creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Economic Commission for Asia and the Far East (ECAFE) was established in 1947 in Shanghai, China as a regional commission of the United Nations (UN) to assist in post-war economic reconstruction. The ECAFE reported to the UN Economic and Social Council. Its Secretariat was part of the UN Secretariat and it worked closely with the Technical Assistance at UN headquarters. Its members were China, Cambodia, Ceylon, Republic of Korea, Laos, Vietnam, Japan, Nepal, Australia, the United Kingdom (UK), Burma, France, India, Indonesia, Netherlands, Philippines, Thailand, the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR), and the U.S. The Commission worked to develop the industry, trade, inland transportation, flood control programs, agriculture, and research and planning activities its region. Its headquarters moved to Bangkok in January 1949.  In 1974, the name was changed to the United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (ESCAP) to reflect both the economic and social aspects of development and the geographic location of its member countries.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Legal Section was established as a special staff section of the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers (SCAP) on October 2, 1945, pursuant to General Order 10, SCAP, October 2, 1945, to advise the Supreme Commander on general legal matters, particularly with regard to Japanese war crimes, and to supervise the prosecution of war criminals. In December 1945 responsibility of the section to prosecute war criminals was limited to violations of the laws and customs of war (Classes "B" and "C"); responsibility for the prosecution of war crimes with international aspects, i.e. crimes against peace (Class "A" war crimes), were assigned to the International Prosecution Section. The specific functions of the Legal Section were to investigate war crimes and to collect and record pertinent evidence; to maintain a central registry of war criminals and suspects and to make recommendations pertaining to their arrest and trial; to recommend the composition, rules, and procedures for military courts, commissions, and tribunals; and to review findings and sentences imposed by war crimes tribunals and to recommend appropriate actions by the Supreme Commander. Because of vested interests of the Allies in the disposition of war criminals, the governments of Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom, the Republic of China, the Netherlands, and France, provided personnel to assist in the investigation and prosecution of war criminals. In June 1946 the Defense Panel of the International Military Tribunal for the Far East (IMTFE) was assigned to the Legal Section. Until 1948 operations of the Legal Section focused on war crimes and, by October 1949, the last war crimes trial by a U.S. tribunal had been completed. Residual activities included the establishment of a clemency and parole program for convicted war criminals. At the same time, as occupation controls over the Japanese were relaxed, the Legal Section became more involved in issues of a non-military nature, with emphasis on governmental and business issues, including the control of foreign exchange and foreign trade.

The SCAP Legal Section was abolished by April 28, 1952.

When President Franklin D. Roosevelt and British Prime Minister Winston Churchill met at Quebec in September 1944 a major topic of discussion was the postwar occupation zones of Germany. As finally agreed upon, the British zone of occupation was to consist of northwest Germany, while the American occupation was to consist of southwest Germany. By this arrangement, American occupation forces would be cut off from port facilities which according to the agreement lay in the British zone. It was therefore agreed that the American military commanders should be given administrative control over a German port in order to assure the flow of supplies to forces of the American occupation. Accordingly the city of Bremen and the dock complex of Bremerhaven (then contained within the city of Wesermuende) were designated to be under the commander of the United States occupation zone. The combined British and American Chiefs of Staff implemented that agreement between the President and Prime Minister by stating that the Bremen Enclave would be under complete American control, including military government. It was understood, however, that American military government would conform to the general policies pursued in the administration of the British zone.

British forces captured Bremen from its German defenders on April 26, 1945. The next day, American Military Government Detachment E2C2, commanded by Colonel Bion C. Welker began the process of military government. By May 1945 the Combined Chiefs of Staff had officially defined the Bremen Enclave area. It was to consist of the city and surrounding land area of Bremen (Hansestadt Bremen and Land Bremen), the rural and urban districts of Wesermuende (Landkreis and Stadtkreis Wesermuende), and the rural districts of Osterholz and Wesermarsch (Landkreis Osterholz and Wesermarsch) The total area of the Enclave was approximately 2,500 square miles containing a population of 676,000.

Soon after the surrender of the German armed forces in May 1945, Detachment E2C2 came under the operational control of the 29th Infantry Division, Ninth U.S. Army. It was transferred to Seventh U.S. Army on June 9, 1945, and remained there until December 10, 1945. By this time there was some confusion over the exercise of authority on the part of both American and British commanders in the area. In addition, the attempt to create the Bremen Enclave out of two German provinces (Land Oldenburg and Provinz Hannover) had also created administrative and economic problems in attempting to reconstitute German authority and prosperity. It was to resolve these difficulties that Lieutenant General Lucius D. Clay, the Deputy Military Governor from the Office of Military Government for Germany (U.S.) and Lieutenant General Sir Brian Robertson, the British Deputy Military Governor, signed an "Agreement on Military Government Responsibility in the Bremen Enclave" on December 10, 1945. Under the Clay-Robertson Agreement, responsibility for military government in the Enclave with the exception of Bremen and Bremerhaven would be turned over to the British. Within Bremen and Bremerhaven itself the old system of administration was to prevail: the Americans would be responsible for military government subject to British policy instruction, unless those instructions interfered with port operations.

The American authorities implemented the Clay-Robertson agreement by transferring governmental authority in Bremen from the Commanding General, Seventh Army, to the Commanding General, Bremen Port Command. The military government detachment itself was reorganized as the Military Government Detachment, Bremen Port Command (Provisional), according to General Orders 46 Headquarters Bremen Port Command dated December 17, 1945. This arrangement lasted until February 23, 1946, when General Orders 14, Headquarters Bremen Port Command discontinued the Military Government Detachment, Bremen Port Command (Provisional), replacing it with the Office of Military Government for Bremen (Non Table of Organization (T/O)). The function of military government, however, continued to be a responsibility of the Bremen Port Command.

Pursuant to authority contained in Cable SC-1316 issued by U.S. Forces, European Theater, on April 5, 1946, the Office of Military Government for Bremen Enclave (U.S.) was established April 15, 1946. General Orders 22, Office of Military Government for Germany (U.S.) dated April 19, 1946, announced the change in military government and also defined the jurisdiction of the new authority. The Office of Military Government for Bremen Enclave (U.S.) was under the command and military government control of the Office of Military Government for Germany (U.S.), otherwise known as OMGUS, subject only to the existing agreements between the occupying powers (an apparent reference to the Clay-Robertson agreement). A letter from OMGUS dated February 11, 1947, subsequently renamed the office the Office of Military Government for Bremen. At the time that OMGUS commenced its responsibilities in Bremen, the military government strength table listed 75 officers, 59 enlisted men, 8 American civilians, and 604 Germans in the city of Bremen and the dock complex of Bremerhaven.

By 1947 it was apparent that the growing bizonal cooperation and economic integration of the American and British zones made a revision of the Clay-Robertson agreement of December 1945 desirable. This was accomplished by another agreement signed by Generals Clay and Robertson which was released in Berlin on January 22, 1947, and made retroactive to January 1. By this agreement a Land Bremen was established, becoming the fourth State in the U.S. zone of occupation and equal with the other three states. The new Land consisted of Stadt Bremen and Stadtkreis Wesermuende, and included the cities of Bremen and Wesermuende (which in February 1947 changed its name to the city of Bremerhaven). The jurisdiction of the military government was also extended by the agreement. Bremen was now to be treated as if it was part of the U.S. zone of occupation, no longer subject to British military government occupation policy: American military government authorities now had complete policy control within Bremen. The supervision of the various Land offices of military government by OMGUS was through command rather than functional channels; each Land Director was responsible for all military government activities within his area. Members of the Land Director's staff were directly responsible to him rather than to the equivalent divisional heads of OMGUS, and the divisional heads of OMGUS exercised no command over the Land Military government divisions.

The objective of military government in Germany was the establishment of democracy which would lead to the eventual peaceful participation by Germany in international relations. To accomplish this, the Germans were under proper safeguards, to be given primary responsibility for running their own affairs in order that they might learn and practice democracy. And as the Germans became increasingly active in self-government the role of the military government correspondingly contracted and became more advisory. Reflecting this changed emphasis, General Orders 7, Headquarters Office of Military Government for Bremen dated September 14, 1948, dissolved many of the old functional divisions, replacing them with new divisions whose offices were headed by advisors. Subsequent reorganizations accelerated this change as Germany moved towards the exercise of national sovereignty. On September 21, 1949, the Cabinet of the German Federal Government was formed, and the Office of Military Government for Germany ended, to be replaced by the Office of the High Commissioner of the United States, Britain, and France. With this change the Director of the Office of Military Government for Bremen also ceased to exist to be replaced by the Office of Land Commissioner for Bremen.

Organization and Outline of the Functions of the Offices of the Department of State January 1944-July 1948, c. 1948: p. 1051-1058 (Jan. 15, 1944 Division of Geography and cartography shall have responsibility in the following matters: (a) assembling, analysis, interpretation and presentation in the form of maps, charts, or reports, of data of a geographic, geodetic or graphic nature on land and water areas throughout the world in  action with current and post-war consideration and negotiations concerning international or inter-regional relations involving questions of political, economic, historic or commercial geography; and the publishing of related geographical information or advise; (b) determining  or revision of population statistics in connection with the creating of immigration quotas for specific areas or countries, when arises; (c) maintenance of the Department’s collection of maps, atlases and gazetteers; and (d) liaison with the United States Geological Survey, Coast and Geodetic Survey, Hydrographic Office, and other departments and agencies in matters of geography, geodesy or cartography. The Office of the Geographer is hereby abolished and its functions, and responsibilities transferred to the Division of Geography and Cartography. Departmental Order 1218, Jan. 15, 1944. Dec. 20, 1944. The Division of Geography and Cartography is hereby transferred to the Office of Public Affairs. The Division shall have responsibility for:… Departmental Order 1301. Jan. 1, 1946 All functions of the Division of Geography and Cartography in the Office of Public Affairs are transferred as of the close of business Dec. 31, 1945 to the Office of Research and Intelligence and the name changed to Division of Map Intelligence and Cartography. Transmittal Letter 8, Jan. 28, 1946. Jan. 1, 1946 Mission of Map Intelligence and Cartography…Letter of Transmittal 8, Jan. 28, 1946. May 1, 1946 transferred to Office of Intelligence Coordination and Liaison Transmittal Letter 19, April 22, 1946. July 1, 1946 Division of Map Intelligence under the general direction of the Director of the Office of Intelligence Coordination and Liaison and in accordance with the over-all intelligence program established by the Advisory Committee on Intelligence and the Special Assistant to the Secretary for Research and Intelligence, the Division of Map Intelligence is responsible for…Transmittal Letter 23, July 17, 1946. Aug. 20, 1946 Name of the division changed to Division of Map Intelligence and Cartography. Functions unchanged. Transmittal Letter 23, Aug 28, 1946. Feb. 4, 1947. Name of division changed to Map Division, functions unchanged. Transmittal letter 43, Feb. 12, 1947. Feb. 6, 1947 Name of the Office of Intelligence Coordination and Liaison changed to the Office of Intelligence Research and the Map Division transferred to the Office of Intelligence collection and Dissemination. Transmittal Letter 45, 1947. March 3, 1947 Map Intelligence Division under the direction of the Director of the Office of Intelligence Collection and Dissemination…Organization Manual, March 3, 1947. Dec. 29, 1947 Map Intelligence Functions of the Division transferred to the Central Intelligence Agency Organization Manual, Jan. 15, 1948.)

Outline of the Functions of the Offices of the Department of State 1789-1943, c. 1943: p. 167 (Oct. 1, 1924 Geographer in the Division of Political and Economic Information (Department's Register 1925, pages 33 and 99, see S.W. Boggs). 1925 transferred to the Division of Publications by Departmental Order 323, of March 3, 1925. June 15, 1925 Geographer The Geographer of the Department and Assistant Chief of the Division of Publications, shall in addition to assuming such administrative duties as may be given to him by the Chief of the Division, be responsible for: (a) Verifying all important geographic statements received or made by the Department. Routine Statements which obviously do not require such verification should not be referred to the Geographer. (b) furnishing geographic information, upon request, to other offices in the Department, and, with the approval of the Chief of the Division of Publications, to persons outside the Department (c) representing the Department on the Immigration Quota Board, U.S. Geographic Board, and on such other boards, committees or congresses dealing with the geographic subjects as may with the approval of the Secretary, be designated. creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The convention concluded between the United States and Great Britain on October 20, 1818, described in Article II that part of the northern boundary from the Lake of the Woods to the crest of the Rocky Mountains. The line was begin at the northwesternmost point of the Lake and run ". . .  due north or south as the case may be, until the said line shall intersect the . . . " 49th parallel of north latitude and from this point ". . . intersection due west along and with the said parallel, shall be the line of demarkation between the territories of the United States, and those of His Britannic Majesty . . . from the Lake of the Woods to the Stony Mountains [i.e. Rocky Mountains]."

No formal boundary commission was established to survey and mark this part of the boundary until 1872. The need for such a survey became apparent in April 1870 when U.S. engineers, surveying near Pembina, South Dakota, for the establishment of a military reservation, discovered that, because the 49th parallel of north latitude had been erroneously marked, the fort of the Hudson's Bay Company at Pembina was actually on U.S. territory.

An agreement between the President of the United States and the British Government allowed the British to occupy the fort until a formal survey of the boundary was accomplished. By notes exchanged in November 1870 between the Secretary of State and the British Minister at Washington it was agreed that, subject to Congressional approval, a joint survey commission be established to survey and mark the northern boundary from the Lake of the Woods to the crest of the Rocky Mountains. On March 19, 1872, the President approved an act (17 Stat. 45) authorizing the establishment of the Commission and specifying that the " . . . engineers in the regular service of the United States shall be employed exclusively as engineers . . . " in conducting the survey. The Presidentappointed Archibald Campbell to represent the United States on the joint Commission.

The survey began in the late summer of 1872, and on September 18, 1872, the U.S. Commissioner held his first meeting with the British Commissioner, Captain (later Major) Donald R. Cameron. Aside from a difference of opinion concerning the exact location of the northwesternmost point of the Lake of the Woods the surveying and marking of the northern boundary was accomplished with little disagreement. At their final meeting on May 29, 1876, the Commissioners approved the data compiled by the surveyors and astronomers.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
On June 3, 1946, all Military Government (MG) detachments were redesignated Liaison and Security Offices. Following this conversion, field work was reduced to denazification, security, reporting, and liaison with both the military and German officials.

Initially each Kreis (district or country) had an MG detachment assigned to it but as early as December 1945, 15 of these detachments were removed and some detachments were covering more than one Kreis. Effective January 10, 1949, Hesse was divided into 10 Districts each responsible for three to five Kreis. This system of administration remained in effect until the Office of Military Government for Hesse (OMGH) was abolished September 20, 1949.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Legal Division was established in 1945 and was initially divided into four branches: Legislation and Legal Counsel, German Administration of Justice, Military Government Courts, and Prisons. By the beginning of 1948, a Legal Advice Branch was added. About the same time, the German Administration of Justice Branch and the Legislation and Legal Advice Branch were combined to form the German Administration of Justice, Legislation and Legal Advice Branch. By the end of 1948, the division had been reduced to two branches. The Prisons, Parole, and Clemency Branch supervised and inspected all prisons in Hesse and considered petitions for release and reduction in sentences. The German Administration of Justice, Legislation, and Legal Advice Branch oversaw the administration of the German court system, examined German legislation, interpreted and forwarded all Control Council laws, and gave advice to all Office of Military Government (OMG) for Hesse units on legal matters. The director of the division was Franklin J. Potter.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
When the Civil Administration Division was established in 1945, it was divided into three branches reflecting its varied duties: Government Organization and Control Branch, Civil Service and Administrative Courts Branch, and the Elective and Civil Organization Branch.

Under the reorganization of April 21, 1948, the functions of the Public Health Division, Public Safety Division, and Public Welfare and Displaced Persons Division were added to the Civil Administration Division. Later that same year, the Denazification Division was abolished, and its functions were also added to the Civil Administration Division.

By mid-summer of 1949 the division was reduced to three branches: Government Affairs, Social Affairs, and Public Safety.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: Wuerttemberg-Baden was initially occupied in May 1945 by the French who established their headquarters at Stuttgart. When the occupation zone boundaries were fixed on July 7, 1945, the formerly autonomous states of Baden and Wuerttemberg were combined into the new Land of Wuerttemberg-Baden with Stuttgart as the capital under the American Zone of occupation. The Commanding officers of the Office of Military Government for Wuerttemberg-Baden (OMGWB) were Colonel William W. Dawson, August 1945-August 1946; Lieutenant Colonel Morris O. Edwards, August 1946-May 1948; Lieutenant Colonel Edward J. Drinkert, June-December 1948; Lieutenant Colonel Joseph H. Rousseau, December 1948-January 1949; and Major General Charles P. Gross, January-September 1949. On September 22, 1949, when OMGWB was abolished, General Gross became the Land Commissioner under the Office of the U. S. High Commissioner for Germany (HICOG).

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Legal Division of the Office of Military Government (OMG) Wuerttemberg-Baden was initially placed under the Government Civilian Administration Staff as part of the Land Government Division. It was divided into four branches, Military Government Courts, German Justice, Prisons, and the Security Review Board. The Prisons Branch was abolished in 1947 and the Legal Advice Branch was added in 1948, but otherwise the organization of the division remained much the same throughout its history.

The functions of the unit, like its structure, remained much the same during the course of its existence. It was concerned with the establishment and operations of the German courts system, prisons, and other legal matters. While, at the beginning, it operated its own court system, it worked concurrently to develop a court and legal system to be run by and for Germans. It additionally provided OMG Wuerttemberg-Baden with legal advice and opinions on both court cases and overall legal matters.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Department of State established the position of Assistant Secretary of State for Far Eastern Affairs in 1949, after the Commission on Organization of the Executive Branch of Government (Hoover Commission) recommended that certain offices be upgraded to bureau level and after Congress increased the number of Assistant Secretaries of State from six to ten (May 26, 1949; P.L. 81-73; 63 Stat. 111). On October 3, 1949, the Office of Far Eastern Affairs became the Bureau of Far Eastern Affairs, headed by the Assistant Secretary. On November 1, 1966, the Department changed the incumbent’s designation to Assistant Secretary for East Asian and Pacific Affairs, as announced in Foreign Affairs Manual Circular 454, dated November 8, 1966.

The specific countries and areas assigned changed over time, but included at various points: Australia, Brunei, Burma, Cambodia, China, Fiji, Indonesia, Japan, Kiribati, Korea, Laos, Malaysia, Marshall Islands, Micronesia, Mongolia, Nauru, New Zealand, North Korea, Pacific Islands, Palau, Papua New Guinea, Philippines, Samoa, Singapore, Solomon Islands, South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand, Timor-Leste, Tonga, Tuvalu, Vanuatu, and Vietnam.

The Office of the Assistant Secretary for East Asian and Pacific Affairs engaged with partners and allies in the region to maintain peaceful and mutually beneficial relations. The Assistant Secretary was responsible for the general conduct of United States (U.S.) foreign relations with the countries assigned to the bureau, and assisted the Secretary of State in providing overall direction, coordination, and supervision of interdepartmental activities of the U.S. Government in these countries. This included ensuring the adequacy of U.S. policy and of the plans, programs, resources, and performance for implementing that policy. Also, the Assistant Secretary was particularly watchful for indications of developing crises and ensured appropriate action was initiated on a timely basis. The Assistant Secretary actively supported chiefs of mission (COMs) and assisted the COMs in carrying out their official duty to implement U.S. foreign policy and lead their missions effectively.

The Assistant Secretary served as the Executive Chairman of the National Security Council (NSC) Interdepartmental Group (NSC-IG) established by the President, with full powers of decision on all matters within the purview of the NSC-IG, unless a member who did not concur requested the upward referral of a matter. The Office directly supervised the policy and operations of the bureau and provided overall guidance to the Foreign Service establishments within the region. The Assistant Secretary exercised the authority conferred on the Secretary of State to authorize leave of absence of chiefs of mission who received compensation in accordance with section 411 of the Foreign Service Act, as amended. It also ensured the provision of an adequate, regular flow of information to posts abroad on U.S. Government policies, policy deliberations, and diplomatic exchanges at Washington, especially on matters that may have resulted in negotiations and representations abroad. Finally, the Assistant Secretary ensured that safety, health, and environmental program requirements affecting posts and operations abroad were implemented.

William Walton Butterworth served as the first Assistant Secretary of State for Far Eastern Affairs from October 3, 1949-July 4, 1950. He was followed by Dean Rusk, March 28, 1950-December 9, 1951; John Moore Allison, February 1, 1952-April 7, 1953; Walter Spencer Robertson, April 8, 1953-June 30, 1959; James Graham Parsons, July 1, 1959-March 30, 1961; Walter Patrick McConaughy, Jr., April 24, 1961-December 3, 1961; William Averell Harriman, December 4, 1961-April 3, 1963; Roger Hilsman, Jr., May 9, 1963-March 15, 1964; and William Putnam Bundy, March 16, 1964-November 1, 1966. 

The Assistant Secretaries of State for East Asian and Pacific Affairs included: William Putnam Bundy, November 1, 1966-May 4, 1969; Marshall Green, May 5, 1969-May 10, 1973; Robert Stephen Ingersoll, January 8, 1974-July 9, 1974; Philip Charles Habib, September 27, 1974-June 30, 1976; Arthur William Hummel, Jr., July 12, 1976-March 14, 1977; Richard Charles Albert Holbrooke, March 31, 1977-January 13, 1981; John Herbert Holdridge, May 28, 1981-December 9, 1982; Paul Dundes Wolfowitz, December 22, 1982-March 12, 1986; Gaston Joseph Sigur, Jr., March 12, 1986-February 21, 1989; Richard H. Solomon, June 23, 1989-July 10, 1992; William Clark, Jr., July 10, 1992-April 23, 1993; Winston Lord, April 23, 1993-February 18, 1997; Stanley Owen Roth, August 5, 1997-January 20, 2001; James Andrew Kelly, May 1, 2001-January 31, 2005; Christopher Robert Hill, April 8, 2005-April 21, 2009; Kurt M. Campbell, June 2, 2009-February 8, 2013; Daniel R. Russel, July 12, 2013-March 8, 2017; Susan Thornton (acting), March 9, 2017-July 2018; W. Patrick Murphy, (acting), July 2018-June 2019), and David R. Stilwell, June 20, 2019-.

The Publications Division produced special thematic pamphlets and special publications. A standard set of pamphlets, special publications, and serial papers dealt a variety of foreign policy initiatives, ranging from democracy (used widely in the nations of the former Soviet Union and elsewhere) and essays on political processes and citizens participation, to articles on market economies and global environmental concerns. It also produced, upon request, pamphlets for other government agencies, U.S. embassies abroad, or domestic representatives of U.S. Information Service (USIS) posts. These pamphlets were published in multiple languages. The Publications Division produced global and regional magazines for distribution by USIS posts. The Division also provided to USIS posts worldwide the Agency-produced bimonthly electronic magazine Global Issues in Transition, the monthly Special Features Service and photo procurement. In addition, the Division arranged copyright clearances and commissioned articles as needed.

On August 31, 1986, the Editorial Services Division and the Publications Division of the Press and Publications Service merged into a single division, the Publications and Editorial Service Division. All but two elements of the Editorial Services Division were incorporated into the new Division. The Publications and Editorial Service Division was more often referred to as the Publications Division, until around 1990 or 1991, when the Publications Division became the official name again.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Committee on Foreign Relations was established on December 10, 1816, when the Senate adopted a resolution offered by James Barbour of Virginia to create 11 standing committees, including one on foreign relations. There were both functional and political reasons for making foreign relations a standing committee. In the Senate's first 27 years, more than 200 separate committees dealt with foreign affairs. No rules governing Senate procedure with respect to either treaties or legislative matters existed. The general practice was to establish a select committee to report on each bill or treaty. The Senate relied on a rather small group of Members with a special interest or background in foreign relations to be appointed members of these select committees. Furthermore, the Senate's rules permitted a select committee to be kept in continuous existence throughout a session by referring to it related subjects. These factors provided an unexpected consistency in the Senate's handling of foreign relations.

By 1816, however, the increased business of the Senate, especially the consideration of nominations and national defense needs arising from the War of 1812, imposed additional burdens on the Senate and provided a further incentive to create standing committees. Since the 2nd session of the 14th Congress, the Committee on Foreign Relations met to consider legislation relating to foreign affairs, treaties (except those with Indian tribes), and nominations of diplomatic and consular representatives, among other subjects. The Committee was instrumental in developing and influencing United States foreign policy, at different times supporting and opposing the policies of Presidents and Secretaries of State.

During 1817-1861, three types of claims were referred to the Committee on Foreign Relations. One type includes claims from diplomatic and consular officers for additional compensation or relief for personal expenses incurred in the conduct of their official duties. The second type includes claims of nondiplomatic personnel for contributions they believed they had made, directly or indirectly, to the U.S. Government through their overseas activities. The third type of claims concerns damage to or loss of private property of Americans at the hands of foreign nationals or damage to foreign owned property resulting from the action of the U.S. Government. Other than claims, the Committee was most often referred to matters related to diplomatic relations with Great Britain, Spain, and their respective colonies (e.g., Canada, West Indies, Mexico, Cuba) and matters concerning present and future States, chiefly Alabama, Louisiana, Florida, and Texas. Also referred to the Committee were boundary disputes and annexation claims between States and territories. 

From 1861-1917, the Committee’s work reflected the transformation of the United States from a minor power into a burgeoning imperial nation during this period. Whereas before 1861, it focused on Great Britain and its colonies and on Western Hemisphere neighbors, by 1917, it demonstrated the expansion of America's worldwide interests. It also dealt with Department of State administrative issues and miscellaneous foreign policy interests of the Senate and the public. The Committee considered, debated, and reported important treaties and legislation, including the purchase of Alaska in 1867.

During 1917-1946, the Committee covered U.S. membership in the League of Nations and U.S. participation in the Permanent International Court of Justice, or World Court. The Foreign Relations Committee was instrumental in the rejection of the Treaty of Versailles in 1919 and 1920. In 1921, the Committee absorbed the Committee on Canadian Relations (created 1892) and Committee on Cuban Relations (created 1889). Other multinational subjects included the Washington Naval Conference of 1921; the Washington Preparatory Committee for the London Economic Conference, 1933; and the second London Naval Conference, 1935. It also handled the rescue and settlement of Jews, which was a recurring issue brought before the Senate, especially the treatment of Jews by European countries. The Committee’s work also encompassed the establishment of the United Nations in 1945; neutrality and aid to the Allies; and World peace.

After 1946, changes were wrought on all committees after the Legislative Reorganization Act of 1946 (Public Law 79-601). For the first time, the Committee had a small professional staff, directed by Francis O. Wilcox, to advise its members. In the postwar world, the Committee's jurisdiction expanded to meet the requirements of the dominant role of the United States in world affairs and of the growing interest in international issues, such as nuclear weapons and disarmament; trade; international energy and investment; international organizations; security agreements; foreign aid; and world environment. The Foreign Relations Committee was instrumental in the passage of the Truman Doctrine in 1947 and Marshall Plan in 1948.

A comparison between the relevant parts of Senate Rule XXV, which defined the jurisdiction of each committee, in 1947 and in 1982 underscores the growth of the Committee's responsibilities since the end of World War II. Under the Legislative Reorganization of 1946, the Committee's jurisdiction included relations of the United States with foreign nations generally; treaties; establishment of boundary lines between the United States and foreign nations; protection of American citizens abroad and expatriation; neutrality; international conferences and congresses; the American Red Cross; intervention abroad and declarations of war; measures relating to diplomatic service; acquisition of land and buildings for embassies and legations in foreign countries; measures to foster commercial intercourse with foreign nations and to safeguard U.S. business interests abroad; the United Nations and international financial and monetary organizations; and foreign loans. 

Between 1947 and 1982, the concept of U.S. neutrality became obsolete and was dropped, but other areas of responsibility were added, including foreign economic, military, technical, and humanitarian assistance; international aspects of nuclear energy, including nuclear transfer policy; international law as it related to foreign policy; oceans and international environmental and scientific affairs as they related to foreign policy; the International Committee of the Red Cross, rather than only the American Red Cross; and the national security and international aspects of trusteeships of the United States. Since 1973, the Committee had responsibility to monitor many executive agreements between the United States and foreign governments that were often used instead of formal treaties.

The role of the Committee expanded in other respects as well, especially in oversight of executive agencies and foreign policy. Rule XXV specified that the Committee shall make comprehensive studies of “national security policy, foreign policy, and international economic policy as it relates to the foreign policy of the United States, and matters relating to food, hunger, and nutrition in foreign countries...." The Committee's jurisdiction extended over the annual authorization bills for and programs of all foreign relations agencies except the Central Intelligence Agency. Since 1968, Committee oversight of executive agreements with foreign governments and the commitment of U.S. Armed Forces to a potential combat situation was extended by the Case Act (Public Law 92-403) and the War Powers Resolutions (Public Law 93-148), respectively.

A bipartisan spirit prevailed as the Committee confronted the perils of the Cold War. However, the state of almost constant crisis that the Cold War spawned eventually resulted in the vast expansion of presidential authority over foreign policy. Since the 1960s, the Committee has sought to redress this imbalance of powers.

The Committee held jurisdiction over all diplomatic nominations. Through these powers, the Committee helped shape foreign policy of broad significance, in matters of war and peace and international relations.

Guide to the Records of the United States Senate at the National Archives 1789-1989, bicentennial ed., 1989: p. 105-111 (10.1 The Committee on Foreign Relations was established on December 10, 1816, when the Senate adopted a resolution offered by James Barbour of Virginia to create 11 standing committees, including one on foreign relations. There were both functional and political reasons for making foreign relations a standing committee. In the Senate's first 27 years, more than 200 separate committees dealt with foreign affairs. No rules governing Senate procedure with respect to either treaties or legislative matters existed. The general practice was to establish a select committee to report on each bill or treaty. The Senate relied on a rather small group of Members with a special interest or background in foreign relations to be appointed members of these select committees. Furthermore, the Senate's rules permitted a select committee to be kept in continuous existence throughout a session by referring to it related subjects. These factors provided an unexpected consistency in the Senate's handling of foreign relations. 10.2 By 1816, however, the increased business of the Senate, especially the consideration of nominations and national defense needs arising from the War of 1812, imposed additional burdens on the Senate and provided a further incentive to create standing committees. From the 2d session of the 14th Congress to the present, the Committee on Foreign Relations has met to consider legislation relating to foreign affairs, treaties (except those with Indian tribes), and nominations of diplomatic and consular representatives, among other subjects. 1817-61 (14th-36th Congresses) 10.11 Three types of claims were referred to the Committee on Foreign Relations. One type includes claims from diplomatic and consular officers for additional compensation or relief for personal expenses incurred in the conduct of their official duties. 10.12 The second type includes claims of nondiplomatic personnel for contributions they believed they had made, directly or indirectly, to the U.S. Government through their overseas activities. 10.13 The third type of claims concerns damage to or loss of private property of Americans at the hands of foreign nationals or damage to foreign owned property resulting from the action of the U.S. Government. 10.14 Other than claims, the subjects of the papers referred to the committee most often relate to diplomatic relations with Great Britain, Spain, and their respective colonies (e.g., Canada, West Indies, Mexico, Cuba) and matters concerning present and future States, chiefly Alabama, Louisiana, Florida, and Texas. 10.17 Territory and State relations: Also referred to the committee were papers relating to boundary disputes and annexation claims between States and territories. 1861-1917 (37th-64th Congresses) 10.20 The subject matter of the committee records reflects the transformation of the United States from a minor power into a burgeoning imperial nation during this period. Whereas its records before 1861 had focused on Great Britain and its colonies and on Western Hemisphere neighbors, by 1917 its records demonstrate the expansion of America's worldwide interests. 10.31 Other subjects: Committee records also document State Department administrative issues and miscellaneous foreign policy interests of the Senate and the public between 1861-1917. 1917-46 (65th-79th Congresses) 10.35 The League of Nations and the World Court The struggle between President Woodrow Wilson and Senators with reservations about U.S. membership in the League of Nations…A longer standing and more popular issue was U.S. participation in the Permanent International Court of Justice, or World Court 10.36 Other multinational subjects documented by records of the committee include the Washington Naval Conference of 1921 (67A - F9); the Washington Preparatory Committee for the London Economic Conference, 1933 (73A - F10); and the second London Naval Conference, 1935 (74A - F9) 10.41 Rescue and settlement of Jews: A recurring issue brought before the Senate was the treatment of Jews by certain European countires.10. 42 Neutrality and aid to the Allies, 10.43 World peace 1947-68 (80th-90th Congress) 10.44 Records of the Foreign Relations Committee after 1946 reflect changes wrought on all committees after the Legislative Reorganization Act of 1946 (Public Law 79-601). For the first time, the committee had a small professional staff, directed by Francis O. Wilcox, to advise its members. In the postwar world, the committee's jurisdiction expanded to meet the requirements of the dominant role of the United States in world affairs and of the growing interest in international issues, such as nuclear weapons and disarmament, trade, international energy and investment, international organizations, security agreements, foreign aid, and world environment. 10.45 A comparison between the relevant parts of Senate Rule XXV, which defines the jurisdiction of each committee, in 1947 and in 1982 underscores the growth of the committee's responsibilities since the end of World War II. In 1947, subjects under the committee's jurisdiction included relations of the United States with foreign nations generally, treaties, establishment of boundary lines between the United States and foreign nations, protection of U.S. citizens abroad and expatriation, neutrality, international conferences and congresses, the American Red Cross, intervention abroad and declarations of war, measures relating to diplomatic service, acquisition of land and buildings for embassies and legations in foreign countries, measures to foster commercial intercourse with foreign nations and to safeguard U.S. business interests abroad, the United Nations and international financial and monetary organizations, and foreign loans. 10.46 Between 1947 and 1982, the concept of U.S. neutrality became obsolete and was dropped, but other areas of responsibility were added, including foreign economic, military, technical, and humanitarian assistance; international aspects of nuclear energy, including nuclear transfer policy; international law as it relates to foreign policy; oceans and international environmental and scientific affairs as they relate to foreign policy; the International Committee of the Red Cross, rather than only the American Red Cross; and the national security and international aspects of trusteeships of the United States. Since 1973, the committee has had responsibility to monitor many executive agreements between the United States and foreign governments that are often used instead of formal treaties. 10.47 The role of the committee has expanded in other respects as well, especially in oversight of executive agencies and foreign policy. Rule XXV now specifies that the committee shall make comprehensive studies of “national security policy, foreign policy, and international economic policy as it relates to the foreign policy of the United States, and matters relating to food, hunger, and nutrition in foreign countries...." The committee's jurisdiction extends over the annual authorization bills for and programs of all foreign relations agencies except the Central Intelligence Agency. Since 1968, committee oversight of executive agreements with foreign governments and the commitment of U.S. armed forces to a potential combat situation has been extended by the Case Act (Public Law 92-403) and the War Powers Resolutions (Public Law 93-148), respectively)

United States Senate Committee on Foreign Relations, August 18, 2021 (The Senate Foreign Relations Committee was established in 1816 as one of the original ten standing committees of the Senate. Throughout its history, the committee has been instrumental in developing and influencing United States foreign policy, at different times supporting and opposing the policies of presidents and secretaries of state. The committee has considered, debated, and reported important treaties and legislation, ranging from the purchase of Alaska in 1867 to the establishment of the United Nations in 1945. It also holds jurisdiction over all diplomatic nominations. Through these powers, the committee has helped shape foreign policy of broad significance, in matters of war and peace and international relations. Members of the committee have assisted in the negotiation of treaties, and at times have helped to defeat treaties they felt were not in the national interest. The Foreign Relations Committee was instrumental in the rejection of the Treaty of Versailles in 1919 and 1920, and in the passage of the Truman Doctrine in 1947 and Marshall Plan in 1948. A bipartisan spirit prevailed as the committee confronted the perils of the Cold War. However, the state of almost constant crisis that the Cold War spawned eventually resulted in the vast expansion of presidential authority over foreign policy. Since the 1960s, the committee has sought to redress this imbalance of powers. creators.administrativeHistoryNote: In 1982, the Office of Program Development and the Office of Training and Management Coordination were merged to create the Office of Training and Program Support (OTAPS). It was staffed by specialists in agriculture, education, health, fisheries, forestry and every other Peace Corps program sector. The Office provided training and program assistance, and information resources to Peace Corps volunteers. Assistance included management of stateside training and a wide range of technical assistance activities from the development of programming and training materials to direct field consultations. In January 1990, the Office of International Operations was eliminated in order to bring the OTAPS in direct contact with the Director's Office. Around 1994, OTAPS was again under the Office of International Operations.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The President's War Relief Control Board was established on July 25, 1942, pursuant to E.O. 9205, July 25, 1942. The Board replaced the President's Committee on War Relief Agencies, established on March 13, 1941, to coordinate the activities of war relief agencies that were exempted from the registration and reporting requirements of the Neutrality Act of 1939 (54 Stat. 4). The Board exercised wartime regulatory powers over voluntary nongovernmental war relief and welfare activities, except the American National Red Cross and established religious organizations. The Board controlled all solicitations, sale of merchandise and services, collections and receipts, and distribution and disposition of funds and contributions for the relief of refugees, of U.S. civilians affected by enemy action, and of armed forces or their dependents. The Board registered and licensed persons and agencies engaged in related fund-raising appeals, defined ethical standards of solicitation and collection of funds, and audited accounts of receipts and expenditures. The Board was chaired by attorney and diplomat Joseph E. Davies, with attorney Charles Phelps Taft and foundation executive Frederick Keppel as the other two members. The Board was terminated on May 15, 1946, pursuant to E.O. 9723, May 14, 1946, with functions transferred to the Advisory Committee on Voluntary Foreign Aid.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Department of State established the position of Assistant Secretary of State for Near Eastern, South Asian, and African Affairs on October 3, 1949, after the Commission on Organization of the Executive Branch of Government (Hoover Commission) recommended that certain offices be upgraded to bureau level and after Congress increased the number of Assistant Secretaries of State from six to ten (May 26, 1949; P.L. 81-73; 63 Stat. 111). On August 20, 1958, the Bureau of African Affairs was formed from the Bureau of Near Eastern, South Asian, and African Affairs. The original bureau was renamed the Bureau of Near Eastern and South Asian Affairs and the Assistant Secretary was renamed accordingly. The Foreign Relations Authorization Act for Fiscal Years 1992 and 1993 (105 Stat. 658) authorized the appointment of an Assistant Secretary of State for South Asian Affairs on October 28, 1991. On August 24, 1992, the Bureau of South Asian Affairs was formed from the Bureau of Near Eastern and South Asian Affairs. The remaining countries and geographic areas were placed in the newly renamed Bureau of Near Eastern Affairs and the Assistant Secretary was renamed accordingly.

The specific countries and areas assigned to the Bureau changed over time, but included at various points: Afghanistan, Algeria, Bahrain, Bangladesh, Ceylon, Cyprus, Egypt, Greece, India, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Libya, Madagascar, Maldives, Morocco, Nepal, Oman, Pakistan, Palestine, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, South Africa, Sudan, Syria, Tunisia, Turkey, United Arab Emirates, and Yemen. 

On January 1, 1956, responsibility for South Africa and Madagascar was transferred from the Bureau of European Affairs to the Bureau of Near Eastern, South Asian, and African Affairs. In the August 20, 1958 reorganization, Egypt and Sudan remained under the Bureau of Near Eastern and South Asian Affairs. On January 15, 1960, Responsibility for the Sudan was transferred to the Bureau of African Affairs. On April 29, 1966, Foreign Affairs Manual Circular 403 established ten Country Directors in the Bureau of Near Eastern and South Asian Affairs, effective July 1. Their responsibilities were: Greece, Turkey, Iran, Cyprus, India-Nepal-Ceylon-Maldives, Pakistan-Afghanistan, Lebanon-Jordan-Syria-Iraq, Saudi Arabia-Kuwait-Yemen-Aden, Israel, and the United Arab Republic. On April 18, 1974, Foreign Affairs Manual Circular 674 transferred responsibility for Greece, Turkey, and Cyprus to the Bureau of European Affairs, effective April 29. It also transferred responsibility for the affairs of Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, and Libya from the Bureau of African Affairs to the Bureau of Near Eastern and South Asian Affairs, effective April 22. On August 24, 1992, India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Afghanistan, and Nepal were transferred to the new Bureau of South Asian Affairs.

The Office of the Assistant Secretary for Near Eastern Affairs led the United States (U.S.) foreign policy in the Middle East and North Africa region through diplomacy, advocacy, and assistance that advanced the interests, safety, and economic prosperity of the American people. In cooperation with regional partners, it promoted democratic values and fostered a free, peaceful, and prosperous Middle East and North Africa. The Office used diplomatic tools and public engagement to end conflict, highlight the value of education, and enhance respect for democratic institutions, including freedom of the press, human rights, religious liberty, and the rule of law. It worked closely with its allies and partners in the region to further these mutual interests and counter extremist ideologies that sought to destabilize the region.

The Assistant Secretary was responsible for the general conduct of United States (U.S.) foreign relations with the countries assigned to the bureau, and assisted the Secretary of State in providing overall direction, coordination, and supervision of interdepartmental activities of the U.S. Government in these countries. This included ensuring the adequacy of U.S. policy and of the plans, programs, resources, and performance for implementing that policy. Also, the Assistant Secretary was particularly watchful for indications of developing crises and ensured appropriate action was initiated on a timely basis. The Assistant Secretary actively supported chiefs of mission (COMs) and assisted the COMs in carrying out their official duty to implement U.S. foreign policy and lead their missions effectively.

The Assistant Secretary served as the Executive Chairman of the National Security Council (NSC) Interdepartmental Group (NSC-IG) established by the President, with full powers of decision on all matters within the purview of the NSC-IG, unless a member who did not concur requested the upward referral of a matter. The Office directly supervised the policy and operations of the bureau and provided overall guidance to the Foreign Service establishments within the region. The Assistant Secretary exercised the authority conferred on the Secretary of State to authorize leave of absence of chiefs of mission who received compensation in accordance with section 411 of the Foreign Service Act, as amended. It also ensured the provision of an adequate, regular flow of information to posts abroad on U.S. Government policies, policy deliberations, and diplomatic exchanges at Washington, especially on matters that may have resulted in negotiations and representations abroad. Finally, the Assistant Secretary ensured that safety, health, and environmental program requirements affecting posts and operations abroad were implemented.

George Crews McGhee served as the first Assistant Secretary for Near Eastern, South Asian, and African Affairs from June 28, 1949 to December 19, 1951. He was followed by Henry Alfred Byroade, April 14, 1952-January 25, 1955; George Venable Allen, January 26, 1955-August 27, 1956; and William Manning Rountree, August 30, 1956-July 6, 1959. 

George Lewis Jones served as the first Assistant Secretary for Near Eastern and South Asian Affairs from July 10, 1959 to April 20, 1961. He was followed by Phillips Talbot, April 21, 1961-September 1, 1965; Raymond Arthur Hare, September 22, 1965-November 30, 1966; Lucius Durham Battle, April 5, 1967-September 30, 1968; Parker Thompson Hart, October 14, 1968-February 4, 1969; Joseph John Sisco, February 10, 1969-February 18, 1974; Alfred Leroy Atherton, Jr., April 27, 1974-April 13, 1978; Harold Henry Saunders, April 11, 1978-January 16, 1981; Nicholas Alexander Veliotes, May 21, 1981-October 27, 1983; Richard William Murphy, October 28, 1983-May 15, 1989; John Hubert Kelly, June 16, 1989-September 30, 1991; and Edward Peter Djerejian, September 30, 1991-August 23, 1992.

Edward Djerejian served as the first Assistant Secretary of State for Near Eastern Affairs from August 24, 1992 to December 17, 1993. He was followed by Robert Halsey Pelletreau, Jr., February 18, 1994-January 24, 1997; Martin S. Indyk, October 14, 1997-November 16, 1999; Edward S. Walker, Jr., January 18, 2000-May 1, 2001; William Joseph Burns, June 4, 2001-March 2, 2005; C. David Welch, March 18, 2005 -December 18, 2008; Jeffrey David Feltman, August 18, 2009-June 11, 2012, Anne Woods Patterson, December 23, 2013-January 6, 2017; Stuart Jones (acting), January 2017-June 2017; David Satterfield (acting), September 2017-June 2019; and David Schenker, June 14, 2019-.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees was established on December 14, 1950 by the United Nations General Assembly. The Office was mandated to lead and co-ordinate international action to protect refugees and resolve refugee problems worldwide. It safeguarded the rights and well-being of refugees. It ensured that everyone could exercise the right to seek asylum and find safe refuge in another State, with the option to return home voluntarily, integrate locally or to resettle in a third country. It also had a mandate to help stateless people.

The High Commissioners included: Gerrit Jan van Heuven Goedhart (Netherlands), 1951-1956; Auguste R. Lindt (Switzerland), 1956-1960; Felix Schnyder (Switzerland), 1960-1965; Sadruddin Aga Khan (Iran), 1966-1977; Poul Hartling (Denmark), 1978-1985; Jean-Pierre Hocke (Switzerland), 1986-1989; Thorvald Stoltenberg (Norway), January 1990-November 1990; Sadako Ogata (Japan), 1991-2000; Ruud Lubbers (Netherlands), 2001-2005; Antonio Guterres (Portugal), 2005-2015; and Filippo Grand (Italy), January 1, 2016-.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Council was a permanent body of the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) responsible to the Assembly. It was composed of 36 Member States elected by the Assembly for a three-year term. In the election, adequate representation was given to States of chief importance in air transport, States not otherwise included but which make the largest contribution to the provision of facilities for international civil air navigation and States not otherwise included whose designation will ensure that all major geographic areas of the world are represented on the Council. The Council convened the Assembly.
 
The Council submitted annual reports to the Assembly; carried out the directions of the Assembly; and discharged the duties and obligations which were laid on it by the Convention on International Civil Aviation (Chicago,  1944). It also administered the finances of ICAO; appointed and defined the duties of the Air Transport Committee, as well as the Committee on Joint Support of Air Navigation Services, the Finance Committee, the Committee on Unlawful Interference, the Technical Co-operation Committee and the Human Resources Committee. It appointed the Members of the Air Navigation Commission and it elected the members of the Edward Warner Award Committee.
 
Another key function of the Council was to appoint the Secretary General. As one of the two governing bodies of ICAO, the Council gave continuing direction to the work of ICAO. In this regard, one of its duties was to adopt international Standards and Recommended Practices (SARPs) and to incorporate these as Annexes to the Chicago Convention. The Council could also amend existing Annexes as necessary.
 
On occasion, the Council could act as an arbiter between Member States on matters concerning aviation and the implementation of the provisions of the Convention; it could investigate any situation which presented avoidable obstacles to the development of international air navigation and it could take necessary steps to maintain the safety and regularity of international air transport.

Presidents of the Council included Edward Warner, 1947-1957; Walter Binaghi, 1957-1976; Assad Kotaite, 1976-2006; Roberto Kobeh Gonzalez, 2006-2013 and Olumuyiwa Benard Aliu, 2014-.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Central Intelligence Group was established under the National Intelligence Authority (NIA) by Presidential directive, January 22, 1946, to plan and coordinate foreign intelligence activities. By National Intelligence Authority Directive 4, April 2, 1946, NIA assumed supervision of the Strategic Services Unit (SSU) dissolution during spring and summer 1946, and assigned some components to Central Intelligence Group at request of Director of Central Intelligence, and effecting incorporation of the remaining units into other War Department organizations. The Central Intelligence Group and National Intelligence Authority were abolished by National Security Act (61 Stat. 495) of July 26, 1947, effective September 18, 1947.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
Often referred to as the Nation's oldest scientific agency, the Coast and Geodetic Survey originated as the Survey of the Coast, established within the Department of the Treasury by an act of February 10, 1807 (2 Stat. 413). Implementation was delayed by lack of suitable instruments and by the War of 1812, and did not begin until 1816, when a survey of New York Harbor was undertaken by Ferdinand Rudolf Hassler, the first Superintendent. Work was suspended pursuant to an act of April 14, 1818 (3 Stat. 425), which repealed such portions of the act of 1807 as permitted civilians to conducts such surveys. Functions ("work and instruments") were transferred to the Department of the Navy, which engaged in a series of disconnected surveys at points along the coast. The Survey of the Coast was revived, under the Department of the Treasury, by an act of July 10, 1832 (4 Stat. 571). By direction of President Andrew Jackson, the Survey was transferred to the Department of the Navy, March 11, 1834, but returned to the Treasury Department on March 27, 1836. Thereafter it was known as the Coast Survey until formally redesignated the Coast and Geodetic Survey in 1878, by an act of June 20, 1878 (20 Stat. 215).

The Coast and Geodetic Survey was transferred to the Department of Commerce and Labor by the act creating that department (32 Stat. 825), February 14, 1903; to the Department of Commerce by the act creating that department (37 Stat. 736), March 4, 1913; and to the newly established Environmental Sciences Services Administration (ESSA), Department of Commerce, by Reorganization Plan No. 2 of 1965 (79 Stat. 1318), effective July 13, 1965.

The Coast and Geodetic Survey surveyed and charted the coasts of the United States and its possessions; studied tides and currents; and compiled and published aeronautical and other charts for purposes of commerce and national defense. It also conducted scientific research on terrestrial magnetism, gravity, and seismology.

The Coast and Geodetic Survey was abolished by Reorganization Plan No. 4 of 1970 (84 Stat. 2090), effective October 3, 1970, which transferred personnel and functions of ESSA to the newly established National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). The Coast and Geodetic Survey became the National Ocean Survey under NOAA, October 9, 1970.

The Office of the Special Representative for Trade Negotiations was established in the Executive Office of the President (EOP) by Executive Order (EO) 11075, January 15, 1963. It was redesignated as the Office of the United States Trade Representative on January 2, 1980 by EO 12188, in accordance with Reorganization Plan No. 3 of 1979. It directed all trade negotiations of the United States and formulated trade policy for the United States.

The United States opened diplomatic relations with Estonia in 1922, and a non-resident Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary, Frederick W.B. Coleman, presented his credentials on November 22, 1922. Coleman, who was also accredited to Latvia and Lithuania, resided at Riga. During his tenure the U.S. Legation at Tallinn was opened on June 30, 1930, with Harry E. Carlson as Charge d'Affaires ad interim.

Subsequent representatives were non-resident envoys. These included Robert B. Skinner, April 2, 1932; John Van A. MacMurray, January 4, 1934; Arthur Bliss Lane, September 10, 1936; and John C. Wiley, November 24, 1938.

Soviet forces occupied Tallinn on June 17, 1940. Walter Leonard was serving as Charge d'Affaires ad interim when U.S. diplomatic officials in Estonia were withdrawn from Tallinn on September 4, 1940. The Legation closed on September 5, 1940.

The first Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary, Lawrence P. Taylor, presented his credentials on August 3, 1995. He was succeeded by Melissa Foelsch Wells, November 3, 1998, and Joseph M. DeThomas, December 11, 2001.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
Full diplomatic relations with Hungary were established at the legation level on October 12, 1945, before the signing of the Hungarian peace treaty of February 10, 1947. H.F. Arthur Schoenfeld was appointed Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary in 1945 and presented his credentials on January 26, 1946. He was succeeded by Selden Chapin, July 9, 1947. Chapin was declared persona non grata by the Hungarian government on February 11, 1949, and he departed Budapest on February 17. Nathaniel P. Davis was appointed to replace him and Davis presented his credentials on October 21, 1949. Succeeding Davis was Christian M. Ravndal, January 11, 1952. 

Ravndal was succeeded by Edward T. Wailes who was appointed as Envoy on July 26, 1956. Wailes arrived in Budapest but the Hungarian national uprising erupted in late summer 1956 and Wailes did not present his credentials. He departed Budapest on February 27, 1957. Thereafter the Legation was headed by a number of Charge d'Affaires ad interim including Garret G. Ackerson, Jr., July 1957 - February 1961; Horace G. Torbert, Jr., February 1961 - December 1962; Owen T. Jones, December 1962 - July 1964; Elim O'Shaughnessy, November 1964 - September 1966; and Richard W. Tims, September 1966 - October 1967.

The Legation was raised to embassy status on November 28, 1966. The first Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary, Martin J. Hillenbrand, presented his credentials on October 30, 1967. He was succeeded by Alfred Puhan, June 16, 1969; Richard F. Pederson, September 10, 1973; Eugene V. McAuliffe, April 28, 1975; Philip M. Kaiser, August 4, 1977; Harry E. Bergold, Jr., March 31, 1980; Nicolas M. Salgo, November 23, 1983; Robie Marcus Hooker Palmer, December 8, 1986; Charles H. Thomas, July 2, 1990; Donald M. Blinken, April 1, 1994; Peter Francis Tufo, December 3, 1997; and Nancy Goodman Brinker, September 26, 2001.

Customs districts and customs offices (known collectively as the Customs Service) were established by an act of Congress on July 31, 1789 (1 Stat. 29). Administration of the customs laws were placed under the office of the Secretary of the Treasury by an act of September 2, 1789 (1 Stat. 65).  The fiscal responsibility for customs collection was placed under the Comptroller of the Treasury, effective October 25, 1792, under the authority of an act of May 8, 1792 (1 Stat. 280).  That function was transferred to the newly established position of Commissioner of Customs by an act of March 3, 1849 (9 Stat. 396). The position was abolished by an act of July 31, 1894 (28 Stat. 205).  The Division of Customs, responsible for the administration of the Customs Service, was established under the direction of the Secretary of the Treasury by authority of an act of March 3, 1875 (18 Stat. 397).  The Customs Service and the Special Agency Service were consolidated to form the Bureau of Customs by an act of March 3, 1927 (44 Stat. 1381).  The Bureau was renamed the United States Customs Service effective August 1, 1973 by Treasury Department Order 165-23 of April 4, 1973.

The Customs Service enforced customs and related laws and collected the revenue from imports; was responsible for the interception and seizure of contraband, including narcotics and illegal drugs; processed persons, carriers, cargo, and mail into and out of the United States; administered navigation laws; detected and apprehended violators of customs laws; enforced export control laws; cooperated with other federal agencies and foreign governments in suppressing illegal traffic in narcotics and pornography; and collected international trade statistics.  Historically, the Customs Service administered navigation aids and lighthouses; this function was transferred to the Lighthouse Board by an act of August 31, 1852 (10 Stat. 119). Functions relating to the protection of seamen and revenue cutters was transferred to the Revenue Marine Division (later the Revenue Cutter Service, the predecessor of the United States Coast Guard) in 1871.  The Bureau of Customs assumed responsibility for vessel documentation by EO 9083, which abolished the Bureau of Marine Inspection and Navigation.

The U.S. Customs Service was abolished on March 1, 2003, with functions transferred to the Bureau of Customs and Border Protection in the Department of Homeland Security.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Records Analysis Division was established in December 1943 to be responsible for the preparation of a history or histories of the Foreign Economic Administration. It took over and continued historical activities that had been begun as early as 1942 in both the Office of Lend-Lease Administration and the Board of Economic Warfare. At first these activities were primarily those of assembling documents or copies of documents considered to be of outstanding historical value, and some information was obtained in interviews. Later, the writing of a series of histories was undertaken. 

When the Foreign Economic Administration was terminated in November 1945 the lend lease historical project was transferred to the Office of the Foreign Liquidation Commissioner of the Department of State, where the work of writing the history of lend lease was continued until, with a few chapters not yet completed, the project was terminated in February 1947. The other history-writing activities of the Records Analysis Division were transferred to the Department of State's Division of Research and Publication. They were terminated in June 1946.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The U.S. Legation in Hungary was established in Budapest on December 26, 1921. U. Grant-Smith presented his credentials as Charge d'Affaires pro tem on January 24, 1922. The first Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary, Theodore Brentano, presented his credentials on May 16, 1922. He was succeeded by J. Butler Wright, June 18, 1927; Nicholas Roosevelt, November 12, 1930; John Flournoy Montgomery, August 1, 1933; and Herbert Claiborne Pell, May 20, 1941.

Hungary severed diplomatic relations on December 11, 1941, and declared war on the U.S. 2 days later. Pell left Budapest on January 16, 1942.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Combined Civil Affairs Committee, known also as CCAC, was established by the Combined Chiefs of Staff in July 1943 to recommend civil affairs policies for enemy or enemy-held areas that were occupied by combined operations and to coordinate military and civilian agency interests in such matters. The U.S. membership consisted of one representative each of the Army, the Navy, and the Department of State, with an additional civilian official, the U.S. Assistant Secretary of War, who served as Chairman of the Committee. The British membership consisted of one representative of the Foreign Office, two from the British Joint Staff Mission, and one additional civilian expert. The Committee continued throughout the war and was abolished in 1949.

From the earliest days of the Republic, Presidents have designated special diplomatic envoys for specific assignments, primarily overseas. The President appointed the first official specifically to bear the title of Ambassador at Large on March 12, 1949, under the authority vested in Article II, Section 2 of the U.S. Constitution that empowers the President, with the advice and consent of the Senate, to appoint Ambassadors, other public Ministers, and Consuls. Presidents have usually appointed Ambassadors at Large to deal with specific foreign policy issues which have been frequently, but not always, spelled out in their commissions.

Richard T. Kennedy served as Ambassador at Large and Special Advisor to the Secretary on Non-Proliferation and Nuclear Energy Policy from December 14, 1982, through January 19, 1993.

Between 1955 and 1961, the head of the Policy Planning function served as Assistant Secretary of State for Policy Planning. creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Department of State created the position of Assistant Secretary of State for American Republic Affairs during the general reorganization of December 20, 1944, after Congress had authorized an increase in the number of Assistant Secretaries of State from four to six (58 Stat. 798, December 8, 1944). This reorganization was the first to assign substantive designations to specific Assistant Secretary positions. The position was temporarily discontinued between June 1947 and June 1949, when American Republic Affairs were handled by an Assistant Secretary for Political Affairs. The Department re-established the position in June 1949 after the Commission on Organization of the Executive Branch of Government (Hoover Commission) recommended that certain offices be upgraded to bureau level and after Congress increased the number of Assistant Secretaries of State from six to ten (63 Stat. 111, May 26, 1949). On October 3, 1949, the Department by administrative action changed the incumbent's designation to Assistant Secretary for Inter-American Affairs. On January 12, 1999, the Bureau assumed responsibility for Canada and was renamed the Bureau of Western Hemisphere Affairs.

Incumbents included Nelson Rockefeller, December 20, 1944 - August 17, 1945; Spruille Braden, August 25, 1945 - June 27, 1947; Edward G. Miller, Jr., June 24, 1949 - December 31, 1952; John M. creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The American Commission to Negotiate Peace was established by, and under the immediate supervision of President Woodrow Wilson, following the signing of the Armistice ending World War I (November 11, 1918). The Commission participated in the peace negotiations at Versailles, January 18 - December 9, 1919. President Wilson personally lead the Commission and selected Secretary of State Robert Lansing, diplomat Henry White, Presidential advisor Edward M. House, and General Tasker H. Bliss to serve as his fellow Commissioners Plenipotentiary. It included a secretariat, administrative officers, and technical advisors.

Notable members of the Commission's staff included Bernard M. Baruch, Archibald Cary Coolidge, Allen W. Dulles, John Foster Dulles, Samuel Gompers, Ulysses Grant III, Joseph C. Grew, Herbert C. Hoover, Edward M. Hurley, Vance McCormick, General Frank R. McCoy, Henry Morgenthau, General John J. Pershing, Nicholas Roosevelt, and Robert A. Taft.

Active U.S. participation in the peace conference ended on December 9, 1919, when the Commission left Paris to return to the United States.

The Board for International Broadcasting (originally proposed as the Overseas Broadcasting Corporation) was established on October 19, 1973, by the Board for International Broadcasting Act of 1973 (87 Stat. 456). It was an independent Federal agency responsible to the President and the U.S. Congress.

The Board oversaw the operations of and made grants to Radio Liberty, which broadcast to the Soviet Union and Afghanistan, and Radio Free Europe, which broadcast to Poland, Romania, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Bulgaria, Estonia, Lithuania, and Latvia. The Board consisted of nine voting members appointed by the President with the advice and consent of the U.S. Senate. 

The Board was terminated on September 30, 1995.

The first Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary, Charles L. Kagey, presented his credentials on February 17, 1922. He was succeeded by Alfred J. Pearson, September 5, 1925; Edward E. Brodie, May 16, 1930; Edward Albright, October 5, 1933; and H.F. Arthur Schoenfeld, July 2, 1937.

The Gambia became independent on February 18, 1965. Mercer Cook, resident at Dakar, Senegal, presented his credentials as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary on August 9, 1965. During Cook's tenure, on September 9, 1965, the Embassy at Bathurst (later Banjul) was established with John G. Gossett as Charge d'Affaires ad interim.

Subsequent Ambassadors were also accredited to Senegal and resident at Dakar. These included William R. Rivkin, January 16, 1967; L. Dean Brown, January 18, 1968; G. Edward Clark, November 24, 1970; O. Rudolph Aggrey, January 17, 1974; and Herman J. Cohen, March 29, 1978. Larry Gordon Piper, the first resident Ambassador, presented his credentials on August 21, 1980.

From August 1982 until June 1984, the Embassy was headed by a Charge d'Affaires ad interim. These were Owen W. Roberts, August 1982 - June 1983; P. Wesley Kriebel, July - November 1983; Alan Logan, November 1983 - April 1984; and Edward Brynn, May - June 1984.

The next Ambassador, Robert Thomas Hennemeyer, presented his credentials on June 20, 1984. He was succeeded by Herbert E. Horowitz, October 24, 1986. From November 1989 through December 1990, the Embassy was headed by a Charge d'Affaires ad interim, including Jimmie Stone, November 1989 - January 1990, and A. Donald Bramante, January - December 1990.

Arlene Render presented her credentials as Ambassador on December 31, 1990. She was succeeded by Andrew J. Winter, October 29, 1993; Gerald W. Scott, February 16, 1996; George Williford Boyce Haley, October 15, 1998; and Jackson McDonald, November 29, 2001.
