The U.S. Legation in Iran (then Persia) was opened at Tehran in 1883. (From 1883 until 1940 the chief of mission was accredited to Persia, thereafter to Iran.) The first Minister Resident and Consul General, S.G.W. Benjamin, presented his credentials on June 11, 1883. He was succeeded by Frederick H. Winston, April 5, 1996; E. Spencer Pratt, November 24, 1886; Truxtun Beale, August 27, 1891; Watson R. Sperry, January 11, 1893; Alexander McDonald, August 29, 1893; Arthur S. Hardy, November 27, 1897; and Herbert W. Bowen, August 27, 1899. 

The next chief of mission, Lloyd C. Griscom, was appointed as Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary; he presented his credentials on December 16, 1901. He was succeeded by Richmond Pearson, May 19, 1903; John B. Jackson, December 12, 1907; Charles W. Russell, March 28, 1910; John L. Caldwell, September 19, 1914; Joseph Saul Kornfeld, April 11, 1922; Hoffman Philip, January 7, 1926; Charles C. Hart, February 9, 1930; and William H. Hornibrook, March 19, 1934. 

From 1934 until 1944 the chief of mission, resident at Tehran, was accredited also to Afghanistan. From March 1936 until December 1940, the Legation was headed by the Charge d'Affaires, and which included Gordon P. Merria, March 1936 - May 1937, and Cornelius Van H. Engert, June 1937 - December 1940.

The next Envoy, Louis G. Dreyfus, Jr., presented his credentials on December 18, 1940. In 1944 the Legation was raised to embassy status and the first Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary, Leland B. Morris, presented his credentials on August 21, 1944. He was succeeded by Wallace Murray, June 5, 1945; George V. Allen, May 11, 1946; John C. Wiley, April 6, 1948; Henry F. Grady, July 2, 1950; Loy W. Henderson, September 29, 1951; Selden Chapin, July 19, 1955; Edward T. Wailes, July 19, 1958; Julius C. Holmes, June 17, 1961; Armin H. Meyer, April 27, 1965; Douglas MacArthur II, October 13, 1969; Joseph S. Farland, May 21, 1972; Richard Helms, April 5, 1973; and William H. Sullivan, June 18, 1977. 

On May 18, 1979, Walter L. Cutler was appointed the next Ambassador but the Government of Iran refused to receive him and he did not go to Tehran. On November 4, 1979, militant Iranian students occupied the Embassy. Fifty-two Americans were held hostage for 444 days. On April 7, 1980, the United States broke diplomatic relations with Iran, and on April 24, 1981, the Swiss Government assumed representation of U.S. interests in Iran.

The United States opened diplomatic relations with the Kingdom of Sardinia in 1840, and opened a legation at Turin. On September 15, 1840, the first U.S. Charge d'Affaires, Hezekiah Gold Rogers, presented his credentials. He was succeeded as Charge by Ambrose Baber, December 1, 1841; Robert Wickliffe, Jr., January 10, 1844; Nathaniel Niles, April 28, 1848; William B. Kinney, August 21, 1850; and John M. Daniel, October 10, 1853. In 1854 the chief of mission was promoted to Minister Resident and John M. Daniel presented his new credentials ca. September 4, 1854.

Following elections during 1859 and 1860, all northern states of the Italian peninsula joined the Kingdom of Sardinia, and the following year the united Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed. The first U.S. Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary to be commissioned to Italy, George P. Marsh, presented his credentials on June 23, 1861. Marsh moved the Legation to Florence in 1865 and to Rome in 1871. He was succeeded by William Waldorf Astor, November  21, 1882; John B. Stallo, November 27, 1885; Albert G. Porter, June 6, 1889; and William Potter, December 28, 1892.

In 1894 the Legation was raised to embassy status. The first U.S. Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary, Wayne MacVeagh, presented his credentials on March 11, 1894. He was succeeded by William F. Draper, June 29, 1897; George V.L. Meyer, February 4, 1901; Henry White, April 16, 1905; Lloyd C. Griscom, March 17, 1907; John G.A. Leishman, July 4, 1909; Thomas J. O'Brien, November 13, 1911; Thomas Nelson Page, October 12, 1913; Robert Underwood Johnson, April 22, 1920; Richard Washburn Child, July 28, 1921; Henry P. Fletcher, April 2, 1924; John W. Garrett, November 20, 1929; Breckinridge Long, May 31, 1933; and William Phillips, November 4, 1936.

George Wadsworth was serving as Charge d'Affaires ad interim when Italy declared war on the United States, December 11, 1941. The Embassy closed shortly thereafter.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Economic Defense Board was established as an interagency advisory board by President Franklin D. Roosevelt on June 30, 1941, by Executive Order (EO) 8839. It was redesignated the Board of Economic Warfare on December 17, 1941, by EO 8982. The Board was comprised of the Vice President, Henry A. Wallace, who served as chair; the Secretaries of State, the Treasury, War, the Navy, Agriculture, and Commerce; the Attorney General; the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs; the Chair of the War Production Board; and the Administrator of the Lend-Lease Administration.

The Board was established "for the purpose of developing and coordinating policies, plans, and programs designed to protect and strengthen the international economic relations of the United States in the interest of national defense." At first the Board functioned chiefly in an advisory, coordinating, and fact-finding capacity, formulating policies to guide the several agencies charged with responsibility for operations pertaining to economic defense. By EO 8900, September 15, 1941, however, the responsibilities for administration of the export-control program that had been previously vested in the Office of the Administrator of Export Control and the Yellow License Unit of the State Department's Division of Controls were transferred, with the personnel and records of those agencies, to the Economic Defense Board. The order also designated the Board as the agency to determine overall estimates of materials and commodities required for export purposes in the interest of economic defense, exclusive of lend-lease operations, and directed that it advise the Supply Priorities and Allocations Board of these requirements and the Office of Production management of the priorities needed.

An executive order of October 28, 1941, specified that the Board was to advise the Department of State regarding lend-lease master agreements and gave the Board authority to review and clear "lend-lease transactions which affect the economic defense of the United States." When the overall supervision of property requisitioning by the Government was vested in the Office of Production Management by an executive order of November 19, 1941, the Economic Defense Board was authorized to initiate action for requisitioning and disposing of property under the priorities and allocations program and the general production and supply plan of the Office of Production Management.

The Board of Economic Warfare was abolished by Executive Order 9361, July 15, 1943, and its functions assumed by the Office of Economic Warfare, Office for Emergency Management.

The U.S. Embassy, Malta, was established at Valletta on September 21, 1964, with Harrison Lewis as Charge d'Affaires ad interim.

The first Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipoteniary, George J. Feldman, presented his credentials on October 5, 1965. He served until September 6, 1967, and was succeeded by Hugh H. Smythe, December 29, 1967 - August 16, 1969; John C. Pritzlaff, Jr., September 4, 1969 - February 24, 1972; John I. Getz, March 9, 1972 - July 18, 1974; Robert P. Smith, September 24, 1974 - October 29, 1976; Lowell Bruce Laingen, January 11, 1977 - January 20, 1979; and Joan Margaret Clark, March 26, 1979 - February 21, 1981. Frank P. Wardlaw served as Charges d'Affaires ad interim from February 1981 through August 1982. The next ambassador, James Malone Rentschler, presented his credentials October 19, 1982; he served until July 26, 1985. He was succeeded by Gary L. Matthews, September 19, 1985 - May 23, 1987; Peter R. Sommer, October 9, 1987 - October 8, 1989; and Sally J. Novetzke, November 9, 1989 - February 28, 1993.

The following officers served as Charge d'Affaires ad interim: William A. Moffitt, Frbruary 1993 - June 1994, and Charles N. Patterson, Jr., June - July 1994. The next ambassador, Joseph R. Paolino, Jr., presented his credentials on July 6, 1994; he served until June 2, 1996. Charles N. Patterson, served as Charge d'Affairs ad interim from June 1996 through July 1997; he was succeeded as charge by Elizabeth Barnett, July 1997 - January 1998. The next ambassador, Kathryn Linda Haycock Proffitt, presented her credentials on January 8, 1998.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Federal Communications Commission, also known as the FCC, was established by the Communications Act of 1934 (48 Stat. 1064), approved June 19, 1934. It regulated the charges and operating practices in interstate or foreign communications, issued broadcast licenses, assigned broadcast frequencies, classified radio and television stations and prescribed the nature of their services. It also enforced radio requirements for some classes of vessels. The seven members of the Commission acted as a unit in determining policy and supervising the staff.

With the imminent reunification of Germany the Embassy at Berlin closed at midnight on October 2, 1990.

The first U.S. Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary, William C. Doherty, presented his credentials on November 26, 1962. He was succeeded by Wilson T.M. Beale, Jr., October 13, 1965; Walter N. Tobriner, December 11, 1967; and Vincent de Roulet, October 23, 1969. Ambassador de Roulet was declared persona non grata on July 20, 1973. He was succeeded by Sumner Gerard, June 4, 1974; Frederick Irving, July 18, 1977; Loren E. Lawrence, April 12, 1979; William Alexander Hewitt, November 1, 1982; Michael Sotirhos, November 12, 1985; and Glen A. Holden, November 21, 1989. 

Ambassador Holden departed Kingston on March 1, 1993. Lacy A Wright, Jr., served as Charge d'Affaires ad interim from March 1993 through November 1994.

The next Ambassador, Jerome Gary Cooper, presented his credentials on November 4, 1994. He was succeeded by Stanley Louis McLelland, February 6, 1998; and Sue McCourt Cobb, September 12, 2001.

The United States opened relations with Japan pursuant to the Treaty of Kanagawa (the Perry Treaty) of March 31, 1854. The first U.S. official, Townshend Harris, was appointed as Consul General  and he took up residence at Shimoda in August 1856. On November 5, 1859, Harris presented his credentials to the Shogunate as Minister Resident.

Harris was succeeded as Minister Resident by Robert H. Pruyn, May 17, 1862; Robert B. Van Valkenburgh, May 4, 1867; and Charles E. De Long, November 11, 1869.

In 1870 De Long was promoted to Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary; he presented his new credentials on June 9, 1872. He was succeeded by John A. Bingham, October 7, 1873; Richard B. Hubbard, July 2, 1885; John F. Swift, May 15, 1889; Frank L. Coombs, June 13, 1892; Edwin Dun, July 14, 1893; Alfred E. Buck, July 3, 1898; and Lloyd C. Griscom, June 22, 1903.

In 1906 the Legation was raised to an embassy and the first U.S. Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary, Luke E. Wright, presented his credentials on May 26, 1906. He was succeeded by Thomas J. O'Brien, October 15, 1907; Charles Page Bryan, November 22, 1911; Larz Anderson, February 1, 1913; George W. Guthrie, August 7, 1913; Roland S. Morris, October 30, 1917; Charles Beecher Warren, September 24, 1921; Cyrus E. Woods, July 21, 1923; Edgar A. Bancroft, November 19, 1924; Charles MacVeagh, December 9, 1925; William R. Castle, Jr., January 24, 1930; W. Cameron Forbes, September 25, 1930; and Joseph C. Grew, June 14, 1932.

Japan declared war on the United States on December 8, 1941 (Tokyo time). Ambassador Grew and the Embassy staff were interned until June 25, 1942, when they departed Japan.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The position of Deputy Secretary of Defense was originally established as the Under Secretary of Defense by Publ. L. 81-36, April 2, 1949. By Publ. L. 81-216, August 10, 1949, the 1949 Amendments to the National Security Act of 1947, the title was changed to Deputy Secretary of Defense.

A second Deputy position was established by Publ. L. 92-596, October 27, 1972, with both Deputies performing duties as prescribed by the Secretary of Defense. The second Deputy position was not actually filled until December 1975, and was abolished by Publ. L. 95-140, October 21, 1977, the law establishing two Under Secretaries of Defense. 

The Deputy Secretary of Defense was delegated to act for the Secretary of Defense and to exercise such powers of the Secretary over all matters for which the Secretary was authorized to act.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Operations Center was the Secretary's and the Department's communications and crisis management center. Working 24 hours a day, the Operations Center monitored world events, prepared briefings for the Secretary and other Department principals, and facilitated communication between the Department and the rest of the world. The Operations Center also coordinated the Department's response to crises and supported task forces, monitoring groups, and other crisis-related activities.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Bureau of Nonproliferation lead U.S. efforts to prevent the spread of weapons of mass destruction (nuclear, chemical, and biological weapons) and their missile delivery systems; to secure nuclear materials in the states of the former Soviet Union; and to promote nuclear safety and the protection of nuclear materials worldwide. It also lead U.S. efforts to promote responsibility, transparency, and restraint in international transfers of conventional arms and sensitive dual-use technology. The Bureau had primary responsibility for leadership in the interagency process for nonproliferation issues; lead major nonproliferation negotiations and discussions with other countries; and participated in all nonproliferation-related dialogues.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
Congress provided for the position of Under Secretary of State in a general government appropriations act adopted on March 1, 1919 (40 Stat. 1224). The Under Secretary subsumed the duties of the Department's Counselor, who had served as the second ranking officer in the Department since 1913. The Under Secretary functioned as the principal deputy and chief assistant to the Secretary of State, served as Acting Secretary of State in the Secretary's absence, and provided guidance and direction to the activities of the Department. Prior to 1944, a number of offices in the Department reported directly to the Under Secretary. In July 1972, the position of Deputy Secretary superseded that of Under Secretary of State.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Secretary of State created the position of Counselor for the Department of State in 1909 as part of a general Department reorganization. In 1912, the position became a Presidential appointment (37 Stat. 372). Between 1913 and 1919, the Counselor served as the Department's second-ranking officer, assuming the role previously exercised by the Assistant Secretary of State. In 1919, the newly-created position of Under Secretary of State subsumed the duties of the Counselor, and the position of Counselor fell vacant. An Act of Congress, May 18, 1937, re-established the position of Counselor of the Department of State (50 Stat. 169). Between 1961 and 1965, the Counselor also served as the Chairman of the Policy Planning Council. The Counselor served as an adviser to the Secretary of State. The Counselor's specific responsibilities have varied over time. On April 30, 1994, the title was changed to Under Secretary of State for Global Affairs.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Country Programs Branch worked out, in collaboration with the Board of Economic Warfare's foreign missions, a program of exports to each friendly country, served as the focal point in the Board and later in the Office of Economic Warfare for the study of problems relating to the internal economies of the importing countries, and advised the other branches regarding the over-all needs and facilities of the countries concerned. The Latin American Exports Division and the Eastern Hemisphere Exports Division were responsible for carrying out the mission of the Branch in their respective areas. The Trade Intelligence Division collected intelligence material on commercial firms and reviewed licenses, freight space, and transportation priority applications for the purpose of preventing American exports from falling into the hands of Axis sympathizers; and the Filed Coordination Division coordinated the operations of the foreign field missions of the Office of Exports and acted as a clearing center for all information originating in the foreign field offices.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: In April 1942 the four geographic division established in November 1941 under the Economic Defense Board were placed under the newly created Office of Economic Warfare Analysis. Within the Office were also established an Economic Intelligence Division, and several administrative units. Toward the end of 1942 the Office was reorganized, and in place of five divisions there were established three branches. The Office of Economic Warfare Analysis had four main objectives: (1) to direct the use of American economic weapons in tightening the British-American blockade of the European continent; (2) to analyze and provide economic information to the armed forces in connection with bombing objectives, the economic potential of the enemy, overseas supply sources, and the economic administration of reoccupied territories; (3) to supply all elements of the Board of Economic Warfare with technical services in the fields of industrial engineering, petroleum, economic intelligence, and cartographic work; and (4) to recommend to the Executive Director ways of dealing with major questions of economic warfare policy referred to the Board proper under the chairmanship of the Vice President and the several agencies represented thereon.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Office of Arms and Munitions Control was established within the Department of State on September 19, 1935, to administer provisions of Joint Resolution 67 (49 Stat. 1081), approved August 31, 1935, which established a National Munitions Control Board to consist of the Secretaries of State, War, the Treasury, the Navy, and Commerce, and imposed registration and licensing requirements on arms and munitions importers and exporters. It was redesignated the Division of Controls on November 22, 1938, pursuant to an act of June 8, 1938 (52 Stat. 631), which provided for the registration of foreign agents in the United States. 

The Division initiated policies of the Department of State relating to international traffic in arms, ammunition, and implements of war to prevent the involvement of the United States in war which would violate United States neutrality. It supervised the fulfillment of the international obligations of the United States under international treaties and agreements, and performed "all necessary duties" in connection with the administration of statutes providing for the preservation of American neutrality. It registered agents in the United States of foreign principals; registered manufacturers, exporters, and importers of arms, ammunition, and implements of war; and issued licenses required for the export of these materials and tin-plate scrap and helium gas. The Chief of the Division served as Executive Secretary of the National Munitions Control Board and performed for the Secretary of State his functions as Chairman of the Board. From July 2, 1940, to September 15, 1941, the Yellow License Unit of the Division, in accordance with directives from the Office of the Administrator of Export Control, issued licenses for the export of defense materials subjected to export control by Presidential proclamation of July 2, 1940, and later proclamations. On September 15, 1941, that function was transferred to the Economic Defense Board. 

The Division of Controls was abolished on October 8, 1941, by Department Order 981 of October 7, 1941. . The Red, White and Blue License Unit was transferred to the newly-created Division of Exports and Defense Aid. The functions of the Registration Unit were transferred to the Division of Foreign Activity Correlation and the Special Division. The Statistics Unit was transferred to the Division of Studies and Statistics.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Bureau of War Trade Intelligence was established on October 15, 1917, replacing the War Trade Intelligence Section of the Exports Administrative Board. The Bureau deteremined the enemy or non-enemy status or affiliations of persons trading with any person or firm in the United States. It supplied the Bureau of Enemy Trade with information concerning applicants for licenses to trade with the enemy. It acted as a clearinghouse of war trade intelligence for the Government and its Allies. After the Armistice its work declined, and the suspension of the "enemy trading lists" on April 29, 1919, still further reduced its activities. On May 12, 1919, it was merged with the Bureau of Enemy Trade under the name of the latter.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
U.S. diplomatic representation in Hawaii (also known as the Sandwich Islands) began in 1843 with the appointment of a commission to the Kingdom. David L. Gregg, who presented his credentials as Commissioner on December 20, 1853, was the first to refer to the U.S. mission as a legation. Subsequent commissioners included James W. Borden, May 21, 1858, and Thomas J. Dryer, June 8, 1861.

James McBride was appointed the first Minister resident; he presented his credentials on June 19, 1863. He was succeeded by Edward M. McCook, July 26, 1866; Henry A. Peirce, July 19, 1869; James M. Comly, September 25, 1877; Rollin M. Daggett, August 21, 1882; George W. Merrill, June 12, 1885; and John L. Stevens, September 23, 1889. In 1890 Stevens was promoted to Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary; he presented his new credentials on September 8, 1890. Stevens was succeeded by James H. Blount, May 23, 1893; Albert S. Willis, November 7, 1893; and Harold M. Sewall, June 7, 1897.

Hawaii was annexed to the United States on August 12, 1898, and on the same date the U.S. Legation at Honolulu was closed.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Passport Bureau was established in the Department of State by a Departmental order of July 3, 1902. It inherited the passport functions held by the Bureau of Accounts since July 11, 1895. The Bureau examined applications for passports and issued passports. It prepared instructions relating to passports for diplomatic and consular officers, conducted correspondence relating to passports, authenticated Department of State seals and seals of other departments; and issued letters of introduction to diplomatic and consular officers.

On May 31, 1907, it was redesignated the Bureau of Citizenship; on August 13, 1918, the Division of Passport Control; and on January 16, 1926, became the Passport Division. It remained the Passport Division until 1952 when it was redesignated the Passport Office.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Home Bureau was established on June 30, 1833, to "have charge of and file and register all domestic correspondence with the Department." It was the caretaker of treaties and foreign gifts in the custody of the Department. It had charge of the seals of the United States and the Department of State. It filed and preserved the returns of copyrights and registered copyright books which were held by the Department. It was responsible for the Department library. From 1834 it was responsible for the preparation and recording of passports and the preparation of related correspondence. (From June 30, 1833 until October 31, 1934, this function had been vested with the Translating and Miscellaneous Bureau). In 1853 it was redesignated the Domestic Bureau, which althought technically abolished by an Act of March 3, 1855, remained in operation under that name until 1870. Most of its functions were transferred to Domestic Records, with passport functions transferred to the newly-established Passport Bureau.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: Unlike the Country Programs Branch, which worked from a geographic viewpoint, the Requirements Branch (which for a few months after November 1942 as the Program Supply Branch) determined the commodity requirements of friendly countries. It obtained from the War Production Board allocations of or priorities on materials required for export and furnished the divisions of the Operations Branch with the information necessary to guide them in their work. Under the direction of the Requirements Branch were the Requisitioning Division and its Compensation Board (both of which had existed since November 1940 under predecessor agencies), which located and requisitioned unused critical and strategic materials and placed such materials wherever they would further the war effort, affording the owners just compensation in case of involuntary requisitioning.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Transportation and Storage Division was responsible for the adequacy of shipping and storage facilities for lend lease material. Specifically, it coordinated activities concerned with the provision of storage and warehousing of lend lease material, maintained liaison relations with U.S. Government agencies and private shipping and storage agencies, reviewed requisitions of foreign governments for storage and warehousing facilities, studied transportation facilities abroad, and through its inspection service, observed the loading, packaging, and cargo movements of lend lease material.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Procurement Control and Materials Distribution Division was responsible for maintaining an equilibrium between requisitions, and the inventory position of lend lease material that was consistent with lend lease policy. In this connection it reviewed all requisitions to determine whether or not the requested material could be furnished from available stock, assumed responsibility for the redistribution of excess or immobile inventory or orders in process, determined monetary losses resulting from the cancellation of orders or redistribution of materials, and maintained liaison relations with the War, Navy, and Treasury Departments and the Maritime Commission.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Bureau of Areas was established on November 13, 1943, as a consolidation of those units of the predecessors of the Foreign Economic Administration that were not assigned to the Bureau of Supplies or to the Office of the Administrator. The units of the Office of Economic Warfare that were transferred to the Bureau of Areas included the area divisions of the Country Programs Branch of the Office of Exports; the Area Branch, excluding the South Pacific Division, of the Office of Imports; and the Enemy and Blockade and Supply Branches of the Office of Economic Warfare Analysis. From the Office of Lend - Lease Administration, the Bureau received the geographic divisions of the Office of Foreign Liaison, the Office of Soviet Supply, and the Overseas Missions Division. From the Office of Foreign Relief and Rehabilitation Operations there were transferred to the Bureau the Divisions of Field Operations, Supply and Transport, Progress Reports, and Program and Requirements. The Bureau also inherited the activities of the Department of State's Office of Foreign Economic Coordination that related to liberated areas.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The U.S. Legation to Korea opened in Seoul on May 20, 1883, when the first Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary, Lucius H. Foote, presented his credentials. In 1885 the grade of the mission was lowered and William H. Parker presented credentials as Minister Resident and Consul General on June 12, 1886. Parker was succeeded by Hugh A. Dinsmore, April 13, 1887; Augustine Heard, May 26, 1890; John M.B. Sill, April 30, 1894; and Horace N. Allen, September 13, 1897. In 1901 Allen was promoted to Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary; he presented his new credentials on October 1, 1901. He was succeeded by Edwin V. Morgan, June 26, 1905. On November 17, 1905, Japan assumed direction of Korean foreign relations, and the Legation closed on November 28, 1905.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The U.S. Embassy in Kuwait was established on September 22, 1967. From 1961 until the opening of the Embassy, diplomatic relations with Kuwait were handled by the U.S. Ambassador in Saudi Arabia. The first resident Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary, John Patrick Walsh, presented his credentials on November 5, 1969. 

The next Ambassador, William A. Stoltzfus, Jr., who presented credentials on February 9, 1972, was also accredited to Bahrain, Oman, Qatar, and the United Arab Emirates. 

Ambassador Stoltzfus was succeeded by Frank E. Maestrone, June 13, 1976; and Francois M. Dickman, October 24, 1979. Philip J. Griffin served as Charge d'Affaires ad interim from August 1983 through September 1984. The next Ambassador, Anthony Cecil Eden Quainton, presented his credentials on September 19, 1984. He was succeeded by W. Nathaniel Howell, September 2, 1987. 

Ambassador Howell was serving when Iraqi armed forces occupied Kuwait, August 2, 1990. The Ambassador and his staff occupied the Embassy until December 13, 1990, when they departed Kuwait.

The Embassy reopened on March 1, 1991, and the next Ambassador, Edward William Gnehm, Jr., presented his credentials on April 2, 1991. He was succeeded by Ryan Clark Crocker, September 7, 1994; James A. Larocco, December 16, 1997; Richard Henry Jones, October 1, 2001.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The U.S. Legation in Laos was opened at Vientiane on August 22, 1950, with Paul L. Guest as Charge d'Affaires ad interim. Donald R. Heath served as non-resident Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary from December 29, 1950, through November 1, 1954.

The first resident Envoy, Charles W. Yost, presented his credentials on November 1, 1954. On August 10, 1955, the Legation was raised to embassy status, and Yost was promoted to Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary, presenting his new credentials on August 19, 1955. Ambassador Yost was succeeded by J. Graham Parsons, October 12, 1956; Horace H. Smith, April 9, 1958; Winthrop G. Brown, July 25, 1960; Leonard Unger, July 25, 1962; William H. Sullivan, December 23, 1964; G. McMurtrie Goldley, July 24, 1969; and Charles S. Whitehouse, Sptember 20, 1973.

Following the conclusion of the Indochina War and the accession of a communist government in Laos, diplomatic relations of the United States with Laos were impaired, and from 1975 until 1992, the Charge d'Affaires ad interim was chief of mission. These included Thomas J. Corcoran, August 1975 - March 1978; George B. Roberts, Jr., March 1978 - September 1979; Leo J. Moser, September 1979 - October 1981; William W. Thomas, Jr., November 1981 - November 1983; Theresa A. Tull, November 1983 - August 1986; Harriet W. Isom, August 1986 - August 1989; and Charles B. Salmon, Jr., August 1989 - August 1992.

Full diplomatic relations were restored in 1992. Charles B. Salmon, Jr., presented his credentials as Ambassador on August 6, 1992. He was succeeded by Victor L. Tomseth, January 8, 1994; Wendy J. Chamberlin, September 5, 1996; and Douglas Alan Hartwick, September 18, 2001.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The United States established diplomatic relations with Latvia on July 28, 1922, and established a legation at Riga on November 13, 1922. The first Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary, Frederick W.B. Coleman, presented his credentials on November 13, 1922. He was also accredited to Estonia and Lithuania.

Coleman was succeeded by Robert P. Skinner, January 28, 1932; John Van A. MacMurray, December 13, 1933; Arthur Bliss Lane, July 2, 1936; and John C. Wiley, October 6, 1938.

Soviet forces occupied Riga on June 17, 1940, and Wiley departed that post on July 25. Earl L. Packer was Charge d'Affaires when the Legation closed, September 5, 1940.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Office of Imports was established in April 1942 to administer the control over imports that was vested in the Board of Economic Warfare by an Executive order of April 13, 1942. It issued directives to the Metals Reserve Company, the Commodity Credit Corporation, the Defense Supplies Corporation, the Defense Plant Corporation, and the U.S. Commercial Company (all of which were subsidiaries of the Reconstruction Finance Corporation) to purchase strategic and critical materials abroad. The Office was also responsible for the receipt from foreign governments of commodities constituting reciprocal aid (reverse lend lease); and it served as the liaison agent between the Board of Economic Warfare and the Combined Raw Materials Board.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Division of Political Studies was established effective January 1, 1943, by Departmental Order 1124, January 14, 1943. It inherited some of the functions previously held by the Division of Special Research.

Under the general supervision of a special assistant to the Secretary of State, the Division prepared studies required in the formulation of foreign policy, particularly with regard to long-range implications of current policies relating to post-war reconstruction.

The Division was abolished by Departmental Order 1218, January 15, 1944, with functions and responsibilities transferred to the newly-established Office of Special Political Affairs.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Bureau of Enemy Trade was established on October 15, 1917, to carry out certain provisions of the Trading With the Enemy Act (40 Stat. 411), approved October 6, 1917. The Bureau issued licenses to trade or carry on other business transactions with or on behalf of an enemy or an ally of an enemy, or for the benefit of an enemy or an ally of an enemy, in cases where such transactions would be to the public interest. It also administered the business of enemy concerns in the United States . It compiled and published an "Enemy Trading List" of firms throughout the world with which trade by American citizens should be prohibited, which included not only enemy firms but neutral firms that dealt with them. In May 1919 the Bureau absorbed the Bureau of War Trade Intelligence.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The U.S. Section of the International Boundary Commission, United States, Alaska, and Canada, was established under the Department of State in 1908. The Commission was founded under the Treaty of 1908 for one specific purpose: the complete reestablishment and mapping of the boundary from the Atlantic Ocean to the Pacific Ocean. The boundary had already been defined by treaty and most of it surveyed by 1874. But between 1874 and 1908 the boundary had become overgrown and monuments obliterated so that it was necessary to reestablish the border demarcation to avoid any uncertainties that could lead to dispute. In 1925, when it was realized that such maintenance would have to be done on a continuous basis, another treaty was signed establishing the Commission as the permanent caretaker of the boundary area and its markers. The boundary vista must have been entirely free of obstruction and plainly marked for the proper enforcement of customs, immigration, fishing and other laws of the two nations. The job of keeping the boundary vista in proper condition fell to the International Boundary Commission. The Commission was made up of two commissioners: one appointed in the United States and one in Canada, each chief of his own staff, equipment and budget. The U.S. Commissioner was appointed by the President and reported to the Secretary of State.

In addition to the upkeep and maintenance of the many boundary markers which delineate the borders, and the clearing of the rights-of-way which separate the United States from its neighbors, the U.S. Section issued annual reports and field reports. The reports prepared from the data obtained from field surveys, included topographical data, reports on the condition of markers, and details of work undertaken to maintain the integrity of the boundary markers and rights-of-way. The Commission was abolished in 1957.

On September 1, after an Egyptian-Israeli agreement was initialed in Jerusalem, calling for the Israeli withdrawal from the Sinai Peninsula, President Ford sent a letter to Congress requesting approval and authorization for a U.S. support role. Henry Kissinger, in his role as Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs, issued a memorandum proposing the organization of the projected support mission. After interagency review, President Ford signed National Security Decision Memorandum 313 for "Establishment of the U.S. Sinai Support Mission."  In the meantime, Congress had somewhat reluctantly approved the mission (Publ. L. 94-110, October 13, 1975) which required a report to Congress every six months. 

The Mission was to coordinate and provide overall management of an American early-warning system in the Sinai, and to maintain the United Nations buffer zone between Egyptian and Israeli forces. 

The Sinai Support Mission (SSM) was headed by a Director reporting to the President through the National Security Council and advised by a Sinai Interagency Board. C. William Kontos was named first Director of the United States Sinai Support Mission on January 15, 1976. The Director had a staff of 14 U.S. government employees in Washington who were detailed from the State Department and the Agency for International Development. These staff provided the technical expertise and staff support. Additional engineering and program support services were provided by Mitre Corporation under contract. Various administrative support services were furnished by the Agency for International Development under an inter-agency agreement. In addition, there was the requirement that no active Department of Defense or intelligence personnel participate in the operation of the system, although they could support the establishment of the system.

The Mission's peacekeeping operation ended April 25, 1982, when Israel completed its withdrawal from the Sinai and Egyptian sovereignty was re-established.

The Office of the Coordinator of Information (OCOI) was established with the appointment of William J. Donovan as COI by Presidential order of July 11, 1941 (6 F.R. 3422). The Coordinator was given authority to collect, analyze, correlate, and make available to the President and certain Government agencies information bearing upon national security; and to carry out, when requested by the President, supplementary activities designed to facilitate the obtaining of information important for national security and not otherwise available to the Government. In the spring of 1942 the Office of the Coordinator was engaged not only in the procurement of information for use in the prosecution of the war but also, by agreement with the President, in the dissemination of information abroad, outside the Western Hemisphere, in support of the war effort. 

By an Executive order of June 13, 1942, which established the Office of War Information (OWI), the powers and duties of the Coordinator that related to the gathering of public information and its dissemination abroad were transferred to OWI. By a military order of the same day (7 F.R. 4469), the Coordinator's office was redesignated the office of the Director of Strategic Services (ODSS) and placed under the jurisdiction of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.

The office of the Director of Strategic Services was abolished by the abolition of the Office of Strategic Services, October 1, 1945.

By an act of July 2, 1940 (54 Stat. 714), Congress provided that whenever the President should deem it necessary in the interest of national defense, he might prohibit or curtail to exportation of any military equipment or munitions, or materials or supplies necessary for the manufacture thereof. In a proclamation of that same date (5 F.R. 2467) the President put an export control program into effect by listing the articles and commodities that could not be exported except when authorized in each case by a license (the list was expanded from time to time) and by vesting responsibility for the administration of the program in an Administrator of Export Control and the Department of State. The licenses were to be issued by the Department of State (the work was handled by its Division of Controls), in accordance with directives issued by the Administrator of Export Control. By a military order, also dated July 2, 1940 (5 F.R. 2491), the President stated that the administration of the export control program was essentially a military function and designated an Army officer, Lieutenant Colonel (later Brigadier General) Russell L. Maxwell, as the Administrator.

The order to make available for defense purposes the materials that could not be exported, an act of October 10, 1940 (54 Stat. 1090), authorized the President to requisition such materials. By an Executive order of October 15, 1940, the Office of the Administrator of Export Control was made responsible for the administration of regulations issued under this authority. Determination of the necessity of requisitioning was to be made by the Secretary of War and the Secretary of the Navy acting through the Joint Army and Navy Munitions Board, and disposition of the requisitioned items was to be handled in similar fashion by that Board.

From July to September 1940 the Administrator of Export Control and a small staff organized the agency, obtained the expansion of the original export control list, and entered into liaison arrangements with various agencies of the Government concerned with exports. On September 5, 1940, the first formal organization order of the Office provided for the establishment of three divisions; in November 1940 two more were added; and a sixth was created on December 23, 1940. Field offices were established in New York on February 1, 1941, and in San Francisco and Los Angeles in June 1941. General administrative services for the Office were performed by the War Department until July 1941, and thereafter by the Division of the Central Administrative Services of the Office for Emergency Management.

By Executive Order 8900 of September 15, 1941, the Office of the Administrator of Export Control, which had been known also as the Office of Export Control, was abolished, and its functions, personnel, and records transferred to the Economic Defense Board. The Office that was thus abolished became, in effect, the Office of Export Control of the Economic Defense Board.

The Office of Strategic Services, known also as OSS, was established by a military order of June 13, 1942, as the principal successor to the Office of the Coordinator of Information. It was assigned, under the jurisdiction of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, to perform two basic functions, (1) gathering, evaluating, and analyzing intelligence in support of the war against the Axis Powers; and (2) planning and executing operations in support of intelligence procurement. The carrying on of military psychological warfare, including propaganda, was also assigned to OSS by the Joint Chiefs of Staff. The military order establishing the agency was modified by an Executive order of March 9, 1943, which directed that certain activities involving the dissemination of propaganda abroad by handled by the Office of War Information rather than by OSS.

William J. Donovan, former Coordinator of Information, served as Director of OSS throughout the life of the agency. 

On September 14, 1945 (by OSS General Order 93), the liquidation of OSS was ordered. By Executive Order 9621, September 20, 1945, OSS was abolished, effective October 1, 1945, and its functions, personnel, and records divided between the Strategic Services Unit (SSU) in the War Department and the Interim Research and Intelligence Service (IRIS) in the Department of State.

The Office of Military Government for Germany (U.S.) (OMGUS) was established, effective October 1, 1945, by General Order 283, U.S. Forces, European Theater (USFET), October 8, 1945, implementing USFET letter AG 014.1 GEC-AGO, September 26, 1945. It was responsible for administering the U.S. zone of occupation and the U.S. sector of Berlin, and for functioning as the U.S. element of organizations comprising the Allied Control Authority, the name given to the four-power occupation control system.

OMGUS functioned, October 1, 1945 - September 1, 1949, as the agent of the following successive Military Governors: General Dwight D. Eisenhower, October 1 - November 10, 1945; General George S. Patton, Jr., (acting), November 11-25, 1945; General Joseph T. McNarney, November 26, 1945 - January 5, 1947; General Lucius Clay, January 6, 1947 - May 14, 1949; and Lieutenant General Clarence R. Huebner (acting), 

May 15 - September 1, 1949.

The transition from military to civilian occupation administration was initiated by the Presidential appointment of John J. McCloy as U.S. High Commissioner for Germany (HICOG), announced May 18, 1949, and establishment in the Department of State of that position by Executive Order 10062, June 6, 1949.

OMGUS was formally abolished, effective December 5, 1949, by General Order 108, European Command, December 1, 1949.

The U.S. Embassy in Madagascar was established at Antananarivo (formerly Tananarive) on June 26, 1960. The first U.S. Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary, Frederic P. Bartlett, presented his credentials on October 5, 1960.

Ambassador Bartlett was succeeded by C. Vaughan Ferguson, Jr., May 21, 1966; and David S. King, April 21, 1967. Ambassador King was also accredited to Mauritius. He was succeeded by Anthony D. Marshall, January 6, 1970. Ambassador Marshall was expelled by the Malagasy Government on June 1, 1971. He was succeeded as Ambassador by Joseph A. Mendenhall, November 15, 1972.

Between 1975 and 1980 the mission was headed by the Charge d'Affaires ad interim, including Gilbert H. Sheinbaum, November 1975 - March 1977, and Robert S. Barrett, March 1977 - June 1980. 

Full diplomatic relations were restored in 1980; Fernando E. Rondon presented his credentials as Ambassador on November 10, 1980. He was succeeded by Robert Brendon Keating, August 11, 1983; Patricia Gates Lynch, August 6, 1986; and Howard K. Walker, September 27, 1989. Ambassadors Rondon, Keating, Lynch, and Walker were also accredited to the Comoros.

Ambassador Walker was succeeded by Dennis P. Barrett, December 3, 1992, and Vicki J. Huddleston, December 12, 1995. 

Howard T. Perlow served as Charge d'Affaires ad interim, July 1996 through August 1998. Ambassador Shirley Elizabeth Barnes presented her credentials on August 30, 1998. She was succeeded by Wanda L. Nesbitt, January 28, 2001.

From the earliest days of the Republic, Presidents have designated special diplomatic envoys for specific assignments, primarily overseas. The President appointed the first official specifically to bear the title of Ambassador at Large on March 12, 1949, under the authority vested in Article II, Section 2 of the U.S. Constitution that empowers the President, with the advice and consent of the Senate, to appoint Ambassadors, other public Ministers, and Consuls. Presidents have usually appointed Ambassadors at Large to deal with specific foreign policy issues which have been frequently, but not always, spelled out in their commissions.

Philip C. Jessup served as Ambassador at Large from March 2, 1949 through January 19, 1953.

The Foreign Procurement and Development Branch negotiated contracts for the importation, stockpiling, and sale of strategic commodities; it engaged in preclusive buying activities; and it encouraged foreign production of strategic materials needed by the United States. It was concerned with the effect of its procurement program on the economies of the exporting countries and prepared studies in connection therewith. The Branch's programs were carried out by its Hides and Leather, Metals, Fiber and Fiber Products, Minerals, and General Commodities Divisions. The Branch also supervised the Pacific Ocean Division, which carried out the directives of the Department of the Navy with regard to projects for the production of supplies on Pacific islands.

In 1946 the records of certain "closed" programs relating to commodities were transferred to the Reconstruction Finance Corporation, while those relating to "open" programs were transferred to the Department of Agriculture's Commodity Credit Corporation or to the appropriate commodity branch of the Department's Production and Marketing Administration.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Requirements and Supply Branch, established in October 1943, presented consolidated foreign and lend lease requirements to the War Production Board or the Combined Petroleum Board for the purpose of obtaining allocations; processed applications to export and applications for the development of such special projects abroad as mines, mills, plants, and factories; assisted the Bureau of Supplies' Trade Relations Staff in advising the Administrator on foreign trade; and represented the Bureau on requirements committees of the War Production Board. The Branch had commodity divisions for metals and minerals, machinery, health supplies and chemicals, and petroleum. Its Operations Division, which inherited functions of the Office of the Administrator of Export Control and its successors in the Economic Defense Board and the Board of Economic Warfare, maintained liaison with the lend lease missions of foreign governments; exercised requisitioning powers with respect to essential commodities not used to the maximum in war production; investigated cases of violations of export regulations; screened applications for export licenses to determine the commercial and political reliability of the consignee; and maintained an information service for exporters in Washington and New York.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: Under the chairmanship of the Administrator, the Policy Committee (originally the Advisory Committee) was concerned with matters of general policy pertaining to all aspects of export control. Three subcommittees of the Policy Committee prepared proposals for the imposition by the President of control over the exportation of specific articles, recommendations for new regulations for control and quotas, and lists of consignees abroad to whom exports were prohibited or curtailed. The Chief of the Planning Division was the Secretary of the Policy Committee.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Office of Protocol, under the direction of the Chief of Protocol, directly advised, assisted, and supported the President of the United States, the Vice President, and the Secretary of State on official matters of national and international protocol, and in the planning, hosting, and officiating of related ceremonial events and activities for visiting heads of state. The Office also was the administrator of Blair House, the President's official guesthouse. In cooperation with the Under Secretary for Management, the Assistant Secretary of State for Administration, the Executive Secretary of the Department, and the regional bureaus, the Office of Protocol served as the coordinator within and between the Department and the White House on all protocol matters for Presidential or Vice Presidential travel abroad. The Chief of Protocol, the Deputy Chief, and four Assistant Chiefs shared responsibility for officiating the swearing in of senior State Department officials, selection boards, and incoming Foreign Service and Civil Service employees.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
In April 1980, the Department of State, by administrative action, established the Bureau of Refugee Programs. The Director held a rank equivalent to an Assistant Secretary of State and served concurrently as Deputy Coordinator for Refugee Affairs. All Directors of the Bureau of Refugee Programs were designated, not commissioned. After March 1979, the Department of State designated certain Ambassadors at Large as Coordinators for Refugee Affairs. The Bureau of Refugee Affairs subsumed duties relating to refugee matters previously exercised by components in the Bureau of Human Rights and Humanitarian Affairs, the Bureau of International Organization Affairs, and the Agency for International Development. Previously, distinct units in the Department of State concerned with refugee affairs existed in the Bureau of United Nations Affairs and the Bureau of Security and Consular Affairs. Also, between September 1966 and June 1975, a Special Assistant for Refugee and Migration Affairs, with rank equivalent to an Assistant Secretary served in the office of the Secretary of State. The Bureau of Refugee Programs was redesignated the Bureau of Population, Refugees, and Migration on May 12, 1994. 

The Bureau of Population, Refugees, and Migration coordinated the Department's policy on global population, refugees, and migration issues and managed migration and refugee assistance appropriations. The Bureau was at the center of a cooperative effort among the State Department, other U.S. Government agencies, private voluntary organizations, and international agencies to implement a more comprehensive international population policy, including broadening of population assistance programs to cover a wider range of reproductive health services; provide assistance to refugees in first-asylum countries and admit refugees to the United States for permanent resettlement; and develop bilateral and multilateral approaches to international migration issues.

Jett served as Charge d'Affaires ad interim from August 1986 through May 1988. The next Ambassador, George Arthur Trail III, presented his credentials on May 13, 1988. He was succeeded by Michael T.F. Pistor, July 1, 1991; Peter R. Chaveas, September 12, 1994; Amelia Ellen Shippy, February 2, 1998; and Roger A. Meece, November 7, 2000.

It worked closely with the British Ministry of Economic Warfare in compiling an economic intelligence file.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Office of Food Programs, an outgrowth of the Requirements and Supply Branch, was established in the Bureau of Supplies in January 1944. It developed and planned the food programs for the Foreign Economic Administration and served as its liaison arm regarding all phases of food activities with the War Food Administration, the appropriate committees of the Combined Food Board, the State, War, and Navy departments, and various international and private relief agencies. The Office approved requirements and submitted allocation requests to the War Food Administration and the War Production Board; reviewed and cleared applications for export licenses covering food and agricultural products; allocated foods under lend lease; initiated programs for the acquisition and management of stockpiles of food; assigned priority ratings; directed the Foreign Economic Administration's participation in relief and rehabilitation programs; and developed and operated programs for the procurement of food abroad and its importation into the United States.

The Under Secretary for Political Affairs was the Department's day-to-day manager of overall regional and bilateral policy issues, and was responsible for integrating political, economic, global, and security issues into the United States' bilateral relationships. There were a number of geographically-defined bureaus and one functional bureau that reported to the Under Secretary. The Assistant Secretaries of the geographic bureaus and office advised the Under Secretary and guided the operation of the U.S. diplomatic missions within their regional jurisdiction. They were assisted by Deputy Assistant Secretaries, office directors, post management officers, and country desk officers. These officials worked closely with U.S. embassies and consulates overseas and with foreign embassies in Washington, D.C.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Office of the General Counsel was at first concerned with general problems of policy involved in economic warfare and with establishing an organization to solve these problems, but during the greater part of the existence of the Board of Economic Warfare the Office performed primarily legal functions. Among the matters it dealt with were the citizenship and draft status of the men being sent abroad on missions; the legal status of operations being carried on abroad by the United States public corporations; the formulation of contracts for purchasing strategic and critical materials abroad; the taking over of Axis properties in Latin America to make them available for war production by friendly foreign producers; changes in legislation pertaining to economic warfare and foreign trade; and enforcement of the Board's regulations controlling private commercial imports.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
By an Executive order of July 15, 1943, the Office of Economic Warfare was established in the Office for Emergency Management, and to it were transferred the functions, personnel, and records of the Board of Economic Warfare, which was abolished by that order. The authority of the Office was limited by a provision in the Executive order that no part of the funds of the Office were to be used for the procurement of services, supplies, or equipment outside the United States except in execution of general economic programs or policies approved by the War Mobilization Committee, which was headed by the Director of War Mobilization. The Executive order also transferred from the Reconstruction Finance Corporation to the Office of Economic Warfare the U.S. Commercial Company, the Rubber Development Corporation, the Petroleum Reserves Corporation, and the Export-Import Bank of Washington, together with their personnel and records.

The Office of Economic Warfare was in existence for only about six weeks; its functions and administrative organization were substantially those of its predecessor. Leo T. Crowley was its head, with the title of Director. By an Executive order of September 25, 1943, the Office and certain other agencies, together with their personnel and records, were transferred to and consolidated in the Foreign Economic Administration, which  was established by that order.

The Office's Area Program Coordination Staff reviewed the economic policies of the Foreign Economic Administration for each country and coordinated these with the over-all supply program, served as a clearance office for instructions from the branches of the Bureau of Supplies to the branches of the Bureau of Areas, and acted as the secretariat for the Foreign Economic Administration's Allocations Committee. creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
Shortly after the outbreak of the war in Europe in September 1939, various foreign governments, notably those of Great Britain and France, placed with American industry cash orders for munitions of war. Need for coordination between the purchases of foreign governments and the United States Government soon developed. To provide a channel for such coordination the President created, on December 6, 1939, the Interdepartmental Committee for Coordination of Foreign and Domestic Military Purchases (also known as the President's Liaison Committee). The original Committee consisted of the Director of Procurement of the Department of the Treasury, the Quartermaster General of the Army, and the Paymaster General of the Navy. In June and July 1940 assistants to the Secretaries of the Treasury and War replaced the Director of Procurement and the Quartermaster General; and in July 1940 the Administrator of Export Control joined the Committee as a member without a vote. As the Treasury Department was directly concerned with the purchases being made by the British and other foreign groups, its administrative facilities were used by the Committee in performing its functions prior to the passage of the Lend - Lease Act of March 11, 1941 (55 Stat. 31).

Liaison with the foreign procurement missions involved on the part of the Committee (1) making available to them airplanes of modern design and other implements of war; (2) helping the missions place contracts with American suppliers at fair prices; and (3) aiding them whenever necessary in creating new facilities for the production of implements of war in the United States. The Committee also cooperated with several American defense committees, concerned with the exportation or procurement of war supplies and established routine procedures for working with them. The most important of these procedures, the forerunner of the lend lease requisition, was implemented by the "Preliminary Negotiations Reports" (PNR), by means of which a foreign war order was referred for approval to the appropriate defense agencies of the Government in order to determine whether it was in conflict with the American defense procurement program.

After the passage and approval of the first Lend-Lease Act of March 11, 1941, the administrative staff in the Treasury Department that provided services for the Committee continued to function as the liaison between the foreign procurement missions and the Government agencies concerned. By a letter to the Secretary of the Treasury on April 14, 1941, the President dissolved the Committee; and by an Executive order of May 2, 1941, he established the Division of Defense Aid Reports to administer the Lend - Lease Act.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: As the head of the agency, Edward R. Stettinius, Jr., responsible for the supervision of all lend lease activities, the Lend - Lease Administrator concerned himself with high policy matters; with dealings with the White House, the Congress, cabinet officers, and head of other agencies; and with public relations, allocation letters, legal matters referred to him by the General Counsel, and Soviet supply matters referred to him by the Senior Administrator in charge of the Division for Soviet Supply. He also served as lend lease representative on the Food Advisory Committee, the Petroleum board, the Board of Economic Warfare, and the American-Canadian Production Committee. His immediate assistant was the Senior Deputy Administrator, who acted for him whenever necessary and who was primarily responsible for matters concerning the finances of lend lease countries. There were also two other Deputy Administrators, one responsible for matters relating to planning and development and the other for supervising the operations of the agency. The Special Assistants, including a Research Assistant, analyzed problems presented to them by the Administrator or Senior Deputy Administrator in terms of the whole lend lease program and prepared progress and status reports based on detailed statistical and fiscal data prepared by the operating divisions.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
From the earliest days of the Republic, Presidents have designated special diplomatic envoys for specific assignments, primarily overseas. The President appointed the first official specifically to bear the title of Ambassador at Large on March 12, 1949, under the authority vested in Article II, Section 2 of the U.S. Constitution that empowers the President, with the advice and consent of the Senate, to appoint Ambassadors, other public Ministers, and Consuls. Presidents have usually appointed Ambassadors at Large to deal with specific foreign policy issues which have been frequently, but not always, spelled out in their commissions.

T. Vincent Learson served as the Ambassador at Large for Law of the Sea Matters and Special Representative of the President for the Law of the Sea Conference from December 11, 1975, through January 21, 1977. He was succeeded by Elliot L. Richardson, who served from March 1, 1977, though October 4, 1980.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
An Act of Congress first authorized an Under Secretary of State for Economic Affairs on August 1, 1946, for a 2-year period as the third-ranking officer in the Department (Public Law 79-590; 60 Stat. 789). The position was not renewed, however, and between 1947 and 1958 the ranking officer in the Department handling foreign economic matters was either a Deputy Under Secretary or an Assistant Secretary of State. On June 30, 1958, Congress re-established the position of Under Secretary for Economic Affairs in the Mutual Security Act (Public Law 85-477; 72 Stat. 274). The following year, the Department of State Organization Act of July 30, 1959, authorized the President to appoint either an Under Secretary for Political Affairs or an Under Secretary for Economic Affairs (Public Law 86-117; 73 Stat. 265). Between 1959 and 1972, during periods when there was no Secretary of State for Economic Affairs, the ranking officer for foreign economic affairs was again either a Deputy Under Secretary or an Assistant Secretary of State. On July 13, 1972, Congress established separate and permanent positions at the Under Secretary of State level for Economic Affairs and for Political Affairs, in the Foreign Relations Authorization Act (Public Law 92-352; 86 Stat. 490). On August 16, 1985, Congress changed the title to include Agricultural Affairs (Public Law 99-93; 99 Stat. 405). The Under Secretary for Economic and Agricultural Affairs served as the principal advisor to the Secretary of State and the Deputy Secretary (previously Under Secretary) on matters relating to foreign economic and commercial policy. Specified duties, responsibilities, and assignments varied over time. Each incumbent was commissioned with a functional designation as part of his title. On May 12, 1994, the title was changed to Under Secretary of State for Economic, Business, and Agricultural Affairs. On December 8, 2011, the title was changed to the Under Secretary for Economic Growth, Energy, and the Environment.

Incumbents included William Lockhart Clayton, August 17, 1946 - October 15, 1947; Clarence Douglas Dillon, July 1, 1958 - June 11, 1959; George Wildman Ball, February 1, 1961 - December 3, 1961; Thomas Clifton Mann, March 18, 1965 - May 31, 1966;  William Joseph Casey, February 2, 1973 - March 14, 1974; Charles Wesley Robinson, January 3, 1975 - April 9, 1976; William Dill Rogers, June 18, 1976 - December 31, 1976; Richard Newell Cooper, April 8, 1977 - January 19, 1981; Myer Rashish, June 29, 1981 - January 20, 1982; W. creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Harriman Mission to London was established pursuant to a Presidential letter of March 6, 1941, appointing W. Averell Harriman as personal representative of the President in London to expedite the furnishing of lend-lease supplies to Great Britain. The Mission was represented on the London committees of the several combined boards, and it gathered information on British supply and production problems. The Mission was responsible to the President and to the Office of Lend-Lease Administration, the Maritime Commission, the War Production Board, the Petroleum Administration for War, and the other United States agencies that it represented. On October 23, 1943, the Mission for Economic Affairs in London superseded the Harriman Mission and inherited its functions and responsibilities.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: Planning problems were submitted by the Administrator in September 1940 to certain committees of the Army Industrial College. As a result of the recommendations of these committees, the Planning Division was established in November 1940. The work of this Division was performed by three sections and by special consultants on petroleum products and other basic commodities. The Programs Section drafted Presidential proclamations, regulations, Executive orders, and administrative orders pertaining to the export control program. It initiated directives and specific rulings for issuance by the Administrator to the State Department's Division of Controls. The Procedures Section assembled data on imports, exports, and the production of commodities and materials essential to national defense and, after it was determined to place a commodity under control, prepared the instructions for licensing. The Projects Section conducted investigations and made comprehensive plans for the coordination of economic power as an effective instrument of national policy. It collected data on trade, agriculture, finance, shipping, and international affairs and integrated this material into concrete proposals. In February 1941 it was organized into 16 committees of experts on particular commodities, headed by an interdepartmental steering committee.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Office of Exports, organized about April 16, 1942, was largely a continuation, greatly expanded, of the Office of Export Control, which had been set up within the Economic Defense Board to administer the export control functions transferred to it from the Office of the Administrator of Export Control and from the Division of Controls of the State Department. By determining whether export licenses should be granted or denied, the Office sought to prevent the depletion of supplies of materials in the United States needed for war purposes, to prevent shipments that would benefit the enemy, and to make critical materials available to other nations when such action would support the war effort.

Although the United States did not open a legation in the Dominican Republic until 1904 it maintained diplomatic contacts through its Charge d'Affaires of the U.S. mission in Haiti. These included John M. Langston, who presented his credentials on March 26, 1884; John E. W. Thompson, March 1, 1885; Frederick Douglass, January 25, 1890; John S. Durham, January 14, 1892; Henry M. Smythe, November 18, 1893; and William F. Powell, February 18, 1898.

The first Minister Resident and Consul General, Thomas C. Dawson, presented his credentials on July 23, 1904. He was succeeded by Fenton R. McCreey, May 18, 1907. Horace G. Knowles, March 7, 1910; and William W. Russell, November 3, 1910. In 1911 the chief of mission was elevated to Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary, and Russell presented his new credentials on September 5, 1911. He was succeeded by James M. Sullivan, September 23, 1913; and William W. Russell, October 7, 1915. Russell served as Envoy during the U.S. occupation of the Dominican Republic from 1916 through 1924. He was succeeded by Evan E. Young, October 28, 1925; Charles B. Curtis, January 28, 1930; H.F. Arthur Schoenfeld, October 9, 1931; R. Henry Norweb, October 7, 1937; Robert M. Scotten, June 21, 1940; and Avra M. Warren, July 4, 1942.

In 1943 Warren was promoted to Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary and the Legation was raised to an embassy. Ambassador Warren presented his new credentials on April 17, 1943. He was succeeded by Ellis O. Briggs, June 3, 1944; George H. Butler, September 19, 1946; Ralph H. Ackerman, August 27, 1948; Phelps Phelps, July 29, 1952; William Pheiffer, June 29, 1953; and Joseph S. Farland, August 7, 1957.

Henry Dearborn was serving as Charge d'Affaires ad interim when the U.S. severed diplomatic relations with the Dominican Republic on August 26, 1960. The Embassy remained closed until January 6, 1962, when it reopened with John Calvin Hill as Charge d'Affaires.

The next Ambassador, John Bartlow Martin, presented his credentials on March 9, 1962. Relations with the Dominican republic were interrupted on September 25, 1963, and Ambassador Martin departed Santo Domingo on September 28. He was succeeded as Ambassador by W. Tapley, Jr., who presented his credentials on March 23, 1964; John Hugh Crimmins, June 29, 1966; Francis E. Meloy, Jr., July 16, 1969; Robert A. Hurwitch, September 5, 1973; Robert L. Yost, May 15, 1978; Robert Anderson, June 22, 1982; Lowell C. Kilday, September 11, 1985; Paul D. Taylor, August 18, 1988; Robert Stephen Pastorino, February 6, 1992; Donna Jean Hrinak, July 22, 1994; Charles Taylor Manatt, December 17, 1999; and Hans H. Hertell, November 29, 2001.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Civilian Production Administration, sometimes referred to as CPA, was established in the Office for Emergency Management by an Executive order of October 4, 1945 (effective November 3, 1945), as the successor to the War Production Board, which was abolished by that order. Its primary purpose was to promote the swift and orderly reconversion of industry form wartime production to a maximum peacetime production free from wartime Government controls, but to do this with due regard for the stability of prices and costs. More specifically, the Administration’s authority was to be used (1) to expand the product of materials that were in short supply; (2) to limit the manufacture of products for which materials or facilities were insufficient; (3) to control the accumulation of inventories so as to avoid speculative hoarding and unbalanced distribution that might curtail production; (4) to grant assistance in the form of priority orders in such fashion as to break bottlenecks that would impede reconversion; (5) to facilitate relief and other essential export programs; and (6) by allocation of scarce materials and facilities, to encourage the production of low-priced items essential to the success of the Government’s stabilization program. 

The head of the agency was the Civilian Production Administrator. He was required to exercise his authority in accordance with general policies established by the Director of War Mobilization and Reconversion. He was authorized to terminate any function vested in the Administration and liquidate all affairs relating to it when he deemed such action to be in the national interest, and to take appropriate steps looking to the eventual liquidation of the Administration. John D. Small was Administrator throughout the existence of the Civilian Production Administration as an independent agency. 

On November 3, 1945, the Civilian Production Administration abolished all organizational units of the War Production Board and set up its own organization. By an Executive order of December 12, 1946, the Administration was abolished as an independent agency, but for some months it remained an autonomous unit in the Office of Temporary Controls, which was established by that order. By an Executive order of April 23, 1947, the President directed that the Administration be entirely liquidated by June 30, 1947, and that its residual functions and its records be transferred to the Secretary of Commerce.

In 1957, the Press Service was renamed the Press and Publications Service to reflect its functions more accurately. The Press and Publications Service produced or acquired and furnished press materials, pamphlets, magazines, and photo services to U.S. Information Service (USIS) posts overseas. It also provided technical direction on the utilization of such products. The Service purchased paper, supplies, equipment and related materials required to support these activities.

The Press and Publications Service supported U.S. foreign policy objectives overseas through a variety of press articles, periodicals, pamphlets, photos, magazines, newspaper supplements, wall newspapers, newsletters, bulletins, leaflets, posters, and other visual materials. The Service served the field by explaining U.S. Government foreign policy issues in economics, democratization, trade, drug enforcement and other global concerns. Some were created for distribution to select groups or to specific audiences. The selective distribution of information materials supplied by the Press and Publications Service and materials produced locally by USIS posts were used for background information and placement in local media.

It produced the Wireless File, a press service which transmitted daily to overseas posts texts of major speeches and official Government statements, analytical and background articles explaining foreign policy and domestic developments, selected materials from U.S. publications, and reports from correspondents on developments pertinent to foreign audiences. The Wireless File was produced in English, Russian, Arabic, French, and Spanish. The Service also produced special country and thematic pamphlets, serial publications, and 4 magazines in 19 languages. Additionally, the Press and Publications Service managed printing and translation facilities in Manila. 

With the abolishment of the Bureau of Policy and Programs on September 30, 1994, all global and regional magazines produced in Washington were eliminated and the remaining functions of the Press and Publications Service transferred to the new Bureau of Information.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Four Party Joint Military Commission (FPJMC) was established by authority of the "Agreement on Ending the War and Restoring the Peace in Vietnam" signed at Paris on January 27, 1973, to facilitate a settlement to the Vietnam War. The Commission included representatives from the United States, the Democratic Republic of Vietnam, the Republic of Vietnam, and the Provisional Revolutionary Government of South Vietnam. According to Article XVI of the Paris Agreement, the Commission's primary tasks were the implementation of the following provisions: enforcement of the cease-fire throughout South Vietnam; enforcement of the cease-fire by U.S. and other foreign countries; enforcement of the cease-fire between all parties in South Vietnam; the withdrawal from South Vietnam of U.S. troops and those of other foreign countries; dismantlement of military bases in South Vietnam of the U.S. and those of other foreign countries; the return of captured military personnel and foreign civilians of the parties; and the mutual assistance of the parties in getting information about those military personnel and foreign civilians of the parties missing in action. FPJMC terminated, March 31, 1973, with functions assumed by the Four Party Joint Military Team (FPJMT), established same date in accordance with Article 10 of the Paris Agreement.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Foreign Information Service Branch, established on July 11, 1941, was the major psychological warfare instrument of the Office of the Coordinator of Information. In the sping of 1942 it was engaged in planning, developing, and executing a program of disseminating news and information about the war effort of the United States to foreign countries outside the Western Hemisphere. It did this by means of short- and medium-wave broadcasts, printed matter, pictures, leaflets distributed by airplanes, and other media of communication. It cooperated with the Federal Communications Commission and the Office of Facts and Figures in analyzing enemy propaganda, and it prepared counter propaganda. It operated through its News, Radio, Picture and Publications, and other divisions. Its functions were transferred to the Office of War Information (OWI) when that Office was established in June 1942 and were carried on by the Overseas Operations Branch of OWI.
