creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The International High Commission was established as a result of the meeting of the Pan-American Financial Congress held in Washington, D.C. in May 1915. It consisted of financial representatives of the American republics. The Secretary of the Treasury was designated as Chairman of the United States Section. The Secretary of Commerce became Chairman in 1921, the Secretary of the Treasury continuing as honorary chairman, and in that year the name of the Commission was changed to "Inter-American High Commission." In 1933, the United States Section was dissolved and its work and records were transferred to the State Department. Its function was to foster improved commercial relations among the American nations, particularly between the United States and South America.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
From November 18, 1976, until April 26, 1983, U.S. diplomatic representation to Cape Verde was handled by a non-resident ambassador. Resident at Bissau in Guinea-Bissau, the Ambassadors Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary, with dates of presentation of credentials, were Melissa F. Wells, November 18, 1976; Edward Marks, October 18, 1977; and Peter J. de Vos, September 24, 1980. During Ambassador Marks's tenure, the U.S. Embassy was established at Praia, January 28, 1978, with Howard McGowan as Charge d'Affaires ad interim.

The first resident Ambassador, Jon Melvin Yates, presented his credentials on April 26, 1983. He was succeeded by Vernon Dubois Penner, Jr., July 15, 1986; Francis Terry McNamara, December 23, 1989; Joseph Monroe Segars, March 24, 1993; Lawrence Neal Benedict, July 30, 1996; Michael D. Metelits, September 15, 1999; and Donald C. Johnson, November 21, 2002.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The U.S. Embassy for the Central African Republic was established at Bangui on February 10, 1961, with W. Wendell Blancke as non-resident Ambassador.  The first resident Ambassador Extraordinary, John H. Burns, presented his credentials on November 29, 1961. He was succeeded by Claude G. Ross, September 16, 1963; Geoffrey W. Lewis, October 23, 1967; Melvin L. Manfull, February 4, 1971; William N. Dale, September 18, 1973; Anthony C.E. Quainton, February 20, 1976; Goodwin Cooke, November 4, 1978; Arthur H. Woodruff, July 10, 1981; Edmund DeJarnette, November 17, 1983; David C. Fields, December 4, 1986; Daniel Howard Simpson, February 6, 1990; Robert E. Gribbin, 3rd., January 16, 1993; Mosina H. Jordan, November 19, 1995; Robert Cephas Perry, February 1, 1999; and Mattie R. Sharpless, December 14, 2001.

From ca. December 4, 1976 through ca. November 29, 1986, the Ambassador was accredited to the Central African Empire. In 1996-1997 the Embassy was closed as a result of civil turmoil in the country; it reopened in 1998.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Foreign Press Bureau-Mail Service was established in November 1917 to supplement the work abroad of the Foreign Press-Wireless and Cable Service. The Service's office was in New York. It cooperated with the Division of Syndicate Features, the Division of Pictures, and representatives of the Committee abroad. It terminated in May 1919. Ernest Poole served as Director. Its function was to compile and to mail weekly for dissemination abroad press material, consisting largely of news and feature articles but including also some posters and pamphlets and pictures to illustrate the articles.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The U.S. Legation in Cuba opened in Havana in 1902. The first Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary, Herbert Goldsmith Squiers, presented his credentials on May 27, 1902. He was succeeded by Edwin V. Morgan, March 1, 1906; John B. Jackson, March 22, 1910; Arthur M. Beaupre, December 18, 1911; William E. Gonzales, August 9, 1913; and Boaz W. Long, January 8, 1920.

In 1923 the Legation was upgraded to embassy status and Enoch H. Crowder became Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary, presenting his credentials on March 5, 1923. He was succeeded by Noble Brandon Judah, December 17, 1927; Harry F. Guggenheim, November 21, 1929; Sumner Welles, May 11, 1933; Jefferson Caffery, February 28, 1934; J. Butler Wright, August 23, 1937; George S. Messersmith, March 8, 1940; Spruille Braden, May 19, 1942; R. Henry Norweb, July 24, 1945; Robert Butler, June 8, 1948; Willard L. Beaulac, September 20, 1951; Arthur Gardner, October 16, 1953; Earle E.T. Smith, July 23, 1957; and Philip Bonsal, March 3, 1959.

The United States severed relations with Cuba in January 1961.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Foreign Press-Wireless and Cable Service began functioning in September 1917. Its main office was in New York. The Service maintained agents in Europe, Asia, and South America. The longest-lived of the Committee's divisions, it was terminated in June 1919, after facilitating transmission to the United States of news concerning the Peace Conference. Walter S. Rogers served as Director. Its function was to disseminate to the world by means of wireless and cables daily news dispatches from the United States.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Four-Minute Men Division was organized privately in Chicago by Donald M. Ryerson, and taken over by the Committee on Public Information on June 16, 1917. At its height it controlled 75,000 speakers throughout the country. In September, 1918, it was consolidated with the Speaking Division to form the Speakers' Bureau. It terminated December 31, 1918. Donald M. Ryerson, William McCormick Blair, and William H. Ingersoll, served successively as Directors. Its function was to provide subjects for four-minute speeches, and to supervise their delivery by a volunteer corps of speakers, whose principal audiences were in theaters throughout the country.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The U.S. Mission to the United Nations was formally established at New York on April 28, 1947, by Executive Order 9844 of April 28, 1947. 

Serving as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary, with dates of entry on duty or presentation of credentials, were Edward R. Stettinius, Jr., January 17, 1946; Warren R. Austin, January 14, 1947; Henry Cabot Lodge, Jr., January 26, 1953; James J. Wadsworth, September 8, 1960; Adlai E. Stevenson, January 23, 1961; Arthur J. Goldberg, July 28, 1965; George W. Ball, June 26, 1968; James Russell Wiggins, October 7, 1968; Charles W. Yost, January 23, 1969; George Bush, March 1, 1971; John A. Scali, February 20, 1973; Daniel P. Moynihan, June 30, 1975; William W. Scranton, March 15, 1976; Andrew J. Young, January 30, 1977; Donald F. McHenry, September 23, 1979; Jeane J. Kirkpatrick, February 4, 1981; Vernon A. Walters, May 22, 1985; Thomas R. Pickering, March 20, 1989; Edward Joseph Perkins, May 12, 1992; Madeleine K. Albright, January 27, 1993; Bill Richardson, February 18, 1997; Richard Holbrooke, August 25, 1999; John D. Negroponte, September 18, 2001; John C. Danforth, who was sworn in on July 1, 2004; and John R. Bolton, August 2, 2005.

Serving as Charge d'Affaires ad interim were Herschel V. Johnson, June 1946; A. Peter Burleigh, September 1998; James B. Cunningham, January 2001; and Anne W. Patterson, January 2005.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The organization of the Speaking Division was approved by a letter of the President dated September 25, 1917. It was transferred on September 1, 1918, to the Four-Minute Men Division, where it was known as the Speakers' Bureau. It terminated in December 1918, and the American National Red Cross took over the direction of tours of speakers previously scheduled. Arthur E. Bestor and J. J. Pettijohn, served successively as Directors.  Its function was to coordinate and make more effective the efforts of the numerous governmental and private speakers' bureaus that were conducting speaking campaigns in support of the national interest. The Division assembled a card catalog of over 10,000 speakers and had available a select group of 300 effective speakers for whom engagements were made.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
Under terms of the London Agreement of 1948, German authorities in the French, British, and American Zones were asked to form a democratic, federal government for the west, while the three powers drafted a statute of occupation to define their powers with relation to the new government. The Germans drafted a constitution that was ratified by the eleven states of western Germany, elections were held, and on September 21, 1949, the government of the Federal Republic of Germany took office. At the same time. Military government was replaced by the Allied High Commission (HICOM), headed by the High Commissioners of the United States, Great Britain, and France.

HICOM was created to exercise supreme Allied authority in the Federal Republic of Germany. As far as the three western zones were concerned, HICOM superseded the quadripartite Allied Control Authority and the US-UK bizonal organization, "Bizonia". All authority previously exercised by the military commanders of the British, French, and American occupying forceswere transferred to the High Commission. HICOM was comprised of the British, French, and American High Commissioners, their deputies and advisers, and a tripartite Allied General Secretariat.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Division of Work With the Foreign Born originated in work done through patriotic organizations of the foreign born, such as the Friends of German Democracy (organized in October 1917) and the American-Hungarian Loyalty League. The Division was formally established in May 1918, and thereafter operated through bureaus (such as the German Bureau) that maintained "direct and continuous contact with fourteen racial groups." Many of the Bureau offices were in New York City. The Division was discontinued in May 1919. Josephine Poche served as Director. Its function was to maintain contact with the foreign-language-speaking residents of the country, to foster their participation in the war effort, and to encourage separatist movements in Germany and Austria-Hungary.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Motion Picture Division, established in the early part of 1942, continued the activities of a predecessor motion picture unit in furthering the inter-American program of the Office of the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs through the medium of motion pictures. The Division cooperated with the motion picture industry to stimulate and expand the production of theatrical feature pictures, short subjects, and news reels designed to further the war effort and promote better understanding between the United States and the other American republics; and it promoted the nontheatrical programs of the Office, which involved the production or procurement of informative and educational short subjects dealing with the war effort and ways of life in the Americas. Activities of the Division involving policy, including the final clearance of motion picture programs with the Department of State, were carried on in Washington. Activities relating to the production, adaptation, and distribution of nontheatrical motion pictures were handled by the Division's New York office, and liaison with the motion picture industry was maintained by the Hollywood office. The Division was abolished in August 1945 and its functions were transferred to the Department of State.

The U.S. Civil Service Commission was established on March 9, 1883, as a permanent commission of three members, pursuant to the Pendleton Civil Service Act of January 16, 1883 (22 Stat. 403). It was abolished effective January 1, 1979, by Reorganization Plan No. 2 of 1978, pursuant to EO 12107, December 28, 1978, and the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 (92 Stat. 1111), October 13, 1978.  

Its function was to recruit persons by open competitive examinations for positions in the Government civil service, to keep the required service records, and to carry out the provisions of the Civil Service Act. During the war, in order to meet the increased demand for civil service employees, the Commission examined approximately one million persons, canvassed the country for available applicants, and cooperated with a number of colleges and technical schools in a training program designed to produce the necessary qualified personnel.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Division of the Federal Register was established within the National Archives Establishment on July 26, 1935, by an Act of Congress, 49 Stat. 500, approved July 26, 1935. 

On June 30, 1949, the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act (63 Stat. 381) transferred the National Archives Establishment (renamed the National Archives and Records Service (NARS) by the same Act of Congress) to the new General Services Administration (GSA), keeping the Division of the Federal Register within NARS. In 1959, as part of a reorganization within GSA, the Division became the Office of the Federal Register, retaining that name when the National Archives (as the new National Archives and Records Administration) gained independence from GSA on April 1, 1985, by way of Public Law 98-497.

In addition to the Federal Register and its supplementary publications, the Office of the Federal Register managed publication of the Code of Federal Regulations (beginning in 1939), the U.S. Government Organization Manual (beginning in 1948), the U.S. Statutes at Large (beginning in 1950), the Public Papers of the Presidents of the United States (beginning in 1957), and the Weekly Compilation of Presidential Documents (beginning in 1965). The Office also coordinated the functions of the Electoral College and administered the constitutional amendment process.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: A protocol of December 19, 1901, between the United States and El Salvador provided for arbitration of the claim of the Salvador Commercial Co., also referred to in El Salvador as the El Triunfo Co., Ltd. In 1894 this company, whose principal stockholders were U.S. citizens, was given the exclusive privilege of establishing and maintaining steam navigation in the port of El Triunfo. Company troubles, including a government decree in 1894 annuling the privileges,gave rise to the claim. The members of the Tribunal were Henry Strong of Canada, Don M. On April 30, 1803, a treaty and two conventions were signed by the United States and France. The treaty ceded Louisiana to the United States. One of the conventions provided for payment of 60 million francs by the United States to France; the other, for payment by the United States to France of a sum not to exceed 20 million francs to be used by France to pay off debts and claims contracted before September 30, 1800, by U.S. citizens against the the French Government. Many of these claims wwre for damages allegedly suffered by U.S. commercial vessels. Three investigators appointed by the U.S. Minister in Paris were to examine the records in the French office relative to such claims. The procedure was slow and complicated. Even if the investigators decided that a debt was due an American citizen, payment could not be made until approval was obtained from the French Government. This procedure gave rise to controversy and confusion in distributing the indemnity. In addition, some categories of claims did not come under the jurisdiction of the convention of April 30, 1803.

On May 18, 1903, John Mercer of Virginia, Isaac Cox Barnet of New Jersey, and William Maclure ofr Virginia were appointed commssioners to examine and liquidate claims of U.S. citizens against France. Nathaniel Cutting served as secretary. The Board held it first meeting in Paris, July 5, 1803, and adjourned December 1, 1804. A total of 356 claims were allowed; 174 were rejected.

The United States opened diplomatic relations with Lebanon in 1942 and opened its Legation in Beirut on November 19, 1942, when George Wadsworth presented his credentials as Diplomatic Agent and Consul General. In 1944 Wadsworth was promoted to Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary and he presented his new credentials on November 16, 1944. He was also accredited to Syria. 

Wadsworth was succeeded as Envoy by Lowell C. Pinkerton, March 6, 1947, and Harold B. Minor, October 18, 1951. The Legation was raised to Embassy status on August 27, 1952, and Minor was promoted to Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary. He presented his new credentials on October 15, 1952. 

Ambassador Minor was succeeded by Raymond A. Hare, September 29, 1953; Donald R. Heath, March 9, 1955; Robert McClintock, January 15, 1958; Armin H. Meyer, January 12, 1952; Dwight J. Porter, June 22, 1965; William B. Buffum, October 13, 1970; and G. McMurtrie Godley, March 15, 1974.

Francis E. Meloy, Jr., was appointed Ambassador on May 1, 1976, and proceeded to his post. On June 16, 1976, Meloy and Economic Counselor Robert O. Waring were kidnapped in Beirut while on their way to meet with President-elect Sarkis. Meloy, Waring, and their Lebanese chauffeur were found dead near a beach several hours later. No demands were made and the assassins were never identified. Richard B. Parker was appointed to succeed him and he presented his credentials as Ambassador on February 15, 1977. He was succeeded by John Gunther Dean, October 10, 1978; Robert Sherwood Dillon, June 26, 1981; Reginald Bartholomew, October 27, 1983; and John Hubert Kelly, August 27, 1986.

John Thomas McCarthy was appointed Ambassador on August 12, 1988. He arrived at Beirut on September 24, 1988, but did not immediately present his credentials. After the withdrawal of all U.S. personnel from Beirut on September 6, 1989, McCarthy resided in Washington, D.C. He visited Lebanon November 18-19, 1989, when he presented his credentials to President Rene Moawad.

The next Ambassador, Ryan Clark Crocker, returned to Beirut in November 1990, and presented his credentials on November 29. The Embassy reopened in March 1991. Ambassador Crocker was succeeded by Mark Gregory Hambley, December 23, 1993; he departed Beirut on September 14, 1994. Vincent Martin Battle served as Charge d'Affaires ad interim from September through October 1994,  followed by Ronald L. Schlicher, October 1994 - February 1996.

Richard Henry Jones presented his credentials as Ambassador on February 2, 1996. He was succeeded by David Michael Satterfield, September 23, 1998; and Vincent Martin Battle, September 12, 2001.

In 1951, the Office of International Trade Policy was functionally subdivided into the Office of International Materials Policy and the Office of Economic Defense and Trade Policy. The Office of Economic Defense and Trade Policy took over the functions, personnel, and equipment of the Commercial Policy Staff, the International Business Practices Policy Staff, and the Economic Security Branch of the Economic Resources and Security Staff. 

The purpose of the Office of Economic Defense and Trade Policy was to promote the strength of the free world through economic ties to prevent inflation and to increase the flow of essential trade. The Office cooperated with other Government agencies to consolidate and strengthen the frame-work of international cooperation in the field of trade policy and economic treaty relationships in order to develop greater political unity and to assure long-run economic stability on which a sustained defense program must rest. The Office also had authority in the Department's jurisdiction over controls of exports to the Soviet bloc.

A Department Circular, dated January 15, 1955, abolished the Office of International Materials Policy and the Office of Economic Defense and Trade Policy and transferred their functions to the new Office of International Trade and Resources (ITR).

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The United States and British Commissioners in their separate opinions issued on October 4, 1821, under terms of article V of the Treaty of Ghent, failed to agree on a settlement of the disputed northwest angle of Nova Scotia and northwesternmost head of the Connecticut River as defined in the l783 peace treaty.  According to the treaty's terms, therefore, the questions were to be submitted for arbitration "to a friendly sovereign or State, to be named for that purpose."  But it was not until 1827, six years after the Commissioners had issued their opinions, that an agreement was reached between the United States and Great Britain to submit the questions to an arbitrator. Albert Gallatin, U.S. minister at London, was authorized to negotiate a convention for the settlement of the dispute.  On September 29, 1827, a convention was signed whereby the contracting powers agreed to submit the northeast Boundary question to a friendly sovereign or state for arbitration. The exchange of ratifications took place on April 2. 1828; and, upon the receipt of notes, dated January 12, 1829, from the United States and British diplomatic representatives at The Hague, the King of the Netherlands agreed to be the Arbitrator. On January 10, 1831, William II, the King of the Netherlands presented his award.  Great Britain did not object to the award.  She thought that it was binding only so far as both countries agreed to accept it. This view left the door open for further negotiations to settle any point that was not acceptable to either country.  President Andrew Jackson presented the King's award to the U.S. Senate.  It was rejected by a vote of 35 to 8 in June 1832. The Senate suggested to the President that he negotiate with Great Britain for a settlement. Not only was the award unsatisfactory to the U. S. Government, but the States of Maine and Massachusetts objected that the boundary line claimed by the United States was unsatisfactory to them. The U. S. Government found necessary to discuss the problem with Maine and Massachusetts to determine a boundary line that would be acceptable to them before it began further negotiations with Great Britain.

Article III of the convention of September 8, 1923, and article IV of the convention of September 10, 1923, between the United States and Mexico provied that each Government could appoint agents and counsel who would have the authority to present to the General and the Special Claims Commissions arguments for or against any claim. This provision led to the establishment of the Agency of the United States (usually referred to as the American Agency or the United States Agency) whose duty was to present and defend all claims before those international claims commissions.  Each claim filed with the Agnecy by a citizen of the United States was assigned an Agency number in order of date of receipt. Afterwards, when the claim was presented by the Agency to either the General Claims Commission or the Special Claims Commission, it was assigned a docket number by one of the two Commission, also in order of date of receipt. Thus most claims bear two numbers. "Agency" numbers run from 1 through 6605, "General" numbers from 1 through 3617, and "Special" numbers from 1 through 3175. The Agency of the United States organized a Research and Information Section to aid the legal staff in gathering all possible information and evidence.

Henry W. Anderson was designated as the Agent of the United States when these Claims Commission were first organized, and he held this position until his resignation on June 30, 1926. J. Reuben Clark, Jr., served in the position from Julky to September 1926 and was succeeed by Clement L. Bouvé, who served until 1931. Claims work was suspended from 1931 to 1934. In 1934, when work on claims was resumed, the Agency was revived and Bert L. Hunt was designated as the Agent. Departmental Order No. 596, dated July 2, 1934, placed the Agency under the supervision of Assistant Secrteraies of State Wilbur J. Carr and R. Walton Moore and Legal Advisor Green H. Hackworth. This three-man group was often referred to as "The Mexican Claims Committee."

Some of the series of records of the Agency, as well as of the General and Special Claims Commission, are not complete, clear cut, or well arranged. These faults may be explained by the peculiar nature of the administrative history of the Commissions and other entities which produced and accumulated the records. For example, the Commissions were not in continuous session during their existence. Frequent periods of inactivity and changes in organization and in methods of procedure were not conducive to the maintenance of well-defined and clear-cut series of records. New series of records came into existence after changes were made in organization and procedures. Often a new series would absorb a part of the records of an earlier series, leaving the old series incomplete.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Special Claims Commission was established by a convention signed by Mexico and the United States on September 10, 1923, for the purpose of adjudicating claims arising from injuries and losses sustained by U.S. citizens during the period from November 20, 1910, to May 31, 1920, as a result of revolution in Mexico. In accordance with the provisions of this convention a three-man commission was established composed of a citizen of the United States, a citizen of Mexico, and a citizen of a neutral country. The Commissioners were as follows: Ernest B. Perry, succeeded by Fred K. Nielsen in 1931, from the United States; Fernando Gonzales Roa from Mexico; and Rodrigo OCtavio of Brazil, neutral chairman, succeeded in 1928 by Kristian Sindballe of Denmark, and in 1931 by Horacio F. Alfaro of Panama. The Commission functioned from 1924 to 1931 but was not in continuous session. During this eight-year period 3,176 claims were filed, 18 were disallowed, and none were allowed. In 1931 activities of the Commission were suspended.

No further progress was made by the two Governments in disposing of the huge mass of unsettled claims until April 24, 1934. On this date the United States agreed to settle for the payment of a lump sum of money, which was to be computed on the basis of amounts awarded on the same class of claims to the Governments of Belgium, France, Germany, Great Britain, Italy, and Spain. The exact amount of this liability was to be computed by a Joint Committee composed of one representative of each Government, whose decision would be accepted as final. The United States representative on the Joint Committee was Edgar Turlington, and the Mexican representative was Manuel J. Sierra. The conclusion reached by the two representatives was that $5,448,020.14 should be paid by Mexico to the United States. Individual U.S. claimants were to receive their awards later from a domestic claims commission known as the Special Mexican Claims Commission. The interests of the United States before the Special and General Claims Commissions were represented by one single agent.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: On July 28, 1926, the United States and Panama signed a convention that provided for the establishment of a commission to settle claims by citizens of each country against the other, most arising after November 3, 1903, when Panama proclaimed its independence. Although the convention was concluded on July 28, 1926, ratifications were not exchanged until October 3, 1931. Another convention, signed December 17, 1932, modified the convention of July 28, 1926. When the Claims Commission was established, Miguel Cruchaga served as Presiding Commissioner, succeeded by D.W. van Heeckeren; Joseph R. Baker was U.S. Commissioner, succeeded by Elihu Root, Jr.; and Horacio F. Alfaro served as Commissioner for Panama. The Commission met in Washington on April 1, 1932, and concluded its work on June 29, 1933. Of 26 claims adjudicated, 15 were of U.S. citizens against Panama and 11 of Panamanians against the United States.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
By an exchange of notes dated December 24, 1923, the United States and Turkey entered into an agreement that provided for a four-member commission (two from each country) to recommend solutions to outstanding claims bteween them. In subsequent communications, the governments agreed that the Commission should undertake a summary examination of the cases to recommend a lump-sum settlement. The U.S. commissoners were Fred K. Nielsen and John W. Connelly, Jr. The commissioners for Turkey were A. Sevki and Mehmet Esat. The Commission met in Istanbul, where the United States presented 898 dossiers; no claims of Turkish citizens against the United States were presented. The records of the Commission are those presented by claimants and include no pleadings by the United States. The Turkish Government did not present rebutting evidence. Cases were discussed by the Commission on the basis of records submitted.

On October 13, 1934, the Commission recommended that Turkey pay the United States $1,300,00. This recommendation was confirmed by an agreement signed on October 25, 1934. The United States was free to distribute that sum among American claimants as deemed proper.

A claims convention between the United States and the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies (anples) provided for payment of 2,115,000 ducats, or about $1,755,450, to the United States in satisfaction of claims of American citizens growing out of seizure and destruction of American vessels and cargoes during the period 1809-12. By an act of March 2, 1833, provision was made for a three-member commission to examine and adjudicate the claims.

The three commssioners were Wyllys Silliman of Ohio, John R. Livingston, Jr. of New York, and Joseph S. Cabot of Massachusetts, who was appointed to fill the vacancy caused by the resignation of Peter V. Daniel. Thomas Swann, Jr., of the District of Columbia was appointed secretary, and John W. Overton of Jentucky served as clerk. The Commission has its first meeting September 18, 1833, and adjourned March 17, 1835, having disposed of the claims. It made about 275 awards, totaling $1,925.034.68.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: On May 7, 1872, a joint resolution (17 Stat. 395) was approved by Congress authorizing the President of the United States to appoint three persons to act as commissioners to inquire into the extent and character of depredations by bands of Indians and Mexicans who crossed the Rio Grande to commit acts endangering the property, lives, and liberty of the citizens of the State of Texas. The Commissioners were ordered to proceed to the frontier areas and take testimony, under oath, of such witnesses as might appear before them. Reports regarding the work accomplished and the evidence collected were to be made periodically. The Commission was organized in New Orleans on July 4, 1872. The Commissioners were Fabius J. Mead, Richard H. Savage, and Thomas P. Robb, Chairman. This Commission was often referred to as the Robb Commission. It functioned, with some recesses, from July 4, 1872, to June 30, 1873. During this period it received 423 petitions and 1,090 depositions. Additional depositions and petitions were received after the Commission expired. The amount of losses and injuries, according to the findings of the Commission, totalled $48,496,235.25. The final report of the Commisison was submitted on June 30, 1873.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: Following the decisions of the U.S. and Venezuela Mixed Claims Commission in 1868, the Government of Venezuela and several U.S. citizens charged the Commission with fraud. After many delays, conventions were signed by the two governments on December 5, 1885, March 15, 1888, and October 5, 1888; they provided that claims that had been before the former commission should be submitted to a new commission. The members of the new commission were John Little, American commissioners and chairman; Jose Andrade, Venezuelan commssioner; and Samuel F. Phillips, succeeded by John V.L. Findlay, the third commissioner. J. Hubley Ashton was U.S. counsel, and Francisco de P. Suarez was appointed secretary. The new commission met in Washington on September 3, 1889, and adjourned September 2, 1890. Sixty-three claims were presented, 49 of which had been before the old commission. The Washington commission awarded $980,572.60.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Research and Information Section, a subdivision of the Agency of the United States, was established to aid the legal staff of the Agency in gathering information and evidence about claims matters. At first its activities were confined to searching, examining, and indexing information from documents of the War Department. Later, as a result of a detailed study of the needs of the Agency, such activities of the Section were extended to documents of the State, Justice, Navy, and Labor Departments. The Section was also given the responsibility for compiling general historical and chronological outlines of events in Mexico, based largely on documentary evidence in the Department of State. In actual practice the Research and Information Section functioned as a general information center on Mexican data and conditions and provided information helpful in the preparation of briefs be members of the legal staff of the Agency of the United States.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The General Claims Commission was created under a convention signed on September 8, 1923, to settle all claims between the United States and Mexico arising after July 4, 1868, except those growing out of the revolution in Mexico, 1910 - 1920. (A Special Claims Commission was established on September 10, 1923, to adjudicate claims arising from injuries and losses sustained by U.S. citizens during the period November 20, 1910, to May 31, 1920, as a result of the revolution in Mexico.) In accordance with the provisions of the convention a three-man commission was established composed of a citizen of the United States, a citizen of Mexico, and a citizen of a neutral country. The three commissioners were: J.R. Baker (succeeded by Nathan L. Miller, Edwin B. parker, and Fred Kenelm Nielsen) of the United States; Genero Fernandez MacGregor of Mexico; and C. Van Vollenhoven of the Netherlands (succeeded by Kristian Sindballe of Denmark and Horacio F. Alfaro of Panama). The Commission functioned from 1924 to 1931, with numerous interuuptions. In 1931, when activities were suspended, 3,617 claims had been filed with the Commission, 54 claims had been disallowed and 94 claims had been allowed for a total amounting to $4,646,926.59.

Work was resumed under an agreement of April 24, 1934, with two commissioners only and under new procedures. The provision for a neutral commissioner was eliminated. U.S. Commissioner oscar W. Underwood and Mexican Commissioner Benito Flores were instructed to appraise separately all claims not yet disposed of and to get together in an attempt to reconcile any differences between them regarding final disposition. A period of three years was allowed for this work. In 1937, when the commissioners filed their report, it was found that they had agreed in the final disposition of only a small number of claims. Little was accomplished by the two Governments toward effecting a final settelment until November 19, 1941, when the United States accepted $40 million as full payment. Individual U.S. claimants were to receive their awards later from a domestic claims commsssion known as the American-Mexican Claims Commission, the whereabouts of whose records is unknown. The interests of the UNited States before the General Claims Commission were represented by an Agent of the United States.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
Congress created the position of Deputy Secretary of State in the Foreign Relations Authorization Act of 1972, approved July 13, 1972 (86 Stat 490), to replace the Under Secretary of State as the second ranking officer in the Department. The Deputy Secretary served as the principal deputy, advisor, and alter ego to the Secretary of State; served as Acting Secretary of State in the Secretary's absence; and assisted the Secretary in the formulation and conduct of U.S. foreign policy and in giving general supervision and direction to all elements of the Department. Specific duties and supervisory responsibilities have varied over time.

Serving a Deputy Secretary of State were John N. Irwin, II, July 13, 1972 - February 1, 1973; Kenneth Rush, February 2, 1973 - May 29, 1974; Robert Stephen Ingersoll, July 10, 1974 - March 31, 1976; Charles W. Robinson, April 9, 1976 - January 20, 1977; Warren Christopher, February 26, 1977 - January 16, 1981; William P. Clark, March 25, 1981 - February 9, 1982; Walter J. Stoessel, Jr., February 11, 1982 - September 22, 1982; Kenneth W. Dam, September 23, 1982 - June 15, 1985; John C. Whitehead, July 9, 1985 - January 20, 1989; Lawrence S. Eagleburger, March 20, 1989 - August 23, 1992; Clifton R. Wharton, Jr., January 27, 1993 - November 8, 1993; Strobe Talbott, February 23, 1994 - January 19, 2001; and Richard Lee Armitage, March 26, 2001 - February 23, 2005; and Robert B. Zoellick, February 23, 2005 - July 2006. John Negroponte took the post on February 27, 2007.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
By articles 12-17 of the Treaty of Washington the United States and Great Britain agreed that all claims on the part of corporations, companies, or private individuals of the two nations arising out of acts against persons or property during the period April 13, 1861 to April 9, 1865, that were not claims referred to in article 1 (Alabama claims), should be referred to a Mixed Claims Commission. The commissioners appointed were Russell Gurney for Great Britain; James Somerville Frazer for the United States; and Count Louis Corti, the Italian Minister to the United States, chosen by both countries. At the Commission's first meeting, September 26, 1871, Corti was selected to preside; Robert Saffiord Hale was received as agent and counsel of the United States; James Mandeville Carlisle was received as counsel of Great Britain; and Henry Howard as agent of Great Britain. Thomas C. Cox, appointed secretary of the Commission on September 27, had charge of the records, concerning which rules were prescribed by the Commission. It met in Washington until May 10, 1873, and then after a recess held the rest of its sessions, from June 10 to September 25, at Newport, Rhode Island.

Adjudicating the claims involved extensive investigation and resulted in considerable documentation. British citizens presented 478 claims for sums totaling, with interest, about $96,000,000. Of the 19 American claims, amounting to less than $1,000,000, exclusive of interest, twelve grew out of the raid on Saint Albans, Vermont, made by Confederates who came across the border from Canada. Others resulted from the detention at Calcutta of American vessels laden with saltpeter and from a raid by Confederate soldiers upon the American steamers Philo Vance and Island Queen on Lake Erie. Documentary evidence regarding the claims was sought by the U.S. agent from the archives of the the departments of the Federal Government and from records of the Confederate Government that were in Federal possession. Testimony was taken in writing all over the United States and in many different parts of the world by special counsel sent out from Washington or by local counsel under the instruction of the U.S. agent. Aid was also obtained from Thomas H. Dudley, who had been the U.S. consul at Liverpool, and Joseph Nunn, vice consul general at London. The cases of American citizens against Great Britain were handled by private counsel with the general aid and supervision of the U.S. agent.

The resulting disposition of the British claims was as follows: 30 dismissed as not within the jurisdiction of the Commission; 258 disallowed as unwarranted; eight withdrawn by the British agent; one dismissed but later refiled; and 181 allowed, for $1,929,819. All the American claims were dismissed.

The records of the Commission and its staff were, upon its termination, deposited in the Department of State.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Treaty of Washington, signed on May 8, 1871, provided in articles 1-11 for the establishment of a tribunal of five commissioners to arbitrate the United States claims against Great Britain arising from the actions of certain Confedearte cruisers. The Tribunal convened in Geneva on December 15, 1871, and the United States and British agents presented their nations' cases. The Tribunal met again on December 16 and then adjourned until June 15, 1872. The two agents were required to prepare their nations' countercases and to make them available to the Tribunal by April 15, 1872. The case of the United States, which supported claims for direct losses resulting from the destruction of vessels and their cargoes by insurgent Confederate cruisers, also supported indirect claims for expendutires incurred in the pursuit of the cruisers and the prolonging of the war, for the loss of the United States merchant fleet to the British flag, and for the increase in insurance rates. Great Britain maintained that the Treaty of Washington did not provide for the arbitration of indirect claims. Fearing for the collapse of the arbitration the United States agent agreed to withdraw to indirect claims. This extra-judicial agreement was formally announced by the President of the Tribunal on June 19, 1872, when the dismissed the indirect claims on the ground that international law was not applicable in such cases.

The final decisions of the Tribunal were announced on September 14, 1872. They were rendered separately for each of the Confederate cruisers and were based on three rules established by article 6 of the Treaty of Washington. Great Britain was held responsible for all the destruction caused by the Alabama, the Florida, and their tenders, but for the destruction by the Shenandoah only after her departure from Melbourne on February 18, 1865. Great Britain was not held liable for the actions of the Georgia, the Sumter, the Nashville, the Tallahasee, or the Chickamauga. The United States was awarded $15.5 million, payable in gold.

The Tribunal, as provided in article 1 of the Treaty of Washington, consisted of five Commssioners or Arbitrators: Charles Francis Adams, representing the United States; Sir Alexander Cockburn, Great Britain; Count Frederic Sclopis, Italy; Jacques Staempfli, Switzerland; and Marcos Antonio d'Araujo, Brazil. Count Sclopis was chosen president. The United States Agent was J.C. Bancroft Davis; we was assisted by William M. Evarts, Caleb Cushing, and Morrison R. Waite. The British Agent was the Lord Chancellor, Lord Hatherly, who prepared the case of Great Britain; he was assisted by Lord Tenterden and Mountague Bernard.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: By a convention of January 19, 1892, the United States and Venezuela agreed to arbitrate the claim of a U.S. firm, the Venezuelan Steam Transportation Co., for alleged wrongful seizure, detention, and employment of the company's steamships Hero, Nutrias, and San Fernando and the imprisonment of their officers, events that took place in Venezuela in 1871-72. The tribunal appointed to arbitrate this claim was composed of Noah L. Jeffries of the United States, Jose Andrade of Venezuela, and Matias Romero of Mexico, succeeded by A. Grip of Sweden. Alexander Porter Morse served as the U.S. agent and Samuel F. Phillips was the Venezuelan agent. Arthur W. Ferguson was appointed secretary. The tribunal met in Washington on October 27, 1894, and adjourned on April 5, 1895.  The March 26, 1895, award partially allowed the claim.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
A convention signed on July 4, 1831, by the United States and France provided for payment of 25 million francs to the United States for unsettled claims of U.S. citizens against the Government of France. The claims were principally for unlawful seizure, capture, sequestration, confiscation, or destruction of American vessels, cargoes, or other property. Some of the alleged acts took place in the 1790's. An act of July 13, 1832, authorized establishment of a domestic claims commssion to examine claims and distribute the 25 million francs amoing U.S. claimants.

The commissioners were George W. Campbell of Tennessee; John K. Kane of Pennsylvania; and Thomas H. Williams of Mississippi (succeeded by Romulus M. Saunders of North Carolina). John E. Frost of the District of Columbia was named secretary. The Commission, which met in Washington, D.C., held its first meeting on August 6, 1832. Its existence was extended twice. It adjourned December 31. 1835. Of 3,148 claims presented, 1,567 were allowed and 1,581 rejected. The total amount awarded was $9,352,193.47. 

The Commission also settled spoliation claims against the Netherlands because it was held that the Dutch Government was under control of France at the time of the seizures.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
A convention, signed January 15, 1880, provided for settlement of claims of French citizens against the United States growing out of the Civil War in America and of U.S. citizens against France arising from the war between France and Mexico, the Franco-Prussian War, and the Insurrection of the Commune. The claims were to be adjudicated by three commissioners; one appointed by the President of the United States, one by the Government of France, and the third by the Emperor of Brazil.

The mebers of the Commission were Asa O. Aldis for the United States, Louis de Geofrey (succeeded by Alexis A. Lefaivre) for France, and Baron de Arinos for Brazil. Washington F. Peddrick served as U.S. secretary, and Leonce Laugel (succeeded by Jules Boeufve) served in a similar capacity for France. The Commission, which met in Washington, D.C., held its first meeting on November 5, 1880. The Commission's existence was extended by conventions signed July 19, 1882, and February 8, 1883. A total of 727 claims were filed by France against the United States, and 19 U.S. claims were filed against France. On March 31, 1884, the commissioners made their final award and adjourned. The ward specified that the United States must pay France a lump sum of $625,566.35, less deductions, and that France pay the United States the sum of 13,659.14 francs, less deductions.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The definitive peace treaty between the United States and Great Britain, signed on September 3, 1783, included in article II a detailed description of the northeast boundary of the United States.  It was the intent of the negotiators by specifically defining the boundary line to prevent misunderstandings between the contracting powers.  The boundary line as described in the treaty, however, was based on inaccurate data, and some of the areas described were poorly defined or unknown. A boundary dispute arose over an area claimed by both Massachusetts and New Brunswick.  Royalists had settled in an area west of the Magaguadavic River, which Massachusetts claimed to be the St. Croix River intended by the negotiators of the definitive peace treaty.  New Brunswick claimed the Scoodic as the true St. Croix, placing the settlers on British territory. On November 19, 1794, John Jay signed a treaty of amity, commerce, and navigation with Great Britain. The Jay Treaty, as it is commonly known, provided in article V for a Commission to settle the St. Croix River dispute.  The Commission was to be composed of one British and one United States Commissioner and a third Commissioner to be appointed jointly by the other two. On May 21, 1796, the President appointed David Howell of Rhode Island as United States Commissioner. Thomas Barclay of Annapolis, Nova Scotia, was appointed as the British Commissioner. The first meeting of the Commissioners convened at Halifax, Nova Scotia, on August 30, 1796.  At this meeting, they agreed upon Egbert Benson of New York as the third Commissioner. The two countries were to be represented before the Commission by agents who would present claims of the countries and documents to support them.  James Sullivan of Massachusetts was commissioned the U.S. agent on May 21, 1796, and Ward Chapman served as the British agent. The Commission conducted its inquiry and on October 25, 1798 declared its decision choosing the Scoodic River as the true, historical St. Croix River, thus settling the immediate dispute, but allowing other potential problems and questions to go unaddressed.  New disputes relating to this boarder became the work of future Commissions and arbitrations.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Treaty of Ghent, concluded December 24, 1814, provided in article IV for a Commission to settle the territorial jurisdiction over the islands in Passamaquoddy Bay and Grand Menan Island, in the Bay of Fundy.  The Commission was to be composed of two Commissioners--one appointed by each of the contracting powers. John Holmes of Massachusetts was appointed by President Madison as the U. S. Commissioner on January 16, 1816, and the British Government's Commissioner, Thomas Barclay, was appointed on September 4, l815.  The agents representing the interests of the two governments were James T. Austin of Massachusetts for the United States, and Ward Chipman for Great Britain.  The first session of the Commission convened at St. Andrews, New Brunswick, on September 23, 1816.  Both governments claimed all the islands in Passamaquoddy Bay and the Island of Grand Menan, in the Bay of Fundy.  The United States declared that the islands were within the 20 leagues of the United States as specified in the treaty of 1783 and that they were not excepted from its territorial limits by any provisions in the treaty.  The British claimed the islands were within Nova Scotian limits. The Commission, after the claims were filed, adjourned with an agreement to meet the following year on May 28, 18l7. This meeting was postponed until early June. During the meetings that followed, the agents presented memorials supporting their countries' claims. The memorials were based, in part, on the interrogation of witnesses in the disputed area, on survey reports, and on colonial documents. The decision reached by the Commission was formally presented in its award, November 24, 1817.  The United States was awarded Moose, Dudley, and Frederick Islands in Passamaquoddy Bay; the remaining islands in that bay and the Island of Grand Menan in the Bay of Fundy were awarded to Great Britain.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The decision of the Commission established under article V of the Jay Treaty determined the source of the St. Croix River--but, when efforts were made to trace the boundary line from the source of the St. Croix River, the two countries disagreed on the location of the line as described in the l783 peace treaty. Efforts were made to settle the dispute. A convention concluded in 1803 by the U.S. minister at London provided for a Commission to determine the boundary line but was never ratified.  Again in 1807 negotiations were held, but the United States and Great Britain failed to reach a formal agreement.  Not until after the War of l8l2 was a treaty ratified that included provisions for settling the boundary dispute. Article V of the Treaty of Ghent, concluded December 24, 1814, addressed the fact that the exact boundary between the United States and Canada had not been ascertained and it was agreed that Commissioners be appointed to address the issues stipulated in the article and survey the boundary. King George III appointed Thomas Barclay as Commissioner on September 4, l8l5. Barclay also was the Commissioner under article IV of the same treaty.  Cornelius P. Van Ness was appointed by President Madison on April 3, 1816, as the Commissioner representing the United States.  Ward Chipman was the British agent before the Commissions established under the 4th and 5th articles of the Treaty of Ghent.  The Commission met several times--with little accomplished at each meeting because of weather conditions, delays in the surveys, and questions of procedure--at St. Andrews, New Brunswick, on September 23, 1816 ; at Boston, Mass., on June 4, 1817; at Burlington, Vt., on May 15, l8l8; at New York, N. Y., on May 3, 1819; at Boston, Mass., on May 11, 1820; and at New York, N.Y., on November 23, 1820, and on May 14, 1821. The Commission recessed on October 4, 1821, so that the Commissioners could prepare their reports.  Numerous issues arose that prevented the parties from reaching an agreement.  The Commissioner's reports were presented at the last meeting of the Commission on April 13, 1822.  The Treaty of Ghent had provided that if the Commissioners failed to agree, the questions should be referred "¿to a friendly sovereign or State¿" for arbitration.  Six years after the final reports were presented, the parties agreed to arbitration by the King of the Netherlands.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: In 1839 the British survey team of Featherstonhaugh and Mudge claimed that some of the previous surveys of the northeast boundary were erroneous and that the interpretation of the wording of the colonial grant of James I to Sir William Alexander was wrong.  The United States, in order to document its boundary claims, considered it necessary to resurvey certain parts of the disputed northeast boundary.  By an act of July 20, 1840 (5 Stat. 402), $25,000 was appropriated to make the new survey. James Renwick, Maj. James D. Graham (later Lieutenant Colonel, Corps of Topographical Engineers), and A. Talcott were appointed as survey Commissioners.  The Commissioners were to examine and report on the findings of Featherstonhaugh and Mudge after they had surveyed the boundary lines claimed by the United States and Great Britain.                         On January 6, l84l, the Commissioners submitted their first report, which stated that they had identified the source of the St. Croix River as determined by the Commission established under article V of the Jay Treaty and that they had surveyed as far north as the weather would permit. By an act of February 27, 1841 (5 Stat. 413), $75,000 was appropriated to continue the survey.  The Commissioners had not completed their survey when they presented another report on January 4, 1842.  Although most of the area surveyed by Featherstonhaugh and Mudge had been explored by the U. S. Commissioners, they requested additional funds to continue the survey.  No funds were appropriated. The U. S. Commissioners submitted a report, dated March 28, 1842, which refuted some of the claims of the British survey team.  The U. S. Commissioners prepared another report, dated January 27, 1843, containing information additional to that contained in the March 28, 1842, report.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: Article I of the Webster-Ashburton Treaty settled the long dispute over the northeast boundary line between the United States and the British provinces in North America by defining the northeast boundary line.  Article VI provided for the establishment of a Commission to survey and mark the line. James Bucknall Estcourt was appointed the British Commissioner, and President John Tyler appointed Albert Smith as the U. S. Commissioner.  he Commissioners met on May 1, 1843, at Bangor, Maine, but they adjourned until June because the weather would not permit them to begin the survey. When they convened at Houlton, Maine, on June 1, they divided the boundary line into several defined units to facilitate the survey.  The joint report of the two Commissioners on the exploring, surveying, and marking of the northeast boundary line was "Signed and Sealed in duplicate, at the City of Washington¿"on June 28, 1847. The duplicate set of the maps, tables, and drawings prepared by the U. S. survey team under the direction of Lt. Col. James D. Graham to accompany the U.S. copy of the final report was destroyed by fire in April 1848.  Under authority of Congress the maps were reconstructed by Graham at a later date.  The "duplicate original" of the tables showing the monuments, distances, and deflections and of the maps prepared by the U. S. survey team to accompany the British copy of the final report was transmitted to Great Britain before the fire. A manuscript copy of this duplicate original was made at a later date for the United States.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The British Minister at Washington, in a note of November 15, 1848, informed the Secretary of State that a boundary marker erected by the Commissioners under terms of the Webster-Ashburton Treaty of 1842 "¿on the road leading from the State of Vermont into Canada has been removed by some Persons and placed about six feet to the southward of the spot where it was originally fixed."  The Minister suggested that the U.S. Government appoint a Commissioner to jointly survey the area with a British Commissioner in order to place the marker at its correct spot. The Secretary of State accepted the British proposal in a note dated May 25, 1849. James D. Graham was designated the U. S. Commissioner, and W. B. Ord was appointed the British Commissioner.  The two Commissioners met at Montreal, Canada, on August 19, 1849.  After the survey was completed and the marker was moved to its correct location at the village of Beebe Plain, the Commissioners prepared a joint report issued on September 19, 1849.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: n its decision of November 24, 1817, the Commission established under article IV of the Treaty of Ghent awarded to the United States the Moose, Dudley, and Frederick Islands in Passamaquoddy Bay.  The remaining islands in that bay and the Island of Grand Menan in the Bay of Fundy were awarded to Great Britain.  No provisions were made in the Treaty of Ghent for the marking of this section of the boundary.  Article II of the convention concluded between the United States and Great Britain on July 22, 1892, provided for the establishment of a Commission "¿to determine upon a method of more accurately marking the boundary line between the two countries in the waters of Passamaquoddy Bay in front of and adjacent to Eastport, in the State of Maine, and to place buoys or fix other boundary marks as they may determine to be necessary." Each country was to appoint one Commissioner. W. F. King of Ottawa, Canada, was appointed the British Commissioner; and Thomas C. Mendenhall. Superintendent of the Coast and Geodetic Survey, was commissioned on September 8, 1892, by Secretary of State John W. Foster as the U.S. Commissioner. The Commissioners met at Ottawa on November 28, 1892. After this meeting the Commissioners examined maps and charts to determine the boundary. Their next meetings were held from March 9 to March 1l, 1893, at Washington, D. C.  Much of the field work was conducted by the Coast and Geodetic Survey under the direction of D. B. Wainright.  The Commissioners met again in March 1894 and prepared a rough draft of their final report.  Disagreement arose over one aspect of the boundary.  In December l894, the Commissioners, through correspondence, suggested to one another alternatives for settling the impasse.  Neither Commissioner was willing to accede to the proposition of the other, but they agreed to meet in April 1895 for additional conferences.  It was decided that a report should be prepared showing what was agreed up on and what was still in controversy.  The Commissioners, however, were not able to agree on a joint report by June 25, 1895, when the Department of State informed Mendenhall that his "¿services as Commissioner of the United States under the Convention of July 22, 1892, were terminated."  The U.S. Commissioner submitted a final report on March 24, 1896, which contains information concerning his negotiations with the British Commissioner and a detailed description of the boundary line and of the methods employed in determining the line and of marking those parts of the line that were agreed upon by the Commissioners.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA), also known as the Hague Tribunal is an international organization based in The Hague. It was established in 1899 as one of the acts of the first Hague Peace Conference, which makes it the oldest institution for international dispute resolution. The seeds of thought that led to the creation of the PCA were planted in the United States. Annual meetings were conducted by the Lake Mohonk Conference on International Arbitration, beginning in 1895, in New York State at the Mohonk Mountain House hotel.

As of 2006, 106 countries were party to the treaty. The Court deals in cases submitted to it by consent of the parties involved and handles cases between countries and between countries and private parties.The PCA is housed in the Peace Palace in The Hague, which was built specially for the Court in 1913 with an endowment from the Carnegie Foundation. From 1922 on, the building also housed the distinctly separate Permanent Court of International Justice, which later became the International Court of Justice in 1946. Unlike the International Court of Justice, the PCA is not an inter-state court. Parties may apply here for arbitration, mediation or examination of the facts. Unlike the ICJ, the Court is not just open to states but also to other parties. Organisations, private enterprises and even private individuals may apply here to resolve a dispute with a state.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
When the United States established diplomatic relations with Mexico in 1825, various incidents had already given rise to claims of citizens of one country against the other country. During the next decade these claims, some of which dated back to Mexico's struggle for independence, continued to increase. Many were based on allegations that U.S. vessels had been fired upon, that U.S. citizens had been illegally arrested and maltreated, and that their property had been confiscated.

The correct this situation the United States and Mexico signed a claims convention on April 11, 1839. It provided that all claims based on injuries to persons and property of citizens of the United States suffered before April 11, 1839, should be referred to a board of four commissioners, two to be named by the President of each country. The Board was to meet in Washington, D.C., and was given a period of eighteen months to decide upon the justice of the claims and the amount of compensation, if any, due from the Mexican Government. In case of differences between the Commissioners, the King of Prussia, or his representative, was to act as umpire.

An act of Congress, approved June 12, 1840 (5 Stat. 383), provided for the appointment of the two U.S. Commissioners and a secretary. On June 16, 1840, President Martin Van Buren appointed William L. Marcy and John Rowan as the U.S. Commissioners; Alexander Dimitry was appointed Secretary. On June 20, 1840, the Mexican President, Anastasio Bustamante appointed Pedro Fernandez and Joaquin Velasquez de Leon as Mexican Commissioners; Lucas de Palacio y Magarola was appointed Secretary. The King of Prussia appointed Baron Roenne, then Minister Resident of Prussia at Washington, as the Umpire.

The Board met in Washington from August 25, 1840, to February 25, 1842. During this time a total of 109 claims was presented to it. The Board, however, reached final decisions in only 72 cases. Awards totalling $439,393.82 were granted in eleven cases, four cases were rejected, and 57 cases were referred to the Umpire. The Umpire rejected four of the 57 cases while awarding to the 53 others a total of $1,586,745.86.

At the end of the eighteen-month period much unfinished business remained. Besides the 37 undecided claims that were under consideration as the Board expired, there were several additional claims of U.S. citizens ready for presentation that the Board was unable to accept or examine because of the lack of time. These additional claims as well as the 37 undecided claims were later taken up by the U.S. Board of Commissioners established in 1849.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: On November 7, 1899, the United States, Germany, and Great Britain signed a convention in which they agreed to submit to arbitration the claims of their citizens residing in Samoa. In addition, any of the signatory powers could submit claims of persons, natives excluded, who were under the protection of that power. The claims grew out of military actions by American, German, and British officers in Samoa, particularly the bombardment of the islands by United States and British naval forces, and covered the period from January 1 to May 13, 1899. King Oscar II of Sweden was chosen as arbitrator. R. Newton Crane served as U.S. Agent. On October 14, 1902, the King held that the United States and Great Britain were responsible for losses caused by their military actions.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
During the War of 1812, the British took possession of a large amount of American property, including enslaved persons, some of whom were voluntary fugitives, while others were taken in predatory excursions. Article I of the Treaty of Ghent, signed on December 24, 1814, contained provisions for restoration of "all territory, places, and possessions" taken by either party during the war. A dispute, however, arose between American and British officials about interpretation of this provision as it affected enslaved people. The dispute was referred, by article V of the convention signed on October 20, 1818, to the Emperor of Russia for arbitration. The Emperor's decision, April 22, 1822, favored the United States. Having settled this point, a convention was signed on June 30, 1822, by the United States and Great Britain providing for a commission of two members from each country, a commissioner, and an arbitrator who would determine the average value of enslaved people and the validity of property claims. Langdon Cheves and Henry Seawell were appointed U.S. commissioner and arbitrator, respectively.

Although the commission, which met in Washington, D.C., August 25, 1823, agreed on some points, it soon ran into insurmountable difficulties. On November 13, 1826, a new convention was signed in which Great Britain agreed to pay $ 1,204,960 in satisfaction of all claims under award of the Emperor of Russia.

An Act of March 2, 1827 (4 Stat. 219), provided for establishment of a domestic claims commission to examine and determine the validity and amount of award, if any, claimants should receive. Langdon Cheves, Henry Seawell, and James Pleasants were appointed commissioners. Aaron Ogden served as clerk. The commission met in Washington, D.C., on July 10, 1827. A total of 1,060 claims were decided before it adjourned on August 31, 1828.

Article I of the Treaty of Ghent, signed on December 24, 1814, contained provisions for restoration of "all territory, places, and possessions" taken by either party during the war. A dispute, however, arose between American and British officials about interpretation of this provision as it affected slaves. The dispute was referred, by article V of the convention signed on October 20, 1818, to the Emperor of Russia for arbitration. The Emperor's decision, April 22, 1822, favored the United States. Having settled this point, a convention was signed on June 30, 1822, by the United States and Great Britain providing for a commission of two members from each country, a commissioner, and an arbitrator who would determine the average value of slaves and the validity of property claims. Langdon Cheves and Henry Seawell were appointed U.S. commissioner and arbitrator, respectively. Although the commission, which met in Washington, D.C., August 25, 1823, agreed on some points, it soon ran into insurmountable difficulties. On November 13, 1826, a new convention was signed in which Great Britain agreed to pay $ 1,204,960 in satisfaction of all claims under award of the Emperor of Russia. An act of March 2, 1827 (4 Stat. 219), provided for establishment of a domestic claims commission to examine and determine the validity and amount of award, if any, claimants should receive. Langdon Cheves, Henry Seawell, and James Pleasants were appointed commissioners. Aaron Ogden served as clerk. The commission met in Washington, D.C., on July 10, 1827. A total of 1,060 claims were decided before it adjourned on August 31, 1828. Records of the Mixed Claims Commission Minutes of the Commission. Aug. 25, 1823-Mar. 26, 1827)

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Decartelization and Deconcentration Division was established within the Office of General Counsel on September 21, 1949. It was responsible for the enforcement of the decartelization and deconcentration laws of the Allied High Commission. It represented the General Counsel on matters relating to the administration, reorganization, and liquidation of properties seized, subject to seizure, or controlled by military government, the Allied High Commissioner, or the U.S. High Commissioner. The Division prepared and reviewed drafts of laws and regulations bearing on decartelization and deconcentration. It ceased to exit by 1955.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
By article 7 of a treaty between the United States and Spain signed December 10, 1898, the United States relinquished claims of its citizens against Spain and guaranteed satisfaction to the claimants. An act of March 2, 1901, provided for a five-member commission to determine and settle American citizens' claims relinquished by this treaty. The commissioners were William E. Chandler, who served as president until he resigned November 10, 1907; Gerrit J. Dickema, succeeded by Harry K. Daugherty; james P. Wood, who became president of the Commission on November 10, 1907, and was succeeded as commssioner by Roswell P. Bishop; William A. Maury; and Wlliam L. Chambers. David Meade Massie was appointed by ther Commission as a salaried commissoner to take testimony in Cuba. William E. Fuller, succeeded by William wallace Brown, was appointed Assistant Attorney General and charged with defense of claims before the Commission.

The first Commission meeting was held on April 8, 1901, and the last on May 2, 1910. A total of 542 claims were filed, of which 354 were for property losses, 152 for damages to seamen of the battleship Maine, and 36 for personal injuries. the claims amounted to $64,931,694.51; final awards totaled $1,387,845.74.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: Article VI of the treaty between the United States and Great Britain, signed November 19, 1794 (Jay's Treaty), provided for a joint commission to determine the amount due British merchants for debts contracted before the Revolutionary War. The members of the five-man commission were Thomas Macdonald and Henry Pye Rich for Great Britain and Thomas Fitzsimmons and James Innes (succeeded by Samuel Sitgreaves) of the United States. The fifth commissioner, chosen by lot, was John Guillemard of Great Britain. Griffith Evans served as secretary. The Commission was organized in Philadelphia on May 29, 1797, and after a series of disagreements disbanded on July 31, 1799, without a final settlement. By a convention between the United States and Great Britain, signed January 8, 1802, the United States agreed to pay Great Britain 600,000 pounds sterling in satisfaction of the claims.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The U.S. Element of the Military Security Board was established as a HICOG organization on September 21, 1949. It was a direct successor of the U.S. Element, Military Security Board which had been functioning under the aegis of the Office of Military Government for Germany (U.S.) (OMGUS) since March 4, 1949. The participants in the London Conference in February 1948 had agreed that the three military governors of the western zones of Germany should set up a Military Security Board to insure that Germany did not rearm or rebuild its war potential. More specific terms of reference for the Board were drafted by the three military governors, in TRIB/P(48)17 (Final), January 17, 1949, and the Military Security Board, now formally established, was directed to assumed certain functions of the Allied Control Council, including the completion of legislation and regulatory work relating to military security, and to monitor compliance with and implementation of Allied laws and regulations through regular inspections. The Board was discontinued on May 5, 1955, with the termination of HICOG.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The establishment of the U.S. Disarmament Administration was announced in a Department of State press release, September 9, 1960. It was responsible for assisting in the formulation of international disarmament and arms control policy and in the negotiation of international agreements in those areas. It was transferred to and absorbed by the Arms Control and Disarmament Agency (ACDA) which had been established as an independent agency by provisions of the Arms Control and Disarmament Act (75 Stat. 638), September 26, 1961. ACDA conducted, supported, and coordinated research for arms control and disarmament policy formulation. It prepared for and managed U.S. participation in international arms control and disarmament negotiations, and prepared, operated, and directed U.S. participation in international arms control and disarmament systems. ACDA was abolished by an act of October 21, 1998 (112 Stat. 2681-767) with functions transferred to the Secretary of State. The ACDA Director was replaced by the office of the Under Secretary of State for Arms Control and International Security Affairs as well as the office of the Senior Advisor to the President and the Secretary of State for Arms Control, Nonproliferation, and Disarmament.

ACDA was the U.S. Government repository of data exchange among nations pursuant to arms control treaties. The Arms Control Community On-line Repository of Treaty Data (ACCORD) database/repository was established by ACDA in 1993 to automate this function. In all subsequent years, the database was updated with the current verified data of all previous information exchanged as a result of the Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) Treaty and the Confidence- and Security-Building Measures (CSBM) Agreement. This computer-based Federal repository allowed exchange data, notifications, and inspection reports to be archived in a single location. To the extent possible, the information was made available in electronic form so that Federal agencies could have immediate access. The repository consisted of both classified and unclassified computer databases, as well as paper copies of data. In 1997 ACDA was adding START, Global Exchange of Military Information data, and data resulting from the Open Skies Treaty. It was expected to add treaty notifications for the Chemical Weapons Convention after that entered into force.

ACDA was abolished on April 1, 1999 in accordance with Public Law 105-277 of October 21, 1998 (112 Stat. 2681-767) and functions transferred to the Secretary of State.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: A convention signed by the United States and Denmark provided for settlement of the claim of Carlos Butterfield & Co. for the seizure and detention of the steamer Benjamin Franklin and the bark Catharine Augusta. The vessels sailed from New York in September 1854 for the Danish island of St. Thomas, where they were allegedly seized and detained until the spring of 1855 by authorities of the island. The loss claimed by the owners was $272,153.37. Sir Edmund Monson, British Minister to Athens, was chosen as sole arbitrator. He decided in favor of Denmark and disallowed the claim on January 22, 1880.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
Article VII of the treaty between the United States and Great Britain, signed November 19, 1794 (Jay's Treaty), provided for a joint commission to settle claims of U.S. citizens against Great Britain arising from the alleged capture or condemnation of American vessels and other property, and claims of British subjects against the United States for losses arising from the capture of their vessels and merchandise.

The five-man commission provided for by article VII was established in 1796. The members were John Nicholl (succeeded by Maurice Swabey) and John Anstey for Great Britain and Christopher Gore and William Pinckney for the United States. The fifth commissioner, chosen by lot, was Colonel John Trumbull of the United States. Francis Moore served as secretary, and Samuel Bayard (succeeded by Samuel Williams and George E. Erving) was chosen as U.S. agent. The Commission, which met in London on August 14, 1796, functioned until July 1799, when it was suspended under article VI.

The convention of January 8, 1802, between the United States and Great Briatin provided that the commissioners in London should reassemble and complete their work. The Commission was brought to a close on February 24, 1804. Approximately $143,428 was awarded in favor of British claimants, while American claimants received about $11,650,000, payable in three installments.
