creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The U.S. Legation in Guatemala was opened in Guatemala City on January 31, 1849, when Elijah Hise presented his credentials as Charge d'Affaires. Previously, and since 1825, U.S. representatives had been accredited to the Central American Republic. 

The first Minister Resident, John L. Marling, presented his credentials on February 14, 1855. He was succeeded by Beverly L. Clarke, July 13, 1858; Elisha O. Crosby, May 28, 1861; Fitz Henry Warren, June 27, 1866; Silas A. Hudson, August 11, 1869; George Williamson, September 9, 1873; Cornelius A. Logan, June 11, 1879; and Henry C. Hall, July 25, 1882. Shortly after his arrival Minister Hall was promoted to Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary; he presented his new credentials on August 10, 1882. He was succeeded by Lansing B. Mizner, June 4, 1889; Romualdo Pacheco, February 28, 1891; Pierce M.B. Young, June 12, 1893; Macgrane Coxe, September 29, 1896; W. Godfrey Hunter, January 25, 1898; Leslie Combs, February 2, 1903; Joseph W.J. Lee, March 19, 1907; William Heimke, May 2, 1908; William F. Sands, October 9, 1909; R.S. Reynolds Hitt, October 14, 1910; William Hayne Leavell, November 29, 1913; Benton McMillin, January 15, 1920; Arthur H. Geissler, July 31, 1922; Sheldon Whitehouse, March 21, 1930; Matthew E. Hanna, October 28, 1933; and Fay A. Des Portes, May 22, 1936.

On May 19, 1943, with the presentation of the credentials of Boaz Long as the first Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary, the Legation was reclassified as an embassy. Ambassador Long was succeeded by Edwin Jackson Kyle, May 8, 1945; Richard C. Patterson, November 24, 1948; Rudolf E. Schoenfeld, April 24, 1951; John E. Peurifoy, November 4, 1953; Norman Armour, October 18, 1954; Edward J. Sparks, July 29, 1955; Lester D. Mallory, February 27, 1958; John J. Muccio, February 1, 1960; John O. Bell, January 30, 1962; and John Gordon Mein, September 22, 1965. On August 28, 1968, Ambassador Mein was murdered by a rebel faction when gunmen forces his official car off the road in Guatemala City and raked the vehicle with gunfire. He was succeeded by Nathaniel Davis, November 21, 1968; William G. Bowdler, October 19, 1971; Francis E. Meloy, Jr., February 7, 1974; Davis E. Boster, October 13, 1976; and Frank V. Ortiz, Jr., July 17, 1979. 

From August 1980 through September 1981 Melvin E. Sinn served as Charge d'Affaires ad interim. The next Ambassador, Frederic L. Chapin, presented his credentials on September 3, 1981. He was succeeded by Alberto Martinez Piedra, August 17, 1984; James H. Michel, October 28, 1987; Thomas F. Stroock, October 31, 1989; Marilyn McAfee, June 16, 1993; Donald B. Planty, August 22, 1996; Prudence Bushnell, October 14, 1999; and John Randle Hamilton, who was sworn in as Ambassador on December 6, 2002.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Diplomatic Bureau has charge of and prepared instructions and letters for Ministers of the United States; received, prepared, filed, and registered despatches; recorded and filed correspondence with foreign ministers; and prepared credential letters, treaties for ratification and exchange, and all drafts of letters that may be necessary. In addition, it transacted and had charge of all matters pertaining to the Diplomatic Department of the United States, except consular business. The Bureau was nominally abolished by an act of March 5, 1855, but it continued to exist as a necessity in the transaction of the Department's business until 1870.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: By a convention of April 28, 1902, the United States and the Dominican Republic settled part of the claim of Emilia C. De Sala and submitted the other part to arbitration. The tribunal established for this purpose met for the first time on March 18, 1903, and adjourned on April 30, 1904, after granting an award of $215,812 to the claimant. The tribunal met in Washington, D.C., and in New York. Fernando E. Guachalla of Bolivia, later replaced by J.M. Ceballos, and Frederick Van Dyne of the United States were named as judges.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: An agreement of December 17, 1930, signed by the United States and Sweden, provided for arbitration of claims of two Swedish motorships against the United States. The motorships Kronsprins Gustaf Adolf and Pacific allegedly suffered financial losses as a result of being detained in 1917-18 by U.S. authorities. The agreement called for the appointment of an arbitrator, a national of either the United States or Sweden. Eugene Borel, professor of international law at the University of Geneva, was chosen. Roberty Perret of Switzerland served as secretary. The U.S. agent was J.A. Metzger; the agent for Sweden was W. Bostrom. The trinunal met in Washington from May 5 to June 2, 1932. The final decision, July 18, 1932, was in favor of the United States.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The European Advisory Commission (EAC) was established, with its seat in London, by a secret protocol signed by the United States, the United Kingdom, and the Soviet Union representatives at the Tripartite Conference in Moscow, November 1, 1943, with responsibility for making recommendations to the three Allied governments on questions connected with the termination of the war in Europe. The Provisional Government of the French Republic was accepted into membership, November 27, 1944. EAC's twelve recommended formal agreements, all of which were eventually accepted by all member governments, concerned surrender terms for, and postwar administration of, Germany and Austria; and armistice terms for Bulgaria. 

The EAC had its seat in London at Lancaster House and started its work on January 14, 1944. William Strang (1st Baron Strang) was the British delegate, while on the American and Soviet side the respective ambassadors were the delegates, John G. Winant and Feodor T. Gousev. The American military advisor was Cornelius Wickersham. George F. Kennen served as political advisor to Winant; he was succeeded by Philip E. Mosely.  

On June 5, 1945 the European Advisory Commission assumed briefly full control over Germany. Members included General Dwight D. Eisenhower for the United States, Field Marshal Sir Bernard Law Montgomery for Great Britain, and Marshal Georgy Zhukov for the Soviet Union. The Commission delimited German territory to its territory of December 31, 1937 minus territory handed over to Poland and the Soviet Union, divided Germany into four zones of occupation under American, British, French, and Soviet military administration and separately divided Berlin into four sectors.

The EAC was abolished, September 10, 1945, pursuant to Section I of the Protocol of the Proceedings of the Berlin Conference (also known as the Potsdam Conference), August 1, 1945. By Sections I and II of same protocol, responsibility for drawing up peace treaties with the former European Axis powers was vested in a Council of Foreign Ministers of China, France, United Kingdom, United States, and the Soviet Union; and responsibility for administering occupied Germany was vested in a Control Council.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: In a protocol of February 17, 1903, the United States and Venezuela provided that all unsettled claims of U.S. citizens against Venezuela should be submitted to a mixed commission for arbitration. The commssion chosen to do this consisted of William E. Bainbridge of the United States, Jose de Jesus de Paul of Venezuela, succeeded by Carlos F. Grisanti, and Charles Augustus Henri Barge of the Netherlands, who served as umpire. Robert C. Morris was U.S. agent; F. Arroyo Parejo was agent for Venezuela. The secretaries were Rudolf Dolge for the United States and J. Padron Uztariz, succeeded by Eduardo Calcano Sanavria, of Venezuela. The Commission met at Caracas on June 1, 1903. Fifty-five claims were filed. The commssioners adjourned on December 26, 1903. The umpire filed his last awards on April 12, 1904.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
In the early period of the Republic instructions from the Department of State to diplomatic and consular officers abroad and their replies to the Department were sent through various shipping houses in New York and through the postmaster and collector of customs of that city. The procedure eventually proved unsatisfactory. On November 18, 1830, William B. Taylor was appointed the first U.S. Despatch Agent at New York, with the duties of transmitting instruction abroad by sending them on the fastest ships and of receiving despatches from abroad and sending them to the Department of State. From time to time the duties of despatch agents were enlarged. The agents assisted in booking passage for Foreign Service officers and their families, in receiving important foreign dignitaries, in extending import courtesies to foreign countries for articles to be displayed at international exhibitions in the United States, in forwarding mail to U.S. naval vessels, in executing passport applications, and in administering oaths. 

Despatch agencies were opened also at Boston and San Francisco. At certain Foreign Service posts despatch agencies were also established. The earliest was at London in 1817, where the agent received the despatches from diplomatic and consular posts in Europe and transmitted tehm on the fastest ships to the United States. Agencies were also operated at Liverpool, Le Havre, Bremen, and Hamburg.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Bureau of Rolls and Library was first established in the Department of State on July 1, 1874.  It was abolished in 1879 and revived in 1882. Its Rolls Division kept the records of the Continental Congress, the laws and treaties of the United States, Presidential orders and proclamations, records of international conferences and commissions, and private collections of papers acquired by purchase.  The Division was responsible for research and correspondence relating to all these records and for publishing the laws and treaties of the United States.  The Library Division of the Bureau had charge of the Department's library and was responsible for storing and distributing the many State Department publications and the publications of the Congress that were apportioned to the Department.  The Bureau was abolished on May 13, 1921, by Department Order No. 203, and most of its functions were transferred to the Division of Publications.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: Applications for land grants in western Georgia (now Mississippi) were made to Georgia State authorities as early as 1785. On January 7, 1795, the Georgia Legislature approved an act by which the greater part of what is now Alabama and Mississippi were sold for 1 1/2 cents an acre to four land companies. Announcement of the sale produced public indignation throughout Georgia. As a result, a newly elected Georgia legislature declared the land sale of 1795 null and void on February 13, 1796. By the time the act had been approved, however, a good part of the disputed land had been sold to private individuals. The claims based on the act of 1795 became known as the Yazoo land claims. In 1802, Georgia ceded to the United States her rights to the territory west of the Chattahoochie River. The task of settling land claims to the ceded territory was left to the Federal Government, primarily the U.S. Congress. Heated arguments took place in Congress concerning settlement of the claims, and finally the matter went to the Supreme Court for decision. The Supreme Court, on March 16, 1810, declared the rescinding act of 1796 unconstitutional. An act of March 31, 1814 (3 Stat. 116), appropriated $5 million to be distributed among claimants as a final settlement. A commission, consisting of Thomas Swann, Francis S. Key, and John Law (3 Stat. 192), was established. The tedious task of deciding cases and distributing the money was begin in 1815. Three years later, the Treasury Department reported a final settlement, the payment of $4,282,151.12. Much of the money did not go to the defrauded claimants but to those who had purchased the claims rights from the original owners.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Operations Coordinating Board (OCB) came into existence in 1953. The principal function of the OCB was the coordination and development by departments and agencies of detailed operational plans to carry out national security policy. Each agency participating in the OCB was represented by a designated board member who was aided by a Board Assistant who served as that agency's focal point for handling OCB matters. The OCB and the Board Assistants met on a regular basis.

The Director of the United States Information Agency (USIA) became a full member of the OCB in 1955; prior to that he attended meetings as an observer. Within USIA, the Office of Plans (IOP) was responsible for supporting the Director on OCB matters. Within IOP, the Special Assistant for Operations Coordinating Board Affairs (IOP/B) coordinated all issues and maintained USIA's primary files on OCB matters.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Department of State established the Office of Occupied Areas on April 8, 1946, to coordinate its activities in Germany, Austria, Japan, and Korea, and placed it under the direction of an Assistant Secretary of State. The Office was dissolved on March 4, 1949. The Assistant Secretary of State was the Departmental member of the State - War - Navy Coordinating Committee and on August 9, 1946, was named as its chairman. He was responsible to the Secretary of State for the coordination of U.S. Government policy falling within the jurisdiction of the Far Eastern Commission. The Department established a new Office of German and Austrian Affairs, and the Office of Far Eastern Affairs assumed responsibility for Japanese and Korean Affairs. Incumbents included John H. Hilldring, April 12, 1946 - August 31, 1947, and Charles E. Saltzman, September 2, 1947 - May 26, 1949.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Office of General Counsel was established on September 21, 1949, pursuant to HICOG Staff Announcement No. 1 of that same date. The Office of General Counsel was the general legal advisor to the Office of the U.S. High Commissioner and its functional elements. The Office provided representation for the High Commissioner on the Law Committee of the Allied High Commission and on all legal matters in multipartite negotiations. The Office initiated policies and procedures and provided advice on matters relating to judicial and penal administration and monitores the administration of justice by German and Occupation authorities. The Office drafted all legislation issued by the High Commissioner, reviewed all German legislation, and reviewed German agreements which were subject to disapproval by the Allied High Commission. The Office of General Counsel was abolished on May 5, 1955, with the termination of HICOG.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: Meeting in Bogotá, Colombia, March 30-May 2, 1948, delegates from all the American republics drafted the Charter for the Organization of American States. The new charter and the Treaty of Pacific Settlement, which was also signed during the conference, reorganized the Pan American system. As established at Bogotá, the OAS had a Secretariat, situated in Washington; a permanent executive body called the Council; a "supreme organ" called the Inter-American Conference; and the Meeting of Consultation of Ministers of Foreign Affairs, designed to consider urgent problems. The Charter of the OAS went into force in December 1951, after two-thirds (fourteen) of the member nations had ratified it.  The United States approved adherence to the Charter on August 28, 1950.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
At the UN General Assembly meeting held in the fall of 1946, the Philippine delegation offered a resolution calling for an international conference on Freedom of Information and Freedom of the Press. UNESCO, then a newly formed component of the UN, offered to sponsor the conference and established a subcommission on Freedom of Information and Freedom of the Press within its Commission on Human Rights. The subcommission helped to gather information and to coordinate various elements of the proposed conference. However, the conference was eventually sponsored by the UN with limited participation by UNESCO. The UN Conference on Freedom of Information convened in Geneva, Switzerland, April 21-24, 1948, with 17 UN members participating.

The Chairman of the U.S. Delegation was William Benton, Assistant Secretary of State for Public Affairs. Lloyd Free, special assistant to the Assistant Secretary, served as technical advisor to the U.S. Delegation. Shortly before the Conference took place, the Office of International Conferences and the Office of International Information (a component of the Office of Public Affairs with Lloyd Free as director) were organized within the Department of State and had various responsibilities for Conference activities, including the Freedom of Information Conference in Geneva.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: This international exposition was held from May 9, 1929, to June 21, 1930, at Seville, Spain.  Spain invited the republics of both Americas that had at one time been in whole or in part under the Spanish flag to participate in an exposition of the arts, sciences, history, industries, commerce, and resources of Spain, Portugal, and the American Republics. Argentina, Brazil, Colombia, Cuba, the Dominican Republic, El Salvador, Guatemala, Mexico, Peru, Portugal, the United States, Uruguay, and Venezuela took part.  The commission representing the United States was headed by Thomas E. Campbell.  The United States constructed three buildings on the exposition site and had both individual and Government exhibits.  The sum of $700,000 was authorized by Public Resolution 65, 68th Congress, approved on March 3, 1925, to meet the expenses of United States participation.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The International Colonial and Overseas Exposition was held in Paris, France, from May 6 to November 15, 1931, to show the industrial, commercial, and cultural development of the French colonies and of the possessions of other countries participating in the exposition.  The United States was represented by a commission headed by C. Bascom Slemp. Other countries that participated were Argentina, Belgium, Canada, Denmark, Great Britain, Greece, Haiti, Holland, Italy, Portugal, and the Union of South Africa.  The United States Government exhibit at the exposition had as its cardinal feature a replica of Mount Vernon, constructed in exact dimensions of the original.  There were also exhibits from the insular possessions of the United States--the Philippine Islands, Hawaii, Guam, Samoa, Alaska, Puerto Rico, the Virgin Islands, and the Panama Canal Zone--and from a number of individual exhibitors.  United States participation was authorized by Public Resolution 95, 71st Congress, and by Public Law 519, 71st Congress, 2d session, the latter authorizing an appropriation of $250,000.  An additional appropriation of $50,000 was made later for participation of the insular possessions of the United States.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
In February, 1946, the United Nations Economic and Social Council established a Preparatory Committee to develop an agenda and proposals for an International Conference on Trade and Employment. The Preparatory Committee was composed of representatives from eighteen countries and held meetings in London (October 5-November 26, 1946) and Geneva (April 10-October 30, 1947).  A special Drafting Committee was established to prepare a charter for the proposed International Trade Organization, based on the discussions during the first meeting of the Preparatory Committee. The Drafting Committee met from January 20-February 5, 1947 at Lake Success, New York.

The International Conference on Trade and Employment, which was attended by representatives from fifty countries, was held in Havana, Cuba, from November 17, 1947, to March 24, 1948, and resulted in the signing of a charter of an International Trade Organization and the establishment of an Interim Commission to function until the Charter was ratified by the required number of countries. However, the United States did not ratify the charter.

A series of reciprocal tariff negotiations was conducted concurrently with the second meeting of the Preparatory Committee in Geneva from April to October, 1947. These negotiations resulted in the signing of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) by twenty-three nations. The Contracting Parties to the GATT met periodically thereafter to revise the tariff agreements and extend them to cover other commodities and countries. The machinery which was established to implement GATT gradually evolved into an organization.

The World's Industrial and Cotton Centennial Exposition was held from December 16, 1884, to June 30, 1885, at New Orleans. The classifications of exhibits at the exposition were as follows:  I, Agriculture; II, Horticulture; III, Manufactured Products, Ores, Minerals, and Woods; IV, Furniture and Accessories; V, Textiles, Fabrics, Clothing, and Accessories; VI, the Industrial Arts; VII, Alimentary Products; VIII, Education and Instruction; IX, Works of Art; and X, Pisciculture.  A Board of United States Executive Departments, composed of one representative from each executive department of the government, was formed pursuant to a Presidential proclamation issued on May 13, 1884, to manage the government's exhibits.  These exhibits were to demonstrate the duties of each department and the workings in general of the federal government. The State Department was represented on this board by Charles S. Hill. The Department's exhibit consisted of articles, many of them from its consular officers, illustrating "The Commerce of the World and the Share of the United States Therein," and was designed to show the resources and channels for development of industry and commercial intercourse. To the Department of State was appropriated the sum of $10,000, to be disbursed under the direction of the board of representatives.  Other acts to aid and encourage the holding of the exposition were approved on February 10, 1888; May 21, 1884; and March 3, 1885.

Invitations on behalf of the U.S. Government were extended to foreign governments through the Department of State.  Austria-Hungary, Belgium, Brazil, France, Great Britain, Haiti, Italy, Japan, Mexico, the Netherlands, Sweden and Norway, Colombia, Costa Rica, Denmark, Germany, Guatemala, Honduras, Jamaica, Nicaragua, Portugal, Russia, Spain, Siam, Turkey, and Venezuela participated.  It is not known whether the last 15 countries sent representatives, but they did participate to the extent of sending industrial exhibits.

The World's Columbian Exposition was held from May 1 to October 30, 1893, to celebrate the four-hundredth anniversary of the discovery of America by Christopher Columbus.  An act of Congress, approved on April 25, 1890, provided for the celebration, designated the city of Chicago to be host to the exposition, and called for the appointment of a commission consisting of two commissioners from each state and territory and from the District of Columbia, together with eight commissioners at large, to be designated as the World's Columbian Commission. The commissioners were appointed by the President.

The act of April 25 also provided that government departments exhibit articles and materials illustrative of their functions and that a board be created to make necessary arrangements and to select, arrange, and protect such exhibits as might be prepared.  The Board of Government, Management, and Control was composed of a representative from each executive department, one from the Smithsonian Institution and National Museum, and one from the U.S. Fish Commission. The representatives were appointed by the President on August 19, 1890.  Sevellon A. Brown, Chief Clerk of the Department of State, was appointed as that Department's representative on the Board. The Government's exhibits were to be housed in buildings erected by the Department of the Treasury at an aggregate cost of $400,000.  The total liability of the government for participation in the exposition was limited to $1,500,000.

The organizations concerned in the operating of the exposition were the World's Columbian Commission, the World's Columbian Exposition, the Board of Lady Managers, the Board of Government, Management, and Control (for government exhibits) and the World's Congress Auxiliary.

Responsibilities for the Department of State concerning this exposition included the notification of the states and territories of the appointments to be made, the calling together of the World's Columbian Commission in Chicago, the preparation of an exhibit of articles and materials to illustrate the functions of the Department, and the despatch of invitations to other governments.

The treaty signed by the United states and Spain provided for a mixed commission to settle claims of U.S. citizens arising from the Cuban insurrection of 1868. The Commission was organized in Washington, May 31, 1871. William T. Otto, succeeded by Kenneth Rayner, Joseph Segar, Joseph T. Stewart, and James Lowndes, served as arbitrator for the United States. Marquis de Potestad, succeeded by Jose Brunetti y Gayoso, was arbitrator for Spain. The umpire was Baron Lederer of Austria, succeeded by M. Bartholdi of France, Baron A. Blanc of Italy, and Count Carl Lewenthaupt of Sweden. The advocate for the United States was Caleb Cushing, succeeded by Thomas J. Durant and Charles C. Suydam. The advocate for Spain was James M. Carlisle, succeeded by John D. McPherson. The secretary of the Commission was George O. Moore, succeeded by George A. Matile and Eustace Collett. A special subcommission was organized at Havana, June 30, 1873, to take testimony in Cuba.

The Washington Commission met on May 31, 1871, and adjourned on December 27, 1882, having settled 140 claims, of which 35 were allowed and 105 rejected. The last awards were dated February 22, 1883, and were posted in the Commission journal on February 23, 1883.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: Participation of the United States in the Grand Exhibition of Japan, which was to be held in Tokyo in 1912, was provided for by an act approved on May 22, 1908.  It authorized the President to accept the invitation of Japan and stated that expenditures for erecting suitable buildings and making appropriate exhibits of arts, industries, manufactures, products of the soil and mines, and of the functions of the United States Government should not exceed $1,500,000.  Three commissioners general, acting under the direction of the Secretary of State, were appointed, and $50,000 was appropriated for their expenses.  The three officials appointed--Francis B. Loomis, Frederick J.V. Skiff, and Francis D. Millet--went to Japan in 1908 and held conferences with Japanese officials regarding the exposition and American participation therein.  The fair was not held in 1912 as proposed, but was postponed until 1917.

 United States.  A commissioner general and five commissioners represented the United States, with offices in Washington and Rio de Janeiro.  In addition to individual exhibits, there were exhibits by the United States Government agencies.  The Government exhibits were accompanied to Rio de Janeiro by departmental representatives.  The sum of $1,000,000 was appropriated for United States participation by a joint resolution of Congress of November 2, 1921.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Northwest Atlantic Fisheries Conference, held in Washington January 26-February 8, 1949, was organized for the purpose of promoting international conservation of fishery resources in the Northwest Atlantic. Plenipotentiary delegates represented the governments of Canada, Denmark, France, Iceland, Italy, Newfoundland, Norway, Portugal, Spain, Great Britain, and the United States.  The Food and Agriculture organization of the United Nations and the International Council for the Exploration of the Sea were represented by observer delegates. The Conference Convention provided for a commission to collect, collate, and disseminate scientific information on international fisheries. Wilbert M. Chapman, Special Assistant to the Under Secretary for Fisheries and Wildlife, Department of State, served as Chairman of the Conference.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: While Western Europe experienced an economic and political recovery after the Second World War, Great Britain and the sterling area (nations that utilize the sterling monetary system) had an increasingly difficult time maintaining their dollar exports and earnings. The crisis manifested itself in the second quarter of 1949 in the form of an unprecedented drain on the sterling area's gold and dollar reserves. Recognizing that an economic setback in Great Britain and the sterling area would have an adverse impact on the economies of Western Europe, the United States, and other parts of the world, representatives of the United States, Great Britain, and Canada held talks in Washington, D.C., September 7-12, 1949, to examine the trade and financial relationships between the sterling area and the dollar area. Representatives to the tripartite economic talks included for the United States, Secretary of the Treasury John W. Snyder, Secretary of State Dean Acheson, and Administrator of the Economic Cooperation Administration Paul Hoffman; for Great Britain, Minister for Foreign Affairs Ernest Bevin, Chancellor of the Exchequer Sir Stafford Cripps, and Ambassador Sir Oliver Franks; for Canada, Secretary of State for External Affairs Lester Pearson, Minister of Finance Douglas C. Abbott, and Ambassador Hume Wrong. The Washington meeting was held in order to examine fundamental causes of the British economic crisis and lay the basis for a permanent solution.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: After Germany overran the Netherlands, Belgium, and France in May and June 1940, the United States called for a Second Meeting of the Ministers of Foreign Affairs of the American Republics. Held in Havana, Cuba, from July 21 to July 30, 1940, the chief purpose of the conference was to prevent the transfer of colonial possessions in the Western Hemisphere to Germany. Accordingly, the conference adopted the Act of Havana, which provided for the provisional administration of European colonies and possessions in the New World should a non-American state (Germany) attempt to assert control over them. The conference also adopted a mutual security resolution which declared that "any outside attack on an American state shall be considered as an act of aggression against the states which signed this declaration". All of the American states signed the declaration. Continental solidarity and economic cooperation were the other major concerns of the American delegation at the conference.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Intercontinental Railway Commission was created as a result of a report of the Committee on Railway Communication adopted by the First International Conference of American States, held in Washington, 1889-90. The report recommended the creation of an International Commission of Engineers to survey the possible routes for a railroad that would connect existing systems and to estimate the costs of each route.

The Congressional appropriation act for the fiscal year ending July 30, 1891, provided $65,000 for the expenses of such a survey and authorized the President to appoint three Commission members from the United States and to detail Army and Navy officers to serve as engineers.

Representatives from Argentina, Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Mexico, Paraguay, Peru, the United States, Uruguay, and Venezuela attended the first meeting of the Commission in Washington on December 4, 1890. Commission members from the United States were Alexander J. Cassatt, Henry G. Davis, and Richard C. Kerens.

The mian work of the Commission (later known as the International Railway Commission) was to organize field parties to undertake the preliminary survey that would determine whether or not it was practical to contruct a railway that would connect the existing railroad systems of the United States and Mexico with those of Central and South America. The Commission organized three field parties, or engineer corps, and sent them to the field under its direct supervision. Each party surveyed an assigned region that had been laid out by the Commission on Surveys. After dispatching the parties, the Commission adjourned on April 22, 1891, having held 19 sessions, and left the transaction of further business in the hands of an Executive Committee.

When the survey parties returned from the field, their records were used in the Washington office for the preparation of the final reports of the Commission. The last meeting of the Executive Committee was on October 10, 1898, and from that date until April 1899, the remaining business of the Commission, which was the distribution of its reports, was in the hands of its secretary.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Paris Universal Exposition was held in Paris from April 1 to November 3, 1867. It was four times as large as any preceding international exposition, and its classifications of exhibit items encompassed practically the whole range of natural and artificial products. Ten large classification groups were provided for objects to be exhibited at the expositon: (1) works of art; (2) apparatus and applications of the liberal arts; (3) furniture and other objects for the use of dwellings; (4) clothing, including fabrics and other objects worn upon the person; (5) products, raw and manufactured, of mining, industry, forestry, etc.; (6) apparatus and processes used in the common arts; (7) food, fresh or preserved, in various states of preparation; (8) livestock and specimens og agricultural buildings; (9) live produce, and specimens of horticultural works; and (10) exposition of objects and methods designed to ameliorate the conditions of the working class. The groups were further divided into 95 classes.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
GATT signatories occassionally negotiated new trade agreements that all countires would enter into. Each set of agreements was called a round. In general, each agreement bound members to reduce certain tariffs. Usually this would include many special-case treatments of individual products, with exceptions or modifications for each country.

The first version of GATT, developed in 1947 during the United Nations Conference on Trade and Employment in Havana, Cuba, was referred to as "GATT 1947". The Havana conference began on November 21, 1947, less than a month after GATT was signed. The ITO Charter was finally agreed in Havana in March 1948, but ratification in some national legislatures proved impossible. The most serious opposition was in the US Congress, even though the US government had been one of the driving forces. In 1950, the United States government announced that it would not seek Congressional ratification of the Havana Charter, and the ITO was effectively dead. So, the GATT became the only multilateral instrument governing international trade from 1948 until the WTO was established in 1995.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
Article 39 of the Charter of the Organization of American States provides for the holding of Meetings of Consultation of Ministers of Foreign Affairs to consider "problems of an urgent nature and of common interest to the American States." Article 40 states that any member state can request such a meeting.  The first meeting took place in Panama at the request of the United States in 1939, after war broke out in Europe. The second meeting took place in Havana, again at the request of the United States, in 1940, after Nazi Germany overran the Low Countries and France. The third meeting took place in Rio de Janeiro, again at the request of the United States, in 1942, after Japan and Germany declared war on the United States.

By late 1950, the other American states and United States policy makers pressed for a fourth meeting of consultation, primarily to consider the threat of communism in the Western Hemisphere. On December 15, 1950, President Harry S Truman addressed the nation concerning "The Present Emergency." Among the points in his speech, Truman announced an emergency program of economic and military preparedness to combat communism. The United States then requested that a meeting of American Republic foreign ministers be called to consult on the situation and to coordinate the common effort required.

The Fourth Meeting of the Ministers of Foreign Affairs of the American States took place in Washington, D.C. from March 26 through April 7, 1951.  The program of the meeting had three major parts. First, the ministers discussed political and military cooperation for the defense of the Americas and for preventing and repelling aggression. Second, they addressed the question of strengthening the internal security of the American Republics.  And, third, they discussed emergency economic cooperation. The chief result of the Washington Conference was the "Declaration of Washington."  The declaration reaffirmed hemispheric solidarity in the face of communist aggression or threats and affirmed inter-American support for actions of the United Nations.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Pan American Exposition was held at Buffalo, N.Y., from May 1 to November 1, 1901, "to fittingly illustrate the marvelous development of the Western Hemisphere during the nineteenth century, by a display of arts, industries, manufactures, and products of the soil, mines, and sea...." Participation of the United States Government in the exposition was provided for by an act of March 3, 1899, which authorized the creation of a government board of agreement to prepare and manage the government's exhibit at the exposition and appropriated the sums of $200,000 to cover the cost of erecting buildings to house this exhibit and $300,000 for expenses of the exhibit.  The Department of State was represented on the government board, and had an exhibit.  Invitations to foreign countries to participate in the exposition were extended by the Department on behalf of the exposition management on January 5, 1900.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The South Carolina Interstate and West Indian Exhibition was held from December 1 1901, to May 30, 1902, in Charleston, South Carolina.C. A joint resolution of Congress of January 21, 1902, appropriated the sum of $90,000 to pay the expenses of the U.S. Government exhibit at the exposition.  An act of July 1, 1902, appropriated the sum of $160,000 to pay legal claims against the exposition company for labor, articles, and services. H.C. McArthur was in charge of the State Department's exhibit. The official invitations to foreign countries to participate in the exposition were sent on May 1, 1901.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Department of State created the position of Assistant Secretary of State for Congressional Relations and International Conferences on December 20, 1944 by Departmental Order 1301, after Congress authorized an increase in the number of Assistant Secretaries in the Department from four to six (58 Stat. 789, approved December 8, 1944). The reorganization was the first to assign substantive designations to specific Assistant Secretary positions. The Office of the Assistant Secretary of State for Congressional Relations and International Conferences. had the responsibility for liaison with the Congress on all matters concerning the Department, with the exception of matters of a fiscal or other administrative character. The Assistant Secretary was the Chairman of a standing Committee on International Conferences of the Secretary’s Staff Committee, and served as the Deputy of the Secretary of State with appropriate staff, to secure coordinated conduct of international conferences and the unified and effective representation of the interests of the United States Government at international conferences. Dean G. Acheson served as the Assistant Secretary of State for Congressional Relations and International Conferences from December 20, 1944 to August 15, 1945. On March 8, 1945, the name was changed to the Office of the Assistant Secretary of State for Congressional Relations to prescribe Foreign Service regulations by Departmental Order 1310.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: By article XI of the treaty signed February 22, 1819, by the United States and Spain, the U.S. Government released Spain from certain claims of American citizens and undertook to make the necessary payments, not to exceed $5 million, to U.S. claimants. The claims arose almost entirely out of alleged seizure, destruction, and detention of U.S. vessels and cargoes. By this treaty, Spain ceded Florida to the United States. A three-man commission was established to decide on the vaildity of claims and the amount, if any, to be awarded to each claimant. The members of the Commission were Hugh Lawson Whitye of Tennessee, William King of Maine, and Littleton Waller Tazewell of Virginia. Tobias Watkins served as secretary. The Commission met in Washington, D.C., June 8, 1821, and continued its work until June 8, 1824. A total of 1,859 claims were presented for adjudication.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The War History Branch came into being as the result of a suggestion by Franklin D. Roosevelt in March 1942. In a letter to the Director of the Bureau of the Budget, Roosevelt proposed the establishment of a committee to oversee the orderly preservation of Federal records documenting the American war effort. The Committee of Records of War Administration was formed and made recommendations to the agencies. In response Secretary of State Cordell Hull issued Departmental Order 1214 on December 15, 1943, announcing establishment of a war history project under Dr. Graham Stuart. Begun by the War Records Unit of the Division of Research and Publication, the work was continued by the War History Branch. Most of the studies were concerned with the work of the various organizational units within the Department, but some were topical in approach. There was to be an overall history based upon the individual studies. The project was never completed, however, and the studies were left at various stages. Some were finished; others were only in the planning stage when the program was abandoned.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Field Operations Division was located in Bremerhaven and was headed by the U.S. Resident Officer. The Resident Officer served as a local representative of the Land Commissioner and the High Commissioner, and directed and administered HICOG programs at the community level. The primary job of the Resident Officer was to foster the development of a democratic way of life among the German population in Bremerhaven. Reorientation and democratization programs such as the cultural exchange program, the film program, and the grant-in-aid program were designed to encourage the adoption of democratic ideas as well as political institutions.

The Resident Officer was also the eyes and ears of the United States at the local level. He observed and reported on political gatherings, the possible possession or manufacture of forbidden weapons, the outbreak of epidemics, refugee problems, and trends in local education. The Resident Officer also maintained contact with the military Commander of the Bremerhaven Port of Embarkation. In addition, he acted as intermediary between the military and German officials and dealt with German complaints of troop violence, traffic law violations, vandalism, non-payment of bills, and requisitioned property.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The HICOG Clemency Board was established on January 6, 1950, pursuant to Staff Announcement No. 63, HICOG, January 6, 1950. The Board was empowered to grant or deny parole and commutation of sentences to applicants who received other than death sentences, and to revoke parole or conditional commutation of sentences. The Board was composed of members appointed by the General Counsel of HICOG from professional personnel of the Prisons and Administration of Justice Divisions in the Office of Chief Counsel, and from the legal advisers of the Laender and the Berlin Sector. The chief of the Prisons Division served as Chairman of the Board, and the Deputy Chief as Executive Secretary. The chiefs of the Prisons Division and the Administration of Justice Division formulated Board policy and directed the general functioning of the Board.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Joint Brazil-U.S. Technical Commission was established as a result of conversations between President Harry Truman and President Gaspar Dutra of Brazil during the summer of 1947. The objective of the Commission was to analyze factors in Brazil which tended to promote or retard economic development and to make broad recommendations on programns to encourage the flow of private capital to Brazil. John Abbink, chairman of the board of McGraw-Hill International Corp. was appointed head of the U.S. Section in July 1948. John C. Cady, Assistant Chief of the American Republics Branch of the Department of State's Division of Foreign Economic Development, was detailed to the Commission to serve as Exeutive Secretary.

The members of the U.S. Section arrived at Rio de Janeiro on September 7, 1948. The Technical Commission was organized into a Central Commission and subcommissions on Agricultural and Livestok Development, Commerce and General Studies, Transportation, Fishing and Fisheries, Eletrical Energy, Banking, Fiscal Problems, Industrial Development, Fuels, Labor and Manpower, and Minerals. The Commission's final report was approved by the Central Commission on February 7, 1949.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: On January 13, 1869, a protocol was concluded between Portugal and Great Britain by which both countries agreed to submit to arbitration their dispute concerning sovereignty over the island of Bulama off the west coast of Africa, and "a certain portion of territory opposite." The contracting powers chose the President of the United States as arbitrator. Assistant Secretary of State J. C. Bancroft Davis prepared a report for the Arbitrator, presenting the problem and summarizing the material presented by Portugal and Great Britain. On April 21, 1870, the award of President Ulysses S. Grant in favor of the Portuguese claim was delivered to the contracting powers by Secretary of State Hamilton Fish.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: After hostilities ceased in 1866 between Spain and the Allied Republics of Peru, Bolivia, Chile, and Ecuador, a state of war still existed. The representatives were: Hamilton Fish for the United States, Mauricio Lopez Roberts for Spain, Manuel Fryere for Peru and Bolivia, Joaquin Godoy for Chile, and Antonio Flores for Ecuador. The armistice was signed at Washington on April 11, 1871.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Tenth Inter-American Conference, held in Caracas, Venezuela, from March 1 through March 28, 1954, was the first to be convoked under the Charter of the Organization of American States (OAS). The charter, which was signed on April 30, 1948, at the Ninth International Conference of American States, entered into force on December 13, 1951.

The U.S. delegation, under the chairmanship of Secretary of State John Foster Dulles, included Henry F. Holland, Assistant Secretary of State for Inter-American Affairs; Mervin L. Bohan, U.S. Representative on the Inter-American Economic and Social Council; John M. Cabot, Ambassador Designate to Sweden; John C. Dreier, U.S. Representative on the Council of the Organization of American States; Herman Phleger, Legal Adviser to the Secretary; Fletcher Warren, Ambassador to Venezuela; Samuel C. Waugh, Assistant Secretary of State for Economic Affairs; W. Randolph Burgess, Deputy to the Secretary of the Treasury; and Andrew N. Overly, Assistant Secretary of the Treasury.  Senators Bourke B. Hickenlooper and Theodore F. Green served as special Congressional advisers to the delegation.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Louisiana Purchase Exposition was held in St. Louis, Missouri, from May 1 to December 1, 1904, to commemorate the purchase from France of the Louisiana Territory. Preliminary steps toward the organization of the celebration were taken by the Missouri State Historical Society and the Louisiana Purchase Exposition Co. by an act of March 3, 1901, Congress appropriated $5,000,000 toward the celebration and authorized the creation of the Louisiana Purchase Exposition Commission, members of which were to be appointed by the President. At that time, it was planned that the dedication of the exposition buildings would take place not later than April 30, 1903. However, the dedication did not take place until a year later. Government exhibits were under the supervision of the U.S. Government Board, on which the State Department was represented. The Department transmitted, on August 22, 1901, invitations for other governments to participate in the exposition.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: In a convention of December 4, 1868, the United States and Peru provided for a mixed commission to decide claims of U.S. citizens against Peru and of Peruvian citizens against the United States. The commissioners were Michael Vidal for the United States and Luciano Benjamin Cisneros for Peru. The Commission has two umpires, Frederico Augusto Elmore, a British subject, and Teodoro Valenzuela, a Colombian citizen. It met in Lima on September 4, 1869, and adjourned on February 26, 1870. Twenty-two claims against Peru and one claim against the United States were presented.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The United States, Great Britain, and Portugal signed a protocol on June 13, 1891, providing for arbitration of a railroad claim of the United States and Great Britain against Portugal. The claim arose when the Portuguese Government cancelled the concession and took possession of the Lourenço Marques Railroad, which had been constructed by American citizens. British subjects also had an interest. The arbitrators, Joseph Blaesi, Andreas Heussler, and Charles Soldan, met in Bern and on March 29, 1900, awarded 15,314,000 francs to the United States and Great Britain.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The United States and Spain signed a convention by which the United States agreed to accept on behalf of certain American claimants, and to distribute among them, inscriptions at 5 percent on the consolidated debt of Spain.  Both parties renounced all claims against each other arising from February 22, 1819, to the date of the signing. An act of June 7, 1836 (5 Stat. 34), provided for appointment of a commissioner to distribute the payments among U.S. citizens having vaid claims. Louis D. Henry was appointed commissioner, John J. Mumford served as secretary, and Cornelius Van Ness, succeede by Wiliam A. Weaver, was appointed as clerk. The commission met on July 30, 1836, in Washington and adjourned on February 1, 1838. A total of 102 claims were decided, of which 68 were allowed and 34 disallowed.

By a convention signed by the United States and New Granada (later the Republic of Colombia), September 10, 1857, claims of U.S. citizens against New Granada that had been presented to the Department of State or to the U.S. Minister at Bogota before September 1, 1859, especially those arising from the riot in Panama, April 15, 1856, were referred to a joint commission. The Commission was composed of one commissioner for each government and an umpire selected jointly. The commissioners were Elias W. Leavenworth of New York and Jose Marcellino Hurtado of Colombia. N.G. Upham of New Hampshire was chosen umpire. The Commission met in Washington on June 10, 1861. It expired on March 9, 1862, before all the claims had been decided.

By a convention signed by the two countries on February 10, 1864, it was agreed to organize a new commission to adjudicate the undecided claims. The new commissioners were Thomas Biddle for the United States and Eustorjio Salgar for Colombia. The umpire was Sir Frederick W.A. Bruce of Great Britain. The Commission completed its work and adjourned on May 19, 1866.

On October 10, 1957, the Department of State elevated the position of Special Assistant for Intelligence to that of the Director of the Bureau of Intelligence and Research, with rank equivalent to that of an Assistant Secretary of State. The Special Assistant for Intelligence, established in 1949, was in charge of intelligence functions that dated back to 1945 when the Department of State first received them after the abolition of the wartime Office of Strategic Services. An Act of Congress (P.L. 99- 3) of August 16, 1985 authorized the appointment of an Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research. Since August 18, 1986, all incumbents served as Assistant Secretaries of State and been commissioned by the President.

W. Park Armstrong, Jr. was the Special Assistant for Intelligence. Directors of the Bureau of Intelligence and Research were: Hugh Smith Cumming, Jr., October 10, 1957-February 19, 1961; Roger Hilsman, Jr., February 19, 1961-April 25, 1963; Thomas Lowe Hughes, April 28, 1963-Augusts 25, 1969; Ray S. Cline, October 26, 1969-November 24, 1973; William G. Hyland, January 21, 1974-November 24, 1975; Harold H. Saunders, December 1, 1975-April 10, 1978; William G. Bowdler, April 24, 1978-December 17, 1979; Ronald I. Spiers, January 28, 1980-October 4, 1981; Hugh Montgomery, October 19, 1981-January 6, 1985; and Morton I. Abramowitz, February 1, 1985-August 18, 1985.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The International Exposition of Electricity at Paris, according to a note from the French Legation to the Department of State, was to be opened on August 1, 1881, and closed on November 15, 1881. Acceptable exhibit items included natural and artifical magnets, apparatus for the generation and transmission of electricity, apparatus for the study of electricity, and exhibits illustrating the applications of electricity. The Department of State gave the circular regarding the exposition to the press and notified Congress of the invitation extended to the United States. The Department organized an honorary commission to represent the United States. Levi P. Morton was selected as honorary commissioner general, and George Walker, Charles R. Goodwin, and George E. Gourand were selected as honorary commissioners. The Assistant Secretary of State was the commissioner general for all matters requiring attention in the United States. Twenty-nine American exhibitors received diplomas and medals awarded by a jury of the exposition.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The dispute between Argentina and Paraguay involved a land area of about 200,000 square miles of the Great Chaco, north of the Pilcomayo River. The dispute had its origin in a treaty of 1865 between Brazil, Argentina, and Uruguay that concerned territorial claims of Paraguay. Until 1870 first Brazil, then Argentina and Uruguay waged war on Paraguay. From 1870 to 1876 negotiations were held between Argentina and Paraguay in an effort to settle the question of ownership of the disputed area. Finally, on February 3, 1876, a treaty was signed at Buenos Aires between Argentina and Paraguay, which submitted the question to arbitration and named the President of the United States as an Arbitrator.  On November 12, 1878, President Rutherford B. Hayes delivered his decision in favor of Paraguay.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
By the terms of a treaty concluded December 24, 1886, the Republics of Costa Rica and Nicaragua agreed to submit to the President of the United States, as arbitrator, the question pending between them regarding the validity of the Treaty of Limits of April 15, 1858.  If the Arbitrator should rule that the treaty was valid, there were questions in two other categories that he should decide upon. One concerned the right of Costa Rica to navigate ships of war or revenue cutters in the San Juan River; the other comprised 11 points of "doubtful interpretation" regarding the boundary between the two countries as stipulated in the Treaty of Limits.

President Grover Cleveland delivered his award on March 22, 1888. He ruled that the Treaty of Limits was valid and that Costa Rica could not navigate war vessels on the San Juan River but could navigate revenue cutters there. He also gave decisions on the 11 points of "doubtful interpretation" relating to the boundary. In rendering his decision President Cleveland made use of the report submitted to him by Assistant Secretary of State George L. Rives.

When the contracting powers began to mark the boundary, in accordance with President Cleveland's award, they encountered a different problem. The marking of the boundary as set by the President was impossible because of shifting sands and the shifting of the river mouth.

A treaty of demarcation was concluded through the mediation of San Salvador on April 8, 1896, and another arbitral proceeding was instituted. Each of the contracting governments appointed two engineers or surveyors to trace and mark the boundary "pursuant to the provisions of the treaty of April 15, 1858, and the arbitral award of the President of the United States." It was provided that, in the event these commissioners could not agree, the point of disagreement would be submitted to a fifth surveyor appointed by the United States. This surveyor had the authority to decide any kind of dispute that arose. Gen. E. P. Alexander was appointed for the United States on February 17, 1897. By July 1900 the Boundary Commission had surveyed and marked the boundary.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Sesquicentennial International Exposition (referred to in part of the legislation as an exhibition) was held in Philadelphia in 1926 to celebrate the one hundred and fiftieth anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence. Participation of the U.S. Government in the exposition was provided for by a joint resolution approved on March 3, 1925.  This resolution established the National Sesquicentennial Exhibition Commission to represent the United States in connection with holding the exposition, and authorized government agencies to prepare for the Exhibition Association such exhibits as it might be in the interest of the United States Government to display. A joint resolution approved on February 26, 1926, authorized the appropriation of $1,186,500 for the selection, purchase, preparation, transportation, arrangement, safekeeping, exhibition, and return of the Government exhibits and for administrative expenses, and an additional sum of $1,000,000 for the construction of buildings for exhibition purposes. The resolution also provided that a Commissioner of the Sesquicentennial Exposition be appointed by the National Commission to carry out the provisions of the resolution. An act of March 3, 1926, appropriated the full amount for the fiscal year 1927.

Each branch of the government participating in the exposition appointed contact officers to facilitate the preparation of the government's exhibits. For the Department of State, J. Butler Wright and E. J. Ayers were appointed.  The exhibits of the United States were illustrative of nearly every branch of government service.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Conference on Near Eastern Affairs at Lausanne, Switzerland, was called at the invitation of Great Britain, France, and Italy. It met from November 20, 1922, to February 4, 1923, and from April 23 to July 24, 1923, in order to write a new treaty with Turkey, which, under the new government of Kemal Pasha, did not recognize the Treaty of Sevres. Represented at the Conference were the British Empire, France, Greece, Italy, Japan, Romania, the Kingdom of the Serbs, Croats, Slovenes, and Turkey. The United States was not officially represented, but had a special mission at the Conference to act as observers, entitled to be heard but with no right to vote, hold office, or to sign agreements or reports. During the first phase of the Conference (November 20, 1922 - February 4, 1923), no agreement could be reached on certain points at issue, and an adjournment took place, during which the Turkish delegates returned home to ascertain the views of their government. The second phase of the Conference began on April 23 and ended on July 24, 1923, with the signing of a treaty of peace and other diplomatic instruments. This treaty restored eastern Thrace, the Bosporus, the Dardenelles, and Smyrna to full Turkish sovereignty, and diminished foreign zones of influence and capitulations, without any need for reparations. The Bosporus, however, remained demilitarized and subject to an international convention, an issue that led to the Montreux Convention Regarding the Regime of the Turkish Straits of 1936. Other points of the Conference involved an agreement between Turkey and Greece concerning the compulsory exchange of minority ethnic groups.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
A disagreement between Argentina and Brazil involving 11,823 square miles of land in the State of Parana, Brazil, and the rivers that formed its boundaries had long been the cause of controversies and wars. Direct negotiations and previous arbitrations had failed to settle the problem.

 To prevent further armed conflict, a treaty was concluded between Argentina and Brazil on September 7, 1889, whereby both countries agreed to submit the controversy to arbitration by the President of United States. His decision was to be made between the following boundary lines: (1) that of the rivers Pepiry-Guacu and San Antonio, the existing boundary of Brazil, or (2) that of the rivers Jangada and Chapeco, the boundary claimed by Argentina. On February 6, 1895, President Grover Cleveland delivered his decision in favor of Brazil.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Colombia-Italy Claims Arbitration of 1897 grew out of claims made against the Colombian Government by Ernesto Cerruti, a native of Italy who had emigrated to Colombia in 1868 and had served as the Italian consul to Colombia from 1870 to 1882. He was also engaged in the operation of a firm, E. Cerruti and Co., that imported chiefly munitions. During the political disturbances of 1876 and 1877 Cerruti furnished munitions to the insurgent State government of Cauce, the State in which he resided.

Political disturbances occurred again in Cauca during 1885, and at this time the Federal Government was successful in putting down the insurrection by the State Government. Cerruti, whose business partners included prominent political and military figures, was arrested and charged with complicity; his property was pillaged and his holdings were confiscated. He was soon released, however, upon the demand of the commander of an Italian warship, who supported his demand with the landing of an armed force. This incident resulted in a break in Italian-Colombian diplomatic relations, but relations were restored by a Spanish-mediated protocol. By the terms of this protocol, Colombia agreed to restore the confiscated property to Cerruti and to submit his other claims to mediation by the Spanish Government.

The decision of the Spanish mediator, delivered on January 26, 1888, led to the return to Cerruti of all his property; and it held that he was entitled to claims against the Colombian Government. The mediator stipulated that a commission composed of three members--one each from Italy Spain, and Colombia--should be set up at Bogotá, Colombia, to which Cerruti would present his claims. The commission met at Bogotá on the appointed date, but it adjourned 3 weeks before it was to expire because Cerruti had failed to present his claims. Cerruti refused to present his claims on the ground that the Colombians would refuse to accept an unfavorable award.

This abortive attempt to settle the claims was followed by a long diplomatic correspondence between the Governments of Italy and Colombia. Another protocol was finally signed on August 18, 1894, by which the Governments of Italy and Colombia agreed to submit all the claims of Cerruti to the arbitration of the President of the United States. The claimant was represented before the Arbitrator by the firm of Coudert Bros. of New York; the Colombian Government was represented by Calderon Carlisle of Washington, D.C.  On March 2, 1897, President Grover Cleveland delivered his decision. The award was in five parts: on three points the award was in favor of the claimant and on two points the claims were disallowed.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Enemy Branch was responsible for planning the economic program to be put into effect when the enemy countries should be occupied. It prepared studies and reports for the industrial disarmament of the enemy to prevent future wars, including analyses of the entire economic structure of the Axis countries. Its staff units and divisions were functional in nature and were concerned with problems relating to industrial disarmament, external economic security, reparations and restitution, requirements and allocations, food and agriculture, foreign trade, consumers' economy, property control, transportaion and communications, and industry of the countries to be occupied. The Branch also included a Japanese and an Austrian Special Services Staff, and it cooperated closely with the Technical Industrial Intelligence Commiutee, a subcommitee of the Joint Intelligence Committee of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.

The records of the Branch were transferred to the Department of State. Intelligence reports accumulated by the Branch were integrated with other intelligence records in the possession of the Reference Division of the Office of Intelligence Collection and Dissemination, Department of State.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: This corporation was originally organized privately on October 30, 1941, under the name Ships, Incorporated, to build an experimental cargo vessel with shallow draft and multiple engines known as the Sea Otter. The Corporation became inactive when the Sea Otter project was abandoned by the Navy Department. The Office of Lend-Lease Administration took over the Corporation in June 1942, under the President's directive that the Administration proceed with a redesigned Sea Otter or Seamobile. In the summer of 1943, cargoes, Inc., also contracted for the construction of experimental helicopters adapted to protecting cargo ships against submarine attack. After the shipping situation improved, the Corporation was liquidated. The final board of directors meeting was held on March 24, 1945, and the Corporation was dissolved on April 30, 1945.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Office of War Crimes Issues, headed by the Ambassador at Large for War Crimes Issues, advised the Secretary of State directly on U.S. efforts to address serious violations of international humanitarian law committed anywhere in the world. These violations primarily concerned large-scale atrocities including genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes. The Office oversaw U.S. support for the creation of courts and other judicial mechanisms to bring perpetrators of international law to justice. After September 11, 2001, the Office played a key diplomatic role with foreign governments whose nationals had been captured in the war on terror. The office also had primary responsibility for policy on Iraqi war crimes. 

The Office of War Crimes Issues worked closely with the regional bureaus in the Department of State, other U.S. Government agencies, foreign governments, the United Nations and other international organizations, and non-governmental organizations. The Ambassador at Large consulted with these entities on a number of issues involving international tribunals and other projects and initiatives designed to address mass atrocities.

The Ambassador and his staff made frequent trips overseas, including to The Hague, the Balkans, Africa and Asia, meeting with high-ranking officials to carry out U.S. government objectives for war crimes issues. Among other activities, the Ambassador met with victims of atrocities, members of Congress and non-governmental organizations.

Nathaniel G. Upham was appointed U.S. commissioner, and Edmund Hornby served as commssioner for Great Britain. Joshua Bates of the United States was selected as umpire. Nathaniel L. Upham was the secretary. The Commission met in London on September 15, 1853, and adjourned on January 15, 1855. The claims of 40 American citizens and 75 Britsih subjects were presented. The awards to American claimants amounted to $329,734.16, and those to British claimants $277,102.88.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: A treaty of July 1, 1863 between the United States and Great Britain provided for settlement of claims of the Hudson's Bay Co. and the Puget's Sound Agricultural Co. The companies, which had extensive holdings in the Oregon Territory, maintained that U.S. authorities had failed to protect their property rights and priveleges. A three-member commission was established to determine rights and claims of the companies and to transfer them to the U.S. Government for money. Alexander S. Johnson was appointed U.S. commissioner. John Rose served as commissioner for Great Britain. Benjamin R. Curtis was selected as umpire. Caleb Cushing srved as counsel for the United States and Charles Dewey Day for Great Britain. The clerks were George Gibbs for the United States and William Finlay Gairdiner for Great Britain. The commissioners held their first meeting in washington, D.C., on January 7, 1865. The final award, September 10, 1869, gave $450,000 to the Hudson's Bay Co. and $200,000 to the Puget's Sound Agricultural Co.

A special agreement of August 18, 1910, between the United States and Great Britain provided for settlement of claims of U.S. citizens against Great Britain and of British subjects against the United States. The U.S. arbitrator was Chandler P. Anderson, succeeded by Robert E. Olds and Roscoe Pound. Charles Fitzpatrick and E. A. Mitchell-Inness served as arbitrators for Great Britain. Henri Fromageot, succeeded by Alfred Nerinex, was chosen as president of the claims tribunal. The agent and counsel for the United states was Severo Mallet-Prevost, succeeded by Robert Lansing and Fred K. Nielsen. Cecil J.B. Hurst served as British agent and counsel.

The first meeting was held at Washington, D.C., on May 13, 1913. The second session was held in Ottawa, and the final one in Washington, D.C., from March 9 to May 1, 1914. The work was then suspended because of World War I. After the War, the tribunal met briefly in Paris and Washington before resuming work in London on October 15, 1923. It disposed of 75 cases after reconvening in London. Of these, 40 were British claims against the United States and 35 were U.S. claims against Great Britain. the final meeting was held on January 22, 1926.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Industrial Division of the U.S. Element, Military Security Board, was established as an agency of HICOG on September 21, 1949, pursuant to Staff Announcements No. 1 and 7, HICOG, September 21, 1949. The Division was responsible for ensuring that that was no manufacture, import, transport, or possession of any arms, war materials, or any other materials or equipment which was prohibited by tripartite agreements. The Division ensured that any retained military buildings and structures converted to industrial use, and all shipyards or factories capable of producing armaments would not be so used as to constitute a security threat. The Division also ensured that any construction or acquisition of merchant shipping would not add to Germany's war potential or violate any tripartite agreement.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Prisons Division was established within the Office of General Counsel on September 29, 1949, succeeding the Prisons Branch of the Legal Division, Office of Military Government for Germany (U.S.). The Division was responsible for the care and treatment of persons sentenced or held in German prisons by U.S. occupation courts. It also processed expulsions and extraditions from Germany and supervised the repatriation of eligible imprisoned displaced persons. The Division provided technical and educational assistance to German authorities responsible for corrections. The Division advised the U.S. High Commissioner on matters relating to convicted war criminals held at Spandau and Landsberg. The Division was abolished on May 5, 1955.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The U.S. Element of the Military Security Board was established as a HICOG organization on September 21, 1949. It was a direct successor of the U.S. Element, Military Security Board which had been functioning under the aegis of the Office of Military Government for Germany (U.S.) (OMGUS) since March 4, 1949. The participants in the London Conference in February 1948 had agreed that the three military governors of the western zones of Germany should set up a Military Security Board to insure that Germany did not rearm or rebuild its war potential. More specific terms of reference for the Board were drafted by the three military governors, in TRIB/P(48)17 (Final), January 17, 1949, and the Military Security Board, now formally established, was directed to assumed certain functions of the Allied Control Council, including the completion of legislation and regulatory work relating to military security, and to monitor compliance with and implementation of Allied laws and regulations through regular inspections. The Board was discontinued on May 5, 1955, with the termination of HICOG.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Tripartite Claims Commission, United States, Austria, and Hungary was established by an agreement signed by the United States with Austria and Hungary on November 26, 1924 (44 Stat. 2213). The Commission was authorized to determine the amounts, if any, to be paid by Austria and Hungary is satisfaction of World War I claims of U.S. citizens, as defined in the treaties of peace concluded by the United States with Austria on August 24, 1921, and with Hungary on August 29, 1921.

Under terms of the Tripartite Agreement of 1924, the three Governments agreed to select a single Commissioner to pass on all claims presented for adjudication. Each country also appointed an Agent and a legal staff, together known as an Agency, to prepare oral and written arguments for presentation to the Commssioner. Since the U.S. Agency of the Mixed Claims Commission, United States and Germany, was already handling similar claims against Germany, the Agent of the United States and his staff were given the additional function of serving as the U.S. Agency of the Tripartite Claims Commission.

The three Governments agreed upon the selection of Edwin P. Parker as Commissioner. He was commissioned by the President of the United States in 1925 and served until his death in 1929. The vacancy was not filled until the appointment of Chandler P. Anderson in 1933. The Agent of the United States was Robert W. Bonynge, who served from the time he was commissioned in 1925 until the Commission completed its work in 1934.  Ludwig Kleinwachter served as the Austrian Agent from January 1926 until October 1926 when Ernst Prossinagg succeeded him. The Hungarian Government was represented by John Pelenyi as Agenbt ad interim during the first meeting. He was succeeded in May 1926 by Alexis de Boer, who served on the Commission continuously thereafter. By agreement of the three Governments, Ephraim P. Bowyer of the United States was made Secretary of the Commssion instead of the three joint secretaries contemplated by the Tripartite Agreement; he served throughout the existence of the Commission.

The first meeting of the Commission was held at Washington, D.C., on January 25, 1926. Under the Tripartite Agreement, all claims had to be presented to the Commission within a year of the first meeting. Claims received after January 25, 1927, as well as those which did not fall within the jurisdiction of the Commission or were withdrawn at the request of the claimants, were referred to the Department of State. By January 25, 1927, 1,631 claims had been filed. Since many of the claims were later subdivided and submitted as two or more separate claims, the aggregate number increased to approximately 3,500. Each claim was given a list number by the Agency of the United States. When a claim was received by the Commission, it was assigned a docket number. Another designation, the item number, was apparently assigned to each case at the time the Commissioner judged it. By May 18, 1934, the Commission had completed its work.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The first systematic efforts to limit armaments on an international scale occurred at the Hague Conferences of 1899 and 1907. Although those efforts were unsuccessful, the Allied Powers (with the exception of the United States) after World War I committed themselves to disarmament in the Treaty of Versailles and in the Covenant of the Leagie of Nations. In 1925 the League of Nations set up a preparatory commission to determine what arms should be limited and how this could be accomplished. BY 1931 several points of agreement had been reached and a draft for discussion at the Disarmament Conference drawn up.

The first phase of the Conference for the Reduction and Limitation of Armaments, at which most the nations of the world were represented, was held at Geneva, Switzerland, from February 8 to July 23, 1932, to discuss proposals relating to disarmament, and, if possible, to conclude agreements. Disagreements over the definitions of categories of war materials, which had obstructed the progress of the preparatory commission continued to hinder the conference. Fearful of Germany, France was reluctant to agree to any type of military limitation. Germany made its own threats to rearm and deadlock ensued. No general agreement was reached by the Conference, but 41 of the nations represented adopted a resolution setting forth the general principles that should be achieved and stating conclusions reached by this first phase.

The Conference adjourned from June to October 1933. When it reconvened, Germany, now under the control of Adolf Hitler, withdrew from the Conference (October 14) and the League of Nations. The Conference then adjourned and reconvened only sproradically thereafter. It ceased to meet after May 1, 1937.
