creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Executive Agreement, signed at Berlin on August 10, 1922 (42 Stat. 2200), created the Mixed Claims Commission, the United States and Germany, for the purpose of determining the exact amount to be paid for satisfaction of claims of the United States and its citizens that had arisen against Germany since July 31, 1914. The Mixed Claims Commission consisted of three members, two Commissioners and one Umpire. Each Government appointed a Commissioner, and the two passed upon the cases presented to them.  

In cases of disagreement the Umpire, chosen jointly by the two Governments, rendered the final decision. Because of illness and death, four Umpires were in turn appointed and in each case the Umpire was a United States citizen.  The Umpires and the dates they began their service were as follows: William R. Day (1922); Edwin B. Parker (1923); Roland W. Boyden (1930); and Owen J. Roberts (1932).

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
On March 22, 1929, the Canadian rumrunner I'm Alone, sailing in the Gulf of Mexico, south of the Louisiana coast, was fired on by the U.S. Coast Guard cutter Dexter. The shooting resulted in the sinking of the Canadian ship and the death of one of its crew members. When the dispute that arose could not be settled by diplomatic negotiation, Canada accepted the proposal that it be submitted to arbitration pursuant to article 4 of he convention concluded by the United States and Great Britain on January 23, 1924, against smuggling intoxicating liquors.

Two distinguished jurists were named as commissioners on the tribunal. Representing Canada was Sir Lyman Poore Duff, Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Canada; the American commissioner was Associate Justice Willis Van Devanter of the U.S. Supreme Court. The tribunal held its first session at Washington, D.C., on January 28, 1932, to discuss procedural matters. Other hearings were held at Ottawa, June 28-30,m 1933, and in washington, December 28, 1934 - January 3, 1935. In their joint final report of January 5, 1935, the commissioners upheld the U.S. contention that the vessel and cargo were American-owned and that no compensation should be paid to the owners. The commissioners, however, recommended a payment of $25,000 to the captain and crew.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: On April 9, 1924, a committee, under the direction of Charles G. Dawes, presented a plan to reorganize the German banking system under Allied supervision. German reparations were set at one billion gold marks annually, gradually increasing over five years to over two billion gold marks. In return, Germany would receive a foreign loan of 800 million gold marks to stabilize its economy. At the London Reparations Conference, July 16 - August 16, 1924, the Allied governments adopted the Dawes Plan and the German Government passed the necessary legislation to encat the economic plan. The United States extended $110 million in support of the German loan.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The International Fishery Exhibition, and exhibition of fish and fishery products, was held in Berlin from April to June 1880. The United States was represented by Commissioner Spencer Baird of Washington. The United States Commissioner of Fish and Fisheries and the Treasury Department's Coast and Geodetic Survey had its exhibits, and there were a number of individual American exhibits.  The two Government exhibits and other exhibits in the American section won a number of gold and silver medals and honorable mentions.  The United States Minister to Germany reported to the Secretary of State on June 22, 1880, that the display of the United States was by far the largest and most comprehensive in the exhibition.  Participation of the United States in this exhibition was provided for by an joint resolution of Congress approved February 16, 1880. By this resolution, the sum of $20,000 was appropriated to enable the United States Commissioner of Fish and Fisheries to exhibit at the Berlin exhibition "a fair anf full collection of the different specimens of American food-fishes, casts thereof, models of, and implements, and so forth, used in the prosecution of American fisheries." This sum was expended under the direction of the Secretary of State.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Centennial International Exposition was held from August 1, 1888, to January 31, 1889, at Melbourne, Australia, to celebrate the centenary of the founding of New South Wales. The United States was represented at the exposition by a commissioner, four assistant commissioners, and two honorary assistant commissioners. Offices of the United States commission were maintained for a time in Washington, D.C., and in San Francisco, in order to furnish information concerning the exposition to all interested parties in the United States. In addition to individual exhibits at the fair, there were two State exhibits, one from Michigan and the other from Rhode Island. American exhibitors had 339 exhibits and received 214 awards. Funds for United States participation in this exposition were authorized by a joint resolution of congress approved on February 1, 1888.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The U.S. Legation at Vienna reopened on September 7, 1946, when Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary John G. Erhardt presented his credentials. He was succeeded by Walter J. Donnelly who presented his credentials on October 25, 1950. From October 16, 1950, until July 27, 1955, the U.S. chief of mission also functioned as the U.S. High Commissioner for Austria.

The mission of the U.S. Embassy was to advance the interests of the United States, and to serve and protect U.S. citizens in Austria. The Ambassador was the personal representative of the President of the United States. As the chief advocate of U.S. policy, he or she was supported by personnel from the Department of State and other Washington agencies. The Embassy reported and analyzed developments in Austria of concern to the United States, and advanced a broad range of U.S. policy initiatives. The Embassy promoted United States' economic and commercial interests, and the export of American agricultural and industrial products and services, and otherwise assists American business, workers and investors. The Embassy engaged the government and a broad range of organizations and individuals in Austria to promote shared values. Among others, these includedindividual freedom, human rights and democracy and the rule of law.

In 1951 the Legation was upgraded to Embassy status and Donnelly presented his credentials as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary on November 28, 1951. He was succeeded by Llewellyn E. Thompson, Jr., September 4, 1952; H. Freeman Matthews, September 4, 1957; James W. Riddleberger, December 12, 1962; Douglas MacArthur II, May 24, 1967; John P. Humes, October 29, 1969; Wiley T. Buchanan, Jr., April 2, 1975; Milton A. Wolf, September 5,1977; Philip M. Kaiser, March 25, 1980; Theodore E. Cummings, September 2, 1981; Helene A. von Damm, June 22, 1983; Ronald S. Lauder, May 7, 1986; Henry Anatole Grunwald, January 20, 1988; Roy M. Huffington, September 11, 1990; Swanee Grace Hunt, December 16, 1993; Kathryn Walt Hall, December 11, 1997; and Lyons Brown, Jr., December 19, 2001.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Peace Corps was established as an operating agency in the Department of State by Department of State Delegation of Authority 85-11, effective March 3, 1961, pursuant to E.O. 10924, March 1, 1961. It was recognized legislatively by the Peace Corps Act (75 Stat. 612), approved September 22, 1961. The Peace Corps was reassigned to the newly established ACTION by Reorganization Plan No. 1 of 1971, effective July 1, 1971. It was made autonomous within ACTION by E.O. 12137, May 16, 1979, and was made an independent agency by Title VI of the International Security and Development Corporation Act of 1981 (95 Stat. 1540), February 21, 1982.The Peace Corps administered and coordinated Federal international volunteer and related domestic volunteer programs.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Division of Research and Publication was established by Departmental Order 560, November 1, 1933. It was charged with the editing and compilation of Foreign Relations of the United States, the session laws, Statutes at Large, Executive orders, and proclamations; with the preparation, custody, and distribution of most publications issued by the Department; the supervision of the Library, the work of the editor of the Territorial Papers of the United States, and of all matters relating to printing and binding. On August 28, 1944, by Departmental Order 1284, it was given responsibility for the preparation of the certification of the Secretary of State to the adoption by the States of amendments to the Constitution and the receipt, certification, and transmittal by the Secretary of certificates of ascertainment of electors of the President and Vice President. The Division was abolished effective September 9, 1946, by Transmittal Letter 33 of October 11, 1946.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: After the failure to arrive at any quadripartite agreement and the adjournment of the Council of Foreign Ministers meeting at London in 1947, a tripartite meeting was convoked early in 1948 to deal with the pressing problems of Germany left unresolved. There were preliminary Anglo-American talks starting on February 19, but the conference did not officially begin until February 23. The Benelux countries were invited to join the talks on February 26, and participated in all matters except those that were the responsibility of the occupying powers. The two major issues discussed were the fusion of the French zone with Bizonia and the establishment of a democratic federal system for the political reorganization of Western Germany. The sessions recessed from March 6 to April 20, while working parties prepared reports and recommendations on these issues. Since there was no conference secretariat, each national delegation accumulated and maintained its own documents, with the British delegation acting as clearinghouse..

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The American and Mexican Joint Commission was established in 1916 to help put an end to depradations on American life and property in Mexico and to arrange compensation for past depradations, the withdrawal of U.S. troops from Mexico, and the pacification of the border between the two countries.

The Government of Mexico designated Luis Cabrera, Ignacio Conillas, and Alberto J. Pani is its Commissioners and notified the Department of State of their appointment on August 4, 1916. The President of the United States appointed Franklin K. Lane, George Gray, and John R. Mott as Commissioners.

The Joint Commission held its first meeting on September 4, 1916, in New York City, and held subsequent meetings in New London, Connecticut; Atlantic City, New Jersey; and again in New York. The Department of State submitted a mass of documentary evidcence to the Commission regarding the disturbance in Mexico. The Mexican Commissioners insisted upon reaching an agreement on the withdrawal of U.S. troops from Mexico and on safeguarding the border before proceeding to the consideration of any other questions. Such a procedure was unacceptable to the U.S. Commissioners, as were the counterproposals of the Mexicans. At the last meeting on January 15, 1917, proposals were advanced for issuing a joint statement on the work and recommendations of the Commission. The Commission adjourned without reaching an agreement or issuing any statement.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
Military Government Detachment E2C2 listed a legal section among its functional offices in August 1945. By June 1946 legal functions had been consolidated in the Legal Branch of the Internal Affairs Division. By November 1946 the Legal Branch had been elevated to full divisional status, which it retained until 1948. The major functions of the Legal Division were the reformation of the German legal system and the trial of offenses committed against military government authority through a series of military government summary, intermediate, and general courts.

The Legal Division was dissolved in November 1948 and replaced by a Legal Adviser in the Public Affairs and Legal Division. This situation was reversed in June 1949 when the Public Affairs and Legal Division was dissolved and the Legal Division reestablished; the latter retained its organization and functions until the end of the Office of Military Government for Germany (U.S) (OMGUS) period. The function of the office in later years was to furnish advice regarding German and international law, as well as assist in furnishing legal advice on the production of military government proclamations and ordinances. The Legal Adviser's office also observed the German legal system to prevent procedures contrary to military policy or regulations.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Council of Foreign Ministers, in Moscow on April 24, 1947, established an Austrian treaty Commission. Composed of representatives from the Soviet Union, the United States, the United Kingdom, and France, the Commission was charged with the responsibility for examining all questions concerning the Austrian Treaty which the Council could not resolve. The Commission met from May 12th to October 11, 1947. It held a total of 85 meetings, in the course of which it considered the question of German assets, Austrian frontiers, a new Austrian government, and economic problems of the Austrian state.  It also undertook the examination of concrete claims cases.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Requirements and Supply Branch, established in October 1943, presented consolidated foreign and lend lease requirements to the War Production Board or the Combined Petroleum Board for the purpose of obtaining allocations; processed applications to export and applications for the development of such special projects abroad as mines, mills, plants, and factories; assisted the Bureau of Supplies' Trade Relations Staff in advising the Administrator on foreign trade; and represented the Bureau on requirements committees of the War Production Board. The Branch had commodity divisions for metals and minerals, machinery, health supplies and chemicals, and petroleum. Its Operations Division, which inherited functions of the Office of the Administrator of Export Control and its successors in the Economic Defense Board and the Board of Economic Warfare, maintained liaison with the lend lease missions of foreign governments; exercised requisitioning powers with respect to essential commodities not used to the maximum in war production; investigated cases of violations of export regulations; screened applications for export licenses to determine the commercial and political reliability of the consignee; and maintained an information service for exporters in Washington and New York.

This office was created as the Division of Customs and Insular Affairs in the Office of the Secretary of War on December 13, 1898, as a result of the acquisition by the United States of a colonial empire following the war with Spain. On December 10, 1900, by order of the Secretary of War, its name was changed to the Bureau of Insular Affairs. The Bureau was responsible for the supervision and liaison with civil governments in Cuba, 1898 - 1902 and 1906 - 1909; Puerto Rico, 1898 - 1900 and 1909 - 1934; and the Philippine Islands, 1898 - 1939; and supervision of the Dominican Customs Receivership, 1905 - 1939, and the Haitian Customs Receivership, 1920 - 1924. During the period of neutrality, 1914 - 1917, the Bureau was concerned with diplomatic problems arising out of belligerent shipping through the ports of Manila, San Juan, and other Philippine and Puerto Rican ports; it also received and transmitted to the Board of Relief or otherwise acted upon numerous applications for the relief of destitute Americans and Filipinos stranded in Europe. Following the entrance of the United States into the war, the Bureau had extensive relations with the War Trade Board, the War Industries Board, and Alien Property Custodian, and the War Finance Corporation on matters affecting the Philippine Islands and Puerto Rico and it supervised the registration of aliens on these islands. Its functions were transferred to the newly created Territories and Island Possessions Division, Department of the Interior, effective July 1, 1939, by Reorganization Plan No. 2.

Chiefs of the Bureau were Brigadier General Clarence R. Edwards, February 12, 1900 - August 23, 1912; Brigadier General Frank McIntyre, August 24, 1912 - January 5, 1929; Brigadier General Charles S. Walcutt (acting), July 17, 1918 - July 1, 1920; Brigadier General Francis LeJau Parker, Janury 6, 1929 - January 8, 1933; Brigadier General Creed F. Cox, January 9, 1933 - May 23, 1937; and Brigadier General Charles S. Burnett, May 24, 1937 - June 30, 1939.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: n 1946 the Department established the Division of Public Studies within the Office of Public Affairs to study public attitudes towards important phases of foreign relations and to foster public understanding of foreign policy questions.  The Division was initially headed by Samuel Shepard Jones.  H. Schuyler Foster became its chief in 1951.  The Division of Public Studies was renamed the Public Opinion Studies Staff late in 1959. The staff analyzed comments from the press, radio, and magazines; statements by outstanding public leaders; views of organizations; various public opinion surveys; and correspondence received by the President and the Secretary of State regarding foreign affairs. This data was circulated within the Department in the form of periodical and special analytical summaries and reports. The staff prepared reports concering European, African, Asian, and Latin American regional issues as well as international topics including the United Nations, foreign aid, and disarmament until budget cuts and reorganizations reduced the staff from 23 in 1953 to one full-time person (Foster)in 1965. After 1965, Foster wrote only weekly analytical reports of opinion on Vietnam and a few other special reports.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Advisory Commission on International Educational and Cultural Affairs was established to replace the Advisory Commission on Educational Exchange in accordance with the provisions of the Mutual Educational and Cultural Exchange Act of 1961 (75 Stat. 527-38)(the Fulbrights-Hays Act).  It was a Presidential adviosry commission that advised the Bureau of Educational and Cultural Affairs, Department State. The Commission was to formulate and recommend to the President policies for exercising his authority under the Act, and to appraise the effectiveness of programs carried out pursuant to it.  The Commission held 93 meetings over the years 1962-1978, as well as several joint meetings with other educational and cultural bodies. Leonard Marks, of the law firm Cohn and Marks, chaired the Commission. The Commission was consolidated into the USICA by Reorganization Plan No. 2 of 1977, which also provided for the merger of the COmmission and the U.S. Advisory Commission on Information into the U.S. Advisory Commission on Public Diplomacy, which may be considered its successor organization.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The U.S. Embassy in Cyprus was established at Nicosia on August 16, 1960, with L. Douglas Heck as Charge d'Affaires ad interim. The first Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary, Fraser Wilkins, presented his credentials on September 19, 1960.

Ambassador Wilkins was succeeded by Taylor G. Belcher, May 11, 1964; David H. Popper, July 18, 1969; Robert J. McCloskey, June 20, 1973; and Rodger P. Davies, July 10, 1974. On August 19, 1974, Ambassador Davies and his administrative section assistant Antoinette Varnava were shot and killed by EOKA-B snipers during a Greek Cypriot demonstration outside the US Embassy in Nicosia.  He was succeeded by William R. Crawford, Jr., August 31, 1974; Galen L. Stone, April 6, 1978; Raymond C. Ewing, October 30, 1981; Richard Wood Boehm, August 28, 1984; Bill K. Perrin, May 3, 1988. Ambassador Perrin departed Nicosia on July 21, 1989, and the Charge d'Affaires became chiefs of mission. They included John U. Nix, July 1989 - July 1990, and Carolyn Huggins, July - November 1990. Robert E. Lamb was appointed the next Ambassador, presenting his credentials on November 30, 1990. He was succeeded by Richard A. Boucher, November 22, 1993; Kenneth C. Brill,  July 11, 1996; Donald Keith Bandler, August 23, 1999; and Michael Klosson, August 29, 2002.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Special Mexican Claims Commission was a domestic claims commission established by an act of Congress of April 10, 1935 (49 Stat. 149). It was assigned the function of reviewing, appraisng, and deciding the claims of U.S. citizens that were filed with the former Special Claims Commission created under the claims convention of September 10, 1923, and was given three years in which to complete its assigned tasks.

The Commission consisted of three members appointed by the President: Edgar E. Witt, chairman, who assumed office on August 23, 1935, James H. Sinclair and Darrel T. Lane. The Commission completed its work on May 31, 1938. It considered and decided on a total of 2,833 claims, of which 1,358 were allowed wholly or in part and 1,475 were disallowed. The total amount of the initial awards was $9,135,041.79, but, as this amount was greater than Mexico had agreed to pay the United States in satisfaction of the claims, the U.S. Government paid its citizens 57 percent of the initial award figure. On thids basis the total amount actually awarded was $5,206,973.86.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: United States Electoral Missions were sent to Nicaragua in 1928, 1930, and 1932, in accordance with an agreement between the Presidents of  Nicaragua and the United States, to supervise the elections and ensure  their being held in a free and impartial manner under the Nicaraguan Constitution. The first of these Electoral Missions was sent to Nicaragua in 1928, under the direction of Gen. Frank R. McCoy.  By action of the Supreme Court of Nicaragua, General McCoy was appointed Chairman of the National Board of Elections, which was composed of Nicaraguan and United States members. Under the National Board were 13 departmental boards and a number of precinct boards, each of which had Nicaraguan members from both liberal and conservative parties and a United States chairman. The United States Electoral Mission supplied the personnel necessary to supervise the elections, execute the acts of the National Board of Elections, advise on matters of policy, inspect the electoral machinery and personnel, and coordinate that personnel with the participating United States Marine forces and the Nicaraguan Guardia Nacional, the national constabulary. Officers and men for the Mission were selected from the United States armed forces.  The work of the Mission ended when the election results were certified by the National Board of Elections to the Nicaraguan Congress. In the elections of 1930 and 1932, similar Missions were established, and the electoral machinery was much the same

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Sino-Japanese dispute between China and Japan, two members of the League of Nations, arose from the aggression by Japan against the territorial and administrative integrity and political independence of China.  This aggression was in violation of the provisions of the Covenant of the League of Nations.  A League resolution of December 10, 1930, provided for a commission of five members to "study on the spot and to report to the Council on any circumstances which, affecting international relations, threatens to disturb peace between China and Japan, or the good understanding between them upon which peace depends."  The commission that was formed became known as the Lytton Commission from the title of its chairman, the Earl of Lytton.  The other members were nationals of Italy, France, Germany, and the United States.  The report of the Lytton Commission, on which Major General Frank McCoy served as the American representative, was an outspoken condemnation of Japan's action.

The International Technical Commission of Aerial Legal Experts, frequently known by the initials C.I.T.E.J.A. (an abbreviation of its French designation, Comite International Technique d'Experts Juridiques Aeriens), was established by a resolution adopted at the First International Conference on Private Air Law, held at Paris, October 27,1925.  First meeting in May 1926 and annually thereafter, the Commission's purpose was to establish a program for the study of private aerial law, prepare texts of international conventions, and elaborate a single international code for aerial law.

The United States sent only unofficial observers to the First Conference at Paris and to the Second Conference, held in Warsaw, October-November 1929.  Other conferences were held in 1933 and 1939. Starting in 1932, the United States sent official representatives to the Commission.  Clarence M. Young, Assistant Secretary of Commerce, and John C. Cooper, Jr., member of the Aeronautical Committee of the American Bar Association, were the first U.S. members.  Stephen Latchford, chief of the Aviation Section, Division of International Communications, served as the head of the U.S. delegation for most of its existence.

The permanent headquarters of the Commission Secretariat were in Paris.  During the Second World War, the Commission continued limited operations supported by the French government.  After the war, the Committee on International Air Law of the newly-created International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) absorbed most of the functions and expertise of the Commission, and rendered it superfluous.  It was liquidated in January 1948, after a brief surge of post war activity.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The formation of the Joint Economic Committees was announced by the United States and Canada on June 17, 1941.  They were to explore the possibilities for greater economic cooperation between Canada and the United States.  The Committee of each country was to study and report to its government on the possible methods of effecting a more economical, more efficient, and better coordinated utilization of the combined resources of the two countries in producing defense requirements; and on plans to reduce postwar economic dislocation.

The Committees maintained close liaison with various joint boards of the United States and Canada and functioned mainly as advisory bodies. They were concerned with a broader range of general economic problems than were any of the joint boards.  They investigated and reported on such joint problems as the use of freight cars, shipping on the Great Lakes, tariff problems, price control, production priorities and allocations, paper shortage, labor problems, Atlantic fisheries, agricultural collaboration, and cooperation in the Pacific Northwest.  The United States Committee was assisted in its research and planning work by the National Resources Planning Board.  In connection with its investigations, the Committee prepared recommendations or resolutions on such matters as export control, shipping coordination, defense production, gold problems, and agricultural collaboration.

On May 14, 1944, the two governments announced their agreement to dissolve the Committees, since the establishment of other agencies rendered further operation unnecessary. The records were maintained by the secretary of the United States Committee. Members of the U.S. Committee were William L. Batt, Harry D. White, Alvin H. Hansen, and Dana Durand.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Emergency Advisory Committee for Political Defense was established at the Conference of Foreign Ministers in Rio de Janeiro, January 1942.  Its inaugural session was held on April 15, 1942.  President of the Committee throughout its existence was Dr. Don Alberto Guani, ex-president of the General Assembly of the League of Nations and previously the Minister of Foreign Affairs and Vice-President of Uruguay.  Members of the Committee included representatives from most Latin American countries. The main function of the committee was to assist member-nations in providing for defense against subversion by Axis agents.  To accomplish this objective, Committee representatives made consultative visits to individual countries, studied and reviewed internal security policies and procedures with officials of the host country, and prepared reports for both the Committee and the host country.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, concluded on February 2, 1848, defined the boundary line between the United States and Mexico and provided for the establishment of a commission to survey and mark the line. The Commission was to begin operations within a year of the exchange of ratifications. The ratified treaties were exchanged on May 30, 1848. Each contracting power as stipulated in the treaty was to appoint a commissioner and a surveyor. John B. Weller was appointed U.S. Commissioner on January 16, 1849; and Andrew B. Gray was appointed surveyor on January 10, 1849. John C. Fremont became U.S. Commissioner to replace Weller; he was replaced by John R. Bartlett on June 15, 1850, when Fremont was elected to the U.S. Senate. The responsibility for supervising the U.S. Section was transferred from the Department of State to the Department of the Interior in JUly 1849.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Bureau of Special Services, established by OWI Staff Order 15, dated march 9, 1943, consisted of divisions of the earlier Bureau of Intelligence of the Office of Facts and Figures, the Bureau of Public Inquiries, and the Bureau of Publications and Graphics.The Bureau of Special Services was a reference and fact-gathering unit for Federal agencies, members of Congress, the White House, and the public. Its services included clipping of items from daily newspapers on specific fields of interest, making weekly and daily reports on press and radio comment, conducting public-opinion surveys to determine the public's response to war programs, and providing research and reference service for operating and policy officials of the Office of War Information. When OWI was terminated in September 1945, this Bureau and its records were transferred to the Bureau of the Budget, where it became the U.S. Information Service of the reestablished Office of Government Reports.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (typically abbreviated GATT) was originally created by the Bretton Woods Conference as part of a larger plan for economic recovery after World War II. The GATT's main purpose was to reduce barriers to international trade. This was achieved through the reduction of tariff barriers, quantitative restrictions and subsidies on trade through a series of different agreements. The GATT was an agreement, not an organization. Originally, the GATT was supposed to become a full international organization like the World Bank or International Monetary Fund (MF). However, the agreement was not ratified, so the GATT remained simply an agreement. The functions of the GATT have been replaced by the World Trade Organization  (WTO) which was established through the final round of negotiations in the early 1990s.

The history of the GATT can be divided into three phases: the first, from 1947 until the Torquay round, largely concerned which commodities would be covered by the agreement and freezing existing tariff levels. A second phase, encompassing three rounds, from 1959 to 1979, focused on reducing tariffs. The third phase, consisting only of the Uruguay Round from 1986 to 1994, extended the agreement fully to new areas such as intellectual property,  services, capital, and agriculture. Out of this round the WTO was born.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Colombo Plan was a regional organization that embodies the concept of collective inter-governmental effort to strengthen economic and social development of member countries in the Asia-Pacific Region. The primary focus of all Colombo Plan activities was on human resources development. The Colombo Plan was not a ¿plan¿ in the economic sense. 

The organization grew out of a Commonwealth Conference of Foreign Ministers, held in Colombo, Sri Lanka (then Ceylon), in January 1950. At this meeting, a Consultative Committee was established to provide a framework within which international cooperation efforts could be promoted to raise the living standards of people in the region. Originally conceived as lasting for a period of six years, the Colombo Plan was extended several times until 1980, when it was extended indefinitely. The "Plan" was not meant to be an integrated master plan to which national plans were expected to conform. It was, instead, a framework for bi-lateral arrangements involving foreign aid and technical assistance for the economic and social development of the region. The principal organs of the Colombo Plan were - the Consultative Committee, the Council and the Secretariat. Administrative costs of the Council and Secretariat are borne equally by the 25 member countries.

Members of the Colombo Plan were Afghanistan, Australia, Bangladesh, Bhutan, Burma (Myanmar) the Fiji Islands, India, Indonesia, Iran, Japan, the Republic of Korea, Laos, Malaysia, The Maldives, Mongolia, Nepal, New Zealand, New_Zealand, Pakistan, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines, Singapore, Sri Lanka, Thailand, the United States, and Vietnam. Britain and Canada withdrew from the Colombo Plan in 1991. Vietnam joined in 1951, withdrew from its membership in 1978 and re-joined again in 2001. Cambodia withdrew from the Colombo Plan in 2004.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
An act of the United States Congress of December 21, 1895 (29 Stat. 1), established a Commission "to investigate and report upon the true divisional line between the Republic of Venezuela and British Guiana." The creation of the Commission was a voluntary movement on the part of the United States. Although the boundary line--whose actual location the Commission set out to ascertain--was of great importance to both  Venezuela and Great Britain, neither of the countries involved was consulted or took part in the creation of the Commission or in the selection of the Commissioners.

Since 1840 the line between Venezuela and British Guiana had been in dispute. Venezuela had proposed arbitration but Great Britain had refused, and diplomatic relations between the two countries had been severed. The United States had also proposed arbitration in vain. In 1895 the United States, in accordance with the Monroe Doctrine, made a firm recommendation to the British that they arbitrate.

In a special message to Congress on December 17, 1895, President Cleveland had proposed that Congress authorize him to appoint a commission to determine where the boundary ought to be and, when the commission had reported, to assume the responsibility for enforcing its decision. The Commissioners,  appointed on  January 4, 1896 under the 1895 act were:  David J. Brewer, President; Richard H. Alvey; Frederic R. Coudert; Andrew D. White; and Daniel C. Gilman.  Severo Mallet-Prevost served as secretary and Perry Allen, as assistant secretary.

The work of the Commission was mainly that of compiling maps, documents, reports, and other information that would be of value to an arbitral tribunal and of use in determining the boundary. Neither the United States nor Great Britain wanted war to develop over the dispute.  Accordingly a court of arbitration was provided for by a treaty of February 2, 1897, between Great Britain and Venezuela.  It consisted of two Justices of the United States Supreme Court, Davis J. Brewer and Melville Weston Fuller; two Englishmen, F. de Martens, who acted as President of the tribunal, and Richard Henn Collins; and a Russian jurist selected by the other four, Baron Herschell. The tribunal met at Paris and a decision was finally rendered in October 1899.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The International Whaling Commission (IWC) was set up under the International Convention for the Regulation of Whaling which was signed in Washington,  D.C. on December 2, 1946.  The purpose of the Convention was to provide for the proper conservation of whale stocks and thus make possible the orderly development of the whaling industry. The main duty of the IWC was to keep under review and revise as necessary the measures laid down in the Schedule to the Convention which govern the conduct of whaling throughout the world. These measures, among other things, provided for the complete protection of certain species; designated specified areas as whale sanctuaries; set limits on the numbers and size of whales which could be taken; prescribed open and closed seasons and areas for whaling; and prohibited the capture of suckling calves and female whales accompanied by calves. The compilation of catch reports and other statistical and biological records were also required. In addition, the Commission encouraged, co-ordinated and funded whale research, published the results of scientific research,  and promoted studies into related matters such as the humaneness of the killing operations.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: At the Third Session of the Council of Foreign Ministers (CFM) in New York, December 1946, it was decided to hold a subsequent meeting in Moscow in March 1947 for the consideration of German and Austrian problems. Pursuant to this meeting, the Ministers appointed Deputies for Germany and Austria. The Deputies for Germany were Robert D. Murphy for the United States, Sir William Strang for Great Britain, Fedor Tarasovich Gusev for the Soviet Union, and Maurice Couve de Murville for France. Murphy was assisted by a U.S. Delegation which included Donald Heath, David Harris, Jacques Reinstein, Howard Trivers, and Carmel Offie. On January 14, 1947, the CFM Deputies convened at Lancaster House in London. This meeting was the only joint meeting of the Deputies for Austria and Germany. Subsequent meetings of the two bodies were held separately. The Deputies invited the views of all the Allies on the settlement of German problems. After gathering testimony, the Deputies submitted proposals to the Council of Foreign Ministers for the peace treaties with Germany and Austria.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: A meeting of the foreign ministers of the United States, Great Britain, and France was held in Paris to discuss problems of common interest.  The existence of the Federal Republic of Germany (FRG), the Organization of  European Economic Cooperation, and the Council of Europe were the main  topics of concern.  The foreign ministers agreed on the accession of the FRG to the International Authority of the Ruhr and on obtaining the cooperation of the German government in matters of common European concern. The Allied High Commissioners were charged with securing FRG action in  such matters.  It was also agreed to discourage the de facto or de jure  recognition of the German Democratic Republic, set up by the Soviets in  East Germany.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: Created at the First Meeting of the Ministers of Foreign Affairs of the American Republics, Panama, 1939, the Inter-American Financial and Economic Advisory Committee (IAFEAC) promoted closer commercial, financial, and economic relations among the republics of the Western Hemisphere throughout the war years.  It recommended the establishment of an Inter-American Bank and an Inter-American Development Commission and pushed collective economic defense measures and inter-American cooperation in the war effort.  In 1942 a Subcommittee on Post-War Problems was created to help plan the transition from a wartime to a peacetime economy in the hemisphere.  Chaired by Harry C. Hawkins of the Office of Economic Affairs of the Department of State, the subcommittee made recommendations to the IAFEAC concerning tariff policies, commodity agreements, economic development, and general trade problems anticipated at the end of the war.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: On August 31, 1945, President Truman wrote British Prime Minister Attlee calling his attention to the plight of the surviving Jewish victims of Nazi and Fascist persecution and urging his consideration of their admission to Palestine.  In reply, the British Government invited the United States to join in the creation of a joint committee of inquiry to examine the situation.  The United States accepted the British suggestion and on December 10, 1945, the membership of the Anglo-American Committee of Inquiry (AACI) was announced.  Composed of six British and six American members, the AACI was charged with gathering information and making recommendations on 1) the effect of Jewish immigration and resettlement on the political, economic, and social conditions of Palestine 2) the position of surviving Jews in Europe and the possibility of relieving the problem by repatriation or resettlement in Palestine and other non-European countries. The Committee conducted investigations in Europe, consulted official and private agencies and individuals, and held hearings in Washington, London, Cairo, and Jerusalem.  On April 20, 1946, the AACI submitted its unanimous report which was made public by the two governments on May 1, 1946.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Administration of Justice Division was established within the Office of General Counsel on September 21, 1949. The Division observed and reviewed all actions by German authorities relating to the administration of justice which were subject to oversight by the Allied High Commission. It observed the operation of the U.S. Courts for Germany and prepared recommendations to the U.S. High Commissioner on matters relating to the administration of justice. The Division considered all applications for clemencyor mitigation of sentences in major war crimes cases and in cases tried by U.S. Courts for Germany or U.S. Military Government Courts subsequent to the enactment of Military Government Ordinance No. 31, and made recommendations to the U.S. High Commissioner. The Division initiated extradition policies, procedures, and processes, and monitored extradition requests involving war crimes; recommended appropriate actions on the extradition of war criminals; and furnished representation on the Extradition Board which processed requests for extradition involving cases other than war crimes. The Administration of Justice Division was abolished on September 19, 1951, pursuant to HICOG Staff Announcement No. 217. Most of its functions were transferred to the newly established Legal Services Division.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: In 1918 a conference was held at Washington under the auspices of the Department of State at which an attempt was made to arrive at a peaceful solution to the dispute between Honduras and Guatemala regarding their boundary. In 1917 a dispute had developed between the two countries when Guatemala sent troops into the area along the Motagua River to halt construction of a railroad by the Cuyamel Fruit Co. This company had a concession to build from the Government of Honduras, but the area was one to which ownership was contested. Guatemala had previously granted a concession in the area to two other foreign countries. At the request of Honduras, the United States exercised its good offices to prevent an armed conflict, and both sides expressed a willingness to accept U.S. mediation. At the Conference both sides presented formal statements of their claims, and an economic survey of the area was made by a representative of the National Geographic Society. Neither party, however, would accept the solution that was offered and the proceedings were suspended.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Commission of Inquiry and Conciliation was set up under a protocol signed on January 3, 1929, by the Bolivian and Paraguayan diplomatic representatives to Washington. The protocol had been initiated by the International Conference of American States on Conciliation and Arbitration that met at Washington in December 1928. The Commission was to investigate the controversy between the Republics of Bolivia and Paraguay resulting from armed conflict at Vanguardia between troops of the two countries. Ownership of the territory which included Vanguardia had long been disputed by Bolivia and Paraguay, and previous arbitrations and treaties had failed to resolve the problem.

The five neutral Commissioners designated by the Governments of the United States, Mexico, Colombia, Uruguay, and Cuba were: Brig. Gen. Frank Ross McCoy, United States; Dr. Fernando Gonzales Roa, Mexico; Dr. Raimundo Rivas, Colombia; Gen. Guillermo Ruprecht, Uruguay; and Dr. Manuel Marquez Sterling, Cuba. Dr. David Alvesteugi and Sr. Enrique Finot represented Bolivia, and Dr. Enrique Bordenave and Dr. Francisco C. Chaves represented Paraguay.

The Commission was successful in arranging for a truce following the fighting at Vanguardia, and it undertook a study of the Chaco region with the assistance of geographers and economists. A report of the Chairman was submitted on September 21, 1929.

Both Bolivia and Paraguay accepted the Commission's proposals and, following the work of the Commission, negotiations were begun by these countries in an effort to finally settle the problem.

The Reciprocity Treaty of 1854 between the United States and Great Britain was terminated in 1866, and the disputes regarding fisheries began anew. By the terms of the Treaty of Washington of 1871 between the United States and Great Britain a commission was created to settle the dispute.

Commissioners appointed under the treaty were: Ensign H. Kellogg for the United States; Alexander T. Galt for Great Britain; and Maurice Delfossee, named by the Austrian Ambassador to Great Britain. The first conference was held on June 15, 1877, at Halifax, and the cases for both sides were concluded at the 77th meeting on November 21, 1877, in conformance with the stipulation that cases be closed within a period of 6 months from the date of organization of the Commission. The award of the Commission, made on November 23, 1877, provided that $5 1/2 million in gold be paid by the United States to Great Britain.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
A treaty of February 8, 1896, between the United States and Great Britain provided for the Bering Sea Claims Commission, ratification for which were exchanged on June 3, 1896. The British claims against the United States concerned the jurisdictional rights of the United States in the Bering Sea and the seizure of British ships by the United States for action that the United States claimed was a violation by the British in the territorial waters of the United States.

A Tribunal of Arbitration of 1893 had decided in favor of Great Britain concerning its claims against the United States for the seizure of vessels. It was the function of the Bering Sea Claims Commission, created by the treaty of 1896, to decide the amount of compensation to which the claimants were entitled.

The Commission met at Victoria, British Columbia, and at San Francisco, Calif., during 1896 and 1897. The Commissioners--Secretary of State Richard Olney and the British Ambassador to the United States, Julian Pauncefote--were appointed by their respective heads of state. In case the Commissioners failed to agree, an umpire was to be appointed by the President of the Swiss Confederation to settle the difference. The award to Great Britain was to be paid by the United States 6 months after it had been finally ascertained.

On December 17, 1897, the Commissioners rendered an award of $473,151.26 against the United States.

On February 22, 1988, National Security Decision Directive 301 (NSDD-301) officially established the U.S. Nuclear Risk Reduction Center (NRRC) within the Department of State. NSDD-301 laid the groundwork for the activities of the NRRC, including Presidential approval of future notifications regimes, the use of pre-formatted notifications and the type of communications equipment to be used. The proper location for the new NRRC was debated for months, but it was finally decided that the NRRC’s role in government-to-government communication was the duty of the Department of State. The Centers’ chief purpose was to reduce the risk of nuclear war by providing direct high-speed transmission of information and notifications required by various agreements. On March 22, 1988, the NRRC was opened and exchanged the first message with the Soviet Union’s NRRC. 

The U.S. concept of Nuclear Risk Reduction came from a Congressional working group sponsored by Senators John Warner (Republican-Virginia) and Sam Nunn (Democrat-Georgia) in the mid-eighties. During the height of the Cold War, they looked at the creation of NRRCs to lessen U.S.-Soviet tensions. President Reagan and General Secretary Gorbachev first discussed this concept of Nuclear Risk Reduction during their November 1985 Geneva Summit. The Nunn-Warner Working Group proposal was further refined during meetings held in late 1985 and 1986 between the U.S. and U.S.S.R. The U.S. NRRC and its Soviet counterpart were formally recognized in a NRRC Agreement signed in Washington, DC by then Secretary of State George Shultz and Foreign Minister Eduard Shevardnadze on September 15, 1987. The NRRC Agreement called for the exchange of Ballistic Missile Launch and Goodwill notifications, as well as those for future agreements. Less than three months later, in December 1987, the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces (INF) Treaty was signed by President Reagan and General Secretary Gorbachev. Subsequently, the NRRC was tasked to exchange INF messages related to inspections, eliminations and conversion activities, and a related database. 

The NRRC began formal operations on April 1, 1988, as the direct government-to-government communications link (GGCL) with its Soviet Union counterpart, located in Moscow in the Ministry of Defense, to support arms control and security agreements. The first treaty notification was transmitted to the Soviet Union’s NRRC five days later and consisted of ballistic missile launch information. The first notification from the Soviet Union was received on June 2, 1988. Since then, the Center’s role expanded to include other international communications links, both bilateral and multilateral, dealing with nuclear, chemical, and conventional arms control treaties and security-building agreements with over 55 foreign governments, including the former Soviet Union republics; participating Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe (CSCE) (and later Organization on Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE)) states; and the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW).

The NRRC received, transmitted, translated, prepared, coordinated, and disseminated all incoming and outgoing messages required for the implementation of arms control treaties and security-building agreements to appropriate U.S. Government entities and partner foreign governments, such as inspection and compliance notifications. The agreements included the INF Treaty, the Ballistic Missile Launch Agreement, the Nuclear Testing Treaties, the Confidence- and Security-Building Measures (CSBM) Agreements, the Conventional Armed Forces in Europe (CFE) Treaty, the Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (START) I Treaty, the New START, the Open Skies Treaty (OS), the Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC), the Additional Protocol (AP), the Hague Code of Conduct against Ballistic Missile Proliferation (HCOC), and other security-related agreements.

An Assistant Secretary of State was appointed within the NSDD-301 Presidential guidance to serve as the Director of the U.S. NRRC. Day-to-day management was provided by the Staff Director, equivalent to an office director. The Deputy Staff Director was an active-duty military officer assigned by the Department of Defense to the NRRC and historically was an Air Force officer with strategic nuclear force experience. To service its various communications links, the NRRC watch center was staffed 24 hours a day by Russian-speaking Department of State Foreign Service Officers, Civil Service, and technical support and communication personnel for three 8-hour shifts per day. The Center sent messages in English and received them in Russian, which later expanded to include French, German, Italian, and Spanish. The NRRC watch officers translated the notifications into English before disseminating them to appropriate U.S. agencies in the arms control community via the Department of State's message system, as well as via interagency wide area information networks.

NSDD-301 remained the guiding document for the NRRC until January 2021 with the adoption of National Security Presidential Memorandum 34 (NSPM-34) to govern the operations of the Center. To reflect the evolving scope of the Center’s risk reduction mission to include nuclear arms control, conventional arms transparency, chemical weapons (CW) destruction, ballistic missile and space launch vehicle awareness, and international cyber incidents, the U.S. Nuclear Risk Reduction Center (NRRC) was renamed the U.S. National and Nuclear Risk Reduction Center (NNRRC).

February 8, 2021 The Nuclear Risk Reduction Center (NRRC) has officially been renamed the National and Nuclear Risk Reduction Center (NNRRC) pursuant to National Security Presidential Memorandum-34. This measure acknowledges the increasingly broad and evolving role the Center has assumed since its inception in 1988, when it was established as a secure, rapid, and reliable means of communication with the Soviet Union on a range of arms control issues. While the communications line with Russia remains a fundamental aspect of the NNRRC’s mission, the Center, which is run by the State Department, has adapted to the evolving international security environment) https://2021-2025.state.gov/renaming-of-the-national-and-nuclear-risk-reduction-center/

Department of State, November 17, 2025 (Archived Content. United States Nuclear Risk Reduction Center (NRRC), Bureau of Arms Control, Verification, and Compliance October 24, 2012 The United States Nuclear Risk Reduction Center (NRRC) exchanges information required by arms control treaties and security-building agreements between the United States and over 55 foreign governments. It consists of a 24-hour watch center operating 365 days a year and staffed by Department of State (DOS) Foreign Service Officers, Civil Servants, and technical support personnel. The Center is part of the Bureau of Arms Control, Verification and Compliance (AVC) at the DOS headquarters, located in the Harry S Truman building in Washington, D.C. When the NRRC began operations on April 1, 1988, it launched a single direct government-to-government communications link (GGCL) with its USSR counterpart located at the Ministry of Defense in Moscow. Since then, the U.S. NRRC’s role has expanded to include the operation of additional international communications links, which have allowed the United States to implement 13 different nuclear, chemical, and conventional arms control treaties and security-building agreements. Since its inception, the NRRC’s role has been to contribute to bilateral and multilateral transparency and mutual understanding through timely and accurate information exchanges. The NRRC receives, transmits, translates, prepares, coordinates, and disseminates all incoming and outgoing messages required for the implementation of 13 arms control treaties and agreements to appropriate U.S. Government entities and partner foreign governments. NRRC officers translate incoming notifications from Russian, French, German, Spanish, and Italian, into English.) https://2009-2017.state.gov/t/avc/rls/199564.htm

The U.S. concept of Nuclear Risk Reduction came from a Congressional working group sponsored by Senators John Warner (R-VA) and Sam Nunn (D-GA) in the mid-eighties…February 22, 1988, National Security Decision Directive number 301 (NSDD-301) officially established the U.S. NRRC within the DOS…An Assistant Secretary of State is appointed within the NSDD-301 Presidential guidance to serve as the Director…NRRC's role was significantly expanded when it was tasked by the NSC to operate the U.S. node of the communications network of the OSCE, the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (then known as the CSCE)…Upon entry into force of the Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC) in 1997, the NRRC established a direct dial-up e-mail system for notification exchange between the U.S. and the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW)…NRRC watch officers translate the notifications into English before disseminating them to appropriate U.S. agencies in the arms control community via the State Department's message system, as well as via interagency wide area information networks…To service its various communications links, the NRRC watch center is staffed for three 8-hour shifts per day) https://web.archive.org/web/20071119210020/http://www.state.gov/t/vci/rls/prsrl/30737.htm

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: In April 1944, the Inter-Allied Commission for the Protection and Restitution of Cultural Material (Vaucher Commission) was established under the chairmanship of Prof. Paul Vaucher as a subcommission of the Conference of Allied Ministers of Education. Composed of representatives of the varied Allied governments, the Vaucher Commission had as its purpose the study of problems relating to protection, restitution, and reparations and the collection and organization of information relating to looting for the eventual use of Supreme Headquarters Allied Expeditionary Force (SHAEF) and particularly of its Civil Affairs Section. This was the agency with which the Roberts Commission's representatives abroad were at first chiefly concerned. The secretariat of the Vaucher Commission functioned as a central bureau for information on looted objects supplied by the different national commissions and issued lists of looted objects for the use of Monuments officers until its dissolution in November 1945.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: By a convention signed November 10, 1858, the United States and Chile agreed to submit the U.S. claim regarding the brig Macedonian to arbitration by King Leopold of Belgium. creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
In a convention signed by the United States and Chile on August 7, 1892, a three-man commission was established to settle claims made by citizens of either country against the government of another. The Commission met July 25, 1893. The U.S. commissioner was John Goode, the Chilean commissioner was Domingo Gana, and the third commissioner and chairman was Alfred de Chaparede of Switzerland. George H. Shields was the U.S. agent, and J. Francisco Vergara Donoso was Chile's agent. The Commission adjourned April 9, 1894, without having decided all the claims presented to it.

In a convention signed by the United States and Chile on May 24, 1897, the earlier Commission was revived and empowered to settle claims that had not been acted on. The Commission met June 15, 1900, and adjourned June 18, 1901. The first Commission awarded $240,564.35 to U.S. claimants. The second Commission awarded $28,062.29 in favor of the United States and $3,000 in favor of Chile.

The claims arose from incidents that took place from about 1817 to 1891.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Third Session of the Council of Foreign Ministers met in New York at the Waldorg-Astoria Hotel from November 4 to December 12, 1946. The principal task of this session was the resolution of issues concerning the draft treaties of peace. After consideration of the recommendations made by the Paris Peace Conference in October 1946, the Council completed the texts of the treaties of peace with Italy, Bulgaria, Hungary, Romania, and Finland. Secretary of State James F. Byrnes signed for the United States in Washington, D.C., on January 20, 1947, and the other powers signed in Paris on February 10, 1947. The U.S. Senate approved ratification on June 4, 1947.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: A resolution was adopted at the Eighth International Conference of America States at Lima, Peru, in 1938, which declared that, in case of a threat to the peace of the Americas from abroad, the foreign ministers of the republics, on the initiative of any one of them, would consult. President Franklin D. Roosevelt, after the outbreak of war in Europe, invoked that resolution by requesting a conference to determine measures that should be taken to preserve peace and neutrality in the Americas. The First Meeting of the Ministers of Foreign Affairs of the American republics opened in Panama on September 21, 1939, and completed its work in eight days. At the Conference the United States promoted resolutions designed to advance hemispheric cooperation in a variety of areas. The most important action of the Conference was the adoption of the Declaration of Panama, which decreed a "safety zone" of three hundred miles around the Western Hemisphere. The Conference also adopted a number of resolutions dealing with neutrality, economic cooperation, and cultural relations./

Deason, Chief of the Office of Foreign Activities, Fish and Wildlife Service, Department of the Interior; and Captain Harold C. Moore, Coordinator for Interdepartmental International Affairs, U.S. Coast Guard. Other agency officials were occasionally invited to assist on specific matters.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: On June 11, 1946, President Truman established by executive order the Cabinet Committee on Palestine and Related Problems.  Comprised of the Secretaries of State, War, and Treasury and their delegates, the Committee considered the recommendations of the AACI and determined future actions of the United States regarding Palestine.  Between June 17 and July 26, 1946, the Cabinet Committee joined a British delegation headed by Sir Norman Brooke in London for a series of meetings concerning implementation of the recommendations of the AACI.  The Anglo-American Cabinet Committee issued a joint statement of policy on Palestine on July 26.  The Palestine problem was subsequently submitted to the UN General Assembly, where the recommendations of the AACI and the Anglo-American Cabinet Committee served as a basis for discussion.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The treaty between the United States and France, concluded on April 30, 1803, provided for the cession of Louisiana to the United States but it did not contain a clear description of the boundary line separating Spanish possessions from U.S. territory. The section of the boundary disputed between these nations lay south of the Red River. This controversry was finally settled by the Adams-Onis Treaty of February 22, 1819, which, in article III, defined the boundary line south of the Red River as beginning ". . . on the Gulph of Mexico, at the mouth of the river Sabine, in the sea, continuing north, along the west bank of the river, to the 32nd degree of latitude; thence, by a line due north to the degree of latitude where it strikes the Rio Roxo of Natchitoches, or Red River. . . ."

Although the Adams-Onis Treaty clearly described this section of the boundary line, the United States in 1829 claimed that the Neches River, which flows to the west of the Sabine River, was the Sabine River referred to in the treaty. When Texas declared its independence of Mexico in 1936, the United States continued to claim the Neches River as the boundary line between the United States and the Republic of Texas.

Two years later, on April 25, 1838, the United States concluded a convention with Texas that authorized the establishment of a Commission to  ". . . run and mark that portion of the said boundary which extends from the mouth of the Sabine, where that river enters the Gulph of Mexico, to the Red River."

Judge John H. Overton of Louisiana was appointed the U.S. Commissioner on January 31, 1839. He met with the Acting Texas Commissioner, Peter B. Dexter, at New Orleans on August 7, 1839, to ". . . make out plans  . . ." for the survey. The U.S. surveyor was John B. Conway. When the Commission reconvened near the Sabine River on November 12, 1939, the Texas Commissioner, David Sample, and the Texas surveyor, George W. Smyth, were present. On January 20, 1840, M. Hunt replaced David Sample as the Texas Commissioner. Hunt announced his resignation to the Commission on May 22, 1840; and Smyth, the Texas surveyor, replaced him. Andrew B. Gray assumed the duties of the surveyor for Texas.

By June 1841 the Commission completed its survey. After considering the question of which river was the Sabine River described in the Adams-Onis Treaty of 1819, the Commission agreed that the more easterly river commonly called the Sabine River was the river intended and that the river to the west of the Sabine--the Neches River--that was claimed by the United States was not the river 

intended.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: A convention concluded between the United States and Great Britain on January 27, 1909, provided for submittal of the question of disputed fishing rights to the Hague Tribunal for arbitration. Seven questions relating to the interpretation and intent of article I of the Treaty of 1818 were to be answered by the Tribunal.  Five members of the Permanent Court at the Hague were selected and agreed upon by the United States and Great Britain. They were:  Dr. H. Lammasch, Doctor of Law, University of Vienna; Jonkeer A. F. de Savornin Lohman, Doctor of Law, the Netherlands; George Gray, Judge, U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals; Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, Doctor of Law, Chief Justice of Canada; and Luis M. Drago, Doctor of Law, Argentine Republic. The decision of the Court, given on September 7, 1910, provided for the protection of New England fishermen and sustained the Newfoundland clam to local jurisdiction. The decision was more of a compromise than a decisive award in favor of either country.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
Provisions for the protection of the North Pacific seal herd in the award of the fur seal arbitration of 1893 provided ineffective. By 1910 the herd that had once numbered some 4 million had been reduced by pelagic sealers to about 100,000. At the invitation off the United States Government, representatives of Russia, Japan, and Great Britain met at Washington with the United States representatives to work out an international agreement that would save the seal herd from eventual destruction. The delegates for the United States were Charles Nagel, Secretary of Commerce and Labor, and Chandler P. Anderson, Counselor for the Department of State.  Delegates for Russia were Pierre Botkine, Mr. Brajnikoff, and Baron Nolde; for Japan, Baron Yasuya Uchida and Hitoshi Duake; and for Great Britain, James Bryce and Joseph Pope.

The Conference first met on May 11, 1911, and within 3 months an agreement had been worked out by the representatives. Under the terms of the agreement the signatory powers bound their nationals not to engage in pelagic sealing; and stipulations were also made for the protection of other sea life and certain plumage birds. To compensate for the losses of revenue that would arise from the restrictions of sealing, the agreement provided that the United States would annually pay Japan and Great Britain a percentage of the proceeds from the strictly regulated land kill.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: A protocol of May 24, 1884, signed by the United States and Haiti, provided for arbitration of the claim of Antonio Pelletier and A. H. Lazare against Haiti. Pelletier, suspected by the Haitian Government of being a pirate and a trader of enslaved people, was arrested and imprisoned and had his vessel confiscated in 1861. Lazare's claim arose from a dispute about a contract concerning establishment of a bank in Port-au-Prince.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Scientific Research Division was established as an element of the U.S. Element, Military Security Board, on September 21, 1949, pursuant to Staff Announcements No. 1 and No. 7, HICOG, September 21, 1949. The Division had responsibility for the implementation in the U.S. Zone of the Law on the Control of Scientific Research (Military Government Law No. 23) and the Law on the Control of Patent Applications in Certain Fields of Research and Manufacture (Allied High Government Law No. 17). The Division was also responsible for the implementation of  Allied High Government Laws No. 22 and 24 as they applied to to conduct of scientific research and the administration of educational and medical establishments and museums. It oversaw matters concerning scientific research as it related to the disarmament and demilitarization of Germany. Specifically, the Division ensured that buildings and equipment of former war research laboratories would not be used for purposes may have constituted a security threat, and ensured that scientific research in Germany would not be used for the purposes of war. The Division also monitored the activities of the German Zonal Meteorological Organization and, when necessary, represented HICOG on meteorological matters during multipartite and international negotiations. The Division ceased to exist by 1953.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: On July 29, 1937, the Division of Protocol and Conferences was divided into the Division of Protocol and the Division of International Conferences by by Departmental Orders 704 and 705. The Division of International Conferences was charged with arrangements for international conferences, congresses, expositions, and conventions in which the United States was to participate, at home and abroad, and in cooperation with other branches of the Government and interested persons and organizations, determination of the extent and character of that participation. It had supervision of the fulfillment of the international obligations of the United States with respect to membership in and expenditures for international treaty commissions, committees, bureaus, and other organizations. This Division was charged with general responsibilities and duties in connection with international civil aviation and particularly with activities of the Interdepartmental Committee on Civil International Aviation (the Chief of the division was the Executive Secretary of the committee and kept its records); with the obtaining of permission for American aviator to make flights in foreign countries and for foreign aviators to make flights in the United States. The Division prepared the Department’s annual publication covering these activities.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: On December 1, 1909, the United States and Chile agreed to submit the Alsop claim to the King of England for final settlement. The claim of Alsop & Co., an American firm, arose out of a complicated agreement arranged by Mr. John Wheelwright in 1876 between the firm and the Bolivian Government. According to the agreement, Bolivia granted special concessions to the firm to partially meet its monetary obligations. The War of the Pacific between Chile and Bolivia, 1879-1883, intervened, and the unsatisfied obligations then became the responsibility of Chile. The U.S. claim against Chile on behalf of the company was $2,803,370.36. On July 5, King Edward VII of England made an award of 2,275,375 bolivianos ($906,666.78) in favor of the claimant.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Fifteenth International Congress of Architects was to be held in Washington, D.C., September 24 - 30, 1939, under the auspices of the Government of the United States and the American Institute of Architects. Foreign governments had been invited by the President to send delegates. Architects from every nation were invited to participate in the Congress and to bring forward their special problems for discussion. Attendance at the Congress was to offer opportunity not only to share in the proceedings but also to examine contemporary progress in the United States in architecture, engineering, town planning, and related fields.

However, on September 8, 1939, as a result of the state of war existing in Europe, the Department of State sent circular telegrams to embassies and legations requesting that they inform their respective foreign offices that the Congress had been postponed indefinitely.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Rio de Janeiro Meeting of Foreign Ministers requested that the  Governing Board of the Pan American Union convoke an Inter-American  Technical Economic Conference at the earliest possible date.  The Conference, under the auspices of the Pan American Union, was scheduled  for March 15, 1945.  It was postponed until November 15, 1945, and further postponed until April 15, 1946.  Because of these postponements, the Inter-American Economic and Social Council convened in a special session on November 15, 1945, to consider urgent economic problems of the hemisphere. On February 20, 1946, the Governing Board of the Pan American Union  finally decided to postpone the Inter-American Technical Economic Conference without fixing a definite date for its convocation.  The Conference was never held.  It was technically replaced by the Inter-American Conference for the Maintenance of Continental Peace and Security, Rio de Janeiro, 1947.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: In October 1944 the Argentine government requested a meeting of American foreign ministers to discuss the non-recognition status imposed on it by the other American republics.  Although the United States opposed such a meeting, Mexico called for a special Inter-American Conference to discuss not only the Argentina problem but the problems of collective security in the Americas.  The conference convened in the castle of Chapultepec near Mexico City on February 21, 1945, and remained in session until March 8, 1945. The most significant result of the conference was adoption of the Act of Chapultepec, which announced the principle that an attack on one American state would be considered as aggression against all.  The Act also called for a regional defense treaty to be negotiated at the end of the war. In addition, the delegates agreed to reorganize the Inter-American system after the war. Although Argentina was excluded from the conference, the American republics invited Argentina to declare war against the Axis and resolved that if Argentina subscribed to the principles embodied in the Act of Chapultepec, she would be eligible for membership in the United Nations.

Article I of the April 11, 1908, treaty which described that section of the international boundary line that runs through Passamaquoddy Bay provided for the Commission to decide on the ". . . location of the line with respect to Pope's Folly Island above Lubec Narrows and with respect to certain fishing grounds east of the dredged channel below Lubec Narrows."  Each government was to present its claim, with supporting documents, within six months after the exchange of ratifications. The Commissioners failed to reach a decision by the end of their allotted six months. Provision was made in the treaty that if a decision was not reached in the case the matter would be submitted to an arbitrator.

The Governments of the United States and Great Britain, in an effort to quickly settle the matter, instructed the Commissioners to decide on a boundary line instead of submitting the case to an arbitrator. Their decision was incorporated into article I of a treaty concluded between the United States and Great Britain on May 21, 1910.

The Centennial International Exhibition was held at Fairmount Park in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania from May 10 to November 10, 1876, to celebrate the one-hundredth anniversary of the independence of the United States. An Act of Congress approved on March 3, 1871, authorized the creation of a United States Centennial Commission to prepare and superintend the execution of a plan for holding the exhibition.

Invitations to participate were sent to foreign governments, and Argentina, Austria, Belgium, Brazil, Chile, China, Denmark, Egypt, France, Germany, Great Britain, Italy, Mexico, Hawaii, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Peru, Portugal, Russia, Spain, Siam, Sweden and Norway, Switzerland, Tunis, Turkey, and Venezuela accepted. Tunis was represented at this exhibition by G. Harris Heap, the United States Consul at Tunis, who served as commissioner for the Bev of Tunis under authority granted him by a joint congressional resolution of February 12, 1876.  All of the states in the United States participated, and many of them contributed funds for the exhibition. 

The following classifications were used for exhibits: I, Raw Materials; II, Materials and Manufactures Used for Food or in the Arts; III, Textile and Felted Fabrics; IV, Furniture and Manufactures of General Use in Construction and Dwellings; V, Tools, Implements, Machines, and Processes; VI, Motors and Transportation; VII, Apparatus and Methods for the Increase and Diffusion of Knowledge; VIII, Engineering, Public Works, and Architecture, etc.; IX, Plastic and Graphic Arts; and X, Objects Illustrating Efforts for Improvement of the Physical, Intellectual, and Moral Conditions of Man. 

The sum of $1,500,000 was appropriated for the exhibition by an act of Congress on February 16, 1876; funds were also appropriated by other legislation to defray the expenses of government exhibits.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: President George Washington appointed the first official U.S. Consul, John Street, in 1795, when Thomas Jefferson was Secretary of State. The United States has had representatives in the Azores ever since, and the U.S. Consulate in Ponta Delgada was the oldest continuously operating U.S. Consulate in the world. At first, the main American Consulate was located on the island of Faial, with  branch offices in Ponta Delgada and, for a short time, a Consular Agent on the island of Flores as well. In 1917 all Consulate operations moved to Sao Miguel (St. Michael).

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: On January 23, 1925, the United States and the Netherlands signed a special agreement to submit thier differences over the sovereignty of the Island of Palmas (Miangas) to arbitration. The dispute over the island, situated about 50 miles soueast of Cape San Agustin, Island of Mindanao, was referred to the Permanent Court of Arbitration at the Hague. The arbitrator was Max Huber; the U.S. agent and counsel was Fred K. Nielsen. The decision of April 4, 1928, stated that the entire island was Netherlands territory.
