creators.administrativeHistoryNote: On JUne 30, 1921, the United States and Norway signed a special agreement that provided for arbitration of Norwegian claims against the United States. The claims arose in World War I, when the United States requisitioned all ships under construction in American shipyards, including fifteen vessels belonging to Norway. The United States also presented one claim (Page brothers' claim) against Norway. The dispute was referred to the Permanent Court of Arbitration at the Hague. Members of the tribunal were Chandler P. Anderson of the United States, Benjamin Vogt of Norway, and James Valloton of Switzerland, who served as president. The agents were C. Frolich Hanssen for Norway and William C. Dennis for the United States. The tribunal met from JUly 22 to October 13, 1922, when it made an award to Norway.

Under the convention of 1858 between the United States and China, signed November 8, 1858, China paid $735,238.97 in settlement of U.S. claims against the Chinese Government. Most of the claims arose from destruction of property and interruption of U.S. business in Canton during December 1856 - January 1857, although a few originated as early as 1841.

By an act of March 3, 1859 (11 Stat. 408), distribution of the $735,238.97 was committed to a board of two commissioners, Charles W. Bradley, U.S. consul at Ningpo, and Oliver E. Roberts, former vice consul at Hong Kong. The commissioners met in Macao, China, November 14, 1859, and formally completed their work of examining and deciding claims on January 13, 1860. creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Tripartite Military Governors Conference was held in Berlin during the recess of the London Conference on Germany, March 6 - April 20, 1948. It was convened in order to implement the decisions of the London Conference. Seven working parties were designated to examine the major issues. The Benelux countries participated along with France, Great Britain, and the United States. The topics studied included the association of the Benelux countries with policy-making on Germany; the fusion of Bizonia and the French zone of occupation; and political, economic, and territorial changes in western Germany. The Military Governors also met with the Minister Residents of the western German Laender to write a German constitution. The working parties prepared reports on their respective issues and progress, and made recommendations to the resumed session of the London Conference.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Paris Peace Commission was established pursuant to an agreement signed by the representatives of the United States and Spain on August 12, 1898, to negotiate and conclude a treaty of peace between the two countries. Commissioners appointed by the United States were William R. Day, Cushman K. Davis, William P. Frye, George Gray, and Whitelaw Reid. The Commission met from October 11 to December 10, 1898, and on the last day signed a treaty of peace.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: At the request of the United States, the Far Easertn Commission established the Inter-Allied Trade Board for Japan. creators.administrativeHistoryNote: Although the Act of Chapultepec called for a regional defense treaty to be negotiated at the end of World War II, the United States delayed in calling a special conference because of the Argentina situation. Finally, in March 1947, President Truman announced that the United States was prepared to call a special conference to carry out the Chapultepec proposal. Accordingly, delegates from the twenty-one American republics met in Petropolis, Brazil (near Rio de Janeiro), from August 15 to September 2, 1947, to discuss a regional defense plan. The delegates drew up a permanent defensive military alliance called the Inter-American Treaty of Reciprocal Assistance (Rio Pact). The treaty gave legal sanction to the principle that the American republics would consider an attack against one of them as an attack against all.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: Two days after the attack on Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, the United States called for a third meeting of the Ministers of Foreign Affairs of the American Republics. The conference met in Rio de Janeiro from January 15 to January 28, 1942, to discuss cooperative action against the Axis. Although the United States attempted to persuade all the American republics immediately to break all relations with the Axis, a compromise resolution was adopted which merely recommended the severing of diplomatic relations with the Axis. The conference adopted a resolution establishing an economic boycott of the Axis, established an extensive program of inter-American economic cooperation, and adopted a series of resolutions aimed at curbing subversive activities in the Americas, and, further, created an Inter-American Joint Defense Board and an Emergency Committee on Political Defense.

The treaty of peace of 1783 between the United States and Great Britain defined, in article II, the boundary line separating the British dependencies in North America from the United States. But it was not until October 27, 1795, that a treaty concluded between the United States and Spain defined the boundary line separating U.S. territory from Spanish possessions. This line, which is referred to as the "Old Southern Boundary," is described in article II of the treaty:

The Spanish colonies of East and West Florida were divided from U.S. territory by a line beginning at ". . . the River Mississippi, at the northernmost part of the thirty-first degree of north latitude . . . " then due east to the middle of the Apalachicola River, ". . . thence along the middle thereof to its junction with the Flint; thence straight to the head of St. Mary's River, and thence down the middle thereof to the Atlantic Ocean." Article II also provided that all ". . . troops, garrisons, or settlements . . . " of either contracting power located on the territory of the other ". . . shall be withdrawn from the said territory within the term of six months after the ratification of this treaty."

In article III the treaty provided for one country to appoint one Commissioner and one surveyor to ". . . run and mark . . ." the line. Article IV of the treaty defined the western boundary of the United States as running south along the middle of the Mississippi River from the northern boundary of the United States to the 31st parallel of north latitude.

President George Washington, on May 24, 1796, appointed Andrew Ellicott as Commissioner and Thomas Freeman as surveyor. Ellicott's journey to Natchez where the Commission was to meet began at Philadelphia on September 16, 1796. The U.S. survey party arrived at Natchez on February 24, 1797. The Governor of Natchez, Manuel Gayoso de Laemos, who was to act as the Spanish Commissioner, met with Ellicott on February 25 and set March 19 as the date the survey wasd to begin. Many problems arose between the U.S. party and Spanish officials--the most complex of which proved to be the Spanish evacuation of posts north of the boundary line. The required evacuation was postponed for more than a year after Ellicott's arrival. It was not until the morning of March 30, 1798, that the Spanish finally left Natchez.

The U.S. party began its survey on April 9, 1798. The swamps, rivers, and wildernesses of the area and Indian hostilities prlonged the survey. Two years later Ellicott completed the task assigned to him.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The International Refugee Organization (IRO) was founded in 1946 to deal with the massive refugee problem created by World War II .  It was established by the Constitution of the International Refugee Organization, adopted by the United Nations General Assembly on December 15, 1946. It was a United Nations specialized agency and took over many of the functions of the earlier United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration (UNRRA).  In 1952 its operations ceased, and it was replaced by the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR). It is the only specialized agency to have ever gone out of existence.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: All aspects of the Foreign Economic Administration's (FEA) relations with the British Empire and countries in the Middle East were handled by this Branch. Its representatives conferred with those of the British Empire on joint aspects of economic warfare and provided for an interchange of economic, political, and military information about lend-lease activities and foreign trade. The Branch was responsible for the field activities of the FEA in the areas indicated by the names of its divisions: The Dominions, India and Southeast Asia, Middle East, United Kingdom and British Colonies, and Turkish Divisions. Its Shipping Control Staff coordinated all shipping activities between the United States and the British Empire, maintaining liaison with the British Ministry of Transport and U.S. shipping authorities. The Reciprocal Aid Requirements Staff presented the requirements of the United States for reverse lend-lease to foreign governments, and the Program Staff prepared the final requirements program for the Britsih Empire. After the war the records of the Branch were divided between the Department of State and the Department of Commerce.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
Sweden proposed a United Nations International Conference on the Human Enviroment during the spring 1968 session of the U.N. Economic and Social Council. The U.N. General Assembly approved the proposal in Resolution 2398, adopted December 3, 1969. Sponsored by 55 member nations, the Conference focused attent of governments and world public opinion on urgent physical and social conditions produced by technology, industrialization, and population. Planners anticipated the action-oriented Conference would produce drafts of international argeeements dealing with major environmental problems. Acknowledged as the first enviromental conference of worldwide siginificance, all member states were expected to send delegations.

Christian A. Herter, Jr., Special Assistant to the Secretary of State for Environmental Affairs, served as the Chief U.S. Delegate to the Conference's Preparatory Committee. The U.S. Government was active in preparations for the Conference from the beginning. Secretary of State William P. Rogers announced on January 26, 1971, his intention to create a committee to advise him on aspects of U.S. participation in the Conference. On February 19, 1971, he announced the appointment of Senator Howard H. Baker, Jr., of Tennessee as Chairman of the Secretary of State's Advisory Committee on the 1972 U.N. Conference on the Human Environment scheduled to be held in Stockholm, Sweden, from June 5 to 16, 1972. Baker, who worked closely with Herter, toured several European, African, and Asiatic nations from August 20 to September 6, 1971, to determine the status of their preparation for the Conference.

The Advisory Committee consisted of 28 members representing a wide spectrum of the U.S. public interested in environmental affairs as well as representatives of the executive branch of the U.S. Government. It served as the principal channel for determining public reactions to proposals on environmental subjects. The Rockefeller, McClellan, and Ford Foundations provided funding, and the University of Georgia Law School and U.S. Environmental Protection Agency detailed itself to the Advisory Committee. Preparatory teams within the U.S. Government, aided by the recommendations and contributions of members of the Advisory Committee and the public, prepared papers on pertinent issues, such as marine pollution and the conservation of soil resources. Regional public hearings were held in six U.S. cities in order to give individuals and organizations an opportunity to present opinions and recommendations.

The final meetings of the Secretary of State's Advisory Committee on the 1972 United Nations Conference on the Human Environment was held at Washington, D.C., April 11-12, 1972. The report was submitted to the Secretary of State in May 1972. The United Nations Conference on the Human Environment convened in Stockholm the following month.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The French National Committee of Liberation was an organization founded in London on June 28, 1940, following the capitulation of France to Germany  in World War II . The Committee was established, on the initiative of General Charles de Gaulle-who had refused to accept France's surrender-for the purpose of carrying on the war against Germany. It undertook to speak for the French government. In June 1943 the Committee developed in liberated North Africa into the French Committee of National Liberation (FCNL) which originally was under both Generals Charles de Gaulle and Henri Giraud and later under the chairmanship of De Gaulle alone. Although the United States could not recognize the French Committee of National Liberation as the government of France, the President was disposed "to see the French Committee for National Liberation exercise leadership to establish law and order under the supervision of the Allied Commander-in Chief." The United States in July 1942 had selected representatives to consult with General de Gaulle and the French Committee in London on all matters relative to the conduct of war which concerned the French.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Office of the Coordinator for Emergency Planning in the Office of Administration was responsible for U.S. Information Agency liaison duties with the Office of Emergency Planning in the Executive Office of the President, and with the Office of Civil Defense in the Department of Defense. The Coordinator for Emergency Planning was J. Albert Bush until he was succeeded by Alfred D. Mittendorf in 1969.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The United States was represented at the Paris Universal Exposition of 1900 by a commissioner general, an assistant commissioner general, a special commissioner, and 18 other commissioners. This commission had a more complex organization than previous such commissions. It had three principal departments, one for exhibits, a second for business, and a third for buildings. The exhibits department had a director-in-chief and 10 subordinate directors, each in charge of one or more groups of exhibits. The business department had a director of affairs, an assistant director of affairs, a librarian, a director of customs, a delegate at the Paris office, and a custodian of exhibits. The building department included the American architect, the French architect, a chief of decoration, and a superintendent of mural decoration. Offices of the commission were maintained in Chicago, Washington, New York, and Paris. The United States constructed a building at the exposition and government departments as well as private citizens of the United States had exhibits. The sum of $1,890,500 was authorized for the expenses of United States participation in this exposition by acts of Congress of July 19, 1897; July 1, 1898; March 3, 1899; and Feb. 9, 1900.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Technical Cooperation Administration (TCA) was established in the Department of State by Executive Order 10159, September 8, 1950, to oversee the technical cooperation programs authorized by Title IV (Act for International Development), Foreign Economic Assistance Act of 1950 (64 Stat. 204), approved June 5, 1950, assuming oversight responsibility for the Institute of Inter-American Affairs. It provided scientific and technical assistance to underdeveloped countries in order to maintain political stability and to further economic and social progress. It was subordinated to the Mutual Security Agency by Executive Order 10458, June 1, 1953, and abolished by Reorganization Plan No. 7 of 1953, effective August 1, 1953, with functions transferred to the Foreign Operations Administration.

It furnished military, economic, and technical assistance to friendly nations. It was abolished by Executive Order 10610, May 9, 1955, effective June 30, 1955, with functions transferred to Department of Defense and to the International Cooperation Administration of the Department of State.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Armistice Agreement with Bulgaria of October 28, 1944 stipulated Article 1 that "On the conclusion of hostilities against Germany the Bulgarian armed forces must be mobilized and put on a peace footing under: supervision of the Allied Control Commission.". Article 11 stipulated that property taken from United Nations territory must be returned to those territories under the supervision of the Control Commission. Article 13 stipulated that property belonging to the Axis powers of Germany and Hungary must not be returned without permission of the Control Commission. Article 18 stipulated that the Commission would "regulate and supervise the execution of the armistice terms under the chairmanship of the representative of the Allied (Soviet) High Command. ... During the period between the coming into force of the armistice and the conclusion of hostilities against Germany, the Allied Control Commission will be under the general direction of the Allied (Soviet) High Command.".

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
Because of a growing feeling that there should be central management of all U.S. resources for any foreign aid overseas, there were continuing efforts to bring all of these programs under a single director. The Department of State established, on January 8, 1951, the Office of International Security Affairs, headed by a Director of International Security Affairs and who would also be an Assistant to the Secretary of State for such affairs.  The new office superseded the Office of the Director of Mutual Defense Assistance. At the same time, with Presidential approval, a new interdepartmental committee -- the International Security Affairs Coordinating Committee (ISAC), superseded the Foreign Military Assistance Coordinating Committee CFMACC). 

The Office of International Security Affairs was to direct all foreign aid activities within the Department, including the overseeing of the Technical Cooperation Administration, and its head was to chair the new International Security Affairs Coordinating Committee, which was to be the vehicle for ensuring the coordination of all foreign aid activities, including the continuing performance of the functions of the abolished FMACC. The Director of International Security Affairs, Thomas D. Cabot, using the mechanism of ISAC, was supposed to pull everything together, assuring both coordination of all programs of aid and their responsiveness to U.S. policy. He was also to coordinate the participation of the United States in NATO and to ensure that the aid programs were fashioned and administered in such a way as to give maximum support to U.S. positions on NATO matters.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Paris Liaison Group was a joint planning and monitoring body, chaired by Embassy staff, with representation from other U.S. agencies in western Europe. The Liaison Group ensured coordination by appropriate U.S. Government Agencies for all noncombatant emergency evacuation planning and implementation. It coordinated with the regional liaison groups ensuring in-country support of the noncombatant emergency and evacuation plan.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Legation's Economic Section was responsible for monitoring and managing the full range of economic relations between the U.S. and Switzerland. The Section interacted with the Swiss Government on bilateral and international economic policy issues; reported on developments in the Swiss economy; facilitated U.S. exports to, and investment in, Switzerland; and advocated U.S. business interests in Switzerland. During the war The Economic Section gathered  economic intelligence on the European Axis powers with emphasis on Germany. The Section targetted German and Italian industries and businesses abroad (mainly in Switzerland) as to their activities, finances, international trading partner agreements, citizenship of their owners/shareholders/board of directors, blacklisting, and the impact on Germany to liquidate specific companies or to change trading polices (blockades/tariffs/bans).

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: During its existence, the Office of Inter-American Affairs (OIAA) created five subsidiary corporations under the laws of the State of Delaware.  The Inter-American Educational Foundation (IAEF) was established on September 25, 1943 in order to carry out most of the education operations of the OIAA. It operated in a manner similar to that employed by the Institute of Inter-American Affairs, using units called "Servicios." As a result of early problems in getting started, the education program was just becoming well established when the OIAA was terminated in May 1946. The IAEF was transferred to the Department of State where it functioned for several years until its programs were completed.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: During its existence, the Office of Inter-American Affairs OIAA) created five subsidiary corporations under the laws of the State of Delaware. All five were transferred to the Department of State in 1946 although some were then in various stages of dissolution.  Among the corporations formed was Prencinradio, Inc.  In May 1942 Prencinradio, Inc., was created to assist Latin American countries to improve existing mass communications media.  Also it helped create new media to improve the dissemination of information in Latin America.  Its powers included the press, cinema, and radio, but in practice its projects excluded the press.  Its principal radio project was an attempt to expand radio facilities in Uruguay.  By the spring of 1945 Prencinradio was in the process of liquidation. In August 1945, with the dissolution of the Radio Division, all information functions were transferred to the State Department.  By the spring of 1946, Prencinradio was no longer functioning.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: This Division, known in 1941 as the Agriculture Division, was established to carry out the Office's food supply program in Latin America. The Division participated in carrying out the cooperative food supply agreements of the Department of State's Institute of Inter-American Affairs to increase the production of foodstuffs for United States armed forces in Latin America, particularly in Panama, and to relieve food shortages in strategic areas, such as northern Brazil, northern Peru, and eastern Nicaragua. It made equipment and supplies available to farmers of Latin America and trained them in modern methods of farming and marketing in order to raise standards of living in that area. The Division also participated in the Amazon Valley Project, which was developed by the Office of the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs, in cooperation with the Brazilian Government to obtain information about agriculture, tropical settlements, tropical diseases, nutrition, labor, and economics in the Amazon Valley that was needed to carry out specific food production and procurement programs in that area.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The U.S.-U.S.S.R. Joint Commission on Korea was established as a result of the Moscow Agreement of December 27, 1945, which was concluded at the Moscow Conference of Foreign Ministers by the Soviet Union, Great Britain, and the United States.  This agreement provided for the establishment of a Joint Commission on Korea to be made up of representatives of the United States and the Soviet Union to consider long-range political and economic problems, including the making of recommendations on the formation of a provisional government for all of Korea.  The Commission first met on March 20, 1946, at Seoul, Korea, as a result of a Joint U.S.-U.S.S.R. Conference held in January and February of that year.  After a number of meetings, the Commission reached an impasse on matters concerning Korean unification.  The Soviets wanted to include in a unified Korean government only those political parties which supported the Moscow Agreement.  Since virtually all Korean parties except for the Communist Party had opposed the "trusteeship" concept announced by the Moscow meeting, the United States held that most Korean parties should be allowed to participate in a unified government, whatever their announced attitude toward the Moscow Agreement.  With discussions at a stalemate, the Joint Commission adjourned sine die on May 8, 1946.  It resumed discussions on May 21, 1947, but by July was once again deadlocked.  Negotiations within the framework of the Moscow Agreement were finally abandoned, and the question of the independence of Korea laid before the United Nations.

On September 17, 1947, the United States brought the Korean problem before the General Assembly of the United Nations.  The Soviets opposed United Nations involvement because the Koreans had not been asked to participate.  On November 14, 1947, the General Assembly passed a US-endorsed resolution to create the United Nations Temporary Commission on Korea (UNTCOK).  Australia, Canada, China, El Salvador, France, India, the Philippines, and Syria sent representatives to serve on UNTCOK, which observed elections held in South Korea, but was not permitted to do so in North Korea.  The report of UNTCOK, approved by a General Assembly resolution on December 12, 1948, stated that a lawful government had been established in the South.  The same resolution created the United Nations Commission on Korea to replace UNTCOK.

Although the United States was not represented on the United Nations Temporary Commission on Korea, some of the records relating to its activities were accumulated or produced by the representatives of the U.S. delegation of the former U.S.-U.S.S.R. Joint Commission, who apparently acted as a liaison (a United Nations Liaison and Election Committee on which some U.S. delegates of the former Commission served was established by the U.S. military command) between the UN Commission and U.S. Army Forces in Korea (USAFIK).

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The United Nations Temporary Commission on Korea (UNTCOK) was established by the United Nations General Assembly on November 14, 1947, to try to break the impasse between the Soviet Union and the United States to  to facilitate Korea-wide elections by May 31, 1948 and consequently oversee the transfer of power to the newly-elected government, hopefully in a unified Korea. UNTCOK was able to function only in the South; elections held south of the thirty-eight parallel on  May 10, 1948 were held by the Commission to be valid; and Syngman Rhee became President of the Republic of Korea on August 15, 1948. On September 31948, the Democratic People¿s Republic of Korea was proclaimed in Pyongyang under the Premiership of Kim Il-sung. UNTCOK was superseded by the United Nations Commission on Korea, pursuant to a General Assembly resolution of December 12, 1948, which declared that a lawful government had been established in South Korea.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The International Cooperation Administration was established within the Department of State by State Department Delegation of Authority 85 of June 30, 1955, pursuant to E.O. 10610 of May 9, 1955. creators.administrativeHistoryNote: An Inter-Allied Governing Authority (Komendatura ) consisting of four Commandants, one from each Power, appointed by their respective Commissioners, was established in July 1945 to direct jointly the administration of the City of Vienna. Each of the Commandants served in rotation, in the position of Chief Commandant, as head of the Inter-Allied Governing Authority. A Technical Staff, consisting of personnel of each of the four Powers, was established under the Inter-Allied Governing Authority, and was organised for the purpose of supervising and controlling the activities of the organs of the City of Vienna responsible for its municipal services. The Inter-Allied Governing Authority operated under the general direction of the Allied Council and received orders through the Executive Committee. By the Control Agreement of June 28, 1946, it was renamed the Vienna Inter-Allied Command.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: DUring World War II thousands of Polish women and children, survivors of the Soviet Gulag, setteld in refugee camps and temporary settlements which had been established world-wide. As early as 1942, the Mexican Government agreed to shelter 20,000 Poles for the dureaction of the war. The agreement was signed on December 31, 1942 by General Wladyslaw Sikorski during his visit to Mexico. AT thsat time, the decision was made that transportation and costs of room and board would be covered by the Ministry of Labour Welfare of the Polish Government-in-exile in London, by the  Polish-American Congress, and various Catholic charity organizations. Colonia Santa Rosa was occupied by Polish refugees for over three years. After the war ended, in accordance with the previous agreement, the camp was closed on December 31, 1946. The Department of State agreed to accept residents of Colonia Santa Rosa as immigrants to the United States. Those children who were orphans were the first to leave and were placed in American orphanages and education institutions. Older girls were placed in private homes as domestics. The rest of the Santa Rosa residents were able to leave Mexico in small groups and settled elsewhere, for the most part in the United States.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
In September 1950, the first U.S.-Burma Economic Cooperation Agreement was signed. For the next decade, the U. S. Government worked closely with the Government of Burma to provide a range of equipment, supplies, training, and technical services through grants, loans, and sales of agricultural commodities. The Government of Burma chose projects and invested its own funds.

Then, following a military coup in 1962, USAID's Mission in Burma closed. However, the United States Government and Government of Burma continued to work together in the years to come. After the coup, funding for ongoing USAID projects continued until they were completed. In June 1966, the United States Government and Government of Burma signed a local currency loan and grant agreement for the construction of schools and hospitals.

In 1978, the Government of Burma requested resumption of the joint development assistance relationship, and the United States agreed, initiating new projects in agriculture and health. USAID focused on the production of maize and oilseed, and the processing and distribution of edible oil. It also worked on improving primary health care and child survival.

After the military coup government's 1988 crackdown on Burma's democratic opposition, USAID once again halted all economic assistance to Burma in 1989. While USAID continued to provide emergency humanitarian assistance, all USAID American staff and contractors were eventually evacuated. USAID did not have a presence again in Burma for the next ten years.

Beginning in 1998, USAID resumed targeted health programs in Burma. Through the World Health Organization, the Food and Agriculture Organization, and international non-governmental organizations (NGOs), USAID supported infectious disease programs to prevent malaria, HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, and avian influenza. USAID also supported ongoing activities focused on improving livelihoods like agriculture and fisheries, water and sanitation, health, and shelter.

On April 4, 2012, Secretary Clinton announced the re-establishment of the USAID mission in Burma. Chris Milligan was sworn in as USAID's Mission Director to Burma on August 29, 2012, the first USAID Country Mission Director in 24 years.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Berlin Air Safety Center (BASC) came into existence immediately after the close of World War II and was one of only three Cold War, four-power organizations to ever exist, the others being Spandau Prison and Military Liaison Missions . Its primary purpose involved diplomatically ensuring the safety of allied air traffic into and out of the western sectors of the divided city against the threat of East German or Soviet air defenses. Formed in the summer of 1945 , the BASC existed until the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989. Located in the Allied Control Authority Building, the BASC was manned continuously by American, British, and French military representatives along with two Soviet representatives - a controller and an interpreter. These officers worked in close cooperation to ensure the safety of allied aircraft 24 hours a day. Coordinating closely with BARTCC (Berlin Air Route Traffic Control Center) air traffic facilities at Tempelhof Airbase, the BASC representatives verified diplomatic clearances, protested Soviet infringements upon allied air corridors, and fielded the political ramifications of east bloc defectors escaping into West Berlin by stolen aircraft.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
When the Department of State established three geographical divisions in 1909, African affairs were the responsibility of the Divisions of Near Eastern and Western European Affairs. Department Order No. 692 of June 15, 1937, transferred responsibility for all African territories except Algeria and the Union of South Africa to the Division of Near Eastern Affairs. A Division of African Affairs was created in the office of Near Eastern Affairs in January 1944. This administrative relationship continued after the establishment of the Bureau of Near Eastern, South Asian, and African Affairs in 1949. On July 18, 1958, Congress authorized an eleventh Assistant Secretary of State (Publ..L. 85-524; 72 Stat. 363), enabling the Department of State to create a bureau to deal with relations with the newly independent nations of Africa. The Bureau of Near Eastern and South Asian Affairs resumed responsibility for relations with the nations of North Africa on April 22, 1974. 

The Bureau, under the direction of an assistant secretary, executed responsibility for the general conduct of foreign relations with the countries within its geographical area of responsibility by applying over-all political, security, economic, public affairs, social, consular, administrative, and other policies and practices. The Bureau maintained and supervised relationships with foreign missions in the United States representing countries within its regional jurisdiction, except on substantive consular matters, and guided the operation of Foreign Service establishments within its area overseas.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Department of State by administrative action created the position of Deputy Under Secretary of State for Administration, after Congress authorized ten Assistant Secretary of State positions (two of which could be at the Deputy Under Secretary of State level) in the Department of State Organization Act of 1949 (63 Stat. 111, approved May 26, 1949). Between 1953 and 1955, the ranking officer in the Department handling administrative matters was the Deputy Under Secretary of State for Administration. The Department re-established the position of Deputy Under Secretary for Administration in 1955, after Congress authorized three Deputy Under Secretary positions in the State Department Organization Act of August 5, 1955 (69 Stat. 536). The Department of State by administrative action changed the title of the position to Deputy Under Secretary of State for Management on July 12, 1971. The position of Deputy Under Secretary for Management was discontinued when an Act of Congress of Oct 7, 1978, established the permanent position of Under Secretary of State for Management (P.L. 85-426; 92 Stat. 968).

The Deputy Under Secretary for Management directed and supervised the activities of the Director General of the Foreign Service; the Director of the Foreign Service Institute; and other staffs concerned with the management of the Department and the Foreign Service.  He was further charged with exercising the Under Secretary's responsibilities for allocation of the Department's resources, for evaluation of overseas programs and of the Department's domestic operations, for insuring that the policy analysis and resources allocation system is operational, and for providing management consulting services.  

The Deputy Secretaries of Administration, the Deputy Under Secretaries of State for Management, and the Under Secretaries of State for Management were: Loy Wesley Henderson, 1955-1961; Roger Warren Jones, 1961-1962; William Horsley Orrick Jr., 1962-1963; William James Crockett, 1963-1967; Idar D. creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
Executive Order 10610, dated May 9, 1955 and effective June 30, 1955, established the International Cooperation Administration (ICA) in the Department of State. A Director led the ICA and reported directly to the Secretary of State. He was responsible for the functions transferred to the ICA from the former Foreign Operations Administration (FOA). The Office of the Director carried out the functions, as assigned by the Secretary of State, under Mutual Defense Assistance Control Act of 1951; section 501(a) ; and of the Mutual Security Act of 1951 (as continued by section 525 of the Mutual Security Act of 1954). It also made the determinations authorized by the last sentence of section 524 (b) of the Mutual Security Act of 1954; and coordinated the functions of the International Cooperation Administration and other affairs of the Department of State. 

ICA Directors were: John B. Hollister, July 1, 1955-September 15, 1957; James H. Smith, Jr., October 8, 1957-January 31, 1959; Leonard J. Saccio, Acting, February 1, 1959-May 29, 1959; James W. Riddleberger, May 29, 1959-February 28, 1961; Henry R. LaBouisse, March 1, 1961-November 3, 1961; and Dr. D. A. FitzGerald, Acting.

DEPARTMENT OF STATE; INTERNATIONAL COOPERATION ADMINISTRATION SECTION 101. Exclusive of the functions transferred by the provisions of section 201 of this order, all functions conferred by law upon, or delegated or otherwise assigned by the President to, the Director of the Foreign Operations Administration, and all functions conferred by law upon, or otherwise placed under the jurisdiction of, the Foreign Operations Administration (including, subject to the provisions of sections 102 (b) and (c) of this order, all functions of agencies, officials, and employees of the Foreign Operations Administration), are hereby transferred to the Secretary of State and the Department of State, respectively. SEC. 102. The following are hereby transferred to the Department of State: (a) All offices of the Foreign Operations Administration, exclusive of the office of Director of the Foreign Operations Administration SEC. 103. (a) The Secretary of State shall establish, with the offices, personnel, and facilities transferred to the Department of State by or under section 102 (a) and 302 of this order, an agency in the Department of State which shall be known as the International Cooperation Administration. The agencies transferred by sections 102 (b) (c) and (d) of this order shall be made a part of or attached to the International Cooperation Administration. The International Cooperation Administration shall be headed by the Director of the International Cooperation Administration referred to in the first sentence of section 103 (b) of this order. The said Director shall report directly to the Secretary of State. Except as may be otherwise provided by the Secretary of State in respect of the matters referred to in section 104 of this order, the functions transferred by section 101 hereof shall be carried out by or under the International Cooperation Administration or the Director thereof. The said Administration, including all its officers and agencies, and all functions transferred by this Part shall be subject to the direction and control of the Secretary of State. To such extent as the Secretary of State shall prescribe, consistent with law and without diminishing assignments made or required to be made by this order to the International Cooperation Administration or the Director thereof, the said Administration and Director shall be deemed to be the successors of the Foreign Operations Administration and the Director thereof, respectively, in respect of transfers to the Department of State and the Secretary of State made by this order. SEC. 104. (a) The Secretary of State, after consultation with the Secretary of  Defense, shall make appropriate arrangements for carrying out the function of coordination referred to in section 102 (c) (1) of Executive Order No. 10575 of November 6,1954. (b) The Secretary of State or, if he shall so direct, the Director of the International Cooperation Administration shall (1) carry out the functions under the Mutual Defense Assistance Control Act of 1951 transferred by section 101 of this order, (2) carry out the functions under section 501 (a) (2) of the Mutual Security Act of 1951 (as continued by section 525 of the Mutual Security Act of 1954) (3) make the determinations authorized by the last sentence of section 524 (b) of the Mutual Security Act of 1954, and (4) coordinate the functions of the International Cooperation Administration and other affairs of the Department of State. creators.administrativeHistoryNote: U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) missions were located in countries where a bilateral program was being implemented. The mission in each country was subject to the direction and guidance of the chief U.S. representative in the country, usually the ambassador. The missions reported to USAID's assistant administrators of the four geographic bureaus.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Organisation for European Economic Co-operation; (OEEC) came into being on 16 April 1948. It emerged from the Marshall Plan  and the Conference of Sixteen (Conference for European Economic Co-operation), which sought to establish a permanent organisation to continue work on a joint recovery programme and in particular to supervise the distribution of aid. The European organisation adopted was a permanent organisation for economic co-operation. The OEEC was also involved in the allocation of Marshall Plan dollars. In late 1957, a European Nuclear Energy Agency was set up under the OEEC. Its first act was to sign a convention establishing security controls on nuclear energy. The same year the OEEC provided the framework for negotiations aimed at determining conditions for setting up a European Free Trade Area, to bring together the Common Market of the Six and the other OEEC members on a multilateral basis. Peter Thorneycroft was responsible for coordination. Following signature of the Rome Treaties on 25 March 1958, an intergovernmental ministerial committee was set up in October by the Council of the Organisation, chaired by Reginald Maudling, to pursue the negotiations.

In September 1961 the OEEC was superceded by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), a worldwide body.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The U.S. Railway Mission in Mexico, begun in November 1942, initially consisted of a small group of technicians but eventually was expanded to 50 railroad technicians in a total staff of over 150.  The Mission was divided into five departments:  (1) Maintenance of Way, (2) Mechanical, (3) Car, (4) Traffic, and (5) Stores and Reclamation.  As its program expanded, Mission officials decided that it would last several years and that a corporate structure would make more efficient use of funds.  The Institute of Inter-American Transportation (IIAT) was created as a subsidiary corporation in June 1943 to administer the Mexican railway program. The Mission undertook an extensive program of rehabilitation while simultaneously maintaining vital rail service.  Its projects included replacement of defective cross-ties and rails, placing a new ballast on roadbeds, construction or repair of bridges, installation of sidetracks, improvement of terminals and repair shops, installation of a reclamation plant, obtaining priorities and licenses for procurement of spare parts in the United States, modernization of administrative and fiscal procedures, and providing technical assistance and instruction.  The Mission concluded its work and was terminated June 30, 1946, and liquidation of IIAT was begun.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: Within the limits of his geographical responsibility, the British Empire and Middle East Division assisted the Lend-Lease Administrator in those phases of his over-all responsibility that related to the continuance of lend-lease matters and to ultimate settlement of lend-lease with foreign governments. Specifically, the Division negotiated the continuation and ultimate termination of lend-lease contractual obligations with respect to and for the countries included within its geographic area. It maintained documentary records of all lend-lease matters within its geographic area. It kept the Deputy Executive Director for lend-Lease, and, though him, the Lend-Lease Administrator, advised as to problems and accomplishments in the lend-lease program for its geographic area. The Division consisted of the Dominions Branch, the United Kingdom Branch, the Middle East Branch, the Australian Branch, the South African Branch, and the Indian-South Asian Branch.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Committee on Post War Programs was established by Departmental Order 1218 of January 15, 1944, to assist the Secretary of State in the formulation of post war foreign policies and the execution of such policies by means of appropriate international arrangements. The Secretary served as Committee chairman. The Under Secrteary of State was vice chairman, and a special assistant to the Secretary, Leo Pasvolsky, was executive director. The Committee dealt with such war-related problems as terms of surrender, occupation, displaced persons, minorities, the treatment of liberated states, foreign petroleum policy, and reconstruction financing. The Committee was abolished on December 20, 1944 by Departmental Order 1301, and functions vested with the Committee on International Conferences.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Department of State established a Bureau of International Cultural Relations on Jun 1, 1959, and subsequently renamed it the Bureau of Education and Cultural Affairs on Apr 17, 1960. The following year, the Department elevated the position of Special Assistant for Coordination of International Educational and Cultural Relations, which headed the Bureau, to the rank of Assistant Secretary of State. The Department had first established a Division of Cultural Relations in 1938. Cultural relations was also part of the responsibilities of the first Assistant Secretary of State for Public Affairs created in 1944. In 1978 the Bureau was abolished and its functions transferred to the International Communications Agency (subsequently the U.S. Information Agency) under Reorganization Plan No. 2 (91 Stat. 1637). On October 1, 1999, pursuant to the integration of the U.S. Information Agency into the Department of State the Bureau was revived.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Department of State established the Bureau of Politico-Military Affairs by an administrative order on September 18, 1969, to enhance the Department's role in the formulation of international security policy, to supervise security assistance and foreign military sales programs, and to direct the issuance of arms export licenses. The Bureau replaced a special component for politico-military affairs that had served under the Office of the Deputy Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs since 1960. The Director of the Bureau of Politico-Military Affairs, who was designated by the Secretary of State, had rank equivalent to an Assistant Secretary of State. The Director became a Presidential appointee, subject to the advice and consent of the Senate, and an Assistant Secretary on April 14, 1986.

The Bureau of Political-Military Affairs provided policy direction in the areas of international security, military coordination and peace operations, and arms trade. Its responsibilities included regional security policy, security assistance, arms transfers (both government-to-government and commercial), humanitarian programs, critical infrastructure protection, burdensharing, complex contingency operations and contingency planning. The Bureau was headed by an Assistant Secretary of State and supported the Secretary and the Under Secretary for Arms Control and International Security Affairs. 

The Bureau of Political-Military Affairs furthered U.S. national security objectives by: managing bilateral political-military relations and conducting formal security dialogues with over 30 countries; maintaining global access for U.S. military forces; controlling access to militarily significant technologies and promoting responsible U.S. defense trade by administering defense trade controls; leading the interagency strategic planning and policy development processes supporting U.S. global mine action activities; serving as the focal point of the Executive Branch liaison with Congress on defense burdensharing matters; leading the interagency effort to promote political-military and defense cooperation on critical infrastructure protection issues; and working closely with the Department of Defense and the Joint chiefs of Staff, the regional bureaus, and the National Security Council for departmental coordination in crisis management, complex contingency operations, and military options and deployment matters. 

The Directors and later Assistant Secretaries of State included: Ronald Ian Spiers, 1969-1973; Seymour Weiss, 1973-1974; George Southall Vest, 1974-1977; Leslie Howard Gelb, 1977-1979; Reginald Bartholomew, 1979-1981; Richard R. Burt, 1981-1982; Jonathan Trumbull Howe, 1982-1984; John Thomas Chain Jr., 1984-1985; Henry Allen Holmes Jr., 1986-1989; Richard A. Clarke, 1989-1992; Robert L. Gallucci, 1992-1994; Thomas Edmund McNamara, 1994-1998; Eric David Newsom, 1998-2000; Lincoln P. Bloomfield, 2001-2005; John Hillen, 2005-2008; Mark Kimmitt, 2008-2009; Andrew J. Shapiro, 2009-2013; and Puneet Talwar, 2014-2015.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The War Trade Board Section was established in the Department of State as the functional successor to the abolished War Trade Board by Departmental Orders No. 143 of July 1, 1919 and of October 7, 1919, under authority of Executive Order (E.O.) 3059, March 3, 1919, and E.O. 3086-A, May 12, 1919, as amended by E.O. 3099, June 23, 1919. It inherited the personnel, functions, records, and public property of the War Trade Board. It continued the work of the Board with regard to the issuance of export and import licenses. The administration of the foreign agents and representatives of the Board was vested in the Consular Bureau. It was abolished by an act of May 27, 1921 (42 Stat. 9) with residual responsibilities devolving upon the Department of State which, by Departmental Order 335 of May 5, 1925, transferred the "files and records" to the Bureau of Indexes and Archives.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The U.S. Legation at Luxembourg opened on July 17, 1903, with Stanford Newel as Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary. From Newel's departure on June 25, 1905, until July 15, 1940, the mission at Luxembourg was a non-resident legation. The U.S. chief of mission in the Netherlands was non-resident Envoy to Luxembourg from August 1905 through April 1922; thereafter, until July 1940 the Envoy to Belgium was non-resident chief of mission.

On May 10, 1940, German forces occupied Luxembourg. George P. Waller was serving as Charge d'Affaires ad interim when the Legation closed, July 15, 1940.

During World War II the United States maintained diplomatic relations with the Luxembourg government-in-exile, represented by the U.S. Envoy to Canada, March 10, 1941 through October 14, 1943, and then by the U.S. Envoy to the governments-in-exile of the occupied nations in London, November 1943 - November 1944.

The U.S. Legation at Luxembourg was re-established on September 23, 1944, with Winthrop S. Green as Charge d'Affaires ad interim. The first U.S. Envoy to reside in Luxembourg, Perle Mesta, presented her credentials on September 21, 1949. She was succeeded by Wiley T. Buchanan, Jr., December 1, 1953. On September 9, 1956, the Legation was raised to Embassy status and Buchanan presented credentials as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary on September 21, 1956.

Ambassador Buchanan was succeeded by Vinton Chapin, October 29, 1957; A. Burks Summers, September 16, 1960; James Wine, May 26, 1961; William R. Rivkin, December 18, 1962; Patricia Roberts Harris, September 7, 1965; George J. Feldman, December 20, 1967; Kingdon Gould, Jr., July 11, 1969; Ruth Lewis Farkas, May 11, 1973; Rosemary L. Ginn, June 8, 1976; James G. Lowenstein, June 21, 1977; John E. Dolibois, October 12, 1981; Jean Broward Shevlin Gerard, October 30, 1985; Edward Morgan Rowell, May 10, 1990; Clay Constantinu, September 7, 1994; and James Catherwood Hormel, September 8, 1999.

Gerald J. Loftus served as Charge d'Affaires ad interim from January 2001 through April 2002. On April 30, 2002, Peter Terpeluk, Jr. presented his credentials as Ambassador.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The National Exposition Commission was established as a Presidential advisory commission by an act of Congress (38 Stat. 77), approved June 23, 1913, to arbitrate disputes between foreign commissioners and the directors of the Panama-Pacific International Exposition, and to represent the United States at the exposition. (The Exposition was held at San Francisco, California, February 20 - December 4, 1915.) The Commission was composed of two civilian employees of the Executive Branch and one member appointed from private life. It was terminated on July 1, 1916.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Advertising Division was established early in 1942 to administer a program to increase advertising revenues in Latin American communications media which had suffered losses due to shifts in wartime production and resulting curtailment of U.S. exports.  The Division encouraged U.S. firms to advertise in Latin America and urged the Latin American media to explain the shortages of items normally sold by the United States in Latin America and to suggest means of conserving scarce goods. The unit was originally a section of the Commercial and Financial Division, and became a separate division of the Department of Economic Development when the latter was formed in 1943.  The Division was terminated March 31, 1946.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
According to State Department records, the first consul to Merida, Charles Thompson Jr., was confirmed on March 3, 1843. The opening of a U.S. Consulate was probably in response to the Mexican government's decree, opening the ports of Sisal and Campeche to duty-free import and export. A consular agent was also maintained in Sisal, a busy port town that attracted many U.S. ships. 

From 1843 until 1897, ten consuls were appointed to represent the United States¿ interests in the Yucatan. Most notable was Edward H. Thompson, the renowned archaeologist and explorer of the Mayan ruins at Chichén Itzá. Thompson was appointed consul by President Grover Cleveland with the understanding that he would be given time away from his Consular duties to explore the Yucatan's many ruins. His book "People of the Serpent" details his exhaustive research at Chichén Itzá and gives a brief summary of how he obtained his consular title.

In 1897, Consulate Merida was closed and the functions of the office were moved to Progreso. The Consulate remained in Progreso for 37 years. The Consulate was moved back to Merida on February 1, 1934. The building was located near the "Parque del Centenario". The Consulate was later moved to downtown Merida not far from the cathedral.

The U.S. government since 1959 leased the previous Consulate building, on Paseo de Montejo at Avenida Colon. The Consul and Vice Consul originally lived in homes located on the Consulate compound. In December of 2001, the lease expired on the property and a temporary extension was signed while an extensive search process for a new location was undertaken. Construction of the new Consulate was completed and is a more secure and functional facility some three blocks from the previous site. The new office building opened for business on November 06, 2006 and is located at Calle 60 No. 338-K x 29 y 31, Col. Alcalá Martín, 97050.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
From the beginning of its existence as an independent country, the United States valued strong diplomatic relations with Tunisia. Two years after the U.S. Declaration of Independence, John Adams (who was to become the second President of the United States) noted that "There are other nations with which it is more urgent to conclude treaties ... By this, I mean Morocco and the Regencies of Algiers, Tunis, and Tripoli." This suggestion was taken seriously and, on March 26, 1799, the first agreement of friendship and trade was concluded between Tunisia and the United States. 

The first American consulate was established in Tunis on January 20, 1800 (although some records attributed to the consulate date as early as 1795), in one of the many diplomatic buildings clustered around the Place de la Bourse in the Medina. In September 1805, U.S. President Thomas Jefferson received a Tunisian special envoy, and in 1865, after the Civil War, another Tunisian ambassador was sent to the U.S. with a message of friendship to the American people. During Tunisia's struggle for independence, leaders of the national liberation movement established good relations with the United States. On May 17, 1956, the U.S. was the first great power to recognize the sovereign state of Tunisia and, soon after that, moved its Embassy to Avenue de la Liberté.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Office of International Information and Cultural Affairs was established by Departmental Order 1336 of August 31, 1945. On August 15, 1947, its name was changed to the Office of Information and Educational Exchange (Departmental Announcement 685).  It was responsible for: the coordination and direction of the formulation of policy and its execution in the field of international information and cultural affairs; the development of policies and programs promoting freedom of information among peoples; the furtherance of international exchanges of persons, knowledge, and skills with other countries; and the coordination of the international exchange programs and activities of other Federal agencies with the overall foreign policy of the United States. The Office was abolished on April 22, 1948, and replaced by the Office of International Information and the Office of Educational Exchange (Department Announcement 12).

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
President John F. Kennedy repeated his calls for an alliance for progress between the United States and its Latin American neighbors in his inaugural address of January 20, 1961  Ten days later, in his first State of the Union address, the President reemphasized his commitment to the Alliance for Progress. He urged the Congress to appropriate the $500 million pledged by the September 13, 1960, Act of Bogota, and expressed his intention to strengthen the authority of the Organization of American States, abolish illiteracy in the hemisphere, and send a Food for Peace mission to Latin America, and to appoint an interdepartmental Task Force on Latin America,

The Task Force on Latin America met for the first time on February 2, 1961. Participants were Adolf A. Berle, Jr., Chairman; Thomas C. Mann, outgoing Assistant Secretary of State for Inter-American Affairs; John M. Leddy, Assistant Secretary of the Treasury for International Affairs; Theodore C. Achilles, Counselor of Department of State; Lincoln Gordon, Consultant; Haydn Williams, Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for International Security Affairs; Wymberly Coerr, Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Inter-American Affairs; and Robert M. Sayre, Executive Secretary 

Mr. Berle briefly explained the purpose of the Task Force. It was an action and not a study group, acting under the direction of the Secretary of State and the President, and was mechanism of transition, pending the appointment of the new Assistant Secretary of State for Latin American Affairs. The Task Force did not supersede the Bureau of Inter-American Affairs which remained responsible for foreign policy operations with respect to Latin America. The Task Force was to insure that problems get the prompt attention of the Secretary of State and the President and that the decisions taken were carried out. It had the longer range responsibility of obtaining general agreement on policies and launching those policies. 

The Task Force dissolved on submission of its final report, July 7, 1961.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The U.S. Consulate in Asmara was first established in 1942. In 1953, the United States signed a mutual defense treaty with Ethiopia. The treaty granted the United States control and expansion of the important British military communications base at Kagnew near Asmara. In the 1960s, as many as 4,000 U.S. military personnel were stationed at Kagnew. On SMarch 11, 1965, it was raised to a U.S. Consulate General. In the 1970s, technological advances in the satellite and communications fields were making the communications station at Kagnew increasingly obsolete. In 1974, Kagnew Station drastically reduced its personnel complement. In early 1977, the United States informed the Ethiopian Government that it intended to close Kagnew Station permanently by September 30, 1977. In the meantime, U.S. relations with Ethiopian Mengistu Haile Miriam were worsening. In April 1977, Mengistu abrogated the 1953 mutual defense treaty and ordered a reduction of U.S. personnel in Ethiopia, including the closure of Kagnew Communications Center and the Consulate General in Asmara. In August 1992, the United States reopened its Consulate in Asmara, staffed with one officer. On April 27, 1993, the United States recognized Eritrea as an independent state, and on June 11, diplomatic relations were established, with a chargé d'affaires ad interim and the U.S. Consulate was raised to an U.S. Embassy. The first U.S. Ambassador arrived later that year.

Since January 2006, the Government of Eritrea did not permit the unimpeded delivery of the U.S. Embassy's diplomatic pouches as called for in the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, a treaty to which the Government of Eritrea was a signatory. The Embassy was unable to receive supplies and materials necessary for its normal operations as a result. In addition, the Government of Eritrea refused to grant visas to State Department technicians who provided vital support for our consular computer systems. For these reasons the Consular Section was closed for public operations except for the provision of necessary services to American citizens.

In the 1970s, technological advances in the satellite and communications fields were making the communications station at Kagnew increasingly obsolete. In 1974, Kagnew Station drastically reduced its personnel complement. In early 1977, the United States informed the Ethiopian Government that it intended to close Kagnew Station permanently by September 30, 1977. In the meantime, U.S. relations with the Mengistu regime were worsening. In April 1977, Mengistu abrogated the 1953 mutual defense treaty and ordered a reduction of U.S. personnel in Ethiopia, including the closure of Kagnew Communications Center and the consulate in Asmara. In August 1992, the United States reopened its consulate in Asmara, staffed with one officer. On April 27, 1993, the United States recognized Eritrea as an independent state, and on June 11, diplomatic relations were established, with a chargé d'affaires. The first U.S. Ambassador arrived later that year.) https://web.archive.org/web/20090114005223/http://www.state.gov/r/pa/ei/bgn/2854.htm

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: After World War II the United States, while maintaining an embassy in Bonn, held that the city of Berlin should only be the capital of a unified Germany. The Department of State established its presence in that city with the U.S. Mission Berlin (USBER). Berlin was an occupied city and under these conditions the U.S. Mission was in many matters under the authority of the U.S. military commander in West Berlin, and not under the authority of the Department of State, and the U.S. military commander could and did sometimes give direction and orders to State Department personnel as the need arose. Yet the Mission also exercised power in its own right, as in vetting high civilian appointments to the city administration. Following the demise of the Berlin Wall and the unification of Germany on 1989-1990, the U.S. Mission Berlin was merged with the U.S. Embassy to the German Democratic Republic (established ca. 1974) to form the U.S. Embassy Office Berlin. From 1990 to 1998 Embassy Office Berlin acted as a satellite of the U.S. Embassy in Bonn.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: SHAEF continued a practice started at Allied Force Headquarters (AFHQ) which was to have civilian officials advise the Supreme Commander about the political implications of proposed actions. These officials, known as Political Officers or Political Advisers, were diplomats appointed by either the British Foreign Office or the U.S. Department of State to serve at SHAEF. The officers gave advice particularly with respect to intelligence matters, psychological warfare, civil affairs and military government, and post-hostilities planning. In September 1944, Ambassador Robert D. Murphy was appointed Political Adviser for German Affairs. The political advisers had their independent staffs. Ordinarily they carried on their activities through the Chief of Staff. but enjoyed direct access to the Supreme Commander, later Military Governor.

The missions reported to USAID's assistant administrators of the four geographic bureaus.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: In the spring of 1942, a Science and Education Division was created in the new Department of Information within the Office of the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs. In late 1943, the name of the division was shortened to the Education Division, a reflection of narrowing functions.  Most of the education operations of the office were carried out by the Inter-American Educational Foundation, Inc. which operated under the Office of the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs until May 1946 when it was transferred to the Department of State. The Education Division was dissolved with the rest of the Department of Information in August 1945.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
In 1922 British shipping interests charged that the American consular officials at Newcastle-on-Tyne had exceeded their authority by attempting to divert passengers from British to American shipping lines. The British Foreign Office insisted that the two accused officials be transferred from Newcastle, and canceled the exequaturs (official consular recognition) of the U.S. Consul and Vice Consul. The Department of State instituted three separate inquiries, which in each case failed to substantiate the charges. The British Government, however, stood by its original accusation.  Secretary of State Charles Evans  Hughes replied by closing the Consulate and ordering the premises sold.  British shipping circles soon complained of delays and loss of money in clearing their ships for American ports because of lack of a Consulate at Newcastle.

In early April 1924 the question was brought to a friendly conclusion.  Great Britain withdrew its charges and  Secretary Hughes announced, through Ambassador Kellogg, his intention to reopen the Consulate at Newcastle-on-Tyne, and to appoint Charles Roy Nasmith as Consul.  Prime Minister Ramay MacDonald's letter to the Ambassador said : "I have the honor to inform you that after further consideration, His Majesty's Government are prepared not to insist upon the charge of exceeding their consular authority, laid about a year and a half ago, against the then American Consul and Vice Consul at Newcastle, and it has therefore been recalled."

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The main function of the Regional Division, established in 1942, was to direct and correlate the activities of the coordination committees. Its Mexican and Guatemalan Section, Central American Section, Caribbean Section, West Coast Section, Brazilian Section, and River Plate Section supervised the operations of these committees and submitted periodic analyses of their activities. The Division maintained working relations with the Department of State, obtaining from it approval for field projects of the coordination committees. The Division was abolished in August 1945 and its functions transferred to the Department of State.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Department of State created the position of Assistant Secretary of State for Public and Cultural Relations during a general reorganization on December 20, 1944, after Congress authorized an increase in the number of Assistant Secretaries in the Department from four to six (Dec 8, 1944; P.L. 78-472; 58 Stat. 798). The Department changed the title to Assistant Secretary of State for Public Affairs in 1946. Initially, incumbents supervised the forerunners of the U.S. Information Agency and the Voice of America.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Office of the Assistant Secretary of State for Economic Affairs was formally established on January 15, 1944, with Dean Acheson, who had previously been assigned to matters concerning economic warfare and liberated areas, as the Assistant Secretary for Economic Affairs. The Office was made responsible for supervising eleven divisions concerned with economic affairs, grouped in the Office of Wartime Economic Affairs and the Office of Economic Affairs, and it inherited the functions of the Office of the Adviser on International Economic Affairs, which had existed in the Office of the Secretary before the war. The Assistant Secretary was the Chairman of the Executive Comittee on Economic Foreign Policy, and he also served on other top policy committees of the Department and on various interdepartmental and international economic committees. In the reorganization of December 20, 1944, William L. Clayton became the Assistant Secretary for Economic Affairs.

The economic activities of the Department expanded rapidly during the defense and early war periods and led to the creation of a number of new divisions and the expanison of existing offices. Most of them were grouped under the Board of Economic Operations, which was created in October 1941. As the war progressed and as problems of the relief and rehabilitation of occupied areas arose, foreign economic activities and the relations between the various agencies concernedwith them grew more complex. On June 24, 1943, the Office of Foreign Economic Coordination was created in the Department, with Dean Acheson as Director, to replace the Board of Economic Operations. This organization lasted only until September 15, 1943, when a new independent agency, the Foreign Economic Administration was established and took over most of the functions of the Office of Foreign Economic Coordination. Thereafter, until the reorganization of January 15, 1944, the economic functions remaining in the Department were handled by four groups of Special Advisers and Advisers (on Supply and Resources, Liberated Areas, the Other American Republics, and the Eastern Hemisphere), under the direction of Assistant Secretary Acheson.

The Office of Wartime Economic Affairs and the Office of Economic Affairs established in January 1944 were abolished on January 26, 1945, in order that their activities might be regrouped in relationship to the post-war economic responsibilities of the Department. They were replaced by the Office of International Trade Policy (known at first as the Office of Commercial Policy) and the Office of Financial and Development Policy. To these were added on October 19 and 20, 1945, the Interim Foreign Economic and Liquidation Service and the Office of Foreign Liquidation, establisged to handle continuing problems connected with lend-lease functions and liberated area requirements and to dispose of surplus war property and of captured enemy property in foreign areas--functions assigned to the Department by the Surplus Property Act of 1944 (58 Stat. 765), a Surplus Property Board regulation of September 25, 1945, and an Executive Order of September 27, 1945.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Department of State created the position of Assistant Secretary of State for Administration during a general reorganization in December 1944, after Congress authorized an increase in the number of Assistant Secretaries in the Department from four to six (58 Stat. 798, approved December 8, 1944). The reorganization was the first to designate substantive designations for specific Assistant Secretary positions. The title for this position has varied over the years. Assistant Secretaries for Administration have supervised a variety of functions ranging from budget and personnel matters to foreign buildings and record keeping. Several of these functions, such as accounting and diplomatic security have become the responsibility of newly created bureaus.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Division of Foreign Activity Correlation was established within the Department of State by Departmental Order 915A, November 22, 1940, to perform such duties with regard to foreign activities as the Secretary of State might direct. On October 8, 1941, it inherited from the Division of Controls functions pertaining to the registration of the agents of alien principals, only to have them transferred to the Department of Justice by an Executive Order of May 29, 1942. Late in October 1941, the Division was directed to interview foreign political leaders promoting movements in the interests of their peoples and also committees of foreign-born groups visiting the Department in order to obtain information as to the purpose, organization, and membership of the groups. On January 7, 1944, it was made responsible for liaison with various war intelligence agencies and for censorship matters, in connection with which it was assigned the overall responsibility of supervising the collection and processing of information from enemy documents after the war. In June 1944, it gained the functions of the Secretary's Liaison office. During the war, the Chief of the Division was a member of the Committee on Political Planning. 

After the war the Division’s focus changed, and by early 1947 it was responsible for the formulation and coordination of Department policy for the collection, evaluation, analysis, research, and dissemination of foreign security information; taking the action necessary to implement this policy; and directing all Departmental programs in this field. The Division formulated Department policy and acted as the Department's sole liaison agent with respect to all matters in the field of foreign security information; participated in the formulation of the Department's travel security policy; and directed and supervised the collection, evaluation, and distribution of all foreign documentary security information, including captured enemy documents. It represented the Department on all interdepartmental boards and committees in this field. The Division was also designated as the Department's clearing point for all security information relating to organization or individuals, except employees of the Department. 

Chiefs of the Division were George Anderson Gordon, 1940-January 14, 1944 (acting), January 15, 1944-1944; Frederick Bronson Lyon, May 1, 1944-1945; and Jack Davis Neal, March 7-April 20, 1946 (acting), April 21, 1946-1948.

On August 27, 1948, the Division of Foreign Activity Correlation was abolished and most of its personnel and functions transferred to the Division of Security and Investigations. At that time, the Division of Security and Investigations became the Division of Security. The rest of the Division of Foreign Activity Correlation moved to the Division of Acquisitions and Distribution in the Research and Intelligence Area.

Lyon, Chief of the Division of Foreign Activity Correlation; In November 1947, the Department’s postwar drive for efficiency and economy targeted the Division of Foreign Activity Correlation (FC), in part because of the running question within the Department: “Just what do all those people do in FC?” With 69 staff members, FC, in liaison with the FBI, the OSS, and the War and Navy Departments reviewed security and intelligence information about individuals, groups, and incidents that threatened the security of the United States. The Department’s January 1948 survey of FC found that it duplicated or completed work similar to that of the Division of Security and Investigation. By February 1948, the Bureau of Administration decided to dissolve FC and transfer most of its duties and staff to the Security and Investigations Division. This occurred on August 27. It performs the following functions: (a) formulates Department policy and acts as the Department's sole liaison agent with respect to all matters in the field of foreign security information; (b) participates in the formulation of the Department's travel security policy; (c) directs and supervises the collection, evaluation, and distribution of all foreign documentary security information, including captured enemy documents; and (d) is designated as the clearing point within the Department for all security information relating to individuals or organizations, except applicants for positions or employees of the Department, the Foreign Service, and individuals sponsored by the Department for international or other organizations or conferences which will continue to be handled by the Division of Security and Investigations.
