creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The governments of Albania, Australia, Belgium, Canada, Denmark, Egypt, France, Great Britain, Greece, India, Luxembourg, Norway, New Zealand, the Netherlands, Czechoslovakia, the Union of South Africa, the United States, and Yugoslavia, to obtain an equitable distribution among themselves of the total assets which had been agreed to at Potsdam on August 1, 1945, and at the Paris Agreement on Reparation From Germany of January 14, 1946, and other assets that may later have been declared to be available as reparation from Germany, established on January 14, 1946, an Inter-Allied Reparation Agency  (IARA). The official functions of the IARA, located in Brussels, Belgium, were to allocate German reparations among the Signatory Governments in accordance with provisions of the Paris Agreement and of any other agreements in force among the Signatory Governments; serve as the medium through which the Signatory Governments received information concerning, and expressed their wishes in regard to, items available as restitution; and deal with all questions relating to the restitution to a Signatory Government of property situated in one of the western zones of occupation in Germany which may be reffered to it by the commander of that zone (acting on behalf of his government). 

Each signatory government was authorized to appoint a delegate to the Agency and an alternate to act in the absence of the delegate. The three commissioners of the Tripartite Commission on the Restitution of Monetary Gold (Tripartite Gold Commission) were also commissioners to the IARA, although the Commission was constitutionally separate from and independent of the IARA. Russell H. Dorr, U.S. representative to the Tripartite Gold Commission, was the first U.S. representative to the IARA, as were Sir Desmond Morton for Britain and Jacques Rueff of France.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Institute of Inter-American Affairs was established as a corporation under the laws of the State of Delaware by the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs on March 31, 1942. It merged with the Inter-American Educational Foundation, Incorporated (which had been similarly established in 1943), and reconstituted as a U.S. Government corporation by an act of August 5, 1947 (61 Stat. 780). It was transferred to the Department of State, effective May 20, 1946, by Executive Order 9710 of April 10, 1946, which abolished the Office of Inter-American Affairs. The Institute was assigned to the Technical Cooperation Administration (TCA) by Executive Order 10159 of September 8, 1950, and, with the TCA, was subordinated to the office of the Director of Mutual Security by Executive Order 10458 of June 1, 1953. The Institute was abolished by Reorganization Plan No. 7, effective August 1, 1953, with functions transferred to the Foreign Operations Administration.

During World War II its function was to aid in improving the health and general welfare of the people of the Western Hemisphere. To further its objective the Institute was granted wide powers, including the power to acquire property, to purchase and deal in foodstuffs and other supplies, to promote programs for the control of disease and the production of nutritive foodstuffs, and to educate doctors, nurses, and other persons. It aided the division of the Department of Basic Economy, Office of the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs, in carrying out their programs by entering into agreements with the governments of the Latin American republics for the operation of cooperative service units in those countries. Each party to an agreement contributed, in accordance with its ability, raw materials, services, and funds. The health, sanitation, and agricultural cooperative service units, known as "Servicios," were usually integral parts of the appropriate ministries of the governments of the Latin American republics. The Institute usually appointed the Director of the Servicio, who also served as the Chief of Field Party for the Institute and was given authority to plan and carry out local projects with the Latin American authorities without referral to Washington.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: From the earliest days of the Republic, Presidents have designated special diplomatic envoys for specific assignments, primarily overseas. The President appointed the first official specifically to bear the title of Ambassador at Large on March 12, 1949, under the authority vested in Article II, Section 2 of the U.S. Constitution that empowers the President, with the advice and consent of the Senate, to appoint Ambassadors, other public ministers, and consuls. Presidents have usually appointed Ambassadors at Large to deal with specific foreign policy issues which have been frequently, but not always, spelled out in their commissions. President Lyndon B. Johnson appointed W. Averell Harriman Ambassador at Large for Southeast Asian Affairs in 1965. In this capacity, Harriman travelled around the world to solicit support for U.S. policies in Vietnam and to investigate the possibilities of a negotiated peace. In 1968, he became the chief U.S. negotiator when preliminary peace talks opened in Paris between the US and North Vietnam.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The selection of appropriate material for the information program was a matter of OIAA concern from its start.  By the fall of 1941 a Content Committee, consisting of the directors of the press, radio, and motion picture units, was operating for this purpose.  Among the organizational changes in the spring of 1942 was the creation of a Directive Council to assist in planning overall policy.  The Council included a Propaganda Committee composed of representatives from the divisions of the Department of Information and the State Department, which assumed the functions of the Content Committee. With the invasion of North Africa imminent in the fall of 1942, the content of information releases to Latin America became a matter of prime concern to the OIAA. 

Planning activities were expanded so that in February 1943, when the Department of Information Services was created, a Content Planning Division was included to insure a high degree of consistency and effectiveness in the materials produced by the Information Department.  To integrate the information program in Latin America with the programs of the Office of War Information (OWI) in other parts of the world, particularly the programs to refute Axis propaganda, the Division prepared daily, weekly, and special "content directives" that pointed out themes to be emphasized by coordination committees and the foreign service missions in Latin America in carrying out their area information programs. In preparing these directives the Division also followed plans and programs communicated to the Office of the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs by the Department of State, intelligence units of the Army and Navy, the Office of Strategic Services (OSS), the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), and the Board of Economic Warfare.

After the Department of Information Services was dissolved in September 1943, the Content Planning Division was transferred to the Department of Information.  In 1945 it was combined for a short time with the Research Division in the Department of Economic Development, and its functions were transferred to the Department of State, with those of the other information divisions, in August 1945.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
On November 4, 1985, the Department of State, by administrative action, established a Bureau of Diplomatic Security headed by a Director holding a rank equivalent to an Assistant Secretary of State. Creation of the new Bureau followed recommendations of the Advisory Panel on Overseas Security (the Inman Panel), which studied means of protecting Department personnel and facilities from terrorist attacks. Congress authorized the Bureau, to be headed by an Assistant Secretary of State for Diplomatic Security, in the Omnibus Diplomatic Security and Anti-terrorism Act of August 27, 1986 (100 Stat. 856). 

The Bureau of Diplomatic Security (DS) was the security and law enforcement arm of the Department of State. It wasd responsible for providing a safe and secure environment for the conduct of U.S. foreign policy and  active in international investigations, threat analysis, cyber security, counterterrorism, security technology, and protection of people, property, and information. Every U.S. diplomatic mission in the world operated under a security program designed and maintained by DS. In the United States, Diplomatic Security personnel protect the Secretary of State and high-ranking foreign dignitaries and officials visiting the United States, investigated passport and visa fraud, and conductd personnel security investigations.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: Sino-American Joint Commission on Rural Reconstruction (JCRR) Established in 1948. After intensive lobbying by Y.C. James Yen, the U.S. Congress included a provision in the China Aid Act of 1948 to fund an independent entity which would take advantage of Yen's experience in the Rural Reconstruction Movement. The JCRR was led by five commissioners, three of whom were Chinese, appointed by the Chinese government, and two of whom were American, appointed by the American President. On the mainland, during the last days of the Chinese Civil War, the JCRR carried out a program of rent reduction, guarantee of tenure security, and formation of cooperatives, in addition to expansion of the agronomic and irrigation programs. By one estimate, this was the largest non-Communist land reform program in China before 1949. But with the impending defeat of the Guomindang (KMT), the JCRR moved to Taiwan, where under the leadership of Chiang Monlin it supervised major land reform, agricultural improvement, and education projects.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Enemy Branch provided assistance in war planning by making studies of the economy of enemy countries for use in estimating the enemy's war potential and in determining bombing objectives that were most vulnerable from an economic viewpoint. The Branch's Economic Intelligence Division interviewed refugees, returned travelers, American business firms, and representatives of various Allied agencies in order to obtain intelligence about conditions in enemy-held areas. It worked closely with the British Ministry of Economic Warfare in compiling an economic intelligence file. Following the termination of the Office of Economic Warfare in 1943 most of the Division's records were commingled with those of the Enemy Branch of the Foreign Economic Administration which were held by the Department of State.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: This Division was originally the Research Section of the Division of Export Licenses of the Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce, beginning active work about July 10, 1918.  On November 12, 1918, the Bureaus of Research and Tabulations were combined into the Bureau of Research and Statistics, with each former Bureau being made into a division.  The general functions of the Division of Research were (1) to investigate and answer requests for information submitted by members and officials of the War Trade Board and other government agencies; (2) to keep at hand in a readily accessible form, information regarding questions constantly before the War Trade Board; and (3) to initiate investigations in order to anticipate inquiries and to prepare reports valuable to the War Trade Board and other war agencies.  Although the domestic conservation program was determined largely by the Food Administration, the Fuel Administration, and the War Industries Board, and administered by trade advisers in the Bureau of Exports, the Division of Research contributed materially to this program.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Special War Problems Division was established on September 1, 1939, as the Special Division, and was renamed the Special War Problems Division on January 15, 1944, when it became a part of the Office of Controls. It became the Special Projects Division on October 3, 1945. The Division handled matters involving the whereabouts and welfare of, the transmission of funds to, and the evacuation and repatriation of United States citizens abroad; obtained representation by a third power of the interests of the United States in enemy or enemy-controlled countries; maintained liaison with the American National Red Cross and the President's War Relief Control Board with regard to the coordination of foreign-relief operations with foreign policy; and handled various matters relating to civilian internees, prisoners of war, and aliens evacuated from designated military areas.

Effective July 29, 1947, by Departmental Announcement 653 of that date, the Special Projects Division was renamed the Division of Protective Services.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Aviation Division was concerned with such international aviation matters as the development of air transportation, the operation or airlines, and the acquisition of landing rights abroad; the presentation of foreign requests for aircraft to the Munitions Assignment Committee (Air) or other allocation authorities; international air mail; and the export of aircraft. It also assisted other agencies in the training of aircraft personnel, both in the United States and abroad; obtained military and civil flight permits for aircraft of the United States in foreign countries; and screened nonmilitary requests for travel priorities.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Economic Cooperation Administration (ECA) was headed by an Administrator for Economic Cooperation, assisted by a Deputy Administrator, both of whom were appointed by the President, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate. The Administrator was responsible to the President and had a status in the Executive Branch of the Government comparable to that of the head of an executive department. During the period of operations of the ECA, he also served as a member of the National Advisory Council on International Monetary and Financial Problems. Paul G. Hoffman served as Administrator during the life of the ECA.

The general functions of the Administrator were to: (1) review and appraise the requirements of participating countries for assistance; (2) formulate programs of U.S. assistance under the Foreign Assistance Act of 1948 (62 Stat. 138), approved April 3, 1948, including approval of specific projects which had been submitted to him by the participating countriues; (3) provide for the efficient execution of any such program as may have been placed in operation; and (4) terminate provision of assistance or take other remedial action  as he deemed necessary in the circumstances.

The Administrator provided for the procurement in the United States of commodities in such a way as to minimize the drain upon the resources of the United States and the impact of such procurement upon the domestic economy, and to avoid impairing the fulfillment of vital needs of the people of the United States. He was empowered to take appropriate steps to facilitate and maximize the use of private channels of trade in furnishing assistance to participating countries.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) was established as an independent agency by the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (48 Stat. 881), approved June 6, 1934. It was organized on July 2, 1934. The mission of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission was to protect investors, maintain fair, orderly, and efficient markets, and facilitate capital formation. The SEC administered Federal laws regulating the distribution of securities to the public and the subsequent trading of such securities. It served as an advisor to U.S. District Courts in connection with reorganization proceedings for debtor corporations in which there was a substantial public interest. The Commission also had certain responsibilities under section 15 of the Bretton Woods Agreement Act of 1945 and under a portion of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The U.S. Legation at Kabul opened on June 6, 1942.  Until then United States diplomatic representation in Afghanistan was headed by a non-resident minister who also served as the American envoy to Persia. The Legation at Kabul was raised to embassy status in 1948. Ambassador Adolph "Spike" Dubs was assassinated while in service on February 14, 1979, and thereafter the chiefs of missions were designated as charge  d'affaires until the Embassy was closed on January 30, 1989.  The U.S. then reduced bilateral assistance and terminated a small military training program. All remaining assistance agreements were ended after the December 1979 Soviet invasion. 

A U.S. liaison office was opened at Kabul on December 22, 2001, and on December 22, 2001, the U.S. recognized the Interim Authority in Afghanistan with a new charge d'affaires ad interim appointed January 2, 2002.

Serving as Envoys Extraordinary and Ministers Plenipotentiary, with dates of presentation of credentials were Cornelius Van H. Engert, July 2, 1942, and Ely E. Palmer, December 6, 1945. Subsequently serving as Ambassadors Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary were Ely E. Palmer, June 5, 1948; Louis G. Dreyfus, Jr., August 16, 1949; George R. Merrell, June 28, 1951; Angus Ward, November 8, 1952; Sheldon T. Mills, May 6, 1956; Henry A. Byroade, March 21, 1959; John M. Steeves, March 20, 1962; Robert G. Neumann, February 19, 1967; Theodore L. Eliot, Jr., November 21, 1973; Adolph Dubs, July 12, 1978; Robert Patrick John Finn, April 3, 2002 - August 1, 2003; Dr. Zalmay Khalilzad, November 24, 2003 - June 20, 2005; Ronald E. Neumann, August 1, 2005 - April 10, 2007; William Braucher Wood, April 16, 2007 - .

Serving as Charge d'Affaires were Charles W. Thayer, June 6, 1942 - July 1942; J. Bruce Amstutz, February 1979 - February 1990; Hawthorne Q. Mills, February 1980 - January 1982; Charles F. Dunbar, January 1982 - May 1983; Edward Hurwitz, June 1983 - March 1986; James M. Ealum, March 1986 - September 1987; Jon D. Glassman, September 1987 - January 1989; and Ryan Crocker, January 2 - April 3, 2002.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Intergovernmental Committee on Refugees was organized in London in August 1938 as a result of the Évian Conference of the month before which had been called by President Franklin D. Roosevelt to consider the problem of racial, religious, and political refugees from central Europe. During its lifetime the Committee sponsored projects for the resettlement of refugees, particularly in the Dominican Republic, took action to facilitate the admission of refugees into countries overseas, and provided legal protection and found new homes for stateless persons.

At the Anglo-American Conference in Bermuda in April 1943 recommendations were made to the Committee and adopted by it in August 1943 for an extension of is mandate and structure in order to take into account not only immediately urgent situations but also the longer-term problems of the post-war period. After the establishment of the United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration (UNRAA) the Committee's responsibilities were limited to refugees in areas in which UNRAA was not active and to refugees who, for one reason or another, did not come within the jurisdication of UNRAA, like stateless refugees. By agreement between the Committee and the United States' War Refugee Board, the Commitee left to the Board and similar national agencies the performance of immediate rescue and relief of persecuted persons from Germany and German-controlled territories.

In July 1944, 37 governments participated in the work of the Committee. Of these, representatives of Brazil, Canada, Czechoslovakia, France, Great Britain, Mexico, the Netherlands, the Soviet Union, and the United States served on its Executive Committee. The United States was represented on the Executive Committee by Myron C. Taylor, Earl G. Harrison, and George L. Warren. The primary responsibility for determining the policy of the United States with regard to the Committee was that of the Department of State. A representative of the Committee in Washington maintained liaison with Government agencies and private individuals and organizations cooperating with the Committee in its relief activities. 

The Committee ceased to exit on June 30,1947 and its functions were transferred to the International Refugee Organization (IRO) of the United Nations. Records of the Committee that were kept in London were inherited by the International Refugee organization. Records of the Washington representative of the Committee went to the Washington office of the IRO. Many related records were maintained and then retired by the Dpartment of State.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The International Information Administration (IIA) was established upon a major Department of State reorganization in January 1952. The Administrator of this new semiautonomous unit reported directly to the Secretary of State. The role combined the duties of the General Manager of International Information and Educational Exchange Program (IE) with most of the overseas information responsibilities of the Assistant Secretary for Public Affairs. The IIA directed the development of international information and educational exchange policies designed to implement and strengthen the foreign policies of the United States; directed the planning of IIA programs; and directed the execution of IAA programs at home and abroad. The Administrator served as chairman of the Psychological Operations Coordinating Committee and, in this capacity, discharged the responsibility of the Secretary of State for international information and educational exchange programs in the interdepartmental field. The IIA included: the International Broadcasting Service, the International Press Service, the International Motion Picture Service, the International Educational Exchange Service, and the International Information Center Service.
 
The IIA Administrators were Wilson C. Compton, January 1952-Februray 1953; Reed Harris, Acting, 1953; and Robert L. Johnson, March 1953-August 1, 1953.

By Reorganization Plan No. 8, of 1953, effective August 1, 1953, the International Information Administration was abolished and most of its functions transferred to the U.S. Information Agency. The International Educational Exchange Service, the program of exchange of persons and students under the Fulbright and Smith-Mundt Acts and other legislation, remained a function of the Department of State under the Assistant Secretary for Public Affairs.

The Administrator of the new unit combined the duties of the General Manager of IE with most of the overseas information responsibilities of the Assistant Secretary for Public Affairs, reporting directly to the Secretary and Under Secretary of State. USIA also absorbed the information functions of the Mutual Security Agency and the Technical Cooperation Administration, already to some extent integrated under IIA. The exchange program under the Fulbright and Smith-Mundt Acts and certain other legislation remained in the Department of State to be administered by the International Educational Exchange Service (IES) under the Assistant Secretary for Public Affairs.)

This agency will be responsible for the foreign information activities formerly performed by the United States International Information Administration, the Mutual Security Agency, the Technical Cooperation Administration and those financed under the Government of Occupied Areas Appropriation…As of August 1 all personnel of the Department engaged in the functions assigned to the USIA will be transferred to the new agency, as well as files and related records…3. creators.administrativeHistoryNote: This Division was created on October 15, 1917, as the Tabulation and Statistics Bureau of the Board, taking over the tabulating and statistical work of the Research Division of the Export Licenses Bureau of the former Exports Administrative Board.  On November 12, 1918, the Bureau became a division of the Bureau of Research and Statistics and remained as such until the transfer of the War Trade Board to the Department of State on July 1, 1919.  The functions of the Division were: 1) tabulating import and export data; (2) checking the use of licenses to detect different forms of abuse, such as over-shipment and altering of licenses; and (3) supplying conversion and stowage factors of commodities for government statistical agencies such as those of the Shipping Board and the War Department.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
On October 1, 1978, the U.S. Congress, in the Foreign Relations Authorization Act for fiscal Year 1979 (92 Stat. 969), authorized the position of Assistant Secretary of State for International Narcotics Matters.,  This title had been given in full in each appointee's commission. The new Assistant Secretary, who headed the Bureau for International Narcotics Matters, replaced a Senior Adviser to the Secretary of State on Narcotics, who had served with a rank equivalent to an Assistant Secretary of State since 1970.  The title of this position was changed from International Narcotics Matters to International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs, February 10, 1995. 

The Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs (INL) advised the President, Secretary of State, other bureaus in the Department of State, and other departments and agencies within the U.S. Government on the development of policies and programs to combat international narcotics and crime. Its programs supported two of the Department's strategic goals: (1) to reduce the entry of illegal drugs into the United States; and (2) to minimize the impact of international crime on the United States and its citizens. Its counternarcotics and anticrime programs complemented the war on terrorism, both directly and indirectly, by promoting modernization of and supporting operations by foreign criminal justice systems and law enforcement agencies charged with the counter-terrorism mission.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Philippine War Damage Commission was established by the Philippine Rehabilitation Act (60 Stat. 128), approved April 30, 1946, to make compensation for physical loss or destruction of or damage to certain kinds of property, public and private, occurring in the Philippines after December 7, 1941, and before October 1, 1945, as a result of military operations. The Commission was chaired by Frank A. Waring. Other Commission members were Francisco A. Delgado and John A. O'Donnell. It held its first meeting on June 3, 1946. According to one Government historian, it "soon became hopelessly mired in bureaucratic red tape". The official historian goes on to say that the Commission was tainted by "slowness, inefficiency, and overt corruption". During its nearly five-year existence the Commission processed more than one million private claims. The first payment to the Philippine Government was made in 1946; the first individual claim was not paid until April 1947. By the time the Commission had finished its business, it had paid out $388 million against claims totaling $1.25 billion. The Commisison last met on March 29, 1951, and it ceased to exist on March 31, 1951, pursuant to provisions of the General Appropriation Act of 1951 (64 Stat. 699).

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Treaty Division was established on April 21, 1928, combining functions formerly vested in the Office of the Solictor and in the Diplomatic Bureau. It drafted treaties and other international agreements and correspondence pertaining to thne negotiation, construction, and termination of treaties. The Division was also charged with maintaining a set of treaties and other international agreements in force top which the United States was a party, as well as those to which it was not a party, together with the pertinent laws, proclamations, Executive orders, and resolutions, maintaining lists of treaties and other international agreements betweenthe United States and foreign governments which were in the process of negotiation or ratification; collecting and keeping available information regarding the application, interpretation, and status of treaties; analysing treaties by subject, and assembling, comparing, and studying the provisions of the same subject in different treaties; examining the text of treatie, conventions, or international agreements to which the United States was a party, with a view to recommending such action as may have been required to obtain the fulfilment by the other party of its duties and obligations and to effect the performance of the duties and obligations of the United States by legislative or administrative acts; and maintaining lists of treaties, conventions, or international agreements expiring or subject to extension with a view to considering the renewal or extension thereof. The Treaty Division was abolished on January 15, 1944, by Departmental Order 1218, with matters of a legal character transferred to the Treaty Branch in the Office of the Legal Advisor.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Office of the U.S. Special Representative in Europe (SRE) was created by the Economic Cooperation Act of 1948 (62 Stat. 138), approved April 3, 1948, to coordinate and supervise recovery programs in the participating European countries. Under the direction of the Special Representative, with the rank of ambassador extraordinary and plenipotentiary, he was appointed by the President and acted as the chief representative of the United States on the Organization for European Economic Cooperation, the Economic Committee for Europe, the European Coordinating Committee, the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) and other European based multinational groups. He also functioned as the direct representative of the Economic Cooperation Administration (ECA) Administrator and as the ECA field headquarters in Europe. In 1951, the Special Representative became the senior American representative for the Mutual Security Agency (MSA) when the ECA was abolished and its responsibilities transferred to the MSA. He coordinated and supervised the activities of the European country missions to develop and advance recovery programs at the local level in cooperation with the participating countries. The Office of the U.S. Special Representative in Europe was abolished in 1953, and replaced by the new U.S. Mission to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and European Regional Organizations (USRO) took over its duties.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
In 1953, the Office of the United States Representative in Europe was abolished and its functions transferred to the new U.S. Mission to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and European Regional Organizations, which had been approved by the President on June 16, 1953. The Chief of the Mission, was appointed by the President, reported to and received instructions from the Secretary of State; and served as the U.S. Permanent Representative on the North Atlantic Council (NAC) and the U.S. representative to the Ministerial Council of the Organization for European Economic Cooperation (OEEC). The USRO only functioned with NATO, OEEC, and other multilateral or supranational organizations as determined, and did not have supervisory powers over the U.S. country teams of Europe. 

At the Washington level, the Secretary of State provided necessary coordination with responsible departments and agencies and action responsibility resided primarily in the Bureau of European Affairs. Administrative services were provided by the Department of State.

Representatives of the Secretary of Defense, Secretary of Treasury, and the Director of the Foreign Operations Administration (FOA) were included in this mission. The Secretary of Defense appointed a principal representative on the USRO, who reported to him through the Chief of USRO, and served as the Defense Adviser to the Chief of USRO concerning the Secretary's responsibilities in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) and for multilateral aspects of the Mutual Security Program (MSP) in Europe, and was the head of the Defense Section of USRO. There was full coordination between the Chief of USRO and Commander-in-Chief, Europe (U.S. CINCEUR). The Chief of USRO could secure advice from U.S. CINCEUR and other military officers designated by the Secretary of Defense or the Joint Chiefs of Staff on problems falling within USRO's responsibility. The Director for FOA appointed a principal representative on USRO, who reported to him through the Chief of USRO, to handle responsibilities for multilateral mutual security program operations in Europe and was the alternate U.S. Representative to the Ministerial Council of the OEEC, the U.S. Observer on ОEEC at the working level, the Economic Adviser to the Chief of USRO, and the head of the Economic Section of USRO. The Secretary of the Treasury appointed a principal representative on USRO, who reported to him, through the Chief of USRO, and was the Financial Adviser to the Chief of USRO. 

The Departments concerned in Washington reached, under the leadership of the Secretary of State, U.S. positions which were transmitted in joint messages to the USRO and carried out by the multilateral team. The USRO sought to work out agreed joint recommendations on multilateral problems to the representative Washington departments concerned. The members of USRO did not initiate directly with officials of other governments, except for those governments' representatives on the multilateral organization, any item of U.S. business.

On July 1, 1967, the U.S. Mission to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and European Regional Organizations was redesignated as the U.S. Mission to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (USNATO).

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Division of Northern European Affairs effectuated the plans and policies formulated by the Office (and after 1949, the Bureau) of European Affairs for the conduct of U.S. relations with Denmark, Finland, Iceland, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, and the territories of those countries and the Polar regions. It directed the day-to-day conduct of U.S. relations with those countries by preparing instructions to U.S. Foreign Service establishments, conferring with foreign diplomatic representatives in the United States, and participating in conferences and meetimgs within the Department and with outside agencies. It received, studied, and evaluated information on its assigned area in order to establish a sound basis for operations and advised other divisions of the current situation. The Division anticipated major problems to be encountered in achieving the objectives and plans of the Office of European Affairs and developed subordinate objectives, plans, and programs. The Division provded the Departmental representative on the Arctic Subcommittee of the Interdepartmental Air Coordinating Committee.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Bureau of Security and Consular Affairs was established on December 24, 1952 upon the enactment of the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1952 (Public Law 82-414; 66 Stat. 174), dated June 27, 1952. The Administrator of the Bureau was ranked equal to that of an Assistant Secretary of State and was an U.S. citizen. The Bureau was responsible for administering and enforcing of immigration law, as it related to the duties and functions of diplomatic and consular officers. The Bureau was responsible for issuing passports and visas. The Administrator of the Bureau was tasked with maintaining close liaisons with Congress, the Commissioner of Immigration and Naturalization, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and with other internal security officers of the government for the purpose of obtaining and exchanging information for use in enforcing the provisions of the Immigration and Nationality Act.

In 1953, the Bureau of Security and Consular Affairs was renamed the Bureau of Security, Consular Affairs, and Personnel when it gained the Office of Personnel. On November 27, 1953, Delegation of Authority No. 74 assigned the Department of State’s responsibilities under the Refugee Relief Act of 1953 (67 Stat. 400) to the Bureau of Security and Consular Affairs. 

On March 1, 1954, the Bureau of Security, Consular Affairs, and Personnel was renamed the Bureau of Inspection, Security, and Consular Affairs. Personnel functions were transferred to the Office of the Assistant Secretary for Personnel and Administration. The Foreign Service Inspection Corps was transferred to the new Bureau on April 5, 1954. On November 3, 1954, Department of State Circular No. 123 announced that the Adviser on Refugees and Displaced Persons had been transferred from the Bureau of International Organization Affairs to the Bureau. 

On December 30, 1954, inspection functions, including the Foreign Service Inspection Corps, were transferred from the Bureau of Inspection, Security, and Consular Affairs to the Office of the Deputy Under Secretary for Administration. Concurrently, the Bureau of Inspection, Security, and Consular Affairs’ name reverted to the Bureau of Security and Consular Affairs. On March 24, 1956, Executive Order 10663 transferred responsibility for the U.S. Escapee Program, which assisted persons fleeing from Soviet-Bloc countries, from the International Cooperation Administration to the Bureau of Security and Consular Affairs.

From 1953 to 1962, the Secretary of State designated incumbents to the Administrator position. The Migration and Refugee Assistance Act of 1962 (Jun 28, 1962; P.L. 87-510; 76 Stat. 123) made the Administrator a Presidential appointee subject to the advice and consent of the Senate. In 1962, the Department transferred the security function to the Deputy Under Secretary for Administration, but the title remained unchanged until 1977. On August 17, 1977, the Foreign Relations Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 1978 (Public Law 95-105; 91 Stat. 847) increased the number of Assistant Secretaries from 11 to 13, making the Administrator of the Bureau of Security and Consular Affairs the Assistant Secretary of State for Consular Affairs and the Bureau was renamed the Bureau of Consular Affairs.

The Assistant Secretary was charged with responsibility over the welfare and protection of U.S. citizens abroad, the issuance of passports and other documentation to citizens and nationals, the protection of U.S. border security, and the facilitation of travel to the United States. 

Robert Walter Scott McLeod served as the first Administrator from February 25, 1953–1957. He was followed by Roderic L. O’Connor (1957–1958), Abba Philip Schwartz (1962–1966), Barbara Mae Watson, Acting (April 1967-1968), Barbara Mae Watson (1968–1974), Leonard Frederick Walentynowicz (1975–1977); and Barbara Mae Watson (1977). When the title changed in 1977, Barbara Mae Watson was the first Assistant Secretary of State for Consular Affairs from 1977-1980. She was the first African American and woman to hold an Assistant Secretary position in the Department of State. She was followed by Diego Cortes Asencio (1980–1983), Joan Margaret Clark (1983–1989), Elizabeth M. Tamposi (1989–1992), Mary A. Ryan (1993–2002), Maura Ann Harty (2002–2008), Janice Lee Jacobs (2008–2014), Michele Thoren Bond (2015–2017), and Carl C. Risch (2017-).

sourceNotes: 66 Statutes at Large 163, 174, 281 June 27, 1952 (Public Law 414 That this Act, divided into titles, chapters, and sections according to the following table of contents, may be cited as the "Immigration and Nationality Act"; Section 101 (a) As used in this Act- (1) The term "administrator'' means the administrator of the Bureau of Security and Consular Affairs of the Department of State. (8) The terms "Commissioner" and "Deputy Commissioner" mean the Commissioner of Immigration and Naturalization and a Deputy Commissioner of Immigration and Naturalization, respectively; Sec. 104 SEC. 104. (a) The Secretary of State shall be charged with the ad-ministration and the enforcement of the provisions of this Act and all other immigration and nationality laws relating to (1) the powers, duties and functions of diplomatic and consular officers of the United States, except those powers, duties and functions conferred upon the consular officers relating to the granting or refusal of visas; (2) the powers, duties and functions of the Bureau of Security and Consular Affairs; and (3) the determination of nationality of a person not in the United States…(b) There is hereby established in the Department of State a Bureau of Security and Consular Affairs, to be headed by an administrator (with an appropriate title to be designated by the Secretary of State), with rank and compensation equal to that of an Assistant Secretary of State. The administrator shall be a citizen of the United States, qualified by experience, and shall maintain close liaison with the appropriate committees of Congress in order that they may be advised regarding the administration of this Act by consular officers. He shall be charged with any and all responsibility and authority in the administration of the Bureau and of this Act which are conferred on the Secretary of State as may be delegated to him by the Secretary of State or which may be prescribed by the Secretary of State. He shall also perform such other duties as the Secretary of State may prescribe. (f) The Bureau shall be under the immediate jurisdiction of the Deputy Under Secretary of State for Administration. SEC. 407. Except as provided in subsection (k) of section 401, this Act shall take effect at 12:01 ante meridian United States Eastern Standard Time on the one hundred eightieth day immediately following the date of its enactment. (c) Within the Bureau there shall be a Passport Office, a Visa Office, and such other offices as the Secretary of State may deem to be appropriate, each office to be headed by a director. The Directors of the Passport Office and the Visa Office shall be experienced in the administration of the nationality and immigration laws, (d) The functions heretofore performed by the Passport Division and the Visa Division of the Department of State shall hereafter be performed by the Passport Office and the Visa Office, respectively, of the Bureau of Security and Consular Affairs. Sec. 105 The Commissioner and the administrator shall have authority to maintain direct and continuous liaison with the Directors of the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the Central Intelligence Agency and with other internal security officers of the Government for the purpose of obtaining and exchanging information for use in enforcing the provisions of this Act in the interest of the internal security of the United States. The Commissioner and the administrator shall maintain direct and continuous liaison with each other with a view to a coordinated, uniform, and efficient administration of this Act, and all other immigration and nationality laws.)

Department of State Bulletin, vol. 28, no. 710, February 2, 1953: p. 195 (The Immigration and Nationality Act was enacted on June 27, 1952, over a Presidential veto, to become effective December 24, 1952. [Footnote: Public Law 414, 82d Cong., 2d sess.]…The act provides for the creation within the Department of State of a Bureau of Security and Consular Affairs, under an administrator. The Bureau will include a Passport Ofﬁce, a Visa Ofﬁce, and such other offices as the Secretary of State may establish, under separate directors.)

Department of State Bulletin, vol. 28, no. 715, March 9, 1953: p. 391 (The Department of State on February 25 (press release 104) announced the appointment of Robert Walter Scott McLeod, of Concord. N. H. as Administrator of the Bureau of Security and Consular Affairs…Mr. McLeod will have responsibility for security and consular affairs. as well as personnel. These responsibilities were formerly under the general supervision of the Deputy Under Secretary of State for Administration. As Administrator of the Bureau of Security and Consular Affairs, Mr. McLeod will have general supervision over the operations of the Office of Security, the Passport Office, the Visa Office, the Office of Protective Services. and the Munitions Office. In addition he will have supervision over the Office of Personnel. He will be directly responsible to Under Secretary of State for Administration Donold Lourie and, through Mr. Lourie, to the Secretary of State.)

Department of State Bulletin, vol. 30, no. 768, March 15, 1954: p. 413 (Press release 102 dated March 1, 1954 Pursuant to instructions of the Secretary of State, the following changes in organization and assignment of responsibility are announced, effective at once: (c) The “Bureau of Security, Consular Affairs and Personnel” is designated the “Bureau of Inspection, Security and Consular Affairs,” under the administration of Mr. McLeod. The functions of personnel administration previously performed by this Bureau are transferred to the office of Assistant Secretary for Personnel Administration. Inspection functions in the Department are made a responsibility of the Administrator, Bureau of Inspection, Security and Consular Affairs, under the general supervision of the Deputy Under Secretary (Administration).)

Department of State Bulletin, vol. 32, no. 812, January 17, 1955: p. 113 (Department circular dated December 30 2. The name of the Bureau of Inspection, Security and Consular Affairs, is changed to “Bureau of Security and Consular Affairs” (SCA).)

Department of State Newsletter, no. 187, February 1977: p. 9, 10 (President Carter has named eight heads of functional bureaus in the Department. Three of the eight are being retained. Nominations of the others are subject to Senate confirmation. Named were: Barbara M. Watson, who is returning as Administrator of the Bureau of Security and Consular Affairs, which she headed from August 1968 to January 1975. Miss Watson, who held the rank of Assistant Secretary, will succeed Leonard F. Walentynowicz; As head of the Bureau of Security and Consular Affairs, Miss Watson was the first woman and also the first black to hold a position at so senior a level in the State Department. If confirmed by the Senate, Miss Watson will administer a $60,000,000 consular program, including executive direction of a bureau comprising nearly 1,000 employees in the United States. She will also have technical direction of 2,000 other employees in over 250 Foreign Service posts over the world. Miss Watson joined the Department in July 1966 as Special Assistant to the Deputy Under Secretary for Administration. She was appointed Deputy Administrator of the Bureau in October 1966, and Acting Administrator in April 1967.)

Department of State Newsletter, no. 193, August-September 1977: p. 3, 5 (Foreign Relations Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 1978, which President Carter signed on August 17. Among other things, the 1978: establishes two new assignat secretaryships in the Department, bestowing this title on ranking officials whose functions otherwise are not changed; Patricia M. Derian and Barbara M. Watson automatically became assistant secretaries of state when the President signed the 1978 Act. They remain in their posts, respectively, as coordinator for human rights and humanitarian affairs and as administrator of consular affairs — but they have the new titles. Ms. Watson's Bureau of Security and Consular Affairs gets a new name — the Bureau of Consular Affairs. The Act says that the persons holding the previous titles on the date of enactment would become assistant secretaries "and shall not be required to be reappointed by reason of the enactment of this section.")

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The U.S. Mission to the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) was established in September 1957, with the appointment of Ambassador Robert Moody McKinney as the first Permanent Representative, but from 1957 through 1999, the Permanent Representative of the USA to the IAEA was not resident in Vienna, Austria but was based in Washington, D.C. In order to have a physical presence in the absence of the Permanent representative, in September 1961, a Resident Representative of the USA to the IAEA was assigned as Principal Officer for the U.S. Mission to the IAEA. This position did not come with an Ambassadorial rank until 1970. In May 1983, the U.S. Mission to the United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO) and the U.S. Mission to the IAEA were merged into, the U.S. Mission to International Organizations in Vienna, under the leadership of a resident Ambassador and Permanent Representative.

The U.S. government maintained an office in Vienna to provide day-to-day contact with, and representation to, the IAEA. Such duties were carried out for most member states by embassy personnel, in addition to their work in connection with relations with Austria. In the case of the U.S., separate diplomatic offices or "missions" represented its interests to the IAEA and the UN-related agencies (principally UNIDO) in Vienna. The U.S. Mission was headed by an Ambassador appointed by the President and confirmed by the U.S. Senate. He or she was assisted by a staff of officers of whom four deal exclusively with IAEA matters, while some of the others are assigned to deal with certain aspects of all of the international organizations, including the IAEA. The Mission provided liaison with the IAEA, evaluated and reported on IAEA plans and activities, consulted with the representatives of other governments, and in other ways advanced the interests of the U.S. government in the IAEA. All officers in the U.S. Mission were employees of the Department of State. Some were Foreign Service Officers or other career employees of the Department of State, while others may have been on loan to the Department from another agency, such as the Department of Energy (DOE), or the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC). The Mission reported to, and received instructions from, the Department of State. Within the Department, several offices had major interests in the IAEA, including the Bureau of International Organizations, the Bureau of Oceans and International Environmental and Scientific Affairs, and the Office of the Ambassador-at-Large for Non-Proliferation. The Department of Energy and the NRC also had continuing interests in many IAEA activities, were kept informed of developments, and were consulted by the Department of State in preparing its instructions to the Mission.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Coordinator determined the policies of the agency, directed the activities of its corporations, and handled top-liaison activities with officials of the United States Government, the governments of the other American Republics, and the heads of private organizations. He was the Chairman of the Inter-American Development Commission and the Committee on Inter-American Affairs and served on other international and interdepartmental committees, including the Mexican -American Commission for Economic Cooperation, the Committee on Inter-American Shipping, the Inter-American Financial and Economic Advisory Committee, the Inter-American Shipping Commission, the Inter-Departmental Committee on Hemisphere Communications, the International Broadcasting Committee, and the Inter-Departmental Committee for Political Warfare. The Coordinator also made funds available for the establishment of the Inter-American Institute of Agricultural Sciences to continue the work, previously carried on by the Inter-American Committee on Tropical Agriculture, of promoting the production of strategic crops, particularly rubber. He had as his immediate assistants a number of special advisors, including the Brazilian Consultant, the Consultant in Port Management, and the Advisor for Civic Projects; the General Counsel; and various committees of the Office. One of his assistants represented the United States Government at the First Pan American Congress of Mining Engineering and Geology held at Santiago, Chile, January 15-23, 1942, at which an all-out mineral production program for pan-American defense was recommended.

Nelson A. Rockefeller served as Coordinator from July 30, 1941 through December 4, 1944. Wallace K. Harrison, heretofor the Deputy Coordinator, served as Coordinator from December 4, 1944 through March 23, 1945.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: Mr. William Phillips was appointed officially as Representative of the Secretary of State of the United States at the Headquarters of the Supreme Allied Commander on September 14, 1943. He was generally referred to as the U.S. Political Advisor or the U.S. Political Liaison Officer and enjoyed the rank of Ambassador. On February 29, 1944, his position title was regularized as Political Officer. His British counterpart was Charles Peake of the Foreign office. From February 29, 1944, he also served as the representative of the Department of State on the London Combined Civil Affairs Committee. Ambassador Phillips took up office at Norfolk House, London in late September 1943 and served until about September 2, 1944.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Permanent Joint Board on Defense, United States and Canada was an advisory body established at Ogdensburg, New York, August 18, 1940, by Prime Minister Mackenzie King of Canada and President Franklin D. Roosevelt for the United States. Its functions were to study sea, land, and air problems, including personnel and materiel, and to consider, in the broad sense, the joint defense of the northern half of the Western Hemisphere by the United States and Canada.  It consisted of both Canadian and American military and civilian members. During the war the Chairman of the United States Section was Fiorello H. La Guardia and the other U.S. members represented the State, War, and Navy Departments; and the Secretariat was provided by the Department of State. At the end of December 1947 the U.S. military representatives were placed under the Joint Chiefs of Staff.

Recommendations of the Board to the two Governments during World War II resulted in the building of the Alaska Highway, the construction of a chain of airfields between Edmonton, Canada and Alaska, and the construction of other projects on Labrador, Newfoundland and Alaska by the United States and Canadian military and civilian forces. Following the war The Board examined every important joint defens measure, including construction of the Distant Early Warning (DEW) Line of radars, the creation of the North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD) in 1958, the bi-national operation of the underwater acoustic surveillance system and high-frequency direction finding network, and the decision to proceed with the North American Air Defence Modernization program in 1985.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Office of Special Political Affairs was created by Departmental Order 1218, January 15, 1944. It was redesignated the Office of United Nations Affairs, January 21, 1948 (Departmental Announcement 943). Secretary of State Dean Acheson upgraded the Office to the Bureau of International Organization Affairs (IO) on June 24, 1949, as part of U.S. efforts to meet the needs of post-World War II diplomacy. Several months later, in October 1949, IO was renamed the Bureau for United Nations Affairs (UNA). (Departmental Announcement 191, October 27, 1949). The Department of State created the position of Assistant Secretary of State for United Nations Affairs in February 1949, using one of the six Assistant secretary positions originally authorized by Congress in 1944 (Dec. 8, 1944; P.L. 78-472; 58 Stat. 798). On Aug 25, 1954, a Department administrative action changed the incumbent's designation to Assistant Secretary of State for International Organization Affairs, and the Bureau was renamed the Bureau of International Organization Affairs. (Department Circular 349, February 4, 1960). 

The Bureau of International Organization Affairs, developed and implemented  U.S. policy in the United Nations (UN), the UN's specialized agencies, and other international organizations. The Bureau worked in cooperation with the U.S. Mission to the UN; the U.S. Mission to the United Nations, Geneva; the U.S. Mission to the United Nations, Rome;  the U.S. Mission to International Organizations in Vienna; the U.S. Mission to the United Nations Education, Science and Culture Organization; and and other international organizations. It worked to advance U.S. policies and interests through multilateral diplomacy. The Bureau worked to ensure that the UN and other international organizations remained viable and effective.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: Officially called "The United States Permanent Mission to the United Nations Office and Other International Organizations in Geneva," the Mission's role was to represent the U.S. government in Geneva. The U.S. Mission handled all dealings and communications with the United Nations and other international agencies in Geneva, as well as with the 100-plus countries that also maintained permanent missions to the UN in Geneva. This "multilateral" role of the Mission dealing with many countries was separate from the "bilateral" diplomacy of the U.S. Embassy in the Swiss capital Bern, which handled relations between the U.S. government and Switzerland. In practice, the Mission carried out its work by attending meetings on any subject of interest to the United States. U.S. Mission staff officers, together with delegates from Washington, were involved in some 300 Geneva-based conferences a year, promoting U.S. policy, representing U.S. interests and helping countries benefit from U.S. experience. The Mission was also the site of bilateral and multilateral negotiations on a variety of security, economic and political issues. During 1993-1994, the United States and North Korea met in Geneva to work out the details of a nuclear agreement under which North Korea agreed to freeze its nuclear program and abide by its obligations under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation treaty. During 1995, the Mission hosted important negotiations on the former Yugoslavia in the lead-up to the Dayton Accords. On September 8, 1995 representatives of the governments of Bosnia, Croatia and Serbia, holding their first face-to-face meeting in nearly two years at the U.S. Mission, agreed on a set of basic principles which were later embodied in the Dayton agreement.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The U.S. Embassy at Belize was established on October 29, 1981, when the Consulate General was raised to embassy status. Malcom R. Barnebey served as Charge d'Affaires ad interim until he was promoted to Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary, presenting his credentials on June 23, 1983. He was succeeded by Keith Guthrie who served as Charge d'Affaires ad interim from July 1985 through September 1987. Robert G. Rich presented his credentials as Ambassador on September 14, 1987. He was succeeded by Eugene L. Scassa, November 22, 1990; George Charles Bruno, August 29, 1994; Carolyn Curiel, January 19, 1998; and Russell F. Freeman, September 11, 2001.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Special Committee on Migration and Resettlement was established by a June 1, 1943 memorandum of the Assistant Secretary of State, Adolph A. Berle, Jr.  Its functions were set forth in terms of reference set forth by the Assistant Secretary the next day: the Committee was to consider issues attending the liberation of enemy-held territories such as the migration of populations and repatriation of military prisoners, forced laborers, and refugees. It was an advisory body, making its recommendations to the Post-War Economic Committee. Ambassador H.F. Arthur Schoenfeld served as Committee chair; Eleanor Lansing Dulles served as Secretary. The Committee included among its members representatives of the War and Nay Departments. The Commitee met for the first time on June 23, 1943 and last and fifteenth meeting on November 4, 1944. The Committee was dissolved in March 1945 on the recommendation of Ambassador Schoenfeld.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Economic Survey Mission to the Philippines, often refered to as the Bell Mission, was a U.S. body appointed to survey the Philippine economy and make recommendations as to its improvement.

In a statement issued to the press on June 29, 1950, President Harry S. Truman announced that the U.S. Government, at the request of the Philippine President, was sending an economic survey mission to make recommendations on measures of self-help which might be taken by the Philippine Government, and to make recommendations on ways in which the United States might be helpful. As Chief of Mission the President named Daniel W. Bell, President of the American Security and Trust Company and former Under Secretary of the Treasury. He acted as the President Truman's personal representative, with the personal rank of Ambassador, and reported directly to the President. On July 7, the Department of State announced the membership of the Economic Survey Mission. Major General Richard J. Marshall (retired), Superintendent of the Virginia Military Institute served as Deputy Chief of Mission, with the personal rank of Minister. He was joined by Edward M. Bernstein, August L. Strand, and Francis McQuillin.

A letter dated July 13, 1950, from the President to Bell, discussed and approved by the National Advisory Council in Action No. 408 of the meeting of July 5, and later slightly revised by the White House and the Bureau of the Budget, set forth the terms of reference for the Mission. The Mission would survey generally the Philippine economy including internal and external finances, public administration, agriculture, mining, industry, domestic and foreign trade and related matters, and would make recommendations concerning both immediate measures necessary to prevent further deterioration and also a longer term plan designed to achieve permanent economic viability and steady progress in Philippine productivity and living standards. It was to work closely with the Philippine Government and maintain close liaison with the Embassy in Manila, but would function as an independent group.

After field trips to the Philippines in the summer of 1950, the Mission submitted its report to the President on October 9, 1950. It recommended that the UnIted States provide the Philippines with $250M in loans and grants over a five-year period. In addition, it recommended that a long-term mission be sent to the Philippines. 

Bell submitted his resignation on October 18, 1950.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Secretary's Open Forum Panel (OFP) was established in May 1967 by Secretary Dean Rusk to encourage "innovation and creativity."

Membership in the Secretary's Open Forum Panel was open to all interested employees of the Department of State, the Agency for International Development (A.I.D.), and U.S. Arms Control and Disarmament Agency CDA). The active membership of the OFP elected a chairman and vice chairman annually. The Director of Planning and Coordination (S/PC) (1970 - 73), who was responsible for encouraging and supporting the work of the OFP, assigned an executive secretary to the Panel. 

In accordance with the Secretary's concept and the Task Force recommendations, the Open Forum Panel met with the Secretary and other senior officers of the Department and discussed ideas and suggestions submitted by employees in the Department or at post aboard; worked closely with S/PC in receiving, transmitting to senior officers, and responding to expressions of divergent opinion and creative dissent on policy matters submitted to the Department by employees'; served as a forum for discussion of policies and programs; was a link with outside individuals and groups, especially youth groups, and, where appropriate, serves as a channel for their ideas.

The Open Forum Panel was still in existence as of 2002.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: SHAEF continued a practice started at Allied Force Headquarters (AFHQ) which was to have civilian officials advise the Supreme Commander about the political implications of proposed actions. These officials, known as Political Officers or Political Advisers, were diplomats appointed by either the British Foreign Office or the U.S. Department of State to serve at SHAEF. The officers gave advice particularly with respect to intelligence matters, psychological warfare, civil affairs and military government, and post-hostilities planning. In September 1944, Ambassador Robert D. Murphy was appointed Political Adviser for German Affairs. The political advisers had their independent staffs. Ordinarily they carried on their activities through the Chief of Staff. but enjoyed direct access to the Supreme Commander, later Military Governor.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
On November 1, 1949, the Bureau of German Affairs was organized to replace the Office of German and Austrian Affairs. All staff were transferred to the new Bureau with the exception of the former Division of Austrian Affairs, which was transferred to the Bureau of European Affairs. The Bureau was created shortly after control over occupied Germany was transferred from the U.S. Army to the Department of State, in preparation for the independence of the newly formed Federal Republic of Germany.

Henry A. Byroade was commissioned by the President as the director of the Bureau. The Director held rank equivalent to an Assistant Secretary of State. His successor, James Williams Riddleberger, was designated as Director by the Secretary of State on May 14, 1952. He was followed by Geoffrey Whitney Lewis who served as Acting Director from 1952 to 1953.

On November 2, 1953, the Bureau of German Affairs was abolished and its functions transferred to the Bureau of European Affairs. The Office of German Affairs was established within the new bureau to discharge the functions formerly performed by the Bureau. Directors included: Geoffrey Whitney Lewis, acting, November 2, 1953-Feburary 7, 1954; Cecil B. Lyon, 1954-1955; Jacques Joseph Reinstein, acting, 1955-1956, Jacques Joseph Reinstein, August 15, 1956-1958; Martin Joseph Hillenbrand, September 7, 1958-1962; Robert Calhoun Creel, 1962-1964; and Alfred Puhan, 1964-1966.

On April 25, 1966, Foreign Affairs Manual Circular 401 established nine Country Directors in the Bureau of European Affairs, effective July 1, 1966. This included the Country Director for Germany. By 1971, Country was dropped by the name. The Country Directors and Directors included: Alfred Puhan, 1966-July 1, 1968; Alexander C. Johnpoll, acting, July 1, 1968-June 1969; and James S. Sutterlin, June 1969-1972.

On April 15, 1972, the Office of the Director for Germany and the Austria and Switzerland functions of the Office of the Director for Austria, Italy, and Switzerland were combined into a new Office of Central European Affairs (EUR/ CE).

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
On March 8, 1945, the Office of the Assistant Secretary for Congressional Relations and International Conferences was changed to the Office of the Assistant Secretary for Congressional Relations by Departmental Order 1310. The Office of the Assistant Secretary for Congressional Relations was responsible for maintaining liaison with the Congress on all matters of interest to the Department, with the exception of matters relating to the budget or to fiscal or other administrative operations. In collaboration with the competent Departmental office or offices, the Office wa responsible for the preparation and presentation to the congress of all legislation (including the submission of treaties and conventions to the Senate for advise and consent to ratification). It was also responsible for liaison with the Bureau of the Budget on all matters of interest to the Department, with the exception of matters involving the budget or fiscal or other administrative operations. On April 11, 1983, the Office was redesigned the Office of the Assistant Secretary of State for Legislative and Intergovernmental Affairs. On October 2, 1987, it was redesignated as the Office of the Assistant Secretary of State for Legislative Affairs.

The Assistant Secretaries for Congressional Relations included: Ernest A. Gross,  March 8, 1949-October 13, 1949; Jack K. McFall, October 15, 1949-Sepember 9, 1952; Robert C. Hill, March 9, 1956-June 26, 1957; William B. Macomber, Jr., October 21, 1957-February 27, 1961; Brooks Hays, February 28, 1961-December 3, 1961; Frederick G. Dutton, December 4, 1961-July 27, 1964; Douglas MacArthur, II, March 14, 1965-March 6, 1967; William B. Macomber, Jr., March 7, 1967-October 2, 1969; David M. Abshire, April 20, 1970-January 8, 1973; Marshall Wright, May 29, 1973-Febuary 2, 1974; A. Linwood Holton, February 28, 1974-January 31, 1975; Robert J. The Assistant Secretary in charge of congressional relations is hereby relieved from responsibility for the coordination and direction of the conduct of international conferences nd section 2, paragraph 2, of Departmental Order 1301 is amended to define the responsibilities of the Assistant Secretary in charge of Congressional relations as follows: (a) The Assistant Secretary in charge of congressional relations shall have responsibility for maintaining liaison with the congress on all matters of interest to the Department, with the exception of matters relating to the budget or to fiscal or other administrative operations. In collaboration with the competent Departmental office or offices, he shall be responsible for the preparation and presentation to the congress of all legislation (including the submission of treaties and conventions to the Senate for advise and consent to ratification). creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The State Department's Bureau of International Organization Affairs developed and implemented the policies of the U.S. Government within the United Nations and its affiliated agencies, as well as within certain other international organizations. The Bureau did this via nine offices in Washington and seven field missions: in New York, Geneva, Vienna, Rome, Paris, Montreal, and Nairobi. Together, the various elements of the Bureau engaged in what was known as "multilateral diplomacy" to promote and defend the many overlapping interests of the American people. Subject areas addressed by the Bureau included: peacekeeping, democracy and human rights, humanitarian and refugee assistance, international trade, economic development, safe food production, transportation safety, public health, terrorism, and the environment. To meet these objectives, the Bureau also promoted effective and efficient management within the international organizations themselves.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: In March 1942 a Division of Inter-American Activities in the United States was established, combining two previously existing units:  the Civic Organizations Section of the Information Division, which worked chiefly with women's groups;  and the Hospitality Section of the Cultural Relations Division, which entertained visiting Latin American officials and others.  The new Division organized a small Lectures and Materials Section to disseminate educational materials and compile lists of speakers.  It became a part of the Department of Information Services when that Department was organized in February 1943. By then Division activities were being carried out by four sections-- Inter-American Centers, Major Key Groups, Spanish and Portuguese Minorities, and a Speakers Service Bureau. The Division of Inter-American Activities in the United States was elevated to departmental status when the Information Services Department was dissolved in September 1943.  By October 1944 the name of the Department had been changed to Department of Special Services.  It consisted of an Education and Teacher Aids Division; a Services and Field Coordination Division, which took over the functions of the former Lectures and Materials Section; a Labor Relations Division; and sections working with reception centers for Latin American visitors, Spanish- and Portuguese-speaking minorities, and key groups. The Labor Relations Division, formed in 1944, continued inter-American labor functions formerly administered by a labor relations unit of the Emergency Rehabilitation Division.  The Division advised the Coordinator, other Government agencies, and private organizations on matters relating to inter-American labor relations, developed programs to promote close relations between labor groups in the United States and Latin America, accumulated data on labor groups in Latin America, and helped prepare various publications. The Department of Special Services was aboolished and most of its functions discontinued in the fall of 1945, except for the Labor Relations Division, which continued to function until the OIAA was terminated in May 1946.  The program of the Education and Teacher Aids Division was transferred to the Office of Education in the Federal Security Agency.
