creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The creation of a science office in the Department of State and a corps of overseas science officers had its origins in several studies undertaken during and after World War II and a 1947 experiment of a small staff of sciences stationed at the U.S. Embassy in London, England. In June 1950, a report entitled “Science and Foreign Relations”, also referred to as the Berker Report, recommended the creation of a science staff in the Department of State, headed by a scientific adviser who would be a Special Assistant to the Under Secretary and the creation of Foreign Service science staffs in U.S. diplomatic missions abroad.

On February 6, 1951, the Office of the Science Adviser was established under the Office of the Under Secretary of State by Departmental Announcement 31. The functions of the former Office of the Consultant to the Secretary of State on international science matters transferred to the new Office. The purpose of the program was to provide advice to the Secretary of State and his staff on policy matters in which scientific developments could affect U.S. foreign relations. The Science Adviser, as a principal staff officer of the Department of State, except in the field of atomic energy matters, was assigned the following responsibilities: participate in the formulation of foreign policy from the standpoint of science and technology; ensure that, in the administration of international programs and policies, proper consideration was given to scientific and technological aspects; and serve as a central point of liaison with the National Science Foundation, the National Research Council, the National Academy of Sciences, and other public and private organizations interested in the formulation and administration of policy relating to science and technology. It also coordinated the Department’s activities in the international exchange of basic scientific information and directed the work of science attachés overseas. The Science Adviser was assisted by a small staff, composed principally of scientists.

On February 7, 1953, the Office of the Science Advisor moved under the new Office of the Under Secretary for Administration, until April 6, 1954, when it returned to the Office of the Under Secretary.

Despite its successful operation, however, the program was curtailed after a few years because of a number of factors, which included a limited budget. After the science attachés returned to Washington at the end of 1955, their positions were not filled, which terminated the scientific attaché program. Meanwhile, the Office of the Science Adviser was maintained in the Department and was constantly called on by other Department units and other agencies for advice and assistance on foreign relations questions in which scientific factors were intertwined. 

Following a review of the Department's science program, the decision was made in the summer of 1957 that the growing importance of scientific developments in formulating foreign policy and carrying on relations with other governments called for a new emphasis in this field. As Walter M. Rudolph, Foreign Affairs Officer who was tasked as the Assistant to the Science Adviser, had been in charge of the Office since 1954; the first task was to obtain the services of a notable scientific administrator with worldwide reputation in his discipline and had the respect of the international scientific community. 

On January 13, 1958, Dr. Wallace R. Brode was appointed as the Science Adviser. He was made directly responsible to the Secretary of State, and participated in daily staff meetings of the Secretary and his principal officials. During 1958, an intensive effort was made to obtain the services of qualified scientists for scientific attachés positions. By the end of the year, the Department's overseas Science Officer Program was firmly reestablished.

The reorganized Office of the Science Adviser brought to the consideration of the Secretary those scientific developments at home and abroad which could have important implications in the formulation and implementation of policy. The Science Adviser and his staff provided assistance to Department officers in working out decisions on issues having scientific implications, backstopped the work of the corps of scientific attachés stationed abroad, represented the Department's interests on various interdepartmental committees, and maintained liaison with governmental, quasi-official, and nongovernmental organizations. To a great extent the work of the science staff was involved in reconciling the scientific objectives of such organizations and of private scientists with the overall objectives and requirements of American foreign policy.

The Office of the Science Adviser cooperated with the National Academy of Sciences in connection with the 1957-58 International Geophysical Year (IGY). The Science Adviser served as an ex-officio member on the U.S.-IGY National Committee. The Office facilitated the planning of those phases of the IGY program which required formal intergovernmental agreements, such as the establishment of earth-satellite tracking stations in Central and South America. 

During 1958 and 1959, the Office of the Science Adviser was actively involved in the preparation of the Antarctic Treaty, which was signed on December 1, 1959 to provide international scientific cooperation and that the Antarctic would be used for peaceful purposes only. In the 1960s, the Office’s functions expanded to include the peaceful uses of outer space and atomic energy.

In the exercise of its responsibilities, the Office worked closely with the geographic and functional units of the Department such as those concerned with disarmament, political and economic affairs, exchange of persons, and passports and visas. Its work frequently required collaboration with other agencies of the Government, and drew upon the technical or scientific resources of these agencies for the solution of foreign affairs problems. 

The Office worked closely with the Office of the President's Special Assistant for Science and Technology. Subjects of mutual concern included: oceanography, the uses of outer space, materials research, and the coordination of governmental activities in the field of science. The President's Special Assistant and the Department's Science Adviser also maintained close liaison through their association on some of the President's principal science committees, including the President's Science Advisory Committee and several of its panels. The Science Adviser also was an observer on the Federal Council for Science and Technology and the chairman of the Council's subcommittee on international science.

The Science Advisers included: Joseph B. Koepfli, February 13, 1951-July 1953; J. W. Joyce, Acting, July 1953-February 1954; Wallace R. Brode, January 13, 1958-September 1960; and Walter G. Whitman, September 1960-September 14, 1962. During February 1954 to January 1954, Walter M. Rudolph, a Foreign Affairs Officer and Assistant to the Science Adviser, was in charge.

On September 14, 1962, the Office of the Science Adviser’s functions were absorbed into the new Office of International Science Affairs.

sourceNotes: Department of State Bulletin, vol. 24, no. 612, March 26, 1951: p. 519 (Office of Science Adviser Established 1. Effective immediately, there is established, under the direction of the Under Secretary of State, the Office of the Science Adviser (U/SA). The Office of the Consultant to the Secretary of State on international science matters provided for in Departmental Announcement 201, November 1, 1949, is hereby abolished and its personnel and functions, as redefined below, are transferred to the Office of the Science Adviser. 2. The Office of the Science Adviser shall function as an integral component of the Department, utilizing the Department's staff services and facilities, and shall conduct its activities pursuant to its own terms of reference and those of other components of the Department as prescribed below and in the Manual of Regulations and Procedures, Volume II, Organization.3. The Science Adviser, as a principal staff officer of the Department, except in the field of atomic energy matters, has been assigned the following responsibilities: a. Participates in the formulation of foreign policy from the standpoint of Science and technology. b. Provides that, in the administration of international programs and policies, proper consideration is given to scientific and technological aspects. c. Serves as a central point of liaison with the National Science Foundation, the National Research Council, the National Academy of Sciences, and other public and private organizations interested in the formulation and administration of policy relating to science and technology. d. Coordinates the activities of the Department in the international exchange of basic scientific information. (Departmental Announcement 31, Feb. 6, 1951.)
Department of State Bulletin, vol. 32, no. 821, March 21, 1955: p. 474 (in the Under Secretary's Office, that of Science Adviser of the Department, was established in 1951)

Department of State Bulletin, vol. 38, no. 971, February 3, 1958: p. 190 (The Department of State announced on January 13 (press release 11) the appointment of Dr. Wallace R. Brode as Science Adviser. He was sworn in by Secretary Dulles on that day and immediately assumed his new duties...Dr. Brode will advise the Secretary and other Department officers on matters relating to scientific developments which affect foreign policy and will direct the work of science attaches overseas)

Department of State Newsletter, No. 18, October 1962: p. 35 (The Department took another step last month to strengthen the link between foreign policy and science by establishing the Office of International Science Affairs...The new office will absorb the functions previously carried out under Dr. Walter G. Whitman who served the Department as Science Adviser from September 1960 to September 1962. During Dr. Whitman's tenure the Science Adviser's functions were expanded to include the peaceful uses of outer space and atomic energy.)

Department of State, April 6, 2020 (February 6, 1951 Dr. Joseph B. Koepfli was appointed as Science Adviser. He served until 1955. The Office of the Science Adviser, under the direction of the Under Secretary of State, replaced the Office of the Consultant to the Secretary on International Science Matters. February 7, 1953 An Act of Congress (67 Stat. 4) established the position of Under Secretary of State for Administration. The new Under Secretary became the third-ranking officer in the Department, but the position was only authorized until December 31, 1954, and was allowed to lapse after two years. Officers reporting to the Under Secretary for Administration were...and the Science Adviser. April 6, 1954 The Office of the Science Adviser was transferred from the Office of the Under Secretary for Administration to the Office of the Under Secretary. January 13, 1958 The position of Science Adviser was revived with the appointment of Dr. Wallace R. Brode)

Science, Technology and American Diplomacy: Science and Technology in the Department of State: Brining Technical Content into Diplomatic Policy and Operations, June 1975:  p. 24-28 (The Berkner Report of June 1950 on Science and Foreign Relations recommended creation of a science staff in the Department of State, headed by a scientific adviser who would be Special Assistant to the Under Secretary. He would also be supported by science staffs in certain overseas missions, integrated into the Foreign Service. Accordingly, the following February, Dr. Joseph B. Koepfli...was appointed Science Adviser; When Dr. Koepfli returned to California Institute of Technology, July 1953, Dr. Joyce became “Acting” until he resigned in February 1954, and Walter M. Rudolph, a Foreign Affairs Officer, took over. The attachés (in London, Paris, and Stockholm) were replaced with other scientists and a fourth was named to the Embassy in Tokyo, but at the end of 1955 the scientific attaché program was completely terminated; By 1956 the State Department science organization had dwindled to a caretaker Foreign Service Officer, Walter M. Rudolph (an economist), supported by two secretaries....Rudolph himself went into print, early in 1957, to make a mild appeal for support. Identified as “Assistant to the Science Adviser” (a vacant office), he noted that his Department “–specifically the Office of the Science Adviser–had been asked by the National Academy of Sciences] to serve on the U.S.-IGY National Committee as ex officio member.”; Accordingly, in January 1958...Secretary Dulles reestablished his science office, naming it “Science Adviser to the Department of State,” and appointed to the post Dr. Wallace R. Brode...He remained in the State Department position until September 1960; Upon his retirement in 1960 he was followed by Dt. Walter G. Whitman; Thus, in September 1962, Dr. Ragnar Rollefson, professor of physics at the University of Wisconsin, was named to succeed Whitman and at the same time the title was changed to “Director of International Scientific Affairs.” His rank and duties were spelled out in a Foreign Affairs Manual Circular, “Director of International Scientific Affairs,” (No. S4, Sept. 14, 1962.))

The Department of State Bulletin, vol. 25, no. 651, December 17, 1951: p. 969 (In accordance with the recommendations of the report, Science and Foreign Relations, the Office of the Science Adviser was established last February in the Department directly under and responsible to the Under Secretary of State)

The Science Adviser of the Department of State, 1960: p. 2, 4-11, 14-17, (As a result of such increased recognition of the need for scientific advice in formulating foreign policy, the wartime experience of several governmental scientific organizations operating overseas, and three major studies of the relation of science and government under taken in the war and postwar period, the Department of State in 1951 established its first formal science program. The basic purpose of the program is to provide advice to the Secretary of State and his staff on those policy matters in which scientific developments may affect U.S. foreign relations. The organizational machinery for the program consists of the Office of the Science Adviser in Washington and the corps of science officers overseas whose activity it directs; The creation of a science office in the Department of State and a corps of science officers abroad had its origins, as stated earlier, in several studies undertaken during and after the war…In 1947 the State Department established at the Embassy at London a small staff of scientists representing various scientific disciplines. This project, carried out on an experimental basis, had as its object the continuation of the liaison between British and American scientists...A survey was made by Dr. Lloyd V. Berkner…published in June 1950 under the title Science and Foreign Relations…the Berkner report recommended the creation of a science staff in the Department to be headed by a Scientific Adviser appointed as Special Assistant to the Under Secretary of State. It proposed also the establishment of science staffs at selected U.S. diplomatic missions abroad, integrated into the normal Foreign Service structure of the missions. Acting on the Berkner report, the Department of State in February 1951 established the Office of the Science Adviser. Dr. Joseph B. Koepfli, of the California Institute of Technology, was appointed Science Adviser and was made directly responsible to the Under Secretary of State. He was assisted by a small staff, composed principally of scientists. In addition, science staffs were established at several missions abroad, to which scientists of international reputation were assigned as attachés...Despite its successful operation, however, the program was curtailed after a few years because of a number of factors, of which undoubtedly the most important was the competing demands of other Departmental activities for their share of a limited budget. Dr. Koepfli returned to the California Institute of Technology in July 1953, and Dr. J. W. Joyce, who served as Acting Science Adviser after that time, resigned in February 1954. The Office of the Science Adviser continued, however, to operate actively in the Department under the guidance of Walter M. Rudolph, a foreign affairs officer...October 1954. After these attachés returned to Washington at the end of 1955, their positions abroad were not filled. Meanwhile, the Science Adviser’s Office was maintained in the Department and was constantly being called on by other Department units and other agencies for advice and assistance on foreign relations questions in which scientific factors were intertwined. Following a review of the Department's science program, the decision was made in the summer of 1957 that the growing importance of scientific developments as an element in formulating foreign policy and carrying on relations with other governments called for a new emphasis in this field. The first task was to obtain the services of a notable scientific administrator with worldwide reputation in his discipline, who enjoyed the respect of the international scientific community. In January 1958 Dr. Wallace R. Brode was appointed Science Adviser to the Secretary...At the time of Dr. Brode's appointment, the Department announced that it would augment embassy offices by assignment of scientific attachés to certain foreign capitals. During 1958 an intensive effort was made to obtain the services of qualified scientists for these positions. In December the Department's overseas Science Officer Program was firmly reestablished...Dr. Brode retired in September 1960, to be succeeded by Walter G. Whitman...The science program of the Department of State, under the direction of the Science Adviser, consists of two basic elements: one is the Science Adviser and his staff in Washington, the other the corps of science officers serving at U.S. embassies abroad. The work of these two groups is coordinated by the Science Adviser to achieve the general objective of interrelating science and foreign policy formulation. To assure that this function of the science program makes its impact at the highest policymaking level, the Science Adviser has been made directly responsible to the Secretary of State and participates in daily staff meetings of the Secretary and his principal officials. Providing scientific advice to the Secretary and his staff constitutes far more than a passive function; the Science Adviser must bring to the consideration of the Secretary those scientific developments at home and abroad which may have important implications in the formulation and implementation of policy. In furtherance of their principal objective, the Science Adviser and his staff perform a variety of functions. These include providing assistance to Department officers in working out day-to-day decisions on issues having scientific implications, backstopping the work of the corps of scientific attachés stationed abroad, representing the Department's interests on various interdepartmental committees, and maintaining liaison with governmental, quasi-official, and nongovernmental organizations. To a great extent the work of the science staff is involved in reconciling the scientific objectives of such organizations and of private scientists with the overall objectives and requirements of American foreign policy; One of the principal activities of the Office of the Science Adviser in recent years was its cooperation with the National Academy of Sciences in connection with the 1957-58 International Geophysical Year. The Office facilitated the planning of those phases of the IGY program which required formal intergovernmental agreements, such as the establishment of earth-satellite tracking stations in Central and South America…During 1958 and 1959 the Office of the Science Adviser was actively involved in the preparation of the Antarctic Treaty proposed by President Eisenhower, which was signed on December 1, 1959, by the United States and 11 other nations. The treaty seeks to provide that the international scientific cooperation which characterized the IGY will continue and that the Antarctic will be used for peaceful purposes only. In the exercise of its responsibilities the science staff works closely with the geographic and functional units of the Department such as those concerned with disarmament, political and economic affairs, exchange of persons, and passports and visas. Its work frequently requires collaboration with other agencies of the Government, and it may draw upon the technical or scientific resources of these agencies for the solution of foreign affairs problems. The staff works closely with the National Academy of Sciences-National Research Council…the Science Adviser to the Secretary of State and the members of his staff work closely on a day-to-day basis with the personnel of the office of the President's Special Assistant for Science and Technology...Subjects of mutual concern include such matters as oceanography, the uses of outer space, materials research, and the coordination of governmental activities in the field of science. The President's Special Assistant and the Department's Science Adviser also maintain close liaison through their association on some of the President's principal science committees. One of these, the President's Science Advisory Committee...The Science Adviser of the Department of State serves on the Committee as one of five observers from various Government agencies, and he is a member of several of its panels. He is also one of the two observers…on the Federal Council for Science and Technology…and he is the chairman of the Council's subcommittee on international science.)

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: A special assistant to act as consultant on petroleum matters was assigned to the Office of the Adviser on International Economic Affairs by Departmental Order 952 of July 9 [sic] 1941. Although there was no Departmental order which established the Office of the Petroleum Adviser, the office is mentioned for the first time in Departmental Order 1024 of January 27, 1942. The Adviser advised the Secretary and the Under Secretary on matters relating to the foreign oil policy of the United States and the oil policies of foreign countries; the foreign organizations and activities of the American oil industry; and the oil resources and production, refining, marketing, and transportation facilities of foreign countries. The Adviser maintained liaison with other executive departments and agencies concerned with petroleum. The Office was abolished by Departmental Order 1218 of January 15, 1944, with functions carried over to the Office of Economic in which was established, on March 24, 1944,  the Petroleum Division

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Bureau of Foreign Agents and Reports was established by a resolution of the War Trade Board on November 2, 1917. It maintained agents and representatives (designated as "special assistants of the Department of State") in 26 countries, whose reports were abstracted in the Washington office and referred to the proper bureau heads or Board members until April 18, 1918, when most of this work was turned over to the Bureau of Research. By June 1, 1918, only seven of the foreign offices were being maintained. In the autumn of 1918 the name was changed to the Bureau of Foreign Agents. The Bureau was abolished along with the War Trade Board and its records and personnel transferred to the Consular Bureau, Department of State, effective July 1, 1919.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: An institute for the study of tropical agriculture had been discussed at inter-American conferences for at least ten years prior to the establishment of the Office for Coordination of Commercial and Cultural relations Between the American Republics (OCCCRBAR) within the Council of National Defense in 1940. During the first year of its existence, the Office of the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs (OIAA) was drawn into the discussion and the Coordinator agreed to administer the project.  The Agricultural Division was established in September 1941, largely for the purpose of carrying out the institute project. The following year, on June 18, 1942, the Inter-American Institute of Agricultural Sciences was incorporated.  It was to be administered as an international body with Pan American Union acting as fiscal agent and was to be located at Turrialba, Costa Rica.  With the incorporation of the Institute, direct involvement in the administration of Institute affairs was taken out of OIAA hands; and the Agricultural Division, which had maintained only a small staff and limited operations throughout its existence, was dissolved.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Governments of the United States and Great Britain, in consultation with the Government of India, agreed to an exchange of representatives on a reciprocal basis between the United States and India on July 21, 1941. An American Foreign Service officer, Thomas W. Wilson, was selected to represent the United States in the capacity of Commissioner, at Delhi. This office at Delhi was formally known as The Commission of the United States to India. (Wilson had been serving as Consul General in Calcutta; he was succeeded there by George R. Merrell). The staff of the Commission were seconded from the U.S. Consulate General at Calcutta. By the time the Coimmission was abolished George R. Merrell was Commissioner. He went on to become the Chief of Mission when the U.S. Embassy was established at New Delhi, November 1, 1946.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The U.S. Legation began filing despatches on February 15, 1823, although the first Minister Resident, Heman Allen, did not present his credentials until April 23, 1824. Succeeding Allen were Charge d'Affaires Samuel Larned, ca. November 9, 1828; John Hamm, May 24, 1831; Richard Pollard, March 13, 1835; John S. Pendleton, May 24, 1842; William Crump, August 18, 1845; and Seth Barton, January 5, 1848.

In 1849 the chief of mission was elevated to Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary; the first envoy, Balie Peyton, presented his credentials on February 16, 1850. He was succeeded by David A. Starkweather, November 22, 1854; John Bigler, October 5, 1857; Thomas H. Nelson, October 4, 1861; Judson Kilpatrick, March 12, 1866; Joseph P. Root, December 2, 1870; Cornelius A. Logan, June 27, 1873; Thomas A. Osborn, August 28, 1877; Judson Kilpatrick, July 25, 1881; Cornelius A. Logan, September 7, 1882; William R. Roberts, July 4, 1885; Patrick Egan, August 9, 1889; James D. Porter, July 4, 1893; Edward H. Strobel, February 6, 1895; Henry L. Wilson, September 14, 1897; John Hicks, October 5, 1905; Thomas C. Dawson, August 20, 1909; and Henry P. Fletcher, September 9, 1910.

In 1914 the Legation was raised to embassy status and Fletcher was promoted to Ambassador; he presented his new credentials as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary on November 19, 1914. He was succeeded by Joseph H. Shea, May 30, 1916; William Miller Collier, September 29, 1921; William S. Culbertson, August 16, 1928; Hal H. Sevier, November 25, 1933; Hoffman Philip, November 7, 1935; Norman Armour, April 21, 1938; Claude G. Bowers, September 7, 1939; Willard L. Beaulac, November 5, 1953; Cecil B. Lyon, June 15, 1956; Walter Howe, June 1, 1958; Robert F. Woodward, May 5, 1961; Charles W. Cole, October 21, 1961; Ralph A. Dungan, December 10, 1964; Edward M. Korry, October 16, 1967; Nathaniel Davis, October 20, 1971; David H. Popper, February 22, 1974; George W. Landau, November 1977; James D. Theberge, March 8, 1982; Harry George Barnes, Jr., November 18, 1985; Charles A. Gillespie, Jr., December 20, 1988; Curtis Warren Kamman, January 14, 1992; Gabriel Guerra-Mondragon, November 24, 1994; John O'Leary, August 19, 1998; and William R. Brownfield, March 25, 2002.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Bureau of Foreign Agents and Reports was established by a resolution of the War Trade Board on November 2, 1917. It maintained agents and representatives (designated as "special assistants of the Department of State") in 26 countries, whose reports were abstracted in the Washington office and referred to the proper bureau heads or Board members until April 18, 1918, when most of this work was turned over to the Bureau of Research. By June 1, 1918, only seven of the foreign offices were being maintained. In the autumn of 1918 the name was changed to the Bureau of Foreign Agents. The Bureau was abolished along with the War Trade Board and its records and personnel transferred to the Consular Bureau, Department of State, effective July 1, 1919.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
During World War II more than 100 committees within the State Department dealt with numerous problems generated by that conflict and developed plans and programs for the postwar period. In late 1944 the Department established the Secretary's Staff Committee, giving it the authority to coordinate and direct these activities. By the terms of its establishing directive (Departmental Order 1301 of December 20, 1944), the Staff Committee replaced both the Policy Committee and the Committee on Postwar Programs, and, with the broadest jurisdiction of any departmental group, it became the final review and advisory body for foreign policy and international relations. Created to be "available for instant consultation with the Secretary," the Committee met at his call or, as was frequently the case, at that of the vice chairman. Its broad objective was to "advise and otherwise assist the Secretary in determining current and long range foreign policy...[based] on the full range and interests of the Department." Its composition was the Secretary of State as chairman, the Under Secretary (vice chairman), the Assistant Secretaries, the Legal Adviser, and the Special Assistant for International Organization and Security Affairs. Participation by others was by special invitation only when necessary. 

The Secretary's Staff Committee was the creation of Secretary Edward R. Stettinius, Jr.: it actively served him, his two Under Secretaries (Joseph C. Grew and Dean C. Acheson), and, to a lesser extent, his successor, James F. Byrnes. Although a few documents are dated after George C. Marshall became Secretary of State, he did not use the Committee, and it was abolished by Departmental Announcement 757 of June 18, 1947.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Economic Cooperation Administration (ECA) was established by the Economic Cooperation Act of 1948 (62 Stat. 138), approved April 3, 1948, to administer the European Recovery Program (Marshall Plan). The purpose of the Administration was to furnish material and financial assistance in a plan of European recovery, in such a manner as to aid them, through their own indiviual and concerted efforts, to become independent of extraordinary outside assistance within the period of operation of the Act. The ECA promoted industrial and and agricultural production; furthered the restoration or maintenance of the soundness of currencies, budgets, and finances; and facilitated and stimulated the growth of international trade.

Participating countries included those countries, including their dependent areas, which signed the Report of the Committee of European Economic Cooperation at Paris on September 22, 1947, as well as any other country, including any of the zones of occupation of Germany, any area under international administration and control, and the Free Territory of Trieste, that was an adherent to a joint program for European recovery.

It reported to both the Department of State and the Department of Commerce. The agency's head was Paul G. Hoffman, a former head of Studebaker. Much of the rest of the organization was also headed by major business figures. The ECA had an office in the capital of each of the sixteen countries participating in the Marshall Plan. ECA was abolished by an act of October 10, 1951 (65 Stat. 373), with functions transferred to the Mutual Security Agency by Executive Order 10300, November 1, 1951, effective December 30, 1951.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Commanding General, U.S. Forces Austria (USFA) was also the U.S. High Commissioner in Austria. In his capacity as High Commissioner, he was responsible directly to the Joint Chiefs of Staff in Washington for all civil affairs matters. As the Commanding General, USFA, he was responsible for military matters to the Commander-in-Chief, European Command in Germany. The civil affairs functions of the headquarters were very closely coordinated with the U.S. Legation in Vienna. 

The single position of USFA Commanding General and U.S. High Commissioner for Austria was held by Gen. Mark Clark from July 5, 1945, to May 16, 1947, and by Lt. Gen. Geoffrey Keyes from May 17, 1947, to September 19, 1950. On October 15, 1950 Headquarters USFA turned over the administration of civil affairs to Mr. Walter J. Donnelly, the first U.S. civilian High Commissioner. Ambassador Llewelyn E. Thompson, Jr., succeeded Donnelly on July 17, 1952. 

The U.S. occupation government in Austria officially terminated on July 27, 1955, as a result of the State Treaty for the Re-establishment of an Independent and Democratic Austria, signed May 15, 1955.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Allied Commission for Austria was established by the Agreement on control machinery in Austria signed in the European Advisory Commission in London on July 4, 1945. It entered into force on July 24, 1945 on the day that the United States gave notification of approval, the last of the four powers to do so. It was supplemented by an agreement of June 28, 1946. Austria was divided into four zones: American, British, French and Russian. Vienna, being the capital, was similarly divided but at its center was an International Zone, sovereignty of which alternated at regular intervals between the Four Powers. The Allied Commission for Austria consisted of an Allied Council, an Executive Committee and staffs appointed by the four Governments concerned. The Commission had its seat in Vienna.

The Four Power Declaration of 4 July 1945 stated that Austria had been restored to its 1937 (pre-Anschluss) frontiers; it was administratively divided into eight provinces and the city of Vienna. The same Allied agreement divided Austria into four occupation zones. The Soviet zone included (1) the province of Burgenland (which had a common frontier with Hungary), (2) the province of Lower Austria (Vienna, which lies within it, received quadripartite occupation), and (3) that part of the province of Upper Austria (Mühlviertel) which lies on the north bank of the Danube River and shares a common frontier with Czechoslovakia and a small part of West Germany. The U.S. zone consisted of (1) the province of Salzburg, and (2) that part of the province of Upper Austria lying on the south bank of the Danube River, both of which have common frontiers with West Germany. The French zone, bordering on Switzerland and Italy, consisted of the provinces of Tirol and Vorarlberg. The British zone included the provinces of Carinthia and Styria which have common frontiers with Italy and Yugoslavia.

The primary tasks of the Allied Commission for Austria were: (a) to ensure the enforcement in Austria of the provisions of the Declaration regarding the defeat of Germany signed at Berlin on 5th June, 1945; (b) to achieve the separation of Austria from Germany; (c) to secure the establishment, as soon as possible, of a central Austrian administrative machine; (d) to prepare the way for the establishment of a freely elected Austrian government; (e) and to provide for the administration of Austria to be carried on satisfactorily. The decisions of the Allied Commission, insofar as they may have required action in the respective zones, were carried out through the occupation authorities. The necessary instructions to those authorities were given by the respective Military Commissioners, in their capacity as Commanders-in-Chief, on the basis of decisions of the Allied Council. 

The Allied Commission for Austria was dismantled following the entry into force of the Austrian State Treaty on July 27, 1955.

The missions reported to USAID's assistant administrators of the four geographic bureaus.

U.S. Agency for International Development, Dec. 10, 2015 (For the past 50 years, USAID has responded to the needs of the Dominican Republic. The Agency currently helps improve governance and reduce corruption across the country and supports the government's implementation of the Dominican Republic-Central America Free Trade Agreement. We also help small businesses and rural communities take advantage of free trade opportunities and employment generation, while protecting natural resources and biodiversity. Additionally, USAID is working to reform the country's health sector, including expanding access to quality health care, improving HIV/AIDS treatment and prevention services, detecting and treating tuberculosis, and implementing a health component under the social security system. USAID also works to improve the quality of primary public school education through teacher training, and providing at-risk youth with life skills, vocational training, and employment opportunities. Mission Contact: Alexandria Panehal, Mission Director) https://www.usaid.gov/where-we-work/latin-american-and-caribbean/dominican-republic

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The U.S. Delegation to the 1st Session of the United Nations General Assembly was named by President Harry S. Truman on December 21, 1945, in a letter to the Secretary of State, in accordance with section 2 (c) of the United Nations Participation Act of 1945 (UNPA), (59 Stat. 619), approved the day before, December 20, 1945. UNPA read, in part: "The President, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, shall designate from time to time to attend a specified session or specified sessions of the General Assembly of the United Nations not to exceed five representatives of the United States and such number of alternates as he may determine consistent with the rules of procedure of the General Assembly. One of the representatives shall be designated as the senior representative."

The President had sent his nominations to the Senate on December 19. All nominations were approved by the Senate the next day. Included in the delegation as representatives were Senator Tom Connally, Chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee; Senator Arthur H. Vandenburg, ranking minority membert of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee; and Mrs. Anna Eleanor Roosevelt, widow of the late President. Alternate representatives included Representative Sol Bloom, Chairman of the House Committee on Foreign Affairs; Representative Charles A. Eaton, ranking minority member of the House Committee on Foreign Affairs; Frank C. Walker, former Postmaster General of the United States; John Foster Dulles, prominent international lawyer; and former U.S. Senator John G. Townshend, Jr. Secretary of State James F. Byrnes actively served as Senior Representative from January 8/9 through January 24, 1946. Ambassador Edward Stettinius, Jr. acted in his stead until June 1946. Herschel V. Johnson served as acting Senior Representative through the remainder of the session.

Attached to the U.S. Delegation was an advisory and expert staff, ten of whom were officers from the U.S. armed forces, and nine from other Government agencies. The Department of State group was headed by five senior advisors, a principal advisor, and a secretary general.

The 1st Session of the General Assembly was held in London, England from January 24, 1946 through May 15, 1947. The Delegation in London was required until the end of the first part of the ifrst session on February 14, 1946.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The U.S. Delegation to the 2nd Session of the United Nations General Assembly was appointed in accordance with section 2 (c) of the United Nations Participation Act of 1945 (UNPA), (59 Stat. 619), approved December 20, 1945. UNPA read, in part: "The President, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, shall designate from time to time to attend a specified session or specified sessions of the General Assembly of the United Nations not to exceed five representatives of the United States and such number of alternates as he may determine consistent with the rules of procedure of the General Assembly. One of the representatives shall be designated as the senior representative."

Included in the delegation as representatives were Ambassador Herschel V. Johnson; Mrs. Anna Eleanor Roosevelt, widow of the late President; and John Foster Dulles, prominent international lawyer. Alternate representatives included Charles Fahy, formerly Legal Advisor of the Department of State; Willard L. Thorp; Francis B. Sayre; and Adlai Stevenson. Virginia C. Gildersleeve, Dean of Barnard College, was appointed as an aAlternate representative, but she never served. She was replaced by retired Major General John H. Hilldring, former Assistant Secretary of State for Occupoed Areas. Secretary of State George C. Marshall served as Senior Representative of the Delegation. During his absence, Ambassador Warren R. Austin acted in his stead. This was the first time that a professional Foreign Service officer was named to the U.S. Delegation, and it was also notable for its lack of Coingressional representation.

The Delegation held its first meeting on September 12, 1947. The 2nd Regular Session of the General Assembly was held in New York from September 30, 1947 through May 14, 1948.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Interdivisional Area Committee on the Far East was a special committee established along with the Country and Area Committee to analyze specific problems relating to U.S. policy in the Far East toward the end of World war II. The Committee concentrated in proposed U.S. actions in the region after Japan's eventual surrender. The Committee considered such topics as the future status of Japanese-occupied European colonies in the Far East, the composition of invasion and occupation forces to be sent into Japan, the future status of the Japanese emperor and various agencies of the Japanese Government during the occupation, the future status of Japanese nationals and their property in areas occupied by Japan, and what forms of government to establish or recognize in such countries as Korea, Formosa, Indochina, Thailand, and Outer Mongolia.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The United States began posting consuls in Tianjin not long after it became a treaty port in mid-nineteenth century and maintained a U.S. consulate there for decades. 

Although representatives of the Department of State were working in Germany with the Office of the Political Adviser from the time that Military Government was established, the six main consular offices - Berlin (Consulate General), Bremen (Consulate),  Frankfurt (Consulate), Hamburg (Consulate General), Munich (Consulate General),  and Stuttgart (Consulate), were not reopened until the spring of 1946. 

Under Military Government the position of these consular establishments was somewhat unusual. Ordinarily, American consular officers were accredited to the government of the territory in which a consulate was located. In occupied Germany, however, consular districts were under one of the Allied military governments. In the case of the U.S. zone of occupation,  the consulates themselves were actually a part of the military government. Thus, requests for services which in normal times would be made directly to the German Government were made instead by the consulates either to the U.S. Military Government (OMGUS) to the Land Military Government which administered the consular district.

To a large extent, the consulates were dependent upon the machinery of military occupation. At the same time, however, they exercised latitude to act somewhat independently from these agencies, and were free to approach municipal authorities directly without burdening military channels, and anticipated a time when a recognized German Government would be formed to which consular offices could be accredited.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: As part of the information program of THE Office for Coordination of Commercial and Cultural Relations between the American Republics (OCCCRBAR) a press or "news" section was established in the Communications Division in the fall of 1940.  The section became a division of the Department of Information when that was created in the spring of 1942 and remained there until early 1944 when the Department of Press and Publications was established, taking press functions out of the Information Department. Press operations were among the largest programs in the Office of the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs, employing about 200 persons throughout most of the war.  Among the press activities were publication and distribution of news and feature articles, magazines and newsletters, pamphlets, books, posters, photographs, and cartoons.  Other activities included supplying newsprint to Latin American countries through the Transportation Division and aiding in bringing leading Latin American journalists to the United States to observe news operations, war plants, and schools of journalism. The Press Division was organized into sections by function.  The names of the sections varied, but by 1944 there were divisions of News, Features, Graphics and Publications, Foreign Languages (for translation), Field Operations, and Administration.  The Department of Press and Publications was abolished in August 1945, and its functions were transferred to the Department of State with other OIAA information functions.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Bureau of Foreign Agents and Reports was established by a resolution of the War Trade Board on November 2, 1917. It maintained agents and representatives (designated as "special assistants of the Department of State") in 26 countries, whose reports were abstracted in the Washington office and referred to the proper bureau heads or Board members until April 18, 1918, when most of this work was turned over to the Bureau of Research. By June 1, 1918, only seven of the foreign offices were being maintained. In the autumn of 1918 the name was changed to the Bureau of Foreign Agents. The Bureau was abolished along with the War Trade Board and its records and personnel transferred to the Consular Bureau, Department of State, effective July 1, 1919.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Inquiry was established in the autumn of 1917 by Colonel Edward M. House at the request of President Woodrow Wilson. It was a group of experts assembled to collect and collate data relating to geographical, ethnological, economic, historic, and political problems of Europe in preparation for the anticipated peace conference to follow World War I. 

The Inquiry was first under the direction of Sidney E. Mezes, a philosopher of religion and president of City College of New York, and later of Isaiah Bowman, a geographer and head of the American Geographical Society. The Inquiry staff was composed largely of geographers, political scientists, historians, and other academicians assigned to various divisions dealing with specific geographic areas or with more general subjects, such as economics, diplomatic history, and international law. At its maximum size, in October 1918, The Inquiry's personnel records listed 126 research collaborators, executives, and staff assistants. 

Key personnel included lawyer David Hunter Miller and James T. Shotwell, historian and director of the National Board for Historical Services. Walter Lippmann, assistant to the Secretary of War, served as the Secretary of the Inquiry. Other noted members of The Inquiry included George L. Beer, Stephen Bonsal, Clive Day, Stephen P. Duggan, Stanley Hornbeck, Robert H. Lord, A.H. Lybyer, Samuel Eliot Morison, Dana G. Munro, W.H. Pitken, William Lytle Schurz, and W.L. Westermann.

The Inquiry undertook studies of virtually every region of the world, collecting and producing nearly 2,000 reports and over 1,000 maps. President Woodrow Wilson used The Inquiry's formal recommendations in drafting the territorial propositions in his Fourteen Points and later incorporated some its suggestions into the peace treaties. 

In December 1918, The Inquiry ceased as an independent body and was absorbed into the Division of Territorial, Economic, and Political Intelligence of the American Commission to Negotiate Peace. Twenty-three members of the former Inquiry staff accompanied President Wilson to the peace conference.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Allied Secretariat constituted the one fixed, continuing staff of the Allied Commission. Its four national components were housed in the Allied Commission Building and worked closely together in the preparation of documents, the reconciliation of texts, and the various other administrative matters for which it was responsible. 

Its main functions were: the preparation of agendas and papers in the English, French, and Russian languages for submission to the Executive Committee or the Allied Council; the reconciliation and issuance of official minutes of Executive Committee and Allied Council meetings; the receipt of all communications addressed to the Allied Commission and their transmitall to the parties concerned; and the transmittal to the Austrian Government, or other parties, of decisions taken by the Executive Committee or the Allied Council.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The U.S. Delegation to the 3rd Regular Session of the United Nations General Assembly was appointed in accordance with section 2 (c) of the United Nations Participation Act of 1945 (UNPA), (59 Stat. 619), approved December 20, 1945. UNPA read, in part: "The President, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, shall designate from time to time to attend a specified session or specified sessions of the General Assembly of the United Nations not to exceed five representatives of the United States and such number of alternates as he may determine consistent with the rules of procedure of the General Assembly. One of the representatives shall be designated as the senior representative."

Included in the delegation as representatives were John Foster Dulles, prominent international lawyer; Mrs. Anna Eleanor Roosevelt, widow of the late President; and Philip C. Jessup, Hamilton Fish Professor of International Law and Diplomacy, Columbia University, New York. Alternate representatives included Benjamin V. Cohen; Willard L. Thorp, Assistant Secretary of State for Economic Affairs; Ernest A. Gross, Legal Advisor to the Department of State; Ambassador Francis B. Sayre, U.S. Representative to the Trusteeship Council; and Ray Atherton. Secretary of State George C. Marshall served as Senior Representative of the Delegation. The Secretary of State was with the U.S. Delegation at Paris from the opening of the session on September 21 until November 21 when he returned to Washington at the request of the President, except for short absences on two successive week-ends on October on the occasion of a consulation with the President in Washington (October 9-11) and a visot to Athens, Greece (October 16-18). During his absence, Ambassador Warren R. Austin acted in his stead. 

The composition of the Delegation was announced on September 7, 1948. The 3rd Regular Session of the General Assembly was held in Paris, France from September 21, 1948 through May 1949.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Subcommittee for the Far East originally began as an ad hoc committee of the State-War-Navy Coordinating Committee (SWNCC). It was formed to study problems relating the the breakup of the Japanese Empire at the end of World War II and the future status of nations and people formerly under Japanese control. With the surrender of Japan, it became a full-fledged subcommittee, responsible for forming strategy on all aspects of postwar policy relating to the Far East, especially Japan, Korea, and China.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Exports Council was established by Executive Order 2645, June 22, 1917, under authority of Title VII of the Espionage Act of 1917 (40 Stat. 219), approved June 15, 1917, to formulate, for the consideration and approval of the President, policies to be carried out by the Export Licenses Division of the Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce, and to make the recommendations necessary to carry out the purposes of export control. Its functions were amended by Executive Order 2687-A, August 21, 1917, which directed the Council to advise the Exports Administrative Board. The Export Council was comprised of the Secretaries of State, Agriculture, and Commerce, and the U.S. Food Administrator. The Chairman of the U.S. Shipping Board was added by the amending Executive order of August 1917. Although the last meeting of the EXports Council was held on August 24, 1917, it was not abolished until it was superseded by the War Trade Council of the of the War Trade Board, pursuant to Executive Order 2729-A, October 12, 1917.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Allied Control Council for Germany was established on June 5, 1945, implementing plans concerning the occupation of post-war Germany announced by the Crimea Conference ("Yalta Conference") Communique of February 3-11, 1945, agreed to by the "Big Three" (the United States, the United Kingdom, and the Soviet Union). The Allied Control Council, comprised of the commanders of the American, British, Soviet, and French zones of occupation, assumed all powers possessed by the German Government, the High Command, and all State, municipal, and local authorities. Initial members of the Allied Control Council included Marshal Georgy Zhukov of the Soviet Union, General Dwight D. Eisenhower of the United States, Field Marshal Bernard Law Montgomery of Great Britain, and General Jean Joseph-Marie Gabriel Lattre de Tassigny of France. The organization of the Allied Control Council was governed by the Agreement on Control Machinery in Germany, approved by the European Advisory Commission on November 14, 1944, as amended on May 1, 1945. (The term "Allied Control Authority" was a rubric that included the entire control machinery in Germany, including the Allied Control Council, the Coordinating Committee, and the Control Staff). The Potsdam Agreement of August 2, 1945, signed by President Harry S. Truman, Prime Minister Clement Attlee, and Marshal Josef Stalin, reiterated the Allied principle of political decentralization and provided for the restoration of local self-government in Germany. It also stipulated that during the period of occupation Germany would be treated as a single economic unit. 

Cooperation by the ACC broke down, as the Soviet representative withdrew on March 20, 1948. After that date, the ACC, even though in existence, no longer met, thus paving the way for the partition of Germany into two states. On September 21, 1949, the western zones were officially combined as the Federal Republic of Germany, and the military occupation ended. The Allied Control Council for Germany was dissolved and in its place instituted the civilian Allied High Commission.

U.S. Occupation Headquarters, World War II, 2001 (The Allied Control Authority (ACA) was established by a tripartite agreement of the United States, United Kingdom, and the Soviet Union dated November 14, 1944.  It was amended to include France on May 2, 1945.  The members held a meeting in Berlin on June 5, 1945; but the first regular meeting of the Control Council, the governing body, was held on July 30, 1945.  The ACA was the supreme governing machinery for Germany following the Second World War. The Control Council  (CONL) was composed of the four commanders-in-chief of the occupying forces of the four Allied governments.  It was the responsibility of each to insure that the decisions of the CONL were implemented in his zone.  It met three times a month in Berlin with the Chair of the meeting rotating each month among the four nations of which the council was composed (the United States, Great Britain, France, and the Soviet Union).)

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The geographic area covered by the Far East and Other Territories Branch was world-wide, covering China, Korea, the Philippines, Thailand, French Indochina, Liberia, Ireland, Greenland, and Afghanistan. In China the Branch was responsible for aiding the United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration (UNRRA) in relief, rehabilitation, and reconstruction activities, for carrying on lend-lease operations, and for helping the Chinese solve their economic problems. The program for the Philippines included relief and rehabilitation, and the Branch worked with the authorities of the Philippine Government in solving their problems. Activities regarding Korea, Thailand, and French Indochina were in the planning stage until VJ-Day.

In 1946 about three-fourths of the records were transferred to the Department of State and the remainder to the Department of Commerce.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
From March 7, 1809, the date of the appointment of Thomas Sumter, Jr., as Minister Plenipotentiary of the United States to the court of the Prince Regent of Portugal in Brazil, until August 6, 1820, when Sumter's successor, John Graham died, the ranking U.S. official in Brazil held the rank of Minister Plenipotentiary. In April 1821 the Portuguese court left Brazil for Portugal and communications from U.S. diplomatic representatives in Brazil cease on July 12, 1821.

The U.S. Legation in Brazil re-opened in 1825. The chief of mission was the Charge d'Affaires, Condy Raguet, who presented his credentials on October 29, 1825. He was succeeded by William Tudor, June 25, 1828; Ethan A. Brown, February 18, 1831; and William Hunter, January 7, 1835.

William Hunter was promoted to Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary and he presented his new credentials on January 1, 1842. He was succeeded by George H. Proffit, December 11, 1843; Henry A. Wise, August 10, 1844; David Tod [sic], August 28, 1847; Robert C. Schenck, August 9, 1851; William Trousdale, October 8, 1853; Richard K. Meade, December 5, 1857; James Watson Webb, October 21, 1861; Henry T. Blow, August 28, 1869; James R. Partridge, July 31, 1871; Henry W. Hilliard, October 23, 1877; Thomas A. Osborn, December 17, 1881; Thomas J. Jarvis, July 11, 1885; Robert Adams, Jr., July 20, 1889; Edwin H. Conger, December 19, 1890; Thomas L. Thompson, September 9, 1893; Edwin H. Conger, August 9, 1897; Charles Page Bryan, April 11, 1898; and David E. Thompson, April 1, 1903.

In 1905 the Legation was elevated to embassy status and David E. Thompson presented his credentials as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary on March 16, 1905. He was succeeded by Lloyd C. Griscom, June 6, 1906; Irving B. Dudley, April 1, 1907; Edwin V. Morgan, June 4, 1912; Hugh S. Gibson, August 8, 1933; Jefferson Caffery, August 17, 1937; Adolf A. Berle, Jr., January 30, 1945; William D. Pawley, June 13, 1946; Herschel V. Johnson, July 22, 1948; James S. Kemper, August 18, 1953; James Clement Dunn, March 11, 1955; Ellis O. Briggs, July 24, 1956; John M. Cabot, July 22, 1959; Lincoln Gordon, October 19, 1961; John W. Tuthill, June 30, 1966; C. Burke Elbrick, July 14, 1969 (on September 3, 1969, Ambassador Elbrick was kidnapped by the Marxist revolutionary group MR-8); William M. Rountree, November 16, 1970; John Hugh Crimmins, August 13, 1973; Robert M. Sayre, June 8, 1978; Langhorne A. Motley, October 6, 1981; Diego C. Asencio, December 20, 1983; Harry W. Shllaudeman [sic], August 5, 1986; Richard Huntington Melton, December 12, 1989; Melvyn Levitsky, June 1, 1994; Anthony Stephen Harrington, February 8, 2000. 

Cristobal R. Orozco served as Charge d'Affaires ad interim from February 2001 until April 23, 2002, when Ambassador Donna J. Hrinak presented her credentials.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Office of the Assistant Legal Advisor for International Organization Affairs was established on February 14, 1947, to render legal services in connection with participation of the United States in international organizations, particularly the United Nations and its principal organs, the Security Council, the General Assembly, the Economic and Social Council, the Trusteeship Council, and the International Court of Justice.

In 1950, functions transferred to the Office of the Assistant of the Legal Adviser for United Nations (U.N.) Affairs. The Office provided legal advice on matters related to the U.S. participation in the U.N., its specialized agencies and other international organizations; international criminal tribunals; U.N. consideration of specific situations; international peacekeeping; multilateral sanctions; the use of force; peaceful settlement of international disputes; matters concerning the International Court of Justice and problems arising out of the presence of the U.N. and other international organizations in the U.S.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: U.S. Forces Austria, USACA Section,  responsible for civil affairs/military government administration, was organized concurrently with the establishment of HQ USFA by General Order 1, HQ USFA, July 5, 1945, as a component of U.S. Forces, European Theater (USFET). The USACA Section provided the U.S. element of organizations comprising the Allied Commission for Austria, the name of the four-power occupation administration established by a U.S., British, French, and Soviet agreement, signed July 4, 1945, and made effective July 24, 1945. The USACA Section also administered occupation government in the U.S. Zone of Austria and U.S. Sector of Vienna. USACA Section was abolished following transfer of U.S. occupation government from military to civilian authority, marked by the Presidential appointment of Walter J. Donnelly as Envoy (later, Ambassador) to Austria and U.S. High Commissioner for Austria, effective September 20, 1950.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The activities of the American Legation, Vienna were reinstituted after the collapse of the German war effort when the Office of the Political Adviser for Austrian Affairs was organized in July 1945. On September 3, 1945,  John G. Erhardt assumed charge of this office and began serving as Political Adviser to the Commanding General, U.S. Forces in Austria (USFA). In January 1946, although a peace treaty had not been concluded, the U.S. Government recognized the Austrian Federal Republic, and on September 7, 1946 Mr. Erhardt presented letters of credence as Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary to the Austrian Government. On September 7, 1946, also, the Commanding General of USFA acquired the additional status and title of U.S. High Commissioner, in which capacity he became the senior representative of the United States as one of four members on the Allied Control Council.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The International Development Advisory Board was established by president Harry S. Truman on September 8, 1950, by Executive Order 10159, pursuant to Title IV of the Act for International Development. It consisted of thirteen persons appointed by the President. Nelson A. Rockefeller served as Chairman. It advised the President on the development of policies of the United States toward underdeveloped countries and how to deal with such problems as military aggression, subversion, hunger, poverty, disease, and illiteracy in these countries. The Board was terminated by Executive Order 10610 of May 9, 1955, which transferred its functions to the Department of State.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The President of the United States was authorized by Joint Resolution 161 of May 29, 1928, to invite representatives of foreign governments to attend the International Civil Aeronautics Conference. The Conference was held at Washington, D.C., December 12-14, 1928, to provide an opportunity for an interchange of views on problems pertaining to aircraft in international commerce and trade. The Conference also celebrated the 25th anniversary of the first powered flight of an airplane by Wilbur and Orville Wright.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Office of the Chief of Counsel for War Crimes (OCCWC) was established in the Office of Military Government for Germany (U.S.) (OMGUS), by General Order 301, Headquarters U.S. Forces in Europe (USFET), October 24, 1946, as successor to the Subsequent Proceedings Division of the Office of the U.S. Chief of Counsel for the Prosecution of Axis Criminality (OUSCCPAC). It was headed by Brigadier General Telford Taylor, appointed Chief of Counsel for War Crimes (CCWC) by same order, having served in OUSCCPAC as staff member in various capacities (May 25, 1945- March 28, 1946) and as Deputy Chief of Counsel in charge of the Subsequent Proceedings Division (March 29-October 23, 1946). OCCWC prosecuted 185 defendants, grouped in twelve ases according to sphere of activity, November 21, 1946-April 14, 1949, before 11 U.S. military tribunals. Of 177 defendants ultimately judged (four of the original defendants having committed suicide and four having been deemed incompetent to stand trial), 35 were acquitted and 142 were convicted, with 25 given the death penalty. OCCWC was formally abolished, June 20, 1949.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The International Sanitary Conference was held in Washington, DC, from January 5 to March 1, 1881, at the invitation of the United States. A joint resolution of Congress, approved May 14, 1880, authorized the President to call a conference of the several powers having jurisdiction over sea ports likely to be infected with yellow fever or cholera in order that an international system of notification might be set up to indicate the actual sanitary condition of these ports and the vessels sailing from them

Delegates were appointed to the Conference from Argentina, Austria-Hungary, Belgium, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, China, denmark, France, Great Britain, Germany, Haiti, Italy, Japan, Liberia, Mexico, the Netherlands, Peru, Portugal, Russia, Span, Sweden and Norway, Turkey, the United States, and Venezuela. The United States was represented by John Hay, James L. Cabell, Thomas J. Turner, J. Hubley Ashton, and James Lowndes.

 The program proposed by the United States inckuded a plan to establish a reliable and satisfactory system of notification among countries as to the existence of contagious and infectious diseases and to set up a uniform system of bills of health. The program was considered by a committee appointed by the conference.

The results of the Conference were embodied in a final act and two conventions. The act contained eight resolutions that related to the public health and the health information services of the various countries, the form of bills of health, the establishment of an organization for the interchange of public health information, and the establishment of an organization to study matters pertaining to yellow fever. The two conventions provided for the creation of a permanent international Sanitary Agency of Notification and for the creation of a temporary sanitary commission for the study of yellow fever.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The International Prime Meridian Conference met in Washington, DC, from October 1 to 22, 1884, at the invitation of the United States. The purpose of the conference, called by the President of the United States pursuant to a Congressional resolution, was to select a suitable meridian of longitude to be employed as a common zero of longitude and a standard of time-reckoning throughout the world.

The Conference was attended by delegates from Austria-Hungary, Brazil, Columbia, Costa Rica, the Dominican Republic, El salvador, France, Germany, Great Britain, Guatemala, Hawaii, Italy, Mexico, Paraguay, Russia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, the United States, and Venezuela. Rear Admiral C.R.P. Rodgers, Lewis H. Rutherford, W.F. Allen, Commander W.T. Sampson, and Cleveland Abbe represented the United States.

The Conference agreed to recommend the meridian at Greenwich as the astronomical and geographic reference meridian of the world. The astronomical day was to begin at midnight mean Greenwich time. This arrangement for a standard time was to begin on January 1, 1885.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Pan American Trade-Mark Conference was held in Washington, D.C., from February 11 to 20, 1929, at the invitation of the United States pursuant to a resolution of the Sixth International Conference of American States. All of the American Republics were represented except Argentina and El Salvador. The Conference adopted and signed a General Inter-American Convention for Trade-Mark and Commercial Protection, a protocol on the inter-American registration of trademarks, and a final act containing twelve resolutions. The more important of these resolutions concerned unfair trade practices, terms used in the convention and protocol, and the calling of a patent conference.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Office of Foreign Relief and Rehabilitation Operations was established in the Department of State on December 4, 1942, pursuant to a Presidential letter of December 3, 1942, allocating funds to the Department "for reconstruction and rehabilitation of territories occupied by the armed forces." The functions of the Office, as conceived by the President, were stated in his two letters of March 19, 1943, and of June 3, 1943, to the Director of the Office and the Secretary of State respectively. In liberated areas the Office was to distribute relief goods and goods for the production of basic civilian necessities; to provide technical advice and services with respect to relief and civilian economy; and to facilitate the restoration of agriculture, housing, and transportation. It was authorized to issue directives to the Government agencies that were equipped to aid in relief work and to utilize the facilities of private organizations and individuals. In the field, the foreign missions of the Office were to be under the control of military authorities, and in matters of foreign policy they were to be guided by the directives of the Secretary of State. Contemplating the establishment of a United Nations relief organization, the President further instructed that the work of the Office in the field be "geared to that of our allies." To accomplish these objectives the Office was authorized to draw funds from the Office of Lend-Lease Administration, much in the same manner as did a foreign lend lease mission.

On the same day that the Office was established Herbert H. Lehman was appointed as its Director.

By an Executive order of September 25, 1943, the Office was merged with other agencies to form the Foreign Economic Administration, and its records were transferred to the Administration.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The United States formally reopened diplomatic relations with the Federal Republic of Germany (West Germany) in May 1955, establishing the U.S. Embassy at Bonn on May 5. The U.S. High Commissioner for Germany, James B. Conant, presented his credentials as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary on May 14, 1955. He was succeeded by David K.E. Bruce, April 17, 1957; Walter C. Dowling, December 3, 1959; George C. McGhee, May 18, 1963; Henry Cabot Lodge, May 27, 1968; Kenneth Rush, July 22, 1969; Martin J. Hillenbrand, June 27, 1972; Walter J. Stoessel, Jr., October 27, 1976; Arthur F. Burns, June 30, 1981; Richard R. Burt, September 16, 1985; and Vernon A. Walters, April 24, 1989.

During Ambassador Walters' tenure the Federal Republic of Germany and the German Democratic Republic were united (October 3, 1990) and the Embassy subsequently relocated to Berlin (ca. July 7, 1999). Following Walters as Ambassador were Richard Holbrooke, October 19, 1993; and Charles E. Redman, October 31, 1994.

Ambassador Redman left his post on June 17, 1996; J.D. Bindnagel served as Charge d'Affairs ad interim until Ambassador John C. Kornblum presented his credentials on September 10, 1997. Ambassador Kornblum was succeeded by Daniel R. Coats, September 12, 2001.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Berlin Conference on West African Affairs was held at Berlin at the invitation of the German Government from November 16, 1884, to February 26, 1885, to regulate trade and commerce with West Africa, particularly in the Congo River Basin. The countries represented at this Conference were Austria, Belgium, Denmark, France, Germany, Great Britain, Italy, Luxembourg, Sweden and Norway, Portugal, Russia, Spain, Turkey, and the United States. The United States was represented by John A. Kasson and Henry S. Sanford. The results of the Conference were embodied in a general act of thirty-eight articles that included declarations concerning the navigation of the Niger and Congo Rivers, the neutrality of the Congo Basin region, and the freedom of commerce.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The quadripartite occupation of Germany, established in 1945, rapidly showed its limitations. Each power tried to impose its methods in its own zone, and ignored what was happening elsewhere. With regard to the Ruhr, France made some demands which were unacceptable to the other powers. The French Foreign Ministry wanted to guarantee the security of France by internalising the ownership of German coal and steel companies. What France really wanted was to avoid the use of the resources of the Ruhr for military purposes, and at the same time, to stop the reintroduction of trusts which would enable Germany to recover its industrial might. The United States and the United Kingdom were in favour of the creation of a control authority for the Ruhr.

In November 1948, the Anglo-American authorities of the Bizone issued a decree Law No 75 on the reorganisation and decentralisation of the coal and steel industries of the Ruhr. But this decision gave the Germans the right to settle the long-term question of ownership. Unhappy with this development, the French immediately suggested the establishment of Allied control over coal and steel. The Americans then proposed that the French participate in the Anglo-American control groups, particularly the Military Office of Security (MOS) already set up by the three Western occupying forces to supervise German disarmament. Meeting in London between 20 April and 2 June 1949, the United States, the United Kingdom, the Benelux countries and France decided in the end to set up the International Authority for the Ruhr (IAR). It was to control the production of coal and steel and the commercial practices of the most industrialised region of Europe. Signed on 28 April by the six countries, the London Agreement provided for coordination between the manufacturing activities of the Ruhr and those of the Organisation for European Economic Cooperation (OEEC). It also prohibited discriminatory practices, helped lower trade barriers and preserved foreign interests in the Ruhr.

The Germans were, on the whole, opposed to this Allied initiative which effectively limited their freedom to act and maintained their country in an inferior position. They were allowed to send their own delegates since the November 1949 `Petersburg agreements which ended German reparations but they did not feel that they were fairly represented. The Social Democratic Party (SPD) and the Liberal Party (FDP) were particularly irritated. On the other hand, the former Christian-Democrat Mayor of Cologne and future German Chancellor, Konrad Adenauer, saw it as a possible starting point for a European federation and hoped that the IAR would rapidly be extended to other European industrial regions.

The signature, on 18 April 1951 in Paris, of the Treaty establishing the European Coal and Steel Community (ECSC) spelled the end of the IAR. The gradual establishment by the Six of a common European market for coal and steel made the IAR's control activities redundant, and it was finally wound up on 27 May 1952.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The U.S. Embassy for Burundi was established at Usumbura (now Bujumbura) on July 1, 1962, with Herbert V. Olds as Charge d'Affaires ad interim. The mission was downgraded to legation status on December 15, 1962, then upgraded to an embassy on September 16, 1963.

Donald A. Dumont presented his credentials as Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary on January 17, 1963. Later that year he was promoted to Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary and he presented his new credentials on September 16, 1963. On December 29, 1965, the Government of Burundi requested Ambassador Dumont's recall, and he left the post on January 11, 1966.

A new ambassador was not appointed for Burundi until 1968 when George W. Renchard presented his credentials as Ambassador Extraordinary and Pleinpotentiary on August 10, 1968. He was succeeded by Thomas Patrick Melady, January 31, 1970; Robert L. Yost, August 19, 1972; David E. Mark, September 4, 1974; Thomas J. Corcoran, April 6, 1978; Frances D. Cook, September 25, 1980; James R. Bullington, April 14, 1983; James Daniel Phillips, November 20, 1986; and Cynthia Shepard Perry, February 12, 1990. Ambassador Perry left her post on February 28, 1993; Leonard J. Lange served as Charge d'Affaires ad interim from March 1993 through June 1994.

Robert Krueger presented his credentials as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary on June 29, 1994. He was succeeded by Morris N. Hughes, Jr., June 27, 1996; Mary Carlin Yates, December 15, 1999; and James Howard Yellin, September 26, 2002.
