creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The U.S. Legation for Cambodia opened on July 11, 1950. Donald R. Heath, who was also accredited to Laos and Vietnam and resident at Saigon, presented his credentials as Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary on July 11, 1950. Legation Phnom Penh was opened to the public on November 14, 1950, with Don V. Catlett as Charge d'Affaires ad interim. On June 25, 1952, the Legation was upgraded to embassy status, and Heath presented his credentials as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary on July 12, 1952. 

The first resident Ambassador, Robert McClintock, presented his credentials on October 2, 1954. He was succeeded by Carl W. Strom, December 7, 1956; William C. Trimble, April 23, 1959; and Philip D. Sprouse, August 20, 1962. Randolph A. Kidder was appointed the next Ambassador on July 9, 1964, and he went to Phnom Penh, but departed the post on September 18, 1964, before presenting his credentials. 

Cambodia severed relations with the United States on May 3, 1965, and the Embassy closed. The Embassy reopened on August 16, 1969, with Lloyd M. Rives as Charge d'Affaires ad interim. Emory Swank presented his credentials as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary on September 15, 1970. He continued to serve, without accreditation, after the proclamation of the Khmer Republic. He was replaced by John Gunther Dean who presented his credentials on April 3, 1974.

United States relations with Cambodia continued after the establishment of the Khmer Republic until the Embassy at Phnom Penh was closed on April 12, 1975, following the evacuation of all U.S. personnel. The U.S. did not have diplomatic representation in Cambodia until November 11, 1991, when a U.S. Mission was established. Career diplomat Charles H. Twining, Jr. served as U.S. Special Representative to the Supreme National Council (SNC). When the freely elected Royal Government of Cambodia was formed on September 24, 1993, the United States and the Kingdom of Cambodia immediately established full diplomatic relations. On May 17, 1994, the Mission was upgraded to embassy status and Twining was promoted to Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary. He was succeeded by Kenneth M. Quinn who presented his credentials on March 28, 1996; Kent M. Wiedemann, August 31, 1999; and Charles Aaron Ray, November 15, 2002.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Office of the U.S. United States High Commissioner for Germany (HICOG) was established on September 21, 1949, pursuant to Executive Order 1006, June 6, 1949. It assumed functions formerly vested with the office of U.S. Military Governor and the Office of Military Government for Germany (U.S.) (OMGUS). The first High Commissioner, John J. McCloy, was confirmed by the U.S. Senate on June 13, 1949, and on July 2, 1949, assumed the duties of military governor, pending the liquidation of OMGUS. The U.S. High Commissioner formally assumed authority under E.O. 10062 and 10063 on September 21, 1949.

Until the establishment of HICOG, the Office of Military Government for Germany (U.S.), a subordinate command of the War Department, and after September 1947, of the Department of Defense, had been responsible for military government in the U.S. zone of occupation. Under terms of the London Agreement of 1948, German authorities in the French, British, and American Zones were asked to form a democratic, federal government for the west, while the three powers drafted a statute of occupation to define their powers with relation to the new government. The Germans drafted a constitution that was ratified by the eleven states of western Germany, elections were held, and on September 21, 1949, the government of the Federal Republic of Germany took office. At the same time. Military government was replaced by the Allied High Commission (HICOM), headed by the High Commissioners of the United States, Great Britain, and France.

HICOM was created to exercise supreme Allied authority in the Federal Republic of Germany. As far as the three western zones were concerned, HICOM superseded the quadripartite Allied Control Authority and the US-UK bizonal organization, "Bizonia". All authority previously exercised by the military commanders of the British, French, and American occupying forceswere transferred to the High Commission. HICOM was comprised of the British, French, and American High Commissioners, their deputies and advisers, and a tripartite Allied General Secretariat.

The U.S. High Commissioner inherited all powers formerly vested with the Military Governor of the U.S. Zone, and all Military Government laws and directives, unless specifically superseded or revoked, continued in effect. The High Commissioner was the supreme U.S. authority in Germany and had the authority, under the immediate supervision of the Secretary of State, to exercise all governmental functions of the United States in Germany (other than the command of military forces), including representation of the U.S. on the Allied High Commission, and also served as the equivalent of a chief of mission to the newly established Federal Republic of Germany.

The office of the U.S. High Commissioner for Germany was abolished on May 5, 1955, by proclamation of the Allied High Commission for Germany. Residual functions were transferred to the Office of the Ambassador to the Federal Republic of Germany, May 6, 1955.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The First Samoan Conference was held at Washington, DC, from June 25 to July 26, 1887. It was attended by representatives from Germany, Great Britain, and the United States, the three major powers most interested in the Samoan Islands. The object of the Conference was to adjust Samoan affairs peacably and to determine the spheres of influence for each government in its relations with the islands. The United States was represented by the Secretary of State; Germany and Great Britain by their respective ministers to the United States.

The Conference considered proposals of the three countries and developed certain points of agreement. On July 26, 1887, the Conference adjourned until each representative could receive from his government further instructions regarding treaty powers. It was planned that the Conference would reconvene pening receipt of these instructions.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Executive Committee on Economic Foreign Policy, an interdepartmental committee, was established on April 18, 1944, pursuant to a letter from the President to the Secretary of State of April 15, to examine problems and developments affecting the foreign economic policy of the United States and to formulate recommendations concerning them for the consideration of the Secretary, and, in appropriate cases, to the President. It was made up of representatives of the State, Treasury, Agriculture, Commerce, and Labor Departments, the U.S. Tariff Commission, and the Foreign Economic Administration; and representatives of the major interdepartmental committees concerned with general economic affairs were invited to participate in the meetings of the Committee and to sit on subcommittees of special interest to them. The subcommittees of the Committee included Committees on Trade Barriers, Private Monopolies and Cartels, Commodity Arrangements, Inter-American Economic Development, Wartime Trade Controls, Stockpiling, and Economic Reconstruction Policies. Related economic committees with which liaison was maintained by its secretariat included the Committees on Shipping, Aviation, Communications, Trade Agreements, Labor Standards and Social Security, Migration and Settlement, and Reciprocity Information; the Inter-American Committee on Post-War Economic Policy; the Advisory Committees on Coffee and Cocoa, and the Policy Committee for Liberated Areas.

The secretariat for the Committee and its subcommittees was at first in the Office of Economic Affairs, but in January 1945 it was placed directly under the Assistant Secretary, and by 1947, under the Under Secretary for Economic Affairs. In addition to performing administrative services for these committees and keeping their records, it was assigned various duties concerning the preparation of programs for their meetings. Policy matters needing consideration by the Committee and its subcommittees were brought to the secretariat's attention by other offices and divisions of the Department; and it in turn brought questions of major policy to the attention of the Department's Policy Committee and Committee on Post-War Programs or their successors in the Secretary's office.

The U.S. Embassy in Cameroon was established at Yaounde on January 1, 1960, with Bolard More as Charge d'Affaires ad interim. Leland Barrows was appointed as the first Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary and he presented his credentials on June 9, 1960. Ambassador Barrows was also accredited to Togo. 

Ambassador Barrows was succeeded by Robert L. Payton, March 4, 1967; Lewis Hoffacker, December 20, 1969; C. Robert Moore, July 22, 1972; Herbert J. Spiro, September 1, 1975; Mabel M. Smythe, October 1, 1977; and Hume A. Horan, July 29, 1980. From 1969 until September 29, 1981, the Ambassador was also accredited to Equatorial Guinea.

Ambassador Horan was succeeded by Myles Robert Rene Frechette, September 8, 1983; Mark L. Edelman, September 9, 1987; Frances D. Cook, December 21, 1989; Harriet Winsar Isom, January 19, 1993; Charles H. Twining, February 28, 1996; John Melvin Yates, January 5, 1999; and George McDade Staples, December 21, 2001.

The U.S. Legation in Canada was opened at Ottawa on June 1, 1927, when the first Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary, William Phillips, presented his credentials. He was succeeded by Hanford MacNider, August 29, 1930; Warren Delano Robbins, May 16, 1933; Norman Armour, August 7, 1935; Daniel C. Roper, May 19, 1939; James H.R. Cromwell, January 24, 1940; Jay Pierrepont Moffat, June 13, 1940; and Ray Atherton, August 3, 1940. Moffat was also accredited to Luxembourg; Atherton to Luxembourg and Denmark.

On November 18, 1943, the Legation was raised to embassy status when Ray Atherton presented his credentials as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary. Ambassador Atherton was succeeded by Laurence A. Steinhardt, November 1, 1948; Stanley Woodward, June 22, 1950; R. Douglas Stuart, July 15, 1953; Livingston T. Merchant, May 23, 1956; Richard B. Wigglesworth, December 15, 1958; Livingston T. Merchant, March 15, 1961; W. Walton Butterworth, December 11, 1962; Harold Francis Linder, September 10, 1968; Adolph W. Schmidt, September 11, 1969; William J. Porter, February 11, 1974; Thomas O. Enders, February 17, 1976; Kenneth M. Curtis, October 5, 1979; Paul Heron Robinson, Jr., July 15, 1981; Thomas Michael Tolliver Niles, September 10, 1985; Edward N. Ney, June 30, 1989; Peter Barry Teeley, July 3, 1992; and James J. Blanchard, August 19, 1993.

The position of ambassador was briefly left vacant after March 29, 1996. James Donald Walsh served as Charge d'Affaires from March 1996 through May 1997, and James G. Weston from June through September 1997.

On September 17, 1997, Gordon G. Giffin presented credentials as Ambassador; he was succeeded by Argeo Paul Cellucci, who presented his credentials on April 17, 2001.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Second International Peace Conference, proposed by the President of the United States and convoked by the Netherlands at the invitation of Russia, met at The Hague from June 15 to October 18, 1907. The program included improvement of the provision in the convention of 1899 relating to the peaceful settlement of international disputes and to the international commission of inquiry, additions to the provisions relating to the laws and customs of war on land, additions to the 1899 convention adapting to maritime warfare the principles of the Geneva Convention of 1864 for the care of sick and wounded soldiers, and the framing of a convention relating to laws and customs of maritime warfare.

Fifty-four nations were represented at the Conference. The United States delegates were Joseph H. Choate, Horace Porter, Uriah M. Rose, David Jayne Hill, George B. Davis, Rear Admiral Charles S. Sperry, and William I. Buchanan.

The actual work of the Conference was done by three committees that were appointed to consider and to report upon two or more items of the Conference agenda. These committees reported to the Conference sitting in plenary session.

The various conventions, declarations, resolutions, and recommendations approved by the Conference were presented in the final act and included: the Convention for the Peaceful Adjustment of International Differences; the Convention Concerning the Limitation of the Employment of Force in the Collection of Contract Debts; the Convention Concerning the Laws and Customs of War on Land; the Convention Concerning the Rights and Duties of Neutral Powers and Persons in Land Warfare; the Convention Regarding the Enemy's Ships of Commerce at the Beginning of Hostilities; the Convention for Regulating the Transformation of Vessels of Commerce into Vessels of War; the Convention in Regard to the Placing of Submarine Mines; the ConventionConcerning the Bombardment of Undefended Ports, Cities, and Villages by Naval Vessels in Time of War; the Convention for the Adaptation of the Principles of the Geneva Convention to Maritime Warfare; the Convention with Regard to Certain Restrictions upon the Right of Capture in Maritime War; the Convention Regarding the Establishment of an International Prize Court; the Convention Concerning the Rights and Duties of Neutral Powers in Case of Maritime War; and a declaration concerning the launching of projectiles from balloons.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Deputy Foreign Ministers held separate meetings in conjunction with each session of the Council of Foreign Ministers and also held meetings during the intervals between formal Council of Foreign Ministers sessions. Assistant Secretary of State James C. Dunn served as Deputy to the Secretary of State for the United States. Ronald I. Campbell, Assistant Under Secretary of State in the British Foreign Office served as Deputy to British Foreign Secretary Ernest Bevin. The Soviet Union was represented by Feodor Tarasovich Gusev, the Soviet Ambassador to Great Britain, and Maurice Couve de Murville, Director General for Political Affairs in the French Foreign Ministry represnted France. The four deputies first met at Lancaster House, London, on January 18, 1945, and agreed to begin consideration of the "understandings" reached by the Council of Foreign Ministers at its first plenary session in London, September 11 to October 2, 1945.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The U.S. Legation at Buenos Aires was opened on December 27, 1823. The chief of mission remained resident until May 1, 1857, when it moved to Parana, where it remained until February 25, 1862. The Legation was raised to embassy status when the first U.S. ambassador presented his letter of credence on January 8, 1915. 

Serving as Minister Plenipotentiary was Caesar A. Rodney who presented his credentials on December 27, 1823. He died at his post on June 10, 1824. Thereafter serving as Charge d'Affaires, with dates of presentation of credentials, were John M. Forbes, August 20, 1825; Francis Baylies, June 15, 1832; William Brent, Jr., November 15, 1844; William A. Harris, July 7, 1846; John S. Pendleton, ca. September 12, 1851, and James A. Peden, January 22, 1855. The chief of mission was upgraded to Minister Resident with the appointment of James A. Peden who presented his new credentials on June 25, 1856. Following Peden were Benjamin C. Yancey, December 1, 1858; John F. Cushman, December 22, 1859; Robert M. Palmer, October 5, 1861; Robert C. Kirk, June 21, 1862; Alexander Asboth, October 20, 1866; H.G. Worthington, September 11, 1868; Robert C. Kirk (second appointment), July 8, 1869; Julius White, May 6, 1873; and Thomas O. Osborn, May 21, 1874. On July 7, 1994, Osborn was recommissioned as Minister Resident/Consul General, and was succeeded by Bayless W. Hanna, October 15, 1885. On February 15, 1888, Hanna presented his credentials as Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary. He was succeeded in this rank by John R.G. Pitkin, October 31, 1889; William I. Buchanan, May 19, 1894; William P. Lord, February 14, 1900; John Barrett, December 21, 1903; Arthur Beaupre, June 17, 1904; Spencer F. Eddy, August 27, 1908; Charles H. Sherrill, June 30, 1909; and John W. Garrett, February 29, 1912.

Following the raising of the legation to embassy status the following served as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary: Frederic Jesup Stimson, January 8, 1915; John W. Riddle, March 8, 1922; Peter Augustus Jay, September 24, 1925; Robert Woods Bliss, September 9, 1927; Alexander W. Weddell, September 18, 1933; Norman Armour, June 19, 1939; Spruille Braden, May 21, 1945; George S. Messersmith, May 23, 1946; James Bruce, August 21, 1947; Stanton Griffis, November 17, 1949; Ellsworth Bunker, May 8, 1951; Albert F. Nufer, August 14, 1952; Willard L. Beaulac, June 1, 1956; Roy Richard Rubottom, Jr., October 20, 1960; Robert McClintock, February 14, 1962; Edwin M. Martin, June 11, 1964; Carter L. Burgess, August 21, 1968; John Davis Lodge, July 23, 1969; Robert C. Hill, February 15, 1974; Raul H. Castro, November 16, 1977; Harry W. Shlaudeman, November 4, 1980; Frank V. Ortiz, November 29, 1983; Theodore E. Gildred, November 6, 1986; Terence A. Todman, June 13, 1989; and James Richard Cheek, July 19, 1993. Ambassador Cheek departed the post on December 18, 1996, with Ronald D. Godard serving as Charge d'Affaires until July 3, 2000 when James Donald Walsh presented his credentials.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Advisory Commission of Railway Experts to the Russian Railway Service Corps, composed of five prominent American railway experts headed by John F. Stevens, arrived in Petrograd on June 17, 1917. It was to advise the Russian Government on the Russian railways with a view to improving thier efficiency, and thus to facilitate the forwarding of American supplies to Russia. The Commission's recommendations were accepted by the Russian Government in August 1917. The Commission terminated its existence with the formation of the Interallied Railway Committee on March 5, 1919.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Bureau of Transportation was created on October 15, 1917, replacing the Transportation Division of the Export Licenses Bureau of the Exports Administrative Board. The Bureau administered and enforced the rules and regulations of the War Trade Board by granting or withholding fueling and provisioning licenses to vessel entering or leaving the United States or its possessions. On June 30, 1919, the functions of the Bureau were transferred to the War Trade Board Section, Department of State.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Interallied Railway Committee was created under the terms of the Interallied Railway Agreement of January and February 1919 between the United States and Japan and subscribed to by the Allied and Associated Powers and the Provisional Government of Russia (at Omsk). The Committee included one representative each from Japan, the United States, Great Britain, France, Italy, Czechoslovakia, China, and the Provisional Russian Government. The Russian representative, L.A. Oustrugoff, served as Chairman, and the American representative, C. Smith, as Secretary. The first meeting was held at Vladivostok on March 5, 1919. Its purpose was to rehabilitate and reestablish efficient transportation on the Chinese Eastern and Siberian Railways by the supervision of railroad operations in the zone of Allied intervention on Siberia and China. In accordance with the terms of the Interallied Railway Agreement, the Committee terminated upon the withdrawal of the last foreign military forces from Siberia on October 25, 1922.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The U.S. Embassy for the Bahamas was established at Nassau on July 10, 1973, with Moncrieff J. Spear as Charge d'Affaires ad interim. The first Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary, Ronald I. Spiers, presented his credentials on September 7, 1973. He was succeeded by Seymour Weiss, September 11, 1974; Jack B. Olson, December 22, 1976; William B. Schwartz, October 11, 1977; Lev E. Dobriansky, March 15, 1983; Carol Boyd Hallett, November 17, 1986; and Chic Hecht, August 23, 1989. Hecht left Nassau on March 1, 1993, and the following served as Charge d'Affaires ad interim: Lino Gutierrez, March - July 1993, and John S. Ford, July 1993 - March 1994. Sidney Williams presented his credentials as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary on March 27, 1994, and was succeeded by Arthur Louis Schechter, October 29, 1998, and J. Richard Blankenship, December 3, 2001.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The U.S. Embassy, Barbados, was established at Bridgetown on November 30, 1966. George Dolgin served as Charge d'Affaires ad interim until November 27, 1967, when Fredric R. Mann presented his credentials as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary. 

Mann was succeeded by Eileen R. Donovan, September 5, 1969; Theodore R. Britton, February 12, 1975; Frank V. Ortiz, Jr., July 29, 1977; Sally A. Shelton, June 7, 1979; Milan D. Bish, December 10, 1981; Thomas H. Anderson, Jr., July 11, 1984; and Paul A. Russo, December 10, 1986. From June 1988 until November 1990 John E. Clark served as Charge d'Affaires ad interim. A new Ambassador, G. Philip Hughes, presented his credentials on November 14, 1990. He was succeeded by Jeanette W. Hyde, April 14, 1994; E. William Crotty, November 24, 1998; and James A. Daley, September 26, 2000. Marcia S. Bernicat served as Charge d'Affaires from August 2001 through March 2002, and Roland W. Bullen served as Charge from March through August 2002. Earl Norfleet Phillips presented his credentials as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary on March 19, 2002.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The United States recognized the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina on April 7, 1992, and established diplomatic relations on August 6, 1992. A U.S. embassy was established at Vienna, Austria, on November 10, 1993; the U.S. Embassy at Sarajevo opened on July 4, 1994. 

The following served as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary, with dates of presentation of credentials: Victor Jackovich, June 23, 1993; John K. Menzies, January 7, 1996; Richard D. Kauzlarich, August 28, 1997; Thomas J. Miller, August 27, 1999; and Clifford G. Bond, November 2, 2001.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The United States opened diplomatic relations with Liberia on February 23, 1864, when Abraham Hanson presented his credentials as Commissioner and Consul General and opened the Legation at Monrovia. He was succeeded as chief of mission by John Seys who presented his credentials as Minister Resident and Consul General on January 2, 1867. He was succeeded by J. Milton Turner, July 19, 1871 (Turner was the first African-American diplomat sent to an African country); John H. Smyth, August 19, 1878; Henry Highland Garnet, December 22, 1881; John H. Smyth, August 4, 1882; Moses A. Hopkins, December 14, 1885; C.H.J. Taylor, June 4, 1887; Ezekiel E. Smith, July 21, 1888; Alexander Clark, November 25, 1890; William D. McCoy, March 28, 1892; William H. Heard, May 6, 1895; Owen L.W. Smith, ca. May 11, 1898; John R.A. Crossland, May 13, 1902; Ernest Lyon, July 27, 1903; William D. Crum, August 25, 1910; George W. Buckner, December 8, 1913; James L. Curtis, December 29, 1915; Joseph J. Johnson, October 8, 1919; Solomon Porter Hood, February 13, 1922; and William T. Francis, November 30, 1927.

The first U.S. Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary, Charles E. Mitchell, presented his credentials in 1931. He was succeeded by Lester A. Walton, October 2, 1935; Raphael O'Hara Lanier, July 1, 1946; and Edward R. Dudley, October 18, 1948. In 1949 Dudley was promoted to Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary; he presented his new credentials on May 6, 1949. He was succeeded by Jesse D. Locker, October 16, 1953; Richard Lee Jones, June 24, 1955; Elbert G. Mathews, September 30, 1959; Charles Edward Rhetts, August 7, 1962; Ben H. Brown, Jr., January 6, 1965; Samuel Z. Westerfield, Jr., December 9, 1969; Melvin L. Manfull, December 22, 1972; W. Beverly Carter, Jr., April 23, 1976; Robert P. Smith, August 6, 1979; William Lacy Swing, August 11, 1981; Edward Joseph Perkins, August 28, 1985; and James Keough Bishop, May 4, 1987.

Peter Jon de Vos, the next Ambassador, arrived at Monrovia on June 28, 1990, however the Government of Liberia was overthrown on September 11, 1990, before he presented his credentials. He continued to serve at Monrovia until July 27, 1992. From 1992 through 1999 the following served as Charge d'Affaires: William H. Twaddell, September 1992 - July 1995; William B. Milam, November 1995 - January 1999; and Donald K. Petterson [sic], February - August 1999.

Bismarck Myrick was appointed Ambassador on July 7, 1999; he presented his credentials on August 20, 1999. He was succeeded by John William Blaney, October 3, 2002.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The United States and Australia established diplomatic relations on January 8, 1940. The U.S. Legation at Canberra opened on July 17, 1940, and was raised to embassy status on July 19, 1946.

Serving as Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary, with dates of presentation of credentials, were Clarence E. Gauss, July 17, 1940, and Nelson T. Johnson, September 12, 1941. Johnson left Australia on April 20, 1945, and was succeeded by John R. Minter, who was serving as Charge d'Affaires ad interim when the Legation was raised to an embassy.

Subsequently appointed as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary were Robert Butler, September 25, 1946; Myron Melvin Cowen, August 20, 1948; Pete Jarman, September 7, 1949; Amos J. Peaslee, August 12, 1953; Douglas Maxwell Moffat, March 27, 1956; William J. Sebald, June 7, 1957; William C. Battle, July 13, 1962; Edward Clark, August 23, 1965; William H. Crook, July 22, 1968; Walter L. Rice, September 11, 1969; Marshall Green, June 8, 1973; James W. Hargrove, February 19, 1976; Philip H. Alston, Jr., May 23, 1977; Robert D. Nesen, June 17, 1981; Laurence W. Lane, Jr., January 7, 1986; Melvin F. Sembler, October 25, 1989; Edward J. Perkins, November 24, 1993; Genta H. Holmes, April 11, 1997; Edward William Gnehm, Jr., August 30, 2000; and J. Thomas Schieffer, August 23, 2001.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Thirteenth International Congress Against Alcohol was held at The Hague from September 11 to 16, 1911, at the invitation of the Government of the Netherlands. United States participation was provided for by an act of Congress that appropriated $4,500 for the sending of several delegates. Other nations represented were Australia, Austria-Hungary, Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, Great Britain, Greece, the Netherlands, Norweay, Portugal, Romania, Sweden, Switzerland, and Uruguay. The program for the Congress included discussions of topics under two main categories: the state and alcoholism, and society and alcoholism. The U.S. delegation submitted a report to ther President on May 10, 1913.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
This conference, preliminary to a more general international conference on communications, was held at Washington, D.C. in October, November, and December 1920, to decide upon the status of former German cable companies and to study all the problems of international communications in order to submit to the Allied and Associated powers proposals and recommendations as to the equitable and just division of the world's communications facilities.

The Conference was attended by delegates from France, Great Britain, Italy, Japan, and the United States. The United States was represented by Walter S. Rogers, Admiral W.S. Benson, Postmaster General A.S. Burleson, and Norman H. Davis.

Specific topics on the agenda of the Conference were referred for study to the following: Subcommittee to Consider the Disposition of the German Cables Ceded to the Five Principal Allied Powers Under Annxes Seven of the Peace Treaty; Subcommittee to Consider the EU-F-GB-I Radio Protocol; Subcommittee on International Cable and Radio Law and Cable Landing Rights; Subcommittee on Improvement of Communications Facilities between the Five Great Powers; and Subcommittee on Universal Communications Union and Telegraph and Radio Conventions.

In addition to preparing reports for the consideration of a later and more general conference, this Conference drafted a convention and regulations covering both telegraph and radio-telegraph communications for submission to the forthcoming World Conference on Electrical Communications.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Office of Administration was established on September 21, 1949, pursuant to Staff Announcement No. 1, HICOG, September 21, 1949, and its organization and functions were set forth in Staff Announcement No. 11, HICOG, September 21, 1949. It succeeded the Provisional Office of Administration, Office of Military Government for Germany (U.S.), which had been established on July 19, 1949, by General Order 26, OMGUS, July 19, 1949. The Office of Administration was responsible for the performance of administrative functions of the Office of the High Commissioner, including the development of organizational structure; the definition and assignment of responsibilities, staffing requirements, and methods of operation for each of the functional elements of HICOG. It maintained the HICOG office of record. It coordinated with the European Command and, after March 1953, the U.S. European Command, on matters relating to the logistical support of HICOG. The Office was redesignated the Office of the Executive Director on February 1, 1952, pursuant to Staff Announcement No. 269, February 6, 1952, and was abolished on May 5, 1955, with the termination of HICOG.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Second International Conference on Emigration and Immigration was held at Havana, Cuba, from March 31 to April 17, 1928, at the invitation of the Cuban Government. The invitation was extended at the request of the Committee of Control, which had been established by the first conference on emigration and immigration held at Rome, Italy, in May 1924.

Delegates were sent to the Second Conference from Argentina, Austria, Belgium, Bolivia, Chile, China, Colombia, Costa Rica, Cubam Czechoslovakia, the Danzig Free State, the Dominican Republic, Ecuador, Egypt, El Salvador, Estonia, France, Germany, Great Britain, Guatemala, Haiti, Holland, Hungary, Italy, Japan, Mexico, Norway, Panama, Paraguay, Peru, Poland, Portugal, the Republic of South Africa, Romania, Spain, Switzerland, Sweden, the United States, Uruguay, and Venezuela. The United States was represented by W.W. Husband, Norval P. Nicols, John W. Kerr, John D. Long, Leo J. Keena, and Henry Carter. As instructed, they took a passive part in the debates of the Conference and abstained from voting.

The Conference met to discuss technical and nonpolitical questions regarding emigration and immigration in order to establish a basis for international cooperation in such matters. The principal questions considered were the manner and means whereby international consideration of emigration and immigration problems could best be conducted, the method to be adopted for carrying on the work of the Conference, and the creation of a suitable body for the latter purpose. The questions on the agenda were referred to five committees appointed by the Conference.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Second Samoan Conference met in Berlin from April 29 to June 14, 1889, and completed the work begun by the First Samoan Conference to reach a peacable adjustment of Samoan affairs.  Germany, Great Britain, and the United States were the participants. The United States was represented by John A. Kasson, William W. Phelps, and George H. Bates. The results of the Conference were embodied in a general act signed on June 14, 1889. The act consisted of eight articles declaring the purpose of the three powers with regard to the independence and neutrality of Samoa and providing for the establishment of a supreme court for Samoa, the investigation and registration of land titles, the administration of Apia, taxation and revenue, and the restriction of traffic in firearms and intoxicants.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
Department of Defense (DoD) Directive 5105.13, dated August 10, 1957, abolished the Assistant Secretary of Defense (Legislative and Public Affairs) and its’ functions were divided and transferred to the new Assistant Secretary of Defense (Public Affairs) and Assistant to the Secretary of Defense (Legislative Affairs). He was appointed by the President with the advice and consent of the Senate. The Assistant Secretary of Defense (Public Affairs) advised and assisted the Secretary of Defense (OSD) in the establishment of policies and systems necessary for effective and economical operation of public information and other public affairs activities of the Department of Defense. His responsibilities included functions such as the supervision and operation of consolidated public information and related activities for all agencies of the Department of Defense located at the seat of government; the formulation of policies and criteria governing Departmentwide public information and public affairs activities; the formulation of policies and criteria for and the performance of security reviews of manuscripts, documents, and other material to be released through the public media, the general public, and the armed forces.; and the provision for the coordinated development and implementation within the Department of Defense of plans, policies, and programs for all aspects of downgrading and declassification of classified material. He collaborated with the other Assistant Secretaries of Defense, the General Counsel of the Department of Defense, and other officials on matters of mutual interest or responsibility. The Assistant Secretary established Freedom of Information policy for the Department of Defense and conducted policy and security review of information originating with the Department. The Office replied to inquiries regarding the Department of Defense. It managed the Armed Forces Radio and Television Service, the Armed Forces Press and Publication Service, and the American Forces Information Service. It maintained a national media pool to deploy, as directed by the Secretary of Defense, to cover U.S. military operations.

The Assistants Secretary of Defense (Public Affairs) included Murray Snyder, March 21, 1957–January 20, 1961; Arthur Sylvester, January 20, 1961–February 3, 1967; Philip G. Goulding, February 28, 1967–January 20, 1969; Daniel Z. Henkin (Acting), January 20, 1969–May 25, 1969; Daniel Z. Henkin, May 25, 1969–January 20, 1973; Jerry W. Friedheim (Acting), January 20, 1973–April 13, 1973; Jerry W. Friedheim, April 13, 1973–September 20, 1974; William Beecher (Acting), September 21, 1974–February 11, 1975; Joseph Laitin, February 12, 1975–December 19, 1975; William I. Greener, Jr., December 21, 1975–July 31, 1976; M. Alan Woods, August 6, 1976–January 21, 1977; Thomas B. Ross, March 7, 1977–January 20, 1981; Henry E. Catto, Jr., May 22, 1981–September 16, 1983; Benjamin Welles (Acting), September 17, 1983–November 1, 1983; Mary Lou Sheils (Acting), November 2, 1983–November 22, 1983; Michael I. Burch, November 23, 1983–June 22, 1985; Fred Hoffman (Acting) , June 23, 1985–October 1, 1985; Robert B. Sims, October 18, 1985–September 20, 1987; Fred Hoffman (Acting), September 21, 1987–February 2, 1988; J. Daniel Howard, February 3, 1988–March 21, 1989; and Louis A. Williams, May 22, 1989–January 20, 1993.

By administrative action, Secretary of Defense Les Aspin changed the title of the Assistant Secretary of Defense (Public Affairs) to the Assistant to the Secretary of Defense (Public Affairs) on January 22, 1993, confirmed by Defense Directive 5122.5, dated December 2, 1993. The Assistant to the Secretary of Defense for Public Affairs was responsible for the functional areas which included Defense public and internal information; audiovisual activities; community relations; review of information intended for public release to ensure compliance with security policies; implementation of the Freedom of Information Act and the access portion of Federal Privacy Act programs within the Department of Defense; long-range coordination and planning of public schedules of senior Defense officials; and providing editorial services to the Secretary and Deputy Secretary of Defense. Liaison was maintained with and assistance was provided to information media and national and civic organizations with respect to matters relating to activities of the Department of Defense. Approvals were required for military participation in public exhibitions, demonstrations, and ceremonies of national or international significance.

The Assistants to the Secretary of Defense for Public Affairs were Vernon A. Guidry, Jr., January 22, 1993–July 18, 1993; Kathleen deLaski, July 19, 1993–August 5, 1994; and Kenneth H. Bacon, September 20, 1994-March 29, 1996.

The National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 1995 (Public Law 103-337), dated October 5, 1994, increased the number of Assistant Secretaries from 10 to 11. The position subsequently reverted to the title Assistant Secretary of Defense (Public Affairs) (ASD(PA)) on March 29, 1996, through DoD Directive 5122.5. The ASD(PA) was the principal staff advisor and assistant to the Secretary and Deputy Secretary of Defense for DoD public information, internal information, community relations, information training, and audiovisual matters. In the exercise of this responsibility, the ASD(PA) developed policies, plans, and programs in support of DoD objectives and operations. The Office ensured a free flow of news and information to the news media, the general public, the internal audiences of the DoD Components, and other appropriate forums, limited only by national security constraints as authorized by Executive Order 12958 and valid statutory mandates or exemptions. The ASD(PA) served as the spokesperson and release authority for DoD information and audiovisual materials to news media representatives; evaluated news media requests for DoD support and cooperation; and determined appropriate level of DoD participation. The Office established and exercised procedures for the administrative management, activation, and direction of the DoD National Media Pool. It oversaw and coordinated, as necessary, the activities of a DoD-level, National Media Pool for potential use in military contingency operations and other activities. The Office monitored, evaluated, and developed systems, standards, and procedures for the administration and management of approved policies, plans, and programs. It issued policy guidance and public affairs guidance to the DoD Components. 

The Office of Assistant Secretary of Defense (Public Affairs) participated with the Under Secretary of Defense (Comptroller) in planning, programming, and budgeting activities, as required. It promoted coordination, cooperation, and mutual understanding among DoD Components and with other Federal, State, and local agencies and the civilian community. The ASD(PA) served on boards, committees, and other groups, and represented the Secretary of Defense outside of the DoD. It oversaw the provision of news clipping services for the OSD, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, and the Military Departments' headquarters. The Office prepared speeches, public statements, Congressional testimony, articles for publication, and other materials for public release by selected DoD and White House officials, as required. It served as official point of contact for public and media appearances by DoD officials, and conducted advanced planning and coordination, as required, with private, public, and media organizations for such events. The Office received, analyzed, and replied to inquiries regarding DoD policies, programs, or activities that were received from the general public either directly or from other Government Agencies. It prepared and provided to the referring office replies to inquiries from the general public that were forwarded from the Congress and the White House. The ASD(PA) evaluated, coordinated, and approved: requests for DoD cooperation in programs involving relations with the public; requests by news media representatives or other non-DoD personnel for travel in military carriers for public affairs purposes; and proposed public affairs guidance, public affairs plans, and public affairs annexes to operations plans. The Office provided DoD assistance to non-Government, entertainment-oriented motion picture, television, and video productions. It evaluated and coordinated the DoD responses to requests for speakers received by DoD and, as required, assisted in scheduling, programming, and drafting speeches for the participation of qualified personnel. In addition, the ASD(PA) exercised authority, direction, and control over the American Forces Information Service (AFIS) (DoDD 5122.10).

The Assistants Secretary of Defense (Public Affairs) included Kenneth H. Bacon, March 29, 1996–January 19, 2001; Victoria Clarke, May 22, 2001–June 20, 2003; Lawrence Di Rita (Acting), August 10, 2003–September 22, 2005; J. Dorrance Smith, January 5, 2006–January 20, 2009; Price Floyd (Performing the duties of), January 2009–February 2010; Douglas B. Wilson, February 11, 2010–March 31, 2012; and George Little (Acting), April 1, 2012–October 8, 2012.

On October 9, 2012, a memorandum from the Secretary of Defense retitled the position again to the Assistant to the Secretary of Defense (Public Affairs).

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: After the failure to arrive at any quadripartite agreement and the adjournment of the Council of Foreign Ministers meeting at London in 1947, a tripartite meeting was convoked early in 1948 to deal with the pressing problems of Germany left unresolved. There were preliminary Anglo-American talks starting on February 19, but the conference did not officially begin until February 23. The Benelux countries were invited to join the talks on February 26, and participated in all matters except those that were the responsibility of the occupying powers. The two major issues discussed were the fusion of the French zone with Bizonia and the establishment of a democratic federal system for the political reorganization of Western Germany. The sessions recessed from March 6 to April 20, while working parties prepared reports and recommendations on these issues. Since there was no conference secretariat, each national delegation accumulated and maintained its own documents, with the British delegation acting as clearinghouse..

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Committee on Public Information (the "Creel Committee") was established as an independent agency by E.O. 2594, April 13, 1917, with George Creel as Chairman, and the Secretaries of State, War, and the Navy as ex officio members. The Committee released government news, issued educational information designed to sustain morale, and administered voluntary press censorship. At first its efforts were confined to the United States, but later it undertook a program to publicize America overseas. Domestic activities ceased with the Armistice, November 11, 1918; foreign operations were discontinued on June 30, 1919, when the Committee ceased to function. The Committee was formally discontinued by E.O. 3154, August 21, 1919, with the Council of National Defense designated as liquidator.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Inter-American Radio Conference, held in Havana, Cuba, from November to December 1937, was the first of its kind ever held in Cuba. The most controversial matter discussed at Havana was North American broadcasting. An agreement was reached whereby the public of the United States could be assured of better broadcasting in the future by the elimination of reception interference caused by high-powered radio stations located in neighboring countries. If an agreement has not been reached, both pan-Americanism and good radio broadcasting service within the United States would have been endangered. The Conference concluded a series of agreements concerning the application of radio to inter-American communications--including aviation, police, broadcasting, ship, fixed service, and amatuer communications.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The U.S. Legation for Austria opened at Vienna on November 7, 1838. In 1867, following the establishment of the Dual Monarchy, the chief of mission was accredited to Austria-Hungary. In April 1901 the Legation was upgraded to embassy status. The Embassy closed on  April 9, 1917, following the Austro-Hungarian decision to sever relations with the United States, which came after the U.S. declaration of war on Germany.

Serving as Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary, with dates of presentation of credentials, were Henry A. Muhlenberg, November 7, 1838, and Daniel Jenifer, March 30, 1842. Jenifer was recalled in July 1845, and was succeeded as chief of mission by William H. Stiles, who served as Charge d'Affaires from August 5, 1845 until August 1, 1849. Subsequent charges included James Watson Webb, February 1850 - May 1850; Charles J. McCurdy, March 1851 - October 1852; Thomas M. Foote, December 1852 - June 1853; Henry R. Jackson, September 1853 - September 1854. On February 8, 1854, Jackson was recommissioned as Minister Resident, and he presented his new credentials on September 28, 1854. He was succeeded by Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary J. Glancy Jones, February 14, 1859; J. Lothrup Motley, November 14, 1861; Henry M. Watts, September 25, 1868; John Jay, June 1, 1869; Godlove S. Orth, May 24, 1875; Edward F. Beale, August 10, 1876; John A. Kasson, August 30, 1977; William Walter Phelps, June 20, 1881; Alphonso Taft, June 30, 1882; John M. Francis, September 11, 1884; Alexander R. Lawton, August 25, 1887; Frederick D. Grant, May 15, 1889; Bartlett Tripp, June 8, 1893; Charlemagne Tower, June 18, 1897; Addison C. Harris, April 13, 1899; and Robert S. McCormick, April 29, 1901. On June 26, 1902, McCormick presented his credentials as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary. He was succeeded by Bellamy Storer, January 3, 1903; Charles S. Francis, May 29, 1906; Richard C. Kerens, April 12, 1910, Frederic Courtland Penfield, September 26, 1913. Penfield left the post on April 7, 1917. Joseph C. Grew was serving as Charge d'Affaires when the Embassy closed on April 9, 1917.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
Diplomatic relations with Austria were resumed October 21, 1921, and the U.S. Mission was established at Vienna on November 26, 1921. Arthur Hugh Frazier served as Charge d'Affaires pro tem until Albert Henry Washburn presented his credentials as Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary, June 19, 1922. Thereafter the U.S. Mission was designated the U.S. Legation. 

Washburn died at his post on April 29, 1930. He was succeeded by Gilchrist Baker Stockton who presented his credentials on May 15, 1930; George H. Earle, 3rd, September 27, 1933; George S. Messersmith, May 23, 1934; and Grenville T. Emmet, September 14, 1937. Emmet died at his post on September 26, 1937. John C. Wiley was serving as Charge d'Affaires ad interim when Austria was annexed by Germany on March 13, 1938. Legation Vienna closed on April 30, 1938.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: At the Teheran Conference, November 28 to December 1, 1943, Great Britain, the United States, and the Soviet Union had agreed that it would be most desirable if Turkey would enter the war on the side of the Allies before the end of the year. Immediately following that Conference, President Franklin D. Roosevelt and Prime Minister Winston S. Churchill met with Turkish President Ismet Inonu at the Second Cairo Conference, December 4 to December 6, 1943. This Conference discussed a possible Turkish entry into the war, affirmed the alliance between Great Britain and Turkey, and noted "the firm friendship between the Turkish people and the United States". As a result of the Anglo-American discussions at the Conference, General Dwight D. Eisenhower was given command of the invasion of western Europe.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The eighteen-power Paris Conference on Reparations was in session from November 9 to December 21, 1945. It was convened upon the invitation of the Governments of the United States, Great Britain, and France, as the powers occupying the three western zones of Germany. Other participating countries included Albania, Australia, Belgium, Canada, Czechoslovakia, Denmark, Egypt, Greece, India, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, the Union of South Africa, and Yugoslavia. James W. Angell, the U.S. representative on the Allied Commission on Reparations for Germany, was the American delegate to the Conference, and D. Maynard Phelps, the deputy U.S. representative on the Allied Commission, was deputy delegate.

The Conference recommended to the participating governments the adoption of the Paris Agreement on Reparations. The agreement established the governing principles and the mechanism for the division of German assets among the 18 nations which were represented at the Conference. In the establishment of reparations shares the Conference was guided by the principle, agrred upon at Yalta, that reparations from Germany should be received in the first instance by those countries which had borne the main burden of the war and suffered the heaviest losses. The Paris Agreement also provided for the establishment of an Inter-Allied Reparation Agency (IARA) at Brussels as the mechanism for the division of German reparations assets.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: At the urging of the United States, the foreign ministers of Great Britain and the Soviet Union, Ernest Bevin and Vyacheslav Molotov, met with Secretary of State James F. Byrnes in Moscow to try and resolve the impasse which had developed at the first Council of Foreign Ministers meeting in London, in late September and early October. At Moscow the Big Three reached agreement concerning the peace settlements for Italy, Bulgaria, Hungary, Romania, and Finland. The agreemment called for the preparation of draft peace treaties by the Council of Foreign Ministers; the convening of a twenty-one nation peace conference to consider the draft treaties and to make recommendations regarding them; the reconsideration and completion of the treaties by the Council of Foreign Ministers in light of those recommendations; and the signing of the final texts of the treaties. At this meeting the foreign ministers, with the agreement of China, also replaced the Far Eastern Advisory Commision by establishing the Far Eastern Commission, the Allied Council for Japan, and a Joint Commission for Korea. In addition, the Big Three discussed at length international control of atomic energy,

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The American Mission for Aid to Greece (AMAG) was established by a United States-Greece agreement, concluded on June 20, 1947, pursuant to the Greek-Turkish Aid Act (61 Stat. 103), approved May 22, 1947. The military component of AMAG consisted of a U.S. Army Group and a U.S. Navy Group, responsible for coordinating procurement and distribution of materiel, but prohibited from giving operational advice to Greek armed forces. The Joint U.S. Military Advisory and Planning Group, Greece (JUSMAPG) was established under AMAG by a joint directive of Secretaries of the Army, the Navy, and the Air Force, December 31, 1947, and issued as JCS 1798/5, January 7, 1948, with responsibility for providing operational and logistical advice to units of Greek armed forces fighting communist guerrilla units. A U.S. Air Force Group was established in AMAG on November 1948. The Greek aid program was extended through FY 1949 by Title III of Foreign Assistance Act of 1948 (62 Stat. 157), approved April 3, 1948; and further extended through FY 1950 by MDAA, Title II. JUSMAPG was abolished; and the U.S. Army, Navy, and Air Force Groups, AMAG, were consolidated under AMAG to form a new organization, Joint U.S. Military Aid Group, Greece (JUSMAG Greece), March 20, 1950, pursuant to JCS 1798/31, approved March 10, 1950. Following the admission of Greece into NATO on February 18, 1952, and the establishment of the U.S. European Command (US EUCOM), August 1, 1952, JUSMAG Greece was placed under US EUCOM by Commander- in-Chief, Europe (US CINCEUR) message 312140Z to Chief, JUSMAG Greece, August 1, 1952.

The Joint U.S. Military Aid Group, Greece changed its name to Office of Defense Cooperation (ODC) in March 1988.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Paris Peace Conference was convened in accordance with the decision of the Interim Meeting of Foreign Ministers (Tripartite) at Moscow, December 16 - 26, 1945, to provide to the other Allied nations an opportunity to express their views on the draft peace treaties with the Axis satellite states of Italy, Romania, Bulgaria, Hungary, and Finland. The twenty-one nation conference opened on July 29, 1946, and was charged with considering and recommending changes in the draft treaties which the Council of Foreign Ministers had prepared during its sessions at London and Paris, January 18 - July 12, 1946. The Conference revealed increasing disagreement between the Soviet Union and the Western Powers, as the former continually objected to the participation of the smaller nations in the treaty-making process.

The initial meetings of the Conference in plenary session were devoted to opening remarks by the various delegates. The articles of the five draft treaties were then distributed to eight commissions for detailed consideration. The commissions reported to the plenary Conference, either approving each article as drafted by the Council of Foreign Ministers or proposing changes. The Conference considered the reports of the commissions in plenary session and drafted its recommendations, which were then submitted to the Council of Foreign Ministers. The Paris Peace Conference completed its work on October 15, 1946.

The Conference produced the Paris peace treaties which were signed on February 10, 1947. The treaties allowed Italy, Romania, Hungary, Bulgaria, and Finland to reassume their responsibilities as sovereign states in international affairs and to qualify for membership in the United Nations. The treaties also incorporated provisions for the payment of reparations, commitment to human rights, the end of the Italian colonial empire in Africa, and numerous border adjustments.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The first legal office of the Treasury was created by statute in 1820.  The original name for the office director was Agent of the Treasury.  The activities were primarily those of a collection agency for the Department.  In 1830, the name was changed to the Office of the Solicitor and its authority and functions greatly expanded.   The Solicitor became the chief law officer of the Department and remained such until 1933 when the Office was transferred to the Department of Justice by Executive Order in 1933.  The Office of the Solicitor was abolished by the Revenue Act of 1934, and the Office of General Councel was established effective June 20, 1934.  Treasury Department Circular No. 519 established the Legal Division which was to function under the direct supervision and control of the General Counsel. The General Counsel was the chief law officer of the Department and was appointed by the President with the advice and consent of the Senate.  The principal and most important role of the General Counsel was to serve as the senior legal and a senior policy advisor to the Secretary and other senior Departmental officials.  The responsibility of the General Counsel include consideration of legal problems relating to broad policy aspects of management of the public debt, administration of Internal Revenue and tariff laws, international cooperation in the monetary and financial fields, law enforcement affairs and similar activities. All chief and legal counsels of the Department and their staffs were part of the Legal Division.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: According to Article 23 and Annex XI of the Treaty of Peace with Italy, signed in Paris on February 10, 1947, the United States, Great Britain, the Soviet Union, and France agreed that they would, within one year of the coming into force of the Treaty, jointly determine the final disposition of Italy's former territorial possessions in Africa, i.e. Libya, Eritrea, and Italian Somaliland. The deputies of the Council of Foreign Ministers were to consider the question of their disposition and to report their recommendations to the Council of Foreign Ministers. The Deputies met in London, October 1947 - July 1948. In order to obtain factual formation upon which to base their recommendations, the Deputies sent an investigative commission to the former colonies to examine conditions there and to determine the views of the local inhabitants. The Deputies submitted their recommendations, which were not unanimous, to the Council of Foreign Ministers on August 31, 1948.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Department of Commerce was a Cabinet department of the United States Government concerned with promoting economic growth. It was originally created as the Department of Commerce and Labor on February 14, 1903. It was subsequently renamed to the Department of Commerce on March 4, 1913, and its bureaus and agencies specializing in labor were transferred to the new Department of Labor. The mission of the Department was to "promote job creation and improved living standards for all Americans by creating an infrastructure that promotes economic growth, technological competitiveness, and sustainable development." Among its tasks were the gathering economic and demographic data for business and government decision-making, issuing patents and trademarks, and helping to set industrial standards. It was  administered by the Secretary of Commerce.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Reconstruction Finance Corporation (RFC) was established as an independent agency by the Reconstruction Finance Corporation Act (47 Stat. 5), approved January 22, 1932, to make loans and provide other types of financial assistance to banks, other credit institutions, and railroads. Later legislation authorized the Corporation to extend financial assistance to business enterprises generally. On June 25, 1940, an amendment to the Reconstruction Finance Corporation Act (54 Stat. 573) granted the Corporation broad powers to engage in financing war-related activities. The Corporation was authorized to make loans or to purchase the capital stock of any corporation "(a) for the purpose of producing, acquiring, and carrying strategic and critical materials as defined by the President, and (b) for plant construction, expansion and equipment, and working capital, to be used by the corporation in the manufacture of equipment and supplies necessary to the national defense." It was authorized also to create subsidiary corporation with power to produce, acquire, and carry strategic and critical materials; to purchase and lease land; to purchase, lease, build, and expand plants; to purchase and produce equipment, supplies, and machinery for the manufacture of arms, ammunition, and implements of war; to lease such plants to private corporations to engage in such manufacture; and, if necessary, to engage in such manufacture itself. These powers were expanded on June 10, 1941 (55 Stat. 249), to include authorization to provide financial aid not only for the manufacture of arms, ammunition, and the implements of war, but also for the manufacture or processing of strategic and critical materials and of any other articles, equipment, facilities, and supplies necessary to the national defense.

The Corporation found it expedient to carry out some of its loan programs through subsidiary corporations. These subsidiaries were legally and financially separate from the parent corporation, but they were staffed on a part-time basis by its employees and many of their directors were members of its Board of Directors.

The Reconstruction Finance Corporation was abolished by Reorganization Plan No. 1of 1957, effective June 30, 1957. The Reconstruction Finance Corporation Liquidation Act (67 Stat. 230), approved July 30, 1953, had provided for RFC's continuation to June 30, 1954, and for termination of its lending powers, effective September 28, 1953. Reorganization Plan No. 2 of 1954 had assigned to appropriate agencies for liquidation of certain functions of the RFC, effective July 1, 1954.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Bureau of Accounts was established in the Department of State in 1870, inheriting functions previously held by the Dispersing Agent. The Bureau had custody of the disbursement of appropriations and was responsible for the care of the building and property of the Department of State. On July 11, 1895, it inherited from the Passport Clerk responsibility for the examination of applications for passports and the issuance of passports; on July 3, 1902, it passed on these functions to the newly-established Passport Bureau. On September 14, 1938, the Bureau of Accounts was redesignated the Division of Accounts with responsibility for all accounts of the Department in Washington, D.C., of the Foreign Service, of international commissions and conferences. The Bureau was abolished by Departmental Order 1218, January 15, 1944, with functions transferred to the Division of Budget and Finance.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Department of State's Bureau of Public Affairs (PA) aimed for an open exchange of information and views between the Department and the American people on the topic of U.S. foreign relations. creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) missions were located in countries where a bilateral program was being implemented. The mission in each country was subject to the direction and guidance of the chief U.S. representative in the country, usually the ambassador. The missions reported to USAID's assistant administrators of the geographic bureaus. 

In 1991, the Pressler Amendment prohibited new obligations for the USAID Mission to Pakistan (USAID/Pakistan). The Mission began to phase out its status by completing ongoing programs.

In January 1993, the Assistant Administrator for Asia obtained approval from the Acting Administrator to merge USAID Mission to Pakistan with the Office of the A.I.D. Representative (AID/REP) to Afghanistan. The AID/REP, located in Pakistan due to unsafe conditions in Afghanistan, had severe budget cuts that required their staff to move from the U.S. Embassy in Pakistan into the USAID’s compound as space became available. The combined mission was called the USAID Mission to Pakistan and Afghanistan. The Mission Director for Pakistan served concurrently as the A.I.D. Representative. The administrative, financial, contracting, legal and program support services were consolidated immediately; however, the AID/REP became the Office of Afghan Field Operations, a separate unit within the new combined Mission.

In seeking this approval, she requested that the USAID Mission Director also be designated the AID/REP. In his approval memorandum of January 21, 1993, the Acting AID Administrator directed the following: "The Mission Director for Pakistan is now also sewing concurrently as the A.I.D. Representative. The proposed consolidation will merge administrative, financial management, contracting, legal and program support services for the two missions. Based on the expressed concern of the Asia Bureau and Ambassador Monjo, however, it is imperative that the Afghan program remain as an identifiable unit within the overall structure of the A. I.D. presence in Pakistan. Our planning will reflect this concern." AID/REP and USAID/Pakistan administrative, financial, contracting, legal and program support services were consolidated immediately. The Afghanistan project portfolio was merged under the Office of Afghan Field Operations, a separate unit within the Combined Mission…As the AID/REP is undergoing a reorganization and developing a new program strategy, the USAID/Pakistan Mission continues in its phase out status under the Pressler Amendment. If Pakistan remains under the new obligation prohibition, its ongoing program should be completed by 1995. USAID/Pakistan also is going through a reorganization to downsize over the next two years; Because of the sensitive nature of the Afghan program in its early stages, AID/REP offices were established in the American Embassy in Islamabad, Pakistan. As the staff expanded…employees were placed in the USAID/Pakistan compound, where they utilized USAID support staff. Shortly after USAID/Pakistan came under the Pressler Amendment (1991) and was planning its staff phase down, the Embassy gave notice that AID/REP should plan on relocating to the USAID/Pakistan compound as space became available. A determination was made at that time, that by the Fall of 1993, such a move would take place. The Afghan Program Office relocated to the USAID compound in early 1993; Memorandum Jan 27 1993 Mission Director for USAID Pakistan is now serving concurrently as the A.I.D. Representative for Afghanistan. The Acting Administrator recently approved the consolidation of the Office of the A.I.D. Representative within USAID/Pakistan. This consolidation merges administrative, financial management, contracting, legal and program support services for the two Missions, while maintaining an identifiable unit for the Afghan program)

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: On April 27, 1945, President Harry S Truman designated Presidential Special Assistant Edwin W. Pauley as his personal representative, with the rank of ambassador, to head the U.S. delegation to the Allied Reparations Commission considering German reparations. At the Crimea Conference the major powers had agreed that Germany would be "obliged to the greatest extent possible to make reparations." After negotiating the formula and methods for exacting reparations, Pauley led the U.S. Reparations Mission to Japan in late 1945 and a third mission concerning Japanese assets in Soviet-occupied Korea and Manchuria in 1946. On March 7, 1947, Pauley transferred to the Department of State and was designated Special Advisor to the Secretary of State on Reparations.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) was established as an independent agency by Reorganization Plan No. 3 of 1970, effective December 2, 1970, consolidating the Department of the Interior's Federal Water Quality Administration; the Federal Radiation Council; and the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare's (HEW) Environmental Health Service. EPA's mission was to control and abate pollution in the areas of air, water, solid waste, pesticides, radiation, and toxic substances. Its mandate was to mount an integrated, coordinated attack on environmental pollution in cooperation with state and local governments.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Office of the Coordinator of Cuban Affairs was established within the Department of State by National Security Action Memorandum No. 213, January 8, 1963, implementing a January 4, 1963, recommendation of the Special Assistant for National Security Affairs, McGeorge Bundy, to the President. The Coordinator of Cuban Affairs acted as chairman of an interdepartmental committee on Cuba and was responsible to the Secretary of State for State Department business and, under his guidance, to the President and the Executive Committee on interdepartmental business. On matters relating to covert operations he reported to the Special Group 5412 of the National Security Council. The Coordinator was directed to appoint a full-time representative in Miami, Florida, to represent the U.S. Government in relations with Cuban refugee organizations and to coordinate the implementation of all related Federal programs.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: On May 1, 1945, the Commodities Division and the War Supply and Resources Division of the Office of International Trade Policy were consolidated into a reconstituted Commodities Division in accordance of Departmental Order 1319, issued April 26, 1945. creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Second Session of the Council of Foreign Ministers was held in Paris in two parts, April 25 to May 16, 1946, and June 15 to July 12, 1946. The meetings were attended by the British Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, Ernest Bevin, French Foreign Minister Georges Bidault, and Soviet Foreign Minister Vyacheslav Molotov. Secretary of States James F. Byrnes was accompanied by Senator Tom Connally, Chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and Senator Arthur H. Vandenberg, also a member of the Committee. There were 42 formal and fifteen informal meetings of the Council during this period. The prolonged meeting produced a substantial degree of agreement on the contents of draft peace treaties with Italy, Bulgaria, Hungary, Romania, and Finland. The ministers also reached an agreement on the convening and procedures for a larger peace conference.

The Potsdam Conference in July and August 1945 established a Council of Foreign Ministers composed of the Big Five (the United States, Great Britain, the Soviet Union, China, and France) to prepare draft peace treaties with Austria, Hungary, Bulgaria, Romania, Finland, and Italy and to propose settlements of outstanding territorial questions. The first meeting was held in London from September 11 to October 2, 1945. It was the first meeting of the prinicipal Allies to be held since the fighting ended. The delegations were led by Ernest Bevin for Great Britain, James F. Byrnes for the United States, Vyacheslav Molotov for the Soviet Union, Georges Bidault for France, and Wang Shih Chien for China.

The first meeting of the Council of Foreign Ministers failed to bring agreement on treaties with Italy, Bulgaria, Hungary, and Romania. There was a conflict between the Soviet Union and the United States over the latter's role in the occupation of Japan.The Conference broke up over the issues of Chinese and French participation, the Soviet delegation insisting that China and France not participate, while the United States and Great Britain maintained that the two should participate.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Allied Council for Japan (ACJ) was established at the Interim Meeting of Foreign Ministers at Moscow, December 26, 1945. Under the chairmanship of the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers (SCAP) it was to advise SCAP in regard to the implementation of the Terms of Surrender,  and of the occupation and control of Japan.The membership of the Allied Council for Japan consisted of the Supreme Commander (or his deputy who served as Chairman and United States member; a Union of Soviet Socialist Republics member; a Chinese member; and a member representing jointly the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand, and India. The Council was to meet not less often than once every two weeks. The Supreme Commander issued all orders for the implementation of the Terms of Surrender, the occupation and control of Japan, and related directives. In all cases action was to be be carried out under and through the Supreme Commander who was the sole executive authority for the Allied Powers in Japan. He was to consult and advise with the Council in advance of the issuance of orders on matters of substance, the exigencies of the situation permitting. His decisions upon these matters was to be be controlling.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The establishment of the Division of Information was authorized by the President in a letter of February 28, 1941, to the Liaison Officer for Emergency Management. The Division's function was to provide a centralized information service for the several constituent agencies of the Office for Emergency Management and thus make unnecessary the establishment of an information unit in each of those agencies. In effect, the Division was a continuation of the Office of Information that had been developed in 1940 as a service unit of the Advisory Commission to the Council of National Defense. By means of conferences, correspondence, the press, radio broadcasts, and motion pictures it informed the public about the policies, programs, procedures, and operations of the emergency agencies.

Robert W. Horton served as the Director of the Division of Information until it was abolished by an Executive Order of June 13, 1942. Its functions relating to specific activities of the constituent agencies of the OFfice for Emergency Management were transferred to those agencies, and its other functions were transferred to the Office of War Information, which was established by the same order.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Department of Agriculture was created by an act of Congress (12 Stat. 387), approved May 15, 1862. Until 1889 the Department was administered by a Commissioner of Agriculture. By an act of Congress (25 Stat. 659), approved February 9, 1889, the powers and duties of the Department were enlarged. It was made the eighth executive department of the Federal Government and the Commissioner became Secretary of Agriculture.

The Department was directed by law to acquire and disseminate useful information on agricultural subjects in the most general and comprehensive sense. The Department conducted research in agricultural and industrial chemistry, the industrial uses of farm products, entomology, soils, agricultural engineering, agricultural economics, marketing, crop and livestock production, production and manufacturing of dairy products, human nutrition, home economics, forestry, and conservation. It made research results available for practical farm application through extension and experiment station work in cooperation with the states.

The Department provided crop reports, commodity standards, Federal meat inspection service, and other marketing services. It sought to eradicate and control plant and animal diseases and pests. It administered Federal law designed to protect the farmer and the consuming public. The Department administered the national forests and in cooperation with the states, promoted better protection and management of forests on private lands. It aided farmers in planning and installing erosion-control and other soil and water conservation measures on their farms. It also assisted in the prevention of floods by planning and aiding in the installation of measures, on farm, grazing, and forest lands and in small stream channels, to retard runoff and reduce damaging effects of floods.

The Department administered price support, acreage and conservation reserve programs, and other production adjustment measures. It cooperated with the states, through a grant-in-aid program, in carrying on the National school lunch program. It made loans to farmers who could not elsewhere get the credit they needed at reasonable terms, both for farm operations and to enable farm tenants and others to become farm owners. It made loans to farmer cooperatives, other non-profit organizations, and commercial concerns for the purpose of financing electric and telephone facilities in rural areas.

The Pan-American Institute of Geography and History (PAIGH) was created in 1928 by a resolution of the sixth Inter-American Conference of Ministers in Havana. The Institute's mission is to encourage, coordinate, and publicize geographic and historical studies concerning the Western Hemisphere and to promote international cooperation among the American nations in these fields. In 1929 the Institute's headquarters were established as a General Secretariat in Mexico City. The organization functioned independently until 1949 when it was absorbed by the Organization of American States (OAS) and became the first of six specialized institutes.

The Institute's work was accomplished through its General Assembly, Directing Council, General Secretariat, Commissions, and National Sections. The General Assembly, usually meeting quadrennially, and Directing Council, usually meeting annually, were responsible for determining administrative and program policies that are implemented by the General Secretariat. In 1943, 1947, 1949, and 1969, respectively, Commissions on Cartography, Geography, History, and Geophysics were created to concentrate efforts in these specialized fields. Most technical work was performed by the Commissions, their Committees, and their Working Groups. A quadrennial Consultation (Conference) was held by each Commission at which current projects were evaluated, new projects were authorized, and scholarly and technical presentations are made. Each member nation was represented in equal numbers in the General Assembly, Directing Council, and Commissions. A National Section was comprised of all the members of a particular nation's delegation to PAIGH.

The War Trade Board was established by Executive Order 2729-A, October 12, 1917, under authority of the Trading with the Enemy Act (40 Stat. 411), approved October 6, 1917.

The Board assumed the functions formerly held by the Exports Administrative Board. It was composed of representatives of the State, Treasury, Agriculture, and Commerce Departments and of the Food Administration, the Shipping Board, and the War Industries Board. The Board licensed exports and imports, rationed supplies to neutrals, and conserved commodities and shipping facilities for American and Allied use. It sought to keep strategic goods out of enemy hands and prohibited the use of enemy credit and financial holdings in the United States. Members of the Board coordinated these functions with those of other government agencies in Washington, D.C., and of the Allied governments associated with the United States during World War I. 

At the end of World War I, the main task of the War Trade Board became the equitable relaxation of wartime controls. Most of this work was completed by June 30, 1919, when the Board was abolished by Executive Order 3059, March 3, 1919, and Executive Order 3086-A May 12, 1919, as amended by Executive Order 3099, June 23, 1919, under authority of the Executive Bureaus Consolidation Act (40 Stat. 556), approved May 20, 1918. It was succeeded by the War Trade Board Section of the Department of State.
