creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Sundry Civil Appropriations Act of April 28, 1904 (33 Stat. 491) created the Thomas Jefferson Statue Commission, composed of the Secretary of State, the chairman of the Committee on the Library of the Senate, and the chairman of the Committee on the Library of the House.  The Commission's duties were to select a site for the statue on publicly owned land in the District of Columbia, to procure plans and designs for the statue, and to report its findings to Congress during the next session.  The total cost of the statue was not to exceed $100,000.  The minute book of the Commission records only two sessions: May 2, 1904 and February 1, 1906.  In May 1906, the Commission arranged for the sculptor Augustus Saint-Gaudens to prepare designs when time would permit.  Saint-Gaudens, however, died before he could undertake the task.

The office of the Special Envoy to China, known also as the Marshall Mission to China, and the George C. Marshall Mediation Mission to China, was a forlorn hope in 1946 to forestall a civil war in China and to bring about a unified government.

General George C. Marshall was appointed as special envoy to China by President Harry S. Truman in a telephone call of November 27, 1945. Details of the mission were hammered out by the White House, the State Department, and the Pentagon in the ensuing weeks. On December 14 General Marshall met with President Truman and Under Secretary of State Dean Acheson and he received his letter of instruction. The United States deemed it essential that "a cessation of hostilities be arranged between the armies of the National Government and the Chinese communists and other dissident Chinese armed forces for the purpose of completing the return of all China to effective Chinese control."

General Marshall arrived in Shanghai on December 20, 1945, and soon thereafter set up a temporary headquarters in Chungking. In the ensuing weeks he met with leaders of both factions, and by late February 1946 was able to get an illusory and fragile agreement which ostensibly ended 18 years of hostility. Despite the agreement Chinese Nationalists forces continued to press their military advantage in Manchuria and North China. 

Faced with increasing intransigence and a growing distrust of General Marshall by both the Nationalists and the Communists, General Marshall pressed the President to recall him. President Truman acceeded and on January 8, 1947, General Marshall departed China.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: On July 29, 1897, the Nicaragua Canal Commission was appointed by President William McKinley, pursuant to an act of June 4, 1897 (30 Stat. 59), to re-examine the proposed canal route and prepare an estimate of construction costs. The Commission, popularly known as the first Walker Commission, was composed of Read Admiral John G. Walker, U.S. Navy, as Chairman; Lewis M. Haupt, professor of civil engineering at the University of Pennsylvania, and Captain O.M. Carter, of the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, who was later replaced by Colonel Peter C. Hains. The Survey was completed in February 1899 and in the following month the Commission reported to the President that a canal across Nicaragua would cost an estimated $118,113,790.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The U.S. Citizens' Commission on NATO was created from a resolution of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) Parliamentarians Conference on November 16, 1957, which recommended that a conference of citizens' groups from member nations be held to explore means of fostering greater cooperation and unity in the Atlantic community. The U.S. Citizens' Commission, appointed by the President of the Senate and the Speaker of the House, was established to prepare for and participate in such conferences.  It took part in the Atlantic Convention held in Paris in January 1962 and made a final report to the Congress before going out of existence on June 30, 1962, its legal expiration date.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: At the urging of the United States, the Council of Foreign Ministers met in Moscow, March 10 to April 24, 1947, in an attempt to iron out differences among the major powers regarding the draft peace treaties for Germany and Austria. Discussion at this meeting centered around the structure of the future German government, the Polish-German frontier, claims and reparations, and the treatment of Germany as a single, unified economic unit. At the meeting the United States, led by Secretary of State George C. Marshall, and Great Britain advocated a federal form of government for Germany while the Soviet delegation sought a centralized state. The only agreement reached was on the foraml dissolution of the Land (state) of Prussia, a large part of which had already been annexed by the Soviet Union and POland.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Department of State by administrative action established the position of Deputy Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs, after Congress authorized three Deputy Under Secretary positions in the State Department Reorganization Act of August 5, 1955 (69 Stat. 536). Prior to the creation of the position of Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs in August  1959, the Deputy Under Secretary for Political Affairs assisted the Secretary and Under Secretary in the formulation and conduct of U.S. foreign policy. He served as the principal coordinator of the policies of the geographic bureaus and maintained overall relationshops between the Department of State and the Department of Defense. After August 1959, the Deputy Under Secretary for Political Affairs served as a focal point for interdepartmental relations, especially those dealing with politico-military issues. During 1969, the Department discontinued the position and created a new Bureau for Politico-Military Affairs.

Serving as Deputy Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs were Robert D. Murphy, August 11, 1955 - August 13, 1959; Livingston T. Merchant, August 21, 1959 - December 3, 1959; Raymond A. Hare, January 25, 1960 - March 5, 1961; U. Alexis Johnson, May 2, 1961 - July 12, 1964 and November 1, 1965 - October 9, 1966; Foy D. Kohler, November 29, 1966 - December 31, 1967; and Charles E. Bohlen, February 11, 1968 - January 22, 1969.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Department of State by administrative action created the position of Deputy Under Secretary for Economic Affairs after Congress authorized three deputy under secretary positions in the State Department Organization Act (69 Stat. 536), approved August 5, 1955. The Deputy Under Secretary for Economic Affairs was the ranking officer in charge of foreign economic matters from August 1955 to June 1958, and again from March 1969 to May 1972. (The posirion was vacant from June 30, 1958 to April 1, 1969.) He was responsible for the economic aspects of foreign policy, coordinated the economic policies of the operating bureaus, and maintained relationships between the Department of State and other departments and agencies concerned with matters of economic and financial policy. The position was discontinued when an act of Congress (86 Stat. 490), approved July 13, 1972, established the permanent position of Under Secretary for Economic Affairs.

Incumbents, with dates of service, included Samuel C. Waugh, August 26, 1955 - October 1, 1955; Herbert V. Prochnow, November 7, 1955 - November 15, 1956; C. Douglas Dillon, March 15, 1957 - June 30, 1958; and Nathaniel Samuels, April 1, 1969 - May 31, 1972.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Bureau of Intelligence and Research (INR) was headed by a director until August 1986, when an Act of Congress (P.L. 99-93) of August 16, 1985, authorized the appointment of an Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research. The Bureau, drawing on all-source intelligence, provided value-added independent analysis of events to Department policymakers, ensured that intelligence activities supported foreign policy and national security purposes; and served as the focal point in the Department for ensuring policy review of sensitive counterintelligence and law enforcement activities. INR's primary mission was to harness intelligence to serve U.S. diplomacy. The Bureau also analyzed geographical and international boundary issues. INR was a member of the U.S. Intelligence Community.

At INR, we are on a mission to deliver and coordinate timely, objective intelligence that advances U.S. diplomacy. ​While INR’s principal customer is the Secretary of State and U.S. diplomats around the globe, INR also provides intelligence assessments and other information for the President, the National Security Council, and other senior policymakers. Each week INR delivers dozens of intelligence assessments, products, and briefings to diplomats and policymakers at home and abroad. As the U.S. government’s leader in foreign public opinion research and polling, we conduct hundreds of surveys annually in more than 100 countries to inform U.S. foreign policy. INR also serves as the IC lead in analytic outreach, working with non-governmental experts to collaborate on research projects and leverage outside expertise to inform Executive Branch policymakers and the IC. From analyzing foreign election results and monitoring and reporting on war and conflict around the world to cyber, emerging technologies and evaluating the impact of climate change on foreign policy, INR delivers intelligence to empower diplomacy.) https://www.state.gov/about-us-bureau-of-intelligence-and-research

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Department of State established the office of Bureau of Far Eastern Affairs in 1949, after the Commission on Organization of the Executive Branch of Government (Hoover Commission) recommended that certain offices be upgraded to bureau level and after Congress increased the number of Assistant Secretaries of State from six to ten (May 26, 1949; Publ. L. 81-73; 63 Stat. 111). On November 1, 1966, the Department by administrative action changed the Bureau's name to Bureau for East Asian and Pacific Affairs. The Division of Far Eastern Affairs, established in 1908, was the first geographical division to be established in the Department of State. 

The Bureau, under the direction of an assistant secretary, executed responsibility for the general conduct of foreign relations with the countries within its geographical area of responsibility by applying over-all political, security, economic, public affairs, social, consular, administrative, and other policies and practices. The Bureau maintained and supervised relationships with foreign missions in the United States representing countries within its regional jurisdiction, except on substantive consular matters, and guided the operation of Foreign Service establishments within its area overseas.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Office of Transportation and Communications was established on January 15, 1944, under Assistant Secretary Adolf A. Berle, Jr., and was placed under the Office of the Assistant Secretary for Economic Affairs on December 20, 1944. From April 1945 to June 1946 it was known as the Office of Transport and Communications Policy. The position of director was left vacant at first but in 1945 was held by Charles P. Taft and George P. Baker successively.  On June 3, 1946, it became the Office of Transport and Communications and in 1949 the Office of Transport and Communications Policy. The Office handled matters relating to the foreign policy aspects of international transportation and communications, functions which had been performed since 1938 by an International Communications Division.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The United States was engaged with Armenia since it achieved independence in 1991. With the opening of the first U.S. embassy in Armenia in 1992, the two countries signed a bilateral agreement on provision of U.S. humanitarian and technical economic assistance. The U.S. aid program, however, dated back to 1988. In that year, a disastrous earthquake in northern Armenia, registering 6.9 on the Richter scale, took over 25,000 lives and left about 500,000 Armenians homeless. The United States was among the 74 countries that responded to the disaster and provided immediate humanitarian aid to the Armenian people.

Following Armenia’s independence, U.S. Agency for International Development’s (USAID) programs in 1992-1998 focused on humanitarian aid, emphasizing food, fuel, medicine and clothing to help Armenia cope with post-earthquake, post-war, and post-Soviet economic collapse.

USAID started provision of more technical support in 1998-2005 and initiated local capacity building activities in addition to humanitarian and direct assistance programs.

In 2005-2012, USAID transitioned from direct assistance to longer-term development initiatives aimed at increasing Armenia’s economic competitiveness, strengthening good governance, and ensuring higher quality and more accessible social and health services. The global financial crisis in 2008 affected Armenia’s economic standing, posing new challenges for the country’s development. After years of double-digit GDP growth, the Armenian economy slowed by 14.4 percent in 2009 and the poverty rate increased from 27.6 percent (2008) to 35 percent (2011). In response, USAID worked with local counterparts to ameliorate the impact of the global financial crisis by supporting the sustainability of Armenia’s economy and creating short-term employment opportunities for vulnerable communities at small-scale infrastructure renovation projects.

Armenia’s borders were closed with two of its four neighbors - Turkey and Azerbaijan - due to the conflict over Nagorno-Karabakh. The closed borders made it more difficult for businesses to thrive and enter new markets. In this context, USAID, along the U.S. Embassy’s fence-mending initiatives, implemented cross-border activities with Turkey aimed at fostering people-to-people and business-to-business ties.

Additionally, USAID worked to increase Armenia’s economic growth and competitiveness, promoted civic participation and participatory governance, expanded access to quality healthcare, and improved the welfare and social inclusion of vulnerable children while promoting inclusive education and equal access to community services. USAID programs sought to ensure that the benefits of growth and good governance, including service delivery and employment opportunities, are also felt outside of the capital Yerevan.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The U.S. Reparations and Restitution Delegation (USRRD) was established by the State Department on April 29, 1947.  Rufus B. Smith served as the first chief of the delegation and was succeeded by Charles L. Hodge in July 1947.  Homer L. Baker was deputy chief of the delegation.  They were assisted by technical aides recruited from large American firms having interests in Japan, including the International Telephone and Telegraph International General Electric Corporation.  The USRRD's basic function was to make surveys of the Japanese economy in order to ascertain what facilities might be removed from Japan as reparation goods without damage to the country's peacetime economy.  Walter E. Hammond was the member of the delegation who was responsible for reparations and restitution investigations regarding American properties seized by the Japanese in Korea.  The activities of the delegation were terminated in December 1949.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Indian Arts and Crafts Board (IACB) was established by 49 Stat. 891, approved August 27, 1935. It promoted the economic development of American Indians and Alaska Natives of Federally recognized Tribes through the expansion of the Indian arts and crafts market. The IACB provided promotional opportunities, general business advice, and information on the Indian Arts and Crafts Act to Native American artists, craftspeople, businesses, museums, and cultural centers of Federally recognized Tribes. Additionally, the IACB operated three regional museums, conducted a promotional museum exhibition program, produced a "Source Directory of American Indian and Alaska Native Owned and Operated Arts and Crafts Businesses," and oversaw the implementation of the Indian Arts and Crafts Act of 1990 (Publ. 101-644).

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The President of the United States established a Board of Examiners for the Foreign Service to develop, and supervise the administration of, examinations prescribed under section 3941 of Title 22 U.S.C.to be given to candidates for appointment in the Foreign Service. The Board  consisted of 15 members appointed by the President (no fewer than five of whom were to be appointed from among individuals who are not Government employees and who were qualified for service on the Board by virtue of their knowledge, experience, or training in the fields of testing or equal employment opportunity). The Board included representatives of agencies utilizing the Foreign Service personnel system and representatives of other agencies which have responsibility for employment testing. The Board was chaired by a member of the Board, designated by the President, who was a member of the Foreign Service.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: At the initiative of Belgium and the United States an International Migration Conference was convened in Brussels, resulting in the 1951 creation of the Provisional Intergovernmental Committee for the Movements of Migrants from Europe (PICMME). A year later PICMME became the Intergovernmental Committee for European Migration (ICEM). ICEM was mandated to help European governments to identify resettlement countries for the estimated 11 million refugees and displaced persons uprooted by World War II, and it arranged transport for nearly a million migrants during the 1950s. The Committee subsequently underwent a succession of name changes from the Intergovernmental Committee for Migration (ICM) in 1980 to the International Organization for Migration (IOM) in 1989, becoming the leading international agency working with governments and civil society to advance the understanding of migration issues and to encourage social and economic development through migration.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The International Conference on Load Lines, held in London, March 3 April 5, 1966, was held at the invitation of the inter-governmental Maritime Consultative Organization to draw up an international convention on load lines. (The purpose of a load line was to ensure that a ship had sufficient freeboard and thus sufficient reserve buoyancy.) In 1906, laws were passed requiring foreign ships visiting British ports to be marked with a load line. It was not until the the 1930 Load Line Convention that there was international agreement for universal application of load line regulations. The 1966 Load Lines Convention re-examined and amended the 1930 rules.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: At the request President Harry S. Truman and Secretary of State Dean Acheson, John Foster Dulles agreed to serve as consultant to the Secretary of State. His appointment was announced by Departrment of State Press Release No. 323 of April 6, 1950, and effective April 19. Dulles was to advise the Secretary on broad problems in the field of foreign affairs and on specific lines of action which the Government should follow. His mandate was not confined to any specific geographic area of the world.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Bureau of Intelligence and Research (INR) was headed by an assistant secretary. The Bureau, drawing on all-source intelligence, provided value-added independent analysis of events to Department policymakers, ensured that intelligence activities supported foreign policy and national security purposes; and served as the focal point in the Department for ensuring policy review of sensitive counterintelligence and law enforcement activities. INR's primary mission was to harness intelligence to serve U.S. diplomacy. The Bureau also analyzed geographical and international boundary issues. INR was a member of the U.S. Intelligence Community.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The General Assemblies of the International Union of Radio Science (URSI) were held at three-year intervals. The main objective of the Assembly was to review current trends in research, present new discoveries and make plans for future research work or for specific projects, especially where it seemed desirable to arrange for cooperation on an international scale. Symposia at the Assembly on selected topics were usually organized by two or more commissions. Most radio scientists attended the General Assemblies solely for these scientific activities, which were open to anyone interested in radio science, whether or not connected with a Member Committee of the Union.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Second Washington Conference (19 June – 25 June 1942) (which did not have a code name because it was hastily called) was regarded at the time as a set of military staff conversations rather than a formal conference. The two delegations were led by Winston Churchill, the British Prime Minister, and U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt. (Immediately before the Conference started, Roosevelt held preparatory talks with Churchill in his home town of Hyde Park, New York, June 19-20.)

The Conference discussed how the Western Allies could best aid the Soviet Union. The Americans were keen to open up a Second Front in France, but the British did not think that it was yet a feasible option and Churchill proposed an developing a joint campaign in the Mediterranean Theater, leading to an attack Italy as the "soft under-belly" of the Axis. Agreement was reached to start preparations for an invasion of the North African colonies of Vichy France (what was to become Operation Torch). One of the first concrete measures taken by Roosevelt to facilitate this strategy was to appoint General Dwight D. Eisenhower as the Commander-in-Chief of U.S. Forces in the European Theater of Operations on June 25. Roosevelt and Churchill also held discussions with members of the Pacific War Council, King Peter II of Yugoslavia and his Foreign Minister, and with Soviet and Chinese representatives with whom they discuss strategic problems.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Potsdam Conference, the final international conference of World War II, was held at Cecilienhof, the home of Crown Prince Wilhelm Hohenzollern, in Potsdam, from July 16 to August 2, 1945. 

The full Conference met on July 17, 1945, Generalissimo Joseph V. Stalin having arrived a day late. Joining him were President Harry S. Truman and British Prime Minister Winston S. Churchill. First on the agenda was how to administer the defeated Nazi Germany. The Conference also considered the establishment of post-war order, peace treaty issues, and countering the effects of war. They were accompanied by their foreign secretaries (James F. Byrnes, V.M. Molotov, and Anthony Eden), their chiefs of staff, and civilian advisors. Joseph Stalin suggested that President Truman preside at the Conference as he was the only head of state attending, to which Churchill agreed.

There were nine formal meetings between July 17 and July 25. The Conference was then interrupted for two days until the results of the British general elections were known. On July 28, Clement R. Attlee joined the Conference as the new-elected British Prime Minister, with his new Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, Ernest Bevin. Discussions continued until August 2.

During the course of the Conference there were regular meetings of the heads of the three governments and their foreign secretaries. In addition, committees appointed by the foreign ministers for preliminary consideration of questions before the Conference met daily. The first declaration issued by the Conference was an "unconditional surrender" ultimatum to Japan. The Conference reversed all German annexations in Europe after 1937 and separated Austria from Germany.  It set forth the goals of the Allied occupation of Germany which were demilitarization, denazification, democratization, and decartelization. The Conference also agreed on the prosecution of Nazi war criminals. The Conference also established a Council of Foreign Ministers composed of the foreign ministers of Great Britain, the Soviet Union, China, France, and the United States. The Council was authorized to draw up treaties of peace with Italy, Romania, Bulgaria, Hungary, and Finland, and to propose settlement of territorial questions outstanding on the termination of the war in Europe.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Teheran Conference took place between November 28 and December 1, 1943, and was the first conference of the Allied heads of state in which Marshal Josef Stalin took part. It succeeded the Cairo Conference (November 23-26, 1943) and was followed by the Yalta Conference (February 4 - 11, 1945) and the Potsdam Conference (July 17 - August 2, 1945). The chief subject of the meeting was the projected Anglo-American invasion of northern Europe in concert with a Soviet offensive in the eastern front. In addition, the Soviet Union agreed to enter the war against Japan following the end of the war in Europe, and, at the insistence of Stalin, the borders of post-war Poland were determined along the Oder and Neisse Rivers and the Curzon line. In the separate protocol, Declaration of the Three Powers Regarding Iran, agreed to on December 1, 1943, the three powers pledged to recognize Iran's independence.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: American representation in Bordeaux dates from March 1778 when France formally recognized the independence of the thirteen colonies on February 6, 1778. The Continental Congress appointed John Bondfield as a commercial agent. This was the first known American diplomatic station in the world. In 1790, President George Washington commissioned Joseph Fenwick of Maryland as the first American consul to Bordeaux. "Fenwick House", built by Victor Louis, also architect of the Grand Theatre, still stands on the quayside and is well-known in Bordeaux. The post was in continuous existence, except during the so-called Franco-American "cold war" of 1798-1800 and the Nazi WWII occupation of 1940-44. In 1962, it became a Consulate General. The CONsulate general was was closed in 1995 for budgetary reasons, in part because as U.S. visas were no longer required for French tourists and businessmen visiting the U.S. for less than three months. Bordeaux was reopened in 2000 as an American Presence Post (APP) when Ambassador Felix G. Rohatyn obtained Congressional approval.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Committee on Commodity Problems was established by the FAO Conference in 1949 to work under the supervision of, and be responsible, to the Council. By decision of the Conference in 1957 it became a Committee of the Council. The Committee was to review international commodity problems affecting production, trade, distribution and consumption, and related economic matters; prepare a factual and interpretative survey of the world commodity situation, to be available directly to member nations; and report and submit suggestions to the Council on policy issues arising out of its deliberations, and to provide these reports and those of its subsidiary bodies to member nations for their information. The Committee held one session during each biennium, convened sufficiently in advance of the Council session and before the regular sessions of the Conference. The Committee could also hold additional sessions.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Office of Policy and Plans determined, developed, coordinated and issued overall International Information Administration (IIA) policy guidances in respect to program content and objectives, with the aid of guidance from the Assistant Secretary for Public Affairs, and the advice of the regional bureaus, the Assistant Secretary for Economic Affairs (E), the Assistant Secretary for United Nations Affairs (UNA), and other areas of the Department as appropriate. It serviced as the only channel for transmission of such guidance to the IIA media services, Public Affairs Officers overseas, other areas of the Department, and other agencies of the Government. The Office directed program planning for the IIA as a whole with the advice of the regional bureaus on program plans applicable to their areas, and the several components of IIA as appropriate. The Office also advised the Assistant Secretary for Public Affairs on international informational and educational exchange considerations that should enter into foreign policy decisions. It performed policy functions as required with respect to the Psychological Strategy Board, the Psychological Operations Coordinating Committee, and related organizations.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
On July 18, 1938, the Division of Cultural Relations was established by Departmental Order 768, dated July 16, 1938, to have general charge of official international activities of the Department of State with respect to cultural relations. This embraced the exchange of professors, teachers, and students; the cooperation in the field of music, art, literature, and other intellectual and cultural attainments; the formulation and distribution of libraries of representative works of the United States and suitable translations thereof; and the preparations for and management of the participation by this Government in international expositions in the field. It was responsible for the supervision of participation by this Government in international radio broadcasts; encouragement of a closer relationship between unofficial organizations of this and of foreign governments engaged in cultural and intellectual activities; and the dissemination abroad of the representative intellectual and cultural works of the United States and the improvement and broadening of the scope of our cultural relations with other countries.

On September 25, 1941, Departmental Order 970 expanded the Division’s duties to take under consideration requests received by the Department for motion pictures wanted or recommended for display abroad, and for foreign-made motion pictures intended for exhibition in the United States. It arranged previews for both the proposed outgoing and incoming films at times and places convenient to a majority of the preview committee and in advance to advise all members as fully as possible concerning the films to be screened and of any rending requests for prints of them. The Division received and filed reports on previews and prepared all necessary authorizations and attestations or refusals of same, in accordance with the findings of the committee. Additionally, the Division received applications for authorizations and attestations of films to conduct pertinent correspondence and kept necessary records in the matters.

Departmental Order 985, date October 9, 1941, ordered the Division to cooperate with the Division of Current Information in the establishment and maintenance of effective liaison with all agencies of the Government concerned with the collection and dissemination of information in which the Department of States had an interest. It designated a delegate to assume full time duties with the Division of Current Information.

On April 15, 1942, Departmental Order 1047 transferred to the Division of Cultural Relations from the Division of American Republics responsibility for the conduct of the Department’s participation in the work of the Interdepartmental Committee of Cooperation with the American Republics, which was established at the instance of the President in May 1938, and under the provisions of Public No. 355, 76th Congress, entitled “An Act to authorize the President to render closer and more effective the relationship between the American Republics,” approved August 9, 1939; and responsibility for matters involved in the administration of Public No. 63, 76th Congress, approved May 3, 1939, and entitled “An Act to amend the Act entitled ‘An Act authorizing the temporary detail of United States employees, possessing special qualifications, to governments of American republics and the Philippines, and for other purposes,’ approved May 25, 1938,” in so far as the demonstration of that Act was vested in the Department of State. This was to provide maximum concentration of responsibility and administration in matters involving cultural cooperative relations with the other American Republics. In carrying out these functions, the Division of Cultural Relations had the responsibility for enlisting the approval of the Division of American Republics of all cooperative projects and personnel assignments, and for enlisting the collaborative of other interested divisions and offices of the Department, and it maintained effective liaison with other interested Departments and agencies of the government.

On April 15, 1942, Departmental Order 1047, the Chief of the Division of Cultural Relations, or in his absence the Acting chief, upon the written authorization of the Assistant Secretary of State and Budget Officer, or in his absence another Assistant Secretary of State, was authorized to certify vouchers and to sign contracts involving obligations and expenditures, other than printing and binding, under the Department of State allotment from the appropriation “ Cooperation with the American Republics”.

On January 15, 1944, Departmental Order 1218 abolished the Division of Cultural Relations and transferred its functions to the Office of Public Information and divided them between the Division of Motion Pictures and Radio, and the Science, Education and Art Division.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
Section 2 of the Act of Congress of July 27, 1789 (1 Stat. 28) establishing a Department of Foreign Affairs, authorized the Secretary to appoint a Chief Clerk, who would have custody of the Department's records whenever the office of the Secretary should be vacant. From 1789 to 1853, when Congress created the position of Assistant Secretary of State, the Chief Clerk was the second-ranking officer of the Department of State, and was responsible for supervision of Department personnel, distribution of correspondence, and day-to-day operations. One of the functions of the Chief Clerk was the issuance of "passports signed by the Secretary of State to American citizens . . . going beyond Sea" . On June 30, 1833, this function was transferred to the Translating and Miscellaneous Bureau. After 1853, the Chief Clerk's duties included at various times custody of archives, distribution of correspondence, and supervision of Department personnel and property. 

Chief Clerks, with dates of their appointment, included Henry Remsen, Jr., July 27, 1789, and September 1, 1790; Roger Alden, January 1, 1790; George Taylor, Jr., April 1, 1792; Jacob Wagner, February 8, 1798; John Graham, July 1, 1807; Daniel Brent, September 22, 1817; Asbury Dickens, August 23, 1833; Aaron Ogden Dayton, December 13, 1836; Aaron Vail,  June 26, 1838; Jacob L. Martin, July 16, 1840; Daniel Fletcher Webster, March 6, 1841; William S. Derrick,  April 24, 1843, and March 11, 1845; Richard K. Cralle, April 10, 1844; Nicholas P. Trist, August 28, 1845; William S. Derrick,  April 15, 1847, and April 25, 1848; John Appleton, January 26, 1848; and William Hunter, Jr., May 17, 1852.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The United States opened diplomatic relations with Ecuador in 1848. Its Legation opened on August 12, 1848, when Van Brugh Livingston presented his credentials as Charge d'Affaires on August 12, 1848. He was succeeded by John Trumbull Van Alen, November 19, 1849; Courtland Cushing, June 3, 1851; and Philo White, December 27, 1853.

The title of the chief of mission was upgraded in 1854 and on September 2, 1854, Philo White presented his credentials as Minister Resident. He was succeeded by Charles R. Buckalew, September 20, 1858; Frederick Hassaurek, July 15, 1861; William T. Coggeshall, September 20, 1866; E. Rumsey Wing, June 23, 1870; and Thomas Biddle. Biddle died at Guayaquil on May 7, 1875, before he presented his letter of credence. Named to replace him was Christian Wullweber who presented his credentials on December 20, 1875. 

The chief of mission was upgraded to Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary with the appointment of Rowland B. Mahany in 1892; he presented his credentials on May 22, 1892. He was succeeded by Edward H. Strobel, July 15, 1894; James D. Tillman, June 3, 1895; Archibald J. Sampson, December 16, 1897; Joseph W.J. Lee, December 30, 1905; Williams C. Fox, April 18, 1907; Evan E. Young, August 8, 1911; Montgomery Schuyler, May 24, 1913; Charles S. Hartman, September 30, 1913; Gerhard A. Bading, May 15, 1922; William Dawson, August 9, 1930; Antonio C. Gonzalez, March 7, 1935; and Boaz Long, April 29, 1938.

On April 14, 1942, the Legation at Quito was upgraded to embassy status with the presentation of new credentials by Boaz Long as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary. He was succeeded as Ambassador by Robert M. Scotten, May 27, 1943; John F. Simmons, July 16, 1947; Paul C. Daniels, May 25, 1951; Sheldon T. Mills, August 19, 1954; Christian M. Ravndal, August 29, 1956; Maurice M. Bernbaum, November 16, 1960; Wymberley DeR. Coerr, March 24, 1965; Edson O. Sessions, September 26, 1968; Findley Burns, Jr., April 9, 1970; Robert C. Brewster, October 1, 1973; Richard J. Bloomfield, May 31, 1976; Raymond E. Gonzalez, July 31, 1978; Samuel Friedlander Hart, December 22, 1982; Fernando Enrique Rondon, August 8, 1985; Richard Newton Holwill, July 27, 1988; and Paul C. Lambert, July 2, 1990.

From February 1992 through November 1993 James F. Mack served as Charge d'Affairs ad interim.

The next Ambassador, Peter F. Romero, presented his credentials on November 16, 1993. He was succeeded by Leslie M. Alexander, August 5, 1996; Gwen C. Clare, August 24, 1999; and Kristie A. Kenney, September 25, 2002.

On February 7, the Government of Ecuador expelled Armando Astorga, an attaché with the Department of Homeland Security working in the U.S. Embassy. Shortly thereafter, on February 18, First Secretary Mark Sullivan was given 48 hours to leave the U.S. embassy in Quito. The Ecuadoran Government accused him of meddling in the Government's internal police policies.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
U.S. diplomatic representation in Chad opened on August 11, 1960, when Alan W. Lukens, resident at Brazzaville, Congo, presented his credentials as Charge d'Affaires ad interim. The U.S. Embassy was established at Fort Lamy (renamed N'Djamena on April 6, 1973)  on February 1, 1961. W. Wendell Blancke, a non-resident Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary, had presented his credentials  on January 9, 1961.

The first resident ambassador, John A. Calhoun, presented his credentials on May 28, 1961. He was succeeded by Brewster H. Morris, August 12, 1963; Sheldon B. Vance, September 23, 1967; Terence A. Todman, August 21, 1969; Edward W. Mulcahy, December 6, 1972; Edward S. Little, December 7, 1974; William G. Bradford, October 15, 1976; and Donald R. Norland, November 17, 1979. 

The Embassy closed on March 24, 1980, due to heavy fighting in the capital, N'Djamena, and did not reopen until January 15, 1982. John Blane was Principal Officer and Charge d'Affaires ad interim until he was succeeded by Jay P. Moffat, who presented his credentials as Ambassador on May 27, 1983. John Blane was promoted to Ambassador and presented his new credentials on September 2, 1985. Succeeding Blane were Robert L. Pugh, October 15, 1988; Richard Wayne Bogosian, August 4, 1990; Laurence Everett Pope, 2nd., September 3, 1993; David C. Halsted, September 12, 1996; and Christopher E. Goldthwait, October 10, 1999.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: In March 1943 Prime Minister Winston Churchill pressed Harry Hopkins, assistant to President Frfanklin D. Roosevelt, to set up a general meeting between himself and the President. After consulting with the Joint Chiefs of Staff, President Roosevelt agreed to meet with the Prime Minister in May in Washington, D.C. The Conference opened on Wednesday, May 12, at the White House. There were six meetings. Representing Great Britain were Churchill, Lord Maxwell Aitken Beaverbrook, Field Marshal Sir John Dill, Field Marshal Sir Alan Alanbrooke, Admiral of the Fleet Sir Dudley Pound, and Air Marshal Sir Charles Portal. The American Delegation was led by President Roosevelt, Harry Hopkins, Admiral William D. Leahy, General George C. Marshall, and Admiral Ernest J. King. The discussion centered upon the conduct of the war, combined planning efforts, and the upcoming invasion of the European continent. Operation Husky, the planned invasion of Sicily, was discussed in detail, as was a putative date (May 1944) for the invasion of Normandy. Also discussed was the seizure of the Azores unless Portugal could be pursuaded by negotiation to grant the use of bases in the islands.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The First Quebec Conference was the sixth war meeting between Franklin D. Roosevelt and Prime Minister Winston S. Churchill. When the President and the Prime Minister parted in Washington in May 1943, they agreed to meet in the late summer again to discuss the leading military and diplomatic problems of the war. Late in June President Roosevelt recommended that this Anglo-American conference be held in Quebec and the conference was tentatively set for the first of September. However, the overwhelming success of the Allied campaign in Sicily made it imperative that the meeting be held earlier.

The Conference itself, code-named Quadrant, was a highly secretized military conference held in Quebec from August 10 to August 25, 1943. Although both Canadian and Chinese officials attended, the major participants at the conference were Roosevelt and Churchill and their civilian and military advisors. The Conference focused on military operations in the Pacific and in Europe. It reaffirmed the overall objectives and strategic concepts for the prosecution of the war and focused on eliminating Italy quickly from the war. The Allies agreed to increase the bombing offensive against Germany and continue the buildup of American forces in Britain prior to a cross-channel invasion of France. It was decided that operations in the Balkans should be limited to supplying guerrillas whereas operations against Japan would be intensified in order to exhaust Japanese resources, cut their communications lines and secure forward bases from which the Japanese mainland could be attacked. In addition to the strategic discussions, which were communicated to the Soviet Union and to Chiang Kai-Shek in China, the Conference also issued a joint statement on Palestine intended to calm tensions as the British occupation was becoming increasingly untenable. The Conference also condemned German atrocities in Poland.

During the Conference, on August 19, Churchill and Roosevelt signed the Quebec Agreement  which outlined the terms of nuclear nonproliferation between Great Britain and the United States. IN a section of the Quebec Agreement, formally entitled "Articles of Agreement governing collaboration between the authorities of the U.S.A. and UK in the matter of Tube Alloys", Britain and the UnIted States agreed to share resources to bring the Tube Alloys [i.e. the Atomic Bomb] project to fruition at the earliest moment.

At the end of the Conference in Quebec, Churchill and Roosevelt continued their conversations in Washington.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The United Nations Monetary and Financial Conference, commonly known as Bretton Woods Conference, was a gathering of 730 delegates from all 45 Allied nations at the Mount Washington Hotel, situated in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, to regulate the international monetary and financial order after the conclusion of World War II. The United States was represented at the conference by Harry Dexter White.

The conference was held from July 1 to July 22,1944, when the agreements were signed to set up the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), and the International Monetary Fund (IMF). The seminal idea behind the Bretton Woods Conference was the notion of open markets. In Henry Morgenthau's farewell remarks at the Conference, he stated that the establishment of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank marked the end of economic nationalism. This meant countries would maintain their national interest, but trade blocks and economic spheres of influence would no longer be their means. The second idea behind the Bretton Woods Conference was joint management of the Western political-economic order, that is, the foremost industrial democratic nations must lower barriers to trade and the movement of capital, in addition to their responsibility to govern the system.

As a result of the conference, the Bretton Woods system of exchange rate management was set up, which remained in place until the early 1970's.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Committee on Commodity Problems was established by the FAO Conference in 1949 to work under the supervision of, and be responsible, to the Council. By decision of the Conference in 1957 it became a Committee of the Council. The Committee was to review international commodity problems affecting production, trade, distribution and consumption, and related economic matters; prepare a factual and interpretative survey of the world commodity situation, to be available directly to member nations; and report and submit suggestions to the Council on policy issues arising out of its deliberations, and to provide these reports and those of its subsidiary bodies to member nations for their information. The Committee held one session during each biennium, convened sufficiently in advance of the Council session and before the regular sessions of the Conference. The Committee could also hold additional sessions.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
Congress created the position of Director General of the Foreign Service in the Foreign Service Act of 1946 (60 Stat. 1000). The first incumbent was appointed on November 13, 1946. Between 1946 and 1980, the Secretary of State designated the Directors General, who held rank equivalent to an Assistant Secretary of State. The Director General became a Presidential appointee, subject to the advice and consent of the Senate, under the Foreign Service Act of 1980 (94 Stat. 2071), approved October 17, 1980. Since November  23, 1975, under a Departmental administrative action, they have concurrently held the title of Director of the Bureau of Personnel.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Provisional International Civil Aviation Organization.(PICAO) convened the first regional meeting dealing with the North Atlantic in March 1946 (the North Atlantic Route Service Conference, in Dublin) and the second in April-May 1946 (the Route Service Conference, in Paris; this meeting was renamed European-Mediterranean Regional Air Navigation Meeting). In both meetings, efforts were made to establish a route pattern to be used by international civil aviation and to determine the ground services and facilities which were required to allow a safe expeditious flow of air traffic.

During PICAO Council’s discussions held in April 1946, it was felt that the Route Service Conferences should be called meetings, as they should be considered as purely technical in character. Moreover, the expression route service was found impossible to translate into French; as the meaning of this English term was not clear, the Council agreed to change the title of those gatherings from PICAO Route Service Conferences to PICAO Regional Air Navigation Meetings (RAN).

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Office of Freedom of Information, Privacy and Classification Review (FPC) was created in 1989. FPC responded to requests under both the Privacy Act and the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA), and was “responsible for the receipt, acknowledgement and processing of external requests for Department record” including “those that have been made by the general public, members of Congress, and other government agencies, and those that have been made pursuant to judicial processes such as subpoenas, court orders and discovery requests.” It was responsible for administering the agency’s information access and document production program with the aid of the Information Request Management System (INFORM).

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Yalta Conference (code-named Argonaut), sometimes called the Crimea Conference, was held from February 4 to 11, 1945, at the former imperial palace at Yalta. The national delegations were led by President Franklin D. Roosevelt, Prime Minister Winston Churchill, and Marshal Joseph Stalin. No other governments were represented nor were they notified of the decisions made at the meeting.

The Conference agreed on a declaration of liberated Europe, allowing for democratic elections in all the liberated territories. It agreed to a conference in April in San Francisco on the proposed world organization, the United Nations (UN). The structure of the UN was considered and the idea of a Security Council was agreed upon. The United States and Great Britain agrred to support the Ukrainian and Byelorussian SoOviet Socialist Republics having separate UN seats. A UN territorial trusteeship would also be applied to existing mandates of the League of Nations and territories detached from the enemy as a result of the war.

As to Germany, the three powers saw the dismemberment, disarmament, and demilitarization of Germany as a "requisite for future peace and security". Germany was to be divided into zones of occupation amongst the Allied, with large sections of eastern Germany annexed by Poland and the Soviet Union. The Germans living in those areas were to be expelled. France was also granted a zone of occupation and membership in the Allied Control Council for Germany. 

Germany would be required to provide reparations for "losses caused by her to the Allied nations in the course of the war". Reparations were allowed in the form of removal of national wealth (machine tools, ships, shares in German enterprises, and so forth), the annual delivery of goods for a period to be fixed, or the use of German labor. The Americans and Russians agreed on the figure of $22 billion.

Poland was to have a "broad democratic provisional government" leading up to "free and unfettered elections as soon as possible on the basis of universal suffrage and secret ballot". In Yugoslavia, the Tito-Subasic Agreement would be put into effect, merging the Royal and Communist governments.

The Soviets agreed to intervene in the war with Japan within three months of the German surrender. In return they would be given the Sakhalin and Kurile Islands and pre-eminent interests over Port Arthur and Darien and its rail connections.

Finally, all Soviet nationals were to be repatriated whether they were willing or not.

The Yalta Conference is often cited as the symbol of Western betrayal or the beginning of the Cold War.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Committee on Commodity Problems was established by the FAO Conference in 1949 to work under the supervision of, and be responsible, to the Council. By decision of the Conference in 1957 it became a Committee of the Council. The Committee was to review international commodity problems affecting production, trade, distribution and consumption, and related economic matters; prepare a factual and interpretative survey of the world commodity situation, to be available directly to member nations; and report and submit suggestions to the Council on policy issues arising out of its deliberations, and to provide these reports and those of its subsidiary bodies to member nations for their information. The Committee held one session during each biennium, convened sufficiently in advance of the Council session and before the regular sessions of the Conference. The Committee could also hold additional sessions.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
On May 26, 1961, President John F. Kennedy, in a letter to the Congress transmitting a foreign assistance bill, indicated that he expected the Secretary of State to become the focal point of responsibility for coordination of foreign economic policies. In facilitating executive branch coordination of foreign economic policies, the Secretary could choose whatever mechanisms he found appropriate, including the formation of interagency working groups. As a result, the Secretary of State delegated to the Under Secretary of State for Economic Affairs responsibility for assuring proper interagency consultation and coordination in this field. The Interdepartmental Committee of Under Secretaries on Foreign Economic Policy thus came into being.

Under the direction of the Under Secretary of State for Economic Affairs, who served as Committee chairman, the Committee met every other Wednesday afternoon. Included among it members were representatives from the Council of Economic Advisers and the head of the Agency for International Development. Joseph D. Coppock served as executive secretary, and it fell to him to circulate the planning papers in advance as well as to follow up actions. 

The Commitee met regularly until late June 1962 when it recessed with the expectation of resuming meetings in the autumnl. It remained inactive, however, for six months. A background paper on the Committee and its future was transmitted under cover of a memorandum from G. Griffith Johnson, Assistant Secretary of State for Economic Affairs, to George C. creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Second Quebec Conference (codenamed "OCTAGON") was a high level military conference held during World War II between the British, Canadian, and American Governments. The Conference was held in Quebec City, September 12 - 16, and was the second conference to be held in Quebec. The chief representatives were British Prime Minister Winston Churchill, Canadian Prime Minister William Lyon Mackenzie King, and President Franklin D. Roosevelt.

The leaders considered strategic plans for final victory over Germany and Japan, continued U.S. economic aid to the United Kingdom, and British naval participation in the conflict against Japan. Also discussed were the demarcation of zones of occupation in post-war Germany and overall policy for governing occupied Germany. The Morgenthau Plan for reducing Germany to an agrarian economy was tentatively approved, although it would be rejected by the President a month later.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Malta Conference (code named ARGONAUT and CRICKET) was held from January 30 to February 3, 1945 between President Franklin D. Roosevelt and British Prime Minister Winston Churchill. The purpose of the Conference was to plan the final campaign against Germany with the Combined Chiefs of Staff. Both leaders agreed on the undesirability of the Red Army advancing into central Europe. Another focal point of discussion was finding a solution for the millions of displaced persons in Europe. Although the Conference began on January 30, 1945,  President Roosevelt did not arrive until February 2, the last day of the Conference.

Also attending the Conference were Secretary of State Edward Stettinius, Jr., Ambassador W. Averell Harriman, Harry L. Hopkins, General of the Army George C. Marshall, Fleet Admiral Ernest J. King, Fleet Admiral William Leahy, British Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden, Major General Laurence S. Kuter (representing General of the Army H.H. Arnold who was unable to attend due to illness), Field Marshal H. Maitland Wilson, Field Marshal Sir Alan Brooke, Air Chief Marshal Sir Charles F.A. Portal, Admiral of the Fleet Sir Andrew B. Cunningham,, General Sir Hastings L. Ismay, and Major General Jacob Devers.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
Because Marshal Joseph Stalin was unable or unwilling to attend the Quebec Conference of August 1943, it was decided that the foreign ministers of Great Britain, the United States, and the Soviet Union should meet as soon as possible to discuss the war situation and wartime cooperation. Accordingly, from October 1 to November 10, 1943, the foreign ministers of the Big Three met in Moscow. It was the first three-power Allied meeting of the war. Heading the American delegation was Secretary of State Cordell Hull. Anthony Eden, Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs led the British delegation, and Vyacheslav Molotov, People's Commissar for Foreign Affairs, led the Soviet delegation.

Discussion at the Conference centered upon measures to shorten the war against Germany and plans for United Nations cooperation after the war. The Conference established a European Advisory Commission, with its seat in London, to study and make recommendations regarding European questions and postwar policy toward Germany, and an Advisory Council for Italy to advise on Italian affairs. The Conference also published a declaration on atrocities and war crimes, as well as the so-called Moscow Declaration (also agreed to by China) on collective security and a postwar international organization.

The most controversial point in the discussions involved the status of the Polish government in exile in London, which the Soviet Union refused to recognize. In addition, the United States and Great Britain assured the Soviets that preparations for a second front in Europe were well under way.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
On October 18, 1973, Congress in the Department of State Appropriations Authorization Act (87 Stat. 453) authorized a Bureau of Oceans and International Environmental and Scientific Affairs and specified that it be headed by an Assistant Secretary of State. The new Bureau, established on October 8, 1974, incorporated the duties and responsibilities of several components in the Department of State, which were then abolished. These were: the Office of International Scientific and Technological Affairs, whose Director had held rank equivalent to an Assistant Secretary of State since 1965; the Office of the Special Assistant to the Secretary for Fisheries and Wildlife and Coordinator of Ocean Affairs; the Office of the Special Assistant to the Secretary for Population Matters; and the Special Assistant to the Secretary for Environmental Affairs. The Department had first appointed a Science Adviser in 1958. 

Although other Assistant Secretaries were commissioned merely as "an Assistant Secretary of State" and then given a functional designation by administrative action, Dr. Dixy Lee Ray, the first incumbent, in light of the legislation that created her position, was commissioned "an Assistant Secretary of State for Oceans and International Environmental and Scientific Affairs." The title has been given in full in all subsequent commissions to this office.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Office of the General Counsel (GC) provided legal advice, counsel, and services to the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) and its officials and ensured that USAID programs were administered in accordance with legislative authorities. The General Counsel (GC) served as the Agency's chief legal officer and was the principal advisor to the administrator on Agency-wide policy matters. The GC also advised on legal matters concerning the operation and administration of USAID programs, and on matters relating to legislation or proposed legislation affecting USAID. The GC provided advice and guidance on congressional investigations and determined what legal courses of action were appropriate for the Agency. GC also maintained liaison with other government organizations to provide advice or assistance in interpreting or applying the legal authorities of the Agency and represented USAID in connection with legal matters affecting it.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Committee on Commodity Problems was established by the FAO Conference in 1949 to work under the supervision of, and be responsible, to the Council. By decision of the Conference in 1957 it became a Committee of the Council. The Committee was to review international commodity problems affecting production, trade, distribution and consumption, and related economic matters; prepare a factual and interpretative survey of the world commodity situation, to be available directly to member nations; and report and submit suggestions to the Council on policy issues arising out of its deliberations, and to provide these reports and those of its subsidiary bodies to member nations for their information. The Committee held one session during each biennium, convened sufficiently in advance of the Council session and before the regular sessions of the Conference. The Committee could also hold additional sessions.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: A number of scientists and conservationists of northern nations with an interest in the preservation and conservation of Arctic animals were concerned about the adequacy of scientific knowledge for the effective management of polar bears. As a consequence, the First International Scientific Meeting on the Polar Bear met at Fairbanks, Alaska, September 6-11, 1965.  Attending were representatives from all five polar bear countries: Canada, Greenland (territory of Denmark), Norway, the United States, and the Soviet Union. The meeting set the stage for additional international conferences and research efforts, which eventually led to a 1973 international agreement on polar bear conservation.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Foreign Service Act of 1946 (60 Stat. 1001), effective November 13, 1946, authorized the establishment of the Board of the Foreign Service. The Appointments and Assignments Board (AAB) was established by and under the general jurisdiction of the Board of Foreign Service. The seven members were composed of four representatives of the Department of State, specifically a representative from the Office of Personnel, and representatives of the geographic bureaus, as well as representatives from the Departments of Labor, Commerce, and Agriculture. It considered the appointments, assignments, and transfers of all officer personnel of the Foreign Service below the rank of career minister that were of concern to more than one department. The AAB was responsible for reviewing individual actions and making recommendations to the Director of Personnel. The Board was not authorized to deal with substantive personnel policy.

Foreign Service and Departmental Personnel Practices of the Department of State, 1954: p. 11, 57 (When we get into the officer grades we have the Appointments and Assignment Board who recommended assignments. That Board is made up of a member of the Office of Personnel who at the present time is Mr. Howard Mace, and representatives of the geographic bureaus in the Department of State, and one representative each of the Departments of Labor, Commerce, and Agriculture. The appointments in the officer category are taken up before the Appointments and Assignment Board which submits the recommended assignments, recommended transfers, etc. to the Director of Personnel, who can either approve, disapprove or modify the recommendations; Appointments and Assignments Board is actually a board under the general jurisdiction of the Board of Foreign Service, and was established by the act of 1946, in cooperation with the Board of Foreign Service. Its members, therefore, parallel the membership of the Board of Foreign Service. That is, we have departmental representation, and in addition to that we have representatives from the Departments of Labor, Commerce, and Agriculture. This Board, of which I am the Acting Chairman [Howard Mace], considers the appointments and transfers of all officer personnel of the Foreign Service, including the assignments of such persons within the Department referred to, whether the Department of State or the other agencies-that is, Commerce, Labor or Agriculture. This board is responsible for reviewing also individual actions and making recommendations to the Director of Personnel. Appointments and Assignments come under his jurisdiction)

This seven-member body, four State Department members and one member each from the Departments of Agriculture, Commerce, and Labor) was authorized to review and recommend the Secretary of State individual appointments and assignments in the Foreign Service below the rank of career minister. creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The FAO Intergovernmental Group (IGG) on Grains represented a forum for intergovernmental consultation and exchange on trends in production, consumption, trade, stocks and prices of wheat and coarse grains, including regular appraisal of the world grain situation and short term outlook. The Group, under FAO auspices, considered changes in national grain policies and examined their international effects as pertaining to the current and prospective grain situation. Membership in the Group was open to all Member Nations and Associate Members of FAO, including Observers from international organizations and institutions. Nearly all grains importing and exporting countries were Members of the IGG on grains. The First Session of the FAO Group on Grains was held in May 1957 and since then it met once in each biennium.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: In response to an invitation of the U.S. Government, representatives of 54 nations met at Chicago from November 1 to December 7, 1944, to "make arrangements for the immediate establishment of provisional world air routes and services: and "to set up an interim council to collect, record and study data concerning international aviation and to make recommendations for its improvement." The Conference was also invited to "discuss the principles and methods to be followed in the adoption of a new aviation convention." Out of the Conference came the Convention on International Civil Aviation, also known as the Chicago Convention, which established the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) a specialized agency of the United Nations charged with coordinating and regulating international air travel. The Convention established rules of airspace, aircraft registration, and safety, and detailed the right of signatories in re4lation to air travel.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
On October 18, 1973, Congress in the Department of State Appropriations Authorization Act (87 Stat. 453) authorized a Bureau of Oceans and International Environmental and Scientific Affairs and specified that it be headed by an Assistant Secretary of State. The new Bureau, established on October 8, 1974, incorporated the duties and responsibilities of several components in the Department of State, which were then abolished. These were: the Office of International Scientific and Technological Affairs, whose Director had held rank equivalent to an Assistant Secretary of State since 1965; the Office of the Special Assistant to the Secretary for Fisheries and Wildlife and Coordinator of Ocean Affairs; the Office of the Special Assistant to the Secretary for Population Matters; and the Special Assistant to the Secretary for Environmental Affairs. The Department had first appointed a Science Adviser in 1958. 

The Bureau of Oceans and International Environmental and Scientific Affairs (OES) was the Department of State's focal point for foreign policy formulation and implementation in global environment, science, and technology issues. The Bureau worked closely with the Executive Office of the President, U.S. Government agencies, Congress, U.S. universities, nongovernmental organizations, private citizens, and other bureaus in the Department of State to formulate U.S. foreign policy on these issues. OES implemented those policies by representing the Department of State at multilateral, regional and bilateral organizations and meetings, including bilateral commissions and common agendas , and through cooperative agreements, such as science and technology framework agreements, with foreign government agencies. 

The Bureau developed and directed the carrying out of policy recommendations relating to U.S. participation in international science and technology programs, in bilateral cooperative programs related to its area of interest, and in the activities of the International Fisheries Commission of which the United States was a member.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Commission for Hydrology (CHy) shaped the water-related activities of the WMO and addressed issues relating to the basic hydrological observation network, water resources assessment, flood forecasting and management, adaptability to climate variability and change and promotes exchange of technology and capacity building. In particular, the outcomes of its deliberations provided guidance to WMO Member countries and WMO Secretariat for the implementation of the Hydrology and Water Resources Programme of  the WMO.

Areas of activity included integrated hydrological networks, hydrological forecasting systems, hydrological aspects of natural disasters and environmental issues, assessment of water use, latest advances in hydrological technology and practical implementation of IWRM principles with particular attention to integrated flood management. This information was incorporated into technical standards, reports or guidelines that could be used by national hydrological and hydrometeorological services of member nations.

The Commission met every four years.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Department's regional bureaus oversaw the U.S. embassies and consulates, and coordinated U.S. foreign relations in their respective geographic areas. Assistant Legal Advisers supervised the attorneys who support those bureaus, dealing with such matters as protection of U.S. citizens and investments, problems in diplomatic and consular relations, interpretation and negotiation of treaties, military base rights and status of force issues, peaceful settlement of disputes, and trade matters. AReas of interest included litigation in U.S. courts involving countries and officials in the region; relations with the governments of Africa and regional and sub-regional organizations; conflict resolution and peace agreements; armed conflict and related UN Security Council actions; border questions; military facility and status of forces agreements; U.S. cooperation in developing legal and political institutions in the region; and restrictions on assistance to or conducting business with certain countries in the region.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: Recommendations for Presidential nominations and appointments under the jurisdiction of the Department of State were made by memorandum from the Secretary of State to the President. These nominations and appointments included not only ambassadors and principal officers of the Department, but also top-level positions in the United Nations, the Inter-American system, and other international commissions, organizations, and conferences where membership requires Presidential appointment. The Presidential Appointments Staff, on behalf of the Under Secretary for Management, had responsibility for assuring the Secretary and the Deputy Secretary that: appropriate consultations and clearances within the Department of State, including the Office of Inspector General, had been completed before selectee recommendations were put forward for approval; that formal security, conflict-of-interest, and medical clearances (if appropriate) were obtained once a selection had been made and White House approval has been received; and that (if appropriate) agreement of the host state or international organization had been obtained.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Department of State established a Bureau of International Cultural Relations on Jun 1, 1959, and subsequently renamed it the Bureau of Education and Cultural Affairs on April 17, 1960. The following year, the Department elevated the position of Special Assistant for Coordination of International Educational and Cultural Relations, which headed the Bureau, to the rank of Assistant Secretary of State. The Department had first established a Division of Cultural Relations in 1938. Cultural relations was also part of the responsibilities of the first Assistant Secretary of State for Public Affairs created in 1944. In 1978 the Bureau was abolished and its functions transferred to the International Communications Agency (subsequently the U.S. Information Agency) under Reorganization Plan No. 2 (91 Stat. 1637). On October 1, 1999, pursuant to the integration of the U.S. Information Agency into the Department of State the Bureau was revived.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Advisory Committee on the Arts (ACA) was established under Section 10 of the International Cultural Exchange and Trade Fair Participation Act of 1956 (70 Stat. 778), and was continued under the Mutual Educational and Cultural Exchange Act of 1961 (75 Stat. 527). It was a public advisory committee the advised the Advisory Commission on International Education and Cultural Affairs regarding cultural exchange in the performing arts. It was made up of ten members selected by the Secretary of State for their expertise in the fields of publishing, music, theater, dance, and the fine arts. Initially attached to the Branch of Cultural Presentation in the International Educational Exchange Service of the Department of State, the Committee received staff support from the Bureau of Educational and Cultural Affairs. The Committee's last meeting was held in 1968 but it was not abolished until July 18, 1973.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The U.S. Legation for Bulgaria was established in 1901. The Consul General at Constantinople, Charles M.  Dickinson, served as the first agent for Bulgaria. Thereafter U.S. representation for Bulgaria was vested in a non-resident diplomatic agent, John B. Jackson, who served as Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary to Greece, Romania, Montenegro, and Serbia, and was resident at Athens, Greece. Other diplomatic agents to Bulgaria included Horace G. Knowles, August 1907 - February 1909; Spencer F. Eddy, 1909; John R. Carter, 1909- 1911; John B. Jackson, 1912 - 1913; and Charles J. Vopicka, 1913 - 1919.

The first resident chief of mission at Sofia was Charles S. Wilson, who served as Charge d'Affaires ad interim from March 18, 1919, until December 5, 1921, when he presented his credentials as Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary. He was succeeded by Henry Wharton Shoemaker, March 28, 1930; Frederick A. Sterling, April 3, 1934; Ray Atherton, October 21, 1937; and George H. Earle III, April 2, 1940. Bulgaria declared war on the United States on December 13, 1941; Earle departed his post in late December 1941. 

The U.S. Legation at Sofia reopened on September 27, 1947, with John Evarts Horner as Charge d'Affaires ad interim. Donald R. Heath presented his credentials as Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary on November 8, 1947. On January 19, 1950, the government of Bulgaria declared Heath persona non grata; he departed Sofia on February 24, 1950, and diplomatic relations were suspended because Bulgaria refused to withdraw false charges of complicity in espionage made against the U.S. minister during the trial of the Bulgarian Communist Party Leader Traicho Kostov. Another U.S. minister was accredited to Bulgaria in 1960 after Bulgaria withdrew as false the charges made against his predecessor. Diplomatic relations were restored in 1959, and the next envoy, Edward Page, Jr., presented his credentials on March 14, 1960. He was succeeded by Eugenie Anderson, August 3, 1962; Nathaniel Davis, June 4, 1965; and John M. McSweeney, October 26, 1966.

The Bulgarian and U.S. Legations at Washington and Sofia were raised to embassy status on November 28, 1966 (this was the last U.S. legation to be upgraded to an embassy), and McSweeney presented his credentials as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary on April 19, 1967. He was succeeded as Ambassador by Horace G. Torbert, Jr., November 4, 1970; Martin F. Herz, April 3, 1974; Raymond L. Garthoff, September 16, 1977; Jack Richard Perry, October 17, 1979; Robert L. Barry, December 8, 1981; Melvyn Levitsky, November 13, 1984; Sol Polansky, September 4, 1987; Hugh Kenneth Hill, September 18, 1990; William Dale Montgomery, October 27, 1993; Avis T. Bohlen, September 5, 1996; Richard Monroe Miles, September 8, 1999; and James W. Pardew, May 13, 2002.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Department of State established a Bureau of International Cultural Relations on Jun 1, 1959, and subsequently renamed it the Bureau of Education and Cultural Affairs on April 17, 1960. The following year, the Department elevated the position of Special Assistant for Coordination of International Educational and Cultural Relations, which headed the Bureau, to the rank of Assistant Secretary of State. The Department had first established a Division of Cultural Relations in 1938. Cultural relations was also part of the responsibilities of the first Assistant Secretary of State for Public Affairs created in 1944. In 1978 the Bureau was abolished and its functions transferred to the International Communications Agency (subsequently the U.S. Information Agency) under Reorganization Plan No. 2 (91 Stat. 1637). On October 1, 1999, pursuant to the integration of the U.S. Information Agency into the Department of State the Bureau was revived.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Republic of Texas was established in 1836, when Texas declared and won its independence from Mexico. The U.S. Government established diplomatic ties with its new neighbor to the south, although it did not formally recognize Texas until late 1837. The consuls who had represented the United States in the settlements of Galvezton (Galveston) and Goliad in the Mexican State of Coahuila Y Texas remained in place and posts at other sites were established later. A Charge d'Affaires was appointed to Harrisburg (Houston) in 1837. Those posts still operating in 1845 were terminated after the United States and Texas agreeed on an annexation resolution; Texas formally became the 28th State of the Union in February 1846.

Consuls at Galveston included:

* David G. Burnet, 1832 - 1834

* Francis Slaughter, 1835 - 1838

* Elisha A. Rhodes, 1839 - Oct. 14, 1842

* A.M. Green, 1843 - 1844

* Duff Green, 1844-1845

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Department's regional bureaus oversaw the U.S. embassies and consulates, and coordinated U.S. foreign relations in their respective geographic areas. Assistant Legal Advisers supervise the attorneys who support those bureaus, dealing with such matters as protection of U.S. citizens and investments, problems in diplomatic and consular relations, interpretation and negotiation of treaties, military base rights and status of force issues, peaceful settlement of disputes, and trade matters. The Office of European Affairs dealt with issues relating to the European Union; the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE); the NATO alliance and defense cooperation issues; democratization and assistance to Eastern Europe and the successor states to the former Soviet Union; and bilateral issues with countries in the region.
