creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The International Council for the Exploration of the Sea (ICES) (Conseil International de l'Exploration de la Mer) (CIEM) was established on July 22, 1902 in Copenhagen. ICES today is a modern intergovernmental organisation that promotes marine research in the North Atlantic.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: Congress authorized the Foreign Service Institute in the Foreign Service Act of 1946 (60 Stat. 1018). The Foreign Service Institute was established on March 13, 1947, to furnish Foreign Service Officers with training throughout their careers. It superseded a Foreign Service School established in 1924 to provide basic instruction in foreign policy questions and consular operations to newly appointed Foreign Service officers. All Directors of the Foreign Service Institute have been designated by the Secretary of State, and hold rank equivalent to an Assistant Secretary of State.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Bureau, under the direction of an assistant secretary, executed responsibility for the general conduct of foreign relations with the countries within its geographical area of responsibility by applying over-all political, security, economic, public affairs, social, consular, administrative, and other policies and practices. The Bureau maintained and supervised relationships with foreign missions in the United States representing countries within its regional jurisdiction, except on substantive consular matters, and guided the operation of Foreign Service establishments within its area overseas. Its geographical area of responsibility included Algeria, Bahrain, Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Libya, Morocco, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Syria, Tunisia, the United Arab Emirates, and Yemen.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Department of State established a Bureau of International Cultural Relations on Jun 1, 1959, and subsequently renamed it the Bureau of Education and Cultural Affairs on April 17, 1960. The following year, the Department elevated the position of Special Assistant for Coordination of International Educational and Cultural Relations, which headed the Bureau, to the rank of Assistant Secretary of State. The Department had first established a Division of Cultural Relations in 1938. Cultural relations was also part of the responsibilities of the first Assistant Secretary of State for Public Affairs created in 1944. In 1978 the Bureau was abolished and its functions transferred to the International Communications Agency (subsequently the U.S. Information Agency) under Reorganization Plan No. 2 (91 Stat. 1637). On October 1, 1999, pursuant to the integration of the U.S. Information Agency into the Department of State the Bureau was revived.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Seventh World Forestry Congress met in Buenos Aires, October 4-18, 1972. The first World Forestry Congress was held in Rome in 1926 and each successive congress generally took place every six years afterward. Gatherings served as forums for governments, universities, civil society and the private sector to exchange views and experiences and to formulate recommendations for implementation at national, regional and global levels. Each Congress also provided an opportunity to examine  the state of forests and forestry in order to discern trends, adapt policies and raise awareness of issues among decision-makers, the public and other parties concerned. Its functions were advisory, not executive, and participants attended the Congress as private individuals. The implementation of recommendations was a matter solely for those to whom they are addressed in light of their own particular circumstances - governments, international organizations, scientific bodies and forest owners, among others. The outcomes were brought to the attention of the Food and Africulture Organization (FAO) Conference which considered endorsing, through a resolution, any declaration emanating from the Congress.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
United Nations Conference on the Application of Science and technology for the Benefit of Less Developed Areas marked the origins of the UN focus on science and technology as useful and important tools for development. It was based on the view that the developing countries “leapfrog” across generations by adopting technologies developed in the industrialized countries. The

conference resulted in a multifaceted approach to science and technology advice: 1. The Committee on Science and Technology for Development (CSTD) was to be a new component of ECOSOC.

2. The Advisory Committee on the Application of Science and Technology for Development (ACAST) was made up of experts in the various fields of science and technology and was created to provide science advice to CSTD and other UN bodies. 3. The Office of Science and Technology (OST) was created as a part of the UN Secretariat to support both of these groups and assist in the implementation of the advice.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Office of the Legal Adviser supported the various functional bureaus of the Department which had crosscutting, worldwide responsibilities for specific program areas.The Office of Human Rights and Refugees (L/HRR) provided legal advice and support to the Bureau of Population, Refugees and Migration and the Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights and Labor. It led U.S. delegations in multilateral negotiations of human rights instruments; acted as counsel to U.S. delegations and participated in negotiations at the UN, the Organization of American States, the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe and elsewhere on matters relating to human rights and refugees. The Office defended U.S. laws and practices in response to a variety of UN, OAS, and OSCE human rights complaint mechanisms, and coordinated U.S. reporting to treaty bodies on U.S. implementation of human rights treaty obligations. It provided legal advice and support throughout the Department on asylum and refugee law, and human rights issues ranging from torture, genocide, and arbitrary detention to freedom of movement, assembly and expression.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The IPU Assembly (formerly known as the Inter-Parliamentary Conference) was the principal statutory body that expressed the views of the Inter-Parliamentary Union on political issues. It brought together parliamentarians to study international problems and make recommendations for action. Delegations attending IPU Assemblies customarily include parliamenatry representatives from all  parties. The Assembly met twice a year (in the spring and autumn) and was held each time in a different country, providing participants with an opportunity to see various national realities.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
In 1957 the Department of State elevated the position of Chief of the Foreign Service Inspection Corps to that of Inspector General of the Foreign Service. Between 1957 and 1980, the Secretary of State designated incumbents, who held rank equivalent to an Assistant Secretary of State. On February 1, 1978, the title of the Office of Inspector General, Foreign Service (S/IG) was changed to the Office of the Inspector General (S/IG). The Foreign Service Act of 1980 (Oct 17, 1980; P.L. 96-465; 94 Stat. 2080) made the Inspector General a Presidential appointee, subject to the advice and consent of the Senate, and changed the title to "Inspector General of the Department of State and the Foreign Service."

The Inspector Generals included: Raymond Clendenin Miller (1957-1960); Gerald Augustin Drew (1960-1962); Norris S. Haselton (1962-1964); Fraser Wilkins (1964-1971); Thomas Watkins McElhiney (1971-1973); James S. Sutterlin (1973-1974); William Everett Schaufele Jr. (1975); Robert Marion Sayre (1975-1978); Theodore Lyman Eliot Jr., 1978; Robert Charles Brewster, 1979-1981; Robert Lyle Brown, 1981-1983; William Caldwell Harrop, 1983-1986; Hugh Byron Hollingsworth (Acting), 1986-1987; Sherman M. Funk, 1987-1994; Jacquelyn W. Williams-Bridgers, 1995-2001; Clark Kent Ervin, 2001-2003; Howard J. Krongard, 2005-2008; and Steve A. Linick, 2013-. Thomas A. Betro was nominated on June 27, 2008 to be the Inspector General; however, the Senate took no action on the nomination.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The J. William Fulbright Foreign Scholarship Board http://exchanges.state.gov/education/ffsb.htm was created by Congress to supervise the educational exchange program. The intent was to establish an impartial and independent body which would assure the respect and cooperation of the academic world for the educational exchange program, particularly in the selection of grantees and of educational institutions qualified to participate. The Board sets policies and procedures for administration of the program, has final responsibility for selection of all grantees, and supervises the conduct of the program both in the United States and abroad. Appointed by the President of the United States, the Board is composed of 12 members drawn from academic, cultural and public life. 

The Fulbright Act of 1945 was an amendment to the Surplus Property Act of 1944. That act appointed the Department of State to be the agency responsible for disposal of surplus war property not on U.S. soil. The resulting funds were to be used by Americans to study in Lend Lease countries and Lend Lease country students to study in the United States. 

The Smith-Mundt Act, three years later, broadened the Fulbright Program to countries other than those Lend Lease countries specified in the original law. It also facilitated the establishment of bi-national centers around the world to coordinate the exchanges between the countries. In 1961, the Fulbright-Hays legislation was passed, extending the Program’s reach even further, and increasing it’s activities. 

Approximately 6,000 new grants are awarded to individuals annually through the Bureau of Educational and Cultural Affairs (ECA) http://exchanges.state.gov/. Grants are given to American students, teachers, and scholars to study, teach, lecture and conduct research in more than 140 countries in the world, and to foreign nationals to engage in similar activities in the United States. 

Individuals are selected on the basis of academic or professional qualifications and potential, plus ability and willingness to share ideas and experiences with people of diverse cultures. 

The primary source of funding for the Fulbright Program is an annual appropriation made by the U.S. Congress to the ECA. Participating governments, as well as host institutions in the United States and abroad, contribute through cost-sharing, as well as by indirect support such as salary supplements, tuition waivers and university housing.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The American Institute in Taiwan (AIT) was the representative office of the United States in Taiwan. The establishment of diplomatic relations with the People's Republic of China (PRC) in 1979 required acknowledgment of the One-China policy and termination of diplomatic relations with the Republic of China. However, the AIT assisted and protected U.S. interests in Taiwan and other areas in the ROC in a non-official manner.

AIT was a non-profit private corporation incorporated in the District of Columbia and founded in 1979 after U.S. established full diplomatic relations. Although AIT was a formally private institution, it was authorized by Section 6 of the Taiwan Relations Act (Publ. L. 96-8) approved April 10, 1979, to perform functions such as issuing visas for tourists and passports for US citizens. With the authorization of Taiwan Relations Act, the Department of State, through a non-official and private contract with AIT, provided AIT guidance and some funding in its operations. In practice the staff of the AIT consisted of largely of employees of the Department of State who are on leave from the Department.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Foreign Aid Steering Group (FASG), also known as the Foreign Assistance Steering Group, was an interdepartmental group established in November 1950. The FASG  along with a number of related task forces, coordinated the preparation of legislative and supporting material in connection with the foreign aid programs to be embodied in the Mutual Security Act of 1951. It was comprised of representatives from the Department of State, the Department of Defense, the Department of the Treasury, the Economic Cooperation Administration (ECA), the Office of the Special Assistant to the President Averell W. Harriman, and the Bureau of the Budget. Willard L. Thorp, Assistant Secretary of State for Economic Affairs, served as Chairman. Representatives from other agencies sometimes attended the group’s meetings, which were held at the Department of Sate. It consisted of an Executive Staff, which became an executive group, and several task forces or groups, they were: Task Force I, European Recovery Program (ERP) and Mutual Security Assistance Program (MSAP); Task Force II, Underdeveloped Areas; Task Force III, Korea; Task Force IV, the Near East and the Palestine Refugee Problem; Task Force V, Japan and the Ryukyus; VI, Congressional Strategy; and VIII, foreign and domestic information program. The Foreign Aid Steering Group held twelve meetings between November 21, 1950, and April 13, 1951.The Steering Group was terminated as of October 12, 1951, with the presentation of the Mutual Assistance program to Congress.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The United Maritime Consultative Council (UMCC) met in Washington in October 1946 for its final session and agreed to recommend to its 18 member governments the establishment through the machinery of the UN of a permanent shipping organization. The Provisional Maritime Consultative Council met in Paris in May 1947 and appointed a committee of three to serve on an inter-organization committee on coordination of activities in the field of safety.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: Shortly after the close of the Washington Conference in mid-February 1974, the Energy Coordinating Group (ECG) convened in Brussels to carry out the mandate given by the Conference and to develop the programme in detail. All of the Washington Conference countries, with the exception of France, participated in the ECG, together with the OECD and the Commission of the European Communities. They were later joined by Austria, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland and Turkey. Representatives of the seventeen countries and the two international institutions met together at the Brussels Palais d'Egmont from early March until November 1974, when their work culminated in agreed proposals for the establishment of the International Energy Agency.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Governing Body was the executive body of the International Labour Office, which acted as the secretariat of the International Labour Organization (ILO). It met three times a year, in March, June and November. It took decisions on ILO policy, decided the agenda of the International Labour Conference, adopted the draft Programme and Budget of the Organization for submission to the Conference, and elected the Director-General. It was composed of 56 titular members (28 Governments, 14 Employers and 14 Workers) and 66 deputy members (28 Governments, 19 Employers and 19 Workers). Ten of the titular government seats were permanently held by states of chief industrial importance (Brazil, China, France, Germany, India, Italy, Japan, the Russian Federation, the United Kingdom and the United States). The other Government members were elected by the Conference every three years. The Employer and Worker members are elected in their individual capacity.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Department of State established a Bureau of International Cultural Relations on Jun 1, 1959, and subsequently renamed it the Bureau of Education and Cultural Affairs on April 17, 1960. The following year, the Department elevated the position of Special Assistant for Coordination of International Educational and Cultural Relations, which headed the Bureau, to the rank of Assistant Secretary of State. The Department had first established a Division of Cultural Relations in 1938. Cultural relations was also part of the responsibilities of the first Assistant Secretary of State for Public Affairs created in 1944. In 1978 the Bureau was abolished and its functions transferred to the International Communications Agency (subsequently the U.S. Information Agency) under Reorganization Plan No. 2 (91 Stat. 1637). On October 1, 1999, pursuant to the integration of the U.S. Information Agency into the Department of State the Bureau was revived.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Washington Diplomatic Conference on the Patent Cooperation Treaty took place from May 25  to June 19, 1970. It concluded with the signing of the Patent Cooperation Treaty which provided a unified procedure for filing patent applications to protect inventions in each of its contracting states. The Treaty entered into force on January 21, 1978 initially with eighteen contracting states, and the first international applications were filed on June 1, 1978. The Treaty was subsequently amended in 1979, and modified in 1984 and 2001. The states party to the PCT, i.e. the Contracting States, constitute the International Patent Cooperation Union.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Department of State by administrative action established the position of Deputy Under Secretary of State, after Congress authorized ten Assistant Secretary of State positions (two of which could be at the Deputy Under Secretary level) in the Department of State Reorganization Act of 1949 (63 Stat. 111) approved May 26, 1949. The position was created as a result of a recommendation made by the Commission on the Organization of the Executive Branch of Government (Hoover Commission). The Deputy Under Secretary assisted the Secretary and Under Secretary in policy development and oversight of non-administrative activities of the Department. The Department replaced this position with a newly-created Deputy Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs in August 1955.

Incumbents were Dean Rusk, May 26, 1949 - March 27, 1950, and H. Freeman Mathews, July 5, 1950 - October 11, 1953.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Diplomatic Convention on Wills met in Washington, D.C. to discuss and agree upon an additional form of last will and testament, or "international will" which, if employed, would dispense to some extent with the search for the applicable law. It followed on the the Hague Convention of 5 October 1961 on the Conflicts of Laws Relating to the Form of the Clauses of a Will, the Convention on the Establishment of a Scheme of Registration of Wills drawn up within the framework of the Council of Europe and signed in Basle on 16 May 1972, and the the Hague Convention of 1 October 1973 concerning the International Administration of the Estates of Deceased  Persons. The Washington Conference agreed upon the Convention providing a Uniform Law on the Form of an International Will of October 26, 1973.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Governing Body was the executive body of the International Labour Office, which acted as the secretariat of the International Labour Organization (ILO). It met three times a year, in March, June and November. It took decisions on ILO policy, decided the agenda of the International Labour Conference, adopted the draft Programme and Budget of the Organization for submission to the Conference, and elected the Director-General. It was composed of 56 titular members (28 Governments, 14 Employers and 14 Workers) and 66 deputy members (28 Governments, 19 Employers and 19 Workers). Ten of the titular government seats were permanently held by states of chief industrial importance (Brazil, China, France, Germany, India, Italy, Japan, the Russian Federation, the United Kingdom and the United States). The other Government members were elected by the Conference every three years. The Employer and Worker members are elected in their individual capacity.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The carry out its duties and responsibilities, the Executive Office had five branches. The Administrative Services Branch arranged and maintained office space, office furnishings, equipment and supplies and warehousing; and managed and maintained all administrative property, supplies, and equipment including an inventory control for all U.S. Operations Mission to Israel (USOM/I) owned property. The Branch assured communication and transportation services including operation of a motor pool; arranged for utilities as required; managed and maintained residential and other real property leased by the Mission; and handled tort claims. Through its Mail and Records Unit, the Branch was responsible for the control and distribution of all incoming and outgoing documents and correspondence of the Mission; proper organization of the records; records inventories; and prompt and orderly destruction or storage of inactive records. The Administrative Services Branch provided printing and reproduction services and internal and external security of all MIssion offices, residences, warehouses, and parking areas.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: PL 480 refers to Public Law 480, also known as Food for Peace, which was a funding avenue by which U.S. food could be used for overseas aid. The full name for Public Law 480 was the Agricultural Trade Development Assistance Act (7 U.S.C. 1721), signed into law on July, 10, 1954, by President Dwight D. Eisenhower. The act had four parts, titles 1, 2, 3 and 5. Title 1 was managed by the United States Department of Agriculture while titles 2, 3 and 5 were managed by the International Cooperation Administration and, subsequently, the Agency for International Development. In 1961, President John F. Kennedy renamed it as "Food for Peace," stating, "Food is strength, and food is peace, and food is freedom, and food is a helping to people around the world whose good will and friendship we want." In late 1961 the staff of the PL 480 Division was reallocated to the Office of Material Resources.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Diplomatic Conference for the Establishment of International Conventions for the Protection of war Victims, frequently referred to as the Fourth Geneva Convention, was the only Geneva Convention that addressed the protection of civilians in times of war. The First, Second, and Third Geneva Conventions of 1949 were concerned with members of armed forces, and all three were revisions of international agreements that existed prior to 1949. Before World War II, no international agreement provided effective protection for civilians in wartime situations. Events that occurred as part of that war prompted the International Committee of the Red Cross, governments, and other entities to establish such an agreement as one component of international humanitarian law. On August 12, 1949, the Diplomatic Conference for the Establishment of International Conventions for the Protection of war Victims adopted the Geneva Convention relative to the Protection of Civilian Persons in Time of War which went into effect on October 21, 1950.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
Upon the termination of the United Maritime Authority on March 2, 1946, the United Maritime Consultative Council (UMCC) was established. Its role was to maintain for the eight months' "transitional period", ending October 31, 1946, a simplified and limited control over international shipping to ensure the availability of vessel tonnage for United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration (UNRRA) shipments and the essential import programmes of various European governments. The UMCC which held its first session in Amsterdam from June 18 to 24, 1946, was asked by the United Nations, through the Secretary General, for its views on "the question of establishing a world-wide inter-governmental shipping organization to deal with technical matters". 

The UMCC met in Washington in October 1946 for its second and final session and agreed to recommend to its eighteem member governments the establishment through the machinery of the UN of a permanent shipping organization. It also agreed, as a temporary measure, pending the creation of permanent body, to form a further interim body, the Provisional Maritime Consultative Council. Annexed to its recommendations were a draft convention for an intergovernmental maritime consultative organizations, the so-called “Washington draft”  The Washington Draft provided for the establishment of an Inter-Governmental Maritime Consultative Organization, consisting of an Assembly of delegates of all member governments, a Council of sixteen governments elected by the Assembly; a Maritime Safety Committee of twelve member governments, and a small Secretariat. The proposed organization would be purely consultative and advisory, without executive powers. Its purpose was to provide machinery in the international shipping field for cooperation among governments, encouragement of the removal of discriminatory practices, exchange of information, and consideration of maritime problems generally.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Experts' Conference on Passports and Frontier Formalities, on April 29, 1947, issued its report to be presented to the United Nations Economic and Social Council. The report contained some forty recommendations for simplification of passport and visa requirements, of currency control and customs and health inspection at frontiers to make travel easier. However, the Conference decided it was not yet possible to return to the pre-1914 regime of complete freedom of travel.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
A Federal appropriations act for the year ending Jun 30, 1875 (Jun 20, 1874; 18 Stat. 90), authorized the President to appoint a Third Assistant Secretary of State. The Secretary of State was authorized to prescribe the duties of the Assistant Secretaries and other Department of State employees, “and may make changes and transfers therein when, in his judgment, it becomes necessary.” The Third Assistant Secretary’s duties varied over the years, including such diverse assignments as: supervision of several geographic divisions; oversight of the Bureaus of Accounts and Appointments; international conferences and commissions; and ceremonials and protocol, including presentation to the President of chiefs of foreign diplomatic missions. The Foreign Service Act of 1924 (May 24, 1924; 43 Stat. 146) abolished numerical titles for Assistant Secretaries of State.

Third Assistant Secretaries of State were: Charles Payson, 1878–1881; Walker Blaine, 1881–1882; Alvey Augustus Adee, 1882–1886; John Bassett Moore, 1886–1891; William Morton Grinnell, 1892–1893; Edward Henry Strobel, 1893–1894; William Woodville Rockhill, 1894–1896; William Woodward Baldwin, 1896–1897; Thomas Wilbur Cridler, 1897–1901; Herbert Henry Davis Peirce, 1901–1906), 1906–1908; William Phillips, 1909; Chandler Hale, 1909–1913; Dudley Field Malone, 1913; William Phillips, 1914–1917; Samuel Miller Breckinridge Long, 1917–1920; Van Santvoord Merle-Smith, 1920–1921; Robert Woods Bliss, 1921–1923; Joshua Butler Wright, 1923–1924; and Benjamin Moran was not commissioned, although his nomination of June 22, 1874, had been confirmed by the Senate.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Office of the Legal Adviser was organized into sections that roughly corresponded with the Department of State's various bureaus, including regional offices that focus on specific areas of the world and functional offices that deal with specific subject matters. The Office of Economic and Business Affairs (L/EB) provided legal advice and support in international negotiations, development of U.S. policy, and the application of U.S. and international law with respect to international economic agreements (including investment, international telecommunications, civil aviation, and trade agreements), imposition of economic sanctions and foreign policy export controls, and other international financial and business issues, such as the extraterritorial application of U.S. laws, foreign debt, antitrust, and the protection of intellectual property.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
An Act of Congress (46 Stat. 1214), approved February 23, 1931, created the position of Legal Adviser of the Department of State, with rank equivalent to an assistant secretary. The Legal Adviser replaced the Solicitor, a Department of Justice employee who had functioned as the Department of State's chief legal officer since 1891. Between 1870 and 1891, the Examiner of Claims had been the chief legal officer of the Department. The Legal Adviser provided legal advice on all problems (domestic and international) arising in the course of the Department's activities. 

Legal Advisers to the Department included Green H. Hackworth, July 1, 1931 - March 1, 1946; Charles Fahy, June 19, 1946 - August 15, 1947; Ernest A. Gross, August 16, 1947 - March 3, 1949; Adrian S. Fisher, June 28, 1949 - January 27, 1953; Herman Phleger, February 2, 1953 - April 1, 1957; Loftus E. Becker, June 13, 1957 - August 15, 1959; Eric H. Hager, September 9, 1959 - January 20, 1961; Abram Chayes, February 6, 1961 - June 27, 1964; Leonard C. Meeker, May 18, 1965 - July 13, 1969; John R. Stevenson, July 14, 1969 - January 1, 1973; Carlyle E. Maw, November 27, 1973 - July 9, 1974; Monroe Leigh, January 21, 1975 - January 20, 1977; Herbert J. Hansell, April 8, 1977 - September 20, 1979; Roberts Bishop Owen, October 4, 1979 - February 16, 1981; Davis Rowland Robinson, July 30, 1981 - February 27, 1985; Abraham D. Sofaer, June 10, 1985 - June 15, 1990; Edwin D. Williamson, September 20, 1990 - November 4, 1992; Conrad Kenneth Harper, May 24, 1993 - June 30, 1996; David Andrews, September 2, 1997 - April 25, 2000; and William Howard Taft IV, April 16, 2001 - .

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The ITU Council was established in 1947 under the name Administrative Council, following a decision taken by the 1947 Plenipotentiary Conference in Atlantic City, New Jersey. It comprises a maximum of 25% of the total number of Member States, which are elected by the Conference with due regard to the need for equitable distribution of Council seats among the five world regions (Americas, Western Europe, Eastern Europe, Africa, Asia, and Australasia). The current Council is comprised of 46 Members. 

The role of Council is to consider, in the interval between Plenipotentiary Conferences, broad telecommunication policy issues to ensure that the Union's activities, policies and strategies fully respond to today's dynamic, rapidly changing telecommunications environment. It also prepares a report on the policy and strategic planning of the ITU. In addition, Council is responsible for ensuring the smooth day-to-day running of the Union, coordinating work programmes, approving budgets and controlling finances and expenditure. Finally, Council also takes all steps to facilitate the implementation of the provisions of the ITU Constitution, the ITU Convention, the Administrative Regulations (International Telecommunications Regulations and Radio Regulations), the decisions of Plenipotentiary Conferences and, where appropriate, the decisions of other conferences and meetings of the Union.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
On July 18, 1969, Press Release 209 announced the establishment of the Office of the Press Relations in the Office of the Secretary, which was composed of the press staff, formerly part of the Bureau of Public Affairs. On February 13, 1978, the Office was transferred to the Bureau of Public Affairs and back to the Office of the Secretary on July 1, 1980. In 1981, the Office of Press Relations was transferred again to the Bureau of Public Affairs.

The Office of Press Relations supported the President and Secretary of State by explaining the foreign policy of the United States and the positions of the Department of State to domestic and foreign journalists. The Office also provided logistical support and expertise to the Secretary of State and other Department officials for events involving media coverage/participation. Specifically, the Office of Press Relations responded to press queries, conducted media interviews, monitored media for breaking international events, and coordinated special press briefings and conference calls. They also supported the Secretary of State’s public events in addition to those of the Deputy Secretary and other senior Department officials. In addition, the Office coordinated interview requests from the national media for senior State Department officials other than the Secretary of State.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Office of the Controller  of the U.S. Operations Mission to Israel (USOM/I) advised and assisted the Mission Director in discharging his responsibility for the financial management of the Mission program. The Controller participated in the formulation and review of existing programs; insured appropriate financial execution of Mission program budgets; reviewed administrative expense estimates and staffing patterns and insured that justifications were appropriate; insured that obligations and expenditures were within allotment limitations; classified obligations and expenditures as between program and administrative allotments; established and maintained accounting records and controls; prepared timely financial reports; audited and certified vouchers as required; and conducted audits concerning project and non-project commodities, counterpart funds, other local currency, procurement practices, and contracts.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Department's regional bureaus oversaw the U.S. embassies and consulates, and coordinated U.S. foreign relations in their respective geographic areas. Assistant Legal Advisers supervised the attorneys who support those bureaus, dealing with such matters as protection of U.S. citizens and investments, problems in diplomatic and consular relations, interpretation and negotiation of treaties, military base rights and status of force issues, peaceful settlement of disputes, and trade matters. Among the issues and the activities which were handled by Assistant Legal Advisor for East Asian and Pacific Affairs were: U.S. commitments in East, South, and Central Asia, and the Pacific, including ANZUS, U.S. bilateral defense treaties, and the Compacts of Free Association; the U.S. military presence in Afghanistan, Australia, Japan, Korea, and the Philippines; relations with the People’s Republic of China; commercial, cultural and other nongovernmental relations with Taiwan; U.S. policy toward Cambodia and Vietnam; Six Party Talks involving North Korea, and Korean Peninsula peace treaty negotiations.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Air Transport Division was established in 1944 under the Department of Transportation, continuing the work of the air-transport unit of the Transportation Division. Through the Civil Aeronautics Authority it arranged for the installation of civilian pilot schools in Mexico. It also conducted surveys of commercial airlines in Latin America, particularly in Mexico; gave assistance in the procurement of aircraft and materials; sponsored the Inter-American Escadrille, which was an organization of private clubs in the United States and Latin America interested in promoting inter-American aviation activites; and arranged for the publication of manuals on airplanes and aviation. The Division was terminated on March 31, 1946.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: On September 28, 1942, the Director of the Office of War Information issued a regulation (OWI Regulation No. 4) to all Government agencies outlining a uniform practice for security classifying and guarding information. To provide a general guidance and advise on specific problems of security, the interdepartmental Security Advisory Board was established in May 1943 under the chairmanship of the Security Officer of the Office of War Information. Other agencies represented on the Board were the War Department, the Navy Department, the Department of Justice, the Office of Censorship, and the Bureau of the Budget. Infractions of security regulations were referred to this Board for action. After the war the Board was continued under the supervision of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The War Information Board, consisting of the Director of the Office of War Information (OWI) and the branch directors, was established to aid the Director in developing policies and formulating general plans for both domestic and overseas programs that would be in harmony with the broad policies developed by the Committee on War Information Policy. After the restriction of domestic operations in 1943 and the separation as far as possible of the work of the Domestic and Overseas Operations Branches, most of the work of policy formulation and control was performed elsewhere. The Board's first meeting was held on March 9, 1943; its last on February 22, 1944.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Special Promotion Division was responsible for creating new methods of carrying propaganda to neutral and Allied countries through packaging and labelling merchandise being shipped abroad by the Office of Lend Lease Administration and other agencies and through sponsoring foreign advertising campaigns. Its packaging and labelling activities were carried on with the cooperation of the Board of Economic Warfare and the Lend Lease Administration. The advertising campaigns sought to persuade American corporations to advertise in neutral and Allied countries in such a way as to create good will for the United States and to provide revenue for sympathetic publications. Another project of the Division was the sending abroad of pamphlets and publications, novelties, and booklets through seamen's organizations. The Division was discontinued on November 11, 1944.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Department of Foreign Affairs was established by an act of July 27, 1789 (1 Stat. 28) and redesignated the Department of State by an act of September 15, 1789 (1 Stat. 68). It was the agency of the United States created by law to assist the President in the formulation and execution of the Nation's foreign policy, and in the conduct of foreign affairs and of certain domestic affairs.

The Department made plans for peace and security among all nations, participated in the United Nations and other international organizations, and furthered international understanding through the dissemination of information and through the development of cultural relations with all peoples. It conducted diplomatic correspondence; negotiated treaties and other international agreements; and participated in international conferences, congresses, expositions, and other similar activities. The Department had jurisdiction over the settlement of international claims and the arbitration of international disputes to which the United States was a party. It coordinated the foreign relations activities of all Federal agencies. It administered the laws for passport and visa control and assisted the National Intelligence Authority in the collection of information. The Department administered the Foreign Service of the United States and preserved the Great Seal of the United States. It formerly published the laws of the United States, maintained custody of Federal records, and administered the Territories.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Civil Aeronautics Board (CAB) was established as an independent agency by Reorganization Plans Nos. III and IV of 1940, effective June 30, 1940. It consolidated the functions of the Civil Aeronautics Authority and the Air Safety Board, both under the Department of Commerce.

Under the Civil Aeronautics Act (52 Stat. 973), approved June 23, 1938, as modified by Reorganization Plans Nos. III and IV of 1940; and as redefined by the Federal Aviation Act of 1958 (72 Stat. 731), August 23, 1958, the CAB promoted and regulated the civil air industry within the United States and between the United States and foreign countries in the interest of the foreign and domestic commerce of the United States, the postal service, and the national defense.

Responsibility for investigating accidents and promoting safety was transferred to the National Transportation Safety Board, Department of Transportation (DOT), by the DOT Act (80 Stat. 931), approved October 15, 1966.

The Civil Aeronautics Board was abolished, effective January 1, 1985, by the Civil Aeronautics Board Sunset Act of 1984 (98 Stat. 1703), approved October 4, 1984, and provisions of Title XVI of the Federal Aviation Act of 1958, contained in the Airline Deregulation Act of 1978 (92 Stat. 1744), October 24, 1978. Functions relating to airline mergers, interlocking directorates, filing agreements, and antitrust exemptions was transferred to the Department of Justice. Responsibilities for rate compensation for mail carriage was transferred to the U.S. Postal Service. The Department of Transportation gained all other functions, effective January 1, 1985, under provisions of the CAB Sunset Act of 1984, the Airline Deregulation Act of 1978, and Title XVI of the Federal Aviation Act of 1958.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Railway Transport Division was established in August 1944 to carry on the activities of an earlier unit in the Transportation Division. It provided technical advisors and missions to assist Latin American countries in the conservation, improvement, and repair of their railroads, helped them make purchases of urgently needed supplies, and administered a training program for technicians working on Latin American railways. Some of the important missions were the United States Railway Mission in Mexico, which was sent to rehabilitate certain key lines of the national Railways of Mexico, and the railway missions to the mining areas of Bolivia and to Ecuador and Colombia. The Division existed until the Office was terminated.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Office of Facts and Figures, known also as OFF, was established within the Office for Emergency Management by Executive Order 8922, October 24, 1941, "for the purpose of dissemination of factual information to the citizens of the country on the progress of the defense effort and on the defense policies and activities of the Government." The Office was directed to formulate programs for the achievement of this objective and to advise with the several agencies of the Government concerning the dissemination of such information. Government agencies were directed to make available to the Director of the Office, upon his request, such information as he might "deem necessary to facilitate the most coherent and comprehensive presentation to the Nation of the facts and figures of national defense." Upon the establishment of the Office of Censorship on December 19, 1941, the Director of the Office of Facts and Figures was appointed a member of the Censorship Policy Board. Throughout the life of the Office its Director was Archibald MacLeish.

The Office of Facts and Figures was at first concerned chiefly with the development of uniform information policies of the Government. With the entrance of the United States into the war in December 1941, it attempted to supervise the relations of the war agencies with the press; but, since it lacked clear authority to perform a war news clearance function, it had to rely chiefly upon its powers of persuasion. It worked closely with the Office of Censorship in attempting to avoid the publication of information that would give "aid and comfort" to the enemy. Early in 1942, under authorization from the White House, it extended its activities to include the clearance of speeches by Government officials and the allocation of radio time among Federal agencies. By agreement with the affected agencies, the clearance of posters and other graphic materials was also added.

Executive Order 9182 of June 13, 1942, abolished the Office of Facts and Figures and transferred its functions and records to the Office of War Information, which was established by that order.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The International Development Act of 1961 (75 Stat. 447) approved September 4, 1961, authorized the President, with the advice and consent of the Senate, to appoint an "Inspector General, Foreign Assistance" to ensure that foreign assistance programs were efficiently administered. On June 20, 1977, the Secretary of State directed the Inspector General of the Foreign Service to perform the functions of the Inspector General of Foreign Assistance. The International Development and Food Assistance Act of 1977 (91 Stat. 541) approved August 3, 1977, formally authorized the transfer of functions, which was completed by July 1, 1978. 

The Inspector Generals, Foreign Assistance were: John Kenneth Mansfield, 1962-1969; Scott Heuer Jr., 1969-1971; Webster B. Todd Jr., 1974-1976; and John Arthur Shaw, 1976-1977.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Department of Information was established in 1942 to bring together and continue the activities of press, radio, motion picture, and education units that had been inherited by the Office of the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs from its predecessor. Its main objective was to carry out the information program of the Office, which was designed to meet and counteract the propaganda programs of the Axis powers and to further close cooperation and decisive joint action on new problems by all the countries of the Western Hemisphere. In 1944 the Press Division was separated from the Department to become the Department of Press and Publications. In August 1945 the Department was abolished and its functions and records were transferred to the Department of State.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: A formal agreement containing provisions for the organization of committees of United States citizens residing in Latin American cities was signed by the Secretary of State on August 16, 1941, and by the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs on August 19, 1941. These coordination committees, as they were called, provided local guidance in adapting the Office's program to local conditions, checked on the effectiveness of the program in each country, and executed programs that could not be handled efficiently by U.S. diplomatic representatives. Most of their activities were related to the press, radio, and motion picture programs of the Office of the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs. As a rule, there was established in the capital city of each country a central coordination committee that was directed by the diplomatic mission in the capital. Regional committees were subordinated to the central coordination committees and received funds and conducted business through the latter. Occasionally a consular officer was authorized to approve local projects. Technically, the committees were autonomous units of volunteers under the direction of the local embassy. Very few members were classed as Office employees and the activities of the committees were financed by grants-in-aid. The coordination committees were first established in 1941 and were continued until the informational activities of the Office were transferred to the Department of State in August 1945.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: A formal agreement containing provisions for the organization of committees of United States citizens residing in Latin American cities was signed by the Secretary of State on August 16, 1941, and by the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs on August 19, 1941. These coordination committees, as they were called, provided local guidance in adapting the Office's program to local conditions, checked on the effectiveness of the program in each country, and executed programs that could not be handled efficiently by U.S. diplomatic representatives. Most of their activities were related to the press, radio, and motion picture programs of the Office of the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs. As a rule, there was established in the capital city of each country a central coordination committee that was directed by the diplomatic mission in the capital. Regional committees were subordinated to the central coordination committees and received funds and conducted business through the latter. Occasionally a consular officer was authorized to approve local projects. Technically, the committees were autonomous units of volunteers under the direction of the local embassy. Very few members were classed as Office employees and the activities of the committees were financed by grants-in-aid. The coordination committees were first established in 1941 and were continued until the informational activities of the Office were transferred to the Department of State in August 1945.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Radio Division was established early in 1942 to further the inter-American program of the Office of the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs through the medium of radio. The Division utilized all broadcasting facilities that were available to it, including international short-wave broadcasts, point-to-point broadcast transmissions beamed to specific countries in Latin America, re-broadcasts of short-wave programs, transcribed programs, and locally produced broadcasts and arranged for their improvement or expansion to increase their effectiveness. Most of the commentator, dramatic, and musical programs of the Division, in English, Spanish, or Portuguese, were planned and produced for broadcasting by its New York office, which also maintained liaison with the major networks of the United States. Some of these programs were "Americanos Todos," a daily series of informative broadcasts in Spanish; "La Nota de la Semana," a weekly presentation of interviews with important personalities; "La Historia en Accion," presenting important phases of the war in dramatic form; and "Saludos Amigos," a musical program featuring famous motion picture stars.

The San Francisco office of the Division was responsible for informational and entertainment programs that were broadcast over high-powered short-wave stations located on the west coast of the United States. The Division's Washington office handled radio field operations through radio field representatives and the coordination committees in Latin America, obtained sponsors in the United States for programs of the Division, and prepared reports relating to radio activities in the other American republics. 

The Division was abolished in August 1945 and its functions were transferred to the Department of State.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Domestic Operations Branch was formed by a consolidation of the central information services of the former Division of Information of the Office for Emergency Management, the operating bureaus of the former Office of Facts and Figures, the service functions and motion picture activities of the former Office of Government Reports, and the Washington news gathering staff of the former Office of the Coordinator of Information. The Branch was responsible for coordinating the dissemination of war information in the United States by all Government agencies and through all channels of information; and for preparing and disseminating comprehensive information pertaining to the work of more than one agency or involving war information policy. The Branch cleared and coordinated releases to the press of information from Government sources to prevent confusion caused by conflicting statements. In the field of radio, it developed a system for the orderly use of time and talent donated by the radio industry and sponsors of radio programs for war information purposes, and it allotted radio time to Government agencies. In the field of advertising, it coordinated the use of newspaper space, radio time, and advertising space donated to the Government to carry advertising on its war information campaigns. It also served as a central point of contact with the motion picture industry regarding needs of the Government for special war information pictures, and it provided a channel of communication between the Government and book and magazine publishers and editors to provide facts on the war effort and information programs promoted by the OWI. Its production activities were curtailed in the summer of 1943, after which it was mainly concerned with planning information campaigns in cooperation with other Government agencies and the communications industries.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Bureau of Graphics was established on July 31, 1944, to include the Graphics Division from the former Bureau of Graphics and Printing and the Poster Clearance and Allocation Division from the Office of Program Coordination. The functions included the clearance, through liaison with the advertising business, of requests of Government agencies for use of outdoor advertising facilities, representation of the Office of War Information in matters pertaining to graphics, both within the Government and in liaison with private industry; the direction of a central service for the creation of graphic materials; the review and clearance of posters proposed for issuance by Government agencies; liaison with the Government Printing Office and commercial printing firms concerning printing and distribution problems; and advising other agencies on printing and distribution problems.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The General Advisory Committee on Arms Control and Disarmement was established on April 2, 1962, pursuant to sec. 26 of Publ. L. 87-297, the Arms Control and Disarmament Act of September 26, 1961 (75 Stat. 632). It was a Presidential advisory committee. Administrative support was provided by the Arms Control and Disarmament Agency. The Committee advised the President, the Secretary of State, and the Director of the Arms Control and Disarmament Agency on matters affecting international arms control, disarmament, and world peace. It was composed of fifteen members appointed by the President and approved by the U.S. Senate. It met at least twice a year with meetings closed to the public. The Committee was abolished on January 1, 1994, with functions absorbed by the President's Scientific and Policy and Advisory Committee.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: On September 30, 1961, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) was established when the Organisation for European Economic Cooperation (OEEC) Convention of December 14, 1960 entered into force. OECD superceded the OEEC, which consisted of 18 European countries with the addition of the United States and Canada with the signing of the convention. Since then, 14 countries became members of the Organisation and they worked with each other to identify problems, discuss and analyze them, and promote policies to solve them.

Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, Jan. 13, 2016 (The Organisation for European Economic Cooperation (OEEC) was established in 1948 to run the US-financed Marshall Plan for reconstruction of a continent ravaged by war. By making individual governments recognise the interdependence of their economies, it paved the way for a new era of cooperation that was to change the face of Europe. Encouraged by its success and the prospect of carrying its work forward on a global stage, Canada and the US joined OEEC members in signing the new OECD Convention on 14 December 1960. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) was officially born on 30 September 1961, when the Convention entered into force. Other countries joined in, starting with Japan in 1964. Today, 34 OECD member countries worldwide regularly turn to one another to identify problems, discuss and analyse them, and promote policies to solve them.) http://www.oecd.org/about/history/

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: On July 17, 1941, President Franklin D. Roosevelt issued a Presidential Proclamation which instructed the Secretary of State, acting in conjunction with the Secretary of the Treasury, the Attorney General, the Secretary of Commerce, the Administrator of Export Controls, and the Coordinator of Commercial and Cultural Relations between the American Republics, to prepare an appropriate list of persons and firms working with or for Axis nations and persons to whom exports from the United States were deemed detrimental to the interests of national defense. As a result of this order the Secretary of State established on July 21, 1941, by Departmental Order 956, the Division of World Trade Intelligence to handle State Department responsibilities pertaining to the Proclaimed List of Certain Blocked Nationals. The Division was at first under the direct supervision of Assistant Secretary Dean Acheson but later became part of the Board of Economic Operations and successor economic offices. On March 1, 1945, by Departmental Order 1311, it was abolished with functions transferred to the Division of Economic Security Controls.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Deputy Directors of the Domestic Operations Branch were assigned fields of war information in which they served as principal representatives of the Office of War Information with various Federal war agencies. They were responsible for the adequacy of information available to the press in their respective fields and for policy decisions on information matters in those fields. In September 1943 they were given the added responsibility of supervising the conduct of all information programs and campaigns falling within the jurisdiction of their assigned agencies. Within the office of each Deputy were program managers who were responsible for specific information programs.

The Deputy Director for Economic Stabilization, War Finance, and Taxation was responsible for liaison with the Treasury Department, the Office of Economic Stabilization, the Office of Civilian Defense, the American National Red Cross, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Security of War Information Committee, the National War Fund, and the Solid Fuels Administration for War. He handled campaigns for economic stabilization, fuel conservation, overseas mail, the American National Red Cross, the National War Fund, the security of war information, and planned spending and saving.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Exports Administrative Board was established by Executive Order (E.O.) 2687-A, August 21, 1917, superseding the Exports Licenses Division of the Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce, Department of Commerce. The Board, which had been meeting informally since June 26, 1917, was composed of representatives of the Departments of State, Agriculture, and Commerce, the U.S. Food Administration, and the U.S. Shipping Board. Vance McCormick served as Chairman. The Board administered and executed the laws relating to the licensing of exports. No commodities on the prohibited lists could be exported without a license issued by the Board. The Exports Administrative Board was abolished and superseded by the War Trade Board, established by E.O. 2729-A, October 12, 1917.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Overseas Operations Branch succeeded to the functions of the Foreign Information Service of the Office of the Coordinator of Information. It planned and carried out the wartime propaganda activities of the Federal Government in all countries outside the continental United States except those in Latin America. In active military zones its agents cooperated with military organizations in psychological warfare. The Branch established outposts in more than twenty neutral and Allied nations, and in areas where it had no representative it provided State Department missions with informational materials for distribution. Operating bureaus of the Branch existed for communications, intelligence, and the support of field offices. Executive Order 9068 of August 31, 1945, which abolished the Office of War Information, transferred the functions and records of the Overseas Operations Branch, including its functions performed abroad, to the Interim International Information Service of the department of State, which later became the Office of International Information and Cultural Affairs.

Sherwood, formerly the Director of the Foreign Information Service of the Office of the Coordinator of Information, served as Director of Overseas Operations until September 1944, when he was succeeded by Edward W. creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The U.S. Information Agency (USIA) was established as an independent agency by Reorganization Plan No. 8 of 1953, effective August 1, 1953, to centralize foreign information dissemination programs. USIA took over the functions of the abolished International Information Administration in the Department of State. It was abolished, effective April 1, 1978 by Executive Order 12048 dated March 27, 1978, in accordance with Reorganization Plan No. 2 of 1977, with its functions transferred to the newly established International Communication Agency (ICA). 

On 1982, ICA was redesignated as the U.S. Information Agency by the United States Information Agency Authorization Act (96 Stat. 291), August 24, 1982. USIA influenced public attitudes in foreign countries in support of U.S. foreign policy objectives. It advised the President, diplomatic personnel, and Executive departments and agencies on the implications of foreign opinion for present and contemplated U.S. policies, programs, and official statements. An act of October 21, 1998 (112 Stat. 2681-761), abolished USIA and its functions transferred to the Department of State, effective October 1, 1999.

The Directors were Theodore Cuyler Streibert, 1953–1956; Arthur Larson, 1956–1957; George Venable Allen, 1957–1960; Edward R. Murrow, 1961–1964; Carl Thomas Rowan, 1964–1965; Leonard Harold Marks, 1965–1968; Frank J. Shakespeare Jr., 1969–1973; James Keogh, 1973–1976; John Edward Reinhardt, 1977–1978; John Edward Reinhardt, 1978–1980; Charles Z. Wick, 1981–1989; Bruce S. Gelbm 1989–1991; Henry Edward Catto Jr., 1991–1993; Joseph Daniel Duffey, 1993–1999; and Penn Kemble (Acting) February 1, 1999-October 1, 1999.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Displaced Persons Commission was established by the Displaced Persons Act (62 Stat. 1009), approved June 25, 1948. The Commission provided for the admission to and resettlement in the United States of eligible displaced persons from western Germany, Austria, and Italy; German expellees; Italian refugees from Venezia Guilia; and displaced and war orphans. The Commission was the government agency to which displaced persons who had been admitted to the United States reported each January and July with respect to employment, place of employment, and residence. The Commission consisted of three members appointed by the President. Ugo Carusi served as Commission chair from August 13, 1948, to December 26, 1950. He was succeeded by John W. Gibson. The Commission was terminated on August 31, 1952, as provided for by the enabling act. Executive Order 10382, August 9, 1952, provided for the transfer of the Commission's records to the Department of State.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Deputy Directors of the Domestic Operations Branch were assigned fields of war information in which they served as principal representatives of the Office of War Information with various Federal war agencies. They were responsible for the adequacy of information available to the press in their respective fields and for policy decisions on information matters in those fields. In September 1943 they were given the added responsibility of supervising the conduct of all information programs and campaigns falling within the jurisdiction of their assigned agencies. Within the office of each Deputy were program managers who were responsible for specific information programs. 

The Deputy Director for Military Information was responsible for liaison with the War and Navy Departments and for the planning, coordination, and execution of war information campaigns sponsored by those Departments.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Bureau of Motion Pictures was established in 1942 to take over the motion picture functions of the Office of Facts and Figures, the Division of Information of the Office for Emergency Management, and the Office of the Coordinator of Government Films of the Office of Government Reports. The motion picture units of the Office for Emergency Management were incorporated into the Office of the Coordinator of Government Films, and the reorganized units became divisions of the Office of War Information's (OWI) Bureau of Motion Pictures. The Bureau reviewed and cleared all motion picture programs sponsored by Federal agencies and served as the central point of clearance and contact for the agencies in their relationships with the motion picture industry. During the first year of its operation the Bureau produced motion picture shorts and slide films dealing with wartime problems such as fuel conservation, salvage, and manpower; but these activities, discontinued in September 1943, were later handled for the Bureau by the War Activities Committee of the motion picture industry.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Bureau of Imports was established on October 15, 1917, to succeed the Imports Division of the Export License Bureau of the Exports Administrative Board. Working in cooperation with trade associations in the allocation of imports, the Bureau had charge of the disposition of all applications for import licenses and of the administration of the War Trade Board's control measures with relation to imports. Such measures were designed to conserve tonnage for essential transportation purposes and to give priority to the procurement of such raw materials and commodities as were needed for Government or essential civilian use. On June 30, 1919, the Bureau was transferred to the War Trade Board Section of the Department of State.

The Deputy Directors of the Domestic Operations Branch were assigned fields of war information in which they served as principal representatives of the Office of War Information with various Federal war agencies. They were responsible for the adequacy of information available to the press in their respective fields and for policy decisions on information matters in those fields. In September 1943 they were given the added responsibility of supervising the conduct of all information programs and campaigns falling within the jurisdiction of their assigned agencies. Within the office of each Deputy were program managers who were responsible for specific information programs. 

The Deputy Director for Pacific Operations was responsible for liaison with the War and Navy Departments, the Combined Chiefs of Staff, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the War Communications Board, the Post Office Department, the Office of Censorship, and the Office of Scientific Research and Development.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Theatrical Division, established in 1943 by a reorganization of the Bureau of Motion Pictures. inherited the functions of a number of earlier divisions of the Bureau. Because of its small number of employees the Division was unable to set up sections defined as such. The records of predecessor divisions were partially reorganized, however, in an effort to bring together materials pertinent to the activities carried on after the middle of 1943. The functions of the Division included coordination of film activities of the various Government agencies, the allocation of raw film stock requested by Government agencies, liaison with the motion picture industry and with newsreel producers, the development of ideas for film subjects, the supplying of background material on short subjects to producing companies, and the distribution of 35 mm. prints of Office of War Information (OWI) films.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The area occupied by U.S. Forces in Germany consisted of the three Laender (States): Bavaria, Hesse, and Wuerttemberg-Baden, as well as the Bremen enclave and the U.S. Sector in Berlin. Land Bavaria encompassed more than half of the area. Following the establishment of the Office of Military Government for Germany in September 1945, a similar organization was established for the administration of each Laender, Enclave and Sector.

The Office of Military Government Bavaria (OMGB) was headed by a Land Director. His office underwent a number of reorganizations from 1945 to 1949. From 1945 to 1946, the Office of the Land Director Bavaria consisted of the Director, his political adviser, the deputy director, and the executive. In 1947, the Administrative Staff joined the organization, and the Personnel and Administration Branch became a division with three branches: Military Personnel, Civilian Personnel, and Administration. In addition, the Public Information and Transportation Branches came under the Land Director's authority. In 1948, the Office of the Land Director absorbed the housing functions of the Social Insurance and Housing Branch of the OMGB Manpower Division. This Branch became known as the Real Estate and Land Resources Branch, later renamed the Real Estate, Land Resources, and Budget Control Branch. By 1949, the Joint Export-Import Agency (JEIA) reported directly to the Land Director.

The Office of Military Government, as supervised by the Land Director, served as the intermediary between the central level of the Office of Military Government for Germany, U.S. (OMGUS) and the local German land government. OMGB received directives, materials, and other items from OMGUS and transmitted them, where appropriate, to the local detachments. It received reports, requests for information, and other inquiries from local detachments to be forwarded to OMGUS. In addition, OMGB performed the function of supervising and coordinating the work of the military government at the operating level. Finally, it remained the agent through which OMGUS directed the formation of the German democratic system of government after the war.

General Patton served as chief administrative officer of Bavaria until the Office of Military Government had been formulated, but the two most important Land Directors during the period 1945 to 1949 were Brigadier General Walter J. Muller (October 1945 to November 1947) and Murray D. Van Wagoner (December 1947 to October 1949). These two individuals performed three functions: 1) the direction of activities of subordinate units, including the issuance of necessary directives, orders, and instructions; 2) administering all matters pertaining to assignment and transfer of U.S. personnel, authorized traveling within the theater, promotions and demotions, awards and decorations, and the issuance of orders to carry out the above in accordance with theater policy; and 3) supervision and advisory duties for German civil agencies and other civilian activities directly or through subordinate Military Government offices. In addition, instructions and interpretations of Military Government policy were given to the German government by the Director through the Bavarian Minister President. The Land Director also had the responsibility for the Liaison and Security Offices (later the Field Operations Division or FOD).

The Political Adviser assisted the Land Director by providing the legal and political expertise in OMGUS and German land government operations. The Deputy Director served as an assistant to the Director, helping to answer inquiries, make public appearances, and carry out the general responsibilities of the office. The Executive (later Assistant Land Director) had direct responsibility for the operations of the Transportation Branch; the Intelligence, Historical, and Reports Branch; the Plans and Operations Branch; the Supply Branch; the Headquarters Commandant; the Public Relations Branch; the Headquarters Third Military Government Regiment; and the Land Resources Budget Control Branch. The Civil Administration Division, the Economics Division, the Internal Affairs and Communications Division, the Information Control Division, the Legal Division, the Manpower Division, and the Finance Division, along with their branches, remained independent of the Office of the Land Director but reported their activities to the Executive Branch.

Later Land Directors for Bavaria included George Schuster and Oron Hale (July 1950 to February 1952), two university professors responsible for the gradual winding down of OMGB. These directors steered the Office of the Land Director away from the handing down of directives and instructions from OMGUS to the German government, and toward the role of an ambassador and adviser. With the formation of the U.S. High Commissioner for Germany (HICOG) in 1949, the title "Land Director" changed to "Land Commissioner." The Land Commissioner continued the work of the Land Director for the rest of HICOG's operational existence.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Office of the Coordinator for Inter-American Affairs (OCIAA) was established in the Office for Emergency Management on July 30, 1941, by authority of Executive Order (E.O.) 8840 of July 30, 1941. It replaced the Office for Coordination of Commercial and Cultural Relations in the Council of National Defense. Its purpose, as stated in the E.O. was "to provide for the development of commercial and cultural relations between the American Republics" and thereby to increase the solidarity of the Western Hemisphere and further "the spirit of cooperation between the Americas in the interest of Hemisphere defense". More specifically, the Office was directed to formulate and execute programs in the commercial and economic fields and the fields of the arts and sciences, education and travel, the radio, the press, and the cinema that would further national defense and strengthen the bonds between the nations of the Western Hemisphere. It was required to work closely with the Department of State in promoting Hemispheric solidarity. It established a number of nonprofit Government corporations to carry out its programs.

The Office was headed by Nelson A. Rockefeller as Coordinator until shortly before its name was changed, by E.O. 9532 of March 23, 1945, to the Office of Inter-American Affairs, which was headed by Wallace K. Harrison as Director. The Office as early as April 1942 lost many of its economic responsibilities to the Board of Economic Warfare (later the Foreign Economic Administration) and in the same year some of its long range cultural activities were taken over by the Department of State. By an executive order of August 31, 1945, the informational activities of the Office of Inter-American Affairs were transferred to the Department of State. 

The Office was abolished by E.O. 9710 of April 10, 1946, effective May 20, 1946, and its remaining functions were transferred to the Department of State.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Radio Bureau, established in June 1942, took over the work of the Radio Section of the Division of Information in the Office for Emergency Management and the Radio Division of the Office of Facts and Figures. It reviewed and cleared for conformance with war information policies all proposed radio programs sponsored by Federal agencies and served as a contact for the agencies in their relations with the radio broadcasting and radio advertising agencies. It channeled Government information programs to the public through both commercially sponsored and sustaining radio shows, obtaining the use of programs with a known audience through the facilities of its several operating plans (the network allocation plan, the national spot allocation plan, and the station announcement plan); and it kept the radio industry informed of the relative importance of the many different demands for contributions of time.

In addition it prepared reports not restricted to any single region or any specific period, to be employed in implementing long-range campaigns, and it maintained a central repository of intelligence material and a central repository of all foreign operational information in Washington.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Office of Administration served as the Director’s principal adviser on matters of administration and management. It developed, interpreted and applied administrative and management policies and procedures necessary to assure effective operation of the Agency’s programs. The Office planned and executed the preparation, preservation and justification of the Agency’s budget. It managed the U.S. Information Agency (USIA) financial affairs. The Office developed, approved and installed the Agency’s organization structure and the assignment of functions and responsibilities therein. It conducted the Agency’s manpower utilization and career development programs; and provided personnel management services. The Office planned for and provided or obtained administrative services; such as procurement; communications and records; travel; and space management and equipment supply.

In 1973, the Office of Administration was changed to the Office of Administration and Management. In 1978, under the International Communication Agency (ICA), it became the Office of Administrative Services and then again the Office of Administration in 1982. In 1982, under the USIA, it was changed to the Office of Administration and Technology. On November 7, 1988, the Technology functions were removed and the name was changed to the Office of Administration.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Department of Basic Economy was established early in 1942 to cooperate with the governments of the Latin American Republics in solving war-related health, sanitation, and food problems, to expedite the procurement of strategic and critical materials, and to promote the general economic development and stability of the Latin American countries. The Department was also concerned with safeguarding the health of the military forces of the United States and its allied that were stationed in other American republics and with increasing the production of war materials in Latin America by improving health and food conditions for workers there. Its program was carried out through the Department of State's Institute of Inter-American Affairs.
