creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The functions of the Book and Magazine Bureau were originally performed by the Office of Facts and Figures. With the establishment of the Office of War Information (OWI) these functions were transferred to the Publications Division of the OWI's Bureau of Publications and Graphics. Following the dissolution of that Bureau in 1943, the functions were successively carried out by parts of the Bureau of Publications, by independent bureaus (the Book Bureau and the Magazine Bureau), and finally, beginning in August 1944, by the Book and Magazine Bureau. The primary function of the Bureau was to promote the war-related information programs of the Government through the media of magazine and books. The Bureau accomplished this by serving in liaison between editors, magazine writers, and literary agents seeking information and those war agencies that could supply such information. Much of the information obtained from Government sources was incorporated in the "Magazine War Guide," a monthly bulletin containing suggestions to editors and writers, which was issued by the Bureau. Similar services were offered to book publishers. Through the Bureau, war agencies had access to the talent of the Writers' War Board, a volunteer organization of leading American writers who prepared programs, speeches, and articles for widely circulated newspapers and magazines. Through its work with the Council on Books in Wartime, the Bureau also made available to war agencies the promotional facilities of numerous publishers, booksellers, and librarians. Before mid-1943 the Bureau engaged in the production of books and magazines, but this activity was eliminated because of a reduction in budget.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Foreign Morale Analysis Division was established in the spring of 1944 under a cooperative arrangement with the Military Intelligence Service of the War Department General Staff to provide information about the morale of the Japanese and social conditions within Japan. It obtained information concerning Japanese morale from interrogation of prisoners, captured documents, and other sources. It prepared analyses and reports on the trend of enemy morale to serve as a guide to officials engaged in planning propaganda strategy and the production of propaganda media. Its work was performed by two groups, one on the Office of War Information and the other in the War Department. The first group translated and analyzed materials available through nonmilitary sources, such as Japanese publications and transcripts of Japanese broadcasts, while the War Department group analyzed materials received from military sources, especially prisoner of war interrogation reports and captured enemy documents. By the spring of 1945 the cooperative unit was known as the Joint Morale Survey and was divided into the Morale Research Unit (Office of War Information) and the Propaganda Section (mainly Army), which was concerned primarily with the analysis of Japanese radio propaganda. The results of the research were presented to interested officials by means of formal reports and special memorandums and in formal and informal conferences. The reports ranged from overall studies of military morale and the effects of Allied propaganda to special studies of subjects investigated upon request.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: This Bureau was organized as the Branches and Customs Division of the Bureau of Exports on October 13, 1917, and became a separate bureau on February 6, 1918. It supervised the administration of branch and cooperative offices and the representatives of the War Trade Board in the United States, and transmitted to the collectors of customs, through the Customs Division of the Department of the Treasury, the rulings of the Board. By December it had 26 general branch offices. Beginning on March 1, 1919, the closing of the branch offices rapidly reduced the number of employees, and on July 1, 1919, several persons were transferred to the War Trade Board Section of the Department of State for the purpose og liquidating the affairs of the Bureau.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Russian Bureau, Inc. was incorporated in the State of Connecticut as the War Trade Board of the United States Russian Bureau, Inc., November 5, 1918, with a capital stock of $5,000,000 owned by the United States Government. The members of the War Trade Board became the directors of the Corporation, and the Chairman of the Board became its President. The Russian Bureau provided and facilitated economic assistance to Russia. It arranged for the shipping of supplies for the American National Red Cross, railway materiel for the Trans-Siberian Railway, and military equipment for Czechoslovak forces in Siberia. It was dissolved by Executive Order (E.O.) 3094-A, June 5, 1919, and E.O. 3099-A, June 24, 1919. Provision was made that its funds be used by the Secretary of State to finance the Interallied Railway Committee and to maintain the Trans-Siberian and Chinese Eastern Railways.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Emergency Rehabilitation Division was organized on July 15, 1942, to meet emergencies resulting from dislocations resulting from the war and natural disasters. Its two main rehabilitation projects were carried out in Ecuador, where the El Oro Technical Mission helped the Ecuadoran Government repair damages caused by the 1941 border dispute with Peru, and in Honduras, where the construction of the Potrerillo - Pito Solo Road provided temporary employment for workers thrown out of work by the disastrous effects of the war on the banana industry. On January 7, 1944, the Division was terminated and its functions and responsibilities were divided between the Division of Health and Sanitation and the Food Supply Division.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Provisional Military Advisory Group (PMAG) was established in U.S. Army Forces in Korea (USAFIK) by General Order 31, USAFIK, August 15, 1948, with responsibility for training and equipping the Republic of Korea (ROK) constabulary and coast guard. ROK national defense organization, with constabulary and coast guard respectively was redesignated army and navy, established, effective December 15, 1948, by ROK Armed Forces Reorganization Act, November 1948. Following the termination of USAFIK, June 30, 1949, PMAG was redesignated the Korea Military Assistance Advisory Group (KMAG), given status as a Department of the Army (DA) administrative unit, and made a component of the American Mission in Korea, by DA message 90992 to Chief, KMAG, July 1, 1949. KMAG was responsible for assisting with organization, equipment, and training of ROK armed forces for purpose of internal security and within limits of ROK economy. This arrangement was confirmed by United States-ROK agreement, concluded January 26, 1950. Following North Korean Army invasion of South Korea, June 25, 1950, KMAG was assigned to newly-activated USAFIK pursuant to General Order 11, Far East Command (FEC), July 4, 1950, and confirmed by General Order 1, USAFIK, July 4, 1950. KMAG was released by the Department of the Army to become an army unit, and assigned to FEC, effective August 29, 1950, by letter from Chief of Manpower Control Division, DA to The Adjutant General, U.S. Army, DAAA G-1 344, August 28, 1950. KMAG was assigned within FEC to Eighth Army in Korea (EUSAK), effective September 14, 1950, by FEC message to EUSAK CX 62333, September 7, 1950. On April 1, 1974, KMAG was eliminated as a subordinate command of Eighth Army and redesignated as Army Section, Joint U.S. Military Assistance Group-Korea (JUSMAG-K).

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Federal Highway Administration was established in the Department of Transportation, effective April 1, 1967, by the Department of Transportation Act (80 Stat. 932), approved October 15, 1966, consolidating functions relating to highway transportation formerly vested in the Department of Commerce and the Interstate Commerce Commission. It administered Federal financial assistance to the states for highway construction; coordinated Federal highway policies; administered miscellaneous programs relating to highway beautification, safety, research and development, and training for state and local highway department employees and foreign highway officials.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Council on International Economic Policy (CIEP) was established, effective Janaury 19, 1971, by a memorandum from President Richard M. Nixon to the newly appointed members of the CIEP dated January 18, 1971. The Council was given statutory recognition by the International Economic Policy Act (86 Stat. 646), approved August 29, 1972. It was an interagency council of the Executive Office of the President and its members included the Secretaries of Agriculture, Commerce, Defense, Labor, Transportation, State, and the Treasury; the Director of the Office of Management and Budget; the Chair of the Council of Economic Advisors; and the Special Representative for Trade Negotiations. The Council considered the full spectrum of international economic policies including trade, investment, balance of payments, and finance, and coordinated these issues with basic foreign policy objectives. The Council was abolished on September 30, 1977, by Reorganization Plan No. 1 of 1977.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Office for Emergency Management, known also as OEM, was established within the Executive Office of the President by an administrative order of May 25, 1940 (5 F.R. 2109). Authority for such action had been set forth in Executive Order 8248 of September 8, 1939, which stated that there should be "in the event of a national emergency, or threat of a national emergency, such office for emergency management as the President shall determine." The Office for Emergency Management was a device whereby the President could coordinate and supervise and, when he wished, personally direct the work of agencies engaged in emergency activities. The functions of the Office, as first stated in general terms in the establishing order, were to assist the President in the clearance of information with respect to measures necessitated by the threatened emergency, to maintain liaison between the President and the national defense agencies, and to perform such additional duties as the President might direct. More specifically, by an administrative order of January 7, 1941 (6 F.R. 192), the President made the Office responsible for keeping him informed about the emergency activities of Government agencies, for assembling and analyzing information concerning additional measures that needed to be taken, and for assisting in the preparation of recommendations for legislation. These functions were performed for about two and half years by or under the direction of the Liaison Officer for Emergency Management--a position held successively by William H. McReynolds, Wayne Coy, and James F. Byrnes. On November 3, 1943, the President accepted the resignation of this officer and appointed no successor, thereby terminating the liaison facilities of the Office.

The Office for Emergency Management existed primarily as a framework within which most the civilian war agencies were set up. Among the more important of these "constituent agencies" of the Office were the Foreign Economic Administration, the National War Labor Board, the Office of Alien Property Custodian, the Office of Civilian Defense, the Office of the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs, the Office of Defense Health and Welfare Services, the Office of Defense Transportation, the Office of Economic Stabilization, the Office of Scientific Research and Development, the Office of War Information, the War Manpower Commission, the War Production Board, the War Relocation Authority, and the War Shipping Administration.

The Office for Emergency Management was abolished progressively, with the Division of Information terminated by Executive Order 9182, June 13, 1942; liaison functions terminated with the resignation of the Liaison Officer  for Emergency Management (the OEM Director), November 3, 1943; and the Division of Central Administrative Affairs abolished, effective November 30, 1944, by Executive Order 9471, August 25, 1944, with the Department of the Interior named as liquidator.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Department of Economic Development was established in September 1943 to carry out the economic development program of the Office of the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs. It cooperated with governmental and private agencies in the economic development of the Latin American republics, particularly in stabilizing their wartime economies. To this end it assisted them in the use and conservation of natural resources, provided technical assistance for the development of industries, sought to remove barriers to trade and commerce and to improve and enlarge markest for United States goods, and encouraged private enteprises in the United States and the other American republics to undertake programs of economic development on a mutually profitable basis. The Department maintained close relations with two international agencies, the Mexican - American Commission for Economic Cooperation and the Inter-American Development Commission. In 1945 it became part of the new Department of Transportation and Economic Development which existed until the Office of Inter-American Affairs was abolished.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Coordinator determined the policies of the agency, directed the activities of its corporations, and handled top-liaison activities with officials of the United States Government, the governments of the other American republics, and the heads of private organizations. He was the Chairman of the Inter-American Development Commission and the Committee on Inter-American Affairs and served on other international and interdepartmental committees, including the Mexican - American Commission for Economic Cooperation, the Committee on Inter-American Shipping, the Inter-American Financial and Economic Advisory Committee, the Inter-American Shipping Commission, the Inter-Departmental Committee on Hemisphere Communications, the International Broadcasting Committee, and the Inter-Departmental Committee for Political Warfare. The Coordinator also made funds available for the establishment of the Inter-American Institute of Agricultural Sciences to continue the work, previously carried on by the Inter-American Committee on Tropical Agriculture, of promoting the production of strategic crops, particularly rubber. He had as his immediate assistants a number of special advisors, including the Brazilian Consultant, the Consultant in Port Management, and the Advisor for Civic Projects; the General Counsel; and various committees of the Office. One of his assistants represented the United States Government at the First Pan American Congress of Mining Engineering and Geology held at Santiago, Chile, January 15-23, 1942, at which an all-out mineral production program for pan-American defense was recommended.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Foreign News Bureau, established on March 14, 1944, by Staff Order No. 28, replaced the Foreign Services Division of the News Bureau. Its basic function was to aid American news agencies, newspapers, and radio stations in exposing enemy propaganda. For this purpose it obtained and sent by teletype to the American press information from such sources as American and Allied monitoring reports, press reports from enemy and enemy-occupied countries, reports of Office of War Information representatives overseas, and State Department cables. The Bureau also prepared supplementary material - in the form of special reports, periodic news columns, and features - summarizing for the press the social, military, political, religious, and propaganda developments in enemy and enemy-occupied countries.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: In accordance with the 1986 recommendation by the United States Advisory Commission on Public Diplomacy, on November 19, 1986, the Office of Research was established as an independent office reporting directly to him and the Deputy Directory. The Office of Research conducted systematic studies of foreign public opinion on policy issues and on the evaluation of Agency programs. Its' policy studies assessed attitudes on security, economic, and other major foreign policy issues in support of the Director’s role as principal advisor to the President on foreign public opinion. It created evaluation studies to provide Agency management with assessments of the effectiveness of agency programs. In addition the Office prepared analyses of foreign media commentary on key issues, and studies on Soviet propaganda and disinformation.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Research Division was established in the Department of Economic Development in 1944 to succeed the Resources Division, which had been established in the immediate Office of the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs early in 1943. It performed research work for all departments and corporations of the Office and assisted in coordinating research projects of Government agencies pertaining to Latin America. The Division prepared reports on political, economic, and social developments in Latin America and provided library and reference service for the entire Office. It was abolished in 1945, but some of its functions were continued by the Department of Administration throughout the lifetime of the Office.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Communications Facilities Bureau planned, provided, operated, and maintained a worldwide communications network for propaganda and information. It was responsible for all matters pertaining to the communications facilities and technical operations of the international broadcasting services of the Overseas Operations Branch. It made surveys of the adequacy of world radio coverage and planned and provided adequate radio coverage to all areas. It was responsible for the construction and operation of broadcasting studios in New York and San Francisco and for the transmission of pictures by radiophoto. Headquarters of the Bureau were in Washington, but sections responsible for planning, radiophoto, studio operations, engineering, and other services were maintained in New York and San Francisco near transmitters.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Advisory Commission on International Communications, Cultural, and Educational Affairs was established on October 30, 1978. By the Reorganization Plan of 1977 and Publ. L. 96-60, as amended, it was redesignated the U.S. Advisory Commission on Public Diplomacy on October 1, 1979. It was an independent, bipartisan statutory presidential advisory committee that oversaw the activities of the U.S. Information Agency.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Department of Transportation was established as the Transportation Division in 1942 to promote the transportation program of the Office of the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs. It made agreements with a number of American republics for the rehabilitation and construction of vessels, railroads, and roads and it furnished them with United States technicians to advise them on maintenance and operational problems. Its programs and projects were carried out by two corporations, the Inter-American Navigation Corporation and the Institute of Inter-American Transportation. The Department of Transportation worked in close collaboration with the Department of State, the War Shipping Administration, the Civil Aeronautics Authority, the Office of Defense Transportation, the War and Navy Departments, and other agencies handling transportation problems. In 1945 it was combined with the Department of Economic Development to form the Department of Transportation and Economic Development, which existed until the Office of Inter-American Affairs was terminated.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Security Office, headed by the Security Officer, was established in February 1943 by order of the Director to coordinate and standardize the security practices of all agencies in Washington, D.C., with regard to security classified materials. Similar offices were attached to the New York and San Francisco offices of the Office of War Information (OWI). The Security Officer, in addition regular security activities with respect to the OWI, served as Chairman of the Security Advisory Board. Rear Admiral R.P. McCullough (Retired) served as Security Officer until early 1945, when he was succeeded by Colonel Eugene M. Winters.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The News Writing Division produced comprehensive reports, special features, press statements, letters for Government officials, answers to public questions, and other items on pertinent phases of the war effort, largely those concerned with two or more Government agencies. These special reports ranged from surveys of the military situation to the outlook for a quick peace to round-ups of the current civilian supply of gasoline, textiles, and foods.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Outpost Service Bureau, with offices in Washington, New York, and San Francisco, was responsible for providing those continuing services required for the efficient operation of Office of War Information (OWI) outposts, including responsibility for financial management and budgeting, the provision of administrative services, and the transportation abroad of individuals, materials, and equipment. Warehousing operations and transportation arrangements for materials, supplies, and equipment were handled by the New York office. In Washington the offices of the Bureau maintained liaison with the Departments of State, War, and the Navy and with other agencies regarding transportation abroad of Outpost personnel and the issuance of passports and military clearances for their travel overseas. The San Francisco office supervised operations on the west coast for Far Eastern outposts of the OWI.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Office of Transition Initiatives (DCHA/OTI) provided assistance targeting key transition, stabilization, and reconstruction needs in the areas of promoting reconciliation, fostering peace and democracy, providing short-term income generation, and jump-starting nascent government operations.  It supported local partners to advance peace and democracy in priority conflict-prone countries.  At the request of and in coordination with the Congress, Department of State, and the appropriate in-country U.S. Ambassadors and USAID field Missions, the Office provided on-the-ground, fast, flexible, catalytic short-term assistance that promoted movement toward political and social stability and democracy.  DCHA/OTI programs in such countries continued until reasonable stability was established and an effective hand-off was completed to longer-term institutional development efforts.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Bureau for Economic Growth, Agriculture, and Trade (EGAT) provided a central Agency focus for the design, implementation, review, coordination, and evaluation of worldwide activities in the areas of economic growth, poverty reduction, education, economic infrastructure, agriculture, environment, natural resources management, and women in development. The Bureau supported national and regional implemented activities in these areas.  The Bureau ensured the quality and capacity of the Agency's technical workforce by overseeing the recruitment, selection, and training for new entry professionals (NEPs); designing, implementing, and coordinating technical training opportunities for all USAID staff working in EGAT's areas of expertise; and liaising with regional Bureaus and Mission Directors to address the continuous learning needs of the staff.

In 2012 the name changed to the Bureau for Economic Growth, Education, and Environment (E3).  The Bureau provided technical leadership, research, and field support for worldwide activities in the areas of economic growth and trade, infrastructure and engineering, education, environment and global climate change, water, and gender equality and women's empowerment.  The Bureau represented the Agency on relevant technical matters in the Inter-agency and with Congress, outside partners, other donors and multilateral institutions. The Bureau also supported research and rigorous impact evaluations to advance Agency strategies and programs in E3 sectors and determined the most effective approaches. E3 encouraged innovation and worked on challenges for development, in education and energy, as well as other methods to identify new ideas and bring them to scale.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Office of Development Credit introduced and oversaw the Development Credit Authority (DCA) as a financing vehicle to accomplish a wide range of development goals and objectives.  DCA used partial loan guarantees to help unlock private financing in support of USAID priorities.  The Office conducted credit risk analyses needed to calculate the level of subsidy required for each credit-funded activity and to ensure prudent risk management of the overall Agency DCA portfolio; was responsible for quality control of financing and economic analyses conducted by the Agency operating units regarding the use of DCA; provided technical assistance in the conduct and scope of these analyses as requested; and provided the necessary training and support to USAID staff and to potential implementing partners on the development, management, and use of credit as a source of project funding. 

Supported by an attorney assigned to the Office of the General Counsel, a budget analyst in the Budget Division, and the Office of the Chief Financial Officer's Credit Team, the Office of Development Credit ensured close coordination with the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) to ensure that USG credit guidelines were respected. Although Missions initiating DCA supported projects assumed responsibility for oversight and monitoring, the Office worked with and through Missions to ensure effectiveness in this area.

U.S. aid to Lebabnon resumed in 1975.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Executive Office served as the focal point for management issues of the Mission and provided advice to the Director on management implications of program administration and implemented management decisions. creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The American embassy in N'Djamena was closed from the onset of the heavy fighting in the city in 1980 until the withdrawal of the Libyan forces at the end of 1981. It was reopened in January 1982. The U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) offices resumed activities in Chad in September 1983.

Before permanently closing its Chad mission in 1995 because of declining funds and security concerns, USAID's development program in Chad concentrated on the agricultural, health, and infrastructure sectors. It also included projects in road repair and maintenance, maternal and child health, famine early warning systems, and agricultural marketing. A number of American voluntary agencies (notably Africare and VITA) continue to operate in Chad.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: In April 1970, the Office of Private Overseas Programs was established. It formed to encourage U.S. private technical assistance organizations to undertake expanded development assistance programs. The Office was responsible for providing leadership in expanding the Agency for International Development's (AID) relationships with the U.S. private, nonprofit, technical assistance community (exclusive of universities and labor unions); promoting maximum private participation in overseas development; and was the Agency's central point of contact with U.S. private organizations.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: In June 1962, the Regional Technical Aid Center (RTAC) was established in Rabat, Morocco, for the purpose of translating technical and training publications form English into French or Arabic, and printing and shipping copies of such materials to Agency for International Development (USAID) missions in Africa and Far Eastern countries. The RTAC also financed a book subsidization program. English language training films were dubbed on a French sound track prior to circulating to missions on a loan basis. In January 1963, it was decided to move the RTAC to Paris for better translators, proximity to printers and film dubbing studios, and better communications with Africa.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Office of the Inspector General (OIG) reviewed the integrity of Agency of International Development's (USAID) operations through audits, appraisals, investigations and inspections. OIG conducted and supervised audits and investigations of USAID programs and operations, and recommended policies designed to promote economy, efficiency and effectiveness, and to prevent and detect fraud and abuse. The Office was semi-autonomous, with its own budget and personnel authorities.OIG provided a means for keeping the Administrator and Congress fully and currently informed about problems and deficiencies relating to the administration of such activities and the necessity for and progress of correction action. By 2004, OIG was responsible for reviewing the integrity of operations for USAID, the Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC), the African Development Foundation (ADF), and the Inter-American Foundation (IAF) through audits, investigations, and inspections.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The major objective of the Finance Department was to establish the Overseas Private Investment Corporation (OPIC) as an aid to U.S. lenders and business enterprises in searching out and financing worthwhile projects in the developing world. The two principal means for accomplishing this were the Corporation's Investment Guaranty Program and its Direct Investment Fund. These two sources of financing were utilized by corporate investors, and all projects assisted by OPIC have private U.S. capital involved. The Finance Department processed loan proposals under the investment guaranty and direct investment programs.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Office of Energy, Environment and Technology (G/ENV/EET) provided analytical, technical, and strategic assistance to U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) Bureaus and Missions to identify energy interventions that contribute to the realization of USAID's development objectives including economic growth, democratization, human health, and environmental stewardship. G/ENV/EET activities that demonstrated the energy development linkage in both rural and urban settings included: energy sector policy and governance, private and public sector capacity building, environmental management, energy efficiency, and renewable energy. Some of the programs related to industrial environmental policy and management, energy policy, energy efficiency, renewable energy, nuclear safety, environmentally sound energy development, and environmental technology. The Office of Energy, Environment, and Technology helped developing countries and emerging economies find market-oriented solutions to their energy and environmental problems. The Office brokered technology cooperation among U.S. energy and environment industries and developing countries, and also helped set energy policy direction for the Agency.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Office of Energy and Infrastructure's assistance programs were to solve problems of high rates of energy use and economic growth accompanied by a lack of energy, especially power in rural areas; severe financial problems, including a lack of investment capital, especially in the electricity sector; and growing energy related environmental threats, including global climate change, acid rain, and urban air pollution.

To address these problems, the Office of Energy and Infrastructure leveraged financial resources of multilateral development banks such as The World Bank and the InterAmerican Development Bank, the private sector, and bilateral donors, to increase energy efficiency and expand energy supplies, enhance the role of private power, and implement novel approaches through research, adoption, and innovation. These approaches included improving power sector investment planning ("least-cost" planning) and encouraging the application of cleaner technologies that use both conventional fossil fuels and renewable energy sources. Promotion of greater private sector participation in the power sector and a wide-ranging training program also helped to build the institutional infrastructure necessary to sustain cost-effective, reliable, and environmentally sound energy systems integral to broad-based economic growth.

The Office of Energy and Infrastructure helped set energy policy direction for the Agency of International Development (A.I.D.), made its projects available to meet generic needs (such as training), and responds to short-term needs of A.I.D.'s field offices in assisted countries

The Office designed seven projects to serve these needs of developing countries, as well as Congressional concerns and A.I.D. initiatives: the Energy Planning and Policy Development; the Energy Efficiency Project; the Private Sector Energy Development Project; the Renewable Energy Applications and Training; the Biomass Energy Systems and Technology; the Energy Technology Innovation Project; and the Energy Training Project.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Foreign Service Buildings Commission, was a joint commission established by the Foreign Service Buildings Act of 1926 (44 Stat. 403) of May 7, 1926. Its duty was to consider, formulate, and approve plans and proposals for the acquisition and utilization of the sites and buildings, and of sites and buildings acquired or authorized for the use of the diplomatic and consular establishments in foreign countries, including the initial furnishings of such buildings and the initial alteration and repair of purchased buildings and grounds. It was discontinued in 1945 and was succeeded by a Foreign Service Buildings Division with expanded powers.

The Commission was composed of the Secretary of State, the Secretary of the Treasury, the Secretary of Commerce, the chairman and the ranking minority member of the Committee on Foreign Relations of the Senate, and the chairman and the ranking minority member of the Committee on Foreign Affairs of the House of Representatives.

The office of United States Ambassador (or formerly Minister/Envoy Extraordinary) to the United Kingdom (known formally as Ambassador to the Court of St. James's) was traditionally, and still is very much so today due to the Special Relationship, the most prestigious position in the United States Foreign Service. Full titles of the chiefs of mission were Minister Plenipotentiary to the Court of St. James's (1785-1811), Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary to the Court of St. James's (1815-1893), and Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to the Court of St. James's (1893-present)

John Adams of Massachusetts, by appointment of Congress of the Confederation, the  presented his credentials as Minister Plenipotentiary to the Court of St. James on June 1, 1785. He was concurrently accredited to the Netherlands. (John Adams became so frustrated with his cool reception at the court that he closed the legation in 1788 and the post remained vacant for four years.) The United States severed relations with the United Kingdom on the outbreak of the War of 1812 - normal relations were restored in 1815.

Although the United States established diplomatic relations with Great Britain in 1792, the records of the London diplomatic post among the National Archives of the United States do not begin until 1826. Whatb became of the records for the period 1702-1825 is unknown 9ecept for those among the Rufus King papers in the New York Historical Society), but the despatches received from the post by the Department of State during this period are to be found in Record Group 59, General Records of the Department of State.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The earliest USAID efforts in South Africa began in 1979.  Working through the Human Rights Fund, USAID supported local non-governmental organizations working on human rights activities.                                                A formal USAID program did not start in South Africa until 1986, when the U.S. Comprehensive Anti-Apartheid Act of 1986 (Public Law 99 - 440) authorized the appropriation of funding for a foreign assistance program to help South African victims of apartheid.  The funding was given directly to private entities.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
In 1991, the Office of Foreign Disaster Assistance (OFDA) established a Disaster Prevention, Mitigation, and Preparedness Division (PMP) to strengthen and give greater coherence to PMP activities within OFDA. PMP activates included prevention of natural phenomenon or potential hazards from having harmful effects on human or economic assets, such as destroying hazardous chemicals or building dams; mitigation to reduce harmful effects of a disaster, such as hurricane straps to reduce wind damage to roofs; and preparedness to structure quick disaster responses after the disaster through training and warning systems. PMP's three strategic goals were to save the greatest number of lives, reduce human suffering, and protect economic assets from disasters; increase awareness of disasters and the possibilities for mitigation within AID development programs, together with those of other donors and the host countries themselves; and ultimately, reduce resources spent on disaster response. To achieve these goals PMP was to integrated disaster PMP concerns into the Agency for International Development (USAID) mainstream programming; to enhance the PMP impact to all USAID resources that contribute to PMP; and to support stand-alone activities that fill PMP gaps in Mission programs or test new initiatives to meet strategy objectives. PMP originally identified seven types of disaster to focus on: famine, conflict, earthquakes, cyclones, floods, volcanoes, and technological disasters (e.g., release of poisonous gases). 

By 1995, the name changed to the Prevention, Mitigation, Preparedness, and Planning (PMPP) Division that oversaw the portfolio of projects designed to prevent or reduce the impact of disasters on the people and economic infrastructure in foreign countries. PMPP invested in partnerships with the US Geological Survey (USGS), the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), the Asian Disaster Preparedness Center, the World Environment Center, and other USAID offices to enhance a country's capacity to manage its owned disasters and hazards, but also promoted the transfer of technology, goods, and services between the US and the host country PMPP programs ranged from investing in drought early warning systems to training local relief workers to manage the response to a disaster more effectively. PMPP programs were designed to prevent, mitigate, prepare, and plan for complex emergencies, which were more the result of human actions than acts of nature.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Planning and Evaluation Division was responsible for the planning and budgeting for Agencywide automation and Agency for International Development/Washington (AID/W) management consulting requirements; contract advisory assistance; evaluation of the Office of Information Resource Management's (IRM) products and services; information management coordination activities; Information Management Council Staff support; Agencywide training coordination for information management; and standards.  During the second half of 1984, the Mandated Management Programs Division was abolished and its functions and staff were reassigned to the Planning and Evaluation Division.

The primary responsibility of the Planning, Management, and Acquisition Division (M/IRM/PMA) was to provide support to the Chief Information Officer (CIO) in developing and implementing the Agency for International Development's enterprise architecture, manage the information technology budget, coordinate the acquisition of Federal information processing resources with other Bureau of Management entities, provide core contract administration services, and provide policy coordination related to computer accessibility for disabled employees.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
As the poorest country in South America, Bolivia has traditionally been a major recipient of U.S. assistance. By the mid-1970's the Agency for International Development was helping the Government of Bolivia pursue a strategy of: 1) increasing agricultural productivity and improving the nutritional level of the subsistence rural dweller; 2) improving the standard of rural health, particularly among the young and, 3) making education more relevant and accessible to rural children and adults.

Its activities aimed at providing credit, extension and technology in agriculture to the small farmers of the central valleys and adjacent lowlands; improving rural access roads in these areas, and stimulating the production of basic food grains. A program was underway to test a low-cost, rural health planning and delivery system, and another project was to  provide potable water and sanitation in these target areas. Curricula reform, decentralization of educational administration, improved rural teacher training and construction of improved school facilities are being undertaken in a variety of United States Agency for International Development (USAID)-supported educational projects.

U.S. interests in the country were predominantly humanitarian and aimed at improving the condition of the rural dweller. Additional, although less significant, interests were the reduction of cocaine trafficking to the United States and maintenance of continued access to Bolivan natural resources such as tin, tungsten and hydrocarbons.

On May 1, 2013, the President of Bolivia, Evo Morales, asked USAID to close its mission. On September 30, 2013, all projects were closed and USAID was no longer administering or implementing any assistance programs in Bolivia. All financial activities also were terminated.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
On May 16, 1949, Departmental Announcement No. 60 redesignated the Office of Controls as the Office of Consular Affairs. The Office of Consular Affairs discharged the responsibility of the Deputy Under Secretary for Administration with respect to the consular program of the Department of State and the Foreign Service, controlling the export of munitions and the security of official operations.

On May 3, 1951, Departmental Announcement No. 97 redesignated the Office of Consular Affairs as the Office of Security and Consular Affairs. This Office discharged the responsibility of the Deputy Under Secretary for Administration with respect to the security and consular programs of the Department of State and the Foreign Service.

The Bureau of Security and Consular Affairs was established on December 24, 1952 upon the enactment of the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1952 (Public Law 82-414; 66 Stat. 174), dated June 27, 1952. It took over the functions of the former Office of Security and Consular Affairs. The Administrator of the Bureau was ranked equal to that of an Assistant Secretary of State and was an U.S. citizen. The Bureau was responsible for administering and enforcing of immigration law, as it related to the duties and functions of diplomatic and consular officers. The Bureau was responsible for issuing passports and visas. The Administrator of the Bureau was tasked with maintaining close liaisons with Congress, the Commissioner of Immigration and Naturalization, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and with other internal security officers of the government for the purpose of obtaining and exchanging information for use in enforcing the provisions of the Immigration and Nationality Act.

As of March 3, 1953, the Bureau of Security and Consular Affairs was renamed the Bureau of Security, Consular Affairs, and Personnel when it gained the Office of Personnel. On November 27, 1953, Delegation of Authority No. 74 assigned the Department of State’s responsibilities under the Refugee Relief Act of 1953 (67 Stat. 400) to the Bureau of Security and Consular Affairs. 

On March 1, 1954, the Bureau of Security, Consular Affairs, and Personnel was renamed the Bureau of Inspection, Security, and Consular Affairs. Personnel functions were transferred to the Office of the Assistant Secretary for Personnel and Administration. The Foreign Service Inspection Corps was transferred to the new Bureau on April 5, 1954. On November 3, 1954, Department of State Circular No. 123 announced that the Adviser on Refugees and Displaced Persons had been transferred from the Bureau of International Organization Affairs to the Bureau. 

On December 30, 1954, inspection functions, including the Foreign Service Inspection Corps, were transferred from the Bureau of Inspection, Security, and Consular Affairs to the Office of the Deputy Under Secretary for Administration. Concurrently, the Bureau of Inspection, Security, and Consular Affairs’ name reverted to the Bureau of Security and Consular Affairs. On March 24, 1956, Executive Order 10663 transferred responsibility for the U.S. Escapee Program, which assisted persons fleeing from Soviet-Bloc countries, from the International Cooperation Administration to the Bureau of Security and Consular Affairs.

From 1953 to 1962, the Secretary of State designated incumbents to the Administrator position. The Migration and Refugee Assistance Act of 1962 (Jun 28, 1962; P.L. 87-510; 76 Stat. 123) made the Administrator a Presidential appointee subject to the advice and consent of the Senate. In 1962, the Department transferred the security function to the Deputy Under Secretary for Administration, but the title remained unchanged until 1977. On August 17, 1977, the Foreign Relations Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 1978 (Public Law 95-105; 91 Stat. 847) increased the number of Assistant Secretaries from 11 to 13, making the Administrator of the Bureau of Security and Consular Affairs the Assistant Secretary of State for Consular Affairs and the Bureau was renamed the Bureau of Consular Affairs.

The Assistant Secretary was charged with responsibility over the welfare and protection of U.S. citizens abroad, the issuance of passports and other documentation to citizens and nationals, the protection of U.S. border security, and the facilitation of travel to the United States. 

Robert Walter Scott McLeod served as the first Administrator from February 25, 1953–1957. He was followed by Roderic L. O’Connor (1957–1958), Abba Philip Schwartz (1962–1966), Barbara Mae Watson, Acting (April 1967-1968), Barbara Mae Watson (1968–1974), Leonard Frederick Walentynowicz (1975–1977); and Barbara Mae Watson (1977). When the title changed in 1977, Barbara Mae Watson was the first Assistant Secretary of State for Consular Affairs from 1977-1980. She was the first African American and woman to hold an Assistant Secretary position in the Department of State. She was followed by Diego Cortes Asencio (1980–1983), Joan Margaret Clark (1983–1989), Elizabeth M. Tamposi (1989–1992), Mary A. Ryan (1993–2002), Maura Ann Harty (2002–2008), Janice Lee Jacobs (2008–2014), Michele Thoren Bond (2015–2017), and Carl C. Risch (2017-).

sourceNotes: 66 Statutes at Large 163, 174, 281 June 27, 1952 (Public Law 414 That this Act, divided into titles, chapters, and sections according to the following table of contents, may be cited as the "Immigration and Nationality Act"; Section 101 (a) As used in this Act- (1) The term "administrator'' means the administrator of the Bureau of Security and Consular Affairs of the Department of State. (8) The terms "Commissioner" and "Deputy Commissioner" mean the Commissioner of Immigration and Naturalization and a Deputy Commissioner of Immigration and Naturalization, respectively; Sec. 104 SEC. 104. (a) The Secretary of State shall be charged with the ad-ministration and the enforcement of the provisions of this Act and all other immigration and nationality laws relating to (1) the powers, duties and functions of diplomatic and consular officers of the United States, except those powers, duties and functions conferred upon the consular officers relating to the granting or refusal of visas; (2) the powers, duties and functions of the Bureau of Security and Consular Affairs; and (3) the determination of nationality of a person not in the United States…(b) There is hereby established in the Department of State a Bureau of Security and Consular Affairs, to be headed by an administrator (with an appropriate title to be designated by the Secretary of State), with rank and compensation equal to that of an Assistant Secretary of State. The administrator shall be a citizen of the United States, qualified by experience, and shall maintain close liaison with the appropriate committees of Congress in order that they may be advised regarding the administration of this Act by consular officers. He shall be charged with any and all responsibility and authority in the administration of the Bureau and of this Act which are conferred on the Secretary of State as may be delegated to him by the Secretary of State or which may be prescribed by the Secretary of State. He shall also perform such other duties as the Secretary of State may prescribe. (f) The Bureau shall be under the immediate jurisdiction of the Deputy Under Secretary of State for Administration. SEC. 407. Except as provided in subsection (k) of section 401, this Act shall take effect at 12:01 ante meridian United States Eastern Standard Time on the one hundred eightieth day immediately following the date of its enactment. (c) Within the Bureau there shall be a Passport Office, a Visa Office, and such other offices as the Secretary of State may deem to be appropriate, each office to be headed by a director. The Directors of the Passport Office and the Visa Office shall be experienced in the administration of the nationality and immigration laws, (d) The functions heretofore performed by the Passport Division and the Visa Division of the Department of State shall hereafter be performed by the Passport Office and the Visa Office, respectively, of the Bureau of Security and Consular Affairs. Sec. 105 The Commissioner and the administrator shall have authority to maintain direct and continuous liaison with the Directors of the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the Central Intelligence Agency and with other internal security officers of the Government for the purpose of obtaining and exchanging information for use in enforcing the provisions of this Act in the interest of the internal security of the United States. The Commissioner and the administrator shall maintain direct and continuous liaison with each other with a view to a coordinated, uniform, and efficient administration of this Act, and all other immigration and nationality laws.)

Department of State Newsletter, no. 187, February 1977: p. 9, 10 (President Carter has named eight heads of functional bureaus in the Department. Three of the eight are being retained. Nominations of the others are subject to Senate confirmation. Named were: Barbara M. Watson, who is returning as Administrator of the Bureau of Security and Consular Affairs, which she headed from August 1968 to January 1975. Miss Watson, who held the rank of Assistant Secretary, will succeed Leonard F. Walentynowicz; As head of the Bureau of Security and Consular Affairs, Miss Watson was the first woman and also the first black to hold a position at so senior a level in the State Department. If confirmed by the Senate, Miss Watson will administer a $60,000,000 consular program, including executive direction of a bureau comprising nearly 1,000 employees in the United States. She will also have technical direction of 2,000 other employees in over 250 Foreign Service posts over the world. Miss Watson joined the Department in July 1966 as Special Assistant to the Deputy Under Secretary for Administration. She was appointed Deputy Administrator of the Bureau in October 1966, and Acting Administrator in April 1967.)

Department of State Newsletter, no. 193, August-September 1977: p. 3, 5 (Foreign Relations Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 1978, which President Carter signed on August 17. Among other things, the 1978: establishes two new assignat secretaryships in the Department, bestowing this title on ranking officials whose functions otherwise are not changed; Patricia M. Derian and Barbara M. Watson automatically became assistant secretaries of state when the President signed the 1978 Act. They remain in their posts, respectively, as coordinator for human rights and humanitarian affairs and as administrator of consular affairs — but they have the new titles. Ms. Watson's Bureau of Security and Consular Affairs gets a new name — the Bureau of Consular Affairs. creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Program Support Division (DCHA/OFDA/PS) provided programmatic and administrative support, including: budget and financial services, procurement planning, contract and grant administration, general administrative support, procurement of technical services, management of information system and computer services, and communication support for both Office of U.S. Foreign Disaster Assistance (DCHA/OFDA) Washington and its field offices. The Division also maintained and developed administrative and programmatic policy as it relates to DCHA/OFDA programs.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Executive Office served as the focal point for management issues of the Mission and provided advice to the Director on management implications of program administration and implemented management decisions. This office had responsibility for ensuring that adequate administrative support and security were provided to the Mission. All functions of the Executive Office were controlled by Manual Order Issuances of the International Cooperation Administration, Foreign Service Regulations, and the Standardized Regulations as pertinent.

Through 1971, the United States Government provided India with about $10 billion in development loans and technical assistance and food aid. In the 10 years prior to that date, U.S. economic assistance averaged slightly more than $600 million annually. Roughly, each year about $300 million was made available in the form of development loans and grants; the balance was provided in food aid, mostly under PL 480, Title I credit sales.

The 1971 Indo-Pakistan war led to suspension of U. S. development programs to Pakistan and India. Subsequently, a large-scale foreign assistance program was resumed in Pakistan but not in India. Although an offer was made to India to continue a scaled-down technical assistance program, in the existing chilly political atmosphere, the Government of India (GOI) indicated that it wished to phase out entirely the U.S. program authorized by the Foreign Assistance Act. Food aid under PL 480 Title I credit sales was also suspended. In 1975 and 1976 shipments resumed again at about half a million tons of wheat valued at about $100 million per year. In 1977, wheat continued to be allocated for India, but it was not sent because of record harvests and high stocks. Vegetable oil worth $25-35 million per year was provided in 1977 and 1978. The United States also continued to contribute to Indian development through its participation in multilateral assistance agencies such as IDA and the World Bank. The U.S. provided over 30 percent of IDA's soft loan replenishment funds which would indirectly amount to over $200 millionof IDA's annual commitments of roughly $600 million to India. 

On July 14, 1977, in a climate of improved relations India between the U.S. and India, the Congress recommended to the President the resumption of AID assistance to India. USAID/India resumed operations as a Mission in May 1978.

To represent the United States in discharging the responsibilities it had assumed pursuant to the Bilateral Agreement, there was created in Rabat a U.S. economic and technical mission, functioning as a subsidiary organization of the American Embassy, whose purpose has been to cooperate with the Government of Morocco in the formulation of plans and in the activation of specific projects which contribute to country economic 

The general objective sought by the United States through the provision of economic and technical assistance to Morocco was to assist the populace to improve its standard of living techniques, 

through accelerated development of agricultural, industrial, natural, and human resources.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The AID program in Syria began in fiscal year 1960, when Syria was still a part of the United Arab Republic. In that year the United States provided $9.6 million of surplus agricultural commodities under Public Law 480, title I, Development Loans totaling $5.7 million, and agreed to assist in developing Syria's civil aviation facilities through a modest Development Grant program.

From early 1961 to August 1962, unsettled political conditions, the separation of Syria from the United Arab Republic, and the unresolved question of the U.S. economic assistance relationship with Syria delayed the procurement and shipment of commodities, and severely hampered the technical advisory work of the civil aviation team. However, in August 1962, the bilateral agreement previously signed with the United Arab Republic was accepted by Syria as covering all AID activity in Syria.

As a consequence of the Six-Day War, Syria severed diplomatic relations with the United States in June 1967. U.S. economic assistance to Syria resumed in late 1974, several months after the restoration of diplomatic relations. The objective of U.S. assistance was to help Syria pursue its economic development program and to further improve U.S. - Syrian relations, and was regarded as essential to peace in the Middle East. Specifically, the USAID program was designed to assist Syria in priority development areas, especially agriculture, transportation, rural development, health, nutrition, and manpower training.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
Even in the early years of independence of the Brazilian Empire, the province of Sao Paulo was significant enough to draw American attention. While the still small provincial capital was isolated at the top of the Serra do Mar (mountains of the sea), its port city of Santos was more accessible. The first American Consulate in the future State of Sao Paulo was established in Santos on April 5, 1830 under Consul George Black. (The Santos Consulate was closed September 28, 1963.) 

With the great coffee boom of the last decades of the 1800's and new rail connections from Santos into the interior, Sao Paulo City began its explosive expansion. On April 10, 1907 an American resident in Sao Paulo, Albert J. Byington, originally from Kansas, was appointed Consular Agent. Byington resigned January 30, 1908, and was replaced on June 18th by William W. Lee, a Brazilian citizen who served until March 5, 1914, taking care of consular business from his home in Rua Santo Amaro.

With a population already in the hundreds of thousands, and a similarly burgeoning economic connection with the United States, the City of Sao Paulo could not long be relegated to a secondary status by the Department of State. A Consulate was established on July 3, 1915, and Vice Consul Robert L. Keiser was appointed to head it.

In the years immediately after World War II, the Consulate occupied parts of two buildings in the old center city, at Largo Sao Francisco, 181, next to the Franciscan Church and Friary, and immediately adjacent at Rua Libero Badaro, 39. From there, the Consulate moved to the Conjunto Nacional Building on Avenida Paulista, between Rua Padre Joao Manoel and Rua Augusta. A fire in September 1978 forced the Consulate to move temporarily to the quarters of the U.S. Trade Center further west on Paulista, until new quarters could be secure.

The Consulate moved to Rua Padre Joao Manoel, 933 and was inaugurated on November 19, 1979. Due to an expanding staff, growing operations and a need to better serve the public, the Consulate moved to the southern part of the city in the Santo Amaro district. The new facility opened on January 21, 2004 with all USG operations consolidated into this one location at Rua Thomas Deloney 381.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The United States recognized the Federation of Nigeria on October 1, 1960, in a congratulatory message from Secretary of State Christian Herter to the Nigerian people, broadcast on Voice of America radio. This message was followed by a congratulatory letter from President Dwight D. Eisenhower delivered to Prime Minister Sir Abubukar Tafawa Balewa on October 2, 1960. Nigeria had been previously under British sovereignty.

The Embassy in Lagos was established on October 1, 1960, with Ambassador Joseph Palmer 2nd in charge pending presentation of his letter of credence (October 4). The U.S. Embassy was transferred from Lagos to Abuja on September 15, 2000.

After the June 12, 1993, presidential election was annulled, and in light of human rights abuses and the failure to embark on a meaningful democratic transition, the United States imposed numerous sanctions on Nigeria. These sanctions included the imposition of Section 212(f) of the Immigration and Nationality Act to refuse entry into the United States of senior government officials and others who formulated, implemented, or benefited from policies impeding Nigeria's transition to democracy; suspension of all military assistance; and a ban on the sale and repair of military goods and refinery services to Nigeria. The U.S. Ambassador was recalled for consultations for four months after the execution of the Ogoni Nine on November 10, 1995.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The establishment of the Communism Analysis Division was announced on December 14,1 959. It provided a continuing situation analysis for countries within the Soviet Orbit (excluding Communist China); analyzed Communist propaganda; and conducted Soviet Orbit audience research.  Ralph K. White served as Chief.

The Soviet Block Division prepared analyses and research reports on the Soviet Union and its satellites and on worldwide communist propaganda.

The East European Division provided the U.S. Information Agency’s programs upon the Communist bloc, and reported about conditions within the Communist bloc that were pertinent to the Agency’s policies and programming.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
After the Second Boer War of 1899–1902, Swaziland became a British protectorate and thus came under the hegemony of the British Empire. In the early years of colonial rule, the British had expected that Swaziland would eventually be incorporated into South Africa. After World War II, however, South Africa’s racial policies induced the United Kingdom to prepare Swaziland for independence. In 1966, the British Government agreed to discuss a new constitution, and Swaziland became independent on September 6, 1968. 

The United States immediately recognized the new nation and established an embassy in the capital Mbabane on September 6, 1968, independence day for Swaziland. Chris C. Pappas, Jr., was appointed as chargé d'affaires ad interim pending the appointment of an ambassador. The first ambassador, Charles J. Nelson was appointed on June 9, 1971. He was accredited to Swaziland, Lesotho, and Botswana while resident in Gaborone, Botswana and until 1979 one ambassador, resident at Gaborone, was accredited to Botswana, Swaziland, and Lesotho. In 1979 a resident ambassador to Swaziland was appointed.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: From 1885 until 1966 the area of southern Africa that is now Botswana was part of the Bechuanaland Protectorate of Great Britain. In June 1964, Britain accepted proposals for democratic self-government in Botswana. The seat of government was moved from Mafikeng in South Africa, to newly established in Gaberones (now Gaborone) in 1965. The 1965 constitution led to the first general elections and to independence on September 30, 1966. The United States immediately recognized the new nation and moved to establish diplomatic relations. An embassy in Gaberones (now Gaborone) was established on September 30, 1966—independence day for Botswana. Charles H. Pletcher was appointed as Chargé d'affaires ad interim pending the appointment of an ambassador. Until 1979 one ambassador, resident at Gaborone, was accredited to Botswana, Swaziland, and Lesotho.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
Prior to 1965, the area of southern Africa that is now Lesotho was a British protectorate by the name of Basutoland. Along with most of the Empire’s other colonies and protectorates, Basutoland gained full independence from Britain in the 1960s. The nation was granted full autonomy on April 30, 1965. On October 4, 1966, Basutoland was granted independence, governed by a constitutional monarchy with a bicameral parliament. At the same time the name of the country was changed to The Kingdom of Lesotho. The United States immediately recognized Lesotho after the nation gained its independence. An embassy in Maseru was established on October 4, 1966, Lesotho’s independence day. Richard St. F. Post was appointed as chargé d'affaires ad interim pending the arrival of an ambassador. 

The United States opened diplomatic relations with Lesotho on October 4, 1966, and opened its embassy  at Maseru that same day. Richard St. F. Post was serving as Charge d'Affaires ad interim. He was succeeded as Charge by Norman E. Barth, July 1968 - August 1969, and Stephen G. Gebelt, October 1969 - December 1970.

The first U.S. Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary, Charles J. Nelson, presented his credentials on September 23, 1971. He was a non-resident Ambassador, accredited also to Botswana and Swaziland, with residence at Gaborone, Botswana. He was succeeded by David J. Bolen, April 25, 1974, and Donald R. Norland, January 6, 1977.

The first resident Ambassador, John R. Clingerman, presented his credentials on November 1, 1979. He was succeeded by Keith Lapham Brown, March 25, 1982; S.L. Abbott, July 3, 1984; and Robert M. Smalley, July 2, 1987. Howard F. Jeter served as Charge d'Affaires ad interim from July 1989 through January 1991. The next Ambassador, Leonard H.O. Spearman, presented his credentials on January 24, 1991; he departed Maseru on April 25, 1993. Karl Hoffman served as Charge d'Affaires ad interim until April 27, 1995, when Bismarck Myrick presented credentials as Ambassador. Ambassador Myrick was succeeded by Katherine Hubay Peterson, September 18, 1998, and Robert Geers Loftis, October 11, 2001.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Water Treaty of February 3, 1944 expanded the duties and responsibilities of the International Boundary Commission (IBC) and renamed it the International Boundary and Water Commission (IBWC). The Commission monitored existing treaties between the United States and Mexico concerning boundary and water matters affecting both countries. It provided international flood control projects for most of the urban an irrigation developments along the U.S.-Mexico border, monitored treaties between the U.S. and Mexico which called for the distribution of waters on the Rio Grande to be divided between the two countries and for the delivery of allotted waters of the Colorado River to Mexico; provided optimum feasible storage in the international storage reservoirs and generation of hydroelectric power, conservation, and regulation of the Rio Grande for its usage by the U.S. and Mexico; operated and maintained structures for the diversion of flood waters on the Rio Grande and for the diversion of irrigation waters on the Rio Grande and Colorado Rivers; and sought solutions for salinity problems on the Rio Grande and Colorado Rivers and for major border sanitation problems.  The Commission was also responsible for the preservation of the international boundary line between the U.S. and Mexico.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Engineering Services Division (ESD), provided oversight, direction, and management of the engineering design and construction program for the entire U.S. Section. ESD designed and developed plans and specifications for construction and renovation of buildings, hydraulic structures, and wastewater treatment plant infrastructure and conducts hydraulic studies, including developing HEC-RAS and HEC-HMS computer models for IBWC projects such as the Canalization, Rectification and Lower Rio Grande Valley Flood Control Projects.  ESD provided license and permit review for projects that may invoke the 1970 Boundary Treaty; and acted as a point of contact for initiating and followup on these projects with the Mexican Section. ESD was responsible for graphic support services and maintained the official record drawings for IBWC projects.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The American Aid Program in the Sudan began in the spring of 1958, when the Sudanese Government decided to seek the assistance of the United States in order to prepare itself to speed up development of its economic potential. Diplomatic relations between the two countries were interrupted as a consequence of the Six-Day War, but after a more than five-year break in diplomatic relations and the absence of an AID program, Sudan and the United States resumed diplomatic relations on July 25, 1972.

Following a request for economic assistance from the Government of Sudan, an eight-day visit was made by an AID team at the beginning of September 1972 to discuss Sudan's development problems and priorities. The team's report showed that balance of payments assistance, either through programs grants or loans, was the Government of Sudan's principal requirement, and that agriculture and transportation were foremost among Sudan's development investment priorities.

An AID Affairs Office was set up as a section of the American Embassy in Khartoum in late June 1973.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Office of East and South Asian Affairs (ANE/ESA) provided liaison and backstopping functions for the Bureau for Asian and Near East (ANE) field Missions. The Office coordinated and participated in the review, approval, implementation, and assessment of proposed assistance from the standpoint of suitability to the country/area development situation and assistance strategy and compatibility with Agency and Bureau policy. The Office also coordinated the review and follow-up of country program strategy plans (CPSP), Results Review and Resource Request documents (R4), Congressional Presentations (CP), Congressional Notifications (CNs/TNs), and any other field documentation that was presented for Washington review. The Office served as USAID/Washington points of contact with USAID's external audiences and respond to stakeholder inquiries and needs for information. With respect to bilateral programs, the Office coordinated USAID participation in multilateral and other donor meetings, particularly the annual Consultative Group meetings. 

The Office of East and South Asian Affairs supported the bilateral and regional activities in the presence countries of Bangladesh, India, Nepal, and Sri Lanka in South Asia and Cambodia, Indonesia, Mongolia, and the Philippines in East Asia. In addition, the Desks were the key link for bilateral and regional activities in the non-presence countries of Afghanistan and Pakistan in South Asia and Burma, China, East Timor, Laos, North Korea, South Pacific Island, Thailand, and Vietnam. The Office acted as the interface for other bilateral and multilateral donor programs in all of the above countries.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
Initial United States diplomatic representation with Ethiopia (then Abyssinia) was opened in 1908 with the appointment of Hoffman Philip as Minister Resident and Consul General. He presented his credentials on July 6, 1909, and represented the United States until February 8, 1910, when he departed Addis Ababa. The position of Minister Resident remained unfilled until Addison E. Southard presented his credentials on March 1, 1928. He was succeeded by Cornelius Van H. Engert on April 30, 1936.

Italian forces occupied Addis Ababa on May 6, 1936, and Engert left the capital on May 4, 1937. A new Minister Resident, John K. Caldwell, presented his credentials on August 31, 1943, and later that year, on December 9, he presented new credentials as Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary. He was succeeded by Felix Cole, October 5, 1945, and George R. Merrell, January 1, 1948. 

In 1949 the Legation was reclassified as an embassy and Merrell presented his credentials as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary on June 28, 1949. He was succeeded by J. Rives Childs, May 14, 1951; Joseph Simonson, October 6, 1953; Don C. Bliss, June 22, 1957; Arthur L. Richards, August 26, 1960; Edward M. Korry, April 20, 1963; William O. Hall, October 27, 1967; E. Ross Adair, July 8, 1971; Arthur W. Hummel, Jr., April 3, 1975; and Frederic L. Chapin, July 21, 1978.

On July 29, 1980, Ambassador Chapin was recalled at the request of the Ethiopian Government. Until June 1992 he was succeeded by a number of Charge d'Affaires ad interim including David A. Korn, June 1982 - July 1985; James Cheek, July 1985 - August 1988; Robert G. Houdek, August 1988 - June 1991; and Marc A. Baas, June 1991 - June 1992.

With the downfall of the Derg junta, under the leadership of Mengistu Haile Mariam, in May 1991, U.S.-Ethiopian relations improved dramatically. Legislative restrictions on assistance to Ethiopia other than humanitarian assistance were lifted and diplomatic relations were upgraded to the ambassadorial level in 1992. On June 24, 1992, Marc A. Baas presented his ambassadorial credentials. He was succeeded by Irvin Hicks, July 22, 1994; David H. Shinn, July 2, 1996; Tibor P. Nagy, Jr., October 12, 1999; and Aurelia E. Brazeal, November 20, 2002.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
In 1969, the Office of the War on Hunger was abolished and its Food for Peace functions were transferred to the new Office of Food for Peace (FFP) that was established to strengthening the use of U. S. food resources in foreign assistance programs has been established by the Agency for International Development (AID). AID Administrator John A. Hannah, in announcing the reorganization said, "The new Office will provide leadership within AID in the use of resources in combating hunger and malnutrition and in furthering the economic development of recipient countries. The Office will enable AID to use food supplied under Public Law 480 for stronger support to economic development, family planning, private enterprise, food production and the growth of democratic institutions. It will seek to assure creative and imaginative uses of food resources in development efforts. The Food for Peace Office will maintain liaison between AID and other governmental agencies on PL 480 matters, and will analyze and recommend food assistance programs and projects to other AID bureaus and Offices.” 

The Office of Food for Peace provided leadership, coordination, and operational support for international food activities. The office developed U.S. Government policy, formal positions, and funding levels for grants and cooperative agreements to the World Food Program (WFP), non-governmental organizations (NGOs), and in selected instances governments, implementing food programs.

In 2020, the Office of U.S. Foreign Disaster Assistance (OFDA) and the Office of Food for Peace were combined into the new Bureau for Humanitarian Assistance to streamline USAID humanitarian responses.

War on Hunger, vol. 3, no. 11, November-December 1969: p. 3 (Administrator John A. Hannah has announced a major organizational change in the Agency for International Development as a step toward meeting foreign aid requirements of the 1970s. The establishment of a Technical Assistance Bureau…new Bureau is headed by an Assistant Administrator, Dr. Joel Bernstein, who was sworn in Sept. 24, 1969…An independent Office of Food for Peace aimed at strengthening the use of U. S. food resources in foreign assistance programs has been established by the Agency for International Development. The new Office is headed by a coordinator who is directly responsible to AID Administrator John A. Hannah. Irwin R. Hedges, who has served as Deputy Assistant Administrator for War on Hunger, has assumed the new post. Food for Peace programs were among the functions of the former Office of the War on Hunger. Other War on Hunger activities have been assumed by a new Technical Assistance Bureau. Dr. Hannah, in announcing the reorganization said, “The new Office will provide leadership within AID in the use of resources in combating hunger and malnutrition and in furthering the economic development of recipient countries. The Office will enable AID to use food supplied under Public Law 480 for stronger support to economic development, family planning, private enterprise, food production and the growth of democratic institutions. It will seek to assure creative and imaginative uses of food resources in development efforts. The Food for Peace Office will maintain liaison between AID and other governmental agencies on PL 480 matters, and will analyze and recommend food assistance programs and projects to other AID bureaus and Offices.”)

The Operations Division (DCHA/OFDA/OPS) develops and manages logistical, operational, and technical support for disaster responses. The Division identifies sources for procurement of relief supplies and manages the stockpiling and transportation of those supplies. DCHA/OFDA/OPS maintains readiness to respond to emergencies through several mechanisms, including: Managing Search and Rescue (SAR) Teams, Maintaining the operational status of the Ground Operations Team (GO Team), and Developing and maintaining the Office’s capability to field Disaster Assistance Response Teams (DART) and Response Management Teams (RMT) in Washington. creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Office of U.S. Foreign Disaster Assistance (OFDA) was responsible for leading and coordinating the U.S. government’s response to disasters overseas. OFDA responded to an average disasters to ensure aid reached people affected by rapid-onset disasters—such as earthquakes, volcanoes, and floods—and slow-onset crises, including drought and conflict. OFDA fulfilled its mandate of saving lives, alleviating human suffering, and reducing the social and economic impact of disasters worldwide in partnership with U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) functional and regional bureaus and other U.S. Government agencies. OFDA experts worldwide and in D.C. helped countries prepare for, respond to, and recover from humanitarian crises. OFDA worked with the international humanitarian community to give vulnerable populations resources to build resilience and strengthen their own ability to respond to emergencies

In 2020, the Office of U.S. Foreign Disaster Assistance and the Office of Food for Peace (FFP) were combined into the new Bureau for Humanitarian Assistance to streamline USAID humanitarian responses.
