creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
In January 1952, the International Educational Exchange Service (IES) was established within the new International Information Administration (IIA) and assumed the functions from the former Office of Educational Exchange. The International Educational Exchange Service developed and conducted, directly and by agreement or contract with public or private agencies, programs for the exchange of persons and for assistance to United States sponsored schools; and assisted foreign governments and American and foreign voluntary organizations in undertaking exchange of persons projects.

Effective August 1, 1953, Reorganization Plan No. 8 of 1953 created the United States Information Agency (USIA) to centralize foreign information dissemination programs. USIA absorbed the information functions of the International Information Administration, the Mutual Security Agency, the Technical Cooperation Administration, and foreign information activities financed under the Government of Occupied Areas Appropriation. Educational exchange programs remained in the Department of State, and accordingly the International Educational Exchange Service (IES) was transferred from IIA and became its own office reporting to the Assistant Secretary for Public Affairs. On July 27, 1956, Department Circular No. 199 established a Deputy Assistant Secretary position in the Bureau of Public Affairs for International Information and Cultural Affairs. As a result, IES was moved under the Deputy Assistant Secretary.

On June 1, 1959, the Department of State established the Bureau of International Cultural Relations under a Special Assistant for Coordination of International Education and Cultural Relations. The International Educational Exchange Service moved from the Bureau of Public Affairs to this new Bureau. On April 17, 1960, in accordance with Department Circular 355, dated April 26, the International Educational Exchange Service was abolished.

The IES Assistant Administrator was Russell L. Riley, 1952-1953; and the IES Directors were Russell L. Riley, 1953-1958; Donald D. Edgar, 1958-1959; and Saxton Bradford, Acting, 1960.

II 1957: 3162-3163 (Following the passage of the Smith-Mundt Act (United States Information and Educational Exchange Act, Public Law 402, January 27, 1948) and the granting of additional funds, OIE [Office of Education and Information Exchange] was split into two units (Departmental Announcements 12, 14, 15, April 22, 1948): Office of International Information (OIL) and Office of Educational Exchange (OEX). The Smith-Mundt Act and the Fulbright Act (Public Law 584, August 1, 1946) made possible great expansion of the exchange program. Late in 1949, the Department of State created (see Public Notice 34 March 6, 1950) the position of a General Manager, who was made responsible for formulating and executing the over-all International Information and Educational Exchange Program (IE), within the directives of the Assistant Secretary for Public Affairs. On January 16, 1952, a major reorganization (Departmental Announcement 4) established the International Information Administration (IIA), described as a “semiautonomous” unit in the Department." The Administrator of the new unit combined the duties of the General Manager of IE with most of the overseas information responsibilities of the Assistant Secretary for Public Affairs, reporting directly to the Secretary and Under Secretary of State. The United States Information Agency (USIA) was established on August 1, 1953,” as independent of the Department of State, but subject to policy guidance therefrom. USIA also absorbed the information functions of the Mutual Security Agency and the Technical Cooperation Administration, already to some extent integrated under IIA. The exchange program under the Fulbright and Smith-Mundt Acts and certain other legislation remained in the Department of State to be administered by the International Educational Exchange Service (IES) under the Assistant Secretary for Public Affairs.)

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The American Aid Program in the Sudan began in the spring of 1958, when the Sudanese Government decided to seek the assistance of the United States in order to prepare itself to speed up development of its economic potential. Diplomatic relations between the two countries were interrupted as a consequence of the Six-Day War, but after a more than five-year break in diplomatic relations and the absence of an AID program, Sudan and the United States resumed diplomatic relations on July 25, 1972.

Following a request for economic assistance from the Government of Sudan, an eight-day visit was made by an AID team at the beginning of September 1972 to discuss Sudan's development problems and priorities. The team's report showed that balance of payments assistance, either through programs grants or loans, was the Government of Sudan's principal requirement, and that agriculture and transportation were foremost among Sudan's development investment priorities.

An AID Affairs Office was set up as a section of the American Embassy in Khartoum in late June 1973.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Disaster Response Division (DRD) was responsible for the aid given in response to disasters and crises that occur overseas. The Division provided humanitarian assistance in response to a declaration of a foreign disaster made by a US Ambassador or the Department of State. In 2001 the Division was renamed the Disaster Response and Mitigation Division (DRM), which was responsible for coordinating with other organizations for the provision of relief supplies and humanitarian assistance. The Division devised, coordinated, and implemented program strategies for the application of science and technology to prevention, mitigation, and national and international preparedness initiatives for a variety of natural and human-caused disaster situations.

U.S. Agency for International Development ADS Chapter 101 Agency Program and Functions, 2020: p. 89, 143 (Bureau for Humanitarian Assistance (BHA) Effective Date: 07/07/2020 The Bureau for Humanitarian Assistance (BHA) fulfills the role of USAID as the lead U.S. Government (USG) Agency for responding to emergencies and disasters overseas with both food and non-food emergency assistance. As the successor to the Offices of U.S. Foreign Disaster Assistance (OFDA) and Food for Peace (FFP) in the Bureau for Democracy, Conflict, and Humanitarian Assistance (DCHA); Bureau for Democracy, Conflict, and Humanitarian Assistance (DCHA) Effective Date: 07/07/2020 Note 1: BHA became operational on June 5, 2020. Information related to the former DCHA offices (OFDA and FFP) is incorporated in the BHA functional statement (see section 101.3.1.16). Note 2: CPS [Bureau for Conflict Prevention and Stabilization] became operational on July 7, 2020. Information related to the former DCHA offices (CMM, CMC, OTI, PPM) is incorporated in the CPS functional statement (see section 101.3.1.18).)

U.S. Agency for International Development ADS Chapter 101 Agency Program and Functions, May 20, 2019: p. 144-147 (Bureau for Democracy, Conflict, and Humanitarian Assistance (DCHA) Effective Date: 11/06/2014 Office of U.S. Foreign Disaster Assistance (DCHA/OFDA). The Disaster Response and Mitigation Division (DCHA/OFDA/DRM) coordinates with USAID offices and others to provide relief supplies and humanitarian assistance. DCHA/OFDA/DRM plans for the level of response needed for an emergency and implements and manages U.S. Government disaster relief and rehabilitation programs worldwide. The Division devises, coordinates, and implements program strategies for the application of the most current science and technology for prevention, mitigation, and national and international preparedness for a variety of natural and man-made disaster situations. DCHA/OFDA/DRM evaluates the impact of previous disaster response initiatives/programs and ensures the integration of this information into future planning and response activities. The Division coordinates with other USAID geographic Bureaus’ donor organizations, United Nations agencies, non-governmental organizations, and private voluntary organizations)

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Office of Environment and Urban Programs (G/ENV/UP) lead the Agency for International Development's (USAID) Making Cities Work strategy, ensuring that sustainable urban management was properly addressed in the Strategic Frameworks of the Agency's operating units. The Office provided policy formulation, design, and implementation support for urban programs that create the policies, institutions, and financing mechanisms needed to enable cities to provide a full range of environmental services and infrastructure; to attract investment in shelter, community facilities, and environmental improvement; and to promote private enterprise. G/ENV/UP facilitated access to outside technical expertise from a broad range of Sustainable Urban Management contractors. The Office assisted USAID Missions and carried out regional activities worldwide through staff based in Regional Urban Development Offices (RUDOs) overseas.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: Since the contracting of its first Housing Guaranty Loan Agreement in 1963, the Office of Housing and Urban Programs has played a role within the Agency for International Development (USAID) and within the international donor community as a leader in the urban development field. The Office worked with USAID mission in developing countries primarily in the areas of housing and related infrastructure, local government, and urban environment. This role was facilitated by the Office's presence in all of the developing areas of the world through its Regional Housing and Urban Development Offices (RHUDOs) and Mission Housing Offices in Latin America, the Caribbean, Asia, Africa, the Near East, and most recently in Eastern Europe and the New Independent States of the former Soviet Union.  The Office also represented USAID and the U.S. Government in international conferences and meetings involving urban programs; maintained contact with U.S. and international institutions active in the field, organized training events, and disseminated information derived from USAID field work and research and development. In 1994, the Office became a unit of the Center for the Environoment and it's name changed to the Office of Environment and Urban Programs.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Office of the Controller advised and assisted the Mission Director in discharging his responsibility for the financial management of the Mission program. The Controller participated in the formulation and review of existing programs; insured appropriate financial execution of Mission program budgets; reviewed administrative expense estimates and staffing patterns and insured that justifications were appropriate; insured that obligations and expenditures were within allotment limitations; classified obligations and expenditures as between program and administrative allotments; established and maintained accounting records and controls; prepared timely financial reports; audited and certified vouchers as required; and conducted audits concerning project and non-project commodities, counterpart funds, other local currency, procurement practices, and contracts.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: Until 1964 Zambia had been a colony of the British Empire, first as Northern Rhodesia and then as a part of the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland. On December 31, 1963, the federation was dissolved into Rhodesia and Northern Rhodesia. On October 24, 1964, Northern Rhodesia gained full independence as the Republic of Zambia. The United States immediately recognized the new nation and moved to establish diplomatic relations. An embassy in Lusaka was established on October 24, 1964, and Robert C. Foulon was appointed as Chargé d’Affaires ad interim pending the appointment of an ambassador. The first ambassador, Robert C. Good was appointed on March 11, 1965. All U.S. Ambassadors to Zambia have held the official title Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary. The U.S. Ambassador to Zambia served concurrently as the U.S. Representative to the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA).

Turkey severed diplomatic relations with the United States on April 20, 1917, after the United States declared war against Germany /wiki/United_States_declaration_of_war_on_Germany_(1917) on April 4, 1917. Normal diplomatic relations were reestablished in 1927.[1]

After Ankara's designation as capital of the Turkish Republic in 1923, the functions of the Embassy were gradually transferred there. The last American ambassador resident in Istanbul, John Van A. MacMurray, moved to Ankara in 1937.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The area on the Horn of Africa on which Djibout is situated had been under French control since 1885 as part of the protectorate of French Somaliland. The area was ruled by the Vichy (French) government from the fall of France in 1940 until December 1942, but Free French and the Allied forces recaptured Djibouti at the end of 1942. In 1957 the colony was given a large measure of self-government and became the French Territory of the Afars and the Issas. In a May 1977 referendum the populace chose independence from France. The Republic of Djibouti was established on

June 27, 1977. The United States immediately recognized the new nation of Djibouti and moved to establish diplomatic relations, and the U.S. Embassy at Djibouti was established on June 27, 1977, with the elevation of the Consulate General. Walter S. Clarke, Charge d'Affaires ad interim, was chief of mission.

The first Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary, Jerrold M. North, presented his credentials on October 27, 1980. He was succeeded by Alvin P. Adams, July 16, 1983; and John Pierce Ferriter, September 30, 1985. Ambassador Ferriter left Djibouti on August 27, 1987; John E. McAteer served as Charge d'Affaires ad interim from August 1987 through September 1988. The next Ambassador, Robert South Barrett IV, presented his credentials on September 5, 1988. He was succeeded by Charles R. Baquet, III, October 10, 1991, and Martin L. Cheshes, January 19, 1994. Ambassador Cheshes departed Djibouti on July 30, 1996. Joseph Phillippe Gregoire served as Charge d'Affaires ad interim from July through September 1996, followed by Terri Robi, September 1996 through January 1998.

Lange Schermerhorn presented his credentials on January 26, 1998. He was succeeded by Donald Y. Yamamoto, who presented his credentials on December 9, 2000.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Bureau of International Commerce was established by Departmental Order 182 of February 1, 1963, consolidating the Bureau of International Programs and the Bureau of International Business Operations. It was responsible for promoting U.S. foreign trade and assisting U.S. businesses abroad. 

On November 17, 1972, the Bureau of Domestic Commerce (BDC) consolidated with the Bureau of International Commerce to form Domestic and International Business Administration. The Administration was responsible for promoting U.S. foreign and domestic commerce, stimulating exports, and planning industrial mobilization. It was abolished, with functions transferred to the Industry and Trade Administration on December 4, 1977.

The International Trade Administration was established in the Department of Commerce by Reorganization Plan No. 3 of 1979, effective January 2, 1980. The Administration promoted world trade and strengthened the international trade and investment position of the United States. It formulated and implemented international economic policy; developed and implemented policies and programs relating to import and export administration; managed an integrated trade development program throughout U.S. industry; and collected, analyzed, and disseminated information on U.S. industrial sectors.

International Trade Administration, Sept. 9, 2015 (The International Trade Administration (ITA) strengthens the competitiveness of U.S. industry, promotes trade and investment, and ensures fair trade through the rigorous enforcement of our trade laws and agreements.  ITA works to improve the global business environment and helps U.S. organizations compete at home and abroad.  ITA supports President Obama’s recovery agenda and the National Export Initiative to sustain economic growth and support American jobs.  ITA is organized into three distinct but complementary business units: The Global Markets unit combines ITA’s country and regional experts, overseas and domestic field staff, and specific trade promotion programs to provide U.S. firms with the full suite of country-specific export promotion services and market access advocacy, while promoting the United States as an investment destination. The Industry and Analysis (I&A) unit brings together ITA’s industry, trade, and economic experts to advance the competitiveness of U.S. industries through the development and execution of international trade and investment policies and promotion strategies. I&A will leverage ITA’s relationships with manufacturing and services industries to increase U.S. exports. The Enforcement and Compliance unit enhances ITA’s responsibilities to enforce U.S. trade laws and ensure compliance with trade agreements negotiated on behalf of U.S. industry. 
On October 1, 2013, ITA implemented a consolidation into these three business units. As a convenience, please consult our concordance list from our previous organizational structure. ITA MISSION Create prosperity by strengthening the international competitiveness of U.S. industry, promoting trade and investment, and ensuring fair trade and compliance with trade laws and agreements. creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The United States Agency for International Development (USAID) created the Task Force on Humanitarian Assistance in Central America (TFHA) in response to a congressional mandate of April 1, 1988 (102 Stat 62) to administer a high-priority program of humanitarian assistance to the Nicaraguan Democratic Resistance, medical care and relief to child victims of the Nicaraguan civil strife, and support to the Verification Commission established to verify compliance with the Sapoa (peace) agreement. The program was enacted pursuant to U.S. policy to advance peace and democracy in Central America, and to preserve and protect U.S. security interests in the region. TFHA reported directly to the USAID Administrator and Ted D. Morse was made its director on April 1, 1988. TFHA established offices in Washington and in Honduras, and held a presence in Costa Rica.  Mr. William Schoux headed the Honduras Office. The program was to end on September 30, 1988; however legislation (102 Stat 2270-53) on October 1, 1988 passed to continue the program through March 31, 1989

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Trade and Development Program (TDP) was established July 1, 1980, pursuant to the provisions of Reorganization Plan No. 2 of 1979 (93 Stat. 1379), to promote economic development in Third World countries and the sale of U.S. goods and services to those countries. TDP, the successor to the Reimbursable Development Program of the Agency for International Development, had substantial day-to-day autonomy while receiving policy and budget guidance from the U.S. International Development Cooperation Agency (IDCA). TDP supported feasibility studies for projects that could be financed by developing countries and undertook by U.S. private industry or Government agencies. TDP operated under the authority of section 607(a) and 661 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 (75 Stat. 424). TDP served as the coordinating and authorizing agency for the provision of government-to-government technical assistance on a reimbursable basis, involving many U.S. agencies or direct host-government contracts with U.S. private firms for project implementation. TDP planning services included: surveys to identify potential projects, conceptual design and pre-feasibility studies, feasibility studies, and design engineering. The TDP helped U.S. industry compete more effectively with other industrialized countries for major development projects in the Third World.

On August 23, 1988, section 2204 of the Omnibus Trade and Competitiveness Act of 1988 (102 Stat. 1328) made the organization a separate component agency of the International Development Cooperation Agency. The organization was renamed, the U.S. Trade and Development Agency, and made an independent agency within the executive branch of the Federal Government on October 28, 1992, by the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 as amended by the Jobs Through Exports Act of 1992 (106 Stat. 3655).

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The U.S. Trade and Development Agency (USTDA), formerly the Trade and Development Program of the International Development Cooperation Agency, was made an independent agency within the executive branch of the Federal Government on October 28, 1992, by the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 as amended by the Jobs Through Exports Act of 1992 (106 Stat. 3655).

The Agency operated under the authority of section 661 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 (75 Stat. 424), which provided funding for planning services including feasibility studies, orientation visits, and trade-related training to assist U.S. firms in becoming involved in development projects having substantial U.S. export potential in project implementation. It funded planning services, such as feasibility studies, for high-priority development projects that were financed by the World Bank or other international financial institutions, or from the host country's own resources. The funded services were performed only by U.S. firms. The Agency could also serve as the coordinating and authorizing agency for the provision of government-to-government technical assistance on a fully reimbursable basis.

By 2012, USTDA's mission was to help companies create U.S. jobs through the export of U.S. goods and services for priority development projects in emerging economies. USTDA linked U.S. businesses to export opportunities by funding project planning activities, pilot projects, and reverse trade missions while creating sustainable infrastructure and economic growth in partner countries.

Following the dissolution of the Austro-Hungarian empire in 1918 at the end of World War I, the Czechs, Moravians, and Slovaks united to form the new nation of Czechoslovakia. The United States recognized Czechoslovakia and commissioned its first ambassador on April 23, 1919. The first Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary, Richard Crane, presented his credentials on June 11, 1919. He was succeeded by Lewis Einstein, December 20, 1921; Abraham C. Ratshesky, May 2, 1930; Francis White, September 7, 1933; J. Butler Wright, October 25, 1934; and Wilbur J. Carr, September 16, 1937. 

German forces occupied Prague (Praha) on March 15, 1939, and Carr closed the Legation on March 21, 1939, leaving Prague on April 6. The United States had no representation to Czechoslovakia until 1941, when it chose to treat with the Czech Government in exile in London. Anthony J. Drexel Biddle, Jr. was appointed Envoy on September 17, 1941, and presented his credentials on October 28, 1941. (Biddle was also the U.S. envoy to Belgium, Greece, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Norway, Poland, and Yugoslavia. He was resident in London.) On July 12, 1943, Biddle presented his credentials as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary; he departed London on December 1, 1943.

Rudolph E. Schoenfeld was serving as Charge d'Affaires ad interim when the Embassy to the Czech government in exile was closed. The Embassy in Prague reopened on May 29, 1945, with Alfred W. Klieforth as Charge d'Affaires ad interim.

The next Ambassador, Laurence A. Steinhardt, presented his credentials on July 20, 1945. He was succeeded by Joseph E. Jacobs, January 5, 1949; Ellis O. Briggs, November 8, 1949; George Wadsworth, December 29, 1952; U. Alexis Johnson, December 31, 1953; John M. Allison, April 24, 1958; Christian M. Ravndal, September 16, 1960; Edward T. Wailes, July 28, 1961; Outerbridge Horsey, January 3, 1963; Jacob D. Beam, August 31, 1966; Malcolm Toon, July 31, 1969; Albert W. Sherer, Jr., March 15, 1972; Thomas R. Byrne, June 23, 1976; Francis J. Meehan, May 30, 1979; Jack F. Matlock, Jr., November 11, 1981; William H. Luers, December 29, 1983; Julian Martin Niemczyk, October 2, 1986; Shirley Temple Black, August 23, 1989; and Adrian Bosora, July 20, 1992.

In June 1992, the Slovak parliament voted to declare sovereignty and the Czech-Slovak federation dissolved peacefully on January 1, 1993. The United States recognized the Czech Republic and Slovakia as independent nations and moved to establish diplomatic relations. The previous ambassador to Czechoslovakia, Adrian A. Basora, continued as the ambassador to the Czech Republic.

U.S. Military Government Courts for Germany was established as an independent unit of OMGUS pursuant to Military Government Ordinance No. 31 (August 18, 1948). These courts were an integrated system of eleven district courts and a court of appeals. The court officers were appointed by the Military Governor and reported to him. This system superseded the summary and intermediate military government courts, previously part of the Administration of Justice Branch of the OMGUS Legal Division and the Military Government Court for Civil Actions.

The U.S. Courts for Germany were established by Staff Announcement No. 1, HICOG, September 21, 1949, with organization and functions set forth in Staff Announcement No. 5, HICOG, September 21, 1949. They succeeded the U.S. Military Government Courts for Germany and formed an independent judicial unit responsible to the High Commissioner.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Evaluation, Development Information and Economic and Social Data Services offices were combined into one operation to form the Center for Development Information and Evaluation (CDIE).  This reorganized and combined Agency for International Development's (AID) central evaluation and information functions for a new perspective on AID's development programs.

The objective of CDIE was to improve the quality of AID and least developed countries (LDC) programs.  CDIE contributed to this object through its leadership of the Agency's evaluation programs and its dissemination of experience with development programs.  The Center was to strengthen the AID's application of its experience through improving the quality and usefulness of development information; improving AID access to evaluation findings, development statistics and project and technical documentation through satellite development information centers in AID Bureaus and Missions; increasing the circulation of impact evaluation findings in forms appropriate to AID managers and project and technical staff; arranging workshops, video presentations, and other educational methods to expose staff to AID and other Agency experience; introducing evaluation findings directly into Agency programming; and improving the AID's decentralized project evolution system with greater discipline in the conduct of evolutions and the use of evolution findings and recommendations.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Development Information Division (DI) was responsible for the Agency for International Development's (USAID) library and in disseminating copies of USAID technical and research reports produced by USAID or USAID contractors; non-USAID development-related books and journals; summaries of USAID projects; agricultural information; technical information; compilations of USAID and other donor project and program experiences; other reference services; information from the microcomputer based Development Information System; and micrographics.  DI produced AID Research and Development Abstracts (ARDA) and selected bibliographies.  DI assisted USAID missions in establishing development information resource centers, improving their document collections, and in using automated technologies and methodologies to improve their access to development information.  ID trained staff on various databases and the Development Information System.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Bureau for Management provided centralized administrative services which included: logistical, financial, operational program support, information technology, and procurement services for the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID).  The Bureau focused on the following priority issues: the Agency operating expense budget; consolidation of USAID and Department of State support services; domestic space management; performance management; overseas space; the Global Acquisition and Assistance System (GLAAS) deployment; enterprise architecture; International Cooperative Administrative Support Services (ICASS); and the Continuity of Operations Program (COOP).

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: President John Tyler appointed the first U.S. consul to Jerusalem in 1844. A permanent consular presence was established in 1857, in a building just inside the Jaffa Gate in the Old City. The mission was designated a Consulate General in 1928. It represented the United States in Jerusalem, the West Bank, and the Gaza Strip as an independent mission, with the Consul General serving as chief of mission.On 23 May 1948 the Consul General, Thomas C. Wasson, who was alos a member of the UN Truce Commission, was assassinated.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
Somalia was formed July 1, 1960, from the unification of the British protectorate of Somaliland with Italian Somaliland. The United States immediately recognized the Somali government and moved to establish diplomatic relations. The U.S. Embassy in the capital Mogadiscio (now Mogadishu) was established on June 25, 1960. Andrew G. Lynch as Chargé d'Affaires served as the ad interim. He was promoted to Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary four days later on July 5, 1960.The American Embassy closed on January 5, 1991, and all U.S. personnel were withdrawn after the collapse of the Siad Barre government. 

Although the U.S. never formally severed diplomatic relations with Somalia, the U.S. Embassy in Somalia has been closed since 1991. The United States maintains regular dialogue with the Transitional Federal Government and other key stakeholders in Somalia through the U.S. Embassy in Nairobi, Kenya. Consular coverage for Somalia was also maintained by U.S. Embassy Nairobi, while American Citizens Services in the self-declared Republic of Somaliland were provided by the U.S. Embassy in Djibouti.

The U.S. Embassy in Mogadishu was re-opened on December 2, 2018, under the direction of Ambassador Donald Yamamoto. U.S. Embassy Nairobi continued to handle consular coverage for Somalia.

The Somali Republic was formed by the union of Somalia, which previously had been under Italian administration as a United Nations trust territory, and Somaliland, which had been a British protectorate until June 26, 1960. Diplomatic relations were established on July 1, 1960, when the U.S. Consulate General at Mogadiscio (now Mogadishu) was elevated to Embassy status, with Andrew G. Lynch as Chargé d’Affaires. The U.S. Embassy in Mogadishu was re-opened on December 2, 2018, under the direction of Ambassador Donald Yamamoto. U.S. Embassy Nairobi continued to handle consular coverage for Somalia.) https://history.state.gov/countries/somalia#:~:text=Re%2Dopening%20of%20the%20U.S.,handle%20consular%20coverage%20for%20Somalia.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
From the partitioning of the Ottoman Empire in 1922 until 1944, Syria had been under the control of France as a part of the League of Nations French Mandate of Syria and Lebanon. The United States appointed George Wadsworth as Agent and Consul General to Syria and Lebanon on October 9, 1942, to provide a quasi-diplomatic presence in Damascus. 

The United States recognized Syria as an independent state on September 8, 1944, when the Syrian Minister of Foreign Affairs, Jamil Mardam Bey, informed the United States that Syria fully recognized and would protect existing rights of the United States and its nationals. This Syrian assurance was in response to a letter sent on September 7, 1944, by the U.S. Diplomatic Agent and Consul General in Syria that offered “full and unconditional recognition” upon receipt of such written assurances. The United States established diplomatic relations with Syria when George Wadsworth presented his credentials as Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary on November 17, 1944. Wadsworth was concurrently the envoy to Syria and Lebanon while resident in Beirut.

The mission was upgraded to an embassy, and the Ambassador presented his credentials to the Syrian government on September 30, 1952. On February 22, 1958, Syria was incorporated, with Egypt, into the United Arab Republic, and the U.S. Embassy in Damascus was re-classified as a Consulate General, effective February 25, 1958. Syria seceded from the Union in 1961 and the mission was re-established as an Embassy on October 10, 1961, but during the Israel-Arab War of 1967, Syria severed relations with the United States, June 6, 1967, and the Ambassador departed the post two days later. In the interim a U.S. Interests Section in Syria was established on February 8, 1974, in the Italian Embassy with Thomas J. Scotes as Principal Officer.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: Until 1955 French Togoland was a United Nations Trust Territory mandated by the U.N. to France. In 1955, French Togoland became the autonomous Republic of Togo within the French Community (Communauté française), although it retained its UN trusteeship status. In 1960 Togo severed its constitutional ties with France, shed its UN trusteeship status, and became fully independent as the Togolese Republic.The United States immediately recognized Togo and moved to establish diplomatic relations. The State Department established an embassy in Yaoundé in nearby Cameroon on January 1, 1960, with Bolard More as Chargé d'affaires ad interim. The Yaoundé embassy was simultaneously accredited to Togo. The embassy in Lomé was established on April 27, 1960, with Jesse M. MacKnight as Chargé d’Affaires ad interim. On June 23, 1960, Leland Barrows was appointed as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to Cameroon with separate accreditation to Togo while remaining resident in Yaoundé. In 1961 a separate ambassador was appointed solely for Togo and resident at Lomé.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The nation of Yugoslavia was formed on December 1, 1918 as a result of the realignment of nations and national boundaries in Europe in the aftermath of The Great War. The nation was first named the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes and was renamed the Kingdom of Yugoslavia in 1929. The kingdom occupied the area in the Balkans comprising the present-day states of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia, Montenegro, Republic of Macedonia, and most of present-day Slovenia and Croatia. The United States recognized the newly formed nation and commissioned its first envoy to the kingdom on July 17, 1919. Previously the USA had had an envoy extraordinary and minister plenipotentiary who was commissioned to Romania, Bulgaria, and Serbia while resident in Bucharest, Romania. Towards the end of the 1930s, the diplomatic relations between Belgrade and Washington were raised from ministerial to the ambassadorial level.

In anticipation of the German occupation, the Legation closed on May 17, 1941. An envoy extraordinary was credentialed to the Yugoslav government-in-exile in England on October 3, 1941, with Anthony J. Drexel Biddle, Jr. as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary and residing in London, England. The Mission was upgraded to an embassy on November 3, 1942. The Yugoslav government-in-exile took residence in Egypt from September 28, 1943 to March 11, 1944. The Embassy moved to Belgrade on March 31, 1945.

After the breakup of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in 1992, the remnants of the nation, comprising the Republics of Serbia and Montenegro, renamed itself the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. On May 21, 1992, the United States announced that it did not recognize the Federal Republic. The ambassador had left Belgrade one week earlier. A series of chargés d’affaires represented the U.S. government until March 23, 1999, when the embassy was closed. The last Embassy personel left the next day and NATO armed forces began military action against Serbia-Montenegro that evening.

In 2001 the United States recognized the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and commissioned an ambassador to Belgrade. In 2003 the parliament of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia ratified the Constitutional Charter, establishing a new state union and changing the name of the country from Yugoslavia to Serbia and Montenegro. The U.S. ambassador continued in his post as the ambassador to Serbia and Montenegro.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The official American presence in Zagreb goes back at least to 1920, when the American Consulate in Zagreb, Kingdom of the Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes, was established. The Consulate remained open in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia until after World War II began in Europe. Until then the consular district was comprised of the Banovine (Provinces) of Drava, Sava, Vrbas, Primorska (sea coast) and in the Banovina of Zeta, the western portion only, as included in the administrative inspectorates of Dubrovnik and Cetinje. This included roughly the territories formerly known as Slovenia, Croatia-Slavonia, western Bosnia, Dalmatia, Hercegovina, and Montenegro. On April 6, 1941, German forces invaded Yugoslvia and on April 10, captured Zagreb. On that same date the fascist Nezavisna Država Hrvatska (Independent State of Croatia) was founded. American diplomatic personnel departed between May 1 and 14, 1941.

The Consulate in Zagreb was reopened after the war on May 9, 1946 and was initially housed in small offices near the Botanical Garden. In 1951, the government of Yugoslavia donated a building now known as Hebrangova 2 to the U.S. Government and, in 1953, the Consulate moved into the building that it was to occupy for the next fifty years. The Consulate was elevated to the status of Consulate General on August 1, 1958, and the first Consul General arrived later that year.

On August 25, 1992, the Consulate General was elevated to the status of Embassy after the establishment of diplomatic relations between the United States of America and the new Republic of Croatia.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Interdepartmental Committee on Trade Agreements, also known as the Trade Agreements Committee (TAC), was established after the enactment of the Reciprocal Trade Agreements Act of 1934 (48 Stat. 943), approved June 12, 1934, to develop proposals for trade negotiations. On June 23, 1934, Secretary of State Cordell Hull wrote to the heads of executive branch departments and agencies concerned with matters of foreign trade. He asked them to designate representatives to serve on the Committee. Executive Orders 9832 (February 25, 1947), 10004 (October 5, 1948), 10082 (October 5, 1949), and 10170 (October 12, 1950) modified the Committee's functions. TAC was established to serve as the central agency of the interdepartmental trade agreements organization; to analyze and consider studies by the Tariff Commission, the Department of Commerce, views presented to the Committee for Reciprocity Information, and other information relating to trade agreements; and to make recommendations to the President on the conclusion of trade agreements. The Committee consisted of representatives of the Department of State (chair and secretary), the Department of Agriculture, the Department of Commerce, the Department of Labor, the Department of Defense (replacing the War Department and the Department of Navy in 1947), the Department of the Treasury, and other agencies of interest, including the Tariff Commission. TAC was terminated by Executive Order 11075 of January 15, 1963, which also created the Office of the Special Representative for Trade Negotiations (STR). STR absorbed the functions of TAC.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The United States opened diplomatic relations with Gabon in 1960. Alan W. Lukens, resident at Brazzaville, Congo Republic, presented his credentials as Charge d'Affaires ad interim on August 17, 1960. W. Wendell Blancke presented his credentials as non-resident Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary on January 13, 1961. During his tenure, the Embassy at Libreville was established, March 20, 1961. The resident ambassador at Libreville was also non-resident ambassador to São Tomé and Príncipe.

The first resident Ambassador, Charles F. Darlington, presented his credentials on October 18, 1961. He was succeeded by David M. Bane, August 14, 1965; Richard Funkhouser, August 9, 1969; John A. McKesson, III, February 4, 1971; and Andrew L. Steigman, August 9, 1975. Beginning with Ambassador Steigman, the U.S. Ambassador to Gabon was also accredited to the Democratic Republic of Sao Tome and Principe, but maintained residence at Libreville. Steigman was succeeded by Arthur T. Tienken, March 6, 1978; Francis Terry McNamara, January 19, 1982; Larry C. Williamson, November 20, 1984; Warren Clark, Jr., September 19, 1987; Keith Leveret Wauchope, December 8, 1989; Joseph Charles Wilson IV, September 17, 1992; Elizabeth Raspolic, November 29, 1995; and James Vela Ledesman, December 16, 1998. Thomas F. Daughton served as Charge d'Affaires ad interim from June 2001 through June 2002. The next Ambassador, Kenneth Price Moorfield, presented his credentials on June 20, 2002.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The country that is now Tanzania comprises the former countries of Tanganyika and Zanzibar. Tanganyika achieved independence from the United Kingdom in December 1961. The United States immediately recognized the new nation and moved to establish diplomatic relations. An embassy in Dar es Salaam was established on December 9, 1961. William R. Duggan was appointed as chargé d'affaires ad interim pending the appointment of an ambassador. The first ambassador, William Leonhart was appointed Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary on August 22, 1962, and presented his credentials to the government on October 3, 1962.

Zanzibar received its independence from the United Kingdom on December 19, 1963, as a constitutional monarchy under the sultan. The U.S. established an embassy in Zanzibar on December 10, 1963, with Frederick P. Picard III as chargé d'affaires ad interim.

On April 26, 1964, Tanganyika united with Zanzibar to form the United Republic of Tanganyika and Zanzibar. The country was renamed the United Republic of Tanzania on October 29, 1964.

An ambassador to Zanzibar had not yet been appointed when that country was united with the Tanganyika. Frank C. Carlucci III was serving as chargé d'affaires ad interim in Zanzibar when the embassy was downgraded to a U.S. consulate on June 27, 1964. Ambassador Leonhart in Dar es Salaam continued to serve as the ambassador to Tanzania.

On August 7, 1998, a bomb detonated outside the U.S. Embassy at Dar es Salaam, killing seven Foreign Service nationals and three Tanzanian citizens, and injuring one U.S. citizen and 76 Tanzanians. The explosion caused major structural damage to the Embassy. The U.S. held Osama Bin Laden responsible.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: Until 1962 Rwanda had been a part of the United Nations Trust Territory of Ruanda-Urundi under the trusteeship of Belgium. In June 1962 the UN General Assembly terminated the Belgian trusteeship and granted full independence to Rwanda and Burundi. The United States immediately recognized the Rwandan government on its independence day, July 1, 1962, and moved to establish diplomatic relations. The U.S. Embassy in the capital Kigali was established on July 1, 1962, with David J.S. Manbey as Chargé d'Affaires ad interim. Charles D. Withers was appointed as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to Rwanda on March 9, 1963.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Office of Population and Reproductive Health provided strategic direction, technical leadership, and support to field programs in population, voluntary family planning, and related reproductive health. It managed programs that advanced and applied state-of-the-art technologies, expanded access to quality services, promoted healthy behaviors, broadened contraceptive availability and choices, and strengthened policies and systems to address family planning and reproductive health needs. 

The Office provided input to decisions concerning the strategic allocation of financial and human resources in the sector and assisted in designing, implementing, monitoring, and evaluating programs; provided a broad range of technical assistance to field missions; ensured compliance with congressional and Administration priorities, directives, and restrictions; and provided information on USAID's population, family planning and reproductive health programs.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Bureau for Global Health (GH) was the Agency's focal point in providing leadership and technical expertise in the areas of child and maternal health and nutrition, HIV/AIDS, infectious disease, population, family planning and related reproductive health, and health systems. It was a primary source of technical expertise to the Agency and other U.S. foreign affairs agencies.  The Bureau provided grants, cooperative agreements, contracts, and indefinite quantity contracts, and technical expertise to carry out the Agency's global health goals and to facilitate programmatic technical support to field missions. It also provided field offices the technical and logistical support needed to meet these goals, which includes collaboration with other donors and USG partners. GH helped ensure compliance with congressional directives and legislative intentions, and contributed technical content for overall program evaluation and performance measurement. The Bureau assisted in workforce planning, recruitment, development, and assignment of headquarters and field staff in the population, health, and nutrition (PHN) sector.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
Albania had been under the domination of the Ottoman Empire since the 14th century but gained a tenuous independence in 1912 after an uprising against the Turks. After suffering invasions and occupations during the First and Second Balkan Wars and the Great War, Albania achieved a relatively stable degree of statehood.

The United States extended de jure recognition to the Government of Albania on July 22, 1922, and opened a legation on December 4, 1922. Following the Italian invasion and takeover of Albania in 1939 the latter abolished its own foreign office. The State Department decided to withdraw U.S. diplomatic and consular representation and on July 11 the U.S. Minister announced that he was closing the Legation the following week. But it was not until September 16, 1939, that all business was concluded and the Legation closed. A U.S. mission operated in Albania shortly after World War II but it was not until March 15, 1991, that the United States reopened diplomatic relations with Albania. The U.S. Embassy at Tirana was established on October 1, 1991.

Serving as Envoys Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary, with dates of their presentation of credentials, were Ulysses Grant-Smith, December 4, 1922; Charles C. Hart, August 1, 1925; Post Wheeler, November 28, 1933; and Hugh Gladney Grant, November 8, 1935.

Following the opening of Embassy Tirana in 1991 the following served as Ambassadors Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary: William Edwin Ryerson, December 21, 1991; Joseph Edward Lake, October 17, 1994; Marisa R. Lino, September 4, 1996; Joseph Limprecht, September 8, 1999 (Ambassador Limprecht died in northern Albania, May 19, 2002); and James Franklin Jeffrey, October 22, 2002 - May 2, 2004; Marcie B. Ries, October 30, 2004 - JUne 16, 2007; and John L. Withers, 2nd, August 29, 2007 - .

In June 2008, allegations surfaced in the media that U.S. Ambassador John Withers and five other members of the U.S. Embassy country team in Tirana were involved in efforts to cover up facts related to the sale of Chinese-origin munitions to the U.S. Department of Defense in contravention of U.S. law. The matter was referred for review to the Department of State Inspector General who subsequently found nothing to substantiate criminal or any other allegations concerning Department of State employees.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Algerian Government had recognized the United States in 1795, but formal diplomatic relations were not established, although the United States had consular representation in Algeria intermittently since 1796. France began to colonize Algeria in 1830 and until 1962, Algeria was under the dominion of France. Independence from France was formally declared on July 3, 1962. The United States and France both formally recognized Algeria on that same day.

The U.S. Embassy at Algiers was established on September 29, 1962 with William J. Porter as Charge d'Affaires ad interim. It was closed on June 10, 1967, after Algeria severed diplomatic relations with the United States. A U.S. Interests Section was maintained in the Swiss Embassy, ca. September 1967 - July 1974. The U.S. Embassy was re-established on November 12, 1974.

Serving as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary, with dates of presentation of credentials, were William J. Porter, December 17, 1962; John D. Jernegan, October 13, 1965; Richard B. Parker, January 17, 1975; Ulric St. Clair Haynes, Jr., July 13, 1977; Michael H. Newlin, October 28, 1981; L. Craig Johnstone, September 9, 1985; Christopher W.S. Ross, September 20, 1988; Mary Ann Casey, September 8, 1991; Ronald E. Neumann, September 18, 1994; Cameron R. Hume, December 28, 1997; and Janet A. Sanderson, October 30, 2000.

Principal officers of the U.S. Interests Section were Lewis Hoffacker, September 1967 - November 1969 and William L. Eagleton, Jr., December 1969 - July 1974.

From the mid-1990's the official U.S. presence in Algeria was limited owing to security concerns. This began to improve after a decade, reflecting the general improvement in the security environment, and the U.S. Embassy has moved toward more normal operations to provide most embassy services to the American and Algerian communities.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
Until 1971, Bahrain had been part of a British protectorate along with the other sheikhdoms in the Persian Gulf. In 1971 the protectorate ended and seven of the other sheikhdoms joined in a federation to become the United Arab Emirates. Bahrain, however, did not join the federation, but declared its independence on August 15, 1971. The United States recognized the State of Bahrain on on the same day and moved to establish diplomatic relations.

The U.S. Embassy, Barain, was established at Manama on September 21, 1971, with John N. Gatch, Jr., as Charge d'Affaires ad interim. The first Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary, William A. Stoltzfus, Jr., presented his credentials on February 17, 1972. He was also accredited to Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, and the United Arab Emirates and was resident at Kuwait. The first ambassador commissioned solely to Bahrain was Joseph W. Twinam in 1974.

Stoltzfus was succeeded by Joseph W. Twinam, June 10, 1974; Wat T. Cluverius, 4th, October 23, 1976; Robert H. Pelletreau, Jr., March 10, 1979; Peter A. Sutherland, July 12, 1980; Donald C. Leidel, November 12, 1983; Sam H. Zakhem, October 6, 1986; and Charles Warren Hostler, October 28, 1989. Hostler left his post on March 1, 1993; David S. Robins served as Charge d'Affaires ad interim until July 18, 1994, when David M. Ransom presented his credentials as Ambassador. Ransom was succeeded by Johnny Young, December 11, 1997, and Ronald E. Neumann, October 9, 2001.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
Since the Mughal Dynasty ceased after the take over by the Crown, the emergence and dissolvment of the Bengal Presidency and the Bengal Province under the British Empire took place. With the termination of British rule in 1947, Bengal was divided into two provinces, West and East Bengal. East Bengal had become a part of Pakistan, named East Pakistan and remained so until 1971. On 26th March 1971, East Pakistan officially seceded, and was to be called Bangladesh and declared itself independent through a radio transmission from Kalurghat, Chittagong. An official interim government was establish on April 10th 1971, that was called Probashi Sharkar led by Prime Minister Tajuddin Ahmed and the Commander in Chief of BDF General M.A.G. Osmani. The administration took refuge in India. After the war ended with West Pakistan, Bangladesh Forces (BDF) and the interim government remained under Indian control in Bangladesh through until March 17th 1971. After the departure of the Indian forces and administration officially in March 19th, many nations initiated diplomatic relations with Bangladesh. The United States followed immediately by initiating recognition of Bangladesh.

The U.S. Embassy, Bangladesh, was established at Dacca (now Dhaka) on May 18, 1972. Serving as Charge d'Affaires ad interim were Herbert D. Spivack, May - October 1972, and Daniel O. Newberry, October 1972 - April 1974.

The first Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary, Davis Eugene Boster, presented his credentials on April 13, 1974. He was succeeded by Edward E. Masters, November 5, 1976; David T. Schneider, March 29, 1978; Jane Abell Coon, August 11, 1981; Howard Bruner Schaffer, September 26, 1984; Willard Ames De Pree, October 5, 1987; William B. Milam, September 1, 1990; Daniel Nathan Merrill, April 5, 1994; John C. Holzman, September 2, 1997; and Mary Ann Peters, September 25, 2000.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Kingdom of Dahomey was an overseas possession of France—part of French West Africa—until 1958. In that year Dahomey became an autonomous republic, and gained full independence in 1960. The United States immediately recognized Dahomey and began the process of initiating diplomatic relations. A U.S. Embassy at Abidjan, Cote d’Ivoire (then named Ivory Coast) was established with Donald L. Norland as Chargé d'Affaires ad interim. The embassy was also accredited also to Dahomey, Niger, and Upper Volta (now named Burkina Faso) while resident at Abidjan. On July 31, 1960, Chargé Norland presented his credentials to the government of Dahomey, to take effect on August 1, 1960. On October 14, 1960, R. Borden Reams was appointed as the ambassador and presented his credentials on November 26, 1960. 

On February 15, 1961, the Embassy in Cotonou, Dahomey was established with Converse Hettinger as Chargé d'Affaires ad interim. Ambassador Reams remained resident in Abidjan. Until June 22, 1961,  relations with the fledgling nation were handled by the non-resident ambassador at Abidjan, Ivory Coast. The first resident ambassador presented his letter of credence on June 22, 1961. In November 1975 Dahomey was renamed Benin and the U.S. Embassy was renamed U.S. Embassy, Benin.

Serving as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary, with dates of presentations of credentials, were R. Borden Reams (non-resident), November 26, 1960; Robinson McIlvaine, June 22, 1961; Clinton E. Knox, August 18, 1964; Matthew J. Looram, Jr., July 21, 1969; Robert Anderson, March 25, 1972; and James B. Engle, November 26, 1974.

From 1976 to 1983 U.S. diplomatic relations with Benin were handled by the following charge d'affaires ad interim: W. Kenneth Thompson, August 1976 - August 1978; John S. Davidson, September 1978 - May 1980; James R. Bullington, June 1980 - July 1983; and Charles H. Twining, July 1982 - October 1983.

Subsequently, chiefs of mission were raised to the ambassadorial level, with the following serving as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary: George E. Moose, November 4, 1983; Walter Edward Stadtler, November 19, 1986; Harriet Winsar Isom, January 26, 1990; Ruth A. Davis, December 24, 1992; John M. Yates, November 24, 1995; Robert C. Felder, November 20, 1998; and Pamela E. Bridgewater, November 24, 2000.

Until 1960 Upper Volta was a French possession as a part of French West Africa. In 1958 Upper Volta became an autonomous republic in the French Community (Communauté française), and achieved independence as the Republic of Upper Volta on August 5, 1960. The U.S. Embassy for Upper Volta (changed to Burkina Faso on August 4, 1984) was established on August 4, 1960. Donald R. Norland, resident at Abidjan, Ivory Coast, presented his credentials as Charge d'Affaires ad interim on August 4, 1960, to take effect from August 5. R. Borden Reams was appointed as non-resident Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary and presented his credentials on December 6, 1960.

The first resident ambassador, Thomas S. Estes, presented his credentials on June 26, 1961. He was succeeded by Elliott P. Skinner, September 14, 1966; William E. Schaufele, Jr., October 16, 1969; Donald B. Easum, December 8, 1971; Pierre R. Graham, July 30, 1974; and Thomas D. Boyatt, September 21, 1978. Boyatt left Ougadougou on October 23, 1980; Larry C. Grahl served as Charge d'Affaires ad interim from October 1980 through November 1981.

Julius Waring Walker, Jr., presented his credentials as the next ambassador on November 18, 1981. He was succeeded by Leonardo Neher, September 21, 1984; David H. Shinn, November 28, 1987; Edward P. Brynn, January 14, 1991; Donald J. McConnell, November 22, 1993; Sharon P. Wilkinson, October 24, 1996; Jimmy J. Kolker, January 11, 2000; and J. Anthony Holmes, December 23, 2002.

Psychological warfare functions of Allied Force Headquarters (AFHQ) were at first charged to the Civil Affairs Section, but were transferred to the Information and Censorship Section of January 5, 1943. On October 23, 1944, the Psychological Warfare Branch was separated from the Information and Censorship Section, and thereafter, until its discontinuance on March 31, 1946, operated as as special staff section of AFHQ. After March 31, 1946, remaining psychological warfare activities in Venezia Giulia were performed by Allied Information Services, Trieste.

The functions of the Branch were to advise the Supreme Allied Commander on all psychological warfare matters; to coordinate the joint directives of the Office of War Information (American) and the Psychological Warfare Executive (British) with the propaganda plans of the Supreme Allied Commander; to cooperate with field commanders and army civil affairs authorities in matters of combat and rear area propaganda; and to plan and supervise psychological warfare activities involving the collection and evaluation of psychological warfare and intelligence, the preparation and dissemination of all Allied propaganda, the utilization of facilities of other arms and services for the dissemination of propaganda material, surveys of public opinion in occupied territories, and the regulation of the political tone of newspapers and radio broadcasts in occupied territories.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The United States recognized the Mutawakkilite Kingdom of Yemen in 1946 and commissioned its first ambassador, J. Rives Childs to the Kingdom of Yemen on August 22, 1946. A diplomatic legation was established in Ta'izz. At that time the ambassador to Saudi Arabia was concurrently commissioned to Yemen while resident in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia. Legation Taiz was opened to the public effective March 16, 1959, with Charles B. Ferguson as Charge d'Affaires ad interim. 

Following a coup d’état in North Yemen in 1962, the nation was renamed Yemen Arab Republic. A period of civil war ensued for the next five years. The United States maintained diplomatic relations with the Kingdom but no ambassador was accredited to the nation. A series of chargés d’affaires maintained the legation during that period. Also during that time, the legation in Ta'izz was raised to embassy status on January 28, 1963 and the embassy was transferred to San'a in 1966.

Each of the following officers served as Charge d'Affaires ad interim: James N. Cortada (February 1963 - August 1964) and Harlan B. Clark (August 1964-August 1966). Robert Stookey was serving as Charge d'Affaires ad interim when Legation Taiz was raised to Embassy status, January 28, 1963 (Embassy transferred to San'a in 1966). Lee F. Dinsmore served as Charge d'Affaires ad interim when the Yemen Arab Republic severed relations with the United States, June 7, 1967. as a consequence of U.S. support for israel during rhe Six-Day War.

A U.S. Interest Section was established in the Italian Embassy on April 10, 1970. Principal Officers were David W. McClintock (Apr 1970 - February 1972) and Robert A. Stein (February - July 1972). The Embassy in San'a was re-established on July 1, 1972, with Stein as Charge d'Affaires ad interim.

The first Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary, William R. Crawford, Jr., was appointed on October 12, 1972. On May 22, 1990, the Yemen Arab Republic and the People's Democratic Republic of Yemen (South Yemen) announced that they were forming a united Republic of Yemen.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Agency Planning Officer was responsible for maintaining continuing liaison with the office of Administration on Planning-Programming-Budgeting System (PPBS) problems, assuring that the Office of Policy (IOP) requirements under Circular 278D were being met. The Agency Planning Officer prepared new policy planning papers, a series of instructions to all Agency elements outlining policy and operational guidance on key subjects for future exploitation by the Agency. He participated in general operational policy (IOP/P) review of all country plans, with attention to assuring that they were in accord with overall Agency policy requirements. The Agency Planning Officer provided policy guidance in connection with the determination of future Agency research projects, as well as assisted in determining the usefulness of completed research. He maintained liaison with the Department of State's Bureau of Educational and Cultural Affairs (CU) planning operations, in coordination with the Office of Policy's (IOP) Cultural Affairs Adviser. The Agency Planning Officer assisted in drawing up operational policy (IOP/P) recommendations to the Director in connection with his membership on the National Security Council, the Senior Interdepartmental Group, and the Committee of Principles. Lastly, the Agency Planning Officer participated in special Office of Policy (IOP) planning projects, as required.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
Mozambique was an overseas possession of Portugal until 1975. On June 25, 1975, Portugal granted independence to Mozambique, much later than other European nations had freed their own African possessions. The United States immediately recognized the new nation and moved to establish diplomatic relations. An embassy in the capital Maputo (then named Lourenço Marques) was opened November 8, 1975, with Johnnie Carson as chargé d’affaires ad interim. On February 4, 1976, Ambassador Willard A. De Pree was appointed as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to Mozambique.

In 1976, the United States extended a $10 million grant to the Government of Mozambique to help compensate for the economic costs of enforcing sanctions against Rhodesia. In 1977, however, largely motivated by a concern with human rights violations, the U.S. Congress prohibited the provision of development aid to Mozambique without a presidential certification that such aid would be in the foreign policy interests of the United States. Relations hit a nadir in March 1981, when the Government of Mozambique expelled four members of the U.S. Embassy staff. In response, the United States suspended plans to provide development aid and to name a new ambassador to Mozambique. Relations between the two countries languished in a climate of stagnation and mutual suspicion.

Contacts between the two countries continued in the early 1980s as part of the U.S. administration's conflict resolution efforts in the region. In late 1983, a new U.S. ambassador arrived in Maputo, and the first Mozambican envoy to the United States arrived in Washington, signaling a thaw in the bilateral relationship. The United States subsequently responded to Mozambique's economic reform and drift away from Moscow's embrace by initiating an aid program in 1984. President Samora Machel paid a symbolically important official working visit to the United States in 1985, where he met President Reagan. After that meeting, a full U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) mission was established, and significant assistance for economic reform efforts began.

creators.biographicalNote:
Gordon Gray (1909-1982), government official, publisher, and educator. A graduate of the Yale Law School, Gray began his professional career as an attorney with a New York Law firm. In 1935, however, he returned to Winston-Salem, North Carolina, to practice law. At approximately the same time, he acquired financial interests in the publishing and broadcasting fields. As operator of radio station WSJS and publisher of the Winston-Salem Journal and the Twin City Sentinel, Gray eventually abandoned the legal profession. As president and publisher of the Piedmont Publishing Company, Gray retained his business interests in publishing and broadcasting throughout his other careers. In 1938, he served as president of the Young Democratic Clubs of North Carolina. From 1938 to 1942 and from 1946 to 1947, he was a member of the North Carolina State Senate.

A lifelong Democrat, Gray served under every president, Democrats and Republicans alike, from Harry Truman to Gerald Ford. During the Truman years, Gray was Assistant Secretary and later Secretary of the Army. He resigned in 1950 to accept the position as president of the University of North Carolina. However, he remained in Washington, D.C. to study United States foreign economic policies as a special assistant to the President. Also, during his tenure as president of the University of North Carolina, he was director of the Psychological Strategy Board. During the early years of the Eisenhower administration, Gray held positions on several committees and boards including the Presidents Committee on International Information Activities and the Atomic Energy Commissions Personnel Security Board. In 1955, he resigned as president of the University of North Carolina and returned to government service on a full- time basis. Involved in advising the president on international and national security affairs, Gray served as Assistant Secretary of Defense for International Security Affairs (1955-1957), director of the Office of Defense Mobilization (1957-1958), and Special Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs (1958-1961).

After the Eisenhower years drew to a close, Gray became more involved in business activities. He did, however, serve as a member of the Presidents Foreign Intelligence Advisory Board from 1961 to 1977. During the 1960's and 1970's he was chairman of the board of Triangle Broadcasting Company, chairman of the board of Summit Communications, Inc., and a member of the board of directors of the J.R. Reynolds Tobacco Company. Gray also served as chairman of the board of trustees for the National Trust for Historic Preservation.

creators.biographicalNote: Charles Hartwell Bonesteel (1909-1977) was born in Plattsburg, New York, the son of Charles Hartwell and Caroline Mead (Hudson) Bonesteel.  He graduated from West Point in 1931 and Oxford University as a Rhodes Scholar in 1934.  In that same year, he married Alice M. Pratt, with whom he had one son, Charles Hartwell IV.  After serving in Europe during World War II, he represented the War Department in the Council of Foreign Ministers in Paris, New York City, and Moscow.  In 1947 and 1948, he was appointed as special assistant to the Under-Secretary of State.  From 1958 to 1960, he was secretary of General Staff of the U.S. Army.  He made general in 1966, while commander-in-chief of United Nations Command in Korea and commanding general of the 8th U.S. Army.  He retired in 1969.  His awards include two Distinguished Service Medals and two Legion of Merit medals.

creators.biographicalNote: Warren Christopher was born on October 27, 1925. He received a B.S. from the University of Southern California in 1945 and an LL.B. from Stanford University in 1949. He has been a lawyer in private practice in Los Angeles since 1950. He served as Deputy Attorney General during the Lyndon Johnson administration, 1967 to 1969, and he served as Deputy Secretary of State during the Carter administration, 1977 to 1981. As Deputy Secretary of State, he handled the negotiations for release of the Americans held hostage in Iran. He also served as Secretary of State during the first years of the Clinton administration, 1993 to 1997. He died on March 18, 2011.

creators.biographicalNote: William John Jorden (b. 1923) was a reporter, writer, and a diplomat. He was a foreign correspondent with the New York Times from 1952 to 1961. He served as Special Assistant to the Under Secretary for Political Affairs on the Policy Planning Council, 1962 to 1965, and Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Public Affairs on the Policy Planning Council, 1965 to 1966. He served as Assistant to former President Lyndon Johnson from 1969 to 1972, and he was U.S. Ambassador to Panama, 1974 to 1978. He wrote a book entitled Panama Odyssey, which was published in 1984.

creators.biographicalNote: Harrison Arlington Williams, Jr., (b. December 10, 1919, Plainfield, New Jersey - d. November 17, 2001, Bedminster, New Jersey) was a Representative and a Senator from New Jersey. He was called to active duty as a seaman in the United States Naval Reserve in 1941; became a naval aviator and was discharged as a lieutenant (jg.) in 1945. Williams was elected on November 3, 1953, as a Democrat to the Eighty-third Congress to fill the vacancy caused by the resignation of Clifford Case; reelected to the Eighty-fourth Congress and served from November 3, 1953, to January 3, 1957; and was an unsuccessful candidate for reelection in 1956 to the Eighty-fifth Congress. He was elected to the United States Senate in 1958; reelected in 1964, 1970 and 1976 and served from January 3, 1959, until his resignation on March 11, 1982. During his tenure in the Senate, he served as chairman, Special Committee on Aging (Ninetieth and Ninety-first Congresses), Committee on Labor and Public Welfare (Ninety-second through Ninety-fifth Congresses), Committee on Human Resources (Ninety-fifth Congress), Committee on Labor and Human Resources (Ninety-sixth Congress). He was one of the congressional targets in the government operation known as "ABSCAM"; convicted of charges related to this effort, and sentenced on February 17, 1982, to three years in prison, of which he served twenty-one months. During subsequent Senate proceedings on an expulsion motion, he resigned his seat on March 11, 1982.

creators.biographicalNote: Ural Alexis Johnson (1908-1997) was a longtime Foreign Service officer and diplomat, specializing in Asian relations. He began working as a language officer in Japan in 1935, and worked for the State Department as a Foreign Service officer until 1977. He was Ambassador to Czechoslovakia from 1953 to 1958; Ambassador to Thailand, 1958 to 1961; Deputy Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs, 1961 to 1964; Deputy Ambassador to South Vietnam, 1964 to 1965; and Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs, 1965 to 1966. He served as Ambassador to Japan from 1966 to 1969, and he once again served as Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs, 1969 to 1973. From 1973 to 1977 he was chief of the U.S. Delegation to SALT (Strategic-Arms Limitation Talks). He retired from the Foreign Service in 1977, but he continued to serve as a consultant to the State Department from 1977 to 1982 and the Department of Defense from 1979 to 1981.

creators.biographicalNote: Thomas Clifton Mann (1912-1999) was born in Laredo, Texas. He graduated from Baylor University in 1934, and from  1934 to 1942, worked as a lawyer on Laredo, Texas. In 1942, Mann joined the Diplomatic Service of the U.S. Department of State, and held various diplomatic posts in Europe, Latin America, and Washington, D.C., through 1955. From 1955 to 1957, Mann served the post of U.S. Ambassador to El Salvador. From October 1957 to August 1960, he served as the Assistant Secretary of State for Economic Affairs, and from August 1960 to January 1961 served as Assistant Secretary of State for Inter-American Affairs. From 1961 to 1966 Mann again held various diplomatic posts in Latin America and Washington, D.C. He resigned from the Department of State in June 1966.

July 14, 2010, Weston, Massachusetts), economist, diplomat, and government official was an Economic and Foreign Service officer in Mexico from 1942 to 1943, in Chile in 1943, in Bolivia from 1943 to 1947, for the Department of Commerce from 1947 to 1950, and in Switzerland  from 1950 to 1956. creators.biographicalNote:
Otto Hilgard Tittmann was born on August 20, 1850, at Belleville, Illinois, where he received his early education.   He subsequently received degrees from Stevens Institute, Washington University, and George Washington University. He joined the Coast and Geodetic Survey on November 10, 1867, as an aid.  He rendered service with field parties on the Atlantic, Gulf, and Pacific Coasts, Puerto Rico, and southeastern Alaska; became Assistant in Charge of Office July 1, 1895; Assistant Superintendent April 18, 1899; and Superintendent December 1, 1900, from which position he resigned April 15, 1915.

From October 7, 1887, Dr. Tittmann was in charge of the Office of Standard Weights and Measures, which was a unit of the Coast and Geodetic Survey prior to the establishment of the National Bureau of Standards. In 1890, he was sent to Paris to bring to the United States the national standard metre.

He was known as a geodesist and served on many scientific expeditions. He was assistant astronomer in the expedition sent to Japan to observe the transit of Venus; a member of the Permanent Commission of the International Geodetic Association; represented the United States in surveying the Alaskan Boundary Line after the modus vivendi of 1899 with Great Britain; served as U.S. Commissioner on the International Boundary Commission relating to the Alaskan Boundary from 1906 to 1915; and United States Commissioner in marking the international boundary line between the United States and Dominion of Canada.

Tittmann was one of the original incorporators of the National Geographic Society and its President from 1915 to 1919. He was a member of the Philosophical Society of Washington (President, 1899); American Philosophical Society; at one time President of the Washington Academy of Sciences; a Fellow and one time Vice President of the American Association for the Advancement of Science; a member of the American Meteorological Society; American Society of Civil Engineers; and the Cosmos Club (President, 1904). He died on August 21, 1938, at his home in Leesburg, Virginia.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
On August 1, 1953, the Office of Policy and Plans (IPO) was created. It took over the functional responsibilities of the International Information Administration's Office of Policy and Plans. In addition it was responsible for collaborating with the Department of State on the Department's exclusive label program.

The Office of Policy and Programs, established on September 17, 1953, by taking over some functions from the former Office of Policy and Plans and Office of Field Programs. It developed, coordinated and issued information policy and program guidance; obtained national and foreign policy from the National Security Council (NSC), the Department of State and other Government agencies; conducted policy relationships between the U.S. Information Agency (USIA) and other government departments; received and processed requests from other government agencies for information program support; reviewed country plans prepared by overseas posts and provided for reappraisal as necessary. It was responsible for program planning to provide the necessary sense of direction and proportion to the operations of the USIA as a whole; to provide for the selection of ideas and events for special emphasis and interpretation to overseas audiences; to effect the proper distribution of Agency resources; and to establish the appropriate levels of country programs and of media support.

On May 2, 1956, the Office of Policy and Programs (IOP) was redesignated as the Office of Policy and Plans (IOP). The Office of Policy and Plans was responsible for determining worldwide foreign information policy and providing guidance to Agency elements in the application of such policy. This Office was also responsible for developing long-range global plans and campaigns to meet overall Agency objectives.

On April 23, 1958, USIA announced that the Office of Policy and Plans was redesignated as the Office of Plans (IOP) to emphasizes the responsibility of the Office for formulating Agency plans. The Office continued to be responsible obtaining foreign policy from the Department of State and other agencies; developing information policy for the Agency; and transmitting these to the operating elements of the Agency.

On August 8, 1962, the Office of Plans was redesignated as the Office of Policy (IOP).
