creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
By National Security Action Memorandum (NSAM) No. 330 of April 9, 1965 (which gave impetus to NSAM's 325 of March 12 and NO. 328 of April 6, 1965), responsibility for policy direction and coordination of all U.S. psychological action programs in Vietnam was delegated to the Director of the U.S. Information Agency (USIA). A new U.S. Mission organization, the Joint U.S. Public Affairs Office (JUSPAO) was established in Saigon which carried out certain functions on behalf of the U.S. Information Agency (USIA), the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), and the Department of Defense (DOD). These functions were assigned to it by the National Security Council (NSC), as well as by USIA and the Department of State. In broad strokes, these functions included coordinating all military and civilian psychological operations activities; promoting the development of Government of Vietnam (GVN) radio, television, motion picture, and information services and related training activities; and carrying out the information and cultural programs of the USIA and the department of State. JUSPAO Saigon staff included military officers from the U.S. Military Assistance Command Vietnam (MACV) as well as civilian personnel from USIA, the Department of State, and USAID.

JUSPAO Saigon had five objectives: to help GVN increase the people's identification with and support for the Government; to help the Government establish a dialogue with the people by means of a nationwide communications network; to induce enemy forces to rally under the Chieu Hoi program, to surrender, or desert; to enhance the image of the GVN with third country audiences; and to increase awareness of and support for American policy in Vietnam.

Barry Zorthian was the first director of the JUSPAO, although his title was Public Affairs Officer in 1965. Edward J. Nickel took over the position in 1968 until Robert Adams Lincoln relieved him in 1971.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Office of the Controller advised and assisted the Mission Director in discharging his responsibility for the financial management of the Mission program. The Controller participated in the formulation and review of existing programs; insured appropriate financial execution of Mission program budgets; reviewed administrative expense estimates and staffing patterns and insured that justifications were appropriate; insured that obligations and expenditures were within allotment limitations; classified obligations and expenditures as between program and administrative allotments; established and maintained accounting records and controls; prepared timely financial reports; audited and certified vouchers as required; and conducted audits concerning project and non-project commodities, counterpart funds, other local currency, procurement practices, and contracts.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Library Division was formed from the nucleus of the collection and personnel of the old Broadcasting Service (IBS) and Press Service (IPS) libraries. The Library had four distinct collections. The first was the book and periodical collection, which was heavily weighted with Russian and Communist materials. The second was the unclassified morgue that covered unclassified intelligence material. The third section was the new expanding classified file, which resembled the unclassified collection, except that all of the documents were classified. The fourth was the propaganda collection that represented an extensive collection of the published propaganda of foreign countries. The last was mainly created by country public affairs officers and other in the field that submitted propaganda examples from their local area. This material was constantly used by the Director and other headquarters personnel, because it was effective in demonstrating the opposition. The Library provided reference service for Agency personnel in Washington and sent responses by telegram or despatch to field personnel.

The Research Library Division conducted general library reference and related services; and provided media services with documented background material. On October 4, 1961, the Research Library Division was renamed the Agency Library. The Agency Library developed and operated the Agency’s general and special reference services to support its domestic and overseas needs, including procurement of books, periodicals, and newspapers for staff use; preparation of research reports on history, life, and culture of the United States; and provision of basic reference and documentation services supplemented by special propaganda materials.

The nucleus of the collection and personnel of this Division is the old IBS and IPS libraries. The Division is headed by Roth Newpher, who headed the IBS Library and Research Staffs for 12 years. The Library has four rather distinct collections. The first section is the book and periodical collection…The collection is heavily weighted with Russian and Communist materials…The second section is the unclassified morgue…unclassified intelligence material. The third section is the classified file. This resembles the unclassified, except that all documents in it are classified. This is a new section for the Agency, and is rapidly expanding…The fourth section is the propaganda collection…It represents an extensive collection of the published propaganda of foreign countries…We must rely heavily on you to send us examples from your area…This material is constantly used by the Director and other headquarters personnel because it is particularly effective in demonstrating the opposition. The Library Division is prepared to give you very rapid service. The Library provides reference service for Agency Personnel in Washington. It can do so by telegram or despatch for you.)

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Panama-Pacific International Exposition was held at San Francisco, California, from February 20 to December 4, 1915, ostensibly to celebrate the completion and opening of the Panama Canal and the four-hundredth anniversary of the directory of the Pacific Ocean, but also to showcase the city's recovery from the 1906 earthquake. A joint resolution approved on February 15, 1911, authorized the President to invite foreign countries to participate in the exposition once certain requirements were met by the exposition company. An act approved on June 23, 1913, made provision for the appointment of members to a national exposition commission. The act also created a government exhibit board to manage the government's exhibits and appropriated the sum of $500,000 to be used by government agencies in the preparation of their exhibits.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Board for International Food and Agricultural Development (BIFAD) was established on April 14, 1976, pursuant to Title XII of the of the International Development and Food Assistance Act of 1975 (89 Stat. 864), approved December 20, 1975. In January 1991 it was renamed the Board for International Food and Agricultural Development and Economic Cooperation (BIFADEC) and in 1995 reverted to its orginal name. It was a public advisory board of the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID).

The Board advised USAID, other Government agencies, and the Congress on all aspects of food and agriculture development assistance, and the mobilization and the utilization of faculty, staff, and other institutional resources of U.S. colleges and universities.

The Board was comprised on seven members appointed by the President, four of whom represented the academic community.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The U.S. Embassy was established at Suva on November 1, 1971, with Robert W. Skiff as Charge d'Affaires ad interim. The first 2 Ambassadors Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to Fiji were also accredited to New Zealand, Tonga, and Western Samoa, and were resident at Wellington. These included Kenneth Franzheim II, who presented his credentials on May 22, 1972, and Armistead I. Selden, Jr., April 17, 1974.

The first resident Ambassador, John P. Condon, presented his credentials on April 11, 1978. He was also accredited to Tonga and Tuvalu. He was succeeded by William Bodde, Jr., August 12, 1980. Fred J. Eckert presented his credentials at Suva on February 25, 1982. In addition to Tonga and Tuvalu, he was also accredited to Kiribati. Succeeding Ambassador Eckert as ambassador at Suva were Carl Edward Dillery, November 1, 1984; Leonard Rochwarger, March 11, 1988; and Evelyn Irene Hoopes Teegan, November 21, 1989. Ambassador Teegan departed Suva on March 5, 1993, and was succeeded by the  Charge d'Affaires, including Michael W. Marine, March 1993 - June 1995; and Bruce N. Gray, June - December 1995.

Subsequent ambassadors were accredited also to Nauru, Tonga, and Tuvalu. Don L. Gervitz presented his credentials on  September 13, 1999, followed by M. Osman Siddique, September 13, 1999. Following Ambassador Siddique's departure from Suva on June 30, 2001, the following served as Charge d'Affaires ad interim: Ronald K. McMullen, June 2001 - June 2002, and Hugh Neighbor, June 2002 - .

The United States has limited its relationship with the interim government established by the illegal December 5, 2006 coup.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The principal objectives of A.I.D. programs in Chile were to increase agricultural production and income of small farmers, and to improve nutrition, especially of the young and poor. Chilean economic progress after the overthrow of the Allende government was slow, but based on sound economic and fiscal principles. Phase-out of USAID programs had been planned for FY 1979 but, because of a recent Chilean Government request, this was rescheduled for FY 1977.

U.S. interests in the country were (1) Chile's economic recovery and continuing foreign debt repayment, and (2) the orderly development of and access to Chile's mineral resources.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
Through 1971, the United States Government provided India with about $10 billion in development loans and technical assistance and food aid. In the 10 years prior to that date, U.S. economic assistance averaged slightly more than $600 million annually. Roughly, each year about $300 million was made available in the form of development loans and grants; the balance was provided in food aid, mostly under PL 480, Title I credit sales.

The 1971 Indo-Pakistan war led to suspension of U. S. development programs to Pakistan and India. Subsequently, a large-scale foreign assistance program was resumed in Pakistan but not in India. Although an offer was made to India to continue a scaled-down technical assistance program, in the existing chilly political atmosphere, the Government of India (GOI) indicated that it wished to phase out entirely the U.S. program authorized by the Foreign Assistance Act. Food aid under PL 480 Title I credit sales was also suspended. In 1975 and 1976 shipments resumed again at about half a million tons of wheat valued at about $100 million per year. In 1977, wheat continued to be allocated for India, but it was not sent because of record harvests and high stocks. Vegetable oil worth $25-35 million per year was provided in 1977 and 1978. The United States also continued to contribute to Indian development through its participation in multilateral assistance agencies such as IDA and the World Bank. The U.S. provided over 30 percent of IDA's soft loan replenishment funds which would indirectly amount to over $200 million of IDA's annual commitments of roughly $600 million to India. 

On July 14, 1977, in a climate of improved relations India between the U.S. and India, the Congress recommended to the President the resumption of AID assistance to India. USAID/India resumed operations as a Mission in May 1978.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The U.S. Agency for International Development (AID) was established within the Department of State on November 3, 1961. AID was responsible for the administration of non-military U.S. foreign assistance programs as defined under the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961. The Agency supported programs in four major areas: population and health, broad-based economic growth, the environment, and democracy. AID also provided humanitarian assistance and aid to countries in crisis and transition.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Financial and Information Services Division (E&E/OM/FIS) provided a wide range of operational and administrative support functions in the area of finance and information management, including the function of the Bureau Controller. Specific activities of the Division included the development and maintenance of critical Bureau financial and information management systems; and maintenance of regularly scheduled distribution of a range of reports required by Agency, Bureau and field staff, including quarterly financial pipeline reports and Freedom Support Act (FSA) and Support for East European Democracy (SEED) reports. The Division provided web site development and training for operating units in information technology (IT) applications; management of Bureau Operating Expenses; and audit management for the Bureau, including General Accounting Office (GAO) and Office of the Inspector General (OIG). The Division also developed and maintained Bureau information databases; tracked vouchers for Bureau-managed activities; managed Bureau Washington deobligations; maintained liaison with other Bureaus and technical offices regarding IT program activities in the region; and coordinated assistance in implementation of the Agency's procurement and accounting systems. The Chief of this Division also served as the Bureau's Controller.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Office of Material Resources (MR) was established on November 4, 1961 and was also known as the Office of Materials Resources. The head of the Office, Herbert J. Waters, served as the Assistant Administrator for Material Resources.

The Office formulated the policies, standards, and procedures governing the various types of commodity assistance. It provided advice and guidance on procurement, utilization, financing and shipping of such commodities. This Office was also charged with seeing that small business enterprises participated equitably in furnishing Agency for International Development (AID) financed commodities and services, and was the focal point for the Agency’s responsibilities in connection with the Food-for-Peace program.

On March 23, 1967, the Office of Material Resources was abolished in accordance with an AID General Notice of that date. The majority of the functions transferred to the new Office of War on Hunger, including the functions of the Assistant Administrator, the Deputy Assistant Administrator, and the Associate Assistant Administrator for Special Resources; as well as the Food for Peace, voluntary foreign aid, and agricultural commodity specialist functions. The Special Assistant (Economics and Trade) and the International Cooperative Development Service functions transferred to the Office of Development Finance and Private Enterprise. The Office of the Special Assistant for Management and Administration transferred to the Office of the War on Hunger except for the Assistant Administrator for Administration who transferred to the Office of Procurement. The remaining functions transferred to the Office of Procurement, which included the Special Ocean Freight Staff.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The U.S. Embassy to the Republic of the Congo was established at Leopoldville on June 30, 1960, with John D. Tomlinson as Charge d'Affaires ad interim. On  August 1, 1964, the Republic of the Congo was renamed the Democratic Republic of the Congo and on June 30, 1966 Leopoldville was renamed Kinshasha. From 1967 through ca. 1970 the chief of mission was accredited to the Democratic Republic of the Congo; from October 27, 1971 through May 17, 1997 the country was named Zaire, and from May 19, 1997, the Democratic Republic of Congo.

On July 25, 1960, Clare H. Timberlake presented his credentials as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary. He was succeeded by Edmund A. Gullion, September 11, 1961; G. McMurtrie Goldley, March 23, 1964; Robert H. McBride, June 29, 1967; Sheldon B. Vance, June 28, 1969; and Deane R. Hinton, August 21, 1974. Ambassador Hinton was declared persona non grata on June 18, 1975; he departed the post on June 21, 1975. He was succeeded by Walter L. Cutler, December 23, 1975; Robert B. Oakley, November 28, 1979; Peter Dalton Constable, October 18, 1982; Brandon Hambright Grove, Jr., September 18, 1984; William Caldwell Harrop, January 28, 1988; and Melissa Foelsch Wells, June 11, 1991.

Ambassador Wells left her post on March 21, 1992. John M. Yates served as Charge d'Affaires ad interim from March 1992 through September 1995, and Roger A. Meece from September through November 1995. 

The next Ambassador, Daniel H. Simpson, presented his credentials on November 23, 1995. He was succeeded by William Lacy Swing, October 13, 1998, Aubrey Hooks, September 4, 2001; Roger A. Meece, August 3, 2004; William J. Garvelink, November 29, 2007; James F. Entwistle, November 4, 2010; and James Christopher Swan, November 1, 2013-December 31, 2016. Ambassador Michael (Mike) A. Hammer was confirmed as the U.S. ambassador to the Democratic Republic of the Congo on September 6, 2018.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The U.S. Agency for International Development (AID) was established within the Department of State on November 3, 1961. AID was responsible for the administration of non-military U.S. foreign assistance programs as defined under the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961. The Agency supported programs in four major areas: population and health, broad-based economic growth, the environment, and democracy. AID also provided humanitarian assistance and aid to countries in crisis and transition.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: As a regional program of the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), US-AEP supported cooperation between governments, businesses, and communities in Asia. US-AEP used a range of flexible program tools to address issues of water supply and quality, air quality, and solid and hazardous waste, and environmental governance. It was established in 1992.  The program was managed by USAID, and supported by eight implementing partners.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Intelligence Production Division, also known as the Production Division, was responsible for answering questions from any part of the U.S. Information Service (USIS) or the U.S. Information Agency (USIA). The Production Division did not always answer these questions itself. If a large and comprehensive study was required, the Division determined the requirements on other appropriate intelligence organizations, including the Department of State, the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), the Department of Defense as well as non-Intelligence Advisory Committee (IAC) agencies such as the Department of Labor, the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Commerce. Requests from the field for information were sent either directly to the Office of Research and Intelligence (IRI) or to the Press Service (IPS), depending on the type of product desired. Both IPS and IRI often worked on the same requests. IRI did the research, and obtained the facts bearing on the subject and placed them in some logical order, irrespective of whether they helped or hindered the cause. IPS utilized these facts, as appropriate in its output.

Announced on December 14, 1959, the Projects and Liaison Staff was established to assist the Director in planning, development, and coordinating major research projects. Irving R. Wechsler served as Chief.

An October 4, 1961 announcement, established the Planning and Review Staff. The Planning and Review Staff (IRR/P) recommended research projects for use in the development of plans, informational policies, and programs. It also reviewed and edited Research and Reference Service (IRR)  studies and reports. Irving R. Wechsler continued to serve as the Chief.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Office of Middle East Affairs supported programs in Algeria, Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Libya, Morocco, Tunisia, West Bank/Gaza, Yemen, and the Middle East Regional Cooperation Program. Egypt, Jordan, Lebanon, Morocco, West Bank/Gaza, and Yemen were U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) posts with a combination of Development Assistance (DA), Economic Support Fund (ESF), and International Development Assistance (IDA)-funded programs. Algeria, Israel, and Tunisia were USAID posts where ESF-funded activities operated. The Office also provided advice and assistance to the Office of Middle East Programs (OMEP), based in the USAID Mission to Egypt, which supported U.S. Government and multi-lateral initiatives and developed programs that address common, transboundary development issues of impact to the Middle East region. Also, the Office lead coordination with the Department of State’s Bureau for Near East and Asia on U.S. Government initiatives that transcend national boundaries and seek to achieve results that benefit the entire region.

AID was responsible for the administration of non-military U.S. foreign assistance programs as defined under the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961. The Agency supported programs in four major areas: population and health, broad-based economic growth, the environment, and democracy. AID also provided humanitarian assistance and aid to countries in crisis and transition.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Office of Management Planning, established November 4, 1961, developed policies and standards in the management area; stimulated Agency-wide management improvement; and conducted management surveys. The Office also conducted research and planning in the field of organization and management practices, program methods, office techniques and procedures. It provided support to the Agency in the programming and operation of automatic data processing (ADP) facilities.

The Office of Data Systems and Management (A/DSM) served as an in-house management consulting firm; operated the Agency for International Development's (AID) computers; regulated and controlled manpower allocations; and provided related management services. Approximately two-thirds of its staff worked on the application of automated data processing (ADP) techniques to the Agency's business. The other third administered Agency-wide management control; coordinated the development of program and management policies and procedures; and provided assistance to Agency officials in solving operational problems.

The Office of Data Systems and Management’s management control functions fell into several areas. The Office controlled the Agency’s overall-position ceilings; determined individual offices' staffing needs; allocated position ceilings; and reported on manpower to the Executive Branch and the Congress. It assured that the organizational structure and functional assignments of the Agency's offices were sound; issued formal organizational charts and functional statements; approved any organizational or functional changes suggested by individual AID offices. The Office controlled the issuance of all Agency directives (Manual Orders, Policy statements, Announcements); approved the issuance of-all in-house reports and forms; and assured that the Agency has a proper records maintenance system. Management assistance, which the management and systems analysts provided, covered the full range of the Agency's activities. Typical analyses focused on the development or improvement of an Agency--wide system or procedure; the solution to a specific management problem that involved one or more Agency offices; and general efforts to improve management efficiency and effectiveness.

In 1969, the Office of Data Systems and Management was abolished and separated into the Office of Management Planning and the Office of Data Systems.

In 1975, the Bureau for Program and Management Services transferred the directives management function from the Office of Data Management to the Office of Management Planning and assigned the latter Office the responsibility for staff support to the new Senior Operations Group.

On April 14, 1983, the Office of Data Management and the Office of Management Planning were combined in to the new Office of Information Resources Management.

The Office of Data Systems and Management (A/DSM) serves as an in-house management consulting firm, operates the Agency's computer, regulates and controls manpower allocations, and provides related management services. Approximately two-thirds of its staff of 105 is working on the application of automated data processing techniques to the Agency's business. The other third administers Agency-wide management control, coordinates the development of program and management policies and procedures, and provides assistance to Agency officials in solving operational problems. A/DSM operates two computers (an IBM 360/30 and a 1401) and processes data for 17 operational systems, including: payroll, personnel, participant training, loan accounting, allotment accounting, commodity statistics, ocean freight transportation, and country financial reporting. Some 350 recurring reports for Agency managers' use are produced by these systems. (A small IBM 360/20 computer is operated independently by the Office of the Controller for processing specialized financial data. USAID Saigon also has a computer which is used for special purposes.) A/DSM will soon install a new, more powerful computer to replace the ones now being used in AID/W. It will handle more data at less cost, and eliminate the present need for some outside computer time on contract. The new equipment will be particularly needed in the coming months as A.I.D. develops an-automated management information system linked to its programming, planning and budgeting system. Prime responsibility for developing the system is assigned to, the Office of Program Policy and Coordination (PPC) with A/DSM systems analysts playing an important roll in automating the system. A/DSM's management control functions fall into several areas: Manpower -controlling the Agency’s overall-position ceilings; determining individual offices' staffing needs; allocating position ceilings; and manpower-reporting to the Executive Branch and the Congress. creators.administrativeHistoryNote: By October 12, 1975, the Agency for International Development (AID) had realigned the country responsibilities of the Bureau for East Asia and the Bureau for Near East and South Asia to achieve a more equitable distribution of program management responsibilities between the two Bureaus. This action redressed the imbalance which had resulted from the termination of AID activities in Indochina and the addition of new requirements to support U.S. initiatives in the Middle East. Concurrently, the Bureaus were redesignated the Bureau for Asia and the Bureau for Near East, respectively.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Office of the General Counsel, established in 1953, conducted the legal affairs of the U.S. Information Agency (USIA), advised on the meaning and intent of all laws applicable to the USIA; counseled USIA officials as to their legal authorities and the limitations thereon; and as to the legal implications of proposed courses of action. It assisted in the drafting of proposed legislation, executive order proposals, regulations, contracts, leases, and other legal matters.  Additionally, the Office of the General Counsel served to supplement the personal relations of the Director of the USIA with Congress after January 1, 1954 when it assumed the congressional liaison function from the Office of Congressional Liaison and Public Information. It also secured the necessary rights clearances for the Agency's activities.

During the reorganization, effective April 1, 1978, that changed the U.S. Information Agency into the International Communication Agency (ICA), the congressional liaison functions were transferred from the Office of the General Counsel to the new Office of Congressional and Public Liaison. The ICA's Office of the General Counsel advised all elements of the Agency on the interpretation of all laws, regulations, and Executive Orders that authorized the Agency's programs or related to the Agency's activities. The Office assisted in the drafting of proposed legislation, Executive Orders, regulations, contracts, leases, and other legal documents. The Office represented the Agency in hearings that arose from disputes on contracts, equal employment opportunity and licensing. The Office secured the necessary rights clearances for the Agency's activities and advised on matters relating to ethical conduct and conflict of interest of Agency employees. In 1981, the Office regained the congressional liaison functions as the it was renamed the Office of the General Counsel and Congressional Liaison.

The General Counsel and legal staff advise all elements of the Agency on the interpretation of all laws, regulations, and Executive Orders that authorize the Agency's programs or relate to the Agency's activities. The Office assists in the drafting of proposed legislation, Executive Orders, regulations, contracts, leases, and other legal documents. The Office represents the Agency in hearings arising from disputes on contracts, equal employment opportunity and licensing. The Office secures the necessary rights clearances for the Agency's activities and advises on matters relating to ethical conduct and conflict of interest of Agency employees. creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Standing Liaison Committee of the State, War, and Navy Departments was established with Presidential approval in April 1938 to coordinate departmental efforts in the execution of national policy, principally in improving relations with Latin America, the Caribbean, and Africa. It was comprised of the Chief of Staff of the Army, the Chief of Naval Operations, and the Under Secretary of State. Its influence in general policy planning diminished after the U.S. entry into the war although it continued to meet until mid-1943.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Bureau for Latin American, was established in 1961 and was the principal line office of the Agency with responsibility for program planning and execution of programs within the region. Programs were administered in accordance with policies and standards established by the Administrator assisted by Agency for International Development (AID) headquarters program and staff offices. On March 3, 1978, the Bureau for Latin America was retitled the Bureau for Latin American and the Caribbean.

[6, 37-39] (AID organization chart, Sept. 25, 1961: Latin American Regional Bureau; By March 1978 the AID Reorganization Task Force appointed by the Administrator in mid-1977, had, for the most part, completed its functional review of the Agency and recommended a number of major changes in program director and organizational structure, many of which were approved by the AID Administrator. Agency for International Development organization chart, effective date: March 3, 1978 Bureau for Latin America and the Caribbean. August 1978 Within a few months by August 1978 the Agency had undergone the following additional changes: 3. The Bureau for Latin America was retitled the Bureau for Latin American and the Caribbean. The Office of Multi-lateral Coordination and Regional Social Development programs was disbanded, and its functional responsibilities are related activities were reassigned to the Office of Development Programs. In addition the Bureau was reorganized, and merged the AID portion of the joint State/AID Office of Panamanian Affairs into the Office of Central America. The Office was retitled the Office of Central American and Panamanian Affairs)

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Office of International Information Programs (IIP) (the Bureau of International Information Programs after May 2003) was the principal international strategic communications service for the foreign affairs community. IIP designed, developed, and implemented a variety of information initiatives and strategic communications programs, including Internet and print publications, traveling and electronically transmitted speaker programs, and information resource services. These were intended for key international audiences, such as the media, government officials, opinion leaders, and the general public in more than 140 countries around the world.                                                

The office's products and services--including web sites and other Internet services, electronic journals, speaker programs, print publications, and CD-ROMs-- were designed to support the State Department's initiatives, as well as those of other U.S. foreign policy organizations. It also managed Information Resource Centers overseas and offered reference specialists based in Washington, D.C., to answer specialized information queries from abroad. 

The IIP was created from elements of the U.S. Information Agency when it merged with the Department of State on October 1, 1999. IIP comprised three offices:  The Office of Geographic Liaison was the first point of contact within IIP for missions overseas and the audiences they served. Its writer-editors, information resource officers, program officers, and translators provided regionally oriented products and services. The Office of Thematic Programs had multifunctional teams organized in one of two ways: along subject-matter lines, such as economic security, or along product lines, such as electronic media. The thematic teams worked closely with the geographic teams in preparing products and services that support Washington initiatives and mission requests. The Office of Technology Services was responsible for developing, interpreting, and applying government-wide technology policies and procedures in support of the Under Secretary for Public Diplomacy and Public Affairs, the Bureau of Educational and Cultural Exchanges, and IIP.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Mission in Cambodia, established in the 1950s and based in the capital city of Phnom Penh, was charged with coordinating infrastructure improvements and generally raising the quality of life for Cambodians through the provision of American aid monies, equipment, and technical assistance.

Between 1955 and 1963, the United States provided $409.6 million in economic grant aid and $83.7 million in military assistance. This aid was used primarily to repair damage caused by Cambodia's war of independence from France, to support internal security forces, and for the construction of an all-weather road to the seaport of Sihanoukville, which gave Cambodia its first direct access to the sea and access to the southwestern hinterlands. Relations deteriorated in the early 1960s. Per the initiative of Norodom Sihanouk, on November 20, 1963 the National Congress of the Sangkum Reash Niyum unanimously voted not to accept grants from the United States in the domains of military, economics, technical or cultural affairs, and the USAID Mission departed Cambodia shortly thereafter.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Collection and Liaison Division, was primarily responsible for collecting the raw and finished intelligence from other intelligence agencies, both within the Government and from foreign governments; falling within the six categories spelled out in the Intelligence Advisory Committee (IAC) Survey. In addition, this Division tried to convince other agencies to produce finished intelligence for the U.S. Information Agency (USIA). To the extent that it succeeded, the work of the Intelligence Production Division was simplified. 

The Collection and Liaison Division also disseminated the raw and finished intelligence which it collected to all elements of USIA. They distributed to the U.S. Information Service (USIS) in the field and to other Government agencies, the finished production turned out by Office of Research and Intelligence (IRI). It was responsible for getting scripts declassified, which utilized paraphrases of some classified material in their preparation.

Another major responsibility of the Collection and Liaison Division was to formulate intelligence requirements. Normally, people had a vague desire for "all the facts" on a given subject. The Division got them to refine and sharpen their requirements until the Division know exactly what they wanted, and how they planned to use the information. It then listed the minimum information to be collected. The Division laid requirements on the other intelligence agencies (Department of State, Department of Defense, Central Intelligence Agency (CIA)) to do production for the USIA when they were better equipped. It laid requirements on the field to collect information when they were the best source. In other words, this Division was the middleman between the user of intelligence and those who collected and produced it. The Collection and Liaison Division was headed by Ed Carroll and later Donald Shea.

The first of these, the Collection and Liaison Division, is primarily responsible for collecting the raw and finished intelligence from other intelligence agencies, both within this Government and from foreign governments; falling within the six categories spelled out in the IAC Survey. In addition, this division has the job of trying to convince other agencies to produce finished intelligence for us. To the extent that it succeeds, the work of the Production Division is simplified. The Collection Division also disseminates the raw and finished intelligence which it collects to all elements of USIA. They distribute to USIS in the field, and to other Government agencies, the finished production turned out by IRI. They are the people responsible for getting scripts declassified which have utilized paraphrases of some classified material in their preparation. Another major responsibility of the Collection and Liaison Division is to formulate intelligence requirements. Normally, people come to us with a vague desire for "all the facts" on a given subject. We then must get them to refine and sharpen their requirements until we know exactly what they want, and how they plan to use the information. We then list the minimum information which must be collected. The Division lays requirements on the other intelligence agencies (State, Defense, CIA) to do production for us when they are better equipped. creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Planning Officer assisted guiding future policy and operational changes in line with the changing times and conditions. The Officer drafted and kept basic guidance papers, the Worldwide Priority Themes, up-to date. It assisted in reviewing all CPPM's to conform to Agency and U.S. Government policies. It prepared Program Action memoranda, documents which were based on survey research and which outlined appropriate action by field posts or by the media services. The Planning Officer sought ideas from a variety of sources. In addition to frequent contact with officers assigned to various Agency elements, the Officer interviewed returning field officers on the broad questions of Agency objectives, accomplishments and efficiencies. The Officer drew on the best thinking from outside the Agency and outside the government. The Planning Officer was responsible for the policy paper "USIA's Role in National Development". The Planning Officer was the head of a National Development Task Force consisting of Office of Policy and Research (IOP) officers and policy officers from the Areas and the Medias. The Group explored how the U.S. Information Agency (USIA) could respond more effectively to this critical issue. The Planning Officer helped affect Agency operations through its active support to the IOP role in the Program Review Committee, which made decisions on all major Agency expenditures. The Planning Office did staff work for the Deputy Director for Policy and Plans. Margot Cutter was the Planning Officer for this time span.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Office of Regional Sustainable Development (LAC/RSD) provided technical leadership and liaison, regional expertise, sectoral strategies, and advice in the areas of economic growth, agriculture, and trade; democracy and governance; education and human resources; population and health; and the environment. 

The Office designed, implemented, and evaluated selected regional projects and was organized into five teams. 

(1) The Broad-Based Economic Growth Team supported economic growth issues including sectoral policy; trade, exports, and markets; agriculture and rural development; micro-enterprise, small business and remittances; financial markets and privatization; legal and regulatory reform; and food security. The team coordinated the technical aspects of food aid programs with DCHA and collaborates with the environment team on habitat preservation, biological diversity, environmental protection, and pollution control and abatement. 

(2) The Democracy and Governance Team supported rule of law and human rights; violence and conflict prevention; civil-military relations; participation and decentralization; governance and accountability; civil society; and political processes such as elections support. 

(3) The Education and Human Resources Team supported basic education, secondary and vocational education; education policy reform, teacher training, and participant training; and provided advice and support for education and training functions. 

(4) The Population, Health, and Nutrition Team supported issues related to family planning and reproductive health; child survival; maternal health; HIV/AIDS; health sector policy reform; tropical and infectious diseases; and sustainability of program impacts. 

(5) The Environment Team supported technical areas related to environmental protection; conservation of tropical forests; urban and industrial pollution; energy; pest and pesticide management; 

global climate change; and coastal resource management.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Interagency Youth Committee (IAYC) was established in April 1962.  Initially membership consisted of the following agencies: Department of State, Department of Defense, Department of Justice, United States Information Agency, the Peace Corps, the Agency for International Development, and the Central Intelligence Agency.  Over time, the makeup of the committee changed.  CIA participation ended and a representative of the White House/National Security Council was added.  The Department of Health, Education, and Welfare also joined the committee.

The Department of State representative served as chair.  Initially the chairman was the Assistant Secretary of State for Educational and Cultural Affairs.  In 1966, general direction of the interagency youth program was transferred to the Deputy Under Secretary for Political Affairs (G) where the position of Special Assistant (Youth), correspondence symbol G/Y, was established.  In 1969, responsibility for the program was transferred to the Counselor (C).  The work of the Committee was directly overseen by the Special Assistant, Youth Affairs(C/Y).

The Committee was established to stimulate and coordinate U.S. Government programs aimed at young leaders overseas, principally in developing countries, and to compete successfully with Communist countries for influence on their future courses of action.

The Committee appears to have ceased action in 1973.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Central African Republic (CAR) was one of the poorest countries in the world and in 1975 the United Nations included it in its list of hard-core least-developed countries among the developing countries.  Agriculture was the CAR's most important economic sector, providing a livelihood for nearly 85 per cent of the population. Major exports were cotton, timber, coffee, and diamonds.

The U.S.'s development strategy reflected a humanitarian concern for the people of the CAR and was aimed at increasing agricultural production and improving the health and skills of the rural poor. The lack of physical infrastructure and scarcity of trained manpower and managerial capacity in the country limited the CAR's absorptive capacity in terms of development assistance projects.

In FY 1976 the U.S. program totalled approximately $600,000. The two major projects were the establishment of a seed production center and the training and equipment of two well drilling teams to provide village drinking water. A FY 1977 project had been approved for technical assistance and equipment to expand fish production.The project was designed to rehabilitate CAR fish stations and assist farmers in the establishment of fish ponds. A project to establish a health delivery system in Ouham province was also in planning.

The U.S. Embassy in Bangui was briefly closed as a result of the 1996-97 mutinies against the Patasse government, It reopened in 1998 with limited staff, but U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) and Peace Corps missions previously operating in Bangui did not return. USAID programs in the CAR subsequently were administred by USAID/East Africa, headquartered in Nairobi, and centered around a rural roads and rehabilitation program, rehabilitating approximately 137 kilometers of rural road between Bozoum and Bossangoa

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The United States recognized the independence of Guinea-Bissau on September 10, 1974. The Embassy at Bissau was established on June 30, 1976, with Dean Curran as Charge d'Affaires.

Melissa Foelsch Wells was appointed the first Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary and she presented her credentials on November 29, 1976. Succeeding her were Edward Marks, October 31, 1977; Peter J. de Vos, September 22, 1980; and Wesley William Egan, Jr., May 12, 1983. Barbara C. Maslak served as Charge d'Affaires ad interim from January 1985 through August 1986. The next Ambassador, John Dale Blacken, presented his credentials on August 27, 1986. He was succeeded by William H. Jacobsen, Jr., November 13, 1989; Roger A. McGuire, October 14, 1992; and Peggy Blackford, November 4, 1995.

The U.S. Embassy suspended operations on June 14, 1998, due to a violent conflict between forces loyal to then-President Joao Bernardo Vieira and a military-led junta. Diplomatic relations with Guinea-Bissau were subsequently under the purview of the U.S. Ambassador to Senegal, resident at Dakar. Subsequently the U.S. Ambasador to Senegal was accredited as the U.S. Ambassador to Guinea-Bissau. 

The United States reopened a diplomatic office in Guinea-Bissau on July 7, 2007 amid fears the West African country was becoming a growing hub for Latin American drug traffickers. The opening of a liaison office was part of a five-year program to return to a full diplomatic presence in Guinea-Bissau. All official U.S. contact with Guinea-Bissau continued to be handled by the U.S. Embassy in Dakar and local employees staffed the U.S. Office in Bissau, American diplomats from the Embassy in Dakar travelled frequently to Bissau to conduct normal diplomatic relations.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
On March 23, 1967, the Office of the War on Hunger (WOH) was established in accordance with an AID General Notice of that date. It gained the following functions, personnel, and records from the former Office of Material Resources: the Assistant Administrator (except the Special Assistant for Economics and Trade and the Special Ocean Freight Staff), the Deputy Assistant Administrator, and the Associate Assistant Administrator for Special Resources; the Food for Peace Division; the Voluntary Foreign Aid Service; the agricultural commodity specialist function from the Industrial Resources Division; and the Office of the Special Assistant for Management and Administration, except for the Assistant Administrator for Administration. From the former Office of Technical Cooperation and Research, WOH gained the Agriculture and Rural Development Service and the Health Service; as well as those concerned with the coordination of Agency research and with the provision of staff support to the Technical Assistance and Resource Council and to the Research Advisory Committee.

The Office coordinated and concentrated the staff functions of AID's food, agriculture development, nutrition, health, population, and family planning programs. President Johnson had assigned to AID the leadership of the U.S. Government's attack on the food population problem. The Office of the War on Hunger was originally headed by Herbert J. Waters, Assistant Administrator, who reported to the Administrator. Other Assistant Administrators included H. Brooks James and Irwin R. Hedges (Acting).

In 1969, the Office of the War on Hunger was abolished and its Food for Peace functions were transferred to the new Office of Food for Peace and the remaining functions to the new Bureau for Technical Assistance.

This Office, and that of Private Resources, was established in March 1967, to implement the presidential directives and to give the War on Hunger greater impact. Besides the Population Service, the Office of the War on Hunger consolidates several activities that had already existed in AID—Food for Freedom, Agriculture and Rural Development, Health, Nutrition and Child Feeding. A Food from the Sea Service was added. Because most of the research and institutional grants projects were in the War on Hunger field the administrative staff for these also was made part of the Office. Evolution of the AID/Washington Organization: A Summary Description of Organization Changes Occurring in AID 1961-1980, December 1980: p. unnumbered (June 1967 Major reorganizations occurred during the first half of 1967. By June AID had: 1. Abolished the Office of Development Finance and Private Enterprise, the Office of Technical Cooperation and Research, and the Office of Material Resources. 4. Established an Office of War on Hunger, transferring to it the Food for Peace and voluntary foreign aid functions from the abolished Office of Material Resources, the agricultural health and research coordination functions form the abolished Office of Technical Cooperation and Research, and establishing a new Population Service in it; Major organization changes occurred in FY 1970. By August 3, AID had: 1. Established a new Bureau for Technical Assistance. The new Bureau was designed to consolidate under single management the central staff functions carried out by the Associate Assistant Administrator for Technical Assistance in the Office of Program and Policy Coordination, and by the Office of War on Hunger, with the exception of the Food for Peace function. Included in the new Bureau was an Office of Science and Technology containing the “research” function. 2. Abolished the Office of War on Hunger and established an Office of Food for Peace to have leadership in the use of P.L. 480 food resources in U.S. overseas development efforts.)

Issuances, 1956-1990 (Department of State Agency for International Development Office of the Administrator AID General Notice Subject: Office of the War on Hunger, March 23, 1967 (Pursuant to AID General Notice dated February 10, 1967, AID/W Reorganization for Increased Emphasis on the Private Sector and the War on Hunger, the Office of War on Hunger is established and the Office of Material Resources [MR] is abolished effective this date. The Office of the War on Hunger (AA/WOH) is headed by Mr. Herbert J. Waters, Assistant Administrator, who reports to the Administrator. The Office of the War on Hunger consists of the Office of the Assistant Administrator, Policy and Evaluation Staff, Management Staff, Reports and Information Staff, AID Research and Institutional Grants Staff, Voluntary Foreign Aid Service (including Disaster Relief), Agriculture and Rural Development Service, Population Service, Nutrition and Child Feeding Service, Health Service, Food from the Sea Service, and Food for Freedom Services. All functions, position ceilings, and personnel assigned to the offices of the Assistant Administrator (except the Special Assistant for Economics and Trade and the Special Ocean Freight Staff), the Deputy Assistant Administrator, and the Associate Assistant Administrator for Special Resources, MR; the Food for Peace Division, MR; Voluntary Foreign Aid Service, MR; Agriculture and Rural Development Service, TCR [Office of Technical Cooperation and Research]; and Health Service, TCR, are transferred to the Office of the War on Hunger. The position ceilings and personnel concerned with the agricultural commodity specialist function in the Industrial Resources Division, MR, are also transferred to AA/WHO. In addition, appropriate TCR position ceilings and personnel concerned with the coordination of Agency research and with the provision of staff support to the Technical Assistance and Resource Council and to the Research Advisory Committee will be transferred to the Office of the War on Hunger. The Special Assistant (Economics and Trade) is transferred with his functional responsibilities to the Office of Development Finance and Private Enterprise as are all functions, position ceilings, and personnel of the International Cooperative Development Service, MR. The functions, position ceilings, and personnel of the Special Ocean Freight Staff in the Office of the Assistant Administrator, MR, are transferred to the Office of Procurement, AA/A. All personnel, position ceilings, and functions of the Office of the Special Assistant for Management and Administration, MR, are transferred to the Office of the War on Hunger except that the Assistant Administrator for Administration will subsequently identify, after consulting with affected offices, appropriate administrative and support positions and ceilings thereof for subsequent transfer to the Office of Procurement as well as appropriate AA/TCR administrative and support positions and ceiling for transfer to AA/WOH or the other offices affected by the AID/W reorganization announced in the February 10, 1967 notice. Pending the reallocation of administrative and support position ceiling, the Office of the War on Hunger will provide administrative services to the Office of Procurement. Records relevant to all reassigned functions will be transferred with them.))

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Office of Program Coordination and Development recruited U.S. speakers to explain U.S. policies and society to overseas audiences, both in person and through electronic media from the United States. The speakers addressed a wide variety of political, economic, and social subjects. provides These expert speakers, sent to U.S. Information Service (USIA) posts, were called American Participants (AmParts). The Office also recruited Professionals-in-Residence as consultants to media outlets, government ministries, parliaments, and other organizations promoting the development of democratic institutions. Also, sports experts traveled abroad to assist foreign sports organizations.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Office of the Comptroller was established by the act creating the Department of the Treasury (1 Stat. 65), September 2, 1789, inheriting certain records and functions of the U.S. Government under the Articles of Confederation. According to section III of the Act of Congress establishing the Treasury Department, it was the Comptroller's duty to "superintend the adjustment and preservation of the public accounts; to examine all accounts settled by the Auditor, and certify the balances arising thereon to the Register of the Treasury; to countersign all warrants drawn by the Secretary of the Treasury, which shall be warranted by law; to report to the Secretary the official forms of all papers to be issued in the different offices for collecting the public revenue, and the manner and form of keeping and stating the accounts of the several persons employed therein. He shall moreover provide for the regular and punctual payment of all monies which may be collected, and shall direct prosecutions for all delinquencies of officers of the revenue, and for debts that are, or shall be due to the United States".

The office was redesignated the Office of the First Comptroller by an act of March 3, 1817 (3 Stat. 367) which created the Office of the Second Comptroller and relieved the Office of the First Comptroller of responsibility for settling military accounts and claims. The duties of the First Comptroller were further modified by an act of March 3, 1849 (9 Stat. 366), which transferred functions relating to receipts and expenditures for collecting customs revenues to the Office of the Commissioner of Customs.

The Dockery Act (28 Stat. 205, approved July 31, 1894) abolished the offices of the Second Comptroller and the Commissioner of Customs and returned their functions to the First Comptroller, who was then renamed the Comptroller of the Treasury.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The National Security Council was established by the National Security Act of 1947 (61 Stat. 496), as amended by the National Security Act Amendments of 1949 (63 Stat. 579). Later in 1949, as part of the Reorganization Plan, the Council was placed in the Executive Office of the President. The National Security Council was the President's principal forum for considering national security and foreign policy matters with his senior national security advisors and cabinet officials. Since its inception under President Truman, the function of the Council was to advise and assist the President on national security and foreign policies. The Council also served as the President's principal arm for coordinating these policies among various government agencies. 

The National Security Council was chaired by the President. When the President was absent, the Vice President could preside at the President's direction. Its regular attendees (both statutory and non-statutory) were the Vice President, the Secretary of State, the Secretary of the Treasury, the Secretary of Defense, the Secretary of Energy, and the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs (also called the National Security Advisor). The Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff was the statutory military advisor to the Council, and the Director of National Intelligence was the intelligence advisor. The Chief of Staff to the President, Counsel to the President, the Director of the Central Intelligence Agency, the Secretary of Homeland Security, the Homeland Security Advisor, the Representative of the United States to the United Nations, and the Assistant to the President for Economic Policy were invited to attend any NSC meeting. The Attorney General and the Director of the Office of Management and Budget were invited to attend meetings pertaining to their responsibilities. The heads of other executive departments and agencies, as well as other senior officials, attended meetings of the NSC when appropriate. 

The day-to-day affairs of the NSC were overseen by the President's National Security Advisor. The National Security Advisor determined the agenda for the NSC, ensured that the necessary papers were prepared and recorded Council actions and Presidential decisions.

An August 2, 1996, decision of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit held that the National Security Council did not exercise substantial authority independent of the President and was therefore not an agency within the meaning of the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA), 5 U.S.C. sec 552 (f). However, the NSC accepted and processed requests from the public and releases information as appropriate on a discretionary basis.

Federal Register, vol. 82, January 28, 2017: p. 9119-9123 (National Security Presidential Memorandum-2 of January 28, 2017 Organization of the National Security Council and the Homeland Security Council Memorandum I hereby direct that my system for national security policy development and decision-making shall be organized as follows: A. The National Security Council, the Homeland Security Council, and Supporting Staff The National Security Act of 1947, as amended, established the National Security Council (NSC) to advise the President with respect to the integration of domestic, foreign, and military policies relating to the national security. There is also a Homeland Security Council (HSC)—established through Executive Order 13228 of October 8, 2001, and subsequently codified in the Homeland Security Act of 2002—that has the purpose of advising the President on matters pertaining to homeland security. Each Council is also responsible for the effective coordination of the security-related activities and functions of the executive departments and agencies. The security threats facing the United States in the 21st century transcend international boundaries. Accordingly, the United States Government's decision-making structures and processes to address these challenges must remain equally adaptive and transformative. Both Councils are statutory bodies that the President will continue to chair. Invitations to participate in specific Council meetings shall be extended to those heads of executive departments and agencies, and other senior officials, who are needed to address the issue or issues under consideration. When the President is absent from a meeting of either Council, the Vice President may preside at the President's direction. The Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs (National Security Advisor) and the Assistant to the President for Homeland Security and Counterterrorism (Homeland Security Advisor) shall be responsible, as appropriate and at the President's direction, for determining the agenda for the NSC or HSC, respectively, ensuring that the necessary papers are prepared, and recording Council actions and Presidential decisions in a timely manner. When international economic issues are on the agenda of the NSC, the National Security Advisor and the Assistant to the President for Economic Policy shall perform these tasks in concert. The NSC and HSC shall have as their regular attendees (both statutory and non-statutory) the President, the Vice President, the Secretary of State, the Secretary of the Treasury, the Secretary of Defense, the Attorney General, the Secretary of Energy, the Secretary of Homeland Security, the National Security Advisor, the Homeland Security Advisor, and the Representative of the United States to the United Nations. When international economic issues are on the agenda of the NSC, the NSC's regular attendees will include the Secretary of Commerce, the United States Trade Representative, and the Assistant to the President for Economic Policy. The Director of National Intelligence and the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, as statutory advisers to the NSC, shall also attend NSC meetings. The Assistant to the President and Chief of Staff, the Assistant to the President and Chief Strategist, the Counsel to the President, the Deputy Counsel to the President for National Security Affairs, and the Director of the Office of Management and Budget are invited as attendees to any NSC meeting. In addition to the NSC and HSC, there is also a single NSC staff within the Executive Office of the President that serves both the NSC and HSC. The staff is composed of regional, issue-focused, and functional directorates and headed by a single civilian Executive Secretary, pursuant to 50 U.S.C. 3021, who is also the Chief of Staff. All policy and staff activity decisions will be transmitted to the Executive Secretary for appropriate distribution and awareness. The purpose of the NSC staff is to advise me, the National Security Advisor, the Homeland Security Advisor, the NSC members, the HSC members, and others in the White House; to facilitate the implementation of Administration policy; and to help coordinate the national-security-related activities of the executive departments and agencies… E. General The President and the Vice President may attend any and all meetings of any entity established by or under this memorandum. This document is part of a series of National Security Presidential Memoranda that shall replace both Presidential Policy Directives and Presidential Study Directives as the instrument for communicating relevant Presidential decisions. This memorandum shall supersede all other existing Presidential guidance on the organization or support of the NSC and the HSC. With regard to its application to economic matters, this document shall be interpreted in concert with any Executive Order governing the National Economic Council and with Presidential Memoranda signed hereafter that implement either this memorandum or that Executive Order.)

In addition to the NSC and HSC, there is also a single NSC staff within the Executive Office of the President that serves both the NSC and HSC…E. creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
Title II refers to a portion of the Agricultural Trade and Development Assistance Act of 1954 (68 Stat. 454), signed into law on July 10, 1954. Executive Order 10900 of January 5, 1961, delegated these responsibilities to the Secretary of State.

The main purpose of Title II programs was to provide for emergency and private assistance programs, particularly donation of U.S. agricultural products to meet humanitarian food needs. Recipients of emergency, or humanitarian relief, and non-emergency (development) food aid included private volunteer organizations, non-governmental organizations (NGO's) and international organizations such as the World Food Programme. Non-emergency aid was used in support of development, health, nutrition, and educational programs.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The establishment of the Executive Secretariat (EXSEC) in the Agency for International Development, effective November 4th, was announced in the AID General Notice dated October 26, 1961. It inherited functions formerly assigned to the ICA Executive Secretariat, and the executive secretariat functions performed through the Office of the Secretary-Treasurer of the Development Loan Fund (DLF). It was responsible for providing staff services and special assistance to the Administrator, the deputy administrators; the assistant Administrators and other senior staff; assuring that policy decisions were properly formulated and disseminated throughout the Agency; serving as coordination point for communications to and from the Office of the Administrator; effecting liaison with the Executive Secretariat in the Department of State; providing services for the Administrator's meetings, and for meetings of committees advisory to the Administrator; and controlling AID participation in international conferences.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Interagency Council on International Educational and Cultural Affairs was established on January 20, 1964, by a Foreign Affairs Manual Circular authorized by the Mutual Educational and Cultural Exchange Act of 1961 (75 Stat. 527), better known as the Fulbright-Hays Act. It was an interagency council under the Department of State and its membership was composed of representatives from the Departments of State; Defense; Health, Education, and Welfare; the Agency for International Development (USAID); the U.S. Information Agency (USIA); and the Peace Corps.

The Council was established to strengthen the coordination of the Federal Government's international educational and cultural programs and policies. It undertook specific projects in fields of common concern, such as the "brain drain," English-language instruction, and exchanges in the fields of law, science, and technology.

The Council was abolished in October 1973.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The U.S. Agency for International Development (AID) was established within the Department of State on November 3, 1961. AID was responsible for the administration of non-military U.S. foreign assistance programs as defined under the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961. The Agency supported programs in four major areas: population and health, broad-based economic growth, the environment, and democracy. AID also provided humanitarian assistance and aid to countries in crisis and transition.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) assistance to Jamaica since its independence in 1962 contributed to reducing the population growth rate, the attainment of higher standards in a number of critical health indicators, and the diversification and expansion of Jamaica's export base. USAID’s primary objective in Jamaica was to increase peace and security through reducing crime and corruption. Other key objectives included fostering broad-based economic growth, strengthening the primary educational system, improving the profitability and competitiveness of key agricultural crops, and reducing the prevalence of HIV/AIDS in most-at-risk populations. In fiscal year 2011, USAID/Jamaica operated a program totaling more than $30 million in development assistance.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The British-American Joint Patent Interchange Committee was established in accordance with the British-American Patent Interchange Agreement of August 24, 1942.  The Agreement provided for the interchange of patent rights, inventions, technical information, designs, and processes between the governments of the United States and Great Britain for war production purposes.  The Agreement was terminated on April 8, 1946.

The Committee's function was to deal with problems arising in connection with operations under the Agreement and to make recommendations to the two governments for necessary action.  Among the principal problems with which the Committee was concerned were (1) the question of reciprocal indemnities, (2) government procurement methods relating to patent rights and unpatented technical information, (3) possible infringement by the American armed forces in England of British-owned patents, (4) the possible need of United States requisitioning powers over patent rights and unpatented technical information, (5) the question whether intergovernmental arrangements should be made for royalty-free disposal at the end of the war of articles embodying patented inventions supplied by one government to the other under Lend-Lease or Reciprocal Aid, (6) secrecy orders covering patent applications filed in the United States and in Great Britain, and (7) the possible need of U.S. Treasury Department regulations to control the transfer of patent rights and unpatented technical information between United States citizens and British subjects.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
On October 2, 1958, Guinea proclaimed itself a sovereign and independent republic, with Sekou Toure as President. The United States established diplomatic relations with the country shortly afterward. Guinea became a one-party dictatorship, with a closed, socialized economy and no tolerance for human rights, free expression, or political opposition. Toure's paranoia ruined relations with foreign nations, including neighboring African states, increasing Guinea's isolation and further devastating its economy.

With Toure still in office, in the mid-1970's U.S. aid to Guinea was limited to agricultural production and training and the development of a model farm.

Following a coup d'etat on December 23, 2008 the United States suspended all aid to Guinea, except for humanitarian assistance and programs in support of the democratic process. Before suspending aid, the U.S. Mission , which included USAID, managed a military assistance program that provided for military education, professionalization, language training programs, and health equipment purchases. 

After Guinea's successful presidential elections in 2010 however, almost all of Guinea's former partners normalized relations. Promoting a transition to democratic, civilian rule was the U.S. Government's highest priority in Guinea. USAID supported the electoral process and promoted good governance and decentralization to bring improved services to the Guinean people. USAID assistance also included a health program focused on HIV/AIDS prevention, and improving maternal and child health and reproductive health, as well as a program to improve food security and nutrition.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
Through 1971, the United States Government provided India with about $10 billion in development loans and technical assistance and food aid. In the 10 years prior to that date, U.S. economic assistance averagedslightly more than $600 million annually. Roughly, each year about $300 million was made available in the form of development loans and grants; the balance was provided in food aid, mostly under PL 480, Title I credit sales.

The 1971 Indo-Pakistan war led to suspension of U. S. development programs to Pakistan and India. Subsequently, a large-scale foreign assistance program was resumed in Pakistan but not in India. Although an offer was made to India to continue a scaled-down technical assistance program, in the existing chilly political atmosphere, the Government of India (GOI) indicated that it wished to phase out entirely the U.S. program authorized by the Foreign Assistance Act. Food aid under PL 480 Title I credit sales was also suspended. In 1975 and 1976 shipments resumed again at about half a million tons of wheat valued at about $100 million per year. In 1977, wheat continued to be allocated for India, but it was not sent because of record harvests and high stocks. Vegetable oil worth $25-35 million per year was provided in 1977 and 1978. The United States also continued to contribute to Indian development through its participation in multilateral assistance agencies such as IDA and the World Bank. The U.S. provided over 30 percent of IDA's soft loan replenishment funds which would indirectly amount to over $200 millionof IDA's annual commitments of roughly $600 million to India. 

On July 14, 1977, in a climate of improved relations India between the U.S. and India, the Congress recommended to the President the resumption of AID assistance to India. USAID/India resumed operations as a Mission in May 1978.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The United States opened diplomatic relations with Kenya and established the Embassy at Nairobi on December 12, 1963. Laurence C. Vass was Charge d'Affaires ad interim.

The first U.S. Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary, William Attwood, presented his credentials on March 2, 1964. He was succeeded by Glenn W. Ferguson, November 4, 1966; Robinson McIlvaine, September 30, 1969; Anthony D. Marshall, January 22, 1974; Wilbert John LeMelle, August 10, 1977; William Caldwell Harrop, July 10, 1980; Gerald Eustis Thomas, November 9, 1983; Elinor Greer Constable, December 11, 1986; Smith Hempstone, Jr., December 7, 1989; Aurelia Erskine Brazeal, September 21, 1993; Prudence Bushnell, September 2, 1996; and Johnnie Carson, September 23, 1999.

Ambassadors Marshall, LeMelle, and Harrop were also accredited to the Seychelles.

On August 7, 1998, a bomb exploded at the rear entrance of the U.S. Embassy in Nairobi, killing 12 U.S. citizens, 32 Foreign Service nationals, and 247 Kenyan citizens. Approximately 5,000 Kenyans, six U.S. citizens, and 13 Foreign Service nationals were injured. The U.S. Embassy building sustained extensive structural damage. The U.S. held Usama Bin Laden responsible.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The U.S. Agency for International Development (AID) was established within the Department of State on November 3, 1961. AID was responsible for the administration of non-military U.S. foreign assistance programs as defined under the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961. The Agency supported programs in four major areas: population and health, broad-based economic growth, the environment, and democracy. AID also provided humanitarian assistance and aid to countries in crisis and transition.

creators.biographicalNote: Alben William Barkley, (1877-1956), American political leader, was Vice President of the United States from 1949 to 1953. Barkley took a more active role in government than most vice presidents before him. He was affectionately called "the Veep", a nickname that clung to him even after he retired from office. Barkley was born in Graves County, Kentucky, on November 24, 1877, the son of tobacco farmer. Following graduation from Marvin College in Clinton, Kentucky, he studied law at Emory College in Oxford, Georgia, and the University of Virginia. He practiced law in Paducah, Kentucky, from 1901 to 1905, when he became prosecuting attorney of McCracken County. He was judge of the McCracken County Court from 1909 to 1913. Barkley was elected to the U.S. Congress as a Democrat from Kentucky's 1st district in 1912. He served seven terms before entering the U.S. Senate in 1927. During four consecutive terms as senator from Kentucky he became a national figure, first as a ranking minority leader and, for ten years beginning in 1937, as majority leader. He was an influential spokesman for the legislative programs of Presidents Franklin D. Roosevelt and Harry S Truman. He was instrumental in guiding much of the New Deal legislation through the Senate, and he consistently supported Truman's Fair Deal program. In 1948, Truman chose Barkley as his presidential running mate. He appointed Barkley to the National Security Council and consulted him on foreign and domestic issues. After leaving the vice presidency in January 1953, Barkley won back his old Senate seat in the 1954 elections. On April 30, 1956, he died suddenly while making a speech at Lexington, Virginia.

creators.biographicalNote: Robert Strange McNamara (b. June 9, 1916, in San Francisco, California-d. July 2009, Washington, D.C.) was a business executive and Secretary of Defense during the Kennedy and Johnson administrations. During World War II he worked on the deployment of the B-29 bomber, and served in the Army Air Forces in India, China, and the Pacific. He was released from active service in April 1946 with the rank of lieutenant colonel. He joined the Ford Motor Company and served in various positions, eventually becoming president of the Ford Motor Company on November 9, 1960. He only served as president for about one month, when President Kennedy appointed him Secretary of Defense. He was sworn in as Secretary of Defense on January 21, 1961, and became heavily preoccupied with the U.S. involvement in Vietnam. In 1967, he commissioned a study of American involvement in Vietnam, which eventually became know as the Pentagon Papers. At odds with President Johnson over American policy in Vietnam, he resigned as Secretary of Defense in early 1968. He served as president of the World Bank from 1968 to 1981.
