creators.biographicalNote: Dean Acheson was born in Middletown, Connecticut, on April 11, 1893. After being educated at Yale University (1912-1915) and Harvard Law School (1915-18) he became private secretary to the Supreme Court Justice, Louis Brandeis from 1919 to 1921. A supporter of the Democratic Party, Acheson worked for a law firm in Washington, D.C., before President Franklin D. Roosevelt appointed him Under Secretary of the Treasury in 1933. During World War II (1941), Acheson served as Assistant Secretary in the Department of State. In 1945 Harry S. Truman selected Acheson as his Under Secretary of State. Over the next two years, Acheson played a role in devising both the Truman Doctrine and the European Recovery Program (ERP), developed a strong personal relationship, with the President often consulting Acheson in the area of foreign policy. Later, Acheson accepted an appointment to the newly created Commission on the Reorganization of the Executive Branch, better known as the Hoover Commission. He was one of four appointments made by Truman to the twelve-member bipartisan commission. He became Truman's Secretary of State in 1949 and served in that position until 1953. Dean Acheson died in Sandy Spring, Maryland, on October 12, 1971.

Hubert Horatio Humphrey, Jr. (1911-1978) was a U.S. Senator and Vice President of the United States. He worked as a pharmacist in his father's drugstore in South Dakota for five years, and married Muriel Buck on September 2, 1936. He left the pharmacy and attended the University of Minnesota where he received a B.A. with high honors in June 1939. He received his M.A. from Louisiana State University in 1940. After graduating, he was director of a worker-education program for the Works Progress Administration, and ran for Mayor of Minneapolis under the Farmer-Labor Party in 1943. He made a strong showing but lost the election. He convinced the Democratic National Committee to merge with the Farmer-Labor Party in 1944, and in 1945 he ran again for Mayor of Minneapolis. He won by the biggest majority in the city's history to that time, and was re-elected in 1947.

Humphrey was elected to the U.S. Senate from Minnesota in 1948, and was re-elected in 1954. Senate majority leader Lyndon B. Johnson assigned Humphrey to the Foreign Relations Committee. In 1960 he became the majority whip in the Senate. After the assassination of President John F. Kennedy in 1963, Lyndon Johnson offered Humphrey the vice presidency. In the 1964 presidential election, Johnson passed over Attorney General Robert Kennedy for the vice presidency to pick Hubert Humphrey, and they were elected. When Johnson announced he would not seek re-election as president in 1968, Humphrey decided to run for the presidency. Robert Kennedy and Eugene McCarthy also sought the Democratic nomination, but Humphrey won the nomination after the assassination of Robert Kennedy. The 1968 Democratic National Convention in Chicago was a disaster, and Humphrey's ratings sank. He lost the election to Richard M. Nixon. He ran for the presidency again in 1972, but Senator George McGovern received the Democratic nomination. He remained in the U.S. Senate, and in 1977 the Senate made him its deputy president pro tempore. On January 13, 1978 he died in Minnesota and his wife, Muriel Humphrey, succeeded him in the Senate.

creators.biographicalNote: Chester Bliss Bowles (b. April 5, 1901, Springfield, Massachusetts-d. May 25, 1986, Essex, Connecticut), government official and Congressman. He graduated from Choate School in 1919 and Yale University in 1924. He worked as a businessman in Springfield, Massachusetts and New York City from 1924 to 1929. In 1929 he co-founded the New York City advertising firm Benton & Bowles, Inc., and was chairman of the board from 1936 to 1941. Bowles worked as the Connecticut State rationing administrator in 1942, the State director in 1942 and 1943, and general manager from July to October 1943. He also worked as the administrator in the Office of Price Administration from 1943 to 1946, was a member of the War Production Board and Petroleum Board for War from 1943 to 1946, and was chairman of the Economic Stabilization Board in 1946. Bowles was Governor of Connecticut from 1949 to 1951, Ambassador to India and Nepal from 1951 to 1953, U.S. Representative from 1959 to 1961, Under Secretary of State in 1961, and the President’s special representative and advisor from 1961 to 1963. Bowles returned to India as U.S. Ambassador and served from 1963 to 1969. He was a resident of Essex, Connecticut, and he is interred in the River View Cemetery in Essex, Middlesex County, Connecticut.

Myron Charles Taylor was born on January 18, 1874 in Lyons, New York.  He received an LL.B. from Cornell University in 1894.  He was admitted to the New York bar the following year, and began practicing law at the firm De Forest and De Forest. He became an expert in corporation law and handled legal matters for various textile companies. On February 21, 1906, he married Anabel Stuart Mack; they had no children.

He eventually abandoned practicing law and devoted his full attention to the reorganization and development of several textile companies.  By 1923 he had divested himself of most of his textile interests and devoted himself to banking and railroad directorships.   In 1927, he became Chairman of the Finance Committee of the U.S. Steel Corporation.  He served as Chairman of Finance from 1927 to 1934.  In 1932, J. Pierpont Morgan stepped aside as Chief Executive Officer, and Taylor assumed full executive power in the company.  He served as Chairman of the Board and CEO of U.S. Steel Corporation from 1932 to 1938.  From 1939 to 1950, Taylor served as Personal Representative of the President of the United States to Pope Pius XII, and from 1950 to 1952 he served as Personal Representative of the President of the United States on Special Missions.  Myron Taylor died in New York City on May 6, 1959.

creators.biographicalNote: Henry Alfred Kissinger (b. May 27, 1923, Furth, Bavaria, Germany - d. November 29, 2023, Kent, Connecticut) served as Secretary of State from 1973 to 1977 under both President Nixon and President Carter. He also served as National Security Advisor from 1968 to 1975 under President Nixon. He was the first person to hold both positions as Secretary of State and National Security Advisor at the same time. He was born as Heinz Alfred Kissinger but changed his name to Henry after immigrating to the U.S. with his family in 1938. After he became a naturalized citizen he went on to serve in the U.S. Army during World War II as a German interpreter. Following the war he went on to earn his Ph.D. in 1954 from Harvard University, where he remained as a faculty member. Before President Nixon selected him as National Security Advisor in 1968 Kissinger also worked as a consultant for several other government agencies. In 1973 he was awarded a Nobel Peace Prize for his involvement in negotiating ceasefires in Vietnam. Following his roles as Secretary of State and National Security Advisor, Kissinger went on to become a faculty member at Georgetown University. In 1985 President Reagan appointed Kissinger as a board member of the President’s Foreign Intelligence Advisory Board, which he served until 1990. Throughout the 1980s and through the 2000s Kissinger went on to hold various positions involved in political and foreign affairs. In 2002 he was appointed by President George W. Bush as chair of the National Commission on Terrorist Attacks Upon the United States.

creators.biographicalNote: John Fitzgerald Kennedy was born on May 29, 1917, to Joseph P. Kennedy and Rose Fitzgerald Kennedy of Brookline, Massachusetts. John Kennedy, the second of nine children, attended Choate Academy (1932-1935), Princeton University (1935-36), Harvard College (1936-40), and Stanford Business School (1941). In 1940, he published a book based on his senior thesis entitled "Why England Slept." The book criticized British policy of Appeasement. In 1941, Kennedy enlisted in the Navy. In August 1943, Kennedy was commanding PT 109 near the Solomon Islands when it was run over a Japanese destroyer. Kennedy was awarded the Purple Heart, and it took the rest of the war for him to recover from his injuries and the malaria he contracted soon after his rescue. In 1945, Kennedy became a special writer for the Hearst press. In 1946, Kennedy was elected to the U.S. House of Representative. In 1952, he ran for and defeated Henry Cabot Lodge, Jr., for the Senate. In 1954, he married Jacqueline Bouvier, and the couple had three children: Caroline, John Jr., and Patrick, who died as an infant. In 1956 he campaigned for the Democratic vice-presidential nomination but lost a close race to Senator Estes Kefauver of Tennessee. After Eisenhower's victory in 1956, Kennedy began to pursue the 1960 Democratic presidential nomination. He won the nomination over Senators Hubert H. Humphrey and Lyndon B. Johnson. With Johnson as his running mate, Kennedy faced Vice-president Richard M. Nixon in the general election. The campaign featured the first televised debate between presidential candidates. Kennedy became the youngest elected president in U.S. history at the age of forty-three, and the first to be born in the twentieth century. He was also the first Catholic to hold the nation's highest office. He was assassinated on November 22, 1963, in Dallas, Texas.

creators.biographicalNote:
Thomas Jefferson (1743-1826) was the third president of the United States, born in Goochland (now Albemarle County), Virginia. He was a member of the Virginia House of Burgesses from 1769 to 1775, and with R. H. Lee and Patrick Henry initiated the inter-colonial committee of correspondence in 1773. He wrote the widely circulated Summary View of the Rights of British America in 1774. Jefferson was a member of the Continental Congress in 1775 and 1776, and was chairman of committee that prepared Declaration of Independence. Jefferson himself wrote and presented the first draft of Declaration to Congress on July 2, 1776. He then signed Declaration with other founding fathers.

Jefferson was Governor of Virginia from 1779 to 1781, and again a member of the Continental Congress from 1783 to 1785. He proposed decimal coinage, a series of provisions later embodied in Ordinance of 1787. He served as U.S. minister to France from 1785 to 1789, and as U.S. Secretary of State from 1790 to 1793. He served as Vice president of the U.S. from 1797 to 1801, and drafted the Kentucky Resolves in 1798, against the Alien and Sedition Acts.

Jefferson was President of the United States from 1801 to 1809, elected by the House of Representatives after a tie in electoral vote (with Aaron Burr, q.v.). His presidential administration is remembered for the purchase of Louisiana from France in 1803 and dispatch of Lewis and Clark to explore it; the war against Algerian pirates from 1801 to 1805; diplomatic trouble with Great Britain over "impressments" of American seamen (Embargo Act of 1807); and prohibition of the importation of slaves. After retirement from presidency, Jefferson lived on his plantation at Monticello near Charlottesville, Virginia. He was instrumental in founding the University of Virginia in 1819. He was a noted naturalist, scholar, and architect, and author of Notes on the State of Virginia in 1785.

creators.biographicalNote:
Benjamin Sumner Welles (1892-1961) graduated from Harvard University in 1914 and began his diplomatic career in 1915 as Secretary of the United States Embassy in Tokyo. From 1917 to 1919 he served in a similar post in Buenos Aires, Argentina. He was Assistant Chief of the Latin American Affairs Division of the Department of State from 1920 to 1921, and Chief of the Division from 1921 to 1922. From 1922 to 1925, he was Minister Plenipotentiary and Envoy Extraordinary to the Dominican Republic, and also in 1922, a delegate to the Congress on Latin American Affairs in Washington, D.C. He served as personal representative of President Calvin Coolidge to offer mediation in the Honduras revolution in 1924, and as a delegate to the Central American Conference in Amapala, Honduras, in 1924. In 1929, he was a member of the Dawes Financial Mission to the Dominican Republic.

Welles, whose area of expertise was Latin American affairs, was named Assistant Secretary of State in 1933, a post he held until 1937, with a brief tenure as Ambassador to Cuba. From 1937 to 1943 he served as Under Secretary of State. He was President Franklin D. Roosevelt's personal envoy on a fact-finding mission to Europe early in 1940, and accompanied Roosevelt to his meeting at sea with Prime Minister Winston S. Churchill of Great Britain in August 1941.

creators.biographicalNote: George Catlett Marshall (b. Dec. 31, 1880, Uniontown, Pennsylvania-d. Oct. 16, 1959), General of the U.S. Army, was commissioned in the infantry in 1902 after graduating from the Virginia Military Institute. He was staff officer with the First Army, then VIII Corps, in France during World War I; aide to General Pershing; and battalion commander in 15th Infantry in China. He became Chief of Staff, U.S. Army (1939-1945), during World War II.  Following resignation from the Army, he was the personal representative of President Truman to mediate peace between the Nationalist and communist Chinese in 1946. He served as Secretary of State from 1947 to 1949, and as Secretary of Defense in 1950 and 1951. The “Marshall Plan” for economic recovery in Europe is named after the General. He was presented a gold medal from the U.S. Congress and awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1953.

William Pierce Rogers was born on June 23, 1913 in Norfolk, New York.  He received an A.B. from Colgate University in 1934, and an LL.B. from Cornell University in 1937.  He was admitted to the New York bar in 1937 and the District of Columbia bar in 1950.  He was the assistant district attorney for New York County from 1938 to 1942, and from 1946 to 1947.  He served in the U.S. Navy from 1942 to 1946.  In 1947 he was chief counsel for the U.S. Senate War Investigating Committee, and from 1947 to 1948 he served as chief counsel for the Truman Committee, U.S. Senate War Investigating Committee.  He also served as chief counsel for the U.S. Senate Investigations Sub-Committee Executive Expenditures Committee, 1948 to 1950.

In 1950 he returned to private law practice with the firm Dwight, Royall, Harris, Koegel & Caskey in New York and Washington, 1950 to 1953.  On January 28, 1953 he was sworn in as Deputy Attorney General, and served in this position until the resignation of Attorney General Herbert Brownell in October 1957.  As Deputy Attorney General, he served on the President's Award for Distinguished Federal Civilian Service Committee, the Government Contract Committee, and as the Special Presidential Representative to the Independence Ceremonies of Togo, Africa.  Rogers was also very active in the political campaigns of 1952 and 1956, accompanying Richard Nixon as one of his chief political advisers.  In October 1957, President Eisenhower selected Rogers as his new Attorney General.  He was sworn in on November 8, 1957.  Rogers resigned from his office on January 21, 1961.  He once again returned to private law practice, as a partner in the firm Royall, Koegel, Rogers & Wells, 1961 to 1969.  He served as Secretary of State from 1969 to 1973, under President Nixon.  In 1973 he became a senior partner in the firm Rogers & Wells.  He died on January 2, 2001.

creators.biographicalNote: George Wildman Ball (1909-1994). He graduated from Northwestern University in 1930, and received his J.D. in 1933. He was admitted to the Illinois bar the following year. Ball began his career of government service working in the General Counsel's Office of the U.S. Department of Treasury from 1933 to 1935. As a government official, he also served in the Lend Lease Administration, which later became the Foreign Economic Administration, from 1942 to 1944). From 1944 to 1945, he was Director of the U.S. Strategic Bombing Survey in London, England, and briefly following World War II, served as General Counsel for the French Supply Council in Washington, D.C., from  1945 to 1946. Ball became the Under Secretary of State for Economic Affairs in 1961, and from 1961 to 1966, served as the Under Secretary of State. He also served as permanent U.S. representative to the United Nations.

creators.biographicalNote: Henry Cabot Lodge (1902-1985) was a journalist, U.S. Senator, and diplomat, and the grandson of statesman Henry Cabot Lodge, Sr. After graduating from Harvard University, he joined the U.S. Army Reserve. He began working as a journalist in Boston and New York in the 1920s, and launched a political career in 1932. He was elected to the Massachusetts legislature in 1932, was reelected in 1934, and was elected to the U.S. Senate in 1936. He resigned from the U.S. Senate in February 1944 to enter active service, and achieved the rank of lieutenant colonel. After World War II, he was reelected to the U.S. Senate in 1946. He played an influential role in the Republican Party, and helped Dwight D. Eisenhower secure the nomination for president. After Eisenhower's election, Lodge was appointed Ambassador to the United Nations, with cabinet rank. He was selected by Richard M. Nixon to run with him on the Republican ticket for the 1960 presidential election. After Kennedy won the election, Lodge was appointed Ambassador to Vietnam. He served in this position from 1963 to June 1965, and August 1965 to April 1967. He served as Ambassador to Germany during the last half of President Johnson's administration. He served as Chief negotiator at the Vietnam Peace Talks in Paris from 1968 to December 1969, and he served as special envoy to the Vatican from 1970 to 1977. He retired in 1977 and moved home to Massachusetts, where he lived until his death in 1985.

creators.biographicalNote:
John Roy Steelman was born in Thornton, Arkansas on June 23, 1900.  Upon graduating from high school he joined the U.S. Army and served in World War I, at the very end of the war.  After the war, he drifted across the country to gain seasonal employment in a variety of manual jobs, then entered Henderson-Brown College in Arkadelphia, Arkansas.  He graduated with a BA from Henderson-Brown College in 1922, and went on to graduate from Vanderbilt University in 1924 with an MA in sociology and a Ph.D. in social ethics and practical sociology in 1925.  He studied for one year as a graduate student at Peabody College in Nashville, Tennessee, and studied at Harvard University in 1926.  He received a doctorate in sociology and economics from the University of North Carolina in 1928.

Dr. Steelman became a professor of sociology and economics at Alabama College, but in 1934 he became a Commissioner of Conciliation for the government, to mediate industrial disputes.  In 1937, he was appointed Director of the Conciliation Service, and oversaw the settlement of thousands of labor-management disputes across the country.  In 1939, Steelman married Emma Zimmerman, whom he met at a union convention.  In 1944, he resigned as Director of the Conciliation Service, and moved to New York for a few months, working as a public relations consultant. Under President Truman in 1945, Steelman became a special assistant to Secretary of Labor Lewis Schwellenbach, and soon became special assistant to the President, in charge of labor matters.  On June 14, 1947, he became Director of the Office of War Mobilization and Reconversion (and temporarily served as Director of Economic Stabilization.)  After this wartime agency was dissolved by the President, Steelman was appointed to the new post of Assistant to the President of the United States, charged with coordinating Federal agency programs and policies.

Steelman also served as chairman of the President's Scientific Research Board, chairman of the President's Special Commission on Higher Education, and liaison officer for the Interdepartmental Committee on Scientific Research and Development.  In 1950, Steelman helped to avert a nationwide railroad strike, and in 1952 he helped settle a United Steel Workers strike.  He left the government in 1953, and went on to serve as director of the Audio-Dynamics Corporation, and a trustee of the Nationwide Investing Foundation.  He died in Naples, Florida on July 22, 1999.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
After the outbreak of war in the Far East in late 1941, Europe lost its hegemony over vast areas of tropical Asia, and was at serious risk of losing others. In the face of such developments, it became necessary to look elsewhere for strategic crops such as rubber (latex), certain fibers, medicinal plants, rice, tea, tropical oilseeds and plants used to produce insecticides, such as rotenone.  The Americas were deemed a valid alternative for fostering the development of tropical crops and stock raising, for which it would be necessary to establish research and education systems to address the region's needs.

The Inter-American Institute of Agricultural Sciences (IICA) was founded in 1942 by the efforts of Secretary of Agriculture Henry Wallace and Ernesto Molestina, Director General of Agriculture of Ecuador.  The Institute¿s headquarters were established in Turrialba, Costa Rica, a region strategically situated between South and North America, with characteristics typical of agriculture in the Americas.  In 1944, the first multilateral Convention on IICA was signed, under which its legal status was recognized by different governments in the hemisphere.

When the Organization of American States (OAS) was created in 1948, IICA became the specialized agency for agriculture of the Inter-American System, consolidating its work by extending its action to every country in the hemisphere. (This task was completed in the 1990s, when Bahamas joined as a member.) By 1964, 21 Member States of the OAS has joined IICA. 

During the 1970s, IICA carried out a number of specialized multinational programs as part of its strategy of hemispheric and humanist projection.  A new Convention on IICA was adopted in 1979, redefining the Institute's objectives, adjusting its cooperation actions with the member countries, and creating the Inter-American Board of Agriculture (IABA) as its new governing body. The organization was also renamed, becoming the Inter-American Institute for Cooperation on Agriculture.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
Concern over fluctuating water levels on Lake of the Woods led the Governments of canada and the United States to refer the matter to the International Joint Commission (IJC) in June 1912. Following a five year study, the IJC made a series of recommendations regarding flow regulation and the need for an engineering board and an international board to regulate and control lake levels. A (Canadian) Lake of the Woods Control Board was formed in 1919 by Canada and Ontario.

A treaty between Canada and the United States, known as the 1925 Lake of the Woods Convention and Protocol, was signed and established elevation and discharge requirements for regulating Lake of the Woods based on the IJC recommendations. The Convention and Protocol stated that whenever the level of the lake rose above elevation 1061 ft. (323.47 m) or fell below 1056 ft. (321.87 m) the rate of discharge of water from the lake would be subject to the approval of the International Lake of the Woods Control Board. 

Although appointed by governments, the Board reported annually (in the spring) to the International Joint Commission. The Canadian Lake of the Woods Control Board had responsibility for regulation of the lake under normal lake levels. With relatively few exceptions, such as the 1985 high water levels which slightly exceeded 1,061 ft., the lake has remained within the water level range where it is under the full authority of the Canadian Board.

The Board was composed of two engineers, one appointed by Canada and one by the United States. The U.S. member was usually appointed from among the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Voice of America (VOA) was established in June 1942. It has been preceded by the Foreign Information Service under the Office of the Coordinator of Information. It was the official broadcasting service of the U.S. Government. It's initial broadcasts were aimed at German-occupied Europe and North Africa. It began to transmit white propaganda radio broadcasts to the Soviet Union on February 17, 1947. Under U.S. law VOA was forbidden to broadcast directly to American citizens, however, VOA programs on shortwave and the Internet were audible in the United States.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: he United States has maintained relations with the Sultanate since the early years of American independence. A treaty of friendship and navigation, one of the first agreements of its kind with an Arab state, was concluded between the United States and Muscat in 1833. This treaty was replaced by the Treaty of Amity, Economic Relations, and Consular Rights signed at Salalah on December 20, 1958. A U.S. consulate was maintained in Muscat from 1880 until 1915. Thereafter, U.S. interests in Oman were handled by U.S. diplomats resident in other countries.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Department's regional bureaus oversaw the U.S. embassies and consulates, and coordinated U.S. foreign relations in their respective geographic areas. Assistant Legal Advisers supervised the attorneys who supported those bureaus, dealing with such matters as protection of U.S. citizens and investments, problems in diplomatic and consular relations, interpretation and negotiation of treaties, military base rights and status of force issues, peaceful settlement of disputes, and trade matters. The Office of Western Hemisphere Affairs handled legal matters relating to relations with the governments of Canada, Latin America, Central America and the Caribbean; U.S. participation in the Organization of American States; Cuba, including assets control, U.S. rights at Guantanamo, and Helms-Burton Act issues; illegal migration and refugee issues, particularly Haiti; foreign assistance; and domestic and international litigation relating to U.S. activities in the region.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: Section 38 of the Arms Export Control Act (22 U.S.C. 2778) authorized the President to control the export and import of defense articles and defense services covered by the United States Munitions List (USML). The statutory authority of the President to promulgate regulations with respect to exports of defense articles and defense services was delegated to the Secretary of State by Executive Order 11958, as amended (42 FR 4311). By virtue of delegations of authority by the Secretary of State, these regulations were primarily administered by the Director of the Office of Munitions Control in the Bureau of Politico-Military Affairs (35 FR 5422). In about 1998-99 the Office of Muntions Control became the Directorate of Defense Trade Controls.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
In the April 17, 1960 reorganization of the Bureau of International Cultural Relations into the Bureau of Educational and Cultural Affairs, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) Relations Staff was redesignated as the Secretariat-U.S. National Commission for UNESCO. By 1963, it was known as the Secretariat to the US National Commission for UNESCO.

In consultation with the Plans and Development Staff, the U.S. National Commission for UNESCO and the Bureau of International Organization Affairs, the Secretariat developed policies governing substantive U.S. participation in UNESCO and related bilateral and multilateral cultural programs. It coordinated activities relating to the participation of the United States in UNESCO, including an information program on UNESCO. The Secretariat consulted with the National Commission for UNESCO on matters related to the UNESCO program, biennial national conferences held by the National Commission, the composition of the delegations to the UNESCO General Conferences, and other matters referred to the Secretary of State to the National Commission for its recommendations. It provided staff functions for the National Commission including services for its meetings, conference and travel arrangements. The Director of the Secretariat served as the Executive Secretary of the U.S. National Commission for UENSCO.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: On September 11, 2008, the Government of Venezuela ordered the expulsion of U.S. Ambassador Patrick D. Duddy. This followed by one day the expulsion of the U.S. Ambassador to Bolivia. On June 25, 2009, through an exchange of diplomatic notes, the United States and Venezuela agreed to rescind the declarations of persona non grata issued in September 2008 and return U.S. Ambassador   Duddy and Venezuelan Ambassador Bernardo Álvarez to their respective posts in Caracas and Washington. Ambassador Duddy returned to his post shortly thereafter.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: Foreign Aid Staff served as the executive staff for the Advisory Committee on Voluntary Foreign Aid.  The Staff maintained a register of private U.S. non-profit agencies approved by the Advisory Committee and whose purposes and programs were determined to be in the public interest; appraised voluntary agency programs, budgets, and operations and suggested means of correlating them with related U.S. Government programs; encouraged and facilitated the activities of voluntary agencies in the field of technical cooperation; developed and maintained a roster of voluntary agencies which have competencies useful in the technical cooperation field; and administered the ICA program of reimbursement to registered American voluntary agencies for ocean freight costs on relief and rehabilitation supplies and surplus foods shipped abroad to countries in conformance with applicable U.S. statues and regulations.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Office of Soviet Union Affairs, and its predecessors, initiated policy with respect to political problems, served as the principal consultant of the Department on political problems and matters of general policy with regard to the Soviet Union, and kept informed of all developments in that region through the examination of communications from Foreign Service posts and from other sources. It cleared all policy actions affecting the assigned area which originated from within and outside the Department. It prepared studies and policy papers, draft memorandums, and instructions to Foreign Service posts on political matters of concern. It acted as liaison with appropriate foreign missions in the United States. It participated in conferences and meetings concerning policy matters relating to the Soviet Union. It drafted and updated policy statements on the Soviet Union. It coordinated work relating to the Soviet Union with that of other offices of the Department and other Federal agencies.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
From the earliest days of the Republic, Presidents have designated special diplomatic envoys for specific assignments, primarily overseas. The President appointed the first official specifically to bear the title of Ambassador at Large on March 12, 1949, under the authority vested in Article II, Section 2 of the U.S. Constitution that empowers the President, with the advice and consent of the Senate, to appoint Ambassadors, other public Ministers, and Consuls. Presidents have usually appointed Ambassadors at Large to deal with specific foreign policy issues which have been frequently, but not always, spelled out in their commissions.

Ellsworth Bunker served as Ambassador at Large from October 11, 1973, through June 30, 1978, leading the negotiating team that drafted the Panama Canal Treaty of 1977.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The U.S. Embassy for Burma was established at Rangoon on September 19, 1947, with Earl L. Packer as Charge d'Affaires ad interim. 

The first Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary, J. Klahr Huddle, presented his credentials on March 3, 1948. He was succeeded by David McK. Key, April 26, 1950; William J. Sebald, July 18, 1952; Joseph C. Satterthwaite, May 10, 1955; Walter P. McConaughy, August 20, 1957; William P. Snow, December 1, 1959; John S. Everton, June 10, 1961; Henry A. Byroade, October 7, 1963; Arthur W. Hummel, Jr., October 1968; Edwin W. Martin, October 1, 1971; David L. Osborn, March 22, 1974; Maurice Darrow Bean, November 8, 1977; Patricia M. Byrne, January 14, 1980; Daniel Anthony O'Donohue, December 26, 1983; and Burton Levin, May 26, 1987. 

The United states downgraded its level of representation in Burma from Ambassador to Charge d'Affaires after the government's crackdown on the democratic opposition in September 1988 and its failure to honor the results of the 1990 parliamentary election. Ambassador Levin left Rangoon on September 30, 1990. Serving as Charge d'Affaires ad interim were Franklin P. Huddle, Jr., September 1990 - September 1994; Marilyn Meyers, September 1994 - October 1996; Kent M. Wiedemann, October 1996 - May 1999; Priscilla A. Clapp, July 1999 - August 2002; and Carmen Maria Martinez, August 2002 - .

Although the ruling State Peace and Development Council (SPDC) changed the name of the country to "Myanmar", the democratically elected, but not convened, Parliament of 1990 did not recognize the name change, and the democratic opposition maintained the use of the name "Burma". Due to unyielding support for the democratically elected leaders, the United States Government likewise used "Burma."

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: Representatives of wheat exporting countries, Argentina, Australia, Canada, and the United States, and Great Britain, a wheat importing country, met in Washington, D.C. from July 10, 1941 through April 22, 1942 to consider steps to be taken toward a solution of various international wheat problems. It was a successor to the International Wheat Advisory Committee which had been established in London in 1933, and whose last meetings had been interrupted at the outbreak of war in September 1939. A Memorandum of Agreement was initialed by the participating representatives on April 22, 1942, and which called for the creation of the International Wheat Council.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
From the earliest days of the Republic, Presidents have designated special diplomatic envoys for specific assignments, primarily overseas. The President appointed the first official specifically to bear the title of Ambassador at Large on March 12, 1949, under the authority vested in Article II, Section 2 of the U.S. Constitution that empowers the President, with the advice and consent of the Senate, to appoint Ambassadors, other public Ministers, and Consuls. Presidents have usually appointed Ambassadors at Large to deal with specific foreign policy issues which have been frequently, but not always, spelled out in their commissions.

Alfred L. Atherton, Jr., served as Ambassador at Large from April 11, 1978, through May 22, 1979.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The United States-Japanese Property Commission was constituted pursuant to the Agreement of June 12, 1952 for the settlement of disputes arising under Article 15(a) of the Treaty of Peace with Japan (parties United States and Japan) of September 8, 1951. However, the Commission appears not to have not met until the following conditions of the Agreement were obtained: "If the Government of an Allied Power is not satisfied with the action taken by the Japanese Government with respect to an application for the return of property, rights, or interests, or with respect to a claim for compensation, the Government of the Allied Power [in this case the United States], within six months after it has been advised by the Japanese Government of such action, may refer such claim or application for final determination to a commission appointed as hereinafter provided."

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Office of the Assistant to the Counselor was established by Departmental Order 769 of August 1, 1938, taking some of the functions of the late office of the Historical Adviser. The Assistant to the Counselor undertook research studies in matters relating to the formulation and execution of the foreign policy of the United States, most particularly on matters of neutrality. The Assistant provided ther Secretary and the Counselor with information on certain historical and constitutional questions and the ascertainment of Presidential electors, and with assisting the Counselor generally in the work of his office. In early 1941, the incumbent, Carlton Savage, became an assistant to the Assistant Secretary of State.

(A second Assistant to the Counselor was provided for by Departmental Order 804 of July 27, 1939; this position was confined to matters relating to intermational aspects of fisheries and international fishery commissions. This position fell vacant in February 1941.)

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The foreign service post at Saigon was raised to legation status on February 17, 1950. Donald R. Heath presented his credentials as Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary on October 22, 1950. Heath was serving when the Legation was raised to embassy status June 25, 1952. During this period Edmund A. Gullion was serving as Charge d'Affaires ad interim.

Succeeding Heath as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary were G. Frederick Reinhardt, May 28, 1955 - February 10, 1957; Elbridge Durbrow, April 16, 1957 - May 3, 1961; Frederick E. Nolting, Jr., May 10, 1961 - August 15, 1963; Henry Cabot Lodge, August 26, 1963 - June 28, 1964; Maxwell D. Taylor, July 14, 1964 - July 30, 1965; Henry Cabot Lodge, August 25, 1965 - April 25, 1967; Ellsworth Bunker, April 28, 1967 - May 11, 1973; and Graham Martin, July 20, 1973 - April 29, 1975.

U. Alexis Johnson arrived at Saigon on June 29, 1964, as the first of a series of Deputy Ambassadors to Vietnam. He was succeeded by William J. Porter, September 1965 - May 1967; Eugene M. Locke, May 1967 - January 1968; Samuel D. Berger, March 1968 - March 1972; and Charles S. Whitehouse, March 1972 - August 1973.

The Embassy and Saigon was closed and all personnel evacuated on April 29, 1975, just prior to the surrender of South Vietnam to North Vietnamese forces.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Office of Controls was established on January 15, 1944, under the direction of Assistant Secretary Adolf A. Berle, Jr., and in December was transferred to the Office of the Assistant Secretary for Administration. The Office was responsible for all control activities of the Department, including passport and visa matters, and it supervised the divisions created to aid United States citizens abroad and to control foreign activities in the United States. On June 18, 1945, a Special Assistant to the Director was designated as the Security Officer of the Department to provide security controls over records, communications, personnel, and property, a function previously performed in the immediate Office of the Assistant Secretary for Administration. On May 16, 1949, the Office of Controls was abolished and its functions transferred to the new Office of Consular Affairs.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Division of Exports and Defense Aid was established by Departmental Order 976 of October 7, 1941. It had responsibility for all matters of foreign policy involved in the Export Control Act of July 2, 1940; the Lend - Lease Act of March 11, 1941; the acts of June 28, 1940 and May 31, 1941 (as they related to priorities or allocations for export); and for the administration of Section 12 of the Neutrality Act of November 4, 1939, the Helium Act of September 1, 1937, and the Tin Plate Scrap Act of of February 15, 1936. The Division was abolished by Departmental Order 1061 of June 18, 1942.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: During World War II the Shipping Division was responsible for the foreign policy aspects of matters concerning international shipping. It analyzed shipping conditions and regulations throughout the world and collaborated with other divisions in issuing instructions to Foreign Service establishments with regard to international shipping. On August 3, 1945, functions relating to shipping requirements and allocations were transferred to it from the Commodities Division of the Office of International Trade Policy. The Division maintained liason with the U.S. Maritime Commission, the War Shipping Administration, and the Combined Shipping Adjustment Board.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Embassy in Kampala was established on October 9, 1962, with Olcott H. Deming as charge d'affaires. In 1973, U.S. Ambassador Thomas Patrick Melady recommended that the United States reduce its presence in Uganda. Melady described the regime of Idi Amin Dada as "racist, erratic and unpredictable, brutal, inept, bellicose, irrational, ridiculous, and militaristic". He left his post on February 9, 1973, and all U.S. diplomatic personnel were withdrawn on November 10, 1973.

Relations improved after the fall of Idi Amin's Dadal (April 11, 1979), and on June 18, 1979, the United States reopened its embassy in Kampala. Relations with successor governments were cordial, although Milton Obote and his administration rejected strong U.S. criticism of Uganda's human rights situation. Under Obote, the security forces had one of the world's worst human rights records. In their efforts to stamp out an insurgency led by Yoweri Museveni's National Resistance Army (NRA), they laid waste to a substantial section of the country, especially in the Luwero area north of Kampala.

The dissolution of the Soviet Union in December 1991 brought an end to the Cold War and created an opportunity to build bilateral relations with the New Independent States (NIS) as they began a political and economic transformation. On December 25, 1991, the United States officially recognized the independence of Ukraine. It upgraded its consulate in the capital, Kyiv, to embassy status on January 21, 1992, with Jon Gundersen as Chargé d'Affaires ad interim.

Successive Ambassadors Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary, with dates of presentation of credentials, were:

* Roman Popadiuk, June 4, 1992

* William Green Miller, October 21, 1993

* Steven Karl Pifer, 1997

* Carlos Pascaul, October 22, 2000

* John A. Herbst, September 20, 2003

* William B. Taylor, Jr., June 21, 2006

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Director of the Intelligence Division from mid 1947 until the end of 1948 was Lieutenant Colonel James R. O'Steen, who was succeeded by Robert H. Cunningham.  Structurally, in addition to Plans and Administration, the Division was divided generally into two parts:  Liaison and Supervision, which worked in conjunction with the Constabulary, Counterintelligence Corps (CIC), and the Liaison and Security Offices in the preparation and submission of intelligence reports; and Analysis and Reports, which operated in conjunction not only with the organizations that worked with Liaison and Supervision, but also with the European Command Intelligence Detachments, other divisions of the Office of Military Government for Hesse (OMGH) and the Office of Military Government (U.S.) (OMGUS), and other Lander intelligence offices, receiving information, evaluating, collating, analyzing, interpreting, and disseminating finished intelligence relating to the mission of the Military Government.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Economics Division began late in 1945 with two branches, each divided into sections. The Administrative Branch included the General Administrative Section, Restitutions Section, Reports and Statistics Section, and German Agencies Section. The Food and Agriculture Branch included the Agriculture Section, Food Section, and Land and Institutions Section.

By the end of 1947 the division had grown to include a Reports and Statistics Branch, a Requirements Branch, an Administration Branch, a German Agencies Branch, a Research Control Branch; a Food and Agriculture Branch with three sections: food, agriculture, and forestry; a Restitution Branch with two sections: Restitution and Monuments, fine arts, and archives; a Trade and Commerce Branch with three sections: Imports and Exports, Trade and Distribution, and Price Control; and an Industry Branch with eight sections: Public Utilities, Program Review, Control and Inspection, Reparations, Mining and Metals Technical Section, Mechanical Industries Technical Section, Building Materials Technical Section, and the Chemicals Technical Section.

On April 21, 1948, the Economics Division was dissolved and the Economics Branch became part of the Bipartite Liaison Division. There it had six sections; German Agencies, which handled liaison with the German Ministry of Economics and Transportation and transportation complaints and investigations with regard to freedom of trade; the Mining/Metals Section which was responsible for the supervision of mining and metal industries; the Mechanical Industries Section which handled supervision of the production of textiles, paper, machinery and equipment, optical instruments, fine-mechanics, and vehicle production; the Building Materials and Construction Section which observed and supervised German governmental agencies, export and import, relating to building materials in actual production; the Chemicals Section surveyed and inspected chemical plants; and the Price Control and Internal Trade Section which supervised all phases of commerce and recommended revision of existing policies.

In July 1949, the Bipartite Liaison Division was abolished and the Economic Affairs Division was created with six branches. These branches included Economics, Finance, Food and Agriculture, Manpower, Property, and Decartelization.

The Antecedents and Organizational Changes of the Office of Refugee and Migration Affairs, March 1979: p. 11, 13-15 (On April 19, 1956 the Department by Circular No. 187 announced the establishment of the Office of Refugee and Migration Affairs (SCA/ORM) in the Bureau of Security and Consular Affairs and directed that the Deputy Administrator of SCA for Refugee Programs (Pierce J. Grety) would direct and supervise ORM. On September 19, 1966, the Office of the Refugee and Migration Affairs (SCA/ORM) was transferred from SCA to S (becoming S/R/ORM) and placed under the direct responsibility of the Special Assistant[ to the Secretary of State for Refugee and Migration Affairs]. George L. Warren was assigned to the S/ORM Staff. In 1969 Clement J. Sobtka was Director of ORM; in 1970 he became Acting Special Assistant to the Secretary for Refugee and Migration Affairs. In 1970 Orson W. Trueworthy was made Director of ORM. In 1971 Raymond W. Laugel became Director of ORM and held that position until 1973 when he was succeeded by Louis A. Wiesner.  In Foreign Affairs Manual Circular No. 700, June 24, 1975, the Department announced the establishment of the position of Coordinator for Humanitarian Affairs (D/HA) in the Office of the Deputy Secretary to replace the position of Special Assistant for Refugee and Migration Affairs. Later that year [1977], the Department in accordance with Section 109 of the Foreign Relations Authorization Act, Fiscal Year 1978 (Public Law 95-105 of August 17, 1977, 91 Stat. 844), created the Bureau of Human Rights and Humanitarian Affairs (HA). The Department designated Derian as Assistant Secretary for HA, James L. Carlin as Deputy Assistant Secretary for Refugee Migration  Affairs, and Shepard C. Lowman as Director of the office of refugee and Migration Affairs.)

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The African and Malagasy Union (AMU) (Union Africaine et Malgache) (UAM) was an intergovernmental organization created in September 1961 to promote cooperation among former French colonies in Africa. The organization derived its name from the name of the continent of Africa and from the former Malagasy Republic, later Madagascar. Twelve francophone countries agreed to maintain close relationships but also a special relationship with the former colonial power, France. Its original aims were to adopt common stands on international issues, to promote economic and culture cooperation, and to maintain a common defense organization. In March 1964 the UAM changed its name to the Afro-Malagasy Union for Economic Cooperation (Union Africaine et Malgache de Cooperation Economique; UAMCE). Subsequently, it confined itself to economic affairs and by 1966 had become inactive. The organization went defunct in 1985.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Department of State established the position of Assistant Secretary of State for European Affairs in 1949, after the Commission on Organization of the Executive Branch of Government (Hoover Commission) recommended that certain offices be upgraded to bureau level and after Congress had increased the number of Assistant Secretaries of State from six to ten (May 26, 1949; P.L. 81-73; 63 Stat. 111). An administrative action changed the incumbent's designation to Assistant Secretary for European and Canadian Affairs on Sep 15, 1983. The Department of State first established a Division of Western European Affairs in 1909, which handled European nations primarily bordering on the Atlantic Ocean and their colonies. The Division of Near Eastern Affairs handled relations with most Central, Eastern, and Southern European countries until after World War I. During the interwar period, responsibility for much of Central and Eastern Europe shifted to the Division of European Affairs, although Greece, Turkey, and Cyprus were handled as part of the Near East until Apr 18, 1974. Following World War II, the Department completed the transfer of responsibility for the former colonies of European nations, except Canada, to the Bureau of Near Eastern, South Asian, and African Affairs and the Bureau of Far Eastern Affairs. 

The Bureau executed responsibility for the general conduct of foreign relations with the countries within its geographical area of responsibility by applying over-all political, security, economic, public affairs, social, consular, administrative, and other policies and practices. The Bureau maintained and supervised relationships with foreign missions in the United States representing countries within its regional jurisdiction, except on substantive consular matters, and guided the operation of Foreign Service establishments within its area overseas.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
Over the decades, the U.S. Mission to International Organizations in Vienna has gone through a variety of changes. The U.S. Mission to the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) was established in September 1957, with the appointment of Ambassador Robert Moody McKinney as the first Permanent Representative, but from 1957 through 1999, the Permanent Representative of the USA to the IAEA was not resident in Vienna, Austria but was based in Washington, D.C. 

In order to have a physical presence in the absence of the Permanent representative, in September 1961, a Resident Representative of the USA to the IAEA was assigned as Principal Officer for the U.S. Mission to the IAEA. This position did not come with an Ambassadorial rank until 1970. 

Amid all these changes, in 1968, another U.S. Mission was opened – the U.S. Mission to the United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO). This U.S. Mission, with its focus on only one UN organizations, was headed by a Principal Officer. The position of Principal Officer to UNIDO was eliminated in 1977 although the Mission, as a separate entity, remained until 1997 when the U.S. withdrew from UNIDO.

In May 1983, the U.S. Mission to UNIDO and the U.S. Mission to the IAEA were merged into, the U.S. Mission to International Organizations in Vienna, under the leadership of a resident Ambassador and Permanent Representative.

The United States Mission to International Organizations in Vienna (UNVIE) worked with seven major organizations of the United Nations system based in Vienna: the International Atomic Energy Agency; the UN Office on Drugs and Crime; the Preparatory Commission of the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty Organization; the UN Office of Outer Space Affairs; the Wassenaar Arrangement; the UN Commission on International Trade Law; and the UN Industrial Development Organization, of which the U.S. was a member until 1997. UNVIE also covered the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis in Laxenburg, Austria. 

UNVIE's mission was to conduct effective multilateral diplomacy with International Organizations in Vienna to advance the U.S. commitment to design and implement global approaches to reduce global threats and seize global opportunities.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The U.S. Embassy to the Republic of the Congo was established at Leopoldville (later Kinshasha) on June 30, 1960, with John D. Tomlinson as Charge d'Affaires ad interim. From 1967 through ca. 1970 the chief of mission was accredited to the Democratic Republic of the Congo; from ca. 1970 through 1997 the country was named Zaire, and from May 19, 1997, the Democratic Republic of Congo.

On July 25, 1960, Clare H. Timberlake presented his credentials as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary. He was succeeded by Edmund A. Gullion, September 11, 1961; G. McMurtrie Goldley, March 23, 1964; Robert H. McBride, June 29, 1967; Sheldon B. Vance, June 28, 1969; and Deane R. Hinton, August 21, 1974. Ambassador Hinton was declared persona non grata on June 18, 1975; he departed the post on June 21, 1975. He was succeeded by Walter L. Cutler, December 23, 1975; Robert B. Oakley, November 28, 1979; Peter Dalton Constable, October 18, 1982; Brandon Hambright Grove, Jr., September 18, 1984; William Caldwell Harrop, January 28, 1988; and Melissa Foelsch Wells, June 11, 1991.

Ambassador Wells left her post on March 21, 1992. John M. Yates served as Charge d'Affaires ad interim from March 1992 through September 1995, and Roger A. Meece from September through November 1995. 

The next Ambassador, Daniel H. Simpson, presented his credentials on November 23, 1995. He was succeeded by William Lacy Swing, October 13, 1998, and Aubrey Hooks, September 4, 2001.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Division of Libraries and Institutes was responsible for the initial formulation of operational policy for the Department with respect to the international exchange of information, knowledge, and skills, so far as such operations involved the establishment of, assistance to, operation of, provision of books and other cultural materials for, and operation of libraries, cultural centers, schools, and other institutions in foreign lands and for other uses by the missions.

The major functions of the Division were the development and maintenance of programs designed to facilitate the interchange of information, knowledge, and skills by the procurement of printed materials and their dissemination through institutional activity and participation in cultural cooperation programs arising from international agreements. The Division was in charge of the interchange of publications, music, art, scientific equipment, and other cultural materials, and the maintenance of the necessary procedures to promote the rapid and effective interchange of cultural materials. It provided assistance in the establishment and effective maintenance of libraries, institutes, and centers. The Division provided assistance, on request, for correlative activities such as library services to diplomatic and consular establishments. It served as a liaison with the book trade. The Division planned and managed the non-governmental translation program for the publication, in foreign languages, of selected materials in English; and, in English, of selected foreign materials. It also provided assistance and counsel to organizations engaged in maintaining schools and other institutions in foreign countries.

Effective July 13, 1951 the Division of Libraries and Institutes was abolished and all of the functions, personnel, funds, property, and records transferred to the new Division of Overseas Information Centers.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Advisory Committee On Voluntary Foreign Aid (ACVFA) was established by Presidential directive on May 15, 1946, to serve as a link between the U.S. Government and private voluntary organizations (PVOs) active in humanitarian assistance and development work overseas. Comprised of 24 private citizens with extensive knowledge of international development, ACVFA helps provide the underpinning for cooperation between the public and private sectors in U.S. foreign assistance programs.

As stated in its charter, the Advisory Committee's role is to: (1) Consult with, provide information to, and advise the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) and other U.S. Government agencies on development issues relating to foreign assistance in which the U.S. Government and PVOs interact; (2) Provide information and counsel to the PVO community on issues of concern regarding their relations with USAID and other U.S. Government agencies; and (3) Foster public interest in the field of voluntary foreign aid and in PVO activities.

ACVFA meetings are held three times a year and provide opportunities for information exchange and consultation between USAID and other governmental agencies and the nongovernmental community. The Committee brings together USAID and PVO officials, representatives from universities, international nongovernmental organizations (NGOs), U.S. businesses, and government, multilateral, and private organizations to foster understanding, communication, and cooperation. The meetings focus on timely topics selected from a wide range of issues and challenges that affect the relationship between the official foreign assistance program and the private voluntary community. Following these deliberations, the ACVFA provides specific recommendations to the USAID Administrator.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The International Radio Consultative Committee or Comité Consultatif International pour la Radio (CCIR) was founded in 1927 as part of the International Telecommunication Union at a conference in Washington, D.C. In 1992 the CCIR was transformed into ITU-R, the Radiocommunication Sector at the Additional Plenipotentiary Conference in Geneva. CCIR's role was to regulate the allocation of radio frequencies and so reduce the interference between radio stations in various countries. Also it had the responsibility for regulating orbital positions of satellites relating to radio communications.CCIR published international engeneering standard documents, among which the standards for the analog and digital radio signals.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
On August 27, 1948, the Division of Foreign Activity Correlation was abolished and most of its personnel and functions transferred to the Division of Security and Investigations. At that time, the Division of Security and Investigations became the Division of Security.

The Division of Security developed and directed the security program of the Department of State and Foreign Service, including the investigation of personnel; security training; secure Department facilities and communication channels; protection of the Secretary and visiting foreign dignitaries; an overseas security program; and furnished recommendations and investigative services with respect to passport, visa, munitions control, and other matters. On May 16, 1949, Departmental Announcement 60 transferred the Division of Security from the Office of Controls to the Office of Consular Affairs, which on May 3, 1951 became the Office of Security and Consular Affairs. The Division gained responsibility for Department identification cards. Chiefs of the Division of Security were Donald L. Nicholson, 1948–1952; and John W. Ford, 1952.

On December 23, 1952, the Division of Security became known as the Office of Security under the Office of Security and Consular Affairs. The Office of Security was then successively under the Bureau of Security and Consular Affairs, 1953; the Bureau of Security, Consular Affairs, and Personnel, 1953; the Bureau of Inspection, Security, and Consular Affairs, 1954; the Bureau of Security and Consular Affairs, 1954; the Office of the Deputy Under Secretary for Administration, August 8, 1962 by Foreign Affairs Manual Circular 79B; the Bureau of Administration, 1971; and the Bureau of Administration and Security, 1985.

On August 26, 1950, the Department of State’s regulations placed the Office of Security in charge of field investigations of employees; a full Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) investigation would follow if evidence of questionable conduct was found. On April 27, 1953, President Dwight D. Eisenhower issued Executive Order (EO) 10450 on security requirements for federal employees, which replaced EO 9835 of March 21, 1947. Heads of federal agencies were responsible for establishing and maintaining security programs. When the Department of State implemented EO 10450, it placed the Office of Security in charge of investigating employees. The FBI would conduct further investigations if there were indications of questionable conduct. Security Hearing Boards were established to review cases, and their findings would be reviewed by the Secretary of State.

By 1962, the Office of Security was responsible for the physical, technical, procedural, and personnel security programs of the Department and its overseas posts. In addition, it was charged with the protection of visiting dignitaries On May 12, 1965, the Office of Security issued a guidance document entitled “The Protection of U.S. Personnel and Installations Against Acts of Terrorism in Latin America” to all Chiefs of Mission in the region. Missions were urged to set up Security Watch Committees to evaluate the local state of security and to devise appropriate measures to improve post security. The following year, an expanded version was sent to all U.S. missions.

The Directors of the Office of Security were John W. Ford, 1952–1953; Dennis A. Flinn, 1953–1956; E. Tomlin Bailey, 1956–1958; and William O. Boswell, 1958–1962. When the Office of Security transferred to the Deputy Under Secretary for Administration, the Director was elevated to Deputy Assistant Secretary for Security. The Deputy Assistant Secretaries for Security included: John F. Reilly, 1962-1963; G. Marvin Gentile, 1964–1974; Victor H. Dikeos, 1974–1978; Karl D. Ackerman, 1978–1982; Marvin L. Garrett, Jr., 1982–1983; and David C. Fields, 1984–1985.

As a result of the June 1985 Inman Panel recommendations, the Office of Security and several initiatives it had gained during the previous two years comprised the bulk of the new Bureau of Diplomatic Security that was established by the Department of State on November 4, 1985 and by the Omnibus Diplomatic Security and Antiterrorism Act (Public Law 99-399) on August 27, 1986.

January 2, 1962 The Office of Security in the Bureau of Security and Consular Affairs was reorganized. The Division of Physical Security was divided into three Divisions: Foreign Operations, Technical Services, and Domestic Operations. The Intelligence Reporting Branch was replaced by an Intelligence Processing Section within the Records and Services Branch. August 8, 1962 Foreign Affairs Manual Circular 79B transferred the Office of Security from the Bureau of Security and Consular Affairs to the Deputy Under Secretary for Administration. John F. Reilly became Deputy Assistant Secretary for Security. May 12, 1965 The Office of Security issued a guidance document entitled “The Protection of U.S. Personnel and Installations Against Acts of Terrorism in Latin America” to all Chiefs of Mission in the region. Missions were urged to set up Security Watch Committees to evaluate the local state of security and to devise appropriate measures to improve post security. The following year, an expanded version was sent to all U.S. missions. History of the Bureau of Diplomatic Security of the United States Department of State, 1st ed., October 2011: p. [iii], 83, 84, 85, 104-105, 167, 285-286 (Chiefs of Security at the U.S. Department of State 1917-2011: Division of Security Donald L. Nicholson. 1948 – 1952; John W. Ford, 1952; Office of Security (SY) John W. Ford, 1952 – 1953; Dennis A. Flinn, 1953 – 1956; E. Tomlin Bailey, 1956 – 1958; William O. Boswell, 1958 – 1962; John F. Reilly, 1962 – 1963; G. Marvin Gentile, 1964 – 1974; Victor H. Dikeos, 1974 – 1978; Karl D. Ackerman, 1978 – 1982; Marvin L. Garrett, Jr., 1982 – 1983; David C. Fields, 1984 – 1985; Despite the success of his training program, Bannerman learned on February 11, 1947, that the Security Office would be merged into the Division of Investigations, which was a part of the Office of Controls. Eight months earlier, the Department created the Division of Investigations, by moving the Office of the Chief Special Agent with its staff of 124 people into the Office of Controls and renaming it. On February 24, the Department transferred the Security Office into Investigations, creating the Division of Security and Investigations; The decision to merge the Security Office into the Division of Investigations arose from several factors. The Division of Management Planning, influenced by Goodrich’s report, urged Panuch to separate the security function into its own division, so that the director of the Office of Controls (CON) could focus upon the managing CON’s multiple divisions. Also, Department managers wanted to improve the efficiency and performance of CON….Although the new Division of Security and Investigations kept the Chief Special Agent’s acronym CSA…The Investigations Division performed investigations of employees, and the concluded investigations were forwarded to the Security Office’s Evaluations branch for review and evaluation, a process which in a way brought the old Chief Special Agent’s office under Bannerman’s umbrella. The new Division of Investigations and Security still retained the duties of protecting the Secretary of State and foreign dignitaries; however, Bannerman’s three tasks: security investigations, the security training program, and the overseas security program provided the focus and structure for the new division; By February 1948, the Bureau of Administration decided to dissolve FC [Division of Foreign Activity Correlation] and transfer most of its duties and staff to the Security and Investigations Division. This occurred on August 27. With the addition of FC’s functions, the Division of Investigation and Security was renamed the Division of Security, and it received a new acronym, SY… SY focused primarily on personnel investigations, but it also operated an overseas security program and conducted the security-training program for the Department and the Foreign Service. Additional responsibilities included physical security of Department of State buildings, advice on Department security programs, recommendations on visas and passports, and protection of the Secretary and visiting foreign dignitaries; Although the Hoover Commission [1949] prompted significant reorganization in other bureaus of the Department, SY was little affected. The Divisions of Security, Visa, Passport, and Protective Services were grouped together into a new Office of Consular Services that replaced the Office of Controls, but retained the old acronym CON. The Office of Security did gain one new task: Department identification cards; Just after Boswell’s reorganization, Crockett’s idea of moving SY to the Bureau of Administration became a reality. On August 8, 1962, SY was transferred to Administration, and its director elevated to Deputy Assistant Secretary of State. John F. Reilly became the first Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Security, and he reported directly to the Deputy Under Secretary of State for Administration; June 1985, the Inman Panel submitted its report to Secretary of State Shultz, and in it, the panel urged the Department to undertake a fundamental reorganization of diplomatic security. The panel recommended creating a Bureau of Diplomatic Security (DS), headed by an Assistant Secretary of State for Diplomatic Security who reported directly to the Under Secretary of State for Management. SY and the several initiatives it had gained during the previous two years comprised the bulk of the new bureau, but the Inman Panel advocated moving several other security-related programs and offices into the bureau, including the Diplomatic Courier Service….The Inman Panel report gained the immediate support of the Secretary of State and Congress. Secretary Shultz appointed Assistant Secretary Lamb to implement the panel’s recommendations and tasked him to complete the reorganization of the Department’s security programs by January 1, 1986. The Department established the Bureau of Diplomatic Security on November 4, 1985, with the new Bureau acquiring the Courier Service, the Rewards for Justice program, as well as ATA and the Emergency Planning program. On August 12, 1986, with overwhelming support, Congress passed the Omnibus Diplomatic Security and Antiterrorism Act (Public Law 99-399), creating the Bureau of Diplomatic Security and providing the new bureau with extensive funding. President Reagan signed the act into law on August 27.)

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The International Radio Consultative Committee or Comité Consultatif International pour la Radio (CCIR) was founded in 1927 as part of the International Telecommunication Union at a conference in Washington, D.C. In 1992 the CCIR was transformed into ITU-R, the Radiocommunication Sector at the Additional Plenipotentiary Conference in Geneva. CCIR's role was to regulate the allocation of radio frequencies and so reduce the interference between radio stations in various countries. Also it had the responsibility for regulating orbital positions of satellites relating to radio communications.CCIR published international engeneering standard documents, among which the standards for the analog and digital radio signals.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
In 1951, the Office of International Trade Policy was functionally subdivided into the Office of International Materials Policy and the Office of Economic Defense and Trade Policy. The Office of International Materials Policy took over the functions, personnel, and equipment of the Petroleum Policy Staff, the Food and Agriculture Branch, and the Industrial Materials Branch of the Economic Resources and Security Staff. 

The purpose of the Office of International Materials Policy, in cooperation with other agencies of the Government; was to develop programs and policies which insured the harmonization of domestic and foreign emergency economic controls designed to stimulate the production of basic materials in short supply; to assure the widest degree of parallel action in the adoption of conservation measures; to provide for the continued export of goods essential to meet the minimum civilian requirements of other parts of the free world; to assure the availability to the United States adequate supplies of basic materials, and to promote the allocation where necessary of materials in short supply. 

A Department Circular, dated January 15, 1955, abolished the Office of International Materials Policy and the Office of Economic Defense and Trade Policy and transferred their functions to the new Office of International Trade and Resources (ITR).

Effective immediately, the Office of International Trade Policy is abolished. There is established an Office of International Materials Policy and an Office of Economic Defense and Trade Policy. The Office of International Materials Policy will take over the functions, personnel, and equipment of the Petroleum Policy Staff, the Food and Agriculture Branch, and the Industrial Materials Branch of the Economic Resources and Security Staff. It will be the purpose of the Office of International Materials Policy, in cooperation with other agencies of the Government; (1) to develop programs and policies which will insure the harmonization of domestic and foreign emergency economic controls designed to stimulate the production of basic materials in short supply; (2) to assure the widest degree of parallel action in the adoption of conservation measures; (3) to provide for the continued export of goods essential to meet the minimum civilian requirements of other parts of the free world; (4) to assure the availability to the United States adequate supplies of basic materials, and (5) to promote the allocation where necessary of materials in short supply. creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Director of the U.S. Operations Mission to Haiti had general responsibility for the entire USOM operation including all program and administrative activities. The Director approved the final Mission program; supervised the staff officers and technical operations division chiefs; took final action on U.S. personnel actions; provided substantive divisions with appropriate operational guidelines; maintained liaison at the highest levels with the Haitian Government and provided primary representation for the USOM; maintained contact with the chief of the diplomatic mission in Haiti, and gave final approval to Mission budgets.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Embassy to Southern Yemen was established in Aden on December 7, 1967, with William L. Eagleton, Jr., as Charge d'Affaires ad interim. However, relations were strained and Southern Yemen was placed on the list of nations that support terrorism. Eagleton served in that capacity when severed diplomatic relations with the People's Democratic Republic of Yemen (PDRY) on October 24, 1969. Edward E. Keller, Jr., was Charge d'Affaires ad interim when the Embassy was closed on October 26, 1969. In 1970, the name of the country was changed to the PDRY. The United States resumed diplomatic relations with the People's Democratic Republic of Yemen on Apr 30, 1990; however, the embassy in Aden was never re-opened. On May 22, 1990, the Yemen Arab Republic and the People's Democratic Republic of Yemen united to form the Republic of Yemen.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Office of the Assistant Director for Refugees, Migration, and Voluntary Assistance was responsible for Foreign Operations Administration (FOA) activities designed to alleviate refugee, migration, and related human problems. The functions of the office included administration of the Escapee Program; provision of staff services for the Advisory Committee on Voluntary Foreign Aid; administration of the ocean freight subsidy program for relief shipments; maintaining liaison with voluntary agencies and civic organizations; and serving as the liaison with the Department of State on all of the above functions. The Office also handled operating functions involved in U.S. Government participation in related programs of international agencies, particularly those of the Intergovernmental Committee on European Migration and United Nations International Children's Emergency Fund (UNICEF), and to some extent those of the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East, United Nations Korean Reconstruction Agency, United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, Organization for European Economic Cooperation (OEEC), North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), and Council of Europe. In 1955, the name changed to the Office of the Deputy Director for Refugees, Migration, and Voluntary Assistance and on June 30, 1955, the position was transferred to the International Cooperation Administration (ICA).

On April 1, 1956, ICA abolished its Office of the Deputy Director for Refugees, Migration and Voluntary Assistance. On that date ICA transferred to the Department of State all activities relating to the United States escapee program, as well as the former ICA responsibilities relating to the formulation of United States policies regarding the assistance programs of the Intergovernmental Committee for European Migration, the United Nations Refuges Fund and the United Nations Children’s Fund. Those functions in this field which remain the responsibility of the Director of the International Cooperation Administration were transferred to the Office of the Deputy Director for Technical Services. These functions were concerned with registration of and relationships with U.S. voluntary agencies which participate in international relief and rehabilitation projects and with staff support for the Advisory Committee on Voluntary Foreign Aid.

The Deputy Director for Management was responsible to the Director and Deputy Director of the Foreign Operations Administration (FOA) for general management of FOA in Washington and overseas by providing the necessary management advice, services, and administrative facilities. 

The Deputy Director for Management collected and compiled program and operational data for use of the Director and the Administration; provided legal advice; assured that, in the formulation and execution of FOA programs, proper consideration was given to the organization, staffing requirements, method of operations and interagency relationships; administered personnel requirements, including control of all recruitment; maintained physical security and personnel security and integrity; formulated administrative fund requirements and provided technical assistance in the development of the program budget; established and administered methods of control over use of funds; and provided public information advice and prepared public reports.
