Article II, section 2 of the U.S. Constitution authorized the President to appoint, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, "Ambassadors, other public Ministers, and Consuls." They were assigned to posts which included legations, consulates general, consulates, vice-consulates, consular agencies, and commercial agencies. The legations were in charge of ministers; no ambassadors were appointed by the United States until 1893. Consular officers were appointed to reside in foreign countries, especially at seaports. Consuls general, consuls, and commercial agents were divided into three classes according to the provisions of an act of August 18, 1856 (11 Stat. 52), which designated the places to which the several classes were to be appointed. 

The consuls general were authorized to communicate with the heads of government in the countries to which they were appointed, and they supervised and gave advice to U.S. consular officers within their consular districts. Consuls general typically supervised one or several deputy consuls general, consuls, and vice consuls 

The chief duties of consuls were to look after the interests of American commerce and seamen; to receive from masters of vessels registers, sea letters, and passports; to recover deserters; to collect and remit the assets of deceased American citizens; to exercise toward their countrymen the role of judges, arbiters, and peacemakers; to serve as registers of marriages, births, and deaths and as notaries issuing passports; and to promote emigration to the United States. Although never admitted publicly, consular officials, like ministers and ambassadors, also gathered intelligence information from the assigned country.

Consular agents served under full consular officers at ports or inland towns different from those at which their principals resided. Commercial agents were appointed by the Department of State and sent abroad to promote U.S. commercial interests. They were not necessarily recognized by the governments of the countries where they resided; sometimes their appointments were secret. 

Until the twentieth century, consular and diplomatic posts operated with a great deal of autonomy from the Department of State in Washington, D.C. Although the posts communicated most matters of consequence, they usually performed their routine duties with little supervision from the Department. 

Throughout the 19th century, ambassadors (or ministers, as they were known prior to the 1893) and consuls were appointed by the President, and until 1856, earned no salary. Many had commercial ties to the countries in which they would serve, and were expected to earn a living through private business or by collecting fees. In 1856, Congress provided a salary for consuls serving at certain posts; those who received a salary could not engage in private business, but could continue to collect fees for services performed.

From 1789 until 1924, the Diplomatic Service, which staffed U.S. legations and embassies, and the Consular Service, which was primarily responsible for promoting American commerce and assisting distressed American sailors, developed separately. The Foreign Service Act of 1924 (the Rogers Act) (43 Stat. 140), approved May 24, 1924,  merged the Diplomatic and Consular services into a single U.S. Foreign Service.

The Foreign Service Act of 1980 was the last major legislative reform to the Foreign Service. It enacted danger pay for those diplomats who serve in dangerous and hostile surroundings along with other administrative changes.

The State-War-Navy Coordinating Committee (SWNCC) was established by a letter of the Secretary of the Navy, on behalf also of the Secretary of War, to the Secretary of State, December 1, 1944, agreeing to a proposal of the Secretary of State (November 19, 1944). It was composed of one representative each of the three departments, with the State Department representative as chair. 

SWNCC considered matters in which they all had a common interest and established policies for their departments on politico-military questions referred to it. The Committee maintained liaison with the Joint Chiefs of Staff in order to obtain military approval for its decisions. The wartime chair of the Committee was the Assistant Secretary of State for European, Far Eastern, Near Eastern, and African Affairs, James Clement Dunn. Among its activities the Committee prepared policy for the control of Japan, drafted directives for the control of Germany and Austria, and coordinated the views of its member agencies on policy for presentation by the United States at international conferences. It formed standing committees for Europe, the Near and Middle East, the Far East, Latin America, Rearmament, Military Information Control, Release of State papers, and Security Control, and ad hoc committees for effecting collaboration among the departments on the security functions of the United Nations and for reviewing directives and procedures for the seizure of enemy records. The Committee''s Security Advisory Board studies the postwar problem of downgrading and declassification of security-classified records and issued regulations for security officers of Federal agencies to follow in declassifying documents. 

Pursuant to the establishment of the Department of the Air Force by the National Security Act of 1947 (61 Stat. 502, approved July 26, 1947), SWNCC was expanded to include an Air Force representative and it was redesignated the State-Army-Navy-Air Force Coordinating Committee (SANACC) by SANACC 12/15/, November 5, 1947, implementing SWNCC 12/14, approved October 3, 1947. 

Soon after the activation of the National Security Council (NSC) in September 1947, SANACC began to submit policy papers to it for its consideration and NSC would in turn ask SANACC to prepare reports for it. It soon became evident that SANACC''s functionsd closely paralleled, and in some cases duplicated, those of the NSC Staff. An ad hoc committee of the NSC was established in March 1948 to study the relationship between SANACC and the NSC. That committee proposed interim terms of reference for SANACC which the Council approved in August 1948. Those terms of reference provided that SANACC''s principal functions would be (a) to advise and assist the NSC, preparing reports and studies requested by it; and (b) to coordinate matters recognized as being part of the Council''s staffing mechanism while at the same time it continued to coordinate matters that did not come before the NSC.

In accordance with the interim terms of reference, the Council made a further review of SANACC six months after approval of the terms of reference. That review resulted in action by the Council to dissolve SANACC. SANACC was terminated, effective June 30, 1949, by SANACC 12/16/, June 6, 1949, approved by the President on the same date, with outstanding cases transferred to departments having primary interest.

The United States established diplomatic relations with the Imamate in 1946. A resident legation, later elevated to embassy status, was opened in Taiz (the capital at the time) on March 16, 1959, and moved to Sanaa in 1966. The United States was one of the first countries to recognize the Yemen Arab Republic (YAR), doing so on December 19, 1962. A major U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) program constructed the Mocha-Taiz-Sanaa highway and the Kennedy memorial water project in Taiz, as well as many smaller projects. On June 6, 1967, the YAR, under Egyptian influence, broke diplomatic relations with the United States in the wake of the Arab-Israeli conflict of that year. Secretary of State William P. Rogers restored relations following a visit to Sanaa in July 1972, and a new USAID agreement was concluded in 1973. 

During a 1979 border conflict between the Yemen Arab Republic and the People''s Democratic Republic of Yemen, the United States cooperated with Saudi Arabia to greatly expand the security assistance program to the YAR by providing F-5 aircraft, tanks, vehicles and training. George H. W. Bush, while Vice President, visited in April 1986, and President Ali Abdullah Saleh visited the United States in January 1990. The United States had a $42 million USAID program in 1990. From 1973 to 1990, the United States provided the YAR with assistance in the agriculture, education, and health and water sectors. Many Yemenis were sent on U.S. Government scholarships to study in the region and in the United States. There was a Peace Corps program with about 50 volunteers. The U.S. Information Service operated an English-language institute in Sanaa. 

On December 7, 1967, the United States recognized the People''s Democratic Republic of Yemen and elevated its Consulate General in Aden to embassy status. However, relations were strained. The PDRY was placed on the list of nations that support terrorism. On October 24, 1969, south Yemen formally broke diplomatic relations with the United States. The United States and the PDRY reestablished diplomatic relations on April 30, 1990, only 3 weeks before the announcement of unification. However, the embassy in Aden, which closed in 1969, was never reopened, and the PDRY as a political entity no longer existed

. 

As a result of Yemen''s actions in the Security Council following the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait, the United States drastically reduced its presence in Yemen including canceling all military cooperation, non-humanitarian assistance, and the Peace Corps program. USAID levels dropped in Fiscal Year (FY) 1991 to $2.9 million, but food assistance through the PL 480 program continued through 2003. The United States was actively involved in and strongly supportive of the 1993 parliamentary elections and continued working to strengthen Yemen''s democratic institutions. The United States supported a unified Yemen during the 1994 civil war. The USAID program, focused in the health field, had slowly increased to $8.5 million in FY 1995, but ended in FY 2000. It was reinvigorated in 2003 and a USAID Mission has re-opened in Sanaa. Yemen also received significant funding from the Middle East Partnership Initiative. Funds went, in large part, to support literacy projects, election monitoring, training for tribal councils, and voter registration for the 2003 parliamentary elections.

The South Pacific Commission (SPC) was a non-political technical assistance agency with an advisory and consultative role which provided, on request of member countries and its own initiative, technical advice, training, assistance and dissemination of information in social, economic and cultural fields to twenty-two governments and administrations of the Pacific region. Altogether, the countries contained approximately five million people scattered over some thirty million square kilometres. Less than two per cent of this area is land.

The South Pacific Commission was established in February 1947 by an agreement signed in Canberra, Australia, known as the Canberra Agreement , by the Governments of Australia, France, the Netherlands, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, and the United States of America. The establishment of the Commission was a response by the then colonial powers to assure the economic and social stability of the Island countries and avoid a repeat of the World War II experience by creating mechanisms for meaningful relations among governments.

As events unfolded and times changed, the Commission began to alter its character. In November 1951 the Canberra Agreement was amended to bring Guam and the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands (TTPI) into the area served by the South Pacific Commission. In 1962 the Netherlands withdrew from the Commission when it ceased to administer its former colony of Dutch New Guinea, now Irian Jaya, part of Indonesia. 

The voices of independent-minded Pacific peoples were being increasingly heard with the first full Island members and the desire by Islanders to change the Commission to what was referred to later as a "Pacific Island Organisation." The first independent and self-governing Pacific States started to articulate Pacific needs and aspirations when admitted to membership: Western Samoa in October 1965, Nauru in July 1969 and Fiji in May 1971.

The political independence of Western Samoa, Nauru and Fiji during the 1960s and early 1970s began the tidal wave of Island sovereignty in the western sense and increased the sound of Island aspiration during "Commission" sessions. This trend continued with the admission of Papua New Guinea in September 1975, Solomon Islands and Tuvalu in November 1978, and Niue and Cook Islands in October 1980. Perhaps the most marked change in the character of the South Pacific Commission came in 1983 at the Twenty-third South Pacific Conference held in Saipan, Northern Mariana Islands. After several years of review and discussion, and following recommendations of the internal review of SPC carried out by the then Secretary General, the Twenty-third South Pacific Conference adopted by consensus a resolution that the Conference''s twenty-seven governments and administrations should have full and equal membership in the Commission thus admitting to the Commission: .American Samoa, Federated State, of Micronesia, French Polynesia, Guam,. Kiribati, Marshall Islands, New Caledonia, Northern Mariana Islands, Palau, Pitcairn Islands, Tokelau, Tonga, Vanuatu, and Wallis and Futuna.

An important aspect of this move was the assumption of financial responsibility by all member governments and administrations on an assessed basis. This also meant the beginning of equal sharing in the decision-making process of the organisation, thus ensuring even greater relevancy to the work programme. The organisation embodied in actual fact its non-political nature to the fullest extent as decision-making was shared equally by member governments irrespective of political status. 

Since 1947 the Commission has changed from an organization aimed at helping dependent territories to one in which all countries (whether governments or administrations) have full and equal membership. The evolution of the Commission has paralleled the political and historical developments of the region, which have in turn influenced the mandate the membership and the activities of the Commission. The Commission (and without any direct intention of doing so) has also inevitably promoted conditions which favoured political development, by furthering the development of the region and by responding to the expressed needs of all member countries. It evolved into a useful and efficient tool for the development of a region that is fast and diverse in both its extremities and its aspirations.

The United States opened diplomatic relations with France during the American Revolution, appointing Benjamin Franklin as Minister Plenipotentiary in 1778. He presented his credentials on March 23, 1779. Franklin was succeeded as Minister Plenipotentiary by Thomas Jefferson, May 17, 1785; William Short, June 14, 1790; Gouverneur Morris, June 3, 1792; James Monroe, August 15, 1794; and Charles Cotesworth Pinckney, 1796. Pinckney arrived in Paris in 1796-97, but was not received by the Directory. He left Paris on February 5, 1797. There was no U.S. representative in Paris until Robert R. Livingston presented his credentials as Minister Plenipotentiary on  December 6, 1801. He was succeeded by John Armstrong on November 18, 1804. Jonathan Russell served as Charge d''Affaires ad interim from September 1810 until November 1911.

The next Minister, Joel Barlow, presented his credentials on November 17, 1811. Barlow was charged with negotiating a commercial treaty with Napoleon, and with securing the restitution of confiscated American property or indemnity therefor. He was summoned for an interview with Napoleon at Wilna, but failed to see the emperor there. He was caught up in the French army''s retreat from Russia and, overcome by exposure, died in the Polish village of Zarnowiec on December 26, 1812. He was succeeded by William H. Crawford, December 14, 1813. The chief of mission was promoted to Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary with the appointment of Albert Gallatin who presented his credentials on July 16, 1816. He was succeeded by James Brown, April 13, 1824, and William C. Rives, October 25, 1829. Levett Harris served briefly as Charge d''Affaires from March through September 1833. Edward Livingston was appointed the next Envoy, presenting his credentials on September 30, 1833. Livingston departed Paris on April 29, 1835, and the Legation was headed by Thomas P. Barton, Charge d''Affaires ad interim until November 8, 1835, when he closed the Legation, having been recalled.

Lewis Cass became the next Envoy, presenting his credentials on December 1, 1836. Cass departed Paris  on November 12, 1842, and the position remained vacant until William R. King presented his credentials on July 1, 1844. King was succeeded by Richard Rush, July 31, 1847; William C. Rives, November 8, 1849; John Y. Mason, January 22, 1854; Charles J. Faulkner, March 4, 1860; William L. Dayton, May 19, 1861; John Bigelow, April 23, 1865; John A. Dix, December 23, 1866; Elihu B. Washburne, March 23, 1869; Edward F. Noyes, September 5, 1877; Levi P. Morton, August 5, 1881; Robert M. McLane, May 14, 1885; Whitelaw Reid, May 21, 1889; and T. Jefferson Coolidge, June 10, 1892.

In 1893 the Legation was reclassified as an embassy and James B. Eustis presented his credentials as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary on May 6, 1893. He was succeeded by Horace Porter, May 26, 1897; Robert S. McCormick, May 2, 1905; Henry White, March 23, 1907; Robert Bacon, December 31, 1909; Myron T. Herrick, William G. Sharp, December 4, 1914; Hugh Campbell Wallace, April 22, 1919; Myron T. Herrick, July 15, 1921; Walter E. Edge, December 18, 1929; Jesse Isidor Straus, June 8, 1933; and William Christian Bullitt, October 13, 1936.

During Bullitt''s tenure, and because of the German military overrun of northern France in June 1940, the Embassy evacuated Paris, moving to Vichy, via La Bourboule. Bullitt departed La Bourboule on July 11, 1940. The next Ambassador, William D. Leahy, presented his credentials at Vichy on January 8, 1941. He departed Vichy on May 1, 1942. S. Pinkney Tuck was serving as Charge d''Affaires ad interim when the Vichy Government severed diplomatic relations with the United States on November 8, 1942.

The Embassy in Paris reopened on December 1, 1944, and Ambassador Jefferson Caffery presented his credentials on December 30, 1944. He was succeeded by David K.E. Bruce, May 17, 1949; James Clement Dunn, March 27, 1952; C. Douglas Dillon, March 13, 1953; Amory Houghton, April 17, 1957; James M. Gavin, March 21, 1961; Charles E. Bohlen, October 27, 1962; Robert Sargent Shriver, Jr., May 25, 1968; Arthur K. Watson, May 6, 1970; John N. Irwin, II, March 23, 1973; Kenneth Rush, November 21, 1974; Arthur A. Hartman, July 7, 1977; Evan Griffith Galbraith, December 2, 1981; Joe M. Rodgers, September 20, 1985; Walter J.P. Curley, July 6, 1989; Pamela Harriman, June 30, 1993; Felix G. Rohatyn, September 11, 1997; and Howard H. Leach, September 4, 2001.

The United States opened its Legation in Brussels, Belgium, in 1832. The Charge d''Affaires served as chief of mission until the first minister resident presented his credentials in 1854. From 1922 until 1949 the chief of mission was also accredited to Luxembourg, but maintained residence in Brussels.

Serving as Charge d''Affaires, with dates of presentation of credentials, were Hugh S. Legare, September 25, 1832; Virgil Maxcy, October 24, 1837; Henry W. Hilliard, September 17, 1842; Thomas G. Clemson, October 7, 1844; Richard H. Bayard, March 1, 1851; and J.J. Seibels, September 12, 1853. In 1854 Seibels was promoted to Minister Resident and on August 6, 1854, he presented his new credentials. He was succeeded by Elisha Y. Fair, September 7, 1858; Henry S. Sanford, May 8, 1861; Joseph Russell Jones, July 21, 1869; Ayres Phillips Merrill, May 18, 1876; William C. Goodloe, March 4, 1878; James O. Putnam, July 12, 1880; Nicholas Fish, July 5, 1882; and Lambert Tree, October 10, 1885.

In 1888 the chief of mission was elevated to Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary, with Lambert Tree presenting his new credentials on September 25, 1888. He was succeeded by John G. Parkhurst, December 20, 1888; Edwin H. Terrell, July 10, 1889; James S. Ewing, June 22, 1893; Bellamy Storer, July 21, 1897; Lawrence Townsend, June 18, 1899; Henry Lane Wilson, May 5, 1905; Charles Page Bryan, February 10, 1910; Larz Anderson, November 18, 1911; Theodore Marburg, January 24, 1913; and Brand Whitlock, February 14, 1914.

In 1919 the Legation was raised to embassy status and Brand Whitlock became Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary, presenting his new credentials on October 3, 1919. He was succeeded by Henry P. Fletcher, May 3, 1922; William Phillips, June 5, 1924; Hugh S. Gibson, May 9, 1927; Dave Hennen Morris, July 6, 1933; Hugh S. Gibson, July 28, 1937; Joseph E. Davies, July 20, 1938; and John Cudahy, January 17, 1940.

Following the German overrun of Belgium in 1940, the Embassy closed on July 15, with Ambassador Cudahy departing on July 18. Rudolf E. Schoenfeld was designated Charge d''Affaires ad interim on November 1, 1940, and represented the United States to the Belgian government in exile in Great Britain. On March 24, 1941, Anthony J. Drexel Biddle, Jr., presented his credentials as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary; he was commissioned also to Czechoslovakia, Greece, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Norway, Poland, and Yugoslavia. Biddle ended his mission on December 1, 1943, and Rudolf E. Schoenfeld resumed as Charge d''Affaires. The mission of the Embassy near the Government of Belgium was terminated on September 8, 1944, and the Embassy was reestablished at Brussels on September 14, 1944. 

Charles Sawyer became the next Ambassador, presenting his credentials on November 8, 1944. He was succeeded by Alan G. Kirk, April, 1, 1946; Robert D. Murphy, November 29, 1949; Myron Melvin Cowen, June 11, 1952; Frederick M. Alger, Jr., July 22, 1953; John Clifford Folger, May 24, 1957; William A. M. Burden, October 26, 1959; Douglas MacArthur 2nd., May 9, 1961; Ridgway B. Knight, June 24, 1965; John S.D. Eisenhower, May 14, 1969; Robert Strausz-Hupe, March 24, 1972; Leonard Kimball Firestone, June 14, 1974; Anne Cox Chambers, June 17, 1977; Charles H. Price II, July 3, 1981; Geoffrey Swaebe, December 2, 1983; Maynard Wayne Glitman, September 28, 1988; Bruce S. Gelb, July 9, 1991; Alan John Blinken, December 2, 1993; Paul L. Cejas, October 6, 1998; and Stephen Brauer, June 12, 2001.

The Second Philippine Commission (the Taft Commission), appointed by President William McKinley on March 16, 1900, and headed by William Howard Taft, was granted legislative as well as limited executive powers. Between September 1900 and August 1902, it issued 499 laws. A judicial system was established, including a Supreme Court, and a legal code was drawn up to replace antiquated Spanish ordinances. A civil service was organized. The 1901 municipal code provided for popularly elected presidents, vice presidents, and councilors to serve on municipal boards. The municipal board members were responsible for collecting taxes, maintaining municipal properties, and undertaking necessary construction projects; they also elected provincial governors. In July 1901 the Philippine Constabulary was organized as an archipelago-wide police force to control brigandage and deal with the remnants of the insurgent movement. After military rule was terminated on July 4, 1901, the Philippine Constabulary gradually took over from United States army units the responsibility for suppressing guerrilla and bandit activities. 

From the very beginning, United States presidents and their representatives in the islands defined their colonial mission as tutelage: preparing the Philippines for eventual independence. Except for a small group of "retentionists," the issue was not whether the Philippines would be granted self-rule, but when and under what conditions. Thus political development in the islands was rapid and particularly impressive in light of the complete lack of representative institutions under the Spanish. The Philippine Organic Act of July 1902 stipulated that, with the achievement of peace, a legislature would be established composed of a lower house, the Philippine Assembly, which would be popularly elected, and an upper house consisting of the Philippine Commission, which was to be appointed by the president of the United States. The two houses would share legislative powers, although the upper house alone would pass laws relating to the Moros and other non-Christian peoples. The act also provided for extending the United States Bill of Rights to Filipinos and sending two Filipino resident commissioners to Washington to attend sessions of the United States Congress. In July 1907, the first elections for the assembly were held, and it opened its first session on October 16, 1907. Political parties were organized, and, although open advocacy of independence had been banned during the insurgency years, criticism of government policies in the local newspapers was tolerated. 

Taft, the Philippines'' first civilian governor, outlined a comprehensive development plan that he described as "the Philippines for the Filipinos . . . that every measure, whether in the form of a law or an executive order, before its adoption, should be weighed in the light of this question: Does it make for the welfare of the Filipino people, or does it not?" Its main features included not only broadening representative institutions but also expanding a system of free public elementary education and designing economic policies to promote the islands'' development. Filipinos widely interpreted Taft''s pronouncements as a promise of independence.

After the Germans invaded France in 1940 and established the so-called Vichy Government, the United States relocated its embassy from Paris to Vichy. The Embassy operated as any other, even after the U.S. entered the war against Germany in late 1941. That changed on November 8, 1942, when American forces landed in French North Africa and the Vichy Government severed ties with the United States as a result. As German forces did not immediately occupy southern France, American diplomats hoped that they might leave directly for Spain, the nearest neutral country. Before leaving, however, French authorities decided to gather at Lourdes all Americans under their control. This gathering eventually included the civilian and military staffs of the Embassy as well as of the consulates at Marseilles, Lyon, Nice, and Tunis; members of the American Red Cross and other relief organizations; the press, not to mention all of the dependents of the foregoing. In all there were 85 men and 65 women. S. Pinkney Tuck, nominal Charge d''Affaires ad interim of the U.S. Embassy, acted as head of the Group.

Most of the Group assembled at Lourdes on November 12. Because of its numbers, the Group was dispersed among four different locations. On November 13, French authorities confined the internees to their lodgings and permitted outside excursions only under police supervision. Nonetheless, while at Lourdes, the members of the Group engaged in sports, church-going, and small self-taught classes. An attempt was made to create "Ther American University of Lourdes," but the geographical dispersion of the Group led to its failure. On January 16, 1943, Germans assumed responsibility for guarding the Group, and on January 15, the Group was shifted to Baden-baden for internment.

The Group arrived at Baden-Baden on January 16 at which time it began thirteen months of residency in the Brenner''s Park Hotel. While there, the Group had adequate supplies of poorly prepared food, especially potatoes. Internees were also allowed use of the Hotel''s garden. Even though wines and liquors generally were reserved only for official uses in wartime Germany, the internees were allowed one-half bottle of wine per person per week. Consumers of spirits were allowed one-half bottle per person per month. To make up for the shortage of spirits, and to raise their own, the internees resorted to making ther own or purchasing what they could from local distilleries.

While at Baden-Baden the Group was isolated from the general population and guarded by the Gestapo and the Kripo (Criminal Police). The Group was not allowed to listen to its own radios, and to ensure compliance, all sets were confiscated, leaving only the Hotel''s. Only German-controlled newspapers and periodicals were available. The Group engaged in sports, weekly movies, church attendance, picnics, but always under guard. Indoor "recreation" included the creation of a "University" which had a board of governors, a president and president emeritus, and ten faculties with deans, instructors, and curricula. The "University" offered courses in modern languages, history, literature, philosophy, music, art, and non-academic subjects. "Graduates" received certificates. The internees also created a library and put on cabaet nights, dramatic performances, and skits.

During internment, the Group maintained correct, but not friendly, contacts with German officials. The local inhabitants of Baden-Baden showed no hostility and some, at no uncertain risk, became quite friendly. As one internee put it: "[I]t is believed that nowhere in the United States could a group of German internees, accompanied by an officer of the FBI, pub-crawl for a whole day through a tourist village . . . , receive wine far in excess of the small village ration at each inn, and dance in public rooms with local women."

On February 19, 1944, the Group departed Baden-Baden for Lisbon. It arrived in that city on February 25 and was exchanged for German and French groups brought from the United States on the repatriation vessel M.S. Gripsholm. The Group departed Lisbon on the Gripsholm on March 7, 1944, thus ending fifteen months of captivity.

Congress created the position of Secretary of State on July 27, 1789 (1 Stat. 28), as the principal officer of the Department of Foreign Affairs (later renamed Department of State). The Secretary was to perform such duties as the President required, in accordance with the Constitution, relating to correspondence, commission, or instructions to U.S. ministers or consuls abroad, and to conduct negotiations with foreign representatives. The Secretary also served as principal advisor to the President in the determination and execution of U.S. foreign policy and in later decades become responsible for overall direction, coordination, and supervision of interdepartmental activities of the U.S. Government overseas, except for certain military activities. The Act of Congress of September 5, 1789, that changed the name of the Department of Foreign Affairs assigned various domestic duties to the Department of State. Nearly all were later reassigned to other agencies.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
Article II, section 2 of the U.S. Constitution authorized the President to appoint, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, "Ambassadors, other public Ministers, and Consuls." They were assigned to posts which included legations, consulates general, consulates, vice-consulates, consular agencies, and commercial agencies. The legations were in charge of ministers; no ambassadors were appointed by the United States until 1893. Consular officers were appointed to reside in foreign countries, especially at seaports. Consuls general, consuls, and commercial agents were divided into three classes according to the provisions of an act of August 18, 1856 (11 Stat. 52), which designated the places to which the several classes were to be appointed. 

The consuls general were authorized to communicate with the heads of government in the countries to which they were appointed, and they supervised and gave advice to U.S. consular officers within their consular districts. Consuls general typically supervised one or several deputy consuls general, consuls, and vice consuls 

The chief duties of consuls were to look after the interests of American commerce and seamen; to receive from masters of vessels registers, sea letters, and passports; to recover deserters; to collect and remit the assets of deceased American citizens; to exercise toward their countrymen the role of judges, arbiters, and peacemakers; to serve as registers of marriages, births, and deaths and as notaries issuing passports; and to promote emigration to the United States. Although never admitted publicly, consular officials, like ministers and ambassadors, also gathered intelligence information from the assigned country.

Consular agents served under full consular officers at ports or inland towns different from those at which their principals resided. Commercial agents were appointed by the Department of State and sent abroad to promote U.S. commercial interests. They were not necessarily recognized by the governments of the countries where they resided; sometimes their appointments were secret. 

Until the twentieth century, consular and diplomatic posts operated with a great deal of autonomy from the Department of State in Washington, D.C. Although the posts communicated most matters of consequence, they usually performed their routine duties with little supervision from the Department. 

Throughout the 19th century, ambassadors (or ministers, as they were known prior to the 1893) and consuls were appointed by the President, and until 1856, earned no salary. Many had commercial ties to the countries in which they would serve, and were expected to earn a living through private business or by collecting fees. In 1856, Congress provided a salary for consuls serving at certain posts; those who received a salary could not engage in private business, but could continue to collect fees for services performed.

From 1789 until 1924, the Diplomatic Service, which staffed U.S. legations and embassies, and the Consular Service, which was primarily responsible for promoting American commerce and assisting distressed American sailors, developed separately. The Foreign Service Act of 1924 (the Rogers Act) (43 Stat. 140), approved May 24, 1924,  merged the Diplomatic and Consular services into a single U.S. Foreign Service.

In 1886 the post at batum was established as a consular agency under the juriusdiction of the Consulate at Odessa. The post was raised to the status of a consulate in 1890, and the appointment of James C, Chambers, the consular agent, as consul was confirmed on May 17, 1890. Chambers resigned on May 23, 1904, and William H. Stuarttook charge of the consulate as vice consul until his death on May 21, 1906. William W. Masterson was appointed as consul on JUne 22, 1906. The post at Batum closed in May 1918, when the Germans overran it. It  reopened in early 1919, only to close for good when the Bolsheviks captured the city in 1921.

The appointment of Brooke B. Williams as the first U. S. consul at Revel was confirmed on February 3, 1858, but Williams resigned before beginning his duties. On January 13, 1859, the appointment of Dr. Charles A. Leas was confirmed. In 1870, when consul Eugene Schuyler was appointed Secretary of the Legation at St. Petersburg, the consulate at Revel was closed. From 1879 until it was closed in May 1917 the post at Revel operated as a consular agency under the jurisdiction of the consulate general at St. Petersburg. The office was reopened as a consulate in 1919. The Secretary of State sent a telegram dated December 31, 1924, informing the consul that the post was to be known as Tallinn.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
Although the Allied Control Commission for Italy (ACC) consisted only of representatives of Great Britain and the United States, it was realized that other powers with an interest in the Mediterranean, notably the Soviet Union, would also desire a mechanism for participation in Italian affairs. Because ACC was a military agency, and directly under the Supreme Allied Commander (SAC), Allied Force Headquarters (AFHQ) as early as July 1943 belived it desirable to establish some separate advisory body through which the political agencies of the interested Allied governments could express their views. In order to give these governments a forum for expressing their views, while still not permitting them to interfere with SAC''s control over the Allied Control Commission, the British resident minister, Harold Macmillan, proposed in early October that an advisory council be established for Italy. He suggested that the council not only advise the Supreme Allied Commander during the period of military responsibility but assume eventually the direction of the armistice control body. This recommendation was presented the the Supremer Allied Commander on October 18, 1943.

At the Moscow Conference of October 1943 the British Government suggest organization of an adviosry council similar to that outlined by Macmillan. The Soviet representative proposed that leadership of ACC Italy pass from the Supreme Allied Commander to this civilian body as soon as military considerations permitted. The Conference decided that the Allied commander in chief should determine when the time had arrived for permitting the Advisory Council to assume the supreme direction of ACC Italy. The terms agreed upon by the Moscow Conference were incorporated by the Combined Chiefs of Staff in a directive of November 26, 1943, to the Supreme Allied Commander. It declared that an Advisory Council for Italy woukld be created immediately and that it would include initially Great Britain, the United States, the Soviet Union, and the French Committee of National Liberation, with provision for later admission of representatives of Greece and Yugoslavia. 

It would be the role of the Council to keep itself closely informed on current Italian affairs and, in particular, to observe the machinery of control in Italy; it was not, however, to concern itself with the military function of the Supreme Allied Commander. The members of the Council were to make joint or several recommendations to their respective governments, but would not have the power to make final decisions. The Council was to gice advice on general matters to the Supreme Allied Commander in his capacity as President of the Allied Control Commission and was authprized to request information or explanations from him and also from technical inter-Allied agencies which might be established in Italy. The Supreme Allied Commander would, however, continue to receive his instruction from the Combined Chiefs of Staff. He would relinquish the presidency of ACC Italy when, in his opinion, the termination of direct military control over Italy was practicable, and at this point the Advisory Council for Italy would assumed direction of the Allied Control Commission.

The Council held it first meeting in Algiers on Novemebr 28, 1943. In late January 1944, after the Italian Government and the Allied Control Commission had moved to Salerno, it entered into residence  in Italy. Members appointed by their respective governments were Harold Macmillan for Great Britain; Robert D. Murphy for the United States; Andrei Vyshinsky, the Soviet Union; Rene Massigli, the French Committee of National Liberation; Jean Politis for Greece; and Miho Kreka, Yugoslavia.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Forest Service administered the national forest system, promoted conservation and use of national forests and grasslands, conducted forest and range research, and assisted and cooperated with administrators of state and private forests.

Systematic Federal activity in forestry had its beginning in 1878, following passage of an act authorizing the Commissioner of Agriculture to appoint a special agent to study general forest conditions in the United States (19 Stat. 143, 167). In 1881 there was established in the Department of Agriculture a Division of Forestry to function primarily as an investigative and information agency. It was superseded on July 1, 1901 by the Bureau of Forestry (31 Stat. 929) and offically designated the Forest Service by the Transfer Act of 1905 (33 Stat. 861, 872), approved February 1, 1905.

In 1891 Congress had authorized the establishment of forest reserves from timberlands on the public domain (26 Stat. 1103), and administration of these reserves was entrusted to the General land Office of the Department of the Interior. In 1901 a Forestry Division was established in that Department and it functioned until 1905 when jurisdiction over the national forest reserves was transferred to the Department of Agriculture and vested in the Forest Service. In 1907 forest reserves were redesignated national forests, and these areas were grouped into six districts. During the following year the Service decentralized the administration of field work by establishing district offices with authority over most matters affecting the national forests within their respective areas.

The growing importance of forest research was highlighted by the establishment in 1910 of the Forest Products Laboratory in Madison, Wisconsin. The passage of the Weeks Act of 1911 (36 Stat. 961) and the Clarke-McNary Act of 1924 (42 Stat. 653) gave considerable impetus to the programs of land acquisition, fire control, and state cooperation. The McSweeney-McNary Act of 1928 (45 Stat. 699) increased considerably the Service''s opportunities and responsibilities for forest research and utilization. 

It also carried out basic research relating to its area of concern and operated conservation and volunteer programs. Special projects which the Forest Service supervised included the forest and range conservation work of the Civilian Conservation Corps, 1933-1942; war-related programs, 1942-1945; the Prairie States Forestry ("Shelterbelt") Project, 1934-1942; and, beginning in 1942, the Cooperative Forest Fire Prevention Program (CFFP), a national defense campaign directed toward the protection of the national forests.

The Forest Service and the Bureau of Land Management (BLM, in the Department of the Interior) managed their lands for multiple uses and for sustained yields of resource outputs without impairing resource productivity. Both agencies sell timber, permit or lease lands for livestock grazing, allow mineral exploration and development in many areas, protect watersheds, manage wildlife habitats, administer recreation uses, and preserve wilderness areas, although they had different rules and regulations governing these activities. The similarity of missions, the proximity of lands and offices, and the existence of one major Federal resource land manager (the Forest Service) outside the Department of the Interior have led to frequent proposals to transfer the Forest Service lands to Interior and/or to merge the BLM and the Forest Service.

The U.S. Legation in Bolivia was established on January 3, 1849, when the Charge d'Affaires, John Appleton, presented his credentials. He was succeeded as Charge d'Affaires by Alexander K. McClung, July 3, 1850; Horace H. Miller, December 18, 1852; and John W. Dana, February 23, 1854.

In 1874 the chief of mission was elevated to Minister Resident and John W. Dana presented his new credentials on September 24, 1854. He was succeeded by John Cotton Smith, March 10, 1859; David K. Cartter [sic], July 28, 1861; Allen A. Hall, September 4, 1863; John W. Caldwell, November 2, 1868; Leopold Markbreit, July 25, 1869; John T. Croxton, April 8, 1873; Robert M. Reynolds, January 30, 1875; S. Newton Pettis, June 2, 1879; Charles Adams, July 8, 1880; George Maney, November 4, 1882; Richard Gibbs, October 16, 1883; William A. Seay, September 19, 1885; S.S. Carlisle, January 17, 1888; and Thomas H. Anderson, December 16, 1889. From June 2, 1879, through October 4, 1890, the chief of mission also served as Consul General.

In 1890 the Minister Resident was elevated to Envoy Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary and Thomas H. Anderson presented his new credentials on October 4, 1890. He was succeeded by Frederic J. Grant, April 12, 1893; Thomas Moonlight, April 14, 1894; George H. Bridgman, July 4, 1898; William B. Sorsby, October 4, 1902; James F. Stutesman, September 8, 1908; Horace G. Knowles, December 28, 1910; John D. O'Rear, August 31, 1913; S. Abbot Maginnis, January 14, 1920; Jesse S. Cottrell, January 6, 1922; David E. Kaufman, May 30, 1928; Edward F. Feely, September 23, 1930; Fay A. Des Portes, November 15, 1933; R. Henry Norweb, August 10, 1936; Robert Granville Caldwell, August 21, 1937; Douglas Jenkins, October 26, 1939; and Pierre de L. Boal, May 23, 1942.

Relations with Bolivia were interrupted on December 20, 1943, and the new government of Bolivia was not recognized by the United States until November 16, 1944. On that date the U.S. mission opened as an embassy, and Walter Thurston presented his credentials as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary. He was succeeded by Joseph Flack, July 15,1946; Irving Florman, February 27, 1950; Edward J. Sparks, June 13, 1952; Gerald A. Drew, December 8, 1954; Philip W. Bonsal, May 10, 1957; Carl W. Strom, May 4, 1959; Ben S. Stephansky, June 29, 1961; Douglas Henderson, December 7, 1963; Raul H. Castro, September 3, 1968; Ernest V. Siracusa, December 5, 1969; William Perry Stedman, Jr., October 3, 1973; Paul H. Boeker, October 26, 1977; and Marvin Weissman, March 26, 1980.

Relations with Bolivia were again interrupted on July 17, 1980. Alexander Watson served as Charge d'Affaires ad interim from July 20, 1980, until September 1981. Relations were resumed and the next Ambassador, Edwin G. Corr, presented his credentials on December 10, 1981. He was succeeded by Edward Morgan Rowell, August 20, 1985; Robert S. Gelbard, October 11, 1988; Charles R. Bowers, August 23, 1991; Curtis Warren Kamman, November 16, 1994; Donna Jean Hrinak, January 14, 1998; and V. Manuel Rocha, August 4, 2000; David Greenlee,  January 17, 2003;  and Philip S. Goldberg, October 13, 2006 At a meeting on September 10, 2008, Bolivian Foreign Minister David Choquehuanca informed Ambassador Philip Goldberg that President Morales had ordered him declared persona non grata (PNG). This followed the Bolivian Government's failure the day before to address security threats to U.S. counternarcotics operations in the Chapare, which caused the withdrawal of U.S. Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) personnel. 

In August 2009, John S. Creamer, August 2009 was appointed Chare d'Affaires ad interim, and was succeeded by Larry L. Memmott in July 2012.

Throughout the past two centuries, dating back to the presidency of George Washington, Consulate Guangzhou (Canton), as America''s oldest diplomatic post in China and one of America''s oldest posts in the Far East, has played a pivotal role in promoting America''s relationship with China. Today, the Consulate promotes trade and commercial ties, engages China across-the board on key American policy objectives, and promotes public diplomacy through visitor exchanges. The Consulate General is the only U.S. mission in China to process American adoptions and immigrant visas, making it one of the U.S. Department of State''s busiest consular-related posts. 

United States diplomatic presence in the Guangzhou area dates back to the founding years of the American republic. In 1784, the American merchant ship Empress of China reached what was then known as the port of Canton transporting ginseng to trade for Chinese black tea. The ship also carried on it Major Samuel Shaw, a 29-year old former Revolutionary War artillery officer, who served as the business agent for this first American trade effort to the "Middle Kingdom". Shaw wrote to Secretary of Foreign Affairs John Jay, recommending that the young United States

appoint a consul and vice consul to Canton. "Such officers,"  he noted, "would have a degree of weight and respect which private adventurers cannot readily acquire, and which would enable them to render essential services to their countrymen." Major Shaw was appointed the first American consul to China, although he would serve "with neither salary nor perquisites but with the confidence and esteem of the United States." 

At that time, Chinese authorities limited trade with the outside world to the port of Canton. All foreign traders were further restricted to living and working on factory compounds established on the banks of the Pearl River. American trade with China increased steadily throughout the early decades of the nineteenth century, although there were long periods during which the office of the U.S. Consul at Canton was unoccupied, and Americans serving at the consulate typically did not speak Chinese. In the wake of the Opium War between China and Great Britain, however, the Chinese government was compelled to expand trading opportunities beyond Canton. After the conclusion of the hostilities, the first U.S. formal mission to China, led by former Congressman Caleb Cushing, brokered the 1844 Treaty of Wangxia, an agreement which secured trading privileges for American merchants and opened new Chinese ports to American vessels. In addition to protecting the interests of United States merchants, American consuls enjoyed greater authority granted by Congress; in 1848 the Consulate was allowed to arraign U.S. citizens charged with offenses 

against the laws of China. The Canton consulate was burned down in 1856, but U.S. diplomats continued to support an expanding American presence in the region throughout the nineteenth century. Within the consular district of Canton, and reporting to the Department of State through canton, there were, for brief periods, consular agencies at Macao, Whampoa, Swatow, Hoikow, Pakhoi, and Kiung-Chow (Hainan island).

Aside from Guangzhou, U.S. Consulates were present in South China in the other opened ports of Fuzhou and Xiamen. However, due to a parsimonious and semi-isolationist U.S. Congress, these consulates frequently remained unoccupied. In fact, British and German officials were often asked to represent U.S. interests. This continued until the mid-1880s when the Shanghai Consul General began administering all consular services in China. At other times, the U.S. Consulate in Guangzhou also shared this responsibility. With the concurrence of the British government, the U.S., in 1873, built a consulate on Shamian Island, a sandy one kilometer long strip of land around which a man-made canal had been dug ten years before to separate it from the rest of the city. 

The Second Sino-Japanese War precipitated the withdrawal of consulate personnel in Fuzhou in 1934 and Canton in 1938. Subsequent to Japan''s surrender to the Allies, many U.S. consulates in China reopened. For several months in 1949, after the Chinese Nationalist government moved its headquarters from Nanjing to Guangzhou, Shamian Island served as the site of the State Department''s "Office of Embassy." As the civil war raged between Chinese Nationalist and Communist forces, the Nationalist government decided once again to move the seat of government to Chungking (Chongqing) and the Office of Embassy followed. Consulate Canton itself was closed in August, 1949, and diplomatic relations between the communist government of mainland China and the United States ceased shortly thereafter.

In the wake of the landmark visits of Secretary of State Henry Kissinger and President Richard Nixon, the United States and China formally re-established diplomatic relations on January 1, 1979. According to an agreement, each country was allowed to set up two consulates. The United States chose Shanghai and Guangzhou (China chose San Francisco and Houston). On August 31 1979, almost 30 years to the day that Consulate Canton had been closed, Vice-President Walter Mondale unveiled the seal for the new U.S. Consulate Guangzhou on the 11th floor of the Dongfang Hotel at 120 Liu Hua Road. Richard L. Williams was appointed the first Consul General in China since 1949. In April 1990, the Consulate returned to Shamian Island when the current Consulate Tower, built on reclaimed land near the Pearl River, was completed at 1 Shamian South Street, next to the White Swan Hotel.

Since reopening, the Consulate''s efforts have focused on two main issues: immigration and commerce. As South China has historically been the home for most Chinese immigrants to America, Guangzhou was designated as the sole immigrant visa processing post for all of China in the early 1980s. Additionally, in 1992 all adoption processing was assigned to Guangzhou. To date, Americans have adopted more than 60,000 children from China (roughly a third of all U.S. foreign adoptions world-wide). Immigrant and nonimmigrant visa numbers have also risen in the past 30 years. Whereas in 1979 the Consulate processed about 27,000 visa applicants (both non-immigrant and immigrant visas), today it adjudicates annually about 121,000 applicants. In order to better accommodate the rising number of applicants, on August 6, 2005, the Consular Section moved to a more spacious office facility at the Tianyu Garden Building on Lin He Zhong Road in Guangzhou¿s

Tianhe district. The facility has 30 interviewing windows available for 23 American staff

and 100 locally-employed personnel.

Following World War II, although representatives of the Department of State were working in Germany with the Office of the Political Adviser from the time that Military Government was established, the six main consular offices - Berlin (Consulate General), Bremen (Consulate),  Frankfurt (Consulate), Hamburg (Consulate General), Munich (Consulate General),  and Stuttgart (Consulate), were not reopened until the spring of 1946. Under Military Government the position of these consular establishments was somewhat unusual. Ordinarily, American consular officers were accredited to the government of the territory in which a consulate was located. In occupied Germany, however, consular districts were under one of the Allied military governments. In the case of the U.S. zone of occupation,  the consulates themselves were actually a part of the military government. Thus, requests for services which in normal times would be made directly to the German Government were made instead by the consulates either to the U.S. Military Government (OMGUS) to the Land Military Government which administered the consular district.

To a large extent, the consulates were dependent upon the machinery of military occupation. At the same time, however, they exercised latitude to act somewhat independently from these agencies, and were free to approach municipal authorities directly without burdening military channels, and anticipated a time when a recognized German Government would be formed to which consular offices could be accredited.

After the War of the Pacific, 1879-83, between Chile and Peru, Chile retained sovereignty over the provinces of Tacna and Arica. Article 3 of the Treaty of Ancon, signed October 20, 1883, provided that the provinces continue in the possession of Chile for a period of 10 years after the ratification of the treaty, after which time a plebiscite would decide whether the territory would remain in the control of Chile or would revert to Peru. The country gaining control, it was further stipulated, would pay the other country 10 million pesos. The treaty further provided for a protocol to prescribe the manner in which the plebiscite would be carried out and the terms of payment of the 10 million pesos.

In 1892 a series of unsuccessful negotiations was begun.  In January 1922, in an effort to settle the problem, the U.S. Government invited Chile and Peru to send representatives to Washington to negotiate directly; and in July of that year, following the negotiations, the two countries asked the President of the United States to arbitrate and to pronounce upon the question of the feasibility of holding a plebiscite. Peru held that article 3 of the Treaty of Ancon was invalid because of the lapse of time from the signing of the treaty, but Chile upheld the treaty. The United States agreed to arbitrate, and by April 1924 the claims of both countries were presented to the Arbitrator. On March 9, 1925, President Coolidge announced his decision that article 3 of the Treaty of Ancon was still valid. The Arbitrator also decided that Peru should receive the province of Tarata, held by Chile since the War of the Pacific.

In accord with the ruling of the Arbitrator, a Plebiscitary Commission was appointed consisting of three members-one appointed by Peru, one appointed by Chile, and the third member, who acted a President of the Commission, appointed by the President of the United States. The Commission had the power and the duty to promulgate all necessary rules and regulations for conducting a plebiscite.  The members of the Plebiscitary Commission were Gen. John J. Pershing, President (succeeded on January 27, 1926, by Maj. Gen. William Lassiter); Don Agustin Edward of Chile; and Manuel de Freyre y Santander, the Peruvian member.

The first session of the Commission was held at Arica during August 1925, at which time April 1926 was selected as the date for the plebiscite. The voting registers were to be opened on March 27, 1926, and of the total population of about 35,000 people, the number of voters could not exceed 6,000. The Registration and Election Boards were to inscribe the names of males, who were able to read and write, or landholders or residents of at least 5 years. On the eve of the registration the Peruvian member of the Commission ordered all Peruvians to abstain from registering because of a conflict between Peruvian and Chilean members. In an effort to counterbalance this order the registers were kept open, unsuccessfully, for an additional period of 30 days. The President of the Commission, General Lassiter, declaring the plebiscite to be abortive, resigned and declared the Commission at an end. Despite Chilean protests that his action exceeded the powers of the President of the Commission and overrode the award of the U.S. President as Arbitrator, the plebiscite failed. Secretary of State Charles Evans Hughes then invited representatives of both Chile and Peru to come to Washington in order to renegotiate a peaceful solution.

During May 1929 a settlement was reached whereby Arica remained in the control of Chile and Tacna reverted to Peruvian control. The Special Boundary Commission, called for as a provision of the award of the Arbitrator, consisted of three members--one appointed by the United States, one by Chile, and one by Peru. The Commission was created to draw the boundary line of the territory covered by article 3 of the Treaty of Ancon. This article defined the boundaries of the provinces of Tacna and Arica.

The records described as records of the Plebiscitary Commission are the records that were turned over to the Arbitrator following the completion of the work of the Commission. This was stipulated in the award of the Arbitrator. The records of the American Delegation were turned over to the Department of State, as were the records of the Special Boundary Commission of which Jay Morrow was Commissioner.

The Philippine Islands came under the control of the United States as a result of the Spanish-American War. By the treaty signed at Paris on December 10, 1898, Spain ceded the Philippine territory to the United States and a Philippine Commission was established by an Executive order of March 16, 1900. In accordance with instructions of the President to the Commission on April 7, 1900, and an Executive order of June 21, 1901, the powers and duties conferred on the Philippine Commission and the Civil Governor were to be exercised under the direction and control of the Secretary of War. An act of Congress of July 1, 1902 (32 Stat. 691) ratified and approved the Presidential instructions and Executive order. In 1907 the Philippine Assembly was established and its members were elected by the Filipino people. The Assembly was in effect the lower house of the Legislature and the Commission was the upper house.

On August 16, 1916, Congress passed the Philippine Autonomy Act (39 Stat. 545), placing the legislative power in the hands of the Filipinos, reenacting the bill of rights, and establishing an almost complete self-government. By provisions of the act the chief executive, the Governor General, continued to be appointed by the President and the Secretary of War continued to have certain statutory duties and powers in connection with the administration of the Philippine Government.

The Hare-Hawes-Cutting Independence Act of January 17, 1933 (47 Stat. 761), fixed the date of political independence for the Philippine Islands as ten years later; provided for a ten-year transition period under an autonomous commonwealth; and stipulated that the act should not become law until it was accepted by the Philippine Legislature. The act was vetoed by the President but was passed over his veto. The Ninth Philippine Legislature met and rejected the act of October 17, 1933.

Subsequently, Philippine leaders agreed to accept legislation similar to the Hare-Hawes-Cutting Act. An act, known as the Tydings-McDuffie Independence Act (48 Stat. 456), was passed on March 24, 1934, and was accepted by the Ninth Philippine Legislature on May 1, 1934. The act, also known as the Philippine Commonwealth and Independence Law, provided that a Commonwealth be established in the Philippine Islands and then, at the end of a ten-year transition period, a Philippine Republic. The former Government of the Philippine Islands was terminated and the authority previously conferred on the Governor General of the Philippine Islands, the Secretary of War, and other officials was given to the President of the United States. He in turn delegated his authority to three agents: a U.S. High Commissioner, who would be his representative in the Philippine Islands; the Secretary of State, who would conduct foreign affairs affecting the Philippines; and the Secretary of War, who would continue to administer certain other affairs pertaining to the Philippines.

The Tydings-McDuffie Independence Act stated that the High Commissioner "shall be the representative of the President of the United States in the Philippine Islands and shall be recognized as such by the government of the Commonwealth of the Philippine Islands, and by the commanding officers of the military forces of the United States, and by all civil officials of the United States in the Philippine Islands." The Commonwealth of the Philippines formally recognized the authority of the High Commissioner under section 1 of the ordinance appended to the Constitution of the Philippines.

Under provisions of Reorganization Plan No. II, submitted to Congress on May 9, 1939, and made effective on July 1, 1939, affairs of the Philippines were to be administered by the Secretary of the Interior. Communications between departments of the Federal Government and the High Commissioner were to normally pass through the Division of Territories and Island Possessions of the Department of the Interior, but, at the request of the President, the High Commissioner communicated directly with the Secretary of State on matters involving or likely to involve foreign affairs of the Philippines and international obligations of the United States relating to the Philippines.

Shortly after the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, on December 7, 1941, Japanese forces invaded the Philippines. The High Commissioner conferred with Naval authorities about the desirability of evacuating employees from Manila by sea. It was decided that the risks involved would be too great and that it would be better for the employees to remain in Manila. On December 24, 1941, the High Commissioner, Francis B. Sayre, received an urgent telephone call from General Douglas MacArthur requesting that he and President Manuel L. Quezon leave Manila within four hours to set up a temporary seat of government at Corregidor. The High Commissioner agreed but, before leaving, instructed Clause A. Buss, his Executive Assistant, to destroy all papers and files that should not fall into enemy hands. 

Few records of the Office of the U.S. High Commissioner survived the war. Nearly all of the records created in the Manila office during 1935-41 period were destroyed to prevent their being captured by the Japanese. In a letter of May 13, 1942, from High Commissioner Francis B. Sayre to Richard R. Ely, Supervisor of Philippine Affairs in the Division of Territories and Island Possessions, Mr. Sayre wrote : "Complete records of appointments made during the months of November and December in the Office of the High Commissioner are not now available due to the fact that it was deemed advisable to destroy the major part of our files before the evacuation of the Office to Corregidor on December 24, 1941. We were permitted to take only a limited quantity of files with use, and nearly all of these had to be destroyed on our departure from Corregidor."

Claude A. Buss, the employee responsible for carrying out the order to destroy the files, in his report to the High Commissioner stated: "We destroyed all our confidential files and everything of record except the personnel cards. We burned telegrams, letters, the compilations of alien property, codes, and cipher tables."

On February 10, 1942, General MacArthur received a message from President Roosevelt suggesting that the High Commissioner and President Quezon should be evacuated from Corregidor. On February 24, the High Commissioner left Corregidor by submarine at 3 o''clock in the morning. After a perilous 13-day trip he reached Australia and from there he flew to the United States, arriving March 13.

During the months of April, May, and June 1942 the High Commissioner, with an office in the new Department of the Interior Building, worked on the problem of getting relief to the civilian population interned in the Philippines. By mid-year 1942 the Philippines had been captured by Japanese forces and affairs relating to the Islands were being handled in the Department of the Interior. By Executive Order 9245, dated September 16, 1942, President Roosevelt transferred the functions, powers, and duties of the High Commissioner, together with its personnel, records, property, and funds, to the Secretary of the Interior. In a letter dated September 16, 1942, the President requested the Office of the High Commissioner, under the direction of the Secretary of the Interior, to undertake the investigation, study, and consolidation of plans for an orderly rehabilitation of the Philippines. 

As the war in the Pacific drew to a close, preparations were begun for the independence of the Philippines. The President''s Executive Order 9616, dated September 14, 1945, stated that : " (1) Executive Order 9245 of September 16, 1942, in hereby repealed and the functions, powers, and duties of the United States High Commissioner to the Philippine Islands, together with the personnel, records, property, and funds of the office . . . are transferred from the Secretary of the Interior to the said United States High Commissioner to the Philippine Islands. (2) All powers and authority of the President in respect to the Philippine Islands and the government of the Commonwealth of the Philippine Islands, its branches, sub-divisions and instrumentalities which be lawfully so delegated are hereby delegated to the United States High Commissioner to the Philippine Islands.

The President of the United States proclaimed the independence of the Philippine Islands by Proclamation NO. 2695, of July 4, 1946. In a letter of the same date to Paul V. McNutt, U.S. Ambassador to the Philippine Islands (and since September 14, 1945, the U.S. High Commissioner), President Truman wrote: "I hereby designate you to liquidate the affairs of the United States High Commissioner to the Philippine Islands immediately following the granting of independence to the Philippine Commonwealth on July 4, 1946, and until Sections 102 and 103 of Reorganization Plan No. 1 of 1946 become law." Reorganization Plan No. 1 was not passed by Congress. In a letter dated June 28, 1947, from the High Commissioner''s office in Manila to Edwin W. Pauley, Special Advisor to the Secretary of State on Reparations, Pauley was notified that "As of June 30 [1947], the liquidation of the Office of the United States High Commissioner to the Philippine Islands will be complete."

Incumbents, with terms of service included: Frank Murphy, November 15, 1935 - December 31, 1936; J. Weldon Jones (acting), January 1, 1937 - February 27, 1937; Paul V. McNutt, February 28, 1937 - July 12, 1939; J. Weldon Jones (acting), July 12, 1939 - August 8, 1939; Francis B. Sayre, August 8, 1939 - October 12, 1942; Harold Ickes (concurrently Secretary of the Interior), October 13, 1942 - September 14, 1945; and Paul V. McNutt, September 14, 1945 - July 4, 1946.

The Overseas Private Investment Corporation (OPIC) was authorized as an independent agency by Public Law 91-175 (83 Stat. 809) of December 30, 1969. The authorities were formerly transferred to the Corporation by Executive Order 11579 of January 19, 1971. OPIC was transferred to the International Development Cooperation Agency on October 1, 1979. It became and independent agency again on April 1, 1999 (112 Stat. 2681-790).

The Overseas Private Investment Corporation mobilized and facilitated the participation of U.S. private capital and skills in the economic and social development of less developed countries and areas, and countries in transition from non-market to market economies, thereby complementing the development assistance objectives of the United States. The Corporation determined whether to provide insurance, financing, or reinsurance operations on a self-sustaining basis, taking into account in it financing operations the economic and financial soundness of projects; utilized private credit and investment institutions and the Corporation's guaranty authority as the principal means of mobilizing capital investment funds; broadened private participation and revolve its funds through selling its direct investments to private investors whenever it could appropriately do so; conducted its insurance operations with due regard to principles of risk management including efforts to share its insurance risks and reinsurance risks; maximize projects sponsored by U.S. small businesses; considered the conduct of its operations the extent to which less developed country governments were receptive to private enterprise, domestic and foreign, and their willingness and ability to maintain conditions which enabled private enterprise to make its full contribution to the development process; fostered private initiate and competition and discouraged monopolistic practices; be consistent as possible with the goals of the US government; supported developmental projects having positive trade benefits for the U.S.; and advised and assisted interested agencies of the US and other organizations with projects and programs relating to the development of private enterprise in less developed countries and areas. The Corporation insured that the country had implemented worker protection rights and that projects had no adverse environmental impacts. It was under the policy guidance of the Secretary of State.

The Corporation had a Board of Directors, a President, and Executive Vice President, and other offices and staff the Board of Directors determined was necessary.  The Board consisted of fifteen Directors including the Chairman. Eight directors, non-government employees, were appointed by the President with the advice and consent of the Senate. At least two of those eight were experienced in small businesses, one in organized labor, and one in cooperatives. Each Director were appointed for  term of no more than three years; and no more than three Directors were appointed for one year. These Directors served until successors were appointed or were reappointed. The Chairman and Vice Chairman of the Board were designated by the President of the U.S. The other Directors were principal U.S. Government officers with duties relating to the Corporation, including the President of the corporation, the Administrator of the Agency for International Development, the U.S. Trade Representation (or a designated Deputy U.S. Trade Representative), and an officer of the Department of Labor. The President of the Corporation was appointed by the President of the U.S. with the consist of the Senate and was the Corporation's Chief Executive Officer and was responsible for the operations and management of the corporation, subject to bylaws and polices established by the Board. The Executive Vice President was appointed by the President of the US with consent of the Senate.

On October 5, 2018, the Better Utilization of Investments Leading to Development Act of 2018 (BUILD Act) authorized the creation of the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation from the merger of the Overseas Private Investment Corporation with the U.S. Agency for International Development’s (USAID) Development Credit Authority and USAID’s existing Legacy Credit portfolio under the Urban Environment Program and any other direct loan programs and non-Development Credit Authority guaranty programs authorized by the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 (22 U.S.C. 2151 et seq.) or other existing predecessor Acts, other than sovereign loan guaranties. The BUILD Act required a reorganization plan, which included October 1, 2019 as the effective date for the abolishment of the Overseas Private Investment Corporation and the creation of the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation.

The concern of the Federal Government with the condition of the nation's roads can be traced to the year 1893, when an Office of Road Inquiry was established by the Secretary of Agriculture in response to increasing demands by supporters of the public interest-driven "Good Roads Movement" during the 1880s. From 1893 to 1912, the Office (under three different designations within the Department of Agriculture) was involved primarily with the investigation of current road construction and maintenance practices and disseminating its findings through publications, lectures, and consultations. In 1896 the Office of Road Inquiry began to encourage construction of "object-lesson" roads, so named because they were to apply new construction methods and materials. On July 1, 1905, the Division of Tests within the Bureau of Chemistry and the Office of Public Roads Inquiries were merged under the new name Office of Public Roads. This period also saw the transfer of various other organizations within the Department of Agriculture to the newly-renamed Office. 

The Federal Highway Act of 1921 expanded the responsibilities of the Bureau of Public Roads (the designation given to the organization in 1918) to include apportioning funds to the states; approving the selection of projects, plans, and materials; and supervising road construction in national forests and parks, on public lands, and in Federal reservations. The Bureau's research activities expanded to include studies on highway design and materials, highway surfaces, and highway maintenance. During this period the Bureau also began to assist the states in formulating highway laws, organizing highway departments, and preparing specifications and standards. During the 1930s the Bureau administered large emergency sums for employing relief labor on highways and eliminating grade crossings. In 1939 the Bureau was transferred to the Federal Works Agency and its name was changed to the Public Roads Administration. During World War II, the Public Roads Administration was involved with the construction of access roads to War industries and military areas. Specific projects of the organization during this period included the Alaska and Canada Highway and the improvement of the Inter-American Highway through Central America. 

After World War II, the Public Roads Administration devoted its efforts toward the realization of various Federal Highway Acts passed during and after the War, which provided for a cooperative program of improvement of primary, secondary, and urban highways throughout the nation. The agency also cooperated with Territorial and foreign governments in establishing long-range highway improvement programs, designing and constructing highways and bridges, and providing information on and instruction in various phases of highway engineering. During this period the Bureau was transferred to the Department of Commerce, where it reverted to its former name, the Bureau of Public Roads, under the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act of 1949. In 1967 the Bureau was renamed the Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) and transferred to the newly-created Department of Transportation.

On August 10, 1970, the Bureau of Public Roads was abolished. Instead of the former bureau structure, FHWA was divided into six new components made up of Planning, Research and Development, Right-of-Way and Environment, Engineering and Traffic Operations, Motor Carrier and Highway Safety, and Administration, each to be headed by an Associate Administrator.
