creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
After the Unilateral Declaration of Independence was issued by the white-majority government of Rhodesia in November 1965, the United States recalled its Consul General from Salisbury, closed the U.S. Information Service (USIS) library, and withdrew its Agency for International Development (USAID) and trade promotion officials. After 1965, the small remaining American consular staff continued to operate under authority of exequaturs issued by Queen Elizabeth II. Following declaration of a republic, the United States closed its Consulate General on March 17, 1970. 

In 1971, despite Administration opposition, the U.S. Congress passed legislation permitting the United States to import strategic materials, such as chrome, from Rhodesia. The legislation, which took effect January 1, 1972, was of little real economic benefit to the Rhodesian economy, and the United States continued to support the balance of the sanctions program. After the legislation was repealed in March 1977, the United States once again enforced all sanctions. 

The United States supported the United Nations and the United Kingdom consistently in their efforts to influence Rhodesian authorities to accept the principles of majority rule. Beginning in 1976, the United States began to take a more active role in the search for a settlement in cooperation with the British. The Anglo-American proposals of late 1977, aimed at bringing a negotiated end to the dispute, lent the weight of the United States to the search for a peaceful settlement and were a counterpart to the Soviet-Cuban use of military power to increase their influence in southern Africa. The United States supported British efforts to bring about and implement the settlement signed at Lancaster House on December 21, 1979 and extended official diplomatic recognition to the new government immediately after independence. A resident Embassy was established in Harare on Zimbabwe''s Independence Day, April 18, 1980. The first U.S. Ambassador arrived and presented his credentials in June 1980. Until the arrival in 1983 of a resident Ambassador in Washington, Zimbabwe''s relations with the U.S. were handled by its Ambassador to the United Nations (U.N.) in New York. 

Iin July 1986, the U.S. Government decided to discontinue future bilateral aid to Zimbabwe as a result of a continuing pattern of uncivil and undiplomatic statements and actions by the Government of Zimbabwe in the United Nations and elsewhere. Aid programs previously agreed upon were not affected by the decision, nor were regional development programs that might benefit Zimbabwe. Full programming was restored in 1988. From 2000, the United States took a leading role in condemning the Zimbabwean Government''s increasing assault on human rights and the rule of law, and joined much of the world community in calling for the Government of Zimbabwe to embrace a peaceful democratic evolution. In 2002 and 2003, the United States imposed targeted measures on the Government of Zimbabwe, including financial and visa sanctions against selected individuals, a ban on transfers of defense items and services, and a suspension of non-humanitarian government-to-government assistance. Despite strained political relations, the United States continued as a leading provider of humanitarian assistance to the people of Zimbabwe, providing about $400 million in humanitarian assistance from 2002-2007, most of which was food aid.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
In September 1965, the Center for Overseas Programs Analysis (COPA) was established. It was an organization that was to “bring to bear comprehensive and rigorously systematic techniques of analysis on the factors which contribute to program success or failure, to program costs, and to program balance and unity”. The Center, of which Howard E. Ball is the Director and John Golden the Deputy Director, was responsible to the Deputy Under Directory for Administration. It was an affiliate of the Foreign Service Institute. The main function of the Center was to augment the Department’s capabilities to solve various problems pertaining to its overseas operations. COPA did not have responsibilities in the field of substantive foreign policy formulation and planning. COPA brought together seasoned career people of the various U.S. international agencies an talented members of the university and business communities in the search for ways to strengthen the execution of overseas programs.

In 1966, the Center for Overseas Program Analysis was redesignated as the Center for International Systems Research (CISR) to help achieve and support foreign policy goals. The Center, under the general direction of the Deputy Under Secretary for Administration, was headed by Director Howard E. Ball and Associate Director John Golden, who held similar positions under COPA. The functions of CISR included: assessing the consequences of increasing or decreasing the amount of specific resources allocated to given countries or regions, along with the timing of such proposed increases or decreases; development of simulated training situations in preparation for crisis management and crisis decision making; defining basis information requirements; and give a range of feasible cost and technological assumptions. The Center cooperated with various Bureaus and Areas in the Department, and worked with other Agencies that participated in overseas operations. It also assisted the Foreign Service Institute in research leading to the development of materials and techniques which will enhance the training program, including the design of new components for the curriculum.

It did not have responsibilities in the field of substantive foreign policy formulation and planning. Neither did its functions impinge on the responsibilities of the Bureau of Intelligence and Research or the Foreign Affairs Research Council. The Center concentrated upon intermediate to long-term types of projects, but did not develop innovations or improvements geared to the short-run performance of overseas operations. 

CISR was abolished by July 1967.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Interdepartmental Committee on the Proclaimed List (or the Interdepartmental Committee on the Proclaimed List of Certain Blocked Nationals), was established as a working committee in the Department of State pursuant to Presidential Proclamation 2497, July 17, 1941, to compile a list of persons working for or with the Axis, and persons to whom exports from the United States were deemed to be detrimental to the national defense. The Committee published the United States Proclaimed List of Certain Blocked Nationals, the effect of which was to prohibit except under license all trading and financial transactions and communications of any type between American citizens both real and juridical and persons included on the List. Any violation of the List subjects the offender to economic sanctions and criminal prosecution. The "Proclaimed List," also known as the "American Black List," was withdrawn effective July 8, 1946.

Committee consisted of representatives of the Departments of State, the Treasury, Justice, and Commerce; the Administrator of Export Control; and the Coordinator of Commercial and Cultural Relations Between the American Republics. The Committee’s membership also included representatives of the British and the Canadian Embassies as well as other United States agencies concerned. Members included from the Department of State: Seymour J. Rubin (Chairman), Walter S. Surrey (Chairman), George W. Baker (Acting Chairman), and George N. Monsma; Department of Commerce: E.E. Schnellbacher; Department of Justice: Simms Carter and Henry Munroe; Foreign Economic Administration: Edmund S. Doty; Office of Inter-American Affairs: Norris Mumper and Louis Keller; and the Department of the Treasury: Paul Gewirtz.

The Proclaimed List was administered by the Division of World Trade Intelligence, followed by the Division of Economic Security Controls. When the Division was abolished, retroactive to July 15, 1947, by Departmental Announcement 650, July 28, 1947, with residual functions transferred to Office of Financial and Development Policy and assigned to new Division of Occupied Areas Economic Affairs.

This list, which was authorized by a Presidential proclamation of July 17, 1941, contained the names of persons in Latin American and elsewhere who were considered to be acting for the benefit of hostile countries or nationals of those countries. Restrictions were placed upon exports to and the use in the United States of assets of such persons. Other regulations applying to persons on the list were contained in an Executive order of April 10, 1940, amending the order of January 15, 1934. These regulations prohibited transactions in foreign exchange, the transfer of credits, and the export of coin and currencies or other transactions designed to evade these prohibitions. The Chairman of the Committee was Assistant Secretary Dean Acheson and the other members represented the Secretary of Treasury, the Attorney General, the Secretary of Commerce, the Administrator of Export Control, and the Coordinator of Commercial and Cultural Relations between the American Republics. The Committee held only one formal meeting, at which the establishment of the State Department’s Division of World Trade Intelligence was decided upon. A working committee, which was also called the Interdepartmental Committee on the Proclaimed List (or the Interdepartmental Committee on the Proclaimed List of Certain Blocked Nationals), prepared the lists. creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Departmental Steering Committee, also known as the Organization to Undertake a Study of the Basic Requirements of the Foreign Service, was established by the Departmental Coordinating Committee in April 1945, in order to conduct studies leading to a basic redraft of Foreign Service legislation, and prepare recommendations for administration of the Foreign Service. The Departmental Steering Committee consisted of high-ranking officers of the Department of State, with the Director of the Office of the Foreign Service serving as chairman. Recommendations from the Steering Committee went to the Departmental Coordinating Committee, then to an inter-departmental supervisory group, and then to a national advisory committee.

Members of the Committee included: Selden Chapin (Chairman), George V. Allen, Ruth W. Ayers, Bernhard G. Bechhoefer, George H. Butler, William E. De Courcy, Walter C. Ferris, Andrew B. Foster, Edmund A. Gullion, Julian F. Harrington, Edward T. Lampson, Frederick Livesey, Charles H. Long, Frank A. March, Harold B. Minor, Archie Palmer, Walter A. Radius, Lionel M. Summers, E. creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The American Working Group on Pact Organization was created, in August 1949, as an interdepartmental committee on foreign assistance correlation. John F. Hickman, Assistant Secretary of State for United Nations Affairs, served as the group's secretary. Ten additional State Department representatives joined Hickman and five members of the National Military Establishment to study and discuss organizational, procedural, and administrative questions related to the North Atlantic Treaty, the pact it called into being, and the Brussels Treaty Council. The working group served both the American team of negotiators engaged in preparing for the first session of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) Council and the two represented agencies by providing informational support and a degree of communication between Departments on matters of mutual interest.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Advisory Committee on Occupied Areas Affairs (OAC) was established August 12, 1946 in pursuance of a directive by the President, dated August 30, 1945 to advise the Department of State on policy toward the occupied areas. It served to pool the resources of the civilian agencies that had an interest in the problems arising from the control of Germany, Japan, Austria, and Korea. The committee served as a forum for the exchange of views and proposals concerning anticipated problems and attempted to improve interdepartmental relationships at the working level by the exchange of information and consultation at the Assistant Secretary level. OAC was terminated by Departmental Announcement 196 of December 13, 1948.

The committee was composed of members from the Departments of State, Agriculture. Treasury, Commerce, and Labor. John Hilldring and Charles E. Saltzman, from the Department of State, served as Chairmen of OAC. Other members included: Department of State: Philander P. Claxton (Deputy Chairman and Alternate), and Leon Weaver (Secretary); Department of Agriculture: L.A. Wheeler, Francis Flood (Alternate), and Fred J. Rossiter (Alternate); Department of Commerce: Thomas C. Blaisdell, and H.W. Parisius (Alternate); Department of Labor: David A. Morse, Philip Kaiser (Alternate), and Arnold Zempel (Alternate); and Department of the Treasury: Frank Southard, Jr., Orvis Schmidt (Alternate), Arthur Stewart (Alternate), and George H. Willis (Alternate).

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Committee on Inter-American Economic Development (lAED) was an inter-departmental committee created in 1944. It consisted of members from the Department of Commerce, the Export-Import Bank, the Department of Agriculture, the Foreign Economic Administration, the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs, and the Department of State. The lAED was a committee of the Executive Committee on Economic Foreign Policy. Its major duties included making recommendations regarding the formation of a general policy for the United States with respect to inter-American economic development and the examination of related problems and developments. It was disbanded in March 1945.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Department established country committees to identify and evaluate present and emerging problems of mutual concern to the geographic and functional offices. The country committees make policy recommendations taking into account political, economic, informational, the United Nations, and other international factors. These committees also served as a medium for the interchange of information gathered from other committees and advised other committees on policy recommendations with regard to the impact proposed policy upon a particular area or country. 

The Committee on the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (CUSSR) was established on February 18, 1946 to deal with the problems relating to the Soviet Union. The Committee was redefined in July 1946 to handle all Eastern and Southeastern Europe and was renamed the Committee on Eastern and Southeastern Europe-Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (CESE-USSR). On January 23, 1947, the Committee Coordinating had approved the recommendation of the European Division to terminate CESE-USSR and to reestablish CUSSR.

In 1946, the CUSSR Representatives were: Robert G. Hooker, Jr. (Chairman), John N. Hazard (Executive Secretary), William A. Brown, Jr. (Secretary), Hubert H. Havlik, Alexander Gerschenkron; John Morrison, Leonard Unger (David Harris replaced him), Howard J. Hilton J. Jr., and Walter Radius.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Committee to Aid Foreign Governments (AFG) was formed, at the direction of Acting Secretary of State Dean Acheson, to formulate the Department of State's position on an ad hoc committee of SWNCC established March 4, 1947, to study the problems of possible requests made to the U.S. by foreign governments for substantial economic, financial, or technical assistance, or for military equipment. The AFG's purpose was to identify countries with urgent need for major assistance, as in the case of Greece and Turkey, not just for long-range security. The AFG was to have a global view, and not confine itself to countries where the British were withdrawing, or countries already receiving assistance. Other considerations were if there was a threat to U.S. security, or a reasonable chance for such aid to be effective, and not to over-extend U.S. financial commitments.

The Inter-American Economic Affairs Committee was created on February 16, 1945 as an interdepartmental subcommittee of the Executive Committee on Economic Foreign Policy. The major function of this subcommittee was to provide long-range plans for the economic development of Latin America. The Committed prepared for the consideration for the Executive Committee recommendations on instructions and advice to the U.S.. representatives on Inter-American economic agencies; the position of the U.S. regarding economic subjects on the agenda of inter-American economic cooperation and participation of the U.S. therein; economic policies and programs of the U.S. as these relate to the American Republics and to their implementation and execution by U.S. Government agencies; and coordination of the activities and research of U.S. Government agencies relating to economic problems in the American Republics exclusive of those sponsored by the Interdepartmental Committee on Cultural and Scientific Cooperation. The Committee on Projects for Inter-American Technical Economic Conference was merged into this Committee on March 23, 1945.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Freedom of Information Committee was established on July 12, 1946 by Departmental Announcement No. 153. This intradepartmental committee correlated the State Department's interest in all matters pertaining to freedom of information that is, dissemination of information to the public from the Department. Among other duties the Committee cleared proposed treaties of friendship and commerce embodying references to freedom of information; performed liaison with the United Nations and the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO); and related matters concerning freedom of information in all international Conferences such as trade and telecommunications conferences. On May 15, 1947, the Freedom of Information Committee was abolished by Departmental Announcement 572 of June 18, 1947.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Intelligence Advisory Board (lAB) was established by Presidential directive of January 22, 1946, to advise the Director of Central Intelligence in carrying out the planning, development, and coordination of all Federal foreign intelligence activities through the Central Intelligence Group (CIG). The Board consisted of four permanent voting members: the Special Assistant to the Secretary of State in Charge of Research and Intelligence; the Assistant Chief of Staff  G-2 of the War Department General Staff (WDGS); the Chief of Naval Intelligence; and the Assistant Chief of Air Staff Intelligence. The Director of Central Intelligence served as a non-voting member and Chairman of the Board. Chiefs of other Intelligence agencies having functions relating to national security were invited to participate in discussion of matters concerning their agencies. As part of its major functions the Board was authorized to concur in recommendations of CIG to the National Intelligence Authority (NIA), and its members were responsible for ensuring the implementation of approved recommendations within their respective departments.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Interdepartmental Committee on Industrial Security (CIS) was established  April 7, 1948 by the State-Army-Navy-Air Force Coordinating Committee (SANACC), SANACC 386/2. Representatives of the following agencies served as permanent members of  the Department of State, the Department of the Army, the Department of the Navy, the Department of the Air Force, the Department of Justice, the Department of Commerce, the Department of the Interior, and the Atomic Energy Commission. creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Working Group on the Framework of Wartime Economic Cooperation (ECWG) was formed on July 31, 1950, on the recommendation of the Committee on Line Economic Warfare Planning,. The ECWG was to coordinate the work of various offices and advise the Secretary of State in the field of economic cooperation in time of war, and to recommend the creation of such international machinery as was necessary to facilitate such economic operation. The Committee worked under the following assumptions: that a national emergency would occur in the near future; that a war would be global rather than limited in nature; and that it was necessary to make maximum use of available international organization and machinery. Made at the request of the National Security Resources Board (NSRB), this study was given high priority because of the Korean War. The mission of the ECWG was completed with the submission of its final report to the NSRB at the end of December 1950.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: Department of State Departmental Order number 1320 dated and effective April 26, 1945, changed the name of the Joint Secretariat of the Executive Staff Committee, established by Departmental Order number 1301 of December 20, 1944, to the Central Secretariat of the Executive Staff Committees. The purpose of the Central Secretariat was to facilitate the work of the responsible officers of the Department in formulating, coordinating, and carrying out major policy decisions. It was not the function of the Secretariat itself to formulate or to implement policy. The Central Secretariat served the Secretary’s Staff Committee and the Coordinating Committee. It provided a channel through which policy matters originating in the offices, divisions, and committees of the Department could be brought to the Executive Staff Committees for consideration. It also assisted in communicating the decisions of the Committees to the responsible officers and prepared periodic reports to the committees in regard to the actions taken on these decisions. The Central Secretariat was also responsible for assisting Department of State representatives on the principal interdepartmental committees in obtaining appropriate Departmental clearance on the important policy matters before final actions were taken. When the Secretary desired, the Central Secretariat was the channel through which recommendations were made by interdepartmental committees to the Secretary of State were brought before the Executive Staff Committees.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Executive Council on Economic Foreign Policy (ECEFP) established the Subcommittee on Foreign Travel (CFT) on October 26, 1945. Its mission was to encourage the dissemination of tourist trade information, produce the cost of passage and accommodations, develop facilities, simplify-formalities, establish exchange programs, and promote international action regarding tourist trade. Chaired by the State Department representative, CFT had members from the Civil Aeronautics Board, the Maritime Commission and the Export-Import Bank. On August 23, 1946, it was reconstituted with less emphasis on operational matters. Its new purpose was examine the purpose of foreign travel, determine the types that should encouraged, the areas to be promoted, the measures to encourage such travel, and feasible the national and international actions. Members from the Department of Commerce, the Department of Treasury, the Department of Justice, the Department of the Interior, and the Department of Agriculture were added. The CFT was reconstituted as an independent committee called the Interdepartmental Committee on Foreign Travel (CFT) on March 7, 1952, after the ECEFP was terminated.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Departmental Dollar Gap Working Group (DDG) was established on March 2, 1950, to consider and prepare the State Department position on the overall question of adjusting the U.S. balance of payments, the DDG was to have assisted State participants in Interdepartmental machinery expected to have been set up by Special Presidential Advisor Gordon Gray to work on his "dollar gap" report to the President. Gray, a former Secretary of the Army, instead of setting up such machinery, requested studies to be prepared by appropriate Executive Agencies. Sending State's studies directly to Gray proved unsatisfactory, and in July 1950 the dormant DDG became the clearance organ for the 15 bodies assigned to State. It also commented on a number of studies from other agencies, and reviewed the draft versions of Gray's "Report to the President on Foreign Economic Policies." With the publication of that report, the DDG had fulfilled its mission and was dissolved December 15, 1950.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The State-Army Committee on Transfer  (SACOT) was established on January 26, 1948, pursuant to letter, dated January 21, 1948, from Secretary of State to Secretary of the Army. It met once, on January 26, 1948, to consider and agree upon plans and arrangements for the transfer of responsibility for administration of non-military aspects of administration of the U.S. Zone of Germany from military to civilian hands. The Committee established working groups which formulated detailed plans for said transfer in February and March 1948. It was made up of representatives from the Department of State and the Department of the Army, including from the Department of State: Charles E. Saltzmann, Chairman; and John L. Kuhn, Secretary; and from the Department of the Army: Major General Daniel Noce. Other members from the Departments of State and Army, were consulted as required for particular problems.

In May 1938, the Committee of Executive Departments and Independent Agencies to Consider the Question of Cooperation with the American Republics was established by the President with responsibility for administering scientific and cultural exchanges with Latin America.  It's name shortened by October 1938 to the Committee on Cooperation with the American Republics, and by November 1938 changed to the Interdepartmental Committee on Cooperation with the American Republics. It was under the immediate direction of the Under Secretary of State as chairman and with a secretariat composed of personnel of the Division of American Republics. The operations were implemented by several acts of Congress since then. This Committee had its own funds by direct appropriation from Congress to the Department of State.

On December 20, 1944, it was renamed the Interdepartmental Committee on Scientific and Cultural Cooperation, corresponding to an enlargement of its functions, and the Assistant Secretary for Public and Cultural Relations became its chairman.  The functions of its secretariat, which had been reassigned several times, were at that time assigned to the Division of Cultural Cooperation of the Office of Public Affairs. During the World War II, the programs formulated by the Committee continued to be primarily long-range in nature rather than temporary instruments of national defense. The Committee was to undertake a permanent, cooperative program for the development of social, economic, cultural and scientific relations with other countries.; and to correlate projects of the departments and agencies of this Government in the economic, scientific and cultural fields designed to increase international understanding and further mutually beneficial cooperative undertakings between nations. It also was assigned responsibility for coordinating training programs mandated by the Philippine Rehabilitation Act, 1946. 

In accordance with the terms of Executive Order 10159, the Interdepartmental Committee on Scientific and Cultural Cooperation and the Advisory Committee on Technical Assistance were abolished effective on the date of the first meeting of the Interdepartmental Advisory Council on Technical Cooperation (TEC) in 1950.

It included representatives of 13 agencies, a number that increased to 20 during the war.  By 1945, 24 agencies and bureaus were represented on this Committee: Department of State: William Benton (Chairman), Ferdinand, Kuhn, Jr. (Vice Chairman), and Raymund L Zwemer (Executive Director); Bureau of the Budget: S. McKee Rosen; Civil Aeronautics Administration: A.S. Koch; Civil Aeronautics Board: Oswald Ryan; Department of Agriculture: Ross E. Moore; Department of Commerce: George Wythe; Department of the Interior: Michael W. Straus; Department of Justice: Herbert Wechsler; Department of Labor: Katharine L. Lenroot; Federal Communications Commission: : Marion H Woodward Federal Security Agency; Worfter Doul Mitchell; Federal Works Agency: E.W. James; Library of Congress: Lewis Hanke; National Archives: Roscoe R. Hill; National Housing Agency: Jacob Crane; Navy Department: Commodore Ellis Reed-Hill; Office of Education: John W. Studebaker; Public Health Service: James A. Doull; Smithsonian Institution: John E Graf; Social Security Board: William L. Mitchell Treasury Department: Herbert E, Gaston, U. S. Tariff Commission: E. B. Brossard; War Shipping Administration: L. P. Nickell. There were also two member ex officio: Pan American Sanitary Bureau: Hugh S. Cumming; and Department of State: Kenneth McIntosh served as the Executive Secretary.

The Interdepartmental Committee on International Social Policy (ISP) was established in January 1947 in accordance with President Harry S. Truman's letter of November 25, 1946. This top-level interdepartmental committee was authorized to examine problems and developments in the social field (labor, social welfare, relief, health, human rights and fundamental freedoms, education, cultural relations, science, information, and related areas) affecting the foreign policy of the United States, to coordinate and formulate recommendations in this area for the consideration of the Secretary of State, the President, and for the guidance of the United States agencies and United States representatives on United Nations committees. Membership on the ISF consisted of representatives at the Assistant Secretary level from the Departments of State. Labor, Agriculture, Commerce, Interior, and the Federal Security Agency. A representative of the Bureau of the Budget participated as a non-voting member. Much of the substantive work of the ISP was performed by six standing committees: Social Welfare Committee; Health Committee; Labor Committee; Non-Self-Governing Territories Committee; Human Rights and Status of Women Committee; and Committee on Cultural Relations, Information, Vocation, and Science. The Interdepartmental Committee on International Social Policy was terminated by Presidential direction in October 1951.

Members of ISP included: Department of State: Willard L. Thorp (Chairman), C. Tyler Wood, (Deputy Chairman), Howard H. Sargeant, Eleanor E. Dennison (Executive Secretary), David Persinger (Assistant Executive Secretary), and Robert W. Shaw (Recording Secretary); Department of Agriculture: Charles F. Brannan and Ross Moore (Alternate); Bureau of the Budget (non-voting) Alvin Roseman and John E. Fobes (Alternate); Department of Commerce: Thomas C. Blaisdell, Jr. and J.C. Miller (Alternate); Federal Security Agency: Ellen S. Woodward and Seville Simons (Alternate); Department of the Interior: C. Girard Davidson and Daniel L. Goldy (Alternate); and Department of Labor: Thacher Winslow and Harry Weiss (Alternate).

The Petroleum Facilities Coordinating Committee (PFCC) was established in August 1945 in order to implement the foreign policy objectives and recommendations set forth in the Department of State's Coordinating Committee Document 52d "Policy with Respect to Fixed Installations Constructed Abroad by the United States Government", in so far as it relates to petroleum facilities. It also advised interested agencies with respect to declaring surplus and disposing of facilities.  Its functions included making lists of petroleum facilities, noting those which could be disposed of, consolidating views of all interested agencies, recommending agreements, be negotiated with foreign governments, and formulating recommendations on specific cases. Tank farms, pipelines, docking facilities, tankers, and even oil drum fabrication plants were disposed of as surplus by the PFCC. The PFCC was terminated May 12, 1947, when its mission was accomplished.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Departmental Committee on Grants to China (CGC) was established on July 7, 1948 to advise the Director of the Office of the Far East in carrying out the Section 404(b) of the China Aid Act of 1948, which gave China grants of 125 million dollars in aid. The Foreign Service Policy Committee (FSPC) was established in the Office of the Assistant Secretary of State for Administration on October 9, 1946 by Departmental Announcement 272. The FSPC was to coordinate and correlate the position of the Department of State on all matters of a substantive or administrative nature affecting the Foreign Service. The Director General of the Foreign Service usually served as Chairman of this five-member intradepartmental committee. The FSPC was responsible for determination of all matters coming before the Board of the Foreign Service; (BFS) the FSPC chairman recommended such matters for consideration of the BFS on the basis of priorities established by the FSPC. Through the FSPC the Department of State was to formulate a unified view to be presented to the interdepartmental BFS. On July 17, 1951, the Department of State announced the termination of the Foreign Service Policy Committee.

Members as of 1947 included: Christian M. Ravndal (Chairman), F.P. Kelly (Executive Secretary), G. Curtiss Murrell (Secretary), Stanley T. Orear, James K. Penfield, Arthur G. Stevens, and Robert E. Ward.

The Travel Policy Committee (TLC) was established by Departmental Regulation No. 183.13 of February 3, 1947. This intradepartmental committee was authorized to advise the Department of State's representatives on the Executive Committee for Economic Foreign Policy (ECEFP) and other interdepartmental and international committees on United States policy pertaining to travel of American citizens abroad and foreign citizens in the United States. The Committee also was authorized to develop such policy and review decisions thereon. The TLC consisted of a representative from each of the following State Department offices: Assistant Secretary for Administration; Under Secretary for Geographic Areas; Legal Adviser; Assistant Secretary for Public Affairs; Assistant Secretary for Economic Affairs; and the Office of Controls. Other State Department officials were invited to serve as consultants to the Committee on matters relating to their fields.

TLC members as of 1947 included: Samuel D. Boykin (Chairman), John W. Sipes (Secretary), Oliver J. Caldwell, George R. Canty, C. Burke Elbrick, Gerald Mokma, George Owen, Robert O. Swain. Technical Advisers: Robert C. Alexander, L. Mason Drury, George S. Knight, William C. McCahon, and John J. Scanlan.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Advisory Committee on Intelligence (ACI) was established May 1, 1946 by Departmental Order 183.5. This intradepartmental body was authorized to advise the Special Assistant to the Secretary of State for Research and Intelligence on matters relating to establishment and coordination of Department intelligence objectives and policies, formulation and prosecution of an integrated program for intelligence research, implementation of Departmental policy with respect to the National Intelligence Authority (NIA), and participation by the Department in centralized operations or projects which the Director of the NIA proposed. The Committee also considered appeals referred to it by its standing Subcommittee on Intelligence Programs and Priorities (SPP). On June 18, 1948, Departmental Announcement 65 abolished the ACI.

The Special Assistant to the Secretary for Research and Intelligence served as Chairman of the Committee. Committee members consisted of the Assistant Secretary for European, Far Eastern, Near Eastern, and African Affairs; the Assistant Secretary for American Republic Affairs; and the Assistant Secretary for Administration. On February 6, 1947, ACI changed its membership to include: the Assistant Secretary for Administration;  the Assistant Secretary for Economic Affairs; the Assistant Secretary for Occupied Areas; the Assistant Secretary for Public Affairs; the Director of American Republic Affairs; the Director of European Affairs; the Director of Far Eastern Affairs; the Director of Near Eastern and African Affairs; the Director of Special Political Affairs; the Director of Intelligence Research; and the Director of Intelligence Collection and Dissemination. The Secretary was Ronald M. Ayer. Representatives of any element of the Department were invited to participate in ACI deliberations whenever a matter of concern to such elements was under consideration.

It was the top technical level coordinating mechanism within the Executive Branch for decisions relating to the European Recovery Program, subject to the approval of the Secretary and the Under Secretary. creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Southeast Asia Aid Policy Committee (SEAC) was established on June 6, 1950, by an informal agreement between the Departments of State and Defense and the Economic Cooperation Administration (ECA), to coordinate federal policy for political, military, and economic aid to Southeast Asia, and to insure that high level aid programs were accomplished successfully. Committee members were Dean Rusk, Assistant Secretary of State for Far Eastern Affairs (Deputy Assistant Secretary Livingston T. Merchant often represented Rusk at SEAC meetings); Major General Harry J. Malony, Special Assistant for Southeast Asian Problems, Office of the Secretary of Defense; and R. Allen Griffin, Director of the Far East Program Division of the ECA. SEAC was primarily a policy consultative group with no direct operational responsibility. The committee met roughly twice a month between its first meeting in July 1950 and August 1951, when it became inact1ve. The functions of the SEAC were assumed in the fall of 1951 by the Mutual Assistance Advisory Committee, an interagency policy coordination group responsible for all Mutual Security Pact countries, including Southeast Asia. The SEAC was formally abolished in the spring of 1953.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Interdepartmental Patent Interchange Committee (IPIC) was established in May 1946. Its creation was in response to the signing of the United States Patent Interchange Agreement with Great Britain, March 27, 1946 (60 Stat. 1566, Treaties and Other International Acts Series 1510). This agreement itself was proposed by the American members of the wartime British-United States Joint Patent Interchange Committee. The committee assisted American and British nationals seeking restitution for alleged infringement of patent rights protecting information, inventions, designs, and processes made available to the other government for military use. The committee also facilitated the exchange of data with the British Government and recommended which federal agencies should undertake indemnity negotiations. The period covered by the agreement began in 1942 and terminated on July 1, 1949, for claims filed by American interests. No such time limit was imposed upon British claims enabling the IPIC to investigate such claims, at a rate of one a year, until 1959. The Department of the Army, the Department of the Navy, the Department of the Air Force, and the Department of Justice assigned up to three representatives each to sit on the IPIC. The Department of State member chaired the committee. No sub- or working committees were created. The Committee met up to four times a year until it was terminated by the Secretary of State on October 30, 1959.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Committee on the Recommendations of the West Indian Conference (WI) was formed by the Executive Committee on Economic Foreign Policy (ECEFP) on September 15, 1944, to examine the economic recommendations made by the West Indian Conference of March 21-30, 1944, which had been held in Barbados under the auspices of the Anglo-American Caribbean Commission (AACC). The Committee was to give special consideration to diversification of the economy of the West Indies and increasing employment, with emphasis on interisland trade and transportation. 

On June 1, 1945, the ECEFP reconstituted this committee, renamed it the West Indian Committee, (WIC) and gave it the mission of studying the Caribbean sugar problem and other economic and social problems of the area, as well as preparing suggestions for the agenda of the next West Indian Conference. Membership of the WIC included members from Commerce. Labor, Treasury, Interior, Foreign Economic Administration, the Tariff Commission and Agriculture. The Department of State provided the Chairman, including Otis E. Mulliken and Thomas Holland. Marten Estey served as the Secretary from the Department of State. The ECEFP dissolved the WIC on January 22, 1947, because the establishment of a Subcommittee of Non-Self-Governing Territories of the Committee on International Social Policy rendered it superfluous.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: On September 23, 1946 by Departmental Announcement 209, Transmittal Letter 32 of September 27, 1946, the Committee Coordinating Board (CCB) was established to provide coordination and general administrative guidance to all Departmental committees subordinate to the Secretary’s Staff Committee. The Coordinating Board attempted to identify and evaluate the Committee system established by the Department of State. The CCB considered proposed establishment of committees, authorities, terms of reference, level of membership, secretariat requirements, proposed changes in existing committees, and terminations.  It heard recommendations for and established committees, coordinated their activities, and evaluated their composition and operations. It furnished advice on operational efficiency, classified committees as to kind; area, functional, policy, operating or informational, and recommended chairman and members from the appropriate divisions. The CCB consisted of four members: one form the Office of the Under Secretary of State, one from the Office of the Under Secretary of State for Economic Affairs, one from the Office of the Assistant Secretary for Administration as Chairman, and the Executive Secretary of the Central Secretariat of the Secretary’s Staff Committee. On. March 23, 1948, Departmental Announcement 1038, the Committee Coordinating Board was terminated by agreement of the interested areas of the Department.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: Established on August 3, 1949 by Departmental Announcement 115, the Policy Service Committee was chaired by the Director of the Executive Secretariat. It established media for interchange of policy information and action responsibility among the various segments of the Department dissemination of policy decisions throughout the Department and its missions, including top policy decisions.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Passenger Shipping Committee (PSC) was established May 1, 1946, by Departmental Regulation No. 183.7. This intradepartmental committee was authorized to consider and coordinate the interests of the Department of State in the procurement and allocation of passenger space on ocean transportation facilities, both official and commercial. Within the Department the PSC established and enforced relative priorities among categories of passengers  who might be accommodated in shipping space obtained by the Department such as use of space for the repatriation of American citizens and foreign nationals to their respective homelands. The Committee consisted of permanent members representing the geographic offices, the administrative offices, and the economic office; other Department officials joined as consultants when appropriate. Members included: A.E. Clattenburg (Chairman), Henry L. Deimel, and Melvin L. Manfull (Secretary). PSC was terminated on July 26, 1949 by Departmental Announcement. 107.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Combined Policy Committee on French Empire Economic Affairs (FEC) worked to combine U.S. and British policy toward French  empire economic affairs, especially in relation to agricultural production of North Africa and military aid to the French forces outside Europe. The FEC’s American members were drawn from the U.S. Policy Committee for French Empire Economic Affairs (US-FEC). It British members included representatives of the British Shipping Mission, the British Food Mission and the British Military Mission. The FEC was the successor to the Combined Committee on North Africa (CCNA) and worked closely with the North Africa Joint Economic Mission (NAJEM) and the French West Africa Economic Mission (FWAJEM) until their dissolution on December 31, 1944. Shortly thereafter, in January 1945, the FEC was superseded by the French Area Committee, which consolidated all economic matters in the French Empire and Metropolitan France.

The Combined French Area Committee was established in Washington to provide a forum for the exchange of views on problems arising in France and the French colonial empire. The Committee was composed of Canadian, British, and American members and discussed combined military, supply, shipping, or financial responsibilities and which were outside the scope of the Combined Chiefs of Staff. The Committee reported as a subcommittee to the Combined Liberated Areas Committee (CLAC). 

The U.S. side of the Combined French Area Committee was known as the French Area Committee and was composed of members of the Departments of State, Agriculture, Commerce, and Treasury, in addition to the War Shipping Administration.

The Information Service Committee was established on February 21, 1944, by Departmental Order 1229 under the chairmanship of the director of the Office of the Foreign Service Administration (later Office of the Foreign Service), for the purpose of strengthening the flow of information to the Foreign Service establishments, “including confidential information about developments of crucial interest in other parts of the world.” The primary purpose of the Committee was to make more efficient dissemination of information to the field vitally needed by American Missions in order to facilitate their conduct of international relations, and to assist field missions in improving the quality of information reported, including events and general trends of local opinion in those countries. The Committee studied, for possible adoption, new techniques in gathering, evaluating, and disseminating intelligence and other information within the Department, and coordinated meetings of the Departmental information Liaison Officers. Its membership included the Special Assistant for Press Relations and informational liaison officers appointed by the Office of Public Affairs and the geographic offices. Officials were designated in the Offices of the Secretary and the Under Secretary to communicate to the committee information not available through other channels, and at various times other offices and divisions were instructed to cooperate with the Committee in making comprehensive background and policy information available to reporting officers in the field. On March 22, 1946, by Transmittal Letter 16 of April 3, 1946, the name of the committee was changed to Policy Information Committee.

Some of the members included: R. Borden Reams (Chairman),  Donald D. Edgar (Vice Chairman), Robert G. Barnes, Ethel G. Christenson, H, Kingston Fleming, Selam Freedman, Virginia M Haaga, Virginia F. Hartley, Barbara F. Hauer, Florence Kirlin, Robert T. Miller, Rowena B. Rommel, Paul P Stewart, and Nancy W. Davis (Secretary).

The Interagency Committee on Food and Agriculture Organization was established by the President, in a letter dated March 30, 1946, to the Secretary of Agriculture. The Committee was to ensure that our Government aided to the fullest extent the proper functioning of the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) of the United Nations (UN). In particular, the Committee assisted in formulating the position which this Government should take in the various fields of activity falling within the general purposes and functions of the FAO. This Committee coordinated US policy toward the UN Food and Agriculture Organization, and prepared position statements for the US delegation to FAO meetings. 

The Committee was chaired by the Department of Agriculture representative, until Secretary of Agriculture Memorandum No. 1365, revised, of May 29, 1969, designated the Assistant Secretary of Agriculture for International Affairs and Commodity Programs to act for the Secretary of Agriculture as the chairman of the U.S.-FAO Interagency Committee. The committee consisted of representatives of U.S. Government agencies which have an interest in the work of FAO, included the Department of Agriculture, the Department of Commerce, the Department of Defense, the Department of Health and Human Services, the Department of Labor, the Department of State, the Department of the Treasury, the bureau of the Budget, the Public Health Service, the Office of Management and Budget, the Chamber of Commerce, and farmers and manufacturers groups. 

Some of the first members of the Committee were: Department of Agriculture: N.E. Dodd (Chairman), L.A. Wheeler (Vice Chairman), Duncan Wall (Secretary), Jesse B. Gilmer, F. Marion Rhodes (Alternate), W.V. Lambert, W.A. Minor, Lyle S. Watts, and O. V. Wells; Department of Commerce: Thomas C. Blaisdell, and Carl Gibboney (Alternate); Department of Interior: A.I. Anderson, and E.D. Eaton (Alternate); Department of Labor: Faith M. William and Edward C. Hollander (Alternate); Department of State: Edward G. Cale, Francis A. Linville (Alternate), Otis E. Mulliken, and Ursula Duffus, (Alternate); Department of the Treasury: George Haas; Bureau of the Budget: Arthur Smithies, Roger Nelson (Alternate) and D.W. Oberdorfer (Alternate); Federal Security Agency: Dr. Thomas Parran, and Dr. James A. Doull (Alternate).

The Director of USDA's International Organizations Staff (IOS), established July 11, 1963 (FSM 1548), under the direction of the Assistant Secretary for International Affairs and Commodity Programs, is designated as vice-chairman. The International Organizations Staff provides liaison and coordinating services essential in maintaining relationships with FAO and with the Department of State and other Departments of the Government to facilitate effective U.S. participation in FAO.  This Staff takes the lead in preparing for FAO meetings, provides the Secretariat of the U.S.-FAO Interagency Committee, distributes FAO publications and documents, and maintains contact with citizen advisory groups interested in the work of FAO. The Forest Service as a unit in the Department of Agriculture shares the Secretary's responsibility.  The Chief is the Forest Service representative on the FAO Interagency Committee and the Director, Division of International Forestry, is his alternate) http://www.fs.fed.us/dirindexhome/fsm/1500/1550.txt

The Departmental Committee on International Social Policy (SIP) was established December 16, 1946, by Departmental Announcement No. 280. The Committee was responsible for the preparation of foreign policy recommendations in the areas of health, cultural relations, labor, social welfare, education, science, information, and human rights on problems under consideration by the Interdepartmental Committee on International Social Policy (ISP), and other problems considered appropriate by consent of the SIP. The Committee was abolished on October 23, 1947 by Departmental Announcement 829.

The Committee was composed of representatives from the Office of the Assistant Secretary for Public and Cultural Relations, the Office of International Trade Policy, the Office of Special Political Affairs, the Office of American Republics, the Office of European Affairs, the Office of Far Eastern Affairs, and the Office of Near Eastern and African Affairs. The Chairman invited representatives of other offices when matters of special interest to such offices were being considered by the Committee.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The U.S. Working Group, Joint Petroleum Discussions was an outgrowth of tripartite financial talks which showed the importance of petroleum in the dollar-sterling problem, these talks were held in Washington September 15-November 6, 1949, primarily between the United States and the United Kingdom. Canada was included as an observer. The discussions were concerned with alleviating the dollar drain on the British caused by petroleum transactions, by studying the balance of payments, projected British oil expansion, and British discrimination against U.S. companies. The U.S. Working Group (JPD), headed by Assistant Secretary George W. Perkins, had members from the Department of  State, the Department of the Interior, the Department of the Treasury, the Department of Commerce, the Department of Defense, the National Security Resources Board, and the Economic Cooperation Administration. They formulated the U.S. position during these discussions recommending an agreement with the British to reduce the dollar drain resulting from U.S. oil company operations in the Sterling area.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Subcommittee on Human Rights and Status of Women was established in January 1947 by the Interdepartmental Committee on International Social Policy (ISP), and authorized to examine problems and developments in the general field of human rights and the status of women which involved the foreign policy of the United States, and to formulate recommendations in this regard for consideration of the ISP. The Subcommittee specifically was responsible for consideration and formulation of recommendations on such matters as concerned the Economic and Social Council on Human Rights and its Subcommissions on the Prevention of  Discrimination and the Protection of Minorities; cooperation with the ISP Subcommittee on Cultural Relations, Information, Education and Science on matters relating to freedom of information; draft bills of human rights and procedures for effective implementation of such rights; and problems and developments relating to the proper recognition and status of women. The Subcommittee consisted of representatives from the Federal Security Agency, the Department of State, the Department of  Justice, the Department of Labor, and the Department of the Interior. Agencies of the United States Government not represented on the Subcommittee were invited to attend meetings and given full voting privileges when subjects of substantial interest to them were considered by the Subcommittee. John M. Cates, Jr. was the Chairman and James Simsarian was the Vice Chairman and Technical Assistant.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The U.S. Policy Committee for French Empire Economic Affairs (US-FEC) was established to formulate U.S. policy prior to meeting with the British in the Combined Policy Committee for French Empire Economic Affairs (FEC). Members of the U.S. committee consisted of representatives of the Department of State, the Department of the Treasury, the War Department, the Foreign Economic Administration, the War Production Board, and the War Shipping Administration. North African agricultural production was the major focus of the committee. It was terminated with the consolidation of all economic matters concerning French Areas, including Metropolitan France, under the French Area Committee at the beginning of 1945. The FEC worked closely with the North Africa Joint Economic Mission (NAJEM) and the French West Africa Economic Mission (FWAJEM) until their dissolution on December 31, 1944.

The U.S. Lend-Lease and Surplus Settlement Committee was established on November 16, 1945 by the Assistant Secretary of State for Economic Affairs. The Committee recommend principles on which the U.S. sought to conclude lend-lease settlements and agreements, including pipeline and inventory disposal agreements, with lend-lease countries. It was to integrate and coordinate the activities of U.S. Government agencies in Lend-Lease settlements and agreements with foreign governments The Committee acted as the primary U.S. Committee with the aid of such subcommittees was necessary in negotiating lend-lease settlements and agreements with foreign governments. It reported on the progress of lend-lease settlement and agreement negotiations and recommended specific settlements and agreements for approval by the U.S. Government. This Committee provided the personnel for the U.S. Working Groups and the U.S. members of the Combined Working Groups on Lend-Lease and Property Settlement.

Members of the Committee included Department of State: Thomas McCabe (Chairman), G.F. Lutheringer (Vice-Chairman), Frank W. Fetter, Chester Lane, Hayden G. Raynor, Benno Schmidt, and Hubert F. Havlik (Principle Secretary); Office of War Mobilization and Reconversion: Harold Stein; and Department of the Treasury: Harold Glasser.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Subcommittee on Labor, established in January 1947 by the Interdepartmental Committee on International Social Policy (ISP), was authorized to examine problems and developments emanating from United States participation in the International Labor Organization (ILO), and to formulate recommendations in this regard for consideration of the ISP. The Subcommittee specifically dealt with such matters affecting United States foreign policy as income security, standards of living, promotion of adequate housing, and the level of availability and productiveness of employment; labor standards and policies, such as regulation of employment working conditions, vocational training, child labor, economic problems of women, labor migration, collective bargaining, and labor-management relations; and international cooperation in improving the administration of relevant laws and services. The Subcommittee consisted of representatives from the Department of Labor, State, Agriculture, Commerce, and from the Federal Security Agency. Agencies of the United States Government not represented on the Subcommittee were invited to attend meetings and given full voting privileges when subjects of substantial interest to them were considered by the Subcommittee.

Members included: Department of Labor: Thacher Winslow (Chairman) and Harry Weiss (Alternate); Department of Agriculture: Louis J Ducoff and Dr. Margaret J. Hagood (Alternate); Department of Commerce: Ralph Hetzel and Edward J. Fitzgerald (Alternate); Federal Security Agency: Wilbur J. Cohen and Miss Maurine Mulliner (Alternate); National Housing Agency: Jacob Crane; Department of State: Daniel M. Horowitz, Cleon O. Swayzee (Alternate), and Bernard Wiesman (Acting Executive Secretary)

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Subcommittee on Non-Self-Governing Territories of the Interdepartmental Committee on International Social Policy (ISP) was established in January 1947 by the ISP, and authorized to examine problems and developments of social and economic character relating to the field of non-self-governing territories which concerned the foreign policy of the United States, and to formulate recommendations in this regard for consideration of the ISP and the Executive Committee on Economic Foreign Policy (ECEFP). Specifically, the Subcommittee was responsible for recommending policy on matters of interdepartmental concern relating to the United Nations Trusteeship system, national advisory commissions for non-self-governing territories, and specialized agencies concerned with social and economic policy in such territories. The Subcommittee also formulated recommendations on the application to non-self-governing territories of any general proposals originating in subcommittees or other sources. The Subcommittee consisted of representatives from the Department of State, the Department of the Navy, the Department of the Interior, the Department of Agriculture, the Department of Labor, the Department of Commerce, and the Federal Security Agency. United States Government agencies not represented on the Subcommittee were invited to attend meetings and given full voting privileges when subjects of substantial interest to them were considered by the Subcommittee.

Members of the Subcommittee included: Department of State: Benjamin Gerig (Chairman), James F. Green (Alternate), and Emil Sady (Secretary); Department of Agriculture: Ross E. Moore and O.S. Aamodt (Alternate); Department of Commerce: Herbert W. Parisius and Carlton L. Wood (Alternate); Federal Security Agency: Mrs. Savilla M. Simons; Department of the Interior: Edwin G. Arnold and Eric Beecroft (Alternate); Department of Labor: Miss Faith M. Williams and Miss Jean Flexner (Alternate); and Department of the Navy: Captain W. F. Jennings.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The United Nations Economic Subcommittee the short name given the Subcommittee on General Economic Policy Questions Arising in International Economic Organizations, which was created by the Executive Committee on Economic Foreign Policy (ECEFP) on May 2, 1947. Its mission was to examine economic policy questions in connection with the work of the United Nations and other international organizations in the economic field. Areas of special interest of the UNEC were to be employment and economic stability, and economic development and reconstruction. In 1949, the symbol for this committee was changed from UNE to UNEC to avoid confusion with a newly created Department of State office. UNEC members included the Department of Agriculture, the Department of Commerce, the Department of Labor, U.S. Tariff Commission, the Securities and Exchange Commission, the Federal Reserve Board, and the Bureau of Budget. The Department of State representative served as chairman. After the abolition of the ECEFP, the UNEC was reconstituted as an independent committee in July, 1951, called the United Nations Economic Committee.

The Board of the Foreign Service (BFS) established the Staff Board (STB), on October 29, 1946, to serve as an advisory body. Membership of the Staff Board coincided with membership on BFS. STB generally consisted of five State Department members, and one member each from the Department of Commerce, the Department of Labor, and the Department of Agriculture. STB formulated recommendations for BFS relating to all matters within the purview of the Board, and was authorized to request from the member Departments such information as it required in the performance of its duties.

Some of the members were: Department of State: Charles Hulten (Chairman); James K. Penfield, Arthur G. Stevens, F.P. Kelly (Executive Secretary), and G. Curtiss Murrell (Secretary); Department of Agriculture: A.R. Johnson; Department of Commerce: E.M. Braderman; and Department of Labor: P.M. Kaiser.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Interdepartmental Policy Committee for Preparations for an International Safety at Sea Conference was established in September 1944 by a meeting of the various agencies of the United States Government interested in the International Safety of Life at Sea Conference. At the urging of the Special Shipping Committee of the Department of State, the Committee was authorized to consider recommendations for a post war International Safety of Life at Sea Conference to revise and improve international agreements relating to the safety of life at sea, including the 1929 safety Convention. The Committee consisted of representatives of the Department of State, the War Department, the Department of the Navy, the Department of Commerce, the Department of Labor, the Department of the Treasury, the U.S. Coast Guard, the U.S. Maritime Commission, the Federal Communications Commission, and the Civil Aeronautics Administration. Subcommittees consisted of a General Committee, Steering Committee, and several technical subcommittees dealing with specific substantive areas of safety at sea.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The International Working Group on Pact Organization was called into being by the Ambassador's Committee on the Washington Security Talks, to study the nature and organization of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (N.A.T.O.) creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Committee on Administrative Planning for Japan (CAPJ) was an intra- departmental committee established by the Deputy Under Secretary for Administration, Carlisle Humelsine, on April 19, 1951. The primary purpose of the Committee was to make plans for the establishment of a U.S. embassy in Japan upon termination of the military occupation with the signing of the Japanese Peace Treaty. This entailed the transfer of certain functions from the Department of the Army to the Department of State as well as the re-establishment of a free-standing Department of State presence in that country. CAPJ's objectives were primarily administrative in nature and did not concern itself with the problems of the peace treaty and related agreements. To facilitate work, the committee established working groups with the following responsibilities: personnel, budget and fiscal matters, organization, operating facilities, special programs, political and legal matters, the economic program and reporting, buildings, public affairs, and  research and intelligence.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Interdepartmental Committee on Prisoners of War (POWC) was established on October 29, 1945, by Department of State Staff Committee paper SC-167A. The POWC was activated on August 19, 1947. This international committee was authorized to study and coordinate the views of interested agencies regarding revision of international agreements relating to prisoners of war and the preparation of a new convention regarding the treatment of civilians of war. The POWC incorporated these views in draft conventions, which represented the position of the United States Government at international conference dealing with the above subjects. The POWC consisted of representatives from the Department of State, the Department of the Army, the Department of the Navy, the Department of the Air Force, the Department of Justice, the Post Office, the Department of the Treasury, and the American Red Cross.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Third Latin American Conference took place at Fort Amador, Canal Zone, January 21-29, 1949, and was sponsored by the United States Air Force under the auspices of the Caribbean Air Command. Conference objectives were to effect close personal liaison between key departmental intelligence officials in Washington and their senior Western Hemisphere field representative; improve the administration, organization, and intelligence gathering efficiency of such field offices; and exchange views regarding important aspects of the current world intelligence picture. Participants in the conference included key intelligence officials from Washington representing the Department of the Army, the Department of the Navy, and the Department of the Air Force; senior military attaches from Western Hemisphere countries; and representatives from the Caribbean Air Command and the United States Embassy, Panama.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The U.S. members of the Joint Editorial Board were William Z. Slany, General Editor of the Foreign Relations of the United States a Series (to October 1977); David F. Trask, the Historian, Office of the Historian, Department of State (from October 1977); Milton 0. Gustafson, Chief of the Diplomatic Branch, National Archives; and S. Frederick Starr, Secretary, Kennan Institute for Advanced Russian Studies, Woodrow Wilson International Center for Scholars. 

The Joint Editorial Board met five times to decide policy and to plan the editorial work. At its first session in Washington in December 1976 the board approved a general prospectus of the collection, the principles and methods to guide its preparation, and the composition of reference materials. At the second meeting in Moscow in June 1977, the board prepared a preliminary model of the collection. During the third session in Washington in February-March 1975, the board adopted an expanded version of the model. 

At the fourth meeting in Moscow in February 1979, it approved the documents and footnotes to be included in the first half of the publication and the illustrations. At the fifth meeting in Washington in June 1979, the Joint Editorial Board approved the documents to be printed in the second half of the collection, their footnotes, the preface, the introduction, the table of contents and various reference aids, and also discussed translations of the documents.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Sixth European Attache Conference took place in Frankfurt, Germany, June 6-14, 1951, and was sponsored by the Department of the Army under auspices of the Commander in Chief, European Command. General conference objectives were to effect close personal liaison between key military departmental intelligence officials in Washington and their senior field representatives in Europe, Africa, and the Near and Middle East; and to improve the administration, organization, and intelligence gathering efficiency of such field offices. Like its immediate predecessor, this conference dealt with a central theme: How can the United States information coverage of critical areas, items, and trends be revitalized and improved? Participants in the conference included key intelligence officials from Washington representing the Department of State, the Department of the Army, the Department of the Navy, the Department of the Air Force, the Central Intelligence Agency, Federal Bureau of Investigation, and Joint Intelligence Group of the Office of the Joint Chiefs of Staff; representatives of the European Command; and senior Army, Naval and Air Attaches from each of the countries of Europe, Africa, and the Near and Middle East.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Ambassadors' Committee on Washington Security Talks was an informal group comprised of the British, French, Dutch, Belgium, and Canadian Ambassadors, with two or three aids each, and Under Secretary Robert Lovett, with four State Department colleagues. 

The Committee first met on July 6, 1948, to explore alternative approaches to best integrate west European political, military, and economical resources into a union dedicated to the military security of that region. The question of supports that the United States might lend to such a pact was introduced at the first meeting and continued to be raised throughout the committee's tenure. 

The committee met twenty times in three rounds of talks. Its deliberations produced the "Washington Paper" (an outline for the N.A.T.O. pact), and the completed draft of the North Atlantic Treaty. The Ambassador's Committee joined in the final meeting the Day the North Atlantic was signed in Washington, April 14, 1949. Many of the committee's members would return to participate in the first session of the N.A.T.O. Council, held in Washington during the following September, but the Committee was not revived.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The International Working Group on the Washington Security Talks was formed in July 1949 to prepare position papers on three general issued arising from the first round of Ambassador's Committee on the Washington Security Talks meetings; (1) general security requirements for the North Atlantic region, (2) geographical limits of the pact, and (3) individual, national security requirements. The papers were prepared by sixteen deputy delegates to the Washington talks under the direction of Counselor Charles Bohlen. The working group produced an outline for the North Atlantic pact that the Ambassador's Committee submitted to their respective governments for the "Washington Paper." The working group met fifteen times before it was abolished along with the Ambassador's Committee in April 1949.

The Interdepartmental Committee for the Resumption of Communications for Liberated and Occupied Areas (RCLA) was established on February 6, 1945, and was authorized to consider problems relating to the reopening of communications with liberated and occupied areas in Europe and the Far East after the Second World War. The Committee consisted of representatives for the Department of State, the War Department, the Post Office Department, the Department of the Treasury, and the Federal Communications Commission. Representatives of other United States agencies (such as the Office of Censorship) and other governments (such as the United Kingdom) were invited to participate in meetings of the Committee when subjects substantial interest to them were considered by the Committee.

Some of the members were: Department of Sate: Francis Cold deWolf (Chairman), O. Fletcher, and Florance A. Trail (Secretary); Federal Communications Commission: John A. Russ; Post Office Department: John J. Gillen, George R. Hartman; and E.J. Mahoney; Treasury Department: Belle Maier, Paul A. parker, and Hamlin Robinson; and War Department: Lieutenant R.S. Spangler and Major J.M. Carson.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: In December 1949 the Foreign Military Assistance Coordinating Committee established the Latin American Working Group consisting of representatives from the Department of State and the Department of Defense to develop necessary operating policy criteria and to formulate a program for military aid to Latin America. This working group began to function in February 1950 and more or less finished its tasks by November of the same year, although some of its activities were still underway in early 1951. Requests from the Latin American countries for various forms of military, naval, and air force assistance were referred to this Latin American Working Group, which prepared a report and a recommendation on each request for submission to the Foreign Military Assistance Coordinating Committee.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Technical Committee on Petroleum (TPC), a technical subcommittee of the Committee on International Commodity Problems (CPC), was formed on April 24, 1946, to investigate certain technical problems to determine the relationship of international petroleum resources to U.S. economic and military needs, and draft a statement on U.S. petroleum policy for approval by the CPC and Executive Committee on Economic Foreign Policy (ECEFP). In carrying out these functions the TPC moved into labor policy questions, and became a forum for interdepartmental consultation on these problems. Because of the importance of petroleum to US foreign policy, the TPC was made a full subcommittee of the ECEFP on April 9, 1948, renamed it the International Petroleum Policy Committee (PPC).  It was charged with evaluating petroleum problems and developments affecting U.S. foreign policy, and with coordinating action on the operating panel. It consisted of representatives from the Department of Commerce, the Department of the Interior, the National Military Establishment, the Tariff Commission, and the National Security Resources Board, and was chaired by the Department of State member. 

With the abolishment of the ECEFP, the PPC was reconstituted as an independent committee on October 2, 1951, by mutual agreement of its member agencies, which now included the Export-Import Bank, the Petroleum Administrator for Defense, and the Materials Security Agency. The work of the PPC included the assignment of petroleum attaches, trade agreements, petroleum reserves in Western Europe, British sterling oil, Latin American oil, and U.S. policy on public loans for foreign petroleum projects.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
On April 3, 1946, the State-War-Navy Coordinating Committee (SWNCC) established a sub-committee for security control known as the Security Advisory Board (SAB). This Board was the successor to the Security Advisory Board of the Office of War Information. When this Board was abolished in November 1945 the Joint Chiefs of Staff recommended the function be continued under SWNCC. The Board had a permanent Secretariat and invited other government agencies to designate security officers to act as liaison with the board. The Department of State representative served as Chairman. 

The board was primarily responsible for advising civilian agencies in the declassification of documents originating in non-military departments; the establishment of top secret control procedures; security clearances of civilian officials; and the conversion of security regulations to civilian agencies for a war-time basis to a peace-time basis. The Board also served as a medium for the exchange of information on security problems offered advice to Federal agencies and departments on all types of security problems.

Some of the members included: Department of State: Hamilton Robinson (Chairman), Frederick B. Lyon (Chairman), Donald L. Nicholson, Finar T. Anderson (Alternate), and Shanette G. Blake (Secretary); Department of the Army Colonel C.C. Blakeney; Department of the Navy: Lieutenant Commander L.L. Lichliter and Lieutenant Commander E.F. Higgins (Alternate); and Department of the Air Force: John S. Arcana.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
As a result of the directives of February 11, 1945 and March 12, 1945, the heads of the Department State, the War Department, the Department of the Navy, the Department of the Treasury, and the Foreign Economic Administrator agreed to set up a committee, composed of representatives of their Departments, to be known as the Information Policy Committee on Germany (IPCOG). It was subsequently agreed that the secretariat of the State-War-Navy Coordinating Committee (SWNCC)would function as the secretariat for this Committee.  The first meeting was held on April 15, 1945 and IPCOG prepared a summary of American policy relating to Germany in the initial post-defeat period. A IPCOG working party prepared a directive to the Commander in Chief of United States Forces of Occupation regarding the military government of Germany, which was approved by IPCOG on April 26 and forward to the Joint Chiefs of Staff for their consideration. On August 2, 1945, the President approved a memorandum from the Secretary of State which terminated the functions of the Informal Policy Committee on Germany and transferred pending matters on the IPCOG agenda to the SWNCC.

The following served as members of this Committee: Department of State: William L. Clayton, Assistant Secretary of State (Chairman); War Department: John J. McCloy, Assistant Secretary of War; Department of the Navy Department: Ralph A. Bard, Under Secretary of the Navy; Department of the Treasury: Henry Morgenthau, Jr., Secretary of the Treasury, Harry D. White, Assistant Secretary of the Treasury, Frank Coe; and Foreign Economic Administration: Leo Crowley, Administrator and H.H. Fowler.
