creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Interim Greece-Turkey Assistance Committee was established on April 7, 1947 by Transmittal Letter 52 of April 11, 1947 in response to President Truman's message to Congress on March 12, 1947 that declared it to be in the national interest to support Greece and Turkey and requested a special appropriation of 400 million dollars for this purpose, together with authority to detail civilian and military personnel and to transfer material to those countries. Pending the establishment of a permanent organization, the Committee served as the principal instrument of coordination for the various offices of the Department concerned with problems  and claims relating to the Greece-Turkey assistance program. Specifically, the committee attempted to identify, analyze, and coordinate policy, operational and organizational plans and recommendations on problems relating to the assistance program for the consideration of the Secretary and Under Secretary. The Committee planed, initiated, and maintained policy supervision over the preliminary operational phases of the program. The Departmental Committee on Aid to Greece and Turkey (CAGT) established on August 5, 1947, superseded the Interim Greece-Turkey Assistance Committee.

The Interim Greece-Turkey Assistance Committee was composed of a representative form each of the following units: Under Secretary of Economic Affairs, Assistant Secretary for Administration, Assistant Secretary for Occupied Areas, Assistant Secretary for Economic Affairs, Assistant Secretary for Public and Cultural Relations, Office of European Affairs, Office of Near Eastern and African Affairs, Office of Financial and Development Policy, and the Office of International Trade Policy. When appropriate, representatives from other units concerned were invaded or requested to participate in the work of the Committee.

National Archives memorandum, Subject: Appraisal of records covered by N1-59-93-30, April 4, 1993 (United States Man and the Biosphere Program (OES/EGC/MAB) The Man and the Biosphere Program was established at the 1970 General conference of the UN Educational, Scientific and Cultural organization (UNESCO). The program is intergovernmental in structure and is oriented toward solving problems arising from the interaction of human activity and natural systems. A part of the program areas are designated as "Biosphere Reserves." The reserves are dedicated to the conservation of characteristic ecosystems and species and the management of land and water resources for sustainable development necessary to meet human needs. Over 110 countries participate in the MAB program. Because of its international character, the Department of State volunteered to serve as the secretariat and coordinating agency for the U.S. Man and the Biosphere Program (U.S. MAB). The purpose of U.S. MAB is to foster harmonious relationships between humans and the biosphere through an international program of policy-relevant research that integrates social, physical and biological sciences to address actual problems. These activities, broadly interpreted, include catalytic conferences and meetings, education and training, and the establishment and use of biosphere reserves as research and monitoring sites. The Department of State established the U.S. National Committee for the Man and the Biosphere Program in 1974. The committee is composed of representatives from supporting Federal agencies and state and private institutions. Among the agencies participating are the Department of Agriculture (Forest Service), Department of Energy, Department of the Interior (Park Service), Department of State, AID, EPA, NASA, NOAA, the National Science Foundation, the Peace Corps, and the Smithsonian Institution. Under direction of the national committee, projects are administered by groups, called directorates, of selected experts whose chairs serve on the national committee.)

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Department of State organized the Office of Management Operations in May 1975 from the former Management Systems Staff, which had developed and examined new management systems and techniques. The Directors of the Office of Management Operations held rank equivalent to an Assistant Secretary of State and were designated by the Secretary of State. On November 1, 1988, the Office of Management Operations became the Office of Management Policy. On November 19, 1989, it became part of a new Bureau of Finance and Management Policy headed by the Chief Financial Officer. 

The Directors included Earl David Sohm, June 8, 1975-July 10, 1976; Clayton E. McManaway, June 28, 1976-January 29, 1977; Joan M. Clark, April 10, 1977-March 20, 1979; Michael M. Conlin, January 31, 1979-January 11, 1980; Robert H. Miller, March 17, 1980-July 10, 1983; Willard A. De Pree, July 11, 1983-April 13, 1987; George E. Moose, April 15, 1987-June 6, 1988; and C. Edward Dillery, June 6-1988-November 19, 1989.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Office of the Associate Director headed the Office of Volunteer Recruitment and Selection (VRS) and was established in 1985. The Office of the Associate Director advised the Director of the Peace Corps and senior staff on Volunteer recruitment and selection issues, as well as matters involving public awareness of the Peace Corps' recruitment efforts. It developed policy, procedures, and objectives to ensure the delivery of Peace Corps trainees in the numbers and general skill categories requested. The Office managed those organizational units that recruited and selected applicants as well as the administrative and infrastructure support for those functions. It also administered the internal planning, personnel, financial and other administrative management systems and processes of VRS. The Office directed research, analyses, studies, and functions related to the mission of VRS; and served as the head of the Volunteer Delivery System Steering Committee Secretariat. Arlen Erdahl was the first Associate Director.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
On May 6, 1944, the Division of Foreign Buildings Operations (FBO) was established  in the Office of the Foreign Service to perform the functions of housing and furnishing diplomatic and consular establishments abroad as required by the Foreign Service Buildings Act of Congress, approved May 7, 1926. It took over from the Division of Foreign Service Administration functions pertaining to the housing and furnishing of diplomatic and consular establishments abroad. The Division of Foreign Building Operations provided and maintained office, residential and other quarters for Foreign Service operations abroad, and provided furnishings for residential quarters. The Division performed the following functions: acquired real properties abroad; purchased and maintained furniture and furnishings for residences and special offices; developed projects on new construction, alternation, repair and property-development; maintained a field staff to supervise construction, maintenance, and property-management operations; and supervised the leasing of offices and residential properties in the field. The Chief of the Division served as the Executive Secretary of the Foreign Service Buildings Commission, a commission established by Congress in 1926 to formulate and approve plans for he acquisition and use of sites and buildings for diplomatic and consular establishments. By 1954, the Division was renamed the Office of Foreign Buildings Operations (FBO). It later managed the curatorial services and Art-in-Embassies programs, which provided high value furnishings and American art at embassies worldwide. 

In 2001, as recommended by the Overseas Presence Advisory Panel, the FBO was realigned to become the standalone Bureau of Overseas Buildings Operations (OBO), reporting to the office of the Under Secretary for Management. In concert with other Department of State bureaus, foreign affairs agencies, and Congress, OBO set worldwide priorities for the design, construction, acquisition, maintenance, use, and sale of real properties and the use of sales proceeds. OBO's mission was to provide safe, secure and functional facilities that represented the U.S. government to the host nation and support Department of State staff in the achievement of U.S. foreign policy objectives.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
On June 4, 1985, the Office of the Coordinator for International Communications and Information Policy was succeeded by the Bureau of International Communications and Information Policy (CIP) and the Coordinator became the new head of CIP. The Bureau was the principal adviser to the Secretary of State on international telecommunications policy issues affecting U.S. foreign policy and national security. The Bureau acted as coordinator with other U.S. Government agencies and the private sector in the formulation and implementation of international policies relating to a wide range of rapidly evolving communications and information technologies. The Bureau promoted U.S. telecommunications interests bilaterally and multilaterally. This Bureau was incorporated into the Bureau of Economic and Business Affairs under the Reorganization Plan of February 5, 1993. The merger took place on May 12, 1994.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Office of the Assistant Legal Adviser for Law Enforcement and Intelligence (L/LEI), established in 1979, coordinated international extradition and promoted mutual legal assistance in criminal and other law enforcement matters. It also negotiated treaties; managed the international extradition caseload; coordinated U.S. and foreign criminal proceedings with foreign policy implications; and assisted U.S. federal and state law enforcement agencies with investigations in foreign countries. The Office advised on proposed legislative initiatives and international agreements on anti-terrorism, narcotics matters, and other law enforcement issues; coordinated the legal/foreign aspects of illicit payments by U.S. firms; and advised on U.S. intelligence activities.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Office of Inter-American Programs, with regard to its respective geographic areas, developed educational and cultural plans, programs, and budget estimates, as well as requirements for program and administrative support. It determined, after consultation with appropriate Bureau of Educational and Cultural Affairs (CU) offices regarding feasibility, the scope and nature of educational and cultural area programs to be conducted. The Office provided program guidelines to the Office of U.S. Programs and Services, and to the Office of Cultural Presentations. It coordinated area program plans and activities with appropriate geographic components of the Department of State (including those of the Agency for International Development (AID)), with the U.S. Information Agency (USIA) and with other Government agencies. The Office also maintained internal Bureau controls on CU communications to and from overseas posts and with foreign embassies in the U.S. which pertained to area educational and cultural plans, programs, and activities.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Office of the Director was established by Reorganization Plan No. 2 of 1979 (93 Stat. 1378), effective July 19, 1979 by Executive Order 12147. The Director was in charge of the U.S. International Development Cooperation Agency, which was established on October 1, 1979 in accordance with Executive Order 12163 of September 29, 1979. The Director was appointed by the President, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate. The Office was primary responsibility for establishing overall development assistance policy and coordination international development activities supported by the United States. The Director served as the principal advisor to the President and the Secretary of State on international development matters and also advised the President on all trade, science and technology, and other matters significantly affecting the developing nations. The Office reported to the President and, on matters relating to foreign policy, to the Secretary of State.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Agency for International Development (USAID) program in Syria began in fiscal year 1960, when Syria was still a part of the United Arab Republic. In that year the United States provided $9.6 million of surplus agricultural commodities under Public Law 480, title I, Development Loans totaling $5.7 million, and agreed to assist in developing Syrian's civil aviation facilities through a modest Development Grant program.

From early 1961 to August 1962, unsettled political conditions, the separation of Syria from the United Arab Republic, and the unresolved question of the U.S. economic assistance relationship with Syria delayed the procurement and shipment of commodities, and severely hampered the technical advisory work of the civil aviation team. However, in August 1962, the bilateral agreement previously signed with the United Arab Republic was accepted by Syria as covering all AID activity in Syria.

As a consequence of the Six-Day War, Syria severed diplomatic relations with the United States in June 1967. U.S. economic assistance to Syria resumed in late 1974, several months after the restoration of diplomatic relations. The objective of U.S. assistance was to help Syria pursue its economic development program and to further improve U.S. - Syrian relations, and was regarded as essential to peace in the Middle East. Specifically, the USAID program was designed to assist Syria in priority development areas, especially agriculture, transportation, rural development, health, nutrition, and manpower training.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: In 1971, the Agency for International Development (AID) combined responsibility for all Supporting Assistance-financed programs from the Bureau for Vietnam, the Bureau for East Asia, and the Bureau for Near East and South Asia into a single Bureau for Supporting Assistance. In 1974, the Bureau for Supporting Assistance was redesignated as the Bureau for East Asia with responsibility for East Asia (transferred from the Bureau for Asia), Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia affairs. At this time the Bureau for Asia was also redesignated as the Bureau for Near East and South Asia and took over from the Bureau for Supporting Assistance work with Cyprus, Egypt, Israel, Jordan, Syria, Malta, and Spain.

Encyclopedia of United States National Security, c. 2006: p. 483 (The first Mutual and Balanced Force Reduction (MBRF) took place in Vienna, Austria in 1973. The U.S. proposed to withdraw 29,000 troops from Europe in return for Soviet withdrawal of 1,700 tanks and 68,000 troops. That would be followed by a reduction by both sides to a total of 900,000 troops apiece. The Warsaw Pact, led by the Soviet Union, proposed removing 20,000 soldiers apiece and freezing troop strengths at this reduced level. Afterward each North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) and Warsaw Pact country would reduce its forces by 15%. In 1989, NAT and the Warsaw Pact agreed to establish a new forum to negotiate troop reductions in Europe. The MBFR talks formally ended Feb. 9 and were replaced by the Negotiation on Conventional Armed Forces in Europe (CFE) on March 9.)

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Operations Staff of the Board of Foreign Scholarships provided under the general supervisor of the Executive Secretary of the Board of Foreign Scholarships, such staff functions as were necessary to enable the Board to fulfill its responsibilities under Public Law 548, 79th Congress. It coordinated Board, Department of State and other agency and overseas binational commission relationships, and arranged for meetings of the Board or of any of its committees. The Staff serviced as the principal point of contact and coordination of the commissions on matters not within the province of other offices of the Bureau of Educational and Cultural Affairs, including program guidance to existing and newly established commissions and the dissemination of information and materials pertaining to the program under the Fulbright Act.

The Office developed educational and cultural plans, programs, and budget estimates, as well as requirements for program and administrative support. It determined, after consultation with appropriative Bureau of Educational and Cultural Affairs (CU) offices regarding feasibility, the scope and nature of educational and cultural area programs to be conducted. The Office provided program guidelines to the Office of U.S. Programs and Services, and to the Office of Cultural Presentations. The Office coordinated area program plans and activities with appropriate geographic components of the Department (including those of the Agency for International Development (AID)), with the U.S. Information Agency (USIA) and with other Government agencies. It also maintained internal Bureau controls on CU communications to and from overseas posts and with foreign embassies in the U.S. which pertained to area educational and cultural plans, programs, and activities.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
On August 1, 1976, established the Office of Combatting Terrorism to further strengthen its efforts against international terrorism under the purview of the Office of the Deputy Under Secretary for Management. It provided a link between the policy and operational aspects of the Department of State's global fight against terrorists. It took over the functions of the Office of the Special Assistant to the Secretary of State and Coordinator. In 1979, the Office for Combatting Terrorism was transferred from the Office of the Under Secretary for Management to the Office of the Deputy Secretary. In 1982, the Office was transferred back to the Office for Combatting Terrorism has been transferred from the Office of the Under Secretary for Management to the Office of the Deputy Secretary.

The Directors of the Office included:  L. Douglas Heck: August 29, 1976-June 6, 1977; Heyward Isham, October 26, 1977-Augsut 1, 1978; Anthony C. E. Quainton, August 16, 1978-August 1, 1981; and Robert M. Sayre, May 11, 1982-1984.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Department of State established the Bureau of Politico-Military Affairs by an administrative order on Sepember18, 1969, to enhance the Department's role in the formulation of international security policy, to supervise security assistance and foreign military sales programs, and to direct the issuance of arms export licenses. The Bureau replaced a special component for politico-military affairs that had served under the Office of the Deputy Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs since 1960. The Director of the Bureau of Politico-Military Affairs, who was designated by the Secretary of State, had rank equivalent to an Assistant Secretary of State. The Director became a Presidential appointee, subject to the advice and consent of the Senate, and an Assistant Secretary on April 14, 1986.

The Directors and later Assistant Secretaries of State for Politico-Military Affairs included: Ronald Ian Spiers, 1969-1973; Seymour Weiss, 1973-1974; George Southall Vest, 1974-1977; Leslie Howard Gelb, 1977-1979; Reginald Bartholomew, 1979-1981; Richard R. Burt, 1981-1982; Jonathan Trumbull Howe, 1982-1984; John Thomas Chain Jr., 1984-1985; Henry Allen Holmes Jr., 1986-1989; Richard A. Clarke, 1989-1992; Robert L. Gallucci, 1992-1994; Thomas Edmund McNamara, 1994-1998; Eric David Newsom, 1998-2000; Lincoln P. Bloomfield, 2001-2005; John Hillen, 2005-2008; Mark Kimmitt, 2008-2009; Andrew J. Shapiro, 2009-2013; and Puneet Talwar, 2014-2015.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: In 1955, the Office of Financial and Development Policy was renamed the Office of International Financial and Development Affairs. The Office of International Finance and Development Affairs was concerned with those financial and economic matters which has an important bearing on the free-world's efforts to achieve a rate of economic progress sufficient to maintain confidence, political stability, and an appropriate military posture. In discharging its responsibilities, this Office dealt with the foreign economic policy aspects of loans, grants, and technical cooperation made available by the United States. It was the function of this Office to encourage, both in broad principle and its specific cases, economic development abroad through investment, including measures on the part of foreign governments which are favorable to the growth of private enterprise and the investment of private capital, and development programs and policies of foreign countries and suggest modification to increase their effectiveness. Another responsibility of the Office of International Financial and Development Affairs was dealing with lend-lease and surplus property.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Foreign Service Inspection Corps was charged with three primary functions. First, to report on the overall effectiveness of all missions or consulates, and the effectiveness of the principal officers in coordinating and directing United States Government activities in each country or consular district. Secondly, to report on the adequacy and effectiveness of the administration of the different posts, including staffing, fiscal operations, housing, communications, and maintenance of records. It also prepared efficiency reports on American personnel at the several posts and to advise the Department of State on placement and career management of their personnel. These efficiency reports made it possible to compare officers and employees with other members of their class on a service wide basis.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Kampuchean Working Group (KWG), also known as the Interagency Working Group on Kampuchea, was organized in 1979 as an interagency task force in the Office of the Secretariat, Office of the Ambassador at Large and Coordinator for Refugee Affairs (S/R). KWG was transferred in 1980 to the newly established Bureau of Refugee Programs. The Kampuchean Working Group administered grants and arranged procurement of supplies for the international organizations and American private voluntary agencies that had relief programs in Thailand and Kampuchea. It was a small operation headed by a Department of State officer, but most staff members were detailed from other government agencies, particularly the U.S. Agency for International Development. There was a counterpart office in Bangkok, Thailand also directed by a Department of State officer and manned primarily by persons employed by voluntary agencies, thus it is termed a joint voluntary agency (JVA) operation.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: President Harry S. Truman issued a confidential Executive Order on July 3, 1945 that created a Cryptographic Security Board. The Executive Order also required the Board to establish the Cryptographic Security Coordinating Committee (CSCC), consisting of three members, one appointed by the Secretary of State, one an officer appointed by the Secretary of War, and one an officer appointed by the Secretary of the Navy. The CSCC performed the functions as directed by the Board. Any committees appointed by the Board, expressed their findings and recommendations to the Board through the CSCC. The Cryptographic Security Coordinating Committee held its first meeting on October 5, 1945 and selected the representative of the Department of State, Mr. Frank McCarthy, as its Chairman.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Advisory Committee on Inter-American Cooperation in Agriculture Education grew out of suggestions originally made by the Continuation Committee of the Conference on Inter-American Relations in the field of Education, held by the Department of State on November 9 and 10, 1939. These suggestions were communicated by Secretary of State Cordell Hull to Secretary of Agriculture Henry A. Wallace, who on June 10, 1940, wrote a letter appointed the original Committee and outlining its functions in general terms. The Committee was set up to advise the Department of State in the realm of agriculture and held its first meeting in November 1940.

The Committee's objective was to work with the land-grant colleges and experiment stations in stimulating interest in agricultural problems common to all the Americas. As a basis for better agricultural understanding, the Committee recommended and urged increased teaching of historical, geographical, and economic backgrounds in all the American republics, and an increase in the study of the written and spoken Spanish and Portuguese in the U.S., and of English in Latin America. The Committee helped increase the number of scholarships and fellowships available for the interchange of professors. Surveys of exiting scholarships and fellowships were made in cooperation with the U.S. Office of Education. The Office Of Education was asked by the Committee to serve as a repository and information center for the various agricultural institutions of all the American countries and as an unofficial accrediting agency to assist in the evaluation of work presented by prospective students. The Committee also planed for the establishment of the Inter-American Institute of Agricultural Sciences.

Memberships of the Committee was made up of the following U.S. agriculture leaders over time: Chairman and later as a member Dean Knowles A. Ryerson, Assistant Dean of Agriculture, University of California; member and later Chairman Homer J. Henney, Dean of Agriculture, Colorado State College; E. N. Bressman, Director, Agricultural Division, Office of the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs; Fred J. Kelly, Chief, Division of Higher Education, U.S. Office of Education; John C. Patterson, U.S. Office of Education; Charles A. Thompson, Chief, Division of Cultural Relations, Department of State; Ross E. Moore and Louis Stanley, U.S. Department of Agriculture; Thomas Barbour, Museum of Comparative Zoology, Cambridge Massachusetts; Richard Bradfield, Cornel University; H. H. Hume, Dean of the College of Agriculture, University of Florida; ;  E. J. Kyle, Agricultural Mechanical College of Texas; J. H. Lee, Dean of the College of Agriculture, University of Louisiana; and T. W. Schultz, University of Chicago.

Soon afterward there came an expansion of inter-American activities throughout the Federal Government, and the committee became one of several comparable bodies appointed by the President to work through the Department of State. Designated as the Advisory Committee on Inter-American Cooperation in Agricultural Education, the group had its first meeting in Nov. 1940 and has met twice a year since then. The committee's object has been to work with the land-grant colleges and experiment stations in stimulating interest in agricultural problems common to all the Americas. As a basis for better agricultural understanding, the committee has recommended and urged increased teaching of historical, geographical, and economic backgrounds in all the republics, and an increase in the study of the written and spoken Spanish and Portuguese in this country, and of English in Latin America. Recognizing that long-time development must be based on adequate training the committee has endeavored to help increase the number of scholarships and fellowships available for the interchange of professors. Surveys of exiting scholarships and fellowships are being made in cooperation with the United States Office of Education. This office was also asked by the committee to serve as a repository and information center for the various agricultural institutions of all the American countries and as an unofficial accrediting agency to assist in the evaluation of work presented by prospective students. Much of the time of the committee has been devoted to plans for the establishment of the proposed Inter-American Institute of Agricultural Sciences. Committee members, in addition to Dean Knowles A. creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Office of Economic Growth (E&E/EG) supported the Bureau for Europe and Eurasia (E&E) objective of creating functional market economies in the former socialist states of Eastern Europe and Eurasia. Specifically, the Office focused on economic restructuring, including energy and infrastructure, macroeconomic policy reform, and developing the microeconomic foundations to sustain competitive economic growth. The Office oversaw the economic growth portfolio of the region, technical assistance activities, and credit programs while providing guidance to the Missions in the E&E region to coordinate economic growth strategies. The Office ensured that the formulation and preparation of country economic growth programs and sector assessments were consistent with technical practices and Bureau guidance and were appropriately integrated into the overall technical policies and strategies of the Agency. The Office was the principal interlocutor between the Missions’ economic growth offices and the Bureau for Economic Growth, Agriculture and Trade (EGAT). The Office managed and designed regionally funded programs such as the Eurasia Foundation, the Partners for Financial Stability, and the Regional Infrastructure Program (RIP). It was also charged with managing some bilaterally funded activities, including 10 Enterprise Funds with authorized funding levels of $1.3 billion. The Office was also responsible to the Agency for coordinating with the Department of State’s Office of the Coordinator for Europe and Eurasia and the National Security Council (NSC) on all matters affecting economic growth activities in the region.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Office of Technical Support (ANE/TS) provided leadership on development issues in the Bureau of Asia and the Near East (ANE) region through analysis, strategy development, program design, technical assistance, and information dissemination in the areas of economics, productive sector development, information technology, social sciences, democracy and governance, natural resources management and environment, agriculture, population, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS), health, nutrition, education, and conflict mitigation. The Office lead the Bureau’s strategic thinking in technical areas, reviewed the performance of Bureau offices and programs, and advised ANE offices on the appropriate allocation of resources. The Office served as the Bureau’s principal point of contact and coordination on all substantive technical aspects of programs in sectors of assigned specialization. It monitored development trends in the region, recommended new strategic directions for the Bureau, including engagement in new areas, as well as the allocation of resources between sectors. The Office recommended new directions for Bureau programs and conducted sectoral analyses and pilot efforts to guide the Bureau’s planning processes and new program development. It helped Missions develop new country strategic plans; conducted periodic reviews of Mission program performance; and provided technical oversight of Mission programs. It made recommendations for how Bureau resources would be allocated among Missions and prioritized sectoral programs throughout the region. The Office maintained close liaison with other U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) Bureaus to provide technical services to Missions; provided technical input for country strategies, impact evaluation, and implementation activities; and supported Missions in formulating strategies and developing programs, especially in new sectoral areas. It also advised the Bureau’s Administrative Officers on skill requirements and personnel qualifications for all Bureau technical positions, assignments, and recruitment.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: Following Ukraine’s independence and the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991, Ukraine began a period of transition toward a market economy and participatory democracy. In 1992, the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) signed a bilateral agreement on humanitarian, economic and technical cooperation with Ukraine to help the country develop its economic, political and societal potential. USAID and the Ukrainian government identified three strategic objectives: to create a broad-based market economy; to help build a participatory democratic political system; and to assist in social sector reforms to ease the difficulties of transition, particularly among the most vulnerable members of society.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: In November 1993, a decision was made to close, the U. S. Agency for International Development (USAID) Mission in Yaounde, along with twenty other missions worldwide. Reason given for the closure were: 1) the need to respond to the new realities of the post- cold war world, entailing a narrower focus of USAID's development priorities, concentrated in fewer countries; 2) the need to devote increasingly scarce resources to those countries - which demonstrate significant progress towards political and economic reforms; 3) Cameroon's economic performance and lack of progress on democratization had, regrettably, failed to match those of many other African countries; and 4) political reform following the flawed presidential elections in late 1992 had advanced very little. The Mission closed in 1994.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Office of Technical Support (ME/TS), housed in the Bureau for Middle East (ME), supported both the the Bureau for Asia (ASIA) and the Bureau for Middle East, regional platforms and field missions with technical staff focused on the unique transformational development issues confronting the Asia and Middle East regions. For these regions, the Office produced technical analyses, developed strategies and sectoral policy guidance, designed programs, monitored and evaluated country progress, and reaches out to the agency, interagency and to the public on technical issues. ME/TS teams encompassed and interconnected the health, education, democracy, economic growth, environment, conflict management, humanitarian, and security sectors. 

For both bureaus, the Office of Technical Support was the principal point of contact with other U.S. Government agencies, international donors, and bilateral and multilateral organizations on strategic technical priorities and concerns. Within the US Government, at the direction of Bureau leadership, ME/TS engaged with other US Government functional or technically-focused agencies and offices, including the State Department’s Bureaus of Oceans and International Environmental and Scientific Affairs (OES); Democracy, Human Rights and Labor (DRL); Economics (EB); International Narcotics and Law Enforcement (INL); and functional teams in the Director of Foreign Assistance (F). It also engaged with coordinating offices for technical issues such as HIV/AIDS, reconstruction and stabilization, and counter-terrorism; and the Department of Commerce, the Department of Justice, the Department of Treasury, the Department of Defense, and The National Security Council on interagency sectoral initiatives. Within the US Agency for International Development (USAID), ME/TS sat on sectoral councils and was the principal point of contact on technical issues related to the region’s foreign assistance planning and program implementation with USAID's technical bureaus.

The Office of Technical Support's main counter parts in the field were the technical staff in USAID missions and the regional platform offices. ME/TS provided the bureaus and field missions with technical advice for country strategic and operational planning, program design, evaluation and implementation. It linked the ASIA and ME bureaus and their field missions with links to USAID pillar bureaus for services, support, research and training, and with access to relevant US or international organizations and initiatives. The Office produced evidence-based analysis to monitor and evaluate progress and to communicate with the public, constituency groups, Congress (with the Bureau for Legislative and Public Affairs), and other stakeholders on technical matters. In coordination with the Office of Strategic Planning and Operations (ASIA/SPO), it planed and managed the Asia and Near East Central Program, including preparing the Operational Plan and annual Performance Reports and leading implementation of regional and cross-cutting activities. The Office advised the Administrative Management Support Team on skill requirements and personnel qualifications for all Bureau technical positions, assignments, and recruitment.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Office of Inspections was responsible for the conduct of independent reviews and assessments of the Agency's program and management operations. The Chief Inspector reported to the Director and the Deputy Director. The Chief Inspector performed the inspection function according to the precepts established by the Director. He was assisted by an Associate Chief Inspector and senior Foreign Service Information Officers (FSIO) with wide field experience. All foreign posts were under study consistent with operational priorities, to assess the effectiveness, efficiency and economy with which resources were employed to accomplish Agency and Mission objectives and to analyze and assess the character and degree of direction and support by Agency elements in Washington and elsewhere. 

Two types of inspections were conducted by the Office. Formal inspections covered all aspects of the post's operations and domestic elements. It provided direction and support of the post; brought innovations of wide operational implication and significant problems to the attention of management; and recommended measures to resolve or relieve such problems as well as problems to which the Agency directed the attention of the Inspectors. Informal inspection were visits to smaller posts or between formal inspections of other posts. It insured that posts and elements performed appropriately, complied with policies and benefit from independent access to the Agency's top management level. 

The Inspection system evaluated the totality of headquarters-field and post-Mission relations for each post and element to arrive at an independent assessment of the manner in which posts, geographical areas, and the medial supported each other in accomplishing the Agency mission abroad. Inspection reports were furnished to the Director, the Post, and Area Director and other offices following each "formal inspection" and where useful in case of "informal" inspection visits. They concluded with recommendations that provided specific options to management in the resolution of problems and the collective adoption of successful program experience. Inspectors' findings were supported by facts and judgements; opinions were identified as views of the Inspectors themselves, either collectively or individually. 

The Office worked with the Inspector-General's office at the Department of State to arrange concurrent inspections of larger posts wherever feasible.

The Chief Inspectors included Daniel P. Oleksiw, Gordon Winkler, and Maurice Lee.

Reorganization Plan No. 2 of 1977, effective April 1, 1978, reorganized the U.S. Information Agency (USIA) into the International Communication Agency and the Office of Inspections was part of the new Associate Directorate of Management (MGT). The Office, in the reorganization of August 24, 1982, moved into the new USIA's Bureau of Management. On July 19, 1983, in accordance with USIA Announcement No. 142 of that date, the Office of Inspections was removed from the Bureau of Management and started to report directly to the USIA Director. In the mid 1980s, the Office of Inspections was merged into the Office of the Inspector General.

The Executive Committee was established on March 18, 1969 to advise the U.S. Information Agency (USIA) Director. It served as the principal body for the review, discussion, and formulation of Agency decisions on major policy, allocation of resources, and operational matters that individual elements were not empowered to make, or on which they could not reach an agreement through means specified in their functional statements in the Manual of Operations and Administration (MOA). The Executive Committee considered all proposals for permanent changes in position and employment ceilings, the reclassification of posts, the initiation or termination of major media products, significant shifts in resources (increase of more than $10,000 in any allocation and reprogramming in excess of $50,000), or any action that committed future overseas or domestic managers to change in program or organization structure that would be difficult to reverse. 

At an initial and midyear program review, the Executive Committee considered the consolidation proposals of each agency element for funding, staffing, and intra-Agency support requirements. Before being considered by the Executive Committee, these proposals were reviewed by the Program Review Group which was chaired by the Assistant Director for Administration and Management and included the Agency Budget Officer, a representative from the Office of Policy and Plans, and the Resource and Operations Analysis Staff.

The Executive Committee was originally limited to four officers: the Deputy Director as Chairman; the Deputy Director for Policy and Plans; the Assistant Director for Administration; and the Executive Secretary. The Associate Director for Research and Assessment was added to the Committee on June 3, 1969, and the General Counsel was added on July 15, 1969. By 1976, the Executive Committee members were: the Director as Chairman;, the Deputy Director; the Deputy Director for Policy and Plans; the General Counsel, the Assistant Director for Administration and Management; the Assistant Director for Research; the Assistant Director for Personnel and Training; and the Assistant Director for Public Information. 

The Chief Inspector and the Agency Budget Officer advised the Executive Committee. It was also supported by the Executive Committee Staff, which analyzed documents submitted to it, prepared studies for the Director, drafted decisions memoranda, reported on actions resulting from the Director's decisions, prepared Committee meeting minutes, and maintained the Agency's master file on these minutes.

This bill would give Congressional recognition and endorsement to the April 1966 decision of the President of the United States and the President of Mexico to set up the joint Commission and would also provide a statutory foundation for the activities of the United States Section of that Commission. The United States Section now includes representatives at the Assistant Secretary level or above of nine Federal agencies and the Chairman of the Interagency Committee on Mexican-American Affairs. creators.administrativeHistoryNote: Arrangements for all International Visitors in the International Visitor Program, which operated under authority of the Mutual Educational and Cultural Exchange Act of 1961 (Fulbright-Hays Act), were made by program officers assigned to the Office of International Visitors. The emphasis of the program was to increase mutual understanding through communication at the personal and professional levels. The International Visitor Program brought participants to the United States from all over the world each year to meet and confer with their professional counterparts and to experience the United States firsthand. The visitors, who were current or potential leaders in government, politics, the media, education, and other fields, were selected by American Foreign Service Officers overseas. Agency program officers worked in concert with a broad range of private, not-for-profit organizations operating under cooperative agreements with USIA. The program also relied on the commitment and skills of volunteer organizations across the country. These organizations were known collectively as "Councils for International Visitors (CIVs)" associated under the umbrella organization of the National Council for International Visitors.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: By October 31, 1984, the Presidential Commission for the German-American Tricentennial completed its work to plan, encourage, develop, and coordinate the commemoration of the 300th anniversary of German settlement in the United States on October 31, 1984. In November 1984, the German-American Contacts Staff was established within the United States Information Agency (USIA) to maintain the records of and continue the work of the Tricentennial through encouragement and dissemination of information on educational, cultural, professional, and social contacts and exchanges between the United States and the Federal Republic of German. The Staff was also known as the Office of German-American Contacts. It was originally located within the Bureau of Educational and Cultural Affairs until December 7, 1987, when it moved directly under the Office of the Director. The Staff had responsibility for the German-American Friendship Garden and for supporting the USIA Director in his role as Coordinator for German-American Contacts. It handled activities associated with the "contacts initiative," including the Interagency Steering Committee for U.S.-German Contacts; the Congress Bundestag Staff Exchange and assorted small ad hoc projects; monitoring and evaluating the range of German-American contacts; stimulating new ones where necessary; and clearing information to the public on both private and public exchange organizations and opportunities connected with Germany.

On January 14, 1983, the Presidential Commission for the German-American Tricentennial was established by Public Law 97-472 (96 Stat. 2603) and extended by Public Law 98-197 (97 Stat. 1353), dated December 1, 1983. The Commission planed, encouraged, developed, and coordinated the 1983 commemoration of the 300th anniversary of German settlement in the United States. One of the projects undertaken by the Commission was to oversee the planning and establishment of a German-American Friendship Garden in the District of Columbia as an enduring symbol of German-American contributions to this country and the lasting friendship between the United States and the Federal Republic of Germany.

The Commission was composed of no more than 40 members from public and private sectors, appointed by the President. Ten members were appointed upon the recommendation of the Speaker of the House of Representatives, and ten other members were appointed upon the recommendation of the President pro tempore of the Senate, in consultation with the majority leader and minority leader of the Senate. The Chief Justice of the United States or his designee was also a member. The Charles Z. Wick, Director of the United States Information Agency (USIA), provided administrative services and staff support to the Commission. He also, at the request of President Ronald Reagan, organized the Commission and acted as the President's personal representative on the Commission. 

The Commission terminated on October 31, 1984; however, its final report entitled "German-American Tricentennial Three Hundred Years of German Immigration to America 1693-1983" was published in 1985. The Commission's records and some functions were transferred to the USIA's German-American Contacts Staff.

sourceNotes: 96 Statutes at Large 2603, January 14, 1983 (Public Law 97-472 That the period commencing January 1, 1983 and ending December 31, 1983 is hereby designated as the "Tricentennial Anniversary year of German Settlement in America", and the President is authorized and requested to issue a proclamation calling upon the people of the United States to issue a proclamation calling upon the people of the United States to observe the year with appropriate ceremonies and activities. There is hereby established a Commission to be known as the Presidential Commission for the German-American Tricentennial (hereinafter referred to as the "Commission") to plan, encourage, develop, and coordinate the commemoration of the German-American Tricentennial. In preparing its plans and carrying out its program, the Commission shall give due consideration to any related plans and programs developed by State, local, private, and foreign groups. The Commission shall be composed of not more than 40 members, appointed by the President, ten of whom shall be appointed upon the recommendation of the Speaker of the House of Representatives, and ten of who shall be appointed upon the recommendation of the President pro tempore of the Senate, in consultation with the majority leader and minority leader of the Senate. One member shall be the Chief Justice of the United States or his designee. The members shall be from the public and private sectors and the President shall designate a member form the private sector as chairman. The Director of the United States Information Agency is authorized to provide administrative services and staff support to the Commission, as necessary. A report of the Commission's activities shall be made to Congress no later than January 31, 1984, upon which date the Commission shall terminate.)

97 Statutes at Large 1353, December 1, 1983 (Public Law 98-197 Whereas in commemoration of the three hundredth anniversary of German settlement in America at Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, on October 6, 1683, the Congress passed Senate Joint Resolution 260, Ninety-seventh Congress, which was signed into law by the President on January 14, 1983, as Public Law 97-472 (hereinafter in this resolution referred to as the "Act"); Whereas the Act established the Presidential Commission for the German-American Tricentennial (hereinafter in this resolution referred to as the "Commission") to plan, encourage, develop, and coordinate the commemoration of the German-American Tricentennial, and provided for the termination of the Commission on January 31, 1984. Whereas one of the key projects undertaken by the Commission is to oversee the planning and establishment of a German-American Friendship Garden in the District of Columbia as an enduring symbol of German-American contributions to this country and the lasting friendship between the United States and the Federal Republic of Germany; and Whereas the President and the Congress are of the opinion that more time will be needed by the Commission beyond its presently scheduled expiration date of January 31, 1984, to complete its work on the German-American Friendship Garden: Now, therefore, be it that the term of the Commission is hereby extended to October 31, 1984,  and the deadline for the report of the Commission's activities to the Congress required by the Act is hereby also extended to that date.)

This commission was established pursuant to PL 97-472 to "plan, encourage, develop, and coordinate the commemoration" of the 300th anniversary of German settlement in what is now the United States. By law the commission could have up to 40 members from the public and private sectors. USIA provided administrative services and staff support. At the time of the creation of the commission, USIA undertook a reinvigorated program of German-American contacts. Key to this was the USIA-chaired Inter-agency Steering Committee (ISC), an official body that paralleled the commission. Program support for the commission and participation and coordination of the ISC were located in the Bureau of European Affairs from the beginning in 1982 through October 1984. In November, both of these duties were transferred to the Bureau of Educational and Cultural Affairs. In 1985, the commission went out of existence and its records and carry-over duties devolved upon USIA. On December 7, 1987, the function was once again reorganized. This time it became a staff office of the Director. The ISC is still in operation. German-American Contacts staff)

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: On July 9, 1962, the U.S. Information Agency (USIA) established a small liaison office, called the Special Projects Office, in Santurce a district of San Juan, Puerto Rico as the result of the expanding programs of the Alliance for Progress. The Office served as a point of contact between the U.S. Information Agency in Washington and various Puerto Rican contractors hired to aid in the output of Spanish language materials for press, radio, television and film audiences in Latin America. Collin E. Ostrander, a USIA Foreign Service officer, served as the Officer in Charge. On April 20, 1964, the Special Projects Office closed and transferred to Washington.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: On October 1, 1994, the Bureau of Information was established. In 1995, the Bureau of Policy and Programs was abolished and many of its functions were transferred to the new Bureau of Information. Additionally certain nonexchange element functions of the Bureau of Educational and Cultural Affairs were also transferred in 1995 to the Bureau of Information, including academic and cultural specialists programs to consolidate programming of speakers and specialists, book programs, and library services. This new consolidated and technologically upgraded Bureau of Information supported U.S. foreign policy objectives by providing instant and in-depth communications with the influence structures of other countries through the electronic information capabilities of the Agency's Wireless File, library and U.S. Information Service (USIS) centers abroad and foreign press centers in the U.S., the programming of U.S. speakers and specialists through overseas travel, and electronic dialogues or interactive television communications. When the U.S. Information Agency (USIA) was abolished October 1, 1999, the educational exchange programs and those in the Bureau of Information were placed in a newly created Bureau of Public Diplomacy in the Department of State.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: On February 27, 1976, the National Commission on the Observance of International Women’s Year approved a recommendation that the Office of International Women's Programs, which was part of the Bureau of International Organization Affairs’ (IO) Directorate for Labor and Women's Affairs, be upgraded, so that it would have direct access to the Assistant Secretary handling international organization affairs and make its influence felt across IO. In June 1976, the International Women’s Program Directorate (IO/IWP) was established headed by an Agency Director and later a Deputy Director. IWP coordinated women's programs which had increasing emphasis in international affairs. The staff attended conferences that included biennial meetings of the Inter-American Commission on Women, the United Nations (UN) Commission on the Status of Women, the meetings of the Economic and Social Council (and as needed the General Assembly) and the UN Seminar programs of the Commission on the Status of Women, as well as some of the seminars of the Inter-American Commission of Women.

sourceNotes: "... To Form a More Perfect Union ..." : Justice for American Women Report of the National Commission on the Observance of International Women’s Year, 1976: p. 243 (The IWY Commission recommends that the Secretary of State direct the Assistant Secretary for International Organization Affairs to upgrade the Office of International Women's Programs to that of Special Advisor for International Women's Programs to the Assistant Secretary, with an appropriate increase of staff. Background The Office of International Women's Programs is a part of the Directorate for Labor and Women's Affairs, one of 15 directorates within the Bureau of International Organization Affairs. This Office, because it affects the work of the entire Bureau and cuts across directorate lines, should be upgraded to have direct access to the Assistant Secretary handling international organization affairs and should make its influence felt in all directorates. The reorganization recommended by the Commission is especially called for now, due to the broadened scope of women's programs offered during the International Decade for Women. Recommendation approved by International Interdependence Committee Feb. 9, 1976; by IWY Commission Feb. 27, 1976.)

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Political Section worked to advance the global partnership between the United States and Australia to serve the countries’ shared interests and values. Political Officers analyzed and reported on political developments and their potential impact on U.S. interests. They also worked with Australian officials to enhance U.S.-Australian cooperation on counter-terrorism, non-proliferation, promoting human rights and democracy, and other mutual priorities. The Political Section worked closely with the U.S. Defense Attaché Office to ensure that the Australia, New Zealand, and United States (ANZUS) alliance continued to serve as a pillar of regional peace and security. The Section also worked to coordinate U.S. and Australian engagement with regional and global institutions, including the United Nations, the East Asia Summit, and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Regional Forum.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: A Department Circular, dated January 15, 1955, abolished the Office of International Materials Policy and the Office of Economic Defense and Trade Policy and transferred their functions to the new Office of International Trade and Resources (ITR). The Office of International Trade and Resources was responsible for work relating to the President's foreign trade program, trade agreements, expanding foreign markets for U.S. exports and trade matters as they affected U.S. economic, political, and defense relations with other countries. These activities in the trade field were performed in coordination with other departments and agencies of the Government. Ben H. Thibodeaux served as its Director.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Economic Section managed the bilateral economic agenda; promoted trade and investment between the U.S. and Peru; and advocated for Peruvian adherence to sound economic policies. The Section also worked to expand cooperation in the areas of environment, science, health, anti-money laundering, and intellectual property protection.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Overseas Private Investment Corporation (OPIC) was authorized as an independent agency by Public Law 91-175 (83 Stat. 809) of December 30, 1969. This legislation also created the position of President of the Corporation. The President was appointed by the President of the United States, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, and served at the pleasure of the President. In making such appointment, the U.S. President was to take into account private business experience of the appointee. The OPIC President also served as the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of the Corporation and was often referred to as the President and Chief Executive Officer. The Office of the President was responsible for the operations and management of the Corporation, subject to bylaws and policies established by the Board of Directors. The authorities were formerly transferred to the Corporation by Executive Order 11579 of January 19, 1971.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Information Support Services Division (ISS), formerly the Communications Program Management Division, was established on December 2, 1990 in the new Office of Administrative Services. The Division was composed of the Mail Management Branch; Printing and Graphics Branch; and the Records Management Branch. Directives and reports functions were performed within the Division Chief’s immediate office.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The USSR Branch was established by Foreign Economic Administration Administrative Memorandum No. 100, dated March 10, 1945. The Branch carried out the Foreign Economic Administration’s activities relating to the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR). The Branch cleared with the President’s Soviet Protocol Committee all questions of exports to the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, and with the State Department all problems relating to imports. Major General C. M. Wessen was the Director.

The USSR Branch arranged for the coordination of Administration activities and programs, with relevant military requests, activities and programs. The Branch established and maintained liaison arrangements on area matters of the administration with international agencies; with agencies of foreign governments; and with the Department of State, the Army, the Navy, the Department of the Treasury, and other governmental agencies, as well as with private relief agencies importers and exporters. It received such requirements and relevant information as were submitted by the Soviet Government, and developed all other requirements not furnished by the Soviet Government; and analyzed all requirements from the viewpoint of area and protocol considerations; and transmitted such requirements, property compiled to the interested member of the Protocol Committee and to the Bureau of Supplies. Information in support of these requirements, was prepared in accordance with the policy of the President’s Soviet Protocol Committee as communicated to the Branch. Such information was designed, as much as possible, to aid the Bureau of Supplies in making an effective presentation to allocating agencies. The USSR Branch received and approved requisitions in accordance with the Protocol existing with the USSR. It issued cash purchase licenses under special arrangement with the Bureau of Supplies. The Branch also considered, in light of supply and shipping programs for the USSR, activities of the Administration relating to relief or lend-lease activities in areas supplied through territory controlled by the USSR.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Office of Material Resources (MR) was established on November 4, 1961 and was also known as the Office of Materials Resources. The head of the Office, Herbert J. Waters, served as the Assistant Administrator for Material Resources.

The Office formulated the policies, standards, and procedures governing the various types of commodity assistance. It provided advice and guidance on procurement, utilization, financing and shipping of such commodities. This Office was also charged with seeing that small business enterprises participated equitably in furnishing Agency for International Development (AID) financed commodities and services, and was the focal point for the Agency’s responsibilities in connection with the Food-for-Peace program.

On March 23, 1967, the Office of Material Resources was abolished in accordance with an AID General Notice of that date. The majority of the functions transferred to the new Office of War on Hunger, including the functions of the Assistant Administrator, the Deputy Assistant Administrator, and the Associate Assistant Administrator for Special Resources; as well as the Food for Peace, voluntary foreign aid, and agricultural commodity specialist functions. The Special Assistant (Economics and Trade) and the International Cooperative Development Service functions transferred to the Office of Development Finance and Private Enterprise. The Office of the Special Assistant for Management and Administration transferred to the Office of the War on Hunger except for the Assistant Administrator for Administration who transferred to the Office of Procurement. The remaining functions transferred to the Office of Procurement, which included the Special Ocean Freight Staff.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: The Political Section's mission was to sustain and deepen the U.S.’ global partnership with Canada in key priority areas such as Afghanistan, the Americas, and the United Nations as well as in the promotion of human rights and good governance throughout the world. Its political officers maintained close contact with a wide range of Canadian political leaders and government officials, third country diplomats, academics, representatives of nongovernmental organizations, journalists, and others of influence, and also spoke to Canadian audiences about U.S. policy priorities and U.S.-Canadian relations. The Section kept the U.S. Government  informed about Canadian political and security (including non-proliferation) issues and developments through regular reporting and analysis. It prepared the chapters on Canada for Congressionally-required reports on human rights, religious freedom, narcotics, terrorism, and trafficking in persons.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
On April 18, 1946, General MacArthur issued Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers (SCAP) General Order No. 18, which established the Diplomatic Section as a special staff section. It was an outgrowth of the Office of the United States Political Advisor for Japan. It dealt with international affairs pertaining to Japan. The Section controlled relationships with foreign diplomatic representatives and supervised other U.S. Department of State agencies in Japan.

More specifically, the Section made recommendations on policies concerning foreign relations of Japan and Korea. It made recommendations concerning establishment of foreign diplomatic missions and consular offices in Japan and Korea and maintained contact with such foreign diplomatic missions and consular offices as were established in Japan. Relationships of foreign diplomatic and consular officials with the Japanese Government were conducted through SCAP and the Diplomatic Section was the SCAP section charged with conduct of SCAP’s relations with such foreign officials. The Section collected, correlated and maintained in useable form information on international affairs relating to Japan and Korea, and from time to time informed and advised SCAP on the aforementioned information as pertinent to conduct his duties. It maintained a branch section in Yokohama for the purpose of performing consular functions, and supervised such other agencies of U.S. Department of State established in Japan. 

The Diplomatic Section maintained contact with U.S. Department of State. It submitted opinions and recommendations to the Department of State through SCAP and the War Department on special subjects when such opinions and recommendations were requested by the Department of State through the War Department. The Section sent reports and information as appropriate to the Department of State through SCAP and the War Department. It also communicated directly with the Department of State on routine matters of interest to that Department, such as personnel, accounts, consular matters, transmittal of publications, press analyses, copies of directives et cetera and receipt of informational material.

Minister George Atcheson, Jr., the Political Adviser, was originally assigned as Chief of Diplomatic Section. Later, the United States Political Adviser to SCAP, William J. Sebald, also served as the Chief of Diplomatic Section. As chairman and member for the United States on the Allied Council for Japan, the chief of the Diplomatic Section was also deputy for the Supreme Commander.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
On February 24, 1947, Transmittal Letter 47, combined the Security Office and the Division of Investigation into the Division of Security and Investigation in order to improve the efficiency and performance of the Office of Controls. The Division of Investigations and Security was charged with protecting the Secretary of State and foreign dignitaries; security investigations; the security training program; and the overseas security program. Thomas F. Finch served as Chief of the Division.

On August 27, 1948, the Division of Foreign Activity Correlation was abolished and most of its personnel and functions transferred to the Division of Security and Investigations. At that time, the Division of Security and Investigations became the Division of Security.

Eight months earlier, the Department created the Division of Investigations, by moving the Office of the Chief Special Agent with its staff of 124 people into the Office of Controls and renaming it. On February 24, the Department transferred the Security Office into Investigations, creating the Division of Security and Investigations; The decision to merge the Security Office into the Division of Investigations arose from several factors. The Division of Management Planning, influenced by Goodrich’s report, urged Panuch to separate the security function into its own division, so that the director of the Office of Controls (CON) could focus upon the managing CON’s multiple divisions. Also, Department managers wanted to improve the efficiency and performance of CON….Although the new Division of Security and Investigations kept the Chief Special Agent’s acronym CSA…The new Division of Investigations and Security still retained the duties of protecting the Secretary of State and foreign dignitaries; however, Bannerman’s three tasks: security investigations, the security training program, and the overseas security program provided the focus and structure for the new division; By February 1948, the Bureau of Administration decided to dissolve FC [Division of Foreign Activity Correlation] and transfer most of its duties and staff to the Security and Investigations Division. creators.biographicalNote: Mark D. Gearan (b. September 19, 1956, Gardner, Massachusetts- ) was a commissioner for the National Commission on Military, National, and Public Service from 2017-2020. Gearan became the Director of the Harvard Institute of Politics on March 1, 2018 and previously served as President of Hobart and William Smith Colleges from 1999-2017. He held senior positions in the Clinton Administration, including White House Deputy Chief of Staff from January 20, 1993 to June 7, 1993; White House Communications Director, June 7, 1993 to August 14, 1995; and as Director of the Peace Corps from September 26, 1995 to August 11, 1999.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
On November 28, 2001, Dr. Anne Peterson, the Assistant Administrator for the Bureau of Global Health, announced the creation of the Office of HIV/AIDS to focus on educating people on the prevention of the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and the acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS); reduce HIV prevalence in young adults; assist children affected by AIDS; support voluntary counseling and testing; develop technologies to fight the transmission; reduce sexually transmitted infections in Africa; and increase the distribution of condoms.

The Office provided strategic direction, technical leadership, and support to field programs and to effectively manage headquarters programs devoted to ending the global HIV/AIDS epidemic. It provided input to decisions concerning the strategic allocation of financial and human resources in the sector and assisted in designing, implementing, monitoring, and evaluating programs. This entailed ensuring the technical integrity of Agency and Mission strategies; providing global technical leadership on the full range of issues related to HIV/AIDS prevention, care, and treatment; managing numerous research and field support programs; supporting USAID Missions in working with partners and other government agencies; and monitoring, evaluating, and reporting on the impact of the Agency’s HIV/AIDS program. The Office of HIV/AIDS served as the Agency’s lead office for implementing the interagency President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) in controlling the HIV/AIDS epidemic by providing technical leadership, monitoring impact, ensuring program integrity, and supporting the transition to local partners.

In 1989, the Department of States renamed the former Office of the Special Coordinator (SC) as the Moscow Embassy Building Control Office (MEBCO) to “develop and executive a long-term plan designed to resolve the current property situation and meet the operational and security requirements of our embassy’s properties in Moscow.” The Office was responsible for construction of the new Embassy building. MEBCO was an independent office responsible for all aspects of the new building project, including the planning, design, project financing, construction, security, acquisition, logistics, budgets, and schedules of the new office building in Moscow. The Director of MEBCO reported directly to the Under Secretary of State of Management and was staffed by Department of State and intelligence community employees.

Generally, the Office of Foreign Buildings Operations (FBO) handled the construction of embassy buildings. However, in the early 1980s, bugs placed by Soviet intelligence were discovered, which compromised the American Embassy in Moscow. MEBCO was established to handle this special situation. Also, the creation of the Office allowed the implementation of the chancery construction project to be kept separate from any one bureau because of the need to coordinate issues involving several bureaus. The MEBCO and the Office of the Inspector General’s Moscow Oversight Team, created in October 1994, worked together from the decision to rebuild the Chancery through the design and construction of a new, secure chancery facility.

On May 15, 2000, the new chancery facility opened, and the Department closed the Moscow Embassy Building Control Office in September 2000.

In January 1993, the Assistant Administrator for Asia obtained approval from the Acting Administrator to merge USAID Mission to Pakistan (USAID/Pakistan) and the Office of the A.I.D. Representative (AID/REP) to Afghanistan. The USAID Mission to Pakistan had began to phase out its status by completing ongoing programs since the Pressler Amendment (1991) prohibited new obligations. The AID/REP, located in Pakistan due to unsafe conditions in Afghanistan, had severe budget cuts that required them to move staff from the U.S. Embassy in Pakistan into the USAID’s compound as space became available. The combined mission was called the USAID Mission to Pakistan and Afghanistan, sometimes abbreviated as USAID/Pakistan. The Mission Director for Pakistan served concurrently as the A.I.D. Representative. The administrative, financial, contracting, legal and program support services were consolidated immediately; however, the AID/REP became the Office of Afghan Field Operations, a separate unit within the new combined Mission.

Although the programs for Afghanistan ended on September 30, 1994, the Mission continued to be known as the USAID Mission to Pakistan and Afghanistan. The programs for Pakistan ended in June 1995, which closed the Mission.

In seeking this approval, she requested that the USAID Mission Director also be designated the AID/REP. In his approval memorandum of January 21, 1993, the Acting AID Administrator directed the following: "The Mission Director for Pakistan is now also sewing concurrently as the A.I.D. Representative. The proposed consolidation will merge administrative, financial management, contracting, legal and program support services for the two missions. Based on the expressed concern of the Asia Bureau and Ambassador Monjo, however, it is imperative that the Afghan program remain as an identifiable unit within the overall structure of the A. I.D. presence in Pakistan. Our planning will reflect this concern." AID/REP and USAID/Pakistan administrative, financial, contracting, legal and program support services were consolidated immediately. The Afghanistan project portfolio was merged under the Office of Afghan Field Operations, a separate unit within the Combined Mission…As the AID/REP is undergoing a reorganization and developing a new program strategy, the USAID/Pakistan Mission continues in its phase out status under the Pressler Amendment. If Pakistan remains under the new obligation prohibition, its ongoing program should be completed by 1995. USAID/Pakistan also is going through a reorganization to downsize over the next two years; Because of the sensitive nature of the Afghan program in its early stages, AID/REP offices were established in the American Embassy in Islamabad, Pakistan. As the staff expanded…employees were placed in the USAID/Pakistan compound, where they utilized USAID support staff. Shortly after USAID/Pakistan came under the Pressler Amendment (1991) and was planning its staff phase down, the Embassy gave notice that AID/REP should plan on relocating to the USAID/Pakistan compound as space became available. A determination was made at that time, that by the Fall of 1993, such a move would take place. The Afghan Program Office relocated to the USAID compound in early 1993; Memorandum Jan 27 1993 Mission Director for USAID Pakistan is now serving concurrently as the A.I.D. Representative for Afghanistan. The Acting Administrator recently approved the consolidation of the Office of the A.I.D. Representative within USAID/Pakistan. This consolidation merges administrative, financial management, contracting, legal and program support services for the two Missions, while maintaining an identifiable unit for the Afghan program)

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The Minority Resource Center (MRC) was established on August 14, 1979, in accordance with Section 123 of Public Law 96-53 (93 Stat. 366), the International Development Cooperation Act of 1979. The Center was responsible for increasing the participation of economically and socially disadvantaged business enterprises in U.S. Agency for International Development’s (USAID) contract, procurement, grant, and research and development activities. At times the Director of the MRC also concurrently served as the Director of the Office of Small and Disadvantaged Business Utilization. 

The Center’s five basic responsibilities were the dissemination of information; the design of programs to assist disadvantaged firms; the identification of opportunities for such firms through market research and planning; the development of support mechanisms for them; and the letting of contracts to involve such firms in development assistance programs. It established, maintained, and disseminated information to and for U.S. small disadvantaged enterprises regarding opportunities in USAID-financed development assistance programs. The MRC designed formal and informal systems to encourage, promote and assist U.S. small and disadvantaged enterprises to participate in USAID programs. It conducted market research, planning, economic, and business analyses and feasibility studies to identify business opportunities. The Center entered into such contracts, cooperation agreements, or other transactions as necessary in the conduct of its function under Section 123 of Public Law 95-53. The MRC also oversaw the administration of the Women's Business Program in accordance with Executive Order 12138 and related initiatives; and designed and maintained automated statistical and other reporting systems including the subcontracting monitoring system (Public Law 100-656), the Agency Consultant Registry Information System (ACRIS), and the Procurement Information Access System (PIAS).
