creators.administrativeHistoryNote: On July 1, 1967, the U.S. Mission to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and European Regional Organizations (USRO) was redesignated as the U.S. Mission to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (USNATO). The USNATO was the official representation of the United States of America to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. It was located at the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) Headquarters in Brussels, Belgium. The USNATO represented U.S. foreign policy interests within the Alliance. The mission was a diverse team of individuals representing numerous U.S. federal agencies. The U.S. Permanent Representative to NATO occupied the U.S. chair in the North Atlantic Council (NAC), which was the principal political decision-making body within NATO.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
On July 28, 1967, the Department of State established the Board of Appellate Review, under the authority of the Secretary of State's responsibilities under the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1952, for the purpose of promoting centralized administrative appeal procedures required by law and regulation or otherwise as provided by the Department. The Board began in the Office of the Deputy Under Secretary for Administration and was transferred to the Office of the Deputy Under Secretary for Management of July 12, 1971, the Office of the Under Secretary for Management on October 1, 1978, and to the Office of the Legal Adviser on July 1, 1979. The jurisdiction of the Board covered appeals from decisions on nationality cases, passport cases, contract cases, and personnel cases.

The Board originally consisted of regular members who served on a full-time basis with one designated as the head. Ad hoc members were designated by the Deputy Under Secretary for Administration, which could include those not employed by the Department or its Foreign Service. On November 30, 1979, the membership changed to consist of regular and ad hoc members as the Legal Adviser designated. Regular members served on a full-time basis. Ad hoc members could be designated from senior officers of the Department of State or from persons not employed by the Department. Regular and ad hoc members were attorneys in good standing admitted to practice in any State of the United States, the District of Columbia, or any Territory or possession of the United States. The Legal Adviser designated a regular member of the Board as Chairman. A member designated by the Chairman acted in the absence of the Chairman. The Chairman or designee presided at all proceedings before the Board, regulated the conduct of  such proceedings, and passed on all issues relating thereto In considering an appeal, the Board acted through a panel of three members, not more than two of whom were ad hoc members. On April 10, 1984, the Chairperson replaced the Chairman.

In 1979, the jurisdiction of the Board included appeals from decisions in the following cases: appeals from administrative determinations of loss of nationality or expatriation; appeals from administrative decision denying, revoking, restricting or invalidating a passport; appeals from final decisions of contracting officers arising under contracts or grants of the Department of State, not otherwise provided for in the Department of State contract appeal regulations; and appeals from administrative decisions of the-Department of State in such other cases and under such terms of reference as the Secretary of State authorized. On April 8, 1986, the Board of Appellate Review’s jurisdiction expanded to hear appeals from administrative determinations denying U.S. Government assistance to U.S. nationals operating in South Africa who did not comply with the Fair Labor Standards. In actuality, the work of the Board mainly involved hearing appeals from persons whom the Department of State has ruled have expatriated themselves and appeals of revocations and denials of passports. Decisions against the Department were not appealable. Decisions against an individual were appealable in the Federal court. It provided its decisions to the office or bureau responsible for the decision from which the appeal arose.

The Board could take any action it considered appropriate and necessary to the disposition of cases appealed to it, which were not subject to review by the Legal Adviser or any other Department official. On October 28, 1991, an expectation for review of the Boards decisions was added for when the Department administratively vacated a Certificate of Loss of Nationality on its own initiative, notwithstanding an intervening decision by the Board sustaining the Department's original determination. The Board could adopt and promulgate rules of procedure approved by the Secretary of State as necessary to govern its proceedings. On January 11, 1984, the Board of Appellate Review began publishing select decisions on appeals from administrative determinations by the Department of State of loss of nationality and denial of passport facilities.

On April 22, 1999, the Board of Appellate Review’s responsibility for appeals from decisions of the Office of Passport Services that constituted adverse action affecting a passport denial, revocation, or limitation was revoked. The most common adverse passport action was denial or revocation based on 22 CFR section 51.70(a), such as being subject to a Federal warrant of arrest or being under court ordered restraint. In these cases, the Board of Appellate Review or other appellate body within the Department of State had no authority to affect the underlying ground for adverse passport action, so there was no change in the existing practice. The Board had infrequently utilized this jurisdiction, and an adverse action could be reviewed without the administrative hearing that the Board conducted in loss of nationality cases. Changes in the applicable laws, their interpretation, and practice thereunder made it even more unlikely that administrative appeals would be taken by the Board.

Because the Board of Appellate Review’s jurisdiction was obsolete or superseded and its functions were exercised by other offices, there was no longer a need for the Board. Accordingly on October 20, 2008, the Board of Appellate Review was eliminated. The Bureau of Consular continued the review of loss of nationality determinations from citizenship and passport denials on a discretionary basis.

Federal Register, vol. 64, 77, April 22, 1999: p. 19713-19715 (22 CFR Parts 50 and 51 [Public Notice 3027] Nationality Procedures Report of Birth Regulation; Passport Procedures-Revocation or Restriction of Passports Regulation AGENCY: Bureau of Consular Affairs, State Action: Final rule…rule amends regulations by replacing the procedures for appeal of adverse passport action. Other agency regulations contain provisions for the organization and operation of the Board of Appellate Appeal of the Department of State. Under this rule, the Board of Appellate Review no longer has jurisdiction to consider appeals from adverse passport actions. EFFECTIVE DATE: April 22, 1999…Board of Appellate Review of the Department of State has had jurisdiction to consider appeals from decisions of the Office of Passport Services that constitute adverse action affecting a passport denial, revocation, or limitation. This jurisdiction has been infrequently utilized, and an adverse action can be reviewed fairly and efficiently without the same kind of administrative hearing that the Board conducts in loss of nationality cases. Changes in the applicable laws, their interpretation, and practice thereunder now make it even more unlikely that administrative appeals will be taken. Accordingly, 22 CFR Part 7 is being amended by eliminating this particular administrative appeal jurisdiction. This amendment to 22 CFR Part 51, Subpart F, reflects that change and replaces an appeal with a request for reconsideration. In current practice, the most common adverse passport action is denial or revocation based upon grounds set forth in 22 CFR section 51.70(a)…no change in existing practice…The rule also amends 22 CFR 51.84 by substituting a more general statement of legal qualifications for representatives for the current reference to the qualification set by the Board)

Federal Register, vol. 73, no. 203, October 20, 2008: p. 62196-62197 (DEPARTMENT OF STATE 22 CFR Parts 7 and 50 [Public Notice: 6398] Board of Appellate Review; Review of Loss of Nationality AGENCY: State Department. ACTION: Final rule. SUMMARY: This rule eliminates the Department's Board of Appellate Review (L/BAR), which had been authorized to review certain Department determinations, in particular those related to loss of citizenship and passport denials. Because L/BAR's jurisdiction has been superseded or made obsolete, and in large part replaced by review of loss of citizenship and passport matters by the Bureau of Consular Affairs, this rule eliminates L/BAR and authorizes on a discretionary basis an alternative, less cumbersome review of loss of nationality determinations by the Bureau of Consular Affairs. DATES: This rule is effective October 20, 2008…The Department published an interim final rule, Public Notice 6298 at 73 FR 41256 (July 18, 2008), with 60 days for post-promulgation comment, amending 22 CFR by removing the regulations in Part 7 that established the Board of Appellate Review (L/BAR) and revising 50.51 to provide for an alternative method of review of loss of nationality determinations on a discretionary basis.)

Request for Records Disposition Authority N1-59-95-11 Dossier, 1996 (BOARD OF APPELLATE REVIEW (L/BAR) The Board of Appellate Review is a quasi-judicial body established in the Department of State under the authority of the Secretary of State's responsibilities under the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1952. The Board was established in 1967. While its jurisdiction is considerably broader, in actuality the work of the Board involves (1) hearing appeals from persons whom the Department of State has ruled have expatriated themselves and (2) appeals of revocations and denials of passports. It provides its decisions to the office or bureau responsible for the decision from which the appeal arose, generally the Bureau of Consular Affairs, Office of Passport Policy and Advisory Services (CA/PPT/PAS). The Board consists of one full-time member and 6 ad hoc members made up of Department officials who sit when cases are heard. While the Board is administratively part of L, it is autonomous and the merits of appeals or decisions of the Board are not subject to review by the Legal Adviser or other Department officials. Decisions against the Department are not appealable. Decisions against an individual are appealable in Federal court. Through the 1980s, the Board averaged about 30 cases per year. In 1990 that began to drop until in 1995, there were only 4 cases. This year, they expect about 10-12 cases.)

creators.administrativeHistoryNote: On December 6, 1989, the of Administration and Information Management's information management functions, including information services, systems operations and plans and development, were transferred to the Bureau of Diplomatic Security, which was renamed the Bureau of Diplomatic Security and Information Management. The remaining functions of the Bureau of Administration and Information Management were redesignated as the Bureau of Administration. This transfer was to protecting Department communications and information systems worldwide. Sheldon J. Krys served as the Assistant Secretary for Diplomatic Security and Information Management. In 1991, the Bureau again became the Bureau of Diplomatic Security.

creators.administrativeHistoryNote:
The U.S. Trade and Development Agency (USTDA), formerly the Trade and Development Program of the International Development Cooperation Agency, was made an independent agency within the executive branch of the Federal Government on October 28, 1992, by the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 as amended by the Jobs Through Exports Act of 1992 (106 Stat. 3655).

The Agency operated under the authority of section 661 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 (75 Stat. 424), which provided funding for planning services including feasibility studies, orientation visits, and trade-related training to assist U.S. firms in becoming involved in development projects having substantial U.S. export potential in project implementation. It funded planning services, such as feasibility studies, for high-priority development projects that were financed by the World Bank or other international financial institutions, or from the host country's own resources. The funded services were performed only by U.S. firms. The Agency could also serve as the coordinating and authorizing agency for the provision of government-to-government technical assistance on a fully reimbursable basis.

The Director served as the head of the USTDA and was appointed by the President, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate. The Director was authorized to work with foreign countries, including those in which the United States development programs were concluded or those not receiving assistance, by providing funds for feasibility studies, architectural and engineering design, and other activities related to development projects which provided opportunities for the use of United States exports.
